name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Commentary: Standing alongside a personal attack on a victim of child rape, Ohio politicians reveal themselves
text:
U.S. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance. (Photo by Drew Angerer/Getty Images)When you stand with vile you reveal yourself. A political ad that ran in Ohio last week sparked nationwide revulsion as perhaps the vilest in American history. It is that bad. 
Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s morally incomprehensible hit piece against Democrat Dr. Amy Acton in the Ohio race for governor will be studied and deconstructed (in all its atrociousness) long after the 2026 midterm elections are over. You know why. 
The decision to platform a mother complicit in the rape of her daughter — as an obscene strategy to blindside a political opponent — went way beyond the pale of personal attacks in the heat of a campaign. It was a sick act by a struggling candidate to capture voter attention that few saw coming. 
The ad featured the estranged mom of Ramaswamy’s gubernatorial rival. Donna Arthur fled Youngstown 48 years ago with Acton’s alleged rapist after the then 12-year-old victim testified against him in court.
The 80-something woman in Ramaswamy’s toxic ad chose to live on the lam with Acton’s fugitive stepfather, Cledith Arthur, until he died in 2004. Neither Acton nor her younger brother saw or spoke to their mother since she skipped town in 1978 with the man arrested, charged, and indicted by a grand jury for raping Acton. 
It was this troubled character, who abandoned her daughter and son as children, that Team Ramaswamy brought direct to camera with scripted venom. Arthur delivered. The performance was staged in a cozy, softly lit kitchen to exude warmth in chilling scene from a twisted story. 
Acton, whom Arthur rejected as a shattered tween in a courtroom, called her now 60-year-old daughter a serial liar with mental health issues who needed help. She warned Ohio voters “don’t let her become your governor.” The message was meant to stop people cold. It did. But after the bombshell went viral so did the backstory. 
The tables turned. So did stomachs as viewers (across the political spectrum) realized how next-level despicable the ad was in elevating an aging abusive mother with a checkered past who ditched a traumatized daughter to run off with the child rapist who assaulted her. 
The Ramaswamy obscenity, thrown on the air less than two weeks before the election, has been widely vilified as the re-victimization of young Acton to win power at any cost. 
Imagine the buried pain it must have triggered. The ad is still running in a shortened version — as if that sanitizes reprehensible. Tellingly, not only does Ramaswamy stand by his viral outrage, but vows to promote it with more than $4 million in bought airtime across the state. 
As disgust grew (and grows by the day) over the exploitation of a tortured childhood for political sport, Ohio’s finger in the wind Republicans responded on a scale from minimal to militant. 
“I would not have run the ad” was the mealy-mouthed comeback from Ohio U.S. Sen. Jon Husted, running in a tight race with former Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown to keep his seat, and Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose, running for a placeholder spot as state auditor against Annette Blackwell, a third-term Cleveland-area mayor. 
“I hope the ad will be taken down,” said an equally mincing former Ohio U.S. Sen. Rob Portman, who added the rising incivility in politics “should concern us all.” 
It took Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine a full day to denounce the weaponization of childhood sexual abuse that gut punched his former state health director who was instrumental in helping Ohioans navigate a frightening and fatal pandemic. 
“It’s just plain wrong,” he said. Finally. “Deeply, deeply troubling.” DeWine also said he stood by his endorsement of Ramaswamy despite the vileness manifested in his contemptible ad for the ages. Ever the profile in cowardice. 
Notably, all the Ohio Republicans who had something to say about the appalling Ramaswamy ad that revictimized the girl who grew up to become the Democratic nominee for Ohio governor — still stand with the GOP nominee for governor who launched the unconscionable clickbait and has never stopped defending it.
Ramaswamy blames backlash to the ad, which has generated massive national and local attention, on (wait for it) a “flawed and failed media” that is “lying about an ad that is about lying.” 
JD Vance, a confessed liar who admitted creating stories out of thin air to command similar exposure, piled on by declaring his disgust not with the vicious strike against a child rape survivor but with Republicans “whining” about it. 
The ad is “not really my concern,” sniffed the smug, amoral veep from Middletown. Couldn’t care less about whether resurfacing Acton’s MIA mother to score political points was appropriate or abhorrent. 
Vance, who also survived an abusive childhood, summoned no compassion or moral clarity about the depravity that drove Team Ramaswamy to malign yesterday’s abused and neglected child for political sport. With JD, power trumps principal. Winning is paramount. Decency is an indulgence. Republicans can’t get hung up on humane if they want control.
Vance’s boss doubled down on defense of the indefensible. Trump embraced the Ramaswamy ad as a gift from heaven and urged the candidate to leave it up. 
He was thrilled the ad blowing up on social media “was hitting pay dirt” and insisted his party own it. But when you stand with vile — smearing a child rape victim to win dirty — you reveal much about yourself. 
Which Ohio Republican will stand with Trump when he returns to Ohio Wednesday? The president welcomes vileness as a means to an end. He demands supporters follow suit or be branded as “disloyal to the Republican Party. Watch who joins him on the stage at the Chillicothe rally. Always revealing.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Commentary: Ohio voters, casting a ballot is our foundational right and responsibility
text:
Voting booths. (Photo by Seth Tupper, States Newsroom.)I am among the many Americans who did not vote in our elections at one time. I believe I was wrong not to do so and I will attempt to convince you current non-voters to change your mind.  
And there are many of you. Even among those registered, ten percent do not cast ballots. In the 2024 national elections, fully ten percent of registered voters did not turn out. That is 18 million registered non-voters in a closely fought election decided by two million votes. 
When I was quite a bit younger and before I knew much history I had little understanding about the long struggle for the right to vote and the democracy of which it is a key part. Most of humanity for most of our history has been governed by narrow cliques of thieving oligarchs or autocratic royals, many of whom relied on violence and terror to retain power. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 Ohio General Election Voter Guide: Races, deadlines, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
At the start of the democratic era it took great courage to stand against the powers that be. But many thousands of people did so anyway, even realizing that they might well pay with their lives to resist. Great numbers of them had to know that they themselves would be unlikely to ever live to exercise the right to vote. They sacrificed their own lives and welfare so that the rest of us could live in a democratic society. Among those epic struggles were the American and French revolutions, but they were not the first. The people of ancient Athens also rose up against tyranny for democracy. Of course there were also many others.  
So I argue that we owe a debt to those who struggled on our behalf. We have a duty to them to vote, and to do so intelligently as best we are able. It is easy to forget that women and minorities were excluded from voting in the United States for long periods of time, and had to struggle mightily for the voting franchise. Some of them paid with their lives. By voting, we can show respect their sacrifices. 
Another argument against voting is that our votes do not count for much. Well, there is some truth to that in the United States, especially with an Electoral College winner-take-all presidential system in which our votes do not count at all if our candidate loses in our state. But on the other hand, there are many state and local offices, as well as school, park, health, safety and other local levies, for which our votes can matter a great deal. And in fact, local elections have a significant impact on the quality of our lives. 
We also hear it said that politicians in general are corrupt and “all the same”. There is a grain of truth to that point of view. Many politicians are indeed narcissistic sociopaths to whom the idea of the public good is close to meaningless. But they are not all like that. In fact, politicians and parties vary in their truthfulness and honesty – at least a third of them are reasonably honest and worth supporting. It is your job as a voter to do some research and support the best of them. If you do not vote, you enable the bad guys. Nowadays it is hard to argue that there are no differences in the two major US political parties.  
To be fair, there are real barriers to voting including onerous registration procedures, long lines at the polls, billionaire dark money in campaigns, and lazy “horse race” journalism that avoids issues. Negative ads and hate media increase public cynicism and increase polarization, of which we have too much already. The consultants who produce untruthful and fear-inducing media know exactly what they are doing.  
It is your job to meet these challenges and support those who are working hard to address them.
If your vote did not matter, they would not work to keep you away from the polls. With freedom comes responsibilities. Voting is one of them. 
Arnold Oliver is Professor Emeritus of Political Science at Heidelberg University in Tiffin, Ohio, and is a member of Veterans For Peace. He is grateful to his former students and colleagues who taught him about the importance of voting.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Can this film change our understanding of the climate and migration crises?
text:
A still from The Welcome Table. (Image courtesy HBO.)
This story was originally published by Capital & Main.
Filmmaker Josh Fox has racked up a lot of miles covering the climate crisis. Sparked by a confounding business offer at his family home nearly two decades ago, his latest project took him around the world to tell stories of people uprooted by extreme weather and natural disasters.
It started in 2008 when a fracking company approached Fox, whose family has long had a home in northeastern Pennsylvania, with a $100,000 offer to lease minerals beneath the property for natural gas development.
Attempting to make sense of the offer, Fox turned to a nearby town already on the frontlines of fracking: Dimock. In that rural Pennsylvanian hamlet, he found families complaining that the natural gas extraction technique had ruined their well water and caused stomach aches and other sicknesses.
That spurred Fox to go deeper and take a road trip, documentary gear in tow, to natural gas-producing areas across the United States where, over and over, he heard testimonials from landowners living near operations of the nascent industry.
He discovered people who would hold a match up to their kitchen faucets — and light their tap water on fire. He strung together such images in the Emmy-winning, Oscar-nominated documentary “Gasland,” a cautionary tale about the risks of the booming industry, which saw the number of fracking wells nationwide multiply 13-fold between 2000 and 2015.
In the years since, the industry has continued to grow, even as climate change-fueled natural disasters have surged in frequency and severity.
In the shadows of “Gasland,” which was pivotal in paving the way for what developed into a potent protest movement against fracking, Fox’s latest film, “The Welcome Table,” shows the result of continued fossil fuel development.
The HBO Original Documentary takes viewers into communities on six continents that Fox visited over a nine-year period. It follows climate migrants who are victims of wildfires — like the 2018 blaze that nearly wiped the town of Paradise, California, off the map — floods and hurricanes, back to the homes from which they fled or to the new ones to which they relocated.
The film visits residents in communities ravaged by drought and mudslides where locals are holding out after fearful neighbors took off. It also features climate migrants who, among the growing number of people seeking refuge in other countries, are hampered or blocked entirely by tightening border policies that don’t take into account the gravity of their hardships.
The film argues that solving the climate crisis and the vast global migration intertwined with it will require collaboration, not division.
Ahead the film’s Oct. 25 national tour kickoff, Fox spoke with Capital & Main about the new film, how it fits into his larger body of work and what it says about the state of the climate crisis.
This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Capital & Main: Some of the first shots in this movie are from the Paradise fire in Northern California in 2018, where you follow a couple who lost their home as they wade through the rubble of their old lives. That was eight years ago. When and how did you know you had a movie on climate migration — a departure from your earlier films on resource extraction?
Josh Fox: So, with “Gasland,” there’s this image of people lighting their water on fire. Ninety-nine percent of people have a kitchen sink. So, when you light the water on fire, they’re like, “Oh f—, that’s just like my kitchen sink.” And people would tell me that they went home to try to light their water on fire, even though they were living nowhere near fracking.
But nobody has [a visceral concept] of their “climate” [the way they have a concept of their tap water]. This is a problem.
“The Welcome Table” is not a climate movie. I think climate change is the background, the backdrop. I felt like what we needed to look at was: How many people are going to lose their homes? How many people are going to be displaced?
I realized that these two issues [climate and immigration] were on such a collision course. And the film focuses on people losing their homes because home is so intrinsic to everyone. Everyone should have a home, or at least has an idea of home, right? Even if they don’t have an idea of “climate.”
“Gasland” was really about one thing — fracking. “The Welcome Table” is about climate change, but also nationalism, border policies and colonialism, and these three things get their own attention in the movie. Was that intentional? 
We have made a tragic error about what the cause of climate change was by focusing on parts per million of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. That’s a symptom. Colonialism is the real cause, and the ideology that goes along with it. What I wanted to show was people’s reaction to loss and crisis. As [a Brazilian community leader named] Gabriel says at the end of the movie, “Home is not a place; home is the people around me.” That’s the only home we have left.
“Gasland,” which came out in 2010, in the early days of natural gas extraction, was a cautionary tale about fracking. “The Welcome Table” is about not listening to that cautionary tale. As our societies have extracted and burned more natural gas, these people who have seen their homes threatened by climate change are living proof of the result.
This is the result of 100 years of influence of the oil industry on our politics. It’s more powerful than anything. Our leaders didn’t want to take it on, and as a result, the world is burning and it’s a disaster. The question is: Can we move on from this extractive ideology, or will it destroy the planet? There are these giant questions that I don’t know the answer to, but it does feel very dire at this moment.
“Gasland” created a lot of buzz, including in and around Dimock, where, 12 years after the film came out, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, then-attorney general, secured a plea deal from a fracking company charged with polluting the area. The deal saw the company agree to pay for a clean water line for residents. Yet, the same day, regulators lifted a vital protection preventing fracking in the town that had been in place for 10 years. Is this the justice you expected for that area, and what does justice for the communities you feature even look like? 
It’s a betrayal in every sense. It would be very helpful to redefine rural Pennsylvania as a place that has been colonized by the oil industry, by the powers that be, and whether you have a Democratic label, like Josh Shapiro, or a red one like [former pro-drilling Republican Gov.] Tom Corbett, this is not what we need.
Josh Shapiro, not only is he politically a hypocrite, but he is a better agent for the oil industry than somebody like Tom Corbett. Josh Shapiro is trying to pretend to be the good guy. Pennsylvania has a history of people who are mealy-mouthed corporate centrists who love to pretend that they are on the side of the working class, but they ignore the working class. It’s incredibly condescending and it’s dehumanizing. The first thing you do when you colonize the place is you dehumanize those people.
After “Gasland,” you faced a broad backlash from the natural gas industry, which argued the film contained falsehoods. That effort included a campaign to disqualify your film from Oscar consideration after it was nominated for best documentary. The disinformation ecosystem has changed a lot since then.
What we’re seeing right now in the arena of truth and misinformation is the toxic data that is everywhere, and it’s polluting the landscape of journalism. Misinformation is more prevalent than fact. Propaganda is more prevalent than journalism.
Right now, we need to imagine. We need to indulge that poetic part of us that is much more human and true. When I started “The Welcome Table,” we were in a different era.
The ideas that sort of bind the movie to what I imagine its audience would be are still there. The principles in there are: human rights and love and generosity. It’s better to share than to be greedy, and be accepting of people, rather than bigoted. Those things I would hope we still have a consensus about.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Catching Our Eye News Roundup, Oct. 28, 2026
text:
The Ohio burgee. (Getty images file photo.)Every morning in the Ohio Capital Journal’s free newsletter, The Eye-Opener, we round up the news and commentary from across Ohio and around the country and world that is catching our attention. We call this feature Catching Our Eye, republished here.
Please subscribe to our free daily newsletter to get all the Ohio news you need to know right to your inbox every weekday morning.
If you already subscribe, please share with your family and friends so they know about the Ohio Capital Journal too: https://ohiocapitaljournal.com/subscribe/

 Catching Our Eye

• Federal election monitors. The Statehouse News Bureau’s Karen Kasler reports, “Feds will send election monitors to three Ohio counties next week.”
The US Department of Justice has informed three Ohio county boards of elections that the federal government will be sending monitors to observe next week’s election. It’s part of what is expected to be the DOJ’s largest-ever election monitoring effort, with the agency planning to send monitors to all 50 states.
The Boards of Elections in Franklin, Medina and Cuyahoga Counties were emailed letters informing them the Civil Rights Division of the DOJ intends to send election monitors to those jurisdictions.
• Gerrymandering. The New York Times reports, “An Extremely Detailed Ranking of the Most Gerrymandered States in America.”
Which state has America’s worst gerrymander? After a year of redistricting battles, we have an answer.
We’ve ranked all 44 states with more than one district by the fairness of their congressional maps. Many of the most notorious gerrymanders are ranked near the top of the list. But there are also some oft-derided maps that we judge to be fundamentally fine. (Ohio ranks No. 7 most-gerrymandered.)
• Ohio Supreme Court. Signal Ohio’s Jake Zuckerman reports, “Is Ohio on the cusp of an all-Republican state Supreme Court?”
Since Statehouse Republicans passed a law in 2021 requiring Ohio Supreme Court candidates to run under party labels on the ballot, reversing a century-old nonpartisan approach, Republicans have gone six for six.
If their undefeated streak continues, they’ll achieve the historically rare feat of total one-party control, a first since 2010.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Brewers blow 12th inning lead, still chasing first World Series title
text:
Fans at the World Series watch party at American Family field react to Cooper Pratt's go-ahead home run in the 12th inning. (Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)The Milwaukee Brewers came tantalizingly close to winning their first World Series title in franchise history Tuesday evening before the Tampa Bay Rays’ Ben Williamson hit a walk-off single to score the winning run in the bottom of the 12th inning, giving the Rays a 4-3 victory. 
A Cooper Pratt home run in the top of the 12th inning had the team just three outs away from the championship but a throwing error with zero outs in the top of the inning sparked a rally for the Rays, who for the first time in the series were able to string together a series of hits. Brewers pitcher Shane Drohan, who had previously pitched just one inning in the playoffs, gave up the game tying and winning runs. 
At American Family Field in Milwaukee a sold out watch party was standing, clapping, cheering and groaning along with the game as if it were happening on the field in front of them and not on the massive screen in center field. 

The game ended around 11:30, with kids out far past their bedtime and lifelong fans on the edge of their seats to watch their hearts get ripped out. 
Watching from the third deck was Chrystal Glynn-Skipini who drove down from Neenah to watch the game in the atmosphere with her niece and great nephew. 
“Why not, how awesome to be with all the other fans,” she said, double crossing her fingers that the team would close out the sweep Tuesday. 
Game five of the series is Wednesday at 7 p.m.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Trone Garriott, Nunn respond to attack ads on Epstein, transgender issues at debate
text:
Democrat Sarah Trone Garriott, left, and Republican Zach Nunn, are competing to represent Iowa's 3rd Congressional District in the 2026 general election. (Photos by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch, photo illustration via Canva)Meeting for the sole debate in Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District, U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn and state Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott responded Tuesday to attacks from their opponent on issues like the Epstein files and transgender athletes and students.
The debate, hosted by KCCI in Des Moines, was aired just a week before Election Day, and follows weeks of the campaigns criticizing one another for being unable to come to a scheduling agreement. The contest is one of the most competitive U.S. House races in the country, according to political forecasters,
While Tuesday was the first time Iowans saw Trone Garriott and Nunn on stage together, many viewers had likely seen campaign ads about the candidates — more than $10.6 million in spending from outside groups was poured into the race, according to Federal Election Commission reports.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Moderators gave the candidates the chance to address some of the claims made in attack ads, including ads criticizing Nunn for his votes related to publicizing files related to Florida financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Nunn voted to pass the “Epstein Files Transparency Act” in 2025, but Democrats have criticized Nunn, as well as other members of Iowa’s federal delegation, for not signing off on the initial discharge petition to force the House to vote on the bill, or voting for an amendment on another measure to compel the release of the Epstein files.
Nunn says votes against releasing files was to protect victim identities
Nunn said he voted against the earlier efforts to release Department of Justice information on Epstein and collaborators, because the proposals would have released the names of Epstein’s victims, which he said would “revictimize the victims.” Some Epstein survivors had their identities revealed in unredacted documents released by the DOJ in early 2026.
“I want to make sure Jeffrey Epstein and all of his accomplices are held fully accountable. He’s a disgusting human being and we’ve been able to lead that legislation here in Iowa,” Nunn said. But “simply opening up and making the files transparent for the victims — their names, their addresses, their background — that’s not fair to the victims.”
He said his vote was to “hold the people who actually did the crime accountable,” and referenced his work in Congress to advocate for providing more federal funding for programs and services for victims of domestic abuse and sexual assault. He said he believed Iowa Republicans were also taking on this issue at the state level.
“It’s not just Jeffrey Epstein,” Nunn said. “This kind of stuff happens right here in Iowa, let’s get after it.”
But Trone Garriott said Nunn’s vote to release the Epstein files only came “when the president had given him permission that he finally joined in and voted to release them.”
“We’ve only gotten half of the files out there, so much is still unknown, and no one has been held accountable,” Trone Garriott said. “We need to make sure that we’ve got someone standing up for us in Washington to make sure that kids are safe.”
Trone Garriott says she voted to give parents a ‘voice’ on transgender issues
Trone Garriott was asked to respond to attack ads criticizing her votes on legislation related to transgender Iowans, including her vote against a 2022 law banning transgender women from participating in women’s sports, and against a 2023 law banning transgender students from using school restrooms that do not align with their sex assigned at birth.
The Democrat said as a mother with two children in Iowa public schools, she cared “deeply about their safety, about health, about fairness” — and said the laws she voted on in regards to transgender students and school athletes were in an effort to allow parents to “have a voice in the decisions that are impacting their children.”
Sand, Lahn call for increasing mental healthcare access, Medicaid oversight in debate

“I believe that we make much better decisions when parents are involved, because parents are the ones who are there, who can see the circumstances, they can understand what’s at stake — and they make the best decisions for our community, that actually help us address the issue,” Trone Garriott said. “Every single one of the bills that was put before me in the Iowa state Senate took away a parent’s voice. I have to stand up for parents’ voices in this process to make sure that things are safe and fair for our kids.”
Nunn claimed Trone Garriott was in the “extreme element of her party” on issues related to transgender issues. The Republican referenced comments from Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Josh Turek, who he said “highlighted the fact that this is wrong and should be stopped.”
He also said Trone Garriott “authored the bill that would teach transgender ideology to kindergartners.” The legislation Nunn referenced has been referred to by Townhall, a conservative news organization, as a bill to “teach sex education in kindergarten classrooms.” The measure relates to Iowa’s Area Education Agencies and does not mention sex education.
Trone Garriott said some of the criticism comes from her support of “Erin’s Law,” a proposal with bipartisan support that would require the state Department of Education to develop guidelines on how schools can teach students in kindergarten through sixth grade about child sexual abuse, with the goal of awareness and prevention.
“Because I was a sexual assault crisis counselor, I also worked to help bring education into classrooms,” Trone Garriott said. “It’s incredibly important that kids have age-appropriate education so that they can ask for help when something is wrong, when they’re being abused. Some of the bills that I’ve been attacked on are bills … to make sure kids have the language to ask for help when they’re being abused.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Our job is to protect your right to vote. Your job is to use it.
text:
Lately, when I talk with Connecticut residents about the upcoming election, they tell me they’re afraid.
Sometimes, they can tell me exactly what they’re afraid of: federal immigration agents showing up at polling places, protesters interfering with voting, their personal information being seized, or even the federal government attempting to stop the election altogether.

Secretary of the State Stephanie Thomas

Other times, people can’t quite put their finger on what’s worrying them. They just know they’re scared.
I understand. For years now, we’ve heard repeated claims about stolen elections, widespread voter fraud, and ineligible people casting ballots. We’ve seen alarming headlines and social media posts predicting everything that could go wrong. Some concerns deserve serious attention. Others are based on speculation or misinformation. But when all of it gets mixed together, it can leave people wondering what to believe and worrying about what might happen next.
But here’s what concerns me most: That fear could accomplish the very thing people are afraid of, which is keeping them from exercising their right to vote.
And that’s why I want Connecticut voters to understand something.
It’s our job to worry about the what-ifs. It’s our job to prepare for them. It’s our job to take the steps necessary to protect voters, election workers, and our elections.
And when I say “our,” I don’t just mean the Secretary of the State’s Office. I mean the Attorney General’s Office, the Connecticut Department of Emergency Services and Public Protection, local election officials in all 169 towns, law enforcement, and the many other state and local agencies and people who have responsibilities for keeping our elections safe, secure, and accessible.
We take those responsibilities seriously. We plan, we prepare, we work together, and we have procedures in place to respond when something doesn’t go as expected.
Our job is to think through what could go wrong before it happens. And most of that work happens long before anyone walks into a polling place.
Earlier this month, election offices in several states received suspicious letters, some containing powder. Federal authorities told us a letter addressed to our office had been intercepted. But before we knew about that letter, we’d already reminded local officials how to handle suspicious mail safely.
We’ve also helped towns prepare for 2026 election law changes, including to help law enforcement understand a new state law establishing restrictions within 250 feet of polling places and other designated election sites. The goal is to protect voters and election workers while making sure officers can still respond to emergencies and perform their lawful duties.
I wish I could promise that nothing unexpected will happen between now and when the polls close at 8 p.m. on Election Day, November 3. But what I can tell you is that we’ve spent months working with state, local, and federal partners to be ready if something we hope never happens does occur.
This is the kind of work most voters never see. And none of it begins the week before an election. It happens year-round, and it involves people from different agencies, political parties, and communities working together.
That’s our job. Your job is to vote.
In the 2018 midterm election, about 65% of Connecticut’s registered voters cast a ballot. In 2022, that figure fell to about 58%.
What will voter turnout look like in 2026?
I hope it will show that Connecticut residents understand what’s at stake; that they realize that the people we elect make decisions about our nation, our state, our towns, the services we rely on, and how public money is spent.
Eligible Connecticut voters have three ways to cast their ballots. They can do it in person during Early Voting through November 1, in person on Election Day November 3, or by absentee ballot.
Find our 2026 Voter Guide in English or Spanish at MyVote.CT.gov. It contains everything you need to know about voting in Connecticut, from how to find your polling place, to the candidates on your local ballot, to the rules about who can legally handle and return someone else’s absentee ballot.
We’re doing our job, Connecticut.
Now it’s time to do yours.
Stephanie Thomas is Connecticut’s Secretary of the State.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Turnout surging in Maryland, as ‘jacked up’ voters head to the polls for early voting
text:
Campaign signs lined up near Wayne K. Curry Sports and Learning Center in Prince George's County during early voting Tuesday. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)Early voting in Maryland is surging, with turnout 67% higher through the first five days of in-person voting than it was at the same time four years ago, according to data from the Maryland State Board of Elections.
Higher voting was recorded in every county in the state, with 309,190 voters having cast ballots through Monday, compared to 185,121 voters after the first five days of voting in 2022. The surge mirrors a national spike in early voting, with more than 34 million Americans already having cast ballots, a week before Election Day on Nov. 3.
Democrats in Maryland have been particularly motivated to vote early, with their numbers up 81% over four years ago, compared to 33% for GOP voters, according to an analysis of state data by Jim Burton, the founder of political and public affairs consulting firm Burton Research and Strategies. 
“They are jacked up to vote,” said Burton, the former executive director of the Maryland GOP. “On the Democrat side, they’re willing to run through a brick building to cast their vote.”
Early voting surges in midterm elections as millions cast their ballots

Monday saw the biggest increases, with Democratic voting up 84% and Republican voting up 49% compared to the fifth day of early voting in 2022. Frederick County saw the biggest surge Monday, with Democratic voting up 146% and GOP voting 67% than four years ago.
Burton said the higher numbers could be voters expressing their displeasure with the administration of President Donald Trump. He added that while the biggest increases appeared to be in suburban areas, the increases could be also be due to local or regional issues, since the surge is being seen everywhere in the state.
Nikki Tyree, the executive director of Maryland’s League of Women Voters, said she thinks big issues like data centers, the cost of living, or Question 3, the proposed constitutional amendment on congressional redistricting, are driving voters this year.
“We’re looking at a midterm that is hanging on so many critical issues that people have been focused on,” Tyree said. “Marylanders have really shown that they’re paying attention to what’s going on.”
In addition to the more than 300,000 who had voted early in person so far, state election officials said voters had returned 305,690 mail-in ballots as of Sunday, about half of the 645,962 mailed out this year.
Early voting began last Thursday and continues through this Thursday. Burton said the first few days and the final day of early voting tend to see the heaviest traffic.
“The candidates and campaigns are still trying to drive turnout,” he said. “I tell my clients … just because what the early-vote demographics are showing doesn’t mean we’re handing in the towel. We have to continue to do our job, and we still have seven days to do it.”
A Burton Research and Strategies analysis of Maryland State Board of Elections early voting data shows it is surging in every county and in both parties, when compared to turnout four years ago. (Graphic courtesy Burton Research and Strategies)
Burton said that even though the increase in Democratic voting is much higher than that of Republicans, it’s too soon to read much into it, as it could simply be the result of differing personal preferences between the parties.
He said Democrats tend to vote by mail of hit the polls early compared to Republicans, who historically tend to stick to voting on Election Day, as they might be “set in their ways.”
Heading into the final days of early voting, and only a week out from Election Day, Tyree thinks the increased turnout is a good sign for the rest of the country.
“I think Maryland is always sort of a microcosm of what’s happening across the country,” she said. “Our little state has so much of what other states encompass…. If our voters are paying attention to the issues that are affecting their daily lives, I think that’s just a small example of what some of the voters who are facing widely publicized races are engaging in as well.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Lamont, Fazio lively in last debate while breaking no new ground
text:
Buoyed by positive polls and a favorable tailwind generated by an unpopular president, Gov. Ned Lamont soldiered through his second and final debate with Republican Ryan Fazio on Tuesday, hewing to a central message of him steering Connecticut to fiscal stability and growth after a lost decade of chronic crises.
Fazio, a 36-year-old state senator from Greenwich seeking statewide office for the first time, once again was the aggressor, this time emphasizing mandates, property taxes and other issues of particular interest to the live audience: the Connecticut Conference of Municipalities convention at Mohegan Sun.
Lamont was more relaxed than in last week’s debate in a largely empty TV studio, playing off an audience with familiar mayors and first selectmen, addressing several by name — and reminding them of their role in shaping a revised housing bill at his invitation after vetoing an initial effort.

Gov. Ned Lamont, who prefers to go without neckties and didn’t wear one in the first debate, answers questions following the Connecticut Conference of Municipalities Gubernatorial Debate at Mohegan Sun’s Earth Expo and Convention Center on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT MIrror

The 72-year-old governor displayed a crispness and a willingness to volley with Fazio largely missing last week, challenging Fazio and other Republicans as failing to oppose President Donald Trump on tariffs, a war in Iran driving up gas prices, and a crackdown on immigration that Lamont called cruel and overreaching.
“I don’t know what happened to the Republicans in the state,” said Lamont, whose home is Greenwich, where local officials plan to erect a statue in the wealthy enclave in tribute to its native son, President George Herbert Walker Bush. “The old Republicans, the Bush Republicans, would stand up. They’d be outraged.”
Fazio distanced himself from Trump without offering comment on a Bush family that has produced two presidents and a U.S. senator but whose brand of politics has lost standing in a GOP dominated by a president who equates the party’s interests with his own, even if he becomes a lame duck next week.

State Sen. Ryan Fazio, Republican challenger, answers a reporter’s question following the Connecticut Conference of Municipalities Gubernatorial Debate at Mohegan Sun’s Earth Expo and Convention Center on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT MIrror

“I’ve criticized Trump administration policies and Democratic administration policies since before I was even in office, and that’s why Gov. Lamont called me bipartisan and objected to others calling me extreme before this general election campaign started,” Fazio said. “I’m an independently minded leader.”
WTNH Channel 8 televised the debate live with two anchors, Dennis House and Kathryn Hauser, posing most of the questions with one wrinkle: Joseph DeLong, the chief executive of CCM, and two members of its “citizens’ assembly” had turns posing difficult questions that neither candidate answered directly.
DeLong challenged Fazio to explain how he could deliver on his promise to cut state taxes and cap municipal property tax increases at a 2% cap or the rate of inflation, whichever is greater. 
“If a city or town school and special education costs rise faster, who covers the difference?” DeLong asked. “Is it the state, local taxpayers, or is the school district going to be required to do drastic cuts?”
Fazio did not reply to those choices but insisted his overall plan would lower costs for municipalities by eliminating unfunded state mandates — and gigged the governor as unreliable on special education reform. 
“The problem is he’s had eight years to accomplish it and hasn’t,” Fazio said.

Gov. Ned Lamont answers a reporter’s question following the Connecticut Conference of Municipalities Gubernatorial Debate at Mohegan Sun’s Earth Expo and Convention Center on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT MIrror

Lamont did not engage on a separate question about mandates, framed around a requirement that municipalities and not the state must advertise public meetings. Instead, he pivoted to dollars his administration has provided, including funding for free school meals.
“I think the answer from Gov. Lamont that those costs are just not that big a deal is not an acceptable answer,” Fazio said. “It’s not just one of these costs that the state is imposing. It’s over 1,000 of them, and the governor increased the number of those costs by over 100 more in just the last five years.”
Hauser pressed Fazio on his opposition to the Lamont administration using surplus state funds to replace expiring federal credits before their expiration caused dramatic increases in premiums.
“Does that remain your position, even for a family that cannot afford coverage, while your proposed cost-cutting reforms take effect?” Hauser asked.

Republican gubernatorial candidate Ryan Fazio at a debate at Mohegan Sun on Oct. 27, 2026. Credit: courtesy WTNH

Fazio said his opposition was about process, not policy.
“The problem with the proposal is that it went outside of the spending caps and would have caused tax increases,” Fazio said. “We can provide this funding through the normal budget process in a state with a $30 billion budget, and I would favor that.”
Fazio pivoted to blame the Lamont administration for approving premium increases.
“Gov. Lamont’s own insurance commission has approved increases in health insurance premiums of 11% and 16%. That’s on his watch. That is the record, and that is not sustainable,” Fazio said.
But he acknowledged to reporters after the debate he was not suggesting they should have been rejected — something that could lead to plans being withdrawn from the Connecticut market.

Gov. Ned Lamont at a debate at Mohegan Sun on Oct. 27, 2026. Credit: courtesy WTNH

Lamont offered the state premium subsidy as one of several examples of Connecticut acting to offset actions or inactions by Trump.
“The Trump administration jacks the price of health insurance on the exchange by $800 a month, pushing people off of health insurance, but not in Connecticut,” Lamont said. “We stepped up, and we are providing support for that. Ryan Fazio did not support that. Those people would be uninsured today.”
Neither candidate warmed to a proposal by CCM’s Citizens’ Assembly to impose tolls and use the money to eliminate the property tax on motor vehicles. A tolls proposal by Lamont in 2019, his first year in  office, fell flat and drove his job approval rating to the bottom of all U.S. governors.
“Joe, you may have heard I actually tried something like that a while back. Nobody wanted to do that. We’re not going to do that,” Lamont said. “But it gets to a bigger story. When I came into office, we had a special transportation fund that had nothing in it, zero. It was on fumes.”

State Sen. Ryan Fazio, Republican challenger, pauses before answering a reporter’s question following the Connecticut Conference of Municipalities Gubernatorial Debate at Mohegan Sun’s Earth Expo and Convention Center on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT MIrror

Lamont turned the question on Fazio, who has proposed a gas tax holiday.
“That’s just the type of mentality that got this state in a pickle eight years ago, and I’m not going to let it happen again. I’m happy to work with the assembly on other ways. We think we can mitigate taxes there. I’m not sure that’s what I’d go for,” Lamont said.
It was an example of the governor and his challenger falling back on messages little changed since the start of the election season.
“After eight years, Gov. Lamont’s had his chance,” Fazio said. “He promised to hold the line on taxes, but he increased your taxes. He promised to cut your property taxes, but property taxes have risen 30 percent on his watch. Now, it’s time for a change.”
Lamont also asked voters to take a closer look.
“Look back, eight years ago, we were lurching from deficit to deficit,” Lamont said. “We had three tax increases in a row. Your mayors and first selectmen, remember, they couldn’t even get a budget done in 2017 until three or four months late. So I do disagree that we’re not in a better place today than we were before.”

Gov. Ned Lamont and Republican gubernatorial candidate Ryan Fazio at a debate at Mohegan Sun on Oct. 27, 2026. Credit: courtesy wtnh

Applause was discouraged during the debate, but the governor got a laugh when he recycled an oft-used line that his opponent in the Democratic primary attacked him for refusing to raise taxes on the wealthy and Fazio cast him as a spendthrift.
“Maybe these two guys should have a debate and then come in and tell me what they’ve decided,” Lamont said, as the municipal officials tittered, then laughed. He landed a punch line, saying loudly, “I do what I think is right every day.”
That got applause.
Did either man hear anything new?
“From him, I really didn’t,” Lamont said. “I just heard him say over and over again, ‘Eight years. What have you done?’ And I said, ‘Eight years, this is what we’ve done to improve our school systems, improve our budget, improve our roads and bridges.’”
Asked the same question, Fazio just smiled and replied, “No.”
CT Mirror reporter Keith M. Phaneuf contributed to this report.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Pete Buttigieg calls for Mississippi to elect Scott Colom to US Senate, send ‘shockwaves’
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
BILOXI – Former U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg on Tuesday pleaded for Mississippi voters to “send shockwaves” by voting for Democratic nominee Scott Colom and rejecting Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith next week. 
Buttigieg was the latest national political figure to campaign in Mississippi in the homestretch before the Nov. 3 midterm elections. The Senate race has also attracted a last-minute barrage of spending as Democrats see an opening and Republicans worry that reliably conservative Mississippi could become a casualty of President Donald Trump’s sinking popularity nationwide. 
Trump hosted a rally for Hyde-Smith in Corinth on Monday, days after former Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned for Colom in Columbus last week.
People hold up signs as former U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg speaks at a rally for Democratic Senate nominee Scott Colom in Biloxi on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. Credit: Michael Guidry/Mississippi Today
Trump’s approval ratings have plummeted nationally amid opposition to increasing consumer prices and an unpopular war in Iran. Democrats have grown optimistic that Colom could pull off an upset in a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in more than four decades. 
READ MORE: Trump rallies for Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi: ‘You like me’
“When you win in Mississippi, it is going to send shockwaves,” Buttigieg told a galvanized crowd in Biloxi. 

 Speaking to hundreds of people at a community center, the Biden administration transportation secretary said Trump and Hyde-Smith are directly responsible for soaring gasoline and grocery prices because of the president’s tariffs and other policies and the Iran war. 
“It’s happening because of decisions that were made in Washington,” Buttigeig said. “This time it’s not because Vladimir Putin decided to start a war. It’s because Donald Trump decided to start a war.” 
Colom repeated his campaign pledges about the need to raise the federal minimum wage and his desire to advocate for policies that help deliver access to affordable healthcare to rural Mississippi, which has some of the most dire health outcomes in the nation. 
“My commitment to you is that I am going to fight to do everything in my power to save our healthcare and save our hospitals,” Colom said.  
Buttigieg said healthcare issues show the Trump administration and Republicans are out of touch.
“Folks are saying, ‘We need help with healthcare,’ and they are saying, ‘OK, let’s build a new ballroom in the White House,'” Buttigieg said. “Folks are saying, ‘I need help affording the things that I buy at the store every week,’ and they are busy protecting whoever is in the Epstein files.”
Earlier in the day, Colom and Buttigieg had a press conference at the Coast Transit Authority in Gulfport, where the two celebrated the 2025 restoration of Amtrak’s Gulf Coast route from Alabama to Louisiana, called the “Mardi Gras Service.” 
The route was shut down after Hurricane Katrina and likely wouldn’t have been resurrected without a significant injection of federal money from Congress’ passage of the bipartisan infrastructure bill in 2021. 
Mississippi Sen. Roger Wicker was one of 19 Republican senators and the only Republican in Mississippi’s congressional delegation who voted for the federal legislation. Both Buttigieg and Colom praised Wicker’s support of the program and denounced Hyde-Smith’s opposition.  
“Let’s be very clear, there was a Republican U.S. senator from Mississippi who voted and acted to bring those dollars to this state,” Buttigieg said. “Just not Cindy Hyde-Smith because she was incapable of doing something without the permission of the then-former president.” 
Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Scott Colom speaks outside the Coast Transit Authority in Gulfport on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. Credit: Michael Guidry/Mississippi TodayPeople wait in line outside a community center in Biloxi before a rally featuring Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Scott Colom and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. Credit: Michael Guidry/Mississippi TodayRachel Ciraldo of Hattiesburg, right, and Evelyn Champagne of Biloxi hold up signs outside a rally for Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Scott Colom in Biloxi on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. Credit: Michael Guidry/Mississippi TodayMusicians play ahead of a rally featuring Democratic Senate nominee Scott Colom in Biloxi on Tuesday, October 27, 2026. Credit: Michael Guidry/Mississippi TodayPeople listen to speakers at a rally for Scott Colom, Democratic nominee for a U.S. Senate seat, in Biloxi on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. Credit: Michael Guidry/Mississippi TodayLadarius Evans of Jackson County and Anthony Hood of Vancleave attend a rally for Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Scott Colom in Biloxi on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026.Former U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg campaigns for Scott Colom, the Democratic nominee for a U.S.  Senate seat, on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, in Biloxi. Credit: Michael Guidry/Mississippi TodayScott Colom, Democratic nominee for a U.S. Senate seat in Mississippi, speaks at a rally in Biloxi on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. Credit: Michael Guidry/Mississippi Today
Hyde-Smith at the time said she opposed the infrastructure legislation because it would increase the national debt, something Colom on Tuesday said was hypocritical because Hyde-Smith hasn’t voiced concerns about the debt increasing under Trump. 
“She doesn’t care about debt,” Colom said. “She cares about politics.” 
Colom also criticized Hyde-Smith for appearing with “Mardi Gras beads” at a ribbon cutting celebrating the reopening of the rail line, calling her dishonest for not disclosing to the public that she voted against the infrastructure bill. 
Buttigieg’s visit to the Magnolia State comes one day after Trump rallied for Hyde-Smith in Corinth in northeastern Mississippi, where he called Colom a “Democrat communist” and accused him of being soft on crime and overly supportive of transgender rights.
Colom called Trump’s description of him lies and pointed to his track record as a district attorney in north Mississippi as evidence that he’s tackled violent crime while in elected office. 
“Can you fill your gas up with those lies?” Colom said of Trump. “Can you pay your grocery bill with those lies?” 
Democratic leaders from outside of the state, such as Harris and Sen. Raphael Warnock of Georgia, have campaigned for Colom in hopes of energizing Democratic turnout on Election Day. 
Hyde-Smith and the GOP have sought to tie Colom to the far-left of the Democratic Party and criticized him for welcoming national Democratic leaders to the conservative state. 
But Colom said Mississippi voters should ask themselves why people such as Buttigieg “care more about roads and bridges” in Mississippi than Hyde-Smith does. 
If Colom wants to pull off an upset, he would need to make significant inroads in the Gulf Coast area, which has become a firewall of support in recent years for Republican candidates. Colom told reporters he believes he’s gained support there because he’s had multiple events in the region and listened to voters’ concerns.
Buttigieg last visited Mississippi in 2024 while he was transportation secretary, to help break ground on a $20-million renovation of Medgar Evers Boulevard in Jackson. He also toured the Medgar and Myrlie Evers Home National Monument and visited the Mississippi Delta, Laurel and Meridian. 
Buttigieg is a potential 2028 Democratic candidate for president and would likely need to shore up support among Black voters to capture the party’s nomination. Mississippi has the largest percentage of Black voters in the nation, but the national party often overlooks Mississippi because of its overall conservative electorate. 
Buttigieg said the national party needs to spend more time in conservative states such as Mississippi because “there’s no such thing as a permanently red state, district or county” and that Southern states deserve better than the incumbents serving them. 
“I think it’s always been a mistake to overlook Mississippi,” Buttigieg said.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Teen found not guilty of homicide in Lincoln Hills counselor death
text:
Lincoln Hills, the youth prison plagued by problems in Wisconsin. (Photo courtesy of the Wisconsin Department of Corrections)The Wisconsin Examiner’s Criminal Justice Reporting Project shines a light on incarceration, law enforcement and criminal justice issues with support from the Public Welfare Foundation.
A jury has found Javarius Hurd, 18, not guilty of reckless homicide in the death of a youth counselor at the Lincoln Hills School for Boys. Hurd was, however, found guilty of battery by a prisoner. 
Hurd had been charged with reckless homicide in the death of Corey Proulx, who died after a confrontation with Hurd in 2024. Prosecutors said that Proulx chased Hurd after the then 16-year-old threw a cup of soapy water in another staff member’s face. Proulx chased Hurd into an outdoor recreational area where, in a scuffle with Hurd, he hit his head on a hard surface. 
After Proulx’s death, the Department of Corrections issued a statement that staff members were collectively mourning. In a press release sent out after the incident, the DOC said that Proulx’s fiancee and daughter “would like everyone to know that Corey was an amazing partner, father, and human being.” 
Hurd’s case became a flashpoint both in and outside of the courtroom. While his attorneys battled prosecutors unsuccessfully to prevent the case from being tried in adult court, Proulx’s death was used by Republican lawmakers to take shots at the approach to juvenile justice taken by Gov. Tony Evers.
Lincoln Hills had become notorious as one of the nation’s largest juvenile prisons where youth suffered abuse and excessive force while guards and counselors were under pressure from  staffing shortages. Recently, Lincoln Hills was found to be in compliance with the requirements set forth after a class action lawsuit over those conditions. As a result, court-ordered monitoring of the facility was halted as new, smaller facilities are being opened around the state. 
A sentencing hearing for Hurd has been set for Friday morning, Oct. 30.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee hosts first gubernatorial forum in eight years. GOP frontrunner no-shows
text:
The 2026 Gubernatorial forum with candidates Jerri Green (D), Lauren Pinkston (I) and David Hatley (I) Republican nominee, U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn did not attend the event
on October 27, 2026 at MTSU in Murfreesboro, Tennessee. Sponsored by Tennessee Press Association and Middle Tennessee State University. (Photo: 
John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Three of the four major Tennessee gubernatorial candidates appeared at a forum one week before the 2026 election and answered questions on a range of topics, including private school vouchers, data centers and toll lanes. 
U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the Republican nominee and favorite to win the race, declined to participate in the forum, continuing a trend among Tennessee GOP candidates of avoiding appearing on stage against their campaign opponents.
Democratic candidate Jerri Green and independent candidate David Hatley both attacked Blackburn at the forum hosted by the Tennessee Press Association and Middle Tennessee State University on the school’s Murfreesboro campus.
Green, a Memphis City Councilmember, said it was a shame the only other candidate with a “path to victory” wouldn’t debate. 
“I’m the only candidate on this stage that won a primary,” Green said.
The press association invited Blackburn, Green, Hatley and Lauren Pinkston, another independent candidate. Blackburn was the only one of the four who declined the invitation.
Hatley is a Washington County hot tub mogul running as a “conservative.” He has put nearly $12 million of his own money into the campaign and refuses to take donations. Hatley is trying to find a lane where he can get enough votes to win without splitting the conservative vote, which could allow Green to win the governor’s race with a plurality.
In his closing remarks, Hatley attacked Green for not supporting the Memphis Safe Task Force and criticized Blackburn for allowing campaign donors to “buy the governor’s office.”
Spoilers or contenders? Two independent candidates for TN governor try to shake up the race

Pinkston is running as a moderate, emphasizing that most voters don’t affiliate with a political party and are fed up with the two-party system. 
Blackburn also refused to debate her Republican gubernatorial primary opponents earlier this year and didn’t debate during her 2024 U.S. Senate reelection campaign. U.S. Sen. Bill Hagerty hasn’t debated in either of his U.S. Senate campaigns. Gov. Bill Lee refused to debate his Democratic Party opponent in 2022. 
The last time Tennessee held debates for statewide offices was in 2018, when Lee debated former Democratic Nashville Mayor Karl Dean and Blackburn took the stage with former Tennessee Gov. Phil Bredesen in their U.S. Senate race. 
Whoever becomes Tennessee’s next governor will face a range of policy decisions
America’s leading artificial intelligence companies started hiring lobbyists earlier this year, ahead of the 2027 legislative session and amid growing backlash to data centers.
The debate over data center expansion has led some local communities to impose construction moratoriums because they worry it’s driving up electricity prices and has negative environmental impacts.
Lawmakers and the next governor are likely to debate whether to pass a state law that preempts local moratoriums on data center construction, paving the way for more. Officials could also look into repealing the generous tax incentives the state offers data centers. 
Green said she would go the other way and implement a statewide moratorium on data center construction, adding that she fought the construction of XAI’s data center in Memphis.
“Elon Musk and his like need to go,” Green said, referring to the CEO of the company that owns XAI.
Pinkston agreed with Green on the moratorium. 
Hatley said he only wants data centers in Tennessee under the right deal.
“We have to have guardrails,” Hatley said. “They need to pay property taxes.”
Blackburn hasn’t publicly taken a stance on whether the state should preempt localities over data centers or whether the state should implement a moratorium.
The candidates on stage differed most from Blackburn’s public position on private school vouchers, where she has called for expanding the program. Blackburn has received million of dollars in support during the gubernatorial primary and the general election from a political action committee, PAC, pushing for private school voucher expansion in the state. 
Blackburn moves $4.8M from US Senate campaign account in apparent legal ‘workaround’

Private school vouchers cost Tennessee taxpayers $310 million a year. Lawmakers expanded the private school voucher program to 35,000 students, funding roughly $7,300 per student to enroll in private schools. The state’s first voucher program provides about $9,000 for about 5,000 low-income students only in Nashville, Memphis and Chattanooga.
Hatley and Pinkston pointed out that most rural counties don’t have private schools and can’t take advantage of the program. 
Green said the whole thing was a “scam” funded by out-of-state interests. 
“Public dollars should go to public schools for the public good,” Green said. 
The next governor will also have to make executive decisions on whether to pursue more toll-lane projects to address a structural deficit in how the state pays for roads. An intergovernmental agency report recommended that state lawmakers consider raising taxes or passing a law that would allow the state to borrow money to cover a $400 million shortfall in the state department of transportation’s budget.
All three candidates at the forum Tuesday also agreed that the state shouldn’t pursue more toll lane projects. 
Green said toll lanes were just “fast track lanes for wealthy people.”
Hatley said he had no idea why the state would pursue toll lane projects after they “failed” in other states.
While Blackburn wasn’t on the stage, her campaign continues to talk on conservative-friendly media.
Blackburn has continued to emphasize that she wants to implement a program similar to President Donald Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency, DOGE. 
Details of the specific cuts are sparse, but when Lee became governor in 2019, he hired the consultancy firm McKinsey to produce a report on ways to reduce government size. During Lee’s eight years in office, the number of state employees modestly increased.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Sand, Lahn call for increasing mental healthcare access, Medicaid oversight in debate
text:
Democratic Auditor Rob Sand and Republican businessman Zach Lahn are competing to become Iowa governor in the Nov. 3, 2026 general election. (Photos by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch, photo illustration via Canva)Both Democrat Rob Sand and Republican Zach Lahn said Tuesday in their final gubernatorial candidate debate that  more work was needed to address mental healthcare and the impact of Medicaid privatization on healthcare providers, but the candidates offered different solutions to improving Iowa’s health system.
Tuesday’s debate, hosted by KCRG-TV9 and The Gazette in Cedar Rapids, was the third for Sand, Iowa’s current state auditor, and Lahn, a businessman with a farm in Belle Plaine. The candidates originally planned four debates but they were unable to reach an agreement on rescheduling a debate with “Iowa Press” on Iowa PBS that had originally been scheduled Oct. 21. Sand withdrew from the Iowa PBS debate following the death of his brother-in-law.
Though Sand did not mention his brother-in-law, Walter E. Lauridsen II, by name, the Democratic candidate said at the debate his family was one of many in the state who have struggled to find psychiatric services in Iowa for people in need. Lauridsen, the brother of Sand’s wife, died earlier in October in a traffic incident near Lucas. Sand said in a social media post sharing the news that “Walter lived with mental health complexities. While this is a difficult and painful time for all of us, we know he is now at peace.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“If you’re one of the families that struggle to find a bed for people, we’re there with you,” Sand said during the debate. “We’ve struggled too. It’s a real problem in our state. We don’t have the availability that we need, and people suffer because of it needlessly.”
Sand also shared another personal story on mental health struggles, speaking about a 2025 incident when a man broke into Sand’s home in Des Moines while his family was away for Thanksgiving. Court records show the man was homeless at the time of arrest, and was later sentenced to two years probation after pleading guilty to burglary and two counts of interference causing injury. He was ordered to receive mental health treatment at an Iowa residential mental health facility, but was set to remain in custody until space was available.
Sand says he remembered having a conversation with the man’s sister after the crime.
“We reached out, and she was just happy to know that he was alive, because she hadn’t heard from him for three years,” Sand said. “This is a man who was living outdoors, saw a warm place. The problem is that we haven’t been paying enough attention to people who are struggling with mental health issues. And then sooner or later, their mental health issue becomes our problem, too, whether it’s because of crime or accidents or anything else. We’ve got to do a better job with this for everyone in this state, because it’s public safety, not just mental health.”
As of a 2023 report, Iowa had two available psychiatric beds per 100,000 individuals, ranking Iowa 51st among all states and Washington, D.C., in availability for state hospital beds available for adults with serious mental health issues.
Lahn says economic growth is key to improving mental healthcare
Lahn similarly said he believed Iowa needs to open additional mental health facilities, and said he believed “there are people that are in prisons in our state that need to be in mental health facilities — and actually, that’s hurting everybody involved.” However, he said the larger conversation on how to address this problem starts with growing Iowa’s economy.
“One thing I’ve learned in running for governor is clearly that we’re dealing with the allocation of scarce resources in the state,” Lahn said. “… I think as we look at, how do we improve access to this, we have to look at priorities that will help us grow as a state. But we cannot just continue to depend on, you know, funding from the federal government for things like this. We have to prioritize growth. If we don’t, we’re just gonna be continuing to put money at something that is not getting the return that we’d like it to have, and not serving the people, and not being able to open up more of these facilities to serve people that do have the mental health needs that need it.”
Sand calls for ending Medicaid privatization
But Sand argued there was a more direct fix for the issue — ending the privatization of Medicaid. Iowa Medicaid was privatized in 2016 under former Gov. Terry Branstad, but Sand said Iowa has seen the privatization of the public health coverage program fail over the past decade. He attributed shortages for mental healthcare and other healthcare to high rates of denied Medicaid coverage and reimbursements by the private managed care organizations (MCOs) that manage the state program. These denials lead to providers shutting down, he said, because they are not being paid.
In 2021, Sand released a report as state auditor which found the percentage of appeals in which judges overturned a reduction or denial of services increased 891% after Medicaid privatization. Sand said these denials not only lead to healthcare facilities closing, but raise healthcare costs across the board.
“It’s not just that people are closing down, because they can’t get paid — other healthcare practitioners have hired new full-time employees, where their entire job is to talk on the phone all day long with these MCOs, to argue about getting paid for the care they provided to people,” Sand said. “Who’s paying that person’s salary? We are. … Privatization of Medicaid in the state of Iowa has driven up costs. It is driven down the quality of care. It has led to mental healthcare practitioners closing their doors.”
Lahn said he understood there were problems with Iowa’s Medicaid system, and called for more oversight of MCOs. But he also said did not believe reversing privatization was the correct solution.
“I think there’s better oversight that we can have with this, but I do not believe the people of Iowa want the government running their healthcare,” Lahn said.
For government oversight, Lahn said he believed the government could take steps to ensure payments to healthcare providers are paid on time, and said the priority would be to pay large bills first.
“One of the issues that I hear from practitioners and hear from providers that sometimes that their largest bills get pushed down to the lower part of the bucket,” Lahn said.
He also said he believed MCOs should not be allowed to have “vertical integration,” meaning the companies involved cannot own healthcare facilities or pharmacies, as well as saying there should be a ban on the use of artificial intelligence when denying claims.
However, Lahn warned removing managed care oversight from Iowa Medicaid would remove “about $1 billion in federal funding” that currently goes to MCOs.
“I do believe there’s better oversight for this,” Lahn said. “I do believe there’s changes we can make to this, but I also believe that the private sector can handle these things better than the government can. But the government has a very distinct role to play in oversight in being the watchdog of these organizations, and I would like to increase that oversight over these organizations, to make sure they are providing the right type of care, they’re paying promptly, and people can have something they should be able to count on — which is just a good service from these companies.”
Agreement on Medicaid work requirements
Despite different opinions on privatization, both candidates said they generally support Medicaid work requirements, implemented on the federal level through the “One, Big Beautiful Bill” Act and similarly placed in Iowa law through a 2025 measure. Lahn said he fully supported work requirements and said he believed Medicaid expansion through the Affordable Care Act “didn’t close this loop” and allowed some able-bodied adults to receive benefits without seeking work.
“I think the people of Iowa just understand, look, if you’re an able-bodied adult, that can seek work, you should be seeking work,” Lahn said. “… But I think one other part of this that we need to make sure we’re focused on, too, is to make sure that only the citizens of the state that are eligible for these programs are getting these programs. I do not believe benefits should be going to illegal immigrants that are in the state.”
Lahn referenced a report from the Center for Immigration Studies, a D.C.-based research organization that advocates for reducing both legal and illegal immigration, which found 59% of “non-citizen households” used one or more public benefit program. Undocumented immigrants are largely banned from receiving any public benefits, but the report argued immigrants, including people in the country illegally, have received “welfare benefits on behalf of U.S.-born citizen children.”
“I think that there’s protections that we can put in place, technology that we can use to make sure that only the people who are eligible for these benefits are getting these benefits,” Lahn said. “And (for) the people who deserve these benefits, that we’re not creating endless bureaucratic paperwork for them, but we’re making it easy for them to be able to get the benefit that they deserve.”
Sand said he believed able-bodied individuals should work. “It’s not an option. If you want to have income, if you wanna have health insurance, that just makes sense,” he said.
He also said because Medicaid work requirements were a federal obligation, and “we are going to follow the law.”
However, Sand said he had concerns about people legitimately in need — who often are working — getting denied access to healthcare because of they were unable to file needed paperwork proving their work history in order to receive health coverage. He referenced a case that received national coverage when Arkansas implemented Medicaid work requirements. A man with a chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder, who was working 30 to 40 hours a week at a poultry plant, meeting the state work requirements, was unable to navigate the monthly reporting system. Because he was unable to report his work hours, he lost Medicaid coverage and could not afford his medication, leading to him losing his job — and eventually losing his life.
“I want able-bodied people to be working, but I want to make sure that what the government is doing is putting in a work requirement and not a paperwork requirement,” Sand said. “It should be simple. It should be straightforward. It should be something that very busy people who do not have a lot of free time on their hands can get done and get done quickly, and the government should take responsibility for making sure that that is happening.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Murkowski and Murkowski endorse Alaska’s Democratic governor candidate
text:
Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, speaks to the Alaska Federation of Natives conference in Anchorage on Oct. 22, 2026. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)Republican U.S. Sen. Lisa Murkowski and her father, Republican former Sen. Frank Murkowski said Tuesday that they are endorsing the election of Democratic candidate for governor Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins.
Kreiss-Tomkins and three Republicans — Dave Bronson, Treg Taylor, and Bernadette Wilson — are running to replace incumbent Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy, who is term-limited and cannot run for re-election this year.
Polling indicates Kreiss-Tomkins, widely known as JKT, has a significant lead, in part because Republican votes are being split among three candidates.
Lisa Murkowski announced her endorsement in an interview with KTUU-TV on Tuesday afternoon.
“JKT is a young Alaskan with a view and a perspective that I think Alaska needs right now,” Murkowski told reporter Rebecca Palsha.
Murkowski has a reputation for bipartisanship in the U.S. Senate and has endorsed the re-election of her colleague, Republican U.S. Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Frank Murkowski, who served as one of Alaska’s two U.S. senators before being elected governor in 2002 — whereupon he appointed his daughter, Lisa, to his vacated Senate seat — joined former Democratic Gov. Tony Knowles and former independent Gov. Bill Walker in endorsing Kreiss-Tomkins via an Anchorage Daily News op-ed published Tuesday.
“We come from different political backgrounds, have different perspectives and have not always agreed on issues facing our state,” the three men said. “But we share a deep commitment to Alaska and its future. That is why we are coming together to support Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins for governor.”
Former Republican Gov. Sarah Palin has not endorsed any of the candidates in this year’s governor race, nor has former Republican Gov. Sean Parnell.
President Donald Trump endorsed Wilson on Oct. 13 during a rally in Wasilla. Speaking at that rally, Dunleavy declined to endorse any specific candidate but said Republican voters should rank all three Republican candidates.
“You need to get out and vote for your governor candidates. There are three of them. I need you to vote for each one of them. Ranked choice voting has foisted this on our shoulders, and the only way we’re going to win is if we all vote for the Republican candidates for governor, and that’s very important,” Dunleavy said.
