name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Medicaid fraud task force recommends more staff, utilizing false claims act
text:
Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird and Solicitor General Eric Wessan present recommendations the final Iowa Medicaid Fraud Elimination Task Force meeting Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Iowa’s Medicaid Fraud Elimination Task Force is sending a draft of recommendations to Gov. Kim Reynolds that suggests the state more than double the fraud investigation and civil enforcement unit to hold fraudsters accountable. 
The task force, which was initiated by Reynolds in July, met for the final time Tuesday and outlined their findings on how to end instances of fraud in the tax-payer supported healthcare system. 
Former state officials who have been vocally opposed to the task force said Tuesday that the initiative was “political theater” and that the conclusions it came to were the same recommendations the former officials suggested months ago. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Kevin Techau, former Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing director, said Attorney General Brenna Bird, who led the task force, could have long ago directed her staff to pursue cases under a state law that allows for lawsuits against parties who have defrauded the state. 
Techau said Bird and Reynolds have been “sitting on their hands” instead of directing staff to file claims under the state’s civil False Claims Act, which he said other state attorneys general have used to pursue cases of fraud and failure to provide Medicaid-funded healthcare.
“Suddenly, they wake up, just before an election, and decide Medicaid fraud is a big issue,” Techau said. “…So, hallelujah! They finally found the answers, but the answers were always sitting there right in front of them.”
Former state officials Kevin Techau, left, and Dean Lerner, right, talk to reporters after the final Iowa Medicaid Fraud Elimination Task Force meeting Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Techau said Iowa nursing homes continue to collect Medicaid funds without providing the care they promise. A recent review of Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services data revealed that Iowa had more insufficient staffing citations at nursing homes in 2025 than any other state.
The task force recommended, according to an executive overview released Tuesday, establishing a “civil fraud team” in the Iowa Attorney General’s Office to make use of the Iowa False Claims Act to recover Medicaid funds from fraudsters. 
“Today, Iowa doesn’t have lawyers that are dedicated to suing these Medicaid fraudsters for the money they took, and the task force is recommending a civil fraud team in my office, something I very much support, to use the Iowa False Claims Act to allow triple damages plus penalties,” Bird said during the meeting. 
Recommendations 
In addition to adding a civil fraud team, the task force recommended growing the Medicaid Fraud Control Unit staff from 9 people to 24 people, including “dedicated prosecutors, investigators, data analysts and a nurse investigator.” 
Eric Wessan, solicitor general for the state, said that “person for person, Iowa’s unit brings more criminal cases than any other unit in the country,” but he said the unit has not grown since 2013. Wessan said that while Medicaid spending has grown 129% since 2013, the Medicaid Fraud Control Unit’s budget has grown 31% in the time period.
“The bottom line is simple: Iowa already does more with less than almost anyone,” Wessan said. “With the right tools, the right people, and the right structure, we can do a great deal more yet.” 
The task force also recommended tougher penalties for Medicaid fraudsters and the establishment of a “Medicaid Fraud War Room” to suspend payments to providers within 24 hours when fraud is suspected, and while it is investigated. 
Stephan Bayens, commissioner at the Iowa Department of Public Safety and a member of the task force, said the investment into the investigation and prosecution side of the issue was “much needed.” 
“In at least some of the public comments that we received, there (were) concerns about staffing levels, and I believe that this is an appropriate recommendation to kind of recognize the good work that’s being done, but also recognize there is capacity that could be addressed with more people.” 
Another section of the task force recommendations calls for revalidating high-risk providers and deactivating providers who are not serving patients. 
It recommended increasing technology and analytical tools for the fraud unit and related departments so they can use data to target reviews of high-risk areas such as in-home care to help ensure, for example, that a caregiver actually showed up to provide the care that was billed to Medicaid. 
Wessan said the task force was also recommending a “program integrity technology unit” within the Iowa Department of Health and Human Services to measure what is spent on “fraud-fighting technology” and what the technology has recovered. 
The task force was also directed to investigate ways to enhance fraud awareness and public reporting of suspected instances of fraud. The task force recommended the state release a video that clearly explains Medicaid fraud and how to report it to the state through avenues such as IowaFraudFighters.gov. 
Wessan said some of the recommendations “can start tomorrow under existing authority” but others will require legislative approval or funding. 
Bird said the draft of the recommendations will be submitted to Reynolds who, upon approval of the recommendations, will release the draft to the public. 
Bird thanked the task force for its work over the past several months. 
“Adopting this report, too, I want people to know this is not the finish line,” Bird said. “This is the starting line. Our message today is unmistakable: Iowa has zero tolerance for anybody who would steal from the taxpayers or exploit vulnerable people who are on Medicaid.”

name: California
title: What local election officials found in Trump’s new claims about California voters
text:
In summary
The Trump administration is demanding that almost every California county review its claims that noncitizens are registered to vote. Some of the information appears outdated, officials say.


Election officials from across California questioned the accuracy of the federal government’s methodology for finding noncitizen voters after the Trump administration threatened them with criminal charges last week.
The counties on Friday were given 48 hours to commit to working with federal authorities and to segregate ballots from a list of people federal authorities claimed were likely noncitizens. 
The letters said the list of names were from the same group of 20,000 people that the Trump administration flagged as noncitizens and then sued California over, demanding that state officials not count those ballots until they verify the voters’ citizenship.
State officials have questioned the accuracy of the data and have refused to comply, saying the federal government risks disenfranchising thousands of voters in an attempt to illegally meddle in state elections. On Tuesday, a federal judge appeared skeptical of the Trump administration’s legal arguments.
Meanwhile, the letters counties received last week threatened potential criminal charges for election officials who “knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens.”
Butte County Clerk-Recorder Keaton Denlay said he received one such letter and a demand to not count ballots from a list of 47 people.
“Upon inspection of the list of names, it appeared to be a print screen of a poorly formatted excel spreadsheet with missing and jumbled information,” he said in a statement. 
Denlay said he reviewed the list and found that 32 of the people were not on Butte County’s active voter rolls and were not sent ballots. Seven others “did not have sufficient information … to match to our voter list with confidence” since the list only contained partial names, partial addresses, no dates of birth, no drivers’ license numbers or Social Security numbers.
Six of the names belonged to people who may not be eligible to vote, but Denlay said California law requires those challenging a voter’s eligibility to have extraordinary levels of proof.“Given the overall inaccuracy of the list provided and its lack of specificity, I believe the Department of Justice has not met that burden,” Denlay said. “There will be no further action taken at this time.”
Fresno County Registrar of Voters James Kus also received a letter, but he said he couldn’t tell how many ballots federal prosecutors wanted him to segregate, since the “not particularly legible” list was a printed sheet, in small font, and “not in a format that facilitates counting or reviewing.” He said the county already follows state and federal voter registration laws.
“We will not be deviating from those legal requirements for this letter,” Kus told CalMatters in an email.
Francisco Diaz, San Benito County registrar of voters, said his office received a demand with 33 names. A preliminary review found that some on the list weren’t registered to vote.
“Hand-delivering a letter via armed federal agents with an arbitrary 48-hour deadline does not circumvent state law,” Diaz said in a statement. “We will not be intimidated by agents with guns for simply doing our jobs, nor will we be rushed into compromising confidential voter data.”
Orange County Registrar of Voters Bob Page said he wasn’t notified of a letter alleging his county had 1,754 “likely aliens” on the voter rolls until after business hours on Friday.
That’s because, he told reporters in an email, federal prosecutors had addressed and hand-delivered the letter not to Page but to Orange County Clerk-Recorder Hugh Nguyen, who handles such documents as marriage licenses and property deeds. 
On Monday, Page said federal agents delivered a correctly addressed letter to his office, along with a “data storage drive.” 
Page planned to respond by the Wednesday deadline, he said.
The messy voter lists counties described fits a pattern, said David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation & Research, a nonprofit whose mission is to restore trust in the American election system
He noted that the Department of Homeland Security recently claimed that Nevada had nearly 16,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls. DHS sent the state the names of only 185 voters. Nevada officials confirmed the voters had attested they were all U.S. citizens.Becker said the Trump administration has been making “broad political claims made with great fanfare” only to have them “fall apart as they’re subjected to scrutiny.” 
“I’m not entirely sure the DOJ wants to get into court and defend its evidentiary claims because I think they would fall apart, just as we’ve seen in other states,” said Becker, a former U.S. Justice Department attorney.
In federal court on Tuesday, Bill Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney in Los Angeles, insisted the federal list of 20,000 people was accurate.
“We stand by the reliability of the information,” he said. “We take our obligations and ethics very seriously.”

name: California
title: Judge says Trump could disenfranchise voters in purge of noncitizens from election rolls
text:
In summary
A federal judge is unlikely to issue a final ruling on the Trump administration’s claim that noncitizens are registered to vote in California until after Election Day.


Saying he had concerns it could disenfranchise voters during the midterm election, a federal judge on Tuesday seemed skeptical of the Trump administration’s demands that California election officials set aside 20,000 ballots that it claimed could have been mailed to noncitizens.
“Some of these may be very valid voters, and that’s my concern about disenfranchisement,”  said U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, an appointee of President Bill Clinton.
Carter said he would issue a formal ruling by Wednesday, but he told the courtroom he was likely going to appoint a special master to weigh the evidence both sides present at a hearing in two weeks. That means his final ruling might not come until after the election.
He said he didn’t want to “just wing it with a ruling” based on last-minute evidence the federal government submitted to the court the night before Tuesday’s hearing.Carter also suggested that his ruling would order federal authorities to stop telling election officials that they could face criminal charges if they didn’t comply with the Trump administration’s demands. The Trump administration on Friday sent letters to California election officials telling them to set aside ballots from suspected noncitizens, and threatened them with criminal charges if they allowed those people to vote.“This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state or county (election) employees cease immediately,” Carter told the courtroom.
Carter’s remarks point to yet another likely legal blow to the Trump administration as it seeks to validate President Donald Trump’s longstanding claims of widespread election fraud favoring Democrats. Experts and election officials say those claims are meritless. 
Bill Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney in Los Angeles, acknowledged that the government’s list of 20,000 people may contain citizens, but he said the possibility that noncitizens were voting illegally was too great a threat.
“I would ask the state how many illegal votes is OK for them?” Essayli said. “It cannot be that the state has a right to facilitate the counting and tabulation of noncitizen votes. There’s no right to that.”
The Trump administration sued California earlier this month saying election officials refused to comply with a 48-hour federal deadline to set aside the ballots of up to 20,000 people the administration had flagged as possible noncitizens until the voters’ citizenship could be verified.
The administration sought a temporary restraining order forcing the state to comply.
California officials argued there was no way they could since they were busy overseeing the election. They also called the demand an illegal effort to meddle in state-run elections that could disenfranchise legal voters.“I just want to make sure the stakes are clear: that what we’re talking about is stripping voting rights from thousands of people until proven otherwise,” said Anne Bellows, a deputy attorney general with the California Department of Justice. 
Judge points to immigrant arrests
State and county officials also have questioned the methodology the federal government used to flag possible noncitizens.
In a court filing, Los Angeles County officials said that a sampling of 200 names from the federal list, which included people from all over California, found that many of them were likely citizens and that most had not voted before and were not sent ballots.  Federal investigators re-reviewed those 200 names and found that only four were citizens, Essayli told the judge.“We stand by the reliability of the information,” he said. “We take our obligations and ethics very seriously.”
Carter noted that, last week, federal prosecutors charged 28 California green card holders for allegedly voting or registering to vote in violation of laws prohibiting noncitizens from participating in elections. 
He said that if noncitizens really are voting in as large of numbers as the Trump administration claims, there’s nothing stopping federal prosecutors from finding them and charging them without the risk of blocking legal voters from having their ballots counted.
“If it’s this big, you’ve got a remedy for goodness sakes,” Carter told Essayli. “Go out and indict.”
After the hearing, Essayli said from the courthouse steps that the state could “resolve this today.”
“They just seem disinterested in getting to the bottom of this,” Essayli said, noting that the number of ballots in question could tip smaller elections. “A lot of elections are decided by tens of votes or hundreds of votes.”
9th Circuit ruled against Trump
The hearing came a day after two judges on a three-judge panel of the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected an emergency effort from the Trump administration to bypass Carter’s courtroom. 
The Trump administration sought an emergency order from the appellate court, claiming that Carter didn’t schedule a hearing fast enough. The two judges said prosecutors’ arguments about urgency didn’t hold up.
Their ruling noted that the prosecutors have been making claims about illegal voters on California’s voter rolls since July and could have taken action any time since, so their “claimed emergency, at least in part, is a self-constructed one.”Judge Mark Bennett, a Trump appointee, noted in a concurring opinion that he had “serious doubts” about the federal government’s claims that prosecutors could “superintend or intervene in a state’s election administration.” 
He wrote that Congress granted states — not the executive branch — authority over elections.In a dissenting opinion, Judge Patrick Bumatay, another Trump appointee, argued that “federal law precludes California from commingling ballots likely cast by aliens with legitimate ballots, because it encourages and induces illegal voting.”
“Stopping that practice for those identified as likely noncitizens is the bare minimum,” Bumatay wrote.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Governor signs bill allowing security spending with campaign funds
text:
Gov. Mikie Sherrill signed a measure, introduced after political killings last year, that lets candidates and elected officials pay for security upgrades with campaign cash. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)Gov. Mikie Sherrill on Tuesday signed legislation allowing candidates and some other fundraising committees to use political contributions to pay for security upgrades needed because of a campaign.
The bill, which won unanimous passage in the Senate but met with a 51-12 Assembly vote divided largely along party lines, allows certain political fundraising committees to fund security upgrades like cameras, gates, and personnel to meet threats that have become increasingly common for individuals seeking or holding office.
It prohibits using campaign funds to pay for firearms or ammunition, and it bars any payments to family members or entities they operate.
Under the new law, security upgrades paid for by campaign accounts are the property of the campaign and must be dissolved once the campaign account closes or an officeholder leaves their position. That can be done by selling devices and equipment at cost or for another reasonable value.
The New Jersey Election Law Enforcement Commission will set regulations further governing the use of campaign funds for candidate security.
The bill’s introduction in February came after a rising tide of political violence in 2025 that included the assassinations of former Democratic Minnesota House Speaker Melissa Hortman and her husband and the conservative activist Charlie Kirk.
Despite its bipartisan sponsorship by Sens. Paul Sarlo (D-Bergen) and Carmen Amato (R-Ocean) and Assemblyman Rob Karabinchak (D-Middlesex), the bill had met with Republican opposition in the lower chamber from members who worried campaign donors were the wrong source to fund security.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana’s bond rating improves, which should save the state money
text:
Fitch Ratings moved Louisiana’s credit from “AA-” to “AA" last week, which is expected to save the state money. (Photo by Wesley Muller/Louisiana Illuminator)One of the three national credit rating agencies upgraded Louisiana’s bond rating at the end of last week. The state should now expect to pay less in interest when it borrows money for roadwork and other construction projects.  
Fitch Ratings moved Louisiana’s credit from “AA-” to “AA,” according to a statement released by the global agency Friday. It attributed the upgrade, in part, to new tax laws Gov. Jeff Landry and the Louisiana Legislature approved two years ago. 
“The upgrade reflects the state’s successful implementation of 2024 revenue policy changes, which reduces a projected structural gap,” said the Fitch report. 
Landry and state lawmakers skirted a major state budget deficit by eliminating an automatic sales tax cut before it took place in 2025. Instead, the governor and legislators raised the sales tax rate further to offset a new income tax reduction. They also freed up more money by shifting revenue dedicated to major transportation projects into accounts for expenses such as healthcare and higher education. 
State Treasurer John Fleming, R-Minden, said the credit rating improvement should be celebrated. 

“We must continue building on this progress to ensure that Louisiana’s finances remain strong for years to come,” he said in a written statement. 
Louisiana Senate President Cameron Henry, R-Metairie, and House Speaker Philip DeVillier, R-Eunice, said the legislature will continue to focus on bringing long-term fiscal stability to the state. 

“We are not done yet, but we are making the changes necessary to secure our state’s fiscal future,” Henry said in a written statement.

A reversal of the new tax policies — for example, a future sales tax rate cut — could cause the rating agency to downgrade Louisiana’s credit in the future, Fitch said in its report. 
“Slow economic growth, the planned partial rollback of the 2024 sales tax increase and the relocation of certain revenue from the general fund to transportation projects could constrain long-term revenue growth,” the report states. “These factors will be important determinants of future financial performance.”

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho reports second influenza death, as health officials report early start to flu season
text:
An influenza vaccine is pictured at the Ellis R. Shipp Public Health Center in West Valley City on Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Idaho health officials on Tuesday reported the state’s second flu death in the 2026-27 influenza season.
The death was of a resident of Elmore County, a rural area outside Boise, who was in their 80s, the regional health agency, Central District Health, announced. The first death, reported last week, was of an Owyhee County man who was older than age 65. 
The deaths come as public health officials say that influenza is spreading earlier in the year than usual. In recent weeks, emergency department and urgent care visits related to the flu have been higher than they were during the same time last year, state health officials say.
Idaho has averaged about 60 reported influenza-related deaths annually for the last five flu seasons, with most reported deaths among people over 50, according to the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare.
Officials at Central District Health say vaccination is the best way to reduce the risk of severe flu illness.
“While most people who get the flu recover without serious complications, some groups are at higher risk for severe illness, hospitalization, and death,” said Dr. Jaime Butler-Dawson, the health district’s epidemiology program manager. “These include adults age 65 and older, pregnant people, young children, people with obesity, and those with weakened immune systems or chronic conditions such as asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), diabetes, or kidney disease.”
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, this year’s vaccines are designed to protect against three different influenza viruses expected to circulate during the flu season.
Symptoms of the flu include fever, cough, sore throat, runny nose, body aches, headache, chills and fatigue. Although most people who get the flu recover after a few days, some can have serious complications that can lead to hospitalization or death.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Montana Public Service Commission postpones vote on NorthWestern Energy merger
text:
(Photo by Scott Olson | Getty Images)The Montana Public Service Commission postponed a decision on the pending merger of NorthWestern Energy and Black Hills Corp until Nov. 10.
Commissioner Jennifer Fielder, who proposed the postponement Tuesday, said staff analysts addressed many of her concerns about the $15.4 billion merger proposal.
However, Fielder requested more time to propose an additional condition to address a concern that two of the groups who have opposed the merger still had.
“I think that there might be some good work we could yet do on that,” Fielder said.
Commissioners Jeff Welborn and Randy Pinocci supported Fielder’s motion to postpone the final decision. Commissioners Annie Bukacek and Kirk Bushman opposed it.
Most of the parties that participated in the case ended up in support of the merger — or agreed not to oppose it — after the utilities addressed their concerns. But 350 Montana and Montana Farmers Union continued to oppose it and suggested conditions the PSC should place on any merger.
Fielder said she wanted to propose one condition the groups had recommended: To reserve a portion of NorthWestern’s acquisition at the coal-fired plant in Colstrip for Montana customers if it would be the most affordable.
Fielder said the additional time would allow members of the public and the parties to review the condition, and it would allow them time to review any additional conditions commissioners wanted to propose.
Bukacek, who has voted to support NorthWestern, urged against the delay.
She said the merger proposal was made more than one year ago, and the PSC should vote this week as scheduled to avoid more staff time and travel costs.
“Enough’s enough,” Bukacek said.
NorthWestern Energy and South Dakota-based Black Hills announced plans to merge in August 2025 pending approval from regulators.
Regulators in Montana will be the last to vote on the deal.
At the meeting Tuesday, roughly 30 people urged the PSC to oppose the merger, citing concerns including the costs more data centers might have on Montana customers.
PSC legal and regulatory staff recommended approval.
Staff cited support from the Montana Consumer Counsel and restrictions aimed to protect NorthWestern’s Montana assets from financial activities of the parent company.
Based on statute, the final day for the PSC to act is Thursday, Nov. 12.
If approved, the new company, to be called Bright Horizon Energy, would operate in Montana, South Dakota, Arkansas, Colorado, Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska and Wyoming.
This story will be updated.

name: Daily Montanan
title: University of Providence to shutter in 2027
text:
The University of Providence (University of Providence photo)The University of Providence, a private liberal arts Catholic school in Great Falls, will close Aug. 20, 2027 the university announced Tuesday, citing ongoing financial struggles.
University President Caroline Goulet said falling enrollment and financial pressures as the reasons for the school closing its doors in a video posted to its website.
The school “pursued multiple paths to secure the university’s future,” she said in a video.“Despite those efforts, we could not find a financially sustainable way forward.”
The school’s board of trustees voted unanimously on Tuesday to shut down the university, which is located on a 44-acre campus made up of 17 buildings near Benefis Hospital. 
“While this chapter of the university’s history is ending, its mission and impact will endure through the generations of graduates, faculty, staff, Sisters and partners who have carried the spirit of Providence into their communities,” Terry Cosgrove, the chairperson of the board, said in a press release. “We are committed to honoring that legacy with the same compassion, dignity and integrity that have guided the university since its founding.”
The board said that a planned closure would be easier than an abrupt one. 
Several webpages created by the university added details about the decision.
“The university’s circumstances also reflect broader pressures reshaping small private colleges across the country, particularly institutions serving smaller and rural communities,” a webpage said, adding a merger and acquisition were also discussed.
In 2025 the university had $28.6 million in revenue and $35.6 million in expenses, with total assets valued at $48.6 million, according to ProPublica.
“The board concluded that closing the university with care was the responsible path forward,” the university said in its communications released Tuesday.
  ‘Questions about what comes next’ 

The university has separate student and facility webpages with additional information about the closure. Students will face decisions about transfers, credits, and degree recognition; whether they can graduate and what happens if faculty leave before the end of the year. 
The Montana University System said in a press release that it would support Providence students seeking to find a new school. The school had 630 students and 244 total employees.
“We know University of Providence students have invested significant time, effort, and resources in their education, and this news brings difficult questions about what comes next,” Montana Commissioner of Higher Education Clayton Christian said in a press release. “Our message to those students is simple: You do not have to navigate this transition alone. The Montana University System is here to help you find a path forward that builds on your progress and supports your goal of earning a degree.”
Staff now face questions dealing with benefits and employment details.
What to do with the school’s endowment is still under consideration, according to the university. Reports show the university having about $20 million in its endowment.
The school is still taking donations, and those will be used to help current students — specifically offering scholarships to cover the cost of tuition for students during the summer 2027 session, and reducing graduate tuition for students.
Existing donors will also be contacted to discuss alternatives true to the “original intent and purpose” of those endowment and scholarship funds.
“The university is working with legal counsel on the steps required to permit use of endowment funds as scholarship support for continuing students, consistent with donor intent and applicable law,” a school webpage says. “These funds would help students complete their education before the university closes.”
  ‘Times change’ 

The school is a private, Roman Catholic liberal arts university, founded in 1932 by the Sisters of Providence.
That religious order, which was founded in 1842 in Montreal, opened schools and hospitals in Montana as early as 1864, according to the university. The Sisters of Providence came to Great Falls in 1892 to open the city’s first hospital and four decades later, the school in cooperation with the Diocese of Great Falls-Billings. 
It was called the College of Great Falls at the time, before changing to the University of Great Falls in 1995 and finally the University of Providence in 2017.
However, about 10 years after the school opened, the Diocese of Great Falls-Billings relinquished control of the university to the Sisters of Providence. 
The Sisters of Providence also grew into a major hospital provider across the West — the healthcare branch of its work, Providence Health & Services, now includes 51 hospitals, 1,002 clinics and 119,000 employees across five states. 
The university said the healthcare service had provided “substantial financial support to keep the university open while it searched for a viable and sustainable operating model.”
Issues at Providence Health also contributed to the university’s demise, as they were contributing about $8 million annually to the school, which was cut, according to the Montana Free Press. 
The school formally declared a financial exigency in December 2025 and sought to address the issues.
Providence Ministries, which is also associated with the university, said the Sisters of Providence saw a need in Great Falls and looked to fill it.
“Because of this ministry, thousands served in hospitals, classrooms, businesses, and communities throughout Montana and beyond,” Mary Anne Sladich-Lantz, president of Providence Ministries said in a press release. “But times change. The path forward for many small, private universities across the country is uncertain. Financial sustainability is no longer feasible.”
  ‘Cannot be measured in dollars alone’ 

The university was known for its nursing program and also had majors in criminal justice, biology, healthcare administration and psychology, among others.
In Great Falls, the news was met with sadness by Mayor Cory Reeves, who called it a “huge loss” for the city.
“For me, this one is personal,” Reeves said in a statement. “It’s where I went to college, earned my degree, and met my wife. The University of Providence will always hold a special place in my heart, and I’m grateful for the role it played in my life.”
He added it was more than losing a college.
“Its impact on Great Falls and Montana cannot be measured in dollars alone,” Reeves added, who said he was “truly saddened” by the news.
The school mostly competed athletically in the Frontier Conference, which also includes a number of other Montana schools. Some sports, including wrestling and soccer, competed separately in the Cascade Collegiate Conference.
The University of Providence had successful sports programs including a volleyball program that has won five Frontier Conference titles — four of which came in the last six years — and advanced to multiple NAIA national tournaments in the last two decades. 
The women’s basketball team made the NAIA’s Final Four during the 2023-24 season, and the school also notably had one of the few wrestling programs in the Mountain West.
Frontier Conference Commissioner Scott Crawford did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico students walk out of classes to protest data centers, US Sen. Heinrich’s permitting bill
authors: Matt Mondschein, Joshua Bowling, Patrick Lohmann
text:
Students from the New Mexico School for the Arts in Santa Fe marched to the Capitol for the "Pull Out the Plug" protest on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)Hundreds of students from New Mexico School for the Arts in Santa Fe and the University of New Mexico in Albuquerque — some donning Halloween costumes — walked out of classes Tuesday and joined protests organized against data centers, pipelines and fossil fuel projects.
The protests, organized by Youth United for Climate Crisis Action (YUCCA), followed a Sunday protest on the Las Cruces campus of New Mexico State University and a coordinated campaign to support a data center moratorium during next year’s legislative session.



“We will not get back the last 20 years of climate progress Project Jupiter will undo,” Isabelle Taylor-Ault, a student organizer and junior at NMSA, said to the crowd outside the Roundhouse in Santa Fe. “You, the adults, the ones supposed to be fighting for us, you may get the privilege of dying of old age, but our children will die from climate change.”
A handful of state lawmakers sitting on the interim Water and Natural Resources Committee — which was meeting on the Capitol’s third floor — headed down to watch the protest unfold.
State Rep. Micaela Lara Cadena (D-Mesilla), a vocal critic of Project Jupiter and one of the first state lawmakers to call for a statewide data center moratorium, told Source NM she was thrilled to see teenagers across the state opposing the development.
Last month, Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland said if elected on Nov. 3, she plans to enact a statewide data center moratorium as an executive order immediately upon taking office. Lara Cadena acknowledged that the Dec. 7 public hearing on whether to give Project Jupiter’s power source an air quality permit — one of the last hurdles the data center needs to clear to become fully operational — could result in a decision before then, but said she plans to continue using her office to hold the industry to account.
“Those permits haven’t been issued yet,” she said.
Protesters — bearing signs with messages like “El agua es vida,” “This sign was not made by AI” and “Make Orwell fiction again” — stood in a circle around the perimeter of the second-floor rotunda, where they began a “Stop Project Jupiter” chant.
As the chant echoed across the rotunda, they marched upstairs to Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham’s fourth-floor office. Standing outside Lujan Grisham’s office, they shouted in unison: “MLG, you can’t hide. You support ecocide.”
Students from the New Mexico School for the Arts in Santa Fe marched to the Capitol for the "Pull Out the Plug" protest on Oct. 27, 2026.  (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)Students from the New Mexico School for the Arts in Santa Fe marched to the Capitol for the "Pull Out the Plug" protest on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)Students from the New Mexico School for the Arts in Santa Fe marched to the Capitol for the "Pull Out the Plug" protest on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)Students from the New Mexico School for the Arts in Santa Fe marched to the Capitol for the "Pull Out the Plug" protest on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)Students from the New Mexico School for the Arts in Santa Fe marched to the Capitol for the "Pull Out the Plug" protest on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)Ahtza Chavez, executive director of Naeva, an Indigenous voter empowerment organization, speaks to protesters Oct. 27, 2026, in front of the office U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM) Protesters gathered Oct. 27, 2026, in front U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich's downtown Albuquerque office to urge him to withdraw his permitting reform bill from the U.S. Senate's consideration. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)A protester critical of U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich's permitting reform bill marches Oct. 27, 2026, in Albuquerque. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM) Protesters march from the University of New Mexico toward U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich's office in downtown Albuquerque on Oct. 27, 2026. They were criticizing Heinrich's permitting reform bill and data centers and urging elected officials not to accept donations from Palantir, the data mining and defense technology firm. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)A protester critical of U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich's permitting reform bill marches Oct. 27, 2026, in Albuquerque. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM) Students from the New Mexico School for the Arts in Santa Fe marched to the Capitol for the "Pull Out the Plug" protest on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)
Office staff told the students Lujan Grisham was out of office, but Kaila Rubbel, a visual arts student at NMSA, waited outside for her turn to write and deliver a letter to the governor. She told Source NM that she wants Lujan Grisham “to take action. I want her to stop this. And I think that not showing up or not doing so shows us who she is.”
Michael Coleman, Lujan Grisham’s communications director, told Source NM in an emailed statement Tuesday that the governor “understands that young New Mexicans are frustrated with the American political system, and she shares their concerns about some of the issues raised during today’s protest.” 
Still, the governor urged the protesters to respect public property and not interfere with government employees “simply doing their jobs.” 
“The governor received the letters the students left in our office, and she plans to read and consider them,” Coleman said. “She hopes the students work to stay informed and continue to participate in the political process.”
In Albuquerque, protesters directed much of their ire toward U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), who recently unveiled a sweeping, bipartisan permitting reform bill that protesters say reduces tribal input and empowers fossil fuel companies to quickly break ground on more harmful projects. 
New Mexico US Sen. Heinrich touts bipartisan permitting reform bill amid environmentalist criticism

More than 100 protesters marched from the UNM bookstore down Central Avenue to Heinrich’s downtown Albuquerque office. In front of a large sign that read “Heinrich is a sellout,” protesters with YUCCA, as well as Indigenous and environmentalist groups, described the bill as a betrayal by a longtime champion for tribal and environmental causes. 
Heinrich’s bill, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, seeks to hasten the federal permitting process for a variety of projects, including data centers, solar arrays, renewable energy transmission lines and more. 
The 400-page bill, cosponsored with U.S. Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah) and two other senators in both parties, has drawn praise from labor unions, as well as both the American Petroleum Institute and the American Clean Power Association. Groups touting bipartisan policy have also lauded it as a step forward on a policy matter that has long frustrated advocates for all types of energy production in the United States.
But critics have said the pros of the bill that Heinrich has touted — namely a prohibition on data centers imposing energy production costs onto ratepayers, and hastening the approvals of renewable energy projects — are far outweighed by the bill’s other provisions. Protesters on Tuesday said the bill erodes hard-fought environmental protections like the National Environmental Policy Act and laws requiring tribal input. 
The All Pueblo Council of Governors, which represents 19 New Mexico pueblos, released a resolution on Tuesday that says the bill’s provisions will combine to ultimately “weaken protections for Pueblo sacred places.”
Outside Heinrich’s office, protesters carried signs decrying “data center giveaways” and “fossil fuel sellouts” and chanted “Kill the bill!” in between speeches.
New Mexico State University students and organizers call for statewide ban on data centers

“We need NEPA. We need our Clean Water Act. We need all of these things because they are the bare minimum for what we need to survive on this land,” Ahtza Chavez, executive director of Naeva, an Indigenous voter empowerment organization, told attendees Tuesday. “And this senator has the gall to say that he’s going to rip that out of our hands. I don’t think so.”
Heinrich’s spokesperson Luis Soriano, in a statement to Source NM on Tuesday, said Heinrich’s bill “actually holds data centers accountable for their energy usage while speeding up the approval of clean energy projects that put cheaper and cleaner electricity on the grid.”
As for tribal consultation, Soriano said that Congress needs to pass the bill to ensure that President Donald Trump’s administration is required to heed tribal input instead of ignoring it.
“The legislation also defends against the Trump administration’s efforts to make all Tribal consultation discretionary and eliminate consultation altogether on cultural landscapes. All of this means stronger Tribal consultation protections, lower utility bills, more good-paying jobs, and a path toward unlocking our clean energy future.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: WA advocates renew calls for state to limit feds’ access to license data
text:
A masked U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent knocks on a car window in Minnesota on Jan. 12. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)SEATTLE — Chris Megargee volunteers at a Shoreline Home Depot to help day laborers frequently targeted by federal immigration authorities. 
As part of the adopt-a-corner program, Megargee and other volunteers provide breakfast and share information so the workers, who are often noncitizens, know their rights if U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents come. 
Since January, ICE officials have detained half a dozen men there, including one this month, who drove their cars to the Home Depot, Megargee said. 
Before arresting each, ICE agents entered the license plate numbers on those cars into a database, and received car registration information to identify the driver, Megargee alleged.
Advocates gathered in Seattle on Tuesday to continue their push for Washington state officials to do more to restrict the ability of the feds to get information from the license plate database.
“We need you to act and slow down this mass deportation and detention machine by continuing to cut off access to the Department of Licensing data that is being used for immigration enforcement,” said Lucía Vázquez Martínez, field director for Service Employees International Union 775. 
Gov. Bob Ferguson noted his administration has acted to curb unfettered access to the state’s data.
“My team has worked to limit Customs and Border Protection access for immigration enforcement, while maintaining access necessary to protect public safety, such as human trafficking investigations that require real-time access to data to protect vulnerable Washingtonians,” he said in a statement Tuesday. 
“Looking ahead to the next two years, this will be an ongoing process for us to adapt to what (the) federal government does next to work around what we do to protect our data,” Ferguson added.
These concerns date back years, but have intensified as President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign has grown in Washington, with surges seen in recent months.
University of Washington researchers connected 356 arrests to federal queries for license data between August 2025 and Oct. 13 of this year. In the first five months of this year, agencies housed under the U.S. Department of Homeland Security searched state Department of Licensing driver and vehicle data over 1 million times, according to the university’s Center for Human Rights.
Washington is one of 19 states that offer driver’s licenses regardless of immigration status. Others require warrants or court orders for federal agencies to access state-held license and vehicle data for immigration purposes, according to the UW researchers. Washington does not.
Ferguson spokesperson Brionna Aho said Tuesday that “our team is reviewing what other states have done, and what is lawful, to require judicial warrants for civil immigration-related requests.”
What the state has already done
Last November, Washington officials cut off ICE’s ability to get this data. This was later expanded to Homeland Security Investigations, also known as HSI.
Between November 2025 and Oct. 12, the Washington State Patrol blocked over 174,000 search attempts from federal agencies, including 89,000 from Customs and Border Protection, 45,000 from HSI and nearly 40,000 from ICE, according to the governor’s office. However, researchers say millions more searches from the Department of Homeland Security have still gone through. 
Aho said shutting off federal access to Department of Licensing data entirely isn’t an option due to “legitimate public safety reasons.”   
The state has taken numerous steps, some of them unprecedented nationwide, to cut off immigration authorities, she said.
These reportedly include blocking searches of the Nlets platform, which police agencies use to share driver’s license data across states, by ICE. The state has also stopped Customs and Border Protection from seeing photos of people searched in Nlets in Washington. A terms-of-use notice in Nlets now also informs those seeking its data that it cannot be used for immigration enforcement.
Federal agents have repeatedly found workarounds to bypass the state’s restrictions. 
“As the federal government has rapidly changed its tactics and the way it uses state data, Governor Ferguson has continually considered and reassessed state agencies’ data practices and taken quick action when necessary,” Aho said in an email. 

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
Washington has also suspended nine searchers associated with CBP and three with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services that were suspected to be connected to immigration enforcement operations.
In this case, the UW researchers say this work by the state to block individual accounts is “not providing meaningful protection for Washingtonians’ data.” They argued the continued federal access violates the Keep Washington Working Act, the 2019 state law that prevents state data from being shared with federal authorities for civil immigration purposes
The state also suspended the ability of ICE and CBP to renew tabs for license plates on undercover vehicles. The Trump administration is suing Washington, and other states, over this policy.

name: VTDigger
title: After probe, concerns over Barre City officer’s credibility puts dozens of criminal cases in limbo
text:
The Barre City Police Department. File photo by Mike Dougherty/VTDigger

A county prosecutor has issued a Brady letter against a Barre City police officer accusing him of having sexual relations with a woman he had arrested while that criminal case remained pending.
Orange County State’s Attorney Colin Seaman wrote in a two-page letter issued Friday that his office “has reason to believe” that Barre City Police Officer Matthew Frey “committed acts that create substantial issues pertaining to his credibility as a witness and conduct as a law enforcement officer in any capacity.”
Often termed a “Brady” or “Giglio” letter, the names refer to national court cases. The letters are filed by prosecutors when an officer’s credibility is called into question and can effectively end a law enforcement career because prosecutors may decide to no longer take cases the officer had investigated.
“Based on the information I have right now, I would not feel comfortable calling him as a witness,” Washington County State’s Attorney Michelle Donnelly said of Frey in an interview.
Frey could not be reached Tuesday for comment. 
After the allegations against Frey came to light, Vermont State Police conducted an investigation and turned the case over for review by the Orange County State’s Attorney’s Office, who declined to prosecute, Adam Silverman, a state police spokesperson, said Tuesday.
Seaman wrote in the letter that Frey was the arresting officer of a woman charged with reckless or gross negligent operation of a motor vehicle, cruelty to a child and resisting arrest in May.
“During the pendency of the criminal charges,” Seaman added, “Matthew Frey began a discreet relationship with the defendant primarily using Snapchat media to exchange messages, including requesting and receiving partially nude pictures of the defendant.”
On Sept. 13, the prosecutor wrote, Frey “invited himself” to that woman’s house, “purposefully placed his motor vehicle in a not readily identifiable manner in the driveway, told the defendant she must keep this meeting a secret and had a sexual encounter with the defendant.”
That woman, Seaman wrote, expressed concern in an Oct. 1 complaint to law enforcement that she was “coerced” by Frey.
“The above actions outline a pattern of behavior that exploits a dangerous power imbalance inherent in law enforcement with persons subject to their potential testimony against them in a criminal proceeding,” Seaman wrote. 
“The Defendant in the criminal case is placed in the role of a victim in this investigation,” the prosecutor added. “They were placed in a position of vulnerability potentially fearing retaliation, favorable or less favorable treatment in their criminal case, and disbelief should they come forward with allegations against the law enforcement officer placing them in this position.”
Seaman could not be reached Tuesday for comment.
Donnelly said Tuesday the matter was referred to the Orange County State’s Attorney’s Office to avoid any conflicts since it involved a law enforcement officer in Washington County. 
“We never want to give even the appearance of a conflict of interest,” Donnelly said.
Donnelly said since the letter was issued Friday she has reviewed all the active criminal and family cases in which Frey was involved to determine which cases need to be dismissed or if they can move forward without him as a witness. 
She said an initial review shows about 90 active criminal and family court cases involving Frey. “We are still looking at how many of those are going to be dismissals or refusals,” Donnelly said. 
Donnelly also said after receiving the letter she dismissed the case brought against the woman Frey arrested in May.
Donnelly added that the letter not only raises credibility concerns with Frey. “It shows, I think, an extreme lack of judgment in the way that he treated somebody that he investigated,” the prosecutor said. 
Donnelly said that she agreed with the decision by Seaman to not bring criminal charges in the matter.
“I think that it was a lack of judgment,” Donnelly said of Frey’s actions. She added that while she believed that there were “professional obligations” Frey did not meet, it did not rise to the level of a crime.
Frey is on paid administrative leave, Barre City Police Chief Braedon Vail wrote in an email Tuesday in response to questions from VTDigger. 
Vail said that an administrative investigation is set to begin this week following the criminal investigation and decision by the prosecutor not to bring any charges.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  After probe, concerns over Barre City officer’s credibility puts dozens of criminal cases in limbo.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Commentary: The Constitution is the real key to protecting our elections
text:
Brigitte Romoleroux proudly wears her “I Voted” sticker after voting at the Main Library in Salt Lake City on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 5, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)The Justice Department has struck out again after U.S. District Court Judge David Barlow dismissed a lawsuit against Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson. While Judge Barlow correctly interpreted federal law, it is important for Americans to know that the ruling helps ensure our elections remain fair and secure.
The Trump administration, to its credit, wants to root out election fraud. But you do not do that by just demanding that states hand over sensitive voter data. The best way to fight election fraud is by following the system outlined in our Constitution.
Article I, Section 4 of the U.S. Constitution says that state legislatures shall determine the time, place and manner of elections to federal office. It also empowers Congress to alter some state election laws. In other words, states take the lead in running elections, Congress plays a secondary role as needed, and the president does what Congress tells him or her to do.
Nowhere does this give the executive branch the authority to make demands beyond those authorized by Congress. Nor does it allow for new election policy to be made via executive order or federal regulation, as recent executive orders and federal regulations around vote by mail (also paused by the courts) would do.
Widespread election fraud is prohibitively difficult to perpetrate in the United States because there are plenty of opportunities to catch it. That is the genius of our constitutionally designed system.
We have 50 state-led election systems administered by thousands of local election officials. These local election officials collect ballots and count votes, while state election officials provide oversight, add local vote tallies together and announce results.
Think about it: To perpetrate voter fraud on a scale that could change the outcome of a federal election, fraudsters would have to overcome the safeguards of dozens of election systems, while getting hundreds (perhaps thousands) of state and local election officials in on their schemes. Even in state races or smaller districts, dozens of state and local election officials would need to be in on the plot for election fraud to sway those elections. Persuading that many individuals from different geographies and independent jurisdictions to get on board with that deception is so difficult it is practically impossible.
Look at Utah if you want to see how difficult pulling off something like that would be.
In the Beehive State, a voter’s identity is verified several times, including when they return a ballot. Ballots themselves contain scannable barcodes so they can be tracked. They also have barcodes on the envelope that, once scanned, can determine whether a voter has already voted in that election. If a signature on the ballot doesn’t match, a voter may also be required to provide a driver’s license or the last four digits of their Social Security number to prove their identity.
In addition, machines are audited for accuracy, have many levels of encryption and are not connected to the internet. There is 24/7 surveillance of ballots, ballots must be handled by at least two election workers, ballots are counted in public and voter rolls are regularly checked and updated to remove ineligible voters.
Federal executive orders that centralize election authority in one or a few federal agencies, by contrast, would mean the number of anti-fraud safeguards shrinks from thousands to a relative handful. This would make election fraud easier to commit because only a single federal system needs to be corrupted instead of dozens of individual state systems, and it can be done from the comfort of Washington, D.C. — far from the eyes of the thousands of state and local anti-fraud checkpoints that safeguard election integrity today.
Both political parties have tried to expand the federal government’s involvement in elections in recent years. Those advocating for these policies should ask themselves a question: Do I want the opposing political party to have greater influence over elections when they take power? If the answer is no, that is a good sign that those federal election policy reforms will not accomplish their goals.
Rather than pursuing proposals that make election fraud easier by centralizing election authority in Washington, D.C., we should strengthen election integrity by enacting measures that further uphold and protect state-led, locally administered elections.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Republicans make plea for unity following ‘hurt feelings’ in US Senate contest
text:
The third-annual Freedom Fry in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)MYRTLE BEACH — At a GOP-energizing event where a long list of Republican nominees took the stage to make their pitch, the underlying theme was a plea for unity in the unexpectedly tight U.S. Senate race.
The third annual Freedom Fry, a title that’s a nod to the host — U.S. Rep. Russell Fry — serves as a fundraiser for the 7th District congressman and get-out-the-vote pep rally for the party faithful.
This year’s event, two months after a special GOP primary for a coveted spot on the ballot, took on the additional mission of bringing together Republicans still upset over the whirlwind race to replace the late U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham as the nominee. Less than a month after his funeral, his younger sister, Darline Graham emerged as the winner of a 10-way contest, aided by the endorsement of President Donald Trump.
Republican Rep. Russell Fry speaks at his third-annual Freedom Fry in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)
According to polls, she’s in a close battle with Democrat Annie Andrews for the next six-year term.
That’s at least partly due to intra-party GOP feuding. The son of U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman, who lost to Graham in the runoff Aug. 25, has publicly endorsed Andrews. Norman himself is refusing to help Graham. And some of Norman’s supporters are encouraging voters to write his name on the ballot. Norman indicated on the night he lost that he’s upset Trump ever got involved.
Attorney General Alan Wilson, the GOP nominee for governor, used part of his allotted time Monday night to address the “hurt feelings” and urge Republicans to vote for Graham.
“I’m just going to say it out loud. It’s the unspoken truth. But here’s the reality we have: this is the only option,” Wilson said after campaigning with Graham elsewhere in Myrtle Beach.
He was addressing about 400 people who paid at least $50 a ticket to hear from candidates at the Hilton Myrtle Beach Resort and eat from the “fry bar.”
“Here’s the thing: Not voting for Darline Graham or voting for Annie Andrews and standing on that election” could put Democrats in control of the U.S. Senate, he said. “You may not intend for that to be the case, but I’m telling you folks,” he continued, that’s “so much greater than the petty differences that we squabble about in our primaries.”
Over the course of two hours, Republicans who took the stage included South Carolina’s GOP nominees for statewide and congressional offices, as well as Texas Sen. Ted Cruz and Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan, chairman of the House Judiciary Committee.
Fry, the primary’s third-place finisher, also spent part of his time to talk up Graham.
“The mission is more important than the personalities, and that’s why everybody needs to get out there and support Darline Graham,” said Fry, who faces Democrat John Vincent on the ballot.
Fry was widely expected to seek the nomination before Trump encouraged Graham to run.
Rumblings over what would happen if Fry ran and won — making him the GOP nominee for both U.S. Senate and the 7th Congressional District — led to the state Election Commission issuing a statement making clear that it is legal in South Carolina for candidates to run for multiple offices simultaneously. Next steps were being discussed: A legislator in the state House was publicly considering running to replace Fry in the U.S. House.
Ultimately, Fry and Norman, who was coming off an unsuccessful run for governor, announced their bids for U.S. Senate after Trump stunned the field by encouraging Graham to run.
After losing, Fry endorsed Graham ahead of the runoff and has appeared with her on stage since, to include introducing her at his event.
U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas speaks at the third annual Freedom Fry in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)
At the Freedom Fry, Cruz applauded Fry for quickly backing her.
“You ran against Darline in a vigorous contest. You didn’t prevail. And you know what? It would be easy to take your ball and go home, and it would be easy to get mad,” said the Texas senator, who’s considered a potential 2028 presidential contender. “You didn’t do that. … We all need to all unify.”
Earlier Monday, the Republican National Committee announced that Trump will return Thursday to rally in South Carolina for the second time in two weeks — this time in Norman’s hometown of Rock Hill.
Fry urged Norman, who did not attend the Freedom Fry, to “step into the sunlight a little bit to help his Republican nominee.”
“As somebody who carried the conservative banner as long as he has, he should step into the arena,” Fry told reporters, referring to the congressman first elected to the state House in 2006. “He didn’t win. I didn’t win either.”
But Norman doubled down on his refusal, telling CNN after the event that the election is “about attempts to ‘force’ a candidate on the voters.”
As he did in a radio interview last week, Norman again suggested the race against Andrews wouldn’t be tight if he’d won the nomination.
“Regardless of the outcome, it didn’t have to be this way as the great people living in South Carolina deserve ‘better!’ Bottom line!! Elections have consequences!!” he wrote in a text to the reporter. As for his son’s op-ed, he wrote, “Warren is EXACTLY RIGHT in his statement!!! My entire family is NOT SUPPORTING her candidacy.”
Norman’s tenure in Congress ends in January, since he chose to run for governor instead of re-election. He placed third in the June primary.
State Sen. Wes Climer, who faces Democrat Mallory Dittmer on the ballot, was among speakers at the Freedom Fry.
Without directly addressing the GOP feuding, he urged attendees to go vote and take friends with them.
“I know that y’all know some friends from church, from work, from the neighborhoods, some good lifelong Republicans who might get a little extra motivation this year,” said Climer, who also lives in Rock Hill. “Right, so just remind them, elections are about choices, and elections have consequences.”
Attorney General Alan Wilson, the GOP nominee for governor, speaks at the third annual Freedom Fry in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)
State GOP Chair Drew McKissick acknowledged the party division as due to the special primary but attributed it to the later-than-normal contest: August instead of June. He indicated there’s still time to unify.
“You have a time span after a primary is over, working to put everything back together again and getting everybody on board and so forth,” he told the SC Daily Gazette. “So we’re in the process of that, and it’s been coming along.”
Trump’s repeated rallies in South Carolina ahead of the general election are unprecedented.
McKissick indicated he’s not worried, despite the polls showing Republicans in trouble in traditional Republican strongholds. Other states Trump’s visiting this week alone include Texas, Ohio, Florida, Kansas and Iowa. Last week, his stops included North Carolina, Iowa and Georgia.
“You are always happy to have the time of the campaigner in chief,” McKissick said. “If he thinks he’s got extra time to come in and make a swing, fine. That helps everybody up and down the team.”
Early voting runs through Saturday. Election Day is Nov. 3.

HATTIESBURG — Southern Miss on Tuesday announced a plan to renovate the 42-year-old home of its nationally renowned baseball program, the only Division I program in the U.S. to boast 10 straight 40-victory seasons and 10 straight NCAA Tournament bids.
The school plans to raise approximately $25 million through private and corporate funding to complete a renovation and expansion of Pete Taylor Park/Hill Denson Field.
“Pete Taylor Park represents so much of what makes Southern Miss baseball special,” said Southern Miss Director of Athletics Jeremy McClain. “The history, the atmosphere and, most importantly, our fans have created an environment unlike any other. This project allows us to honor those traditions while making a significant investment in what comes next for our program.”
Jackson-based Weir Boerner Allin Architecture, which has designed numerous athletic facilities across the South including Dudy Noble Field at Mississippi State, partnered with Southern Miss to do master planning for the project. Seating capacity would increase to approximately 6,500. The largest crowd to date was 6,346, which included more than  2,000 standing room only. Southern Miss has sold out its season tickets of approximately 4,600 tickets for four straight seasons.
A planned renovation of Pete Taylor Park at Southern Miss would include this seating down the first base line. Credit: Courtesy of Southern Miss Athletics
The proposed stadium renovation would include all chairback seating and the addition of eight more luxury suites to the existing 12. Said McClain, “We wish we had room for 20 more suites because we could sell that many more.”
The master plan includes an indoor pitching laboratory and hitting facility with  high-tech sports science equipment to improve performance. Southern Miss coach Chrisian Ostrander, who has guided the Golden Eagles to 143 victories over three seasons called the proposed performance center “a game changer for player development, the backbone our our program.”
Southern Miss is calling the baseball stadium project “Where Tradition Meets Tomorrow, ” McClain said.
“The vision is not to change what makes The Pete special. It is to build around it,” he said. “We want our longtime fans to walk into the renovated ballpark and still feel everything they love about Southern Miss baseball, while the next generation of Golden Eagles experience a facility built for the future.”
McClain said he is confident Southern Miss can raise the money.
“We’ve had several preliminary meetings with potential donors,” he said. “We’ve confident we can get to the finish line soon and move forward with the project. Our baseball program is nationally competitive and we want to continue to invest in its future.”
Fund-raising will include naming rights to the performance center, as well as different enhanced seating areas in the ballpark, McClain said. Already this year, Renasant Bank bought the naming rights to the former M.M. Roberts Stadium in a deal that will pay the university $13.7 million over 10 years.

name: Nevada Current
title: Conservation group sues feds for failing to protect rare Nevada toad and fish
text:
Amargosa toad, Oasis Valley speckled dace. (Photos: Center for Biological Diversity, Bureau of Land Management)A conservation group sued the federal government Tuesday for failing to make a timely decision on whether to list a rare Nevada toad and fish as endangered or threatened species.
The Center for Biological Diversity sued the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Tuesday for allegedly violating the Endangered Species Act after federal wildlife managers failed to issue a 12-month finding on whether to list the Amargosa toad and the Oasis Valley speckled dace, as required by federal law.
Last year, a review by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service found there was substantial evidence that both the toad and fish may be eligible for listing, after the Center filed petitions to protect both species under the Endangered Species Act. But the agency missed the legally required deadline to issue a final decision on whether to protect the toads and fish.
The Amargosa toad and Oasis Valley speckled dace live in spring-fed habitats along the Amargosa River in Oasis Valley near Beatty in Nye County. The Amargosa toad is only found along a 14 mile stretch of the Amargosa River, with a population estimated at about 2,000 individuals.
The area has also attracted gold mining company AngloGold Ashanti, which has proposed several potential mines in the area.
“The Amargosa toad and Oasis Valley speckled dace are at the center of a bullseye surrounded by gold mining activity that threatens to push them over the edge to extinction,” said Patrick Donnelly, Great Basin director at the Center for Biological Diversity. “Endangered Species Act protections are urgently needed for these species before AngloGold’s mines suck dry the water they need for survival.”
According to the petitions, both the rare toad and fish are threatened with extinction due to groundwater pumping from seven proposed gold mining operations along the Amargosa. Six of those projects are being proposed by British multinational miner AngloGold Ashanti, including what is potentially the largest greenfield gold discovery in Nevada in more than a decade.
AngloGold Ashanti has claimed their Arthur Gold Deposit could contain about 16 million ounces of gold resources, nearly five times as much gold as Nevada produces annually.
AngloGold Ashanti’s North Bullfrog Project, which is currently in the permitting phase, is about nine miles north of the Town of Beatty. The project would span about 5,400 acres of public lands and would withdraw up to 2,500 acre-feet of water per year from Oasis Valley, perhaps enough to serve about 7,500 homes.
The conservation group said “the combined groundwater drawdown from these projects could substantially reduce flows or dry up springs along the Amargosa River that the toads and fish depend on for survival.”
“The Amargosa River is a crown jewel of the Mojave Desert, and we shouldn’t sacrifice it for gold mining,” said Donnelly. “The Amargosa toad and Oasis Valley speckled dace are emblems of Nevada’s remarkable biodiversity. We won’t rest until they get the protections they urgently need and deserve.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: With 1 week until Election Day, Montana absentee votes exceed 225,000
text:
A sign noting where to vote by precinct is on display at the Helena Civic Center during a primary vote on Tuesday, June 2, 2026 in Helena, Montana. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)One week from Election Day, more than 209,000 Montanans have already cast their ballot this midterm. 
The Montana Secretary of State’s office sent out just under 525,000 absentee ballots to registered voters in October and as of Tuesday afternoon, 225,698 have been returned — roughly 43%.  
That number is tracking well ahead of the 2022 midterm election, when the state reported 284,000 absentee ballots were received by the day before Election Day. 
Montana’s electorate has grown every year since 2002, but saw a jump in registered voters in recent years following a surge of in-migration after the COVID-19 pandemic. Montana has roughly 5% more registered voters in the state compared to the 2022 midterm, with the Secretary of State’s Office reporting 805,418 registered voters as of Tuesday.
But overall voter turnout in 2022 was also historically low by Montana standards. Less than 500,000 voters cast ballots, the lowest number of midterm votes since 2004, according to data from the secretary of state. 
Current absentee votes received by Tuesday exceed 48% of the total votes cast in 2022. 
Compared to the 2018 midterm election, during President Donald Trump’s first term in office, absentee ballots returned so far amount to 44% of total votes cast in 2018. 
Sheridan County leads with the highest percentage of absentee ballots with 51% of absentee ballots returned, followed by Lewis and Clark and Fergus counties at 48%. 
Missoula County leads among the state’s most populous counties with 47% of ballots returned. 
Roosevelt, Lincoln, Big Horn and Glacier counties have returned the lowest percentage of absentee ballots, with less than 33% returned to the state. 
Montana doesn’t require voters to register with a party affiliation, so early returns don’t offer much in the way of specific data points for contested partisan races. But nationwide in many states that do have party registration, Democratic voters lead in early returns. 
Absentee ballots must be received by 8 p.m. on Election Day, Nov. 3.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Former teacher fights license suspension over alleged incident with student
text:
A former Davenport elementary school teacher is suing the Iowa Board of Educational Examiners over its move to suspend his teaching license due to allegations of inappropriate contact with a former student. (Stock photo via Getty Images)A former Davenport elementary school teacher is contesting the state’s efforts to suspend his teaching license due to allegations of inappropriate contact with a former student.
Julian Lira is taking the Iowa Board of Educational Examiners to court and seeking judicial review of the board’s recent decision to suspend his teaching license for three years.
In his lawsuit, filed in Polk County District Court, Lira is appealing the board’s Sept. 24, 2026, final order in his disciplinary case. Lira alleges that before the matter was turned over to the board for final action, an administrative law judge on June 30, 2025, issued a proposed decision for the board to consider.
According to the lawsuit, the judge’s proposed decision included a finding that Lira had “briefly touched (a former student’s) chest” at a wedding reception and described this as a “brief, inappropriate interaction.” The lawsuit asserts the judge concluded that a public letter of reprimand was the appropriate sanction in the case.
The judge’s proposed decision was then forwarded to the board, which issued a final order that, according to the lawsuit, “expressly deleted the last three sentences” of the judge’s proposed decision, all of which were related to the seriousness of offense and the appropriateness of a public reprimand.
The board retained the judge’s finding that “Lira had an inappropriate interaction with a former student at a wedding reception,” and then opted to impose a three-year license suspension, the lawsuit claims.
In addition, the lawsuit asserts, the board imposed additional conditions on Lira’s potential license reinstatement, calling for consultation with a doctor for a psychosexual evaluation, as well as a mental health evaluation and possible counseling or treatment.
According to the lawsuit, the board identified “no additional aggravating factual findings” to justify the enhanced penalty it favored, and the board supplied no explanation for not agreeing with the judge’s proposed sanction in the case.
Lira is asking the court to reverse the board’s final decision and dismiss the disciplinary complaint against him. In the alternative, Lira argues, the court should vacate the board’s decision and remand the matter back to the board for a new hearing before a different administrative law judge.
The State of Iowa, which does not comment on pending litigation, has yet to file a response to the lawsuit.
The disciplinary case appears to stem from allegations that surfaced in late 2023, when WHBF TV reported that Lira had been arrested and charged with misdemeanor lascivious conduct with a minor while the two were guests at a wedding reception on Oct. 7, 2023.
Prosecutors later dropped the criminal charge, saying they could not show Lira — who had briefly served as the alleged victim’s teacher in the third and sixth grade — was in a position of authority over the victim at the time of the alleged incident.
Court records indicate that earlier, in 2019, Lira was criminally charged with sexually abusing a young girl who was a relative of his at the time. A jury subsequently found Lira not guilty of sexual abuse in the second degree, court records show.
