name: Mississippi Today
title: Watch: How the fatal Senatobia shooting unfolded in 25 seconds
authors: Julie Lee, Sarah Whites-Koditschek, and Mukta Joshi
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Julie Lee is a data reporter at Mississippi Today. Sarah Whites-Koditschek and Mukta Joshi are investigative reporters at Mississippi Today spending a year as New York Times Local Investigations fellows. They report for the Deep South Today Investigative Reporting Center in collaboration with The New York Times.
Reporters for Mississippi Today closely examined video footage and broke down key moments of the police confrontation that ended with the fatal shooting of 1-year-old Kohen Wiley in a Walmart parking lot this summer.
The frame-by-frame review shows how a tip that two women were running out of the store escalated in a matter of seconds, with five officers surrounding their car, guns raised. The video analysis also catalogs the moments cited by several experts who said the police unnecessarily escalated the encounter and put themselves in harm’s way.
The Mississippi attorney general, Lynn Fitch, announced last week that the state would not pursue criminal charges against Hunter Foster, the Senatobia police officer who shot Kohen. The toddler was sitting on his mother’s lap as a second woman drove. Foster fired at the car as it drove in the direction of two officers, and Fitch ruled his actions were justified. 
That decision came after a state investigation that relied heavily on the video shown here.
The footage begins just after 2 p.m. on June 14, inside a small room with video monitors near the store entrance. A Walmart employee steps in, interrupting police officers who are discussing an unrelated incident.

Outside, the two women, one of whom is carrying Kohen, run toward a gray sedan in the parking lot, Walmart surveillance footage shows. Latoya Ferrell, carrying a box of diapers, gets in to drive. Kohen’s mother, Vellesiya Wiley, climbs into the passenger seat with her son. 
It is unclear if the officers knew who the women were or why they were running. No one in the video accuses the women of a crime, hints at why they are running or mentions a child. 
An incident report that Senatobia officers filed later said baby clothes and a large box of Pampers Easy Ups diapers were stolen. The report says the diapers were “under rang,” a term for when an item is skipped at self-checkout or a cheaper item is scanned instead. Neither woman has been charged.
As the officers run toward the car, it backs out of its parking spot. They shout, “Stop!” 
The first person to draw a gun is a deputy from the Tate County Sheriff’s Office. He points it at the ground and holsters it almost immediately as the car continues to reverse. Meanwhile, Foster draws his gun. He is the first officer to aim at the car, 20 seconds after the Walmart employee alerted the officers.

Jeremy Bauer, a forensic reconstruction expert who reviewed body-worn camera footage from Foster and two other officers, said the car was still backing up when Foster pointed his gun at it.
Russ Hicks, a retired law enforcement officer and instructor from Washington, said, “What concerns me is taking out the gun so quickly on this kind of a case.” Hicks consults with police departments on use of force and de-escalation techniques.
As the driver backs out of her parking space, she hits an SUV, momentarily coming to a stop. The officers close in around the car, continuing to yell, “Stop,” and drawing their weapons. By the time the car accelerates forward, all five officers have drawn their guns.

The car accelerates toward Foster and a sheriff’s deputy. The front wheel appears to turn left, away from Foster. As the car’s bumper approaches Foster’s leg, he fires one shot at the windshield, about 25 seconds after the Walmart employee ran in. He fires at least two more shots into the side window. 
An analysis of body-worn camera footage indicated the audio was at times mismatched to the video by fractions of seconds. The analysis indicated that Foster’s video had a larger lag, though still less than one-third of a second. For that reason, Mississippi Today muted the footage from his camera.

According to Bauer, the forensic reconstruction expert, Foster fires the first shot when his right leg is in front of the bumper and his left leg is beside the car. 
Bauer said it was hard to tell if Foster was grazed by the car. He noted that Foster’s balance was not disrupted and said there was “no definitive evidence of an impact.”

It is unclear in the videos whether any of the other officers who were close to the car were hit, Bauer said. He saw no evidence of possible contact with the other officers beyond one officer who braced his hand on the hood of the car. 
Veronica Roberson, Kohen’s grandmother, said Mississippi Bureau of Investigation officials told her when she viewed the footage that one officer — not Foster — was struck by the car. She said she was told that the officer who was struck was a sheriff’s deputy who was standing in front of the car. 
Walmart surveillance video seems to show him jumping out of the way in time. But the Walmart camera was recording at a lower frame rate than body-camera footage, so it is difficult to determine whether it accurately captured his movement. Other camera angles appear to show the car veer closer to him, and the deputy can be seen lifting his leg and bracing his hand against the car.

The videos released Thursday are a portion of the camera footage collected by state investigators, though they appear to capture the critical moments around the time of the shooting.
Leaked footage published by Darkhorse Press, a Mississippi news outlet, on Oct. 20 included a clip of Foster and another officer talking outside the hospital where Kohen was pronounced dead. In that video, which starts about 20 minutes after the shooting, Foster asks whether the 1-year-old had been hit, saying, “I didn’t even see a baby in her lap,” adding an expletive. That clip was not included in the footage released by the state Thursday. 
Foster was placed on administrative leave by the Senatobia Board of Aldermen on June 16, two days after the incident. He resigned last Wednesday.

name: WyoFile
title: Teton County sheriff’s candidate calls suspension ‘political,’ keeps campaigning
text:
KHOL 89.1 Jackson Hole Community Radio produced this story with editing support from WyoFile.
Teton County Sheriff Deputy Eric Snow is still campaigning for sheriff and bashing the office that suspended him, which he aims to lead.  
Snow’s comments come a week before the election and a week after his suspension for reasons that remain guarded by the sheriff’s office. Snow said he’s being disciplined for “failure to act” during an arrest last week. 
His suspension follows two highly scrutinized DUI arrests. In the first, Snow charged a Jackson man with a DUI and jailed him despite what the Teton County Sheriff’s Office said was a lack of evidence. In the second, he did not charge a DUI despite a field test indicating intoxication. 
In his first interview since being put on leave, the Republican candidate called his suspension a “no-win situation.” Snow denounced the decision by Lt. Mark Priest as retaliation for challenging their boss, Teton County Sheriff Matt Carr, a Democrat seeking his third term as sheriff.
Snow also defended his arrest track record and claimed Carr has turned the office into a “political instrument.” 
Carr said he had no role in putting Snow on leave and denied allegations that he weaponized the office. In the three-way race, which also includes independent Chris Glenn, Carr has also faced scrutiny for offering a job to his one-time primary opponent, a former Jackson police officer, during the election. 
Carr did, however, say that at least two of Snow’s recent arrests “reflect a pattern of behavior that’s very concerning, that is not reflective of the type of law enforcement we want in our community.” 
Carr said that he would release Snow’s personnel file, which would include any past department reviews, only if Snow first agreed to that.  
Snow declined to do so and told KHOL that, “Cops are afforded some level of privacy.” 
Mark Jackowski, Snow’s attorney, said he reviewed what was represented by the sheriff’s office to constitute Snow’s personnel file and was unable to ascertain any “pattern of behavior” and that the suspension “smacks of retaliation.” 
“I will not be surprised if this matter ends up being litigated,” Jackowski said. “While the sheriff was able to rid himself of a Democrat primary opponent by offering him a job, he couldn’t do that with respect to Snow.” 
Teton County Sheriff’s Deputy Eric Snow said he was dismissed for “failure to act” during an arrest, a point he disputes.  (Evan Robinson-Johnson/KHOL)
Why is Snow on leave? 
The sheriff’s and county attorney’s offices have declined to confirm or provide his suspension letter, citing personnel policy. A pending records request filed by KHOL for all records relating to Snow’s suspension has been received by the county clerk’s office.  
In a press release, Snow states that he was cited for a policy called “fail to act” related to an arrest he made early on Oct. 21. Court records show he pulled over a Driggs, Idaho, woman for speeding and, after being told she was on release for a June DUI, administered a portable breath test, which showed her blood alcohol level to be more than twice the legal limit. 
Despite that result, Snow did not conduct a DUI investigation. That would have included a field test investigating signs of intoxication, such as a field sobriety test. Snow said that omission led to his suspension. 
“I know I’m under the microscope,” Snow said. “So, I chose the path that had the strongest legal foundation to support the arrest.”
Snow instead charged the Idaho woman for violating her previous DUI release order. A defense attorney, he said, could “not argue with a release order violation. You can argue with the DUI.” 
Carr declined to comment on how he viewed the case, but said his office is treating Snow as it would any deputy. Lt. Mark Priest, second-in-command at the sheriff’s office, put Snow on leave.
“Every single arrest that our deputies make, every report they write, everything they do, we look at it. We look at everything. We’re not just picking out Eric’s,” Priest told KHOL. 
Snow felt his actions have been under more scrutiny since a July arrest he made, he told KHOL. The sheriff’s office referred that arrest to the state for an independent evaluation. The Wyoming Division of Criminal Investigation, in turn, advised elevating the case to the FBI, which determined it did not meet the threshold for a civil rights violation, the sheriff’s office said. 
Snow stands by the arrest of a Jackson man, whom he charged with speeding and arrested on suspicion of drug-impaired driving, he said. 
“[If] you’ve got somebody who’s demonstrating impairment, getting them off the road is the right choice,” Snow said. Jackowski added that the evidence of impairment dissipates over time. 
A field breath test and evaluation by a drug recognition expert found no evidence of impairment. Snow said the sheriff’s office declined his request to test the man’s blood for drugs beyond what the state typically looks into. Carr said the blood is preserved and had been tested for “everything in the world.” Snow declined to state which other drugs he wanted to test for.
Snow’s expertise called into question 
In his press release, Snow claims that Priest tried to have him “decertified” as a drug recognition expert after Snow ran advertisements highlighting the credentials. 
But a phone recording requested by KHOL and provided by the county shows a more complicated request related to Snow’s July arrest. 
In a recording from Sept. 21, months after the first DUI arrest, Priest talked to Lt. Evan Storch for about eight minutes. Storch, who is with the Laramie County Sheriff’s Office, runs the state’s drug recognition expert training. Storch trained Snow.
In the recording, Priest asks Storch to advise Snow to pause conducting DRE evaluations, not outright revoke his ability to do so, until the end of the election or until the Jackson man’s case “clears up.” 
Defense attorneys had “latched onto” a newspaper article covering questions about Snow’s July arrest, Priest said, and at least one party had chosen to exclude Snow’s testimony from a pending case.
“His supervisors immediately noticed it was not a good arrest. There was not any probable cause there,” Priest told Storch in the recorded call. “I’m trying to avoid making him look bad.”  
In response, Storch told Priest he wouldn’t decertify Snow without having “definitive details” but that he would give Snow “some advice about how to proceed.” 
Reached by phone, Storch told KHOL that he was surprised to be asked to intervene with Snow’s capacities “so close to the election.” He said “nothing” in Snow’s July case “would give me pause to decertify Snow.” He declined further comment. 
In the recorded call, Priest acknowledged that the request was a “very slippery slope” during the election season. 
Many sheriff’s deputies appear to back Carr 
In his interview with KHOL, Snow accused Carr of violating a Wyoming law that prohibits a public official or employee from using “public funds, time, personnel, facilities or equipment for political or campaign activity.” 
Snow claims that has happened several times, including at a GOP-sponsored sheriff’s debate on Oct. 5 where more than a dozen officers stood and sat in the back of the library auditorium. Dressed in uniform, the officers clapped intermittently after the two-term incumbent spoke. GOP moderators asked them to hold their applause, though some later continued.
About 14 sheriff’s deputies line the back wall in the Teton County Library auditorium during a candidate forum hosted by the Teton County GOP. (Sophia Boyd-Fliegel/KHOL)
“What you witnessed at the Republican debate was a crime on the part of the sheriff,” Snow said. “By him asking everyone to be there, that’s misuse of office.”
Carr said he didn’t ask deputies to attend. 
“I was [as] surprised as anyone,” Carr said. 
Snow said on-duty deputies should not have attended the forum. 
“If you’re getting paid by the taxpayer, you shouldn’t be going to a political event,” Snow said. 
Lt. Priest confirmed deputies were not asked to attend, adding that he himself is a Republican, who grew up in Wyoming. 
“Everybody wanted to be there,” Priest said.

name: VTDigger
title: Pownal will consider a 5-year permitting pause on data center facilities
text:
Some in the Pownal area are concerned the former Green Mountain Race Track site is being eyed for a data center. The selectboard is considering a moratorium on such projects. File photo by Holly Pelczynski/Bennington Banner

This story by Jim Therrien was first published in the Bennington Banner on Oct. 26, 2026.
POWNAL — The Pownal Select Board is considering a town moratorium on data center facilities amid concerns the former Green Mountain Race Track site is being eyed for a center.
Other towns in Vermont and around the country have enacted or discussed moratoriums for such centers — especially the large-scale facilities associated with artificial intelligence development, which would create a significant new demand for electricity and water for cooling purposes.
The 144-acre former track site off Route 7 near the Williamstown, Massachusetts, line is located along the Hoosic River and believed to have significant groundwater supplies. The property has been for sale, and rumors have surfaced about a possible purchase by an unidentified party, town officials have said.
Five-year pause
Board member Jeannie Alexander noted the data center rumors during an Oct. 22 meeting, and the fact that other communities in Vermont have enacted or proposed data center permitting moratoriums.
She said that after researching data center issues, she has concerns that an outright ban on the centers “might not be legally binding,” adding, “I think a moratorium is probably the way to go.”
Alexander then suggested wording for a five-year moratorium — to be considered by the board and by Pownal residents during a future board meeting.
A moratorium, she said, would give the town time to enact zoning or other regulation aimed at controlling the impacts of a large data center facility.
‘Irresponsible to wait’
Alexander said Monday in an email, “It is my understanding that a number of developers have been interested in that site in particular. It would be foolish and irresponsible to wait until after the fact to try and protect our town’s natural resources.”
She added, “It’s obvious that the powers that be in Montpelier aren’t coming to save us or any other small town in Vermont, and so we had better be prepared to take care of ourselves and our neighbors. There are significant issues with water quality in Pownal, and energy bills are already too high. We must begin taking seriously the impact that today’s decisions will have on our great-grandchildren.”
She said she supports responsible and sustainable growth, adding that the proposed moratorium “would require the Conservation Commission and the Planning Commission to work together to determine what sort of potential development we could work to attract. Moratoriums on (large power- and water-using) data centers are one of the only issues folks on the left and right are in agreement over. If some tech billionaire wants to make more money off of data centers, they can damn well do it somewhere else. Not Pownal.”
Lawmakers supportive
On the state level, Sen. Seth Bongartz, D-Bennington District, and Rep. Jonathan Cooper, D-Pownal, agreed that the town is right to try to protect its interests.
A bill to regulate large data centers “sailed through both chambers on its way to the governor, because it was designed to protect towns like Pownal from situations like this,” Cooper said Monday in an email. “The bill (H.727) had remarkably broad support: It was unanimously passed out of a committee with five Democrats, three Republicans, and one independent. It was subject to just one roll call vote on its way to the governor, and that was 26-3 in favor of the bill.” 
He added, “I applaud the town select board for listening to its residents, but I worry that in the absence of state law the town will not be able to rely on services of the Attorney General’s office if there is a challenge to the moratorium.”
The Legislature will return to this topic in the next session, Cooper said, adding, “What little opposition the bill actually garnered while it was in the Legislature tended to focus on the unlikelihood of the state needing such regulation, and the adequacy of our existing framework to manage this new phenomenon. I don’t think too many Vermonters are taking great comfort in that line of thinking.”
‘A balanced bill’
Bongartz said in an email: “We passed a balanced data center bill this past session. It controlled water usage and noise. It also required that any center be deemed to be in the public interest, either via building new transmission capacity and/or lowering rates for other users.”
He added, “For reasons that are unfathomable to me, (Gov. Scott) vetoed that bill and left us exposed to an application for a data center with no guardrails in place. His explanation made no sense.”
Scott has contended that Vermont already has strong environmental and other regulations in place to consider applications for permits for data centers.
Bongartz said, however, that the Pownal board “is right to be concerned. A moratorium makes sense until we can get a comprehensive bill regulating the environmental and social impacts of data centers through the Legislature and signed by the governor.”
Last year’s final bill version “will likely get reintroduced,” he said. “It will then likely get amended to some degree as it works its way through the committee process. I do not see it getting weaker. People want to be protected.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Key accountability index for CT schools ticked up last year
text:
Connecticut’s Next Generation Accountability Index for public schools showed modest improvement across most categories in the 2025-26 school year, the State Department of Education said Tuesday.
The index combines 12 factors, including test scores and chronic absenteeism, to produce one number representing the performance of Connecticut schools. For the 2025-26 school year, the statewide index came out to 72.2, a slight improvement over the previous year’s 71.8 but below its pre-pandemic 2018-19 score of 74.2.
Among the highlights were the 4-year graduation rate, which reached 91.2%, and the proportion of students demonstrating postsecondary readiness, which reached 49.9%. Both numbers were the highest for their respective categories since the index was introduced for the 2014-15 school year.
CSDE opted to focus on the latter measure during its press conference. 
According to Chief Performance Officer Ajit Gopalakrishnan, postsecondary readiness has been rising thanks to recent state investments in dual credit courses. Connecticut used some of its federal COVID relief funding to expand those courses, and the General Assembly recently gave the program a line item in the state budget, allowing it to continue after federal dollars dried up.
However, Gopalakrishnan said the program needs further investment from the General Assembly to meet demand. His comment drew a laugh from Education Committee Ranking Member Rep. Lezlye Zupkus, R-Prospect, who was also in attendance.
Education Commissioner Charlene Russell-Tucker said CSDE is still determining just how much additional funding it needs for the dual credit programming.
In the 2025-26 school year, 34.6% of 11th and 12th graders earned three or more college credits through dual credit courses. That’s a more-than 12% increase over what it was during the pandemic.
“It’s not a promise of a credit. It’s actual college credit that goes on a transcript,” Gopalakrishnan said.
At the press conference to highlight the impact of dual credit programming were two high school students, Bena Mejia Romero of Stratford and Evan Gaudio of Wallingford.
Romero, who immigrated with her family from Honduras when she was six, said the dual credit courses she’s taken in medicine have encouraged her to explore becoming a nurse practitioner or doctor.
“I feel more prepared to take on that next step because I’ve begun exploring the field,” Romero said.
Gaudio said he learned how to use CAD software in his dual credit coursework to design a load-bearing structure and a 3D-printed car. He said the class taught him how to work on a timeline and was a “phenomenal confidence booster.”

Students also meet the postsecondary readiness threshold if they meet certain benchmarks on ACT, SAT, AP or IB tests. Postsecondary readiness among high needs students has risen 8.9% since the pandemic. Among Hispanic and Latino students, it has risen 10.2%, and among Black students, it has risen 12.2%.
Chris Todd, executive director of the Office of Early College Programs at the University of Connecticut, said last year, 43% of dual credit students at UConn identified as first generation, and 41% received fee waivers to attend at no cost.
One key use of the accountability index for CSDE is to identify schools that need additional support. If schools score particularly poorly, the state offers them administrative support from the department’s turnaround office, and they also become eligible for additional funding through Title I. 
This year, the state identified 72 schools for this enhanced support. Those include nine from Bridgeport and 15 from Hartford — both districts that have been the subject of state intervention regarding their finances. New Haven, which has also reported severe funding challenges, has eight schools on the list.
Although most factors on the accountability index improved, growth in Math and English Language Arts moved in the opposite direction. According to Gopalakrishnan, growth measures how much individual students’ test scores improve from one year to the next. A lower growth number on the accountability index means those scores didn’t rise quite as quickly as they did the previous year.
CT Mirror reporter Sasha Allen contributed to this story.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Commentary: Water pipeline discussion is about choosing our future, or letting scarcity choose it for us
text:
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers' Omaha District Oahe Project hydropower house on the Missouri River near Fort Pierre is pictured on July 16, 2025. (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers photo by Delanie Stafford)Imagine if Lake Oahe were filled with oil instead of water.
We would treat it as one of the country’s greatest economic assets. Pipelines would be flowing. Industries would be built around it. The cost of moving oil west would be a budget line item.
Water deserves the same kind of thinking. The difference is that we see the price of gasoline every time we stand at the pump, while generations of public investment have masked much of the true cost of water by the time it pours from a kitchen faucet.
Most of us barely notice the water portion of the monthly utility bill. Yet we will pay about $1.50 for a 20-ounce bottle, the equivalent of nearly $10 a gallon.
That is why we should look differently at the Western Dakota Regional Water System’s proposed pipeline. The latest published estimate is about $4.5 billion to move Missouri River water roughly 165 miles west through a massive pipeline and major pumping facilities.
Will South Dakota be ready when other states come for our water?

The conversation is about to become more visible. The system plans to begin a public campaign in January to build awareness of the project. Before the debate centers on the $4.5 billion price tag, we should ask a more basic question: What is the water worth?
The system secured a future-use permit for 20,765 acre-feet of Missouri River water annually, the equivalent of about 18.5 million gallons a day based on projected needs through 2080. Spread $4.5 billion of construction cost across 50 years at that volume, and the simple capital cost comes to roughly 1.3 cents per gallon before financing, treatment, pumping and operating expenses.
A penny or two a gallon does not make a $4.5 billion project cheap. It does make the number look different.
To decide whether it is worth doing, we must also ask what the water would make possible and what happens without it.
Generations of public investment made dependable water affordable. In the process, we forgot what scarcity costs.
The Lewis & Clark Regional Water System offers a useful reminder. It took decades and hundreds of millions of dollars to build and now serves roughly 350,000 people in South Dakota, Iowa and Minnesota. Its system is designed to deliver about 44 million gallons a day, more than twice the capacity proposed for Western Dakota.
Imagine southeastern South Dakota without the Lewis & Clark system. Growth would have been harder, more expensive and increasingly constrained by local water supplies.
The Western Dakota proposal did not emerge from a wish list. A 2019 South Dakota School of Mines study found that existing supplies could meet demand during average years but become less reliable during prolonged drought.
The pressure is easiest to see around Rapid City, Box Elder and Ellsworth Air Force Base.



Quotation







Generations of public investment made dependable water affordable. In the process, we forgot what scarcity costs.


Pactola Reservoir, high in the Black Hills, remains under drought pressure. Rapid City moved it to alert status and extended water restrictions year-round as inflows fell well below normal. The Bureau of Reclamation cut winter releases from Pactola in half to conserve water.
Pactola’s managers are doing what reservoir managers are supposed to do: storing water from wetter years for use during dry ones.
Then add growth.
Not everyone in the Black Hills wants more of it. A new regional water supply would make more development possible.
But the demand projections behind the pipeline are based largely on population and water-use trends planners already expect. Without another supply, growth may slow, become more expensive or go elsewhere. Infrastructure is expensive. Scarcity is expensive, too. The pipeline would not create growth so much as remove water as a limit.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Rapid City is already growing, and Ellsworth’s impending B-21 mission is adding to population, housing and infrastructure demand.
Ellsworth has also shown how expensive it can be to lose water you already have. The Air Force is spending roughly $12.5 million on a water system to restore dependable service to residents whose private wells were affected by PFAS contamination while providing additional system capacity. Federal documents estimate the contamination plume extends approximately 25 miles south-southeast along Boxelder Creek toward the Cheyenne River.
Water is remarkably inexpensive until the water you already have is no longer usable.
That brings us back to $4.5 billion.
If this were oil, we would understand the investment almost instinctively. Missouri River water is one of South Dakota’s great assets, and using a portion of it for western South Dakota’s future should not be dismissed simply because getting it there is expensive.
The question is not whether $4.5 billion is a lot of money. Of course it is.
The question is what South Dakota wants the future of western South Dakota to look like, and whether we choose that future while we still have options or allow water scarcity to choose it for us.
Water has a way of settling arguments. Eventually.

name: WyoFile
title: Judge declines to hold Laramie County Sheriff Kozak in contempt, but sets deadline for records dispute
text:
A judge denied Monday a request to hold Laramie County Sheriff Brian Kozak in contempt of court in a lawsuit concerning immigration arrest records.  
While acknowledging that Kozak and his counsel, Laramie County Attorney Mark Voss, didn’t fully comply with a court order requiring them to produce immigration arrest records, Laramie County Judge Robin Cooley wrote in her decision that there wasn’t clear evidence showing their noncompliance was willful. 
A Colorado law firm requested records from the Laramie County Sheriff’s Office related to a deputy’s April immigration arrest of Mario Fabian Valenzuela-Robles, a Mexican national with three children who are U.S. citizens. The legal practice, Lichter Immigration, is representing Valenzuela-Robles in ongoing immigration proceedings, and the evidence is vital to his defense in federal court, the firm has said. 
Alleging that it faced barriers to obtaining certain records, Lichter Immigration, represented by former Wyoming GOP Chair Drake Hill, sued Kozak and his office in July. Later that month, Cooley ordered Kozak to provide additional records concerning Valenzuela-Robles’ detention. 
But Kozak and Voss didn’t fully comply with that order, missing the agreed-upon deadline by two days. Some documents were in a format the plaintiffs couldn’t open or read. Kozak’s office didn’t provide a log explaining why certain documents were withheld. Because of these shortcomings, Lichter Immigration requested Cooley to hold Kozak and his office in contempt of court. 
But noncompliance alone, Cooley wrote in her decision, “does not establish civil contempt.” 
“Plaintiffs have not proven by clear and convincing evidence that the failure to comply was willful,” Cooley wrote. Kozak also noted this point. “The law says you have to willfully, you know, withhold the evidence, and so of course we didn’t do that,” he said in a phone call to WyoFile. 
That being said, Cooley continued, just because the defendants’ noncompliance wasn’t willful “does not make it acceptable.” 
She noted that the defendants helped draft the terms of the order compelling production of records. Cooley also pointed out that Hill had asked Voss in an August letter to address concerns about the records. 
The defendants’ failure to address those concerns “prolonged a dispute that should have been resolved without the necessity of further Court proceedings,” Cooley wrote. 
While declining to hold Kozak in contempt, Cooley ordered the sheriff and Voss to provide within 10 days a log explaining why certain records were withheld, records in a readable format and written explanations addressing each of the alleged missing records the plaintiffs had identified. 
Kozak said he had talked with Voss and expects to comply with the order in the next couple of days.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Return of the lame-duck session with RI General Assembly set to reconvene after November election
text:
Rhode Island Superior Court Associate Justice Luis Matos stands alongside Gov. Dan McKee during an Aug. 12, 2026, news conference announcing his nomination to the state Supreme Court. McKee has yet to formally submit the nomination to lawmakers for advice and consent. (Photo by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current)For the first time in six years, state lawmakers are set to reconvene after the Nov. 3 election to consider the appointments of five magistrates and potentially four other judges, including Gov. Dan McKee’s pick for the Supreme Court.
Superior Court Presiding Justice Joseph A. Montalbano last week recommended Timothy G. Healy and Kara Hoopis Manosh for magistrate positions in the state’s highest trial court, subject to advice and consent from the Senate. All Rhode Island magistrates serve 10-year terms unlike judges who serve lifetime appointments.
Also up for consideration are Robert A. Ragosta and Therese M. Picard, who Family Court Chief Judge Michael Forte recommended for appointments to become magistrates in August. In addition, Forte recommended the reappointment of Traffic Tribunal Magistrate Erika Kruse Weller in January.
Senate spokesperson Greg Paré confirmed Tuesday that the chamber has received all five nominations.
“We anticipate potentially receiving (other) appointments from the governor and the judiciary,” Paré wrote in an email to Rhode Island Current Tuesday.
McKee in August nominated Superior Court Judge Luis Matos to fill the vacancy created on the state’s high court by Justice Maureen McKenna Goldberg’s retirement in the spring. The governor lost to Democratic rival Helena Bounnano Foulkes in the Sept. 9 primary. 
Foulkes faces independent Ken Block, Republican Aaron Guckian and two other independent candidates in the Nov. 3 general election.
State law requires the governor to formally transmit a Supreme Court nomination to both the House and Senate before lawmakers can provide advice and consent. But McKee has not yet done so, despite praising Matos as the most qualified of five candidates he interviewed — including former House Speaker K. Joseph Shekarchi — during an Aug. 12 press conference.
“The governor has not forwarded a name to the House for a Supreme Court appointment, so there is no return date for the House,” chamber spokesperson Larry Berman wrote in an email to Rhode Island Current.
McKee also has yet to announce his decision to fill two Superior Court vacancies from a total of eight candidates recommended by the Judicial Nominating Commission on Aug. 12. The pair of vacancies opened when Montalbano became presiding justice and Jeffrey Lanphear retired.
The governor is also considering five candidates for a District Court chief judge recommended by the Judicial Nominating Commission on Friday. The vacancy was created by the Oct. 9 retirement of Jeanne E. LaFazia, who stepped down after 16 years on the bench.
The governor’s shortlist includes former state Sen. Stephen Archambault and District Court judges James Caruolo, Mary McCaffrey, J. Patrick O’Neill and Debra Saunders.
McKee’s office did not respond to requests for comment on the status of his judicial picks.
Paré said the Senate may also consider three additional Traffic Tribunal magistrates selected by its chief judge.
The Rhode Island Senate is scheduled to meet Nov. 5 to formally receive appointments and refer them to the Judiciary Committee. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)
When will they meet?
State law requires a seven-calendar-day waiting period after lawmakers receive a nomination before they can consider it. The House and Senate must separately confirm Supreme Court nominees within 60 days of submission, while the Senate has 90 days to confirm other judicial nominees. 
If lawmakers fail to meet those deadlines, the governor must submit another nominee.
Senate President Valarie Lawson outlined five meeting dates in an Oct. 21 email to senators, opening with a reminder that the chamber was “anticipating receipt of judicial appointments” requiring lawmakers’ advice and consent.
The full 38-member Senate is scheduled to meet Nov. 5 to formally receive appointments and refer them to the Judiciary Committee, which is scheduled to hold hearings Nov. 17 and 18. The Senate is set to consider nominations on Dec. 1, with a second session the following day if needed.
Lawmakers last reconvened following a summer recess in December 2020, when the COVID-19 pandemic prompted an unusual lame-duck session at Rhode Island College to pass a state budget and consider judicial nominations, including those of Supreme Court justices Melissa Long and Erin Lynch Prata.
“We’ve gotten used to a legislature that once they go home in June they don’t come back,” John Marion, executive director of Common Cause Rhode Island, said in an interview.
Marion said these sessions were more common when turnover in the judiciary created more vacancies or lawmakers returned to override vetoes by Republican governors.
“It’s certainly not without precedent to see lame-duck legislatures do this,” Marion said. “It’s not mischievous — this is their duty under the way the law reads.”
All 38 senators face reelection. Nine House lawmakers chose not to run again for a seat in the chamber.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Republican gubernatorial candidate’s campaign loans near $13M
text:
Oklahoma Republican gubernatorial candidate Mike Mazzei waves during a midterm election rally at the Choctaw Event Center, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Durant, Oklahoma. (Photo by Jessica Tobias/For Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – Republican gubernatorial nominee Mike Mazzei has loaned himself nearly $1.9 million more to fuel his campaign for governor, according to campaign finance reports.
That brings the total that the Republican has loaned his campaign to nearly $13 million, a record for a gubernatorial candidate, according to the reports that document campaign contributions and spending from Aug. 19 until Oct. 19. 
Mazzei had raised nearly $3.5 million in other contributions, records show, bringing his total to $16.5 million, including the money he’s loaned himself.
He had about $1.6 million on hand.
His campaign did not respond to a request for comment. 
Mazzei previously told Oklahoma Voice that he views those personal loans as a “good investment” in Oklahoma, and said he was not sure he would receive enough donations to offset all the debt. The Oklahoman in June had reported that Mazzei put up some business assets as collateral.
Mazzei faces Democratic nominee Cyndi Munson, 41, on the Nov. 3 general election ballot.
The Oklahoma Ethics Commission on Tuesday was having technical issues. Munson’s most recent report was not available.
Munson’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment.
Independents Jerry Griffin, 82, of Tulsa, Robert E. Brooks Sr., 47, of Moore, and Orlando Lynn Bush, 61, of Edmond are also on the ballot.
Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt cannot run again due to term limits.
Whoever Oklahomans elect as their next governor on Nov. 3 will be paid $185,000 a year, according to Senate staff.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Minnesota candidates, outside groups, spent big in weeks leading up to Nov. 3 election
text:
Minnesota Capitol. Photo courtesy of Minnesota House Public Information Services.Candidates for Minnesota’s statewide offices, alongside their deep-pocketed outside allies, have poured millions of dollars into what will likely be the most expensive midterm election in state history, according to campaign finance documents released Tuesday.
Sen. Amy Klobuchar, the Democratic nominee for Minnesota governor who has served in the U.S. Senate for 20 years, has raised over $15.5 million as of Oct. 19. Gov. Tim Walz’s fundraising in his 2022 reelection pales in comparison to Klobuchar’s — Walz had raised about $5.7 million around this time four years ago. 
The money sloshing into races this year reflects the deregulated campaign finance environment of the past 15 years, since the U.S. Supreme Court’s rulings siding against campaign rules on First Amendment grounds, beginning with Citizens United vs. FEC. The money is also a reflection of the fiercely competitive atmosphere and high stakes of a potential Democratic-Farmer-Labor trifecta.
Since launching her campaign at the end of January, Klobuchar has spent nearly $13.5 million, with most of her expenses going to advertising. As of Oct. 19, Klobuchar’s campaign had over $2 million in cash, meaning she will have plenty to spend in the final days of the campaign.
House Speaker Lisa Demuth, the GOP nominee for governor, raised $3.6 million as of Oct. 19, about $1.3 million of which came from an August public subsidy payment. The state provides the subsidy to candidates who agree to spending and fundraising limits. Klobuchar opted out of the subsidy so she could blow through the voluntary spending caps. That allowed Demuth to receive a larger payment.
Demuth’s campaign spent $3.5 million this year, over $2.2 million on digital and tv ads.
Demuth’s candidacy has been bolstered by a super PAC that has provided the most significant outside money in support of a statewide Republican candidate in years. Restore Sanity is mostly funded by the Restoration of America PAC, which is primarily financed by Wisconsin billionaire duo Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein. The Uihleins own one of North America’s largest distributors of shipping and packaging supplies.
Restore Sanity has raised over $16 million this year — over $15 million from the Uihlein-funded Restoration of America PAC. Restore Sanity has spent over $5 million on digital and TV ads and direct mailers in favor of Demuth, and it has spent over $9 million on negative ads and mailers opposing Klobuchar’s campaign.
For the first time, Restore Sanity spent money outside of the governor’s race: $330,000 on digital ads against Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon, who is seeking a fourth term.
The Democratic-Farmer-Labor-aligned Alliance for a Better Minnesota raised $8.5 million this year, mostly from the We All Do Better PAC, which received most of its money from an arm of the Democratic Attorneys General Association. Alliance for a Better Minnesota has spent over $4.7 million on ads against Republican attorney general candidate Ron Schutz, and $3 million on ads against Demuth.
Renew Minnesota, a Republican-aligned independent expenditure group, is spending heavily on contested Minnesota legislative races. It’s mostly funded by a large national Republican committee based in Arlington, Virginia, and the Minnesota Private Business Council. Jim Schultz, a former Republican attorney general candidate, is president of the council.
All 201 seats in the Minnesota Legislature are up for grabs next week, and Republicans and Democrats are spending heavily to try to win a majority.
Renew has spent over $9 million this year and is spending heavily on battleground Minnesota Senate races. The group has spent $658,000 on ads against Sen. Grant Hauschild, DFL-Hermantown; $556,000 on ads against Sen. Aric Putnam, DFL-St. Cloud; and $534,000 on ads against Kristy Janigo, the Democratic candidate running for a Maple Grove-area Senate seat left open by retiring Republican Sen. Warren Limmer.
The Republican and Democratic House caucuses are fundraising to take control of the chamber, as the House was split 67-67 in the last legislative session.
House Democrats have raised $7.8 million and have $1.8 million cash on hand. Among the caucus’ top donors are the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee ($1.2 million), Education Minnesota’s political action committee ($625,000) and labor unions like LIUNA, AFSCME and SEIU, which each donated over $200,000.
House Republicans have raised over $2.6 million and have over $700,000 in cash. Among its top donors include the International Union of Operating Engineers ($125,000), former Target CEO Bob Ulrich ($100,000) and the North Central State Carpenters PAC ($65,000).
Senate Democrats, who are hoping to grow their one-seat majority, have raised over $8.5 million and have nearly $2.5 million in cash. Among the caucus’ top donors include the DLCC ($1.2 million), the AFSCME Working Families Fund based in D.C. ($775,000) and Education Minnesota’s PAC ($625,000).
Senate Republicans have raised $3.5 million this year and have over $2.1 million in cash. Its top donors include a Republican-aligned PAC called Building American Greatness ($225,000), Marty Davis, CEO and president of the quartz surfaces manufacturer Cambria Company ($100,000), and Ulrich, the former Target CEO ($100,000).

name: VTDigger
title: Southwestern Vermont rail gets an upgrade to help the region’s economy
text:
West Street looking East in Rutland. Seen on Thursday, September 1, 2022. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
The Vermont Agency of Transportation is acquiring $60.3 million in federal dollars to replace 60 miles of rail for freight travel between Rutland and North Bennington, according to an announcement earlier this week.
The funding comes from the federal Department of Transportation, and was supported by U.S. Rep. Becca Balint, D-Vt., U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and U.S. Sen. Peter Welch, D-Vt. 
“Repairing and upgrading our transportation infrastructure is a win-win for Vermont’s rural communities,” said the Vermont delegation in a joint press release. “This federal funding will help improve safety and reliability on the Vermont Railway, and support the development of rural towns up and down the Western Corridor.”
The investment will go toward the Western Corridor railway between Rutland and Bennington counties, upgrading the “old stick rail” — a traditional jointed track using bolts to connect steel rail together creating small gaps, said Vermont Agency of Transportation Rail Director Dan Delabruere. The track will be replaced by continuously welded rail, which is heavier and does not have joints that slow down travel, Delabruere said. 
The revamped rail will improve safety and efficiency of moving freight, which allows for faster shipping of more goods for businesses, reducing costs for companies and customers, Delabruere said. 
Shipping large volumes is challenging for businesses, so more efficient rail transport will hopefully be a boon for the local economy, said Sarah Furman, executive director of the Chamber & Economic Development of the Rutland Region 
“It’s a step in the right direction,” Furman said. “We need to do more to encourage more businesses here and to keep the businesses that we have, so every little bit helps, and I think this is a large investment that’s going to make a big difference.”
On the map
The investment helps to further revitalize the rail industry, which the southwestern region saw wane in the 20th century.
The Rutland Railroad passenger rail service ceased in 1953, said Paul Searls, Vermont historian and Vermont State University professor, which was a “huge blow” to the region’s economy. 
After that rail service ended, the region faced a one-two punch to the economy with the advent of the interstate highway development curving down the eastern part of the state, constructed between 1958 and 1982, Searls said. The interstate development did not extend to Rutland and Bennington counties, further isolating the region economically, Searls said. 
The region’s economic leaders and environmentalists battled over the development of an upgraded four-lane, limited-access highway system crossing the western part of the state over the decades, Searls said, and plans to fully connect the southwestern region through an interstate has yet to come to fruition. 
Herbert Ogden, a former Windsor County senator and a founder of the Vermont Chapter of the Sierra Club, formed the Vermont Association of Railroad Passengers in 1972, and lobbied to bring back passenger service to reduce car travel to lessen the environmental impacts of transportation in the state, Searls said. 
A passenger rail line was restored with the launch of Amtrak’s Ethan Allen Express in 1996, with Rutland as its last stop. In 2015, the state took on an initiative to extend the Western rail corridor project to Burlington, which was completed in 2022. 

Dan Delabruere, Vermont’s rail and aviation bureau director, emcees a celebration in St Albans in July 2021, to mark the return of Amtrak service in Vermont after 16 months. File photo by Riley Robinson/VTDigger

Establishing passenger rail from Rutland through Bennington County and over to New York is part of the Agency’s future rail plans, Delabruere said. 
While this investment is focused on freight travel, the upgrade of the Western corridor rail in southwestern Vermont is necessary if the state decides to pursue passenger rail in the region, Delabruere said. “This is a step that could benefit that decision,” he said.  
The railroad connection already exists in the southwestern region, so improving the rail network is minimally disruptive, economical and environmentally efficient, said Christopher Parker, former executive director of the Vermont Rail Action Network, a community organization that advocates for better passenger and freight rail in the state.
Investing in freight and passenger train travel is worthwhile in order to grow the region’s economy, attracting tourists and new residents to the region, Parker said.
“Rutland doesn’t have an interstate, and having the train is a big deal for people who live there and work there,” Parker said. “It’s also a big deal in terms of putting Rutland on the map and making Rutland economic opportunities possible.”

name: VTDigger
title: Blunder over legal process impedes school merger studies in some regions
text:
A school bus in Vermont pictured in January 2026. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

School board members who met in St. Albans expected to kick off the process of discussing district mergers under this year’s education reform law. Instead, the Sept. 29 meeting devolved into a public information session because members didn’t think the meeting was properly warned, according to local facilitator John Everitt. 
The kerfuffle among districts in the Group 17 region was just a preview of how confusion over the minutia of public process would get merger study meetings — scheduled to happen across the state in a tight timeline — off to a slow start.
Committee meetings in five regions have been canceled or postponed because this year’s education reform law, Act 170, is unclear about who is responsible for warning meetings or posting information such as agendas, according to Dave Younce, the state’s lead facilitator. The law outlines a process for districts and supervisory unions to consider merging with each other, a move that supporters say would save on administrative and maintenance costs.  
The legal ambiguity has led facilitators and school district leaders to point fingers at each other in some regions, with each denying it’s their responsibility to warn meetings or post information. In regions where there’s disagreement, committees don’t plan on scheduling new meetings until the legislators or the Vermont secretary of state’s office provides an interpretation of the law, Younce said. 
“If it’s end of November and we’re still struggling to get clarity, I think it does put our timelines into risk,” Younce said in an interview. 
Committees have to submit final reports to the state in September 2027, and any resulting merger proposals would go before local voters on Town Meeting Day in 2028. 
Although the process is in the early stages, Heather Stephenson, a Londonderry parent of two, said she’s concerned that it’s difficult for parents and taxpayers to find clear information about merger study meetings. 
Stephenson said she doesn’t want information to be solely disseminated by school districts or supervisory unions because in her area, most kids go to independent high schools and many go to independent middle schools. Notices from districts might not reach parents with kids in independent schools, she said, or taxpayers without kids. 
“It’s important to be in the room when the process begins, not halfway through,” Stephenson said. 
Sen. Seth Bongartz, D-Bennington, who chairs the Senate Education Committee, said the disagreement between facilitators and school districts is “just making it more complicated than it needs to be.” 
Bongartz said that under Vermont’s 2015 education reform law, the initial meeting of each merger committee was warned by the superintendent from the committee’s largest school district. The committees then warned their own subsequent meetings, he said. Bongartz said he thinks committees should follow the same process now. 
Meanwhile, Younce said the Vermont Learning Collaborative, which the state hired to facilitate the merger study process, has gotten legal advice that it might not be necessary to warn committee meetings at all. Younce works for the collaborative in his role as lead facilitator. 
The collaborative also doesn’t plan to create a statewide website or publish information on each region’s process, Younce said. “The local school districts are the entities that have to educate their voters,” he said. 
Still, the organization has provided some materials on its website such as updated maps of merger committee regions and an attachment listing information from local districts’ websites. 
While the learning collaborative declines to assume responsibility for warning meetings or sharing information about them, some districts are concerned about taking on the role themselves. 
A handful of districts have gotten legal advice that it isn’t their responsibility to post information and warn meetings, according to Chelsea Myers, executive director of the Vermont Superintendents Association. 
Myers said her organization has been advocating for a “central repository” for statewide information on the merger study process. 
“It’s just that no one wants to own that piece of it,” Myers said. 
When asked if the Vermont Agency of Education would consider creating a webpage for merger committee information, Toren Ballard, a spokesperson for the agency, said that “the Agency cannot satisfy another legal entity’s obligations under the Open Meeting Law.” 
Ballard said the agency believes it was clear and consistent with the law to have school districts and supervisory unions keep community members informed. 
Younce said he’s been in touch with legislators and the secretary of state’s office to get clear guidance within the next week. 
Bryan Mills, the office’s chief of staff, told VTDigger in an email Tuesday that the office didn’t have any guidance on the issue.

name: WyoFile
title: DOJ election monitors will return to Cheyenne, but this time they’ve agreed to stay 100 yards from polling places
text:
Laramie County Clerk Debra Lee confirmed Tuesday that the Department of Justice will send officials to Cheyenne next week to monitor Wyoming’s general election. In a press release, Lee said she expects the visit to go better than the last one, when Gov. Mark Gordon and other local officials were caught off guard by federal monitors’ “aggressive” behavior, raising concerns about interference. 
In a Monday meeting, the DOJ confirmed its plans and also agreed to comply with a recent opinion by Wyoming Attorney General Keith Kautz, which concludes state law places limits on the federal monitors’ actions, according to the release. 
“We are committed to following Wyoming law and protecting the rights of our citizens to vote privately, safely, securely, and without disruption or interference,” Lee said in the statement. 
In August, local and state officials butted heads with the feds after two DOJ election monitors appeared at a Cheyenne polling place on primary election day, catching the governor and others off guard. Gordon later described the federal monitors’ conduct as “aggressive” and “irregular,” while Clerk Lee said it “was a poorly managed exercise and one that showed complete disregard for our state laws and administration of our elections.” 
Email records indicate Secretary of State Chuck Gray was the only state official to be notified in advance that federal agents would monitor voting in Cheyenne, the Wyoming Tribune Eagle reported in September.
However, things are expected to go differently this time, Lee said. 
“Unlike their visit during the Primary Election, however, monitors won’t be allowed inside polling places and must remain 100 yards from the polls, in accordance with state law and a recent Wyoming Attorney General’s opinion,” Lee said Tuesday. 
In the opinion, requested by Lee’s office, Kautz writes that “in the absence of a court order, settlement agreement or consent decree, Wyoming County Clerks and their election judges not only have the authority to exclude the general public, including DOJ election monitors,… our law requires that they do so.” 
In a virtual meeting Monday, the Justice Department told county officials “they had received the Attorney General’s opinion and would conduct observations and interviews only with voters who agree to be interviewed, outside the 100-yard restricted boundary around polling places, as required by state law,” according to the release. 
Monitors will also identify themselves to voters, the release states, and wear official badges issued by the clerk’s office. 
While federal election observers aren’t new to other states, it’s a unique experience for Wyoming, according to the release. 
“Former senior staff of the Wyoming Secretary of State contacted by Lee said they had no recollection of DOJ monitors visiting Wyoming polls in at least 40 years, if ever,” the release states. 
Meanwhile, the Trump administration has long said it plans to ramp up monitoring efforts across the country. Earlier this month, the DOJ confirmed to WyoFile that it would “have a presence in Wyoming in the general election” but did not provide further details. 
DOJ spokesperson Kiersten Pels told States Newsroom on Monday that about 1,000 monitors will be involved nationally but that the department won’t disclose the full list of monitored locations until Election Day, when voters will decide who controls Congress. 
President Donald Trump has repeatedly cast doubt on the integrity of the upcoming elections, saying Tuesday he would respect the outcome of the elections “if they’re honest.” He also told supporters to “cheat like hell, like they [the Democrats] do.” 
The monitoring follows the Justice Department’s efforts to obtain states’ voter data, which it successfully procured from Wyoming in 2025 with the assistance of Secretary of State Gray.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico announces new screwworm cases, creating infested zone in Las Cruces
text:
A pinned specimen of a full-grown New World screwworm fly. (Image via Texas A&M)New Mexico agriculture officials on Tuesday announced two more confirmed cases of New World screwworm, and a new infested zone in Las Cruces.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The two cases in Doña Ana County include a sheep on the New Mexico State University campus and a cow at an off-campus location. They follow four confirmed cases last week in Otero and Grant counties.
With the new Las Cruces cases, state and federal officials say they are expanding surveillance and fly-trapping on the NMSU campus and establishing a 12.4-mile infested zone in the area.
“Early detection is critical to containing New World screwworm and protecting animal health,” State Veterinarian Dr. Samantha Holeck with the New Mexico Livestock Board said in a statement. “We encourage the campus community to know the warning signs and report suspicious wounds or infestations promptly.”
Residents can view the current infested-zone map at ScrewwormNM.org to determine whether it includes their properties. Animals located within infested zones are required to be inspected within five days of any movement.
“Protecting animal health requires awareness and action from all of us,” New Mexico Secretary of Agriculture Jeff Witte said in a statement. “With cases now confirmed in Doña Ana County, we encourage the NMSU community and surrounding residents to stay vigilant, recognize the warning signs and report concerns quickly.”
The discovery last year of the screwworm’s reemergence has raised widespread concerns for the cattle industry across much of Mexico, along with New Mexico, Texas and Arizona. 
The New World screwworm, a maggot named for its behavior of feeding on live tissue, can cause serious injury and death, primarily to animals and rarely to humans. Warning signs include wounds that fail to heal or become worse; maggots within wounds; and other unusual signs to injuries, including discharge and irritation.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Braun nixes appeal that he order Indiana Election Commission meeting
text:
Indiana Election Commission members, from left, John Westercamp, Beth Boyce, Suzannah Wilson Overholt and Karen Celestino-Horseman during a meeting on April 8, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Republican Gov. Mike Braun won’t direct the Indiana Election Commission to meet ahead of Election Day to review pending campaign misconduct allegations.
Braun responded Tuesday to a request from Lincoln Party secretary of state candidate Greg Ballard for the commission to take up those complaints earlier than its scheduled Nov. 20 meeting.
Ballard’s appeal on Monday to the governor came the same day that a judge handling a lawsuit filed by Ballard rejected his motion seeking a court order for a commission meeting.
In a response letter released by the governor’s office, Braun said he would not intervene.
“While no process is ever perfect, I am satisfied that the Commission has managed the business of election law competently and efficiently,” Braun’s letter said. “As the Marion County Superior Court noted in its decision denying your motion for preliminary injunction, you have offered no evidence that the meeting scheduled for November 20 is insufficient to address any pending allegations of campaign finance violations.”
Ballard has criticized the Election Commission — made up of two Republicans and two Democrats — as overly partisan as he pushed for it to consider the campaign finance complaints against Republican candidate Max Engling and Democrat Beau Bayh.
State law gives Braun and Election Commission Chair Beth Boyce, who is also the Johnson County Republican chair, authority over calling meetings of the panel.
“Based on yesterday’s disappointing ruling, the election commission got away with it,” Ballard said Tuesday. “They got away with it. They simply wanted to run out the clock.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: North Carolina joins ‘overcharging’ lawsuit against Dollar General
text:
Dollar General operates more than 1,100 stores in North Carolina. (Photo: Greg Childress/NC Newsline)North Carolina State Attorney General Jeff Jackson and 19 of his colleagues in other states announced Tuesday they’re suing Dollar General for overcharging customers. The bargain retailer is accused of raising prices for products at the register without updating sticker prices on shelves.  
Jeff Jackson (Photo: Greg Childress/NC Newsline)
At a press conference Tuesday, Jackson called Dollar General a habitual offender that has been “ripping people off,” even after being told repeatedly to resolve the problem.
“They are illegally overcharging families and they have been, we believe, for years, so today, we’re taking them to court to stop this behavior,” Jackson said. 
The lawsuit is part of a multi-state complaint against Dollar General that includes the Federal Trade Commission. In addition to North Carolina, Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Connecticut, Florida, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Utah and Wisconsin also joined the lawsuit. 
“Dollar General has betrayed the trust of millions of American consumers and imposed significant financial harm on communities and consumers who are already struggling to make their paychecks last,” Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a statement.
Dollar General denied in a statement that it has ”willfully disregarded the affordability needs of our customers.”
“Nothing could be further from the truth,” it said. “Our goal is 100% accuracy between shelf and register prices in every store.”
The retailer acknowledged that price discrepancies do occur, but said “store teams are instructed, empowered, and expected to make things right for the customer” when mistakes happen.
However, Jackson said the NCDOJ, through its consumer protection division, has uncovered internal documents that show Dollar General was aware of the overcharging, “knew that it was systemic and chose not to fix the problem.”
“That means they’ve broken the law,” Jackson said. “That means we have good evidence for a strong case that directly impacts families in North Carolina.”
NC attorney general creates new complaint tool for gas tax cheats

Jackson said the overcharges are sometimes a dime, a quarter or a dollar or more. 
“Sometimes people catch it,” Jackson said. “Usually they don’t. Usually they just pay the extra money. They go on about their lives. 
Dollar General operates more than 1,100 stores across the state, and in some rural areas, it’s the only local option for basic goods, food and supplies.
Jackson said NCDOJ will ask the court to order Dollar General to take verifiable action to stop overcharging customers. The NCDOJ will also seek penalties. 
He noted that the N.C. Department of Agriculture recently fined 10 Dollar General Stores in Eastern North Carolina for overcharging customers. The Department of Agriculture regularly conducts inspections to ensure that sticker prices match prices at the register. 
Those 10 stores are in Hertford, Pamlico, Carteret, Transylvania, Craven, Onslow, Buncombe, and Scotland counties. In addition, Dollar General stores have also failed audits in previous years in Franklin, Alamance, Transylvania, Montgomery, Brunswick, Hyde, Lee, and Moore counties. 
Jackson said the families that Dollar General overcharged deserve money back. He said it’s too early to say how that would take place.
“Ultimately, that’s going to be a question for the court and part of our advocacy to the court,” he said. “There are some different ideas in play here, but I can tell you, our consumer division routinely finds a way to get customers their money back when they’ve been ripped off.”
Jackson urges Dollar General customers to check their receipts before leaving the store and to demand that the store correct the price if they’re charged more than the price on the shelf. Complaints can be filed with the state Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services’ Standards Division using this complaint form or at 984-236-4751.

name: VTDigger
title: Voter voices from east to west
text:
Susan and Mark Boutwell of Hartland sit in a booth at Snap’s Restaurant in Bristol on Sunday Oct. 25. Photo by Theo Wells-Spackman/VTDigger
VTDigger reporters visited a variety of sites across Vermont in recent weeks, asking voters directly about the issues they care most about this election season. This week we’ll bring you those voices as we approach Election Day on Nov. 3.
BRISTOL — Beaming sun illuminated the remaining red leaves on Sunday, bringing a steady stream of Vermonters to two Addison County dining institutions. 
For a fraction of those brunchgoers, that peace was briefly shattered by a VTDigger reporter’s inquiries about their perspectives on next week’s general election. But like other attempts to capture the atmosphere surrounding Vermont’s most closely watched race — Democrat/Progressive Amanda Janoo’s challenge to Republican Gov. Phil Scott — the resulting snapshot showed more worry about the challenges facing Vermont than clarity about who voters will select to solve them.
Among those savoring a meal in a window-side booth at Snap’s Restaurant in Bristol were two voters, Susan and Mark Boutwell of Hartland, who had yet to be fully won over by either gubernatorial candidate.
Mark, 67, who recently retired from leading Senior Solutions in southeastern Vermont, said affordability issues for older residents were at the top of his mind.
“Many older Vermonters aren’t going to be able to afford higher heating oil prices,” for example, he said.

READ MORE

Mark said he was also concerned about homelessness among older adults, and added that he was “not convinced” by Scott’s efforts to address the state’s housing crisis. In general, he tends to vote for Democrats, he said, but hasn’t made up his mind about the governor’s contest this year.
Susan, a 68-year-old former communications professional and news editor, likewise expressed uncertainty, despite being “really interested in that race.”
Education reform is a particularly important issue for her, she said, with property taxes a pressing problem as electeds in Montpelier work toward economic sustainability for the state’s education finance apparatus. But Susan said she was unsure about school district consolidation as an approach to that goal.
“I’m not convinced it will save money,” she said, adding “what are you getting in return?”
Essex Junction’s Ben Bivins, 40, who emerged from Snap’s in a hurry bearing an order for takeout, said he thinks the state is due for a change in leadership strategy.
For one thing, “property taxes are crazy,” Bivins said, which he argued contributes to Vermont’s sinking birth rates and outflow of young people. He said he generally supports Janoo’s progressive agenda, and added that legislative experimentation might be called for in this moment.
“I’m down to try anything at this point, because what’s been going on the last couple years ain’t cuttin’ it,” Bivins said.

Rosie’s Restaurant in Middlebury on Sunday Oct. 25. Photo by Theo Wells-Spackman/VTDigger

Fifteen miles down the road, Tim Seniff paused on the way out of Rosie’s Restaurant in Middlebury to explain that a desire for political balance in the Statehouse and a distaste for the two-party system usually leads him to vote for independent or third-party candidates where possible.
The Warren-based estate gardener and chef said he intends to do so again next week, having grown increasingly worried about the state’s financial management in recent years. Vermont often greenlights spending its residents can’t really afford, Seniff argued, including on the much-debated motel program designed to provide emergency housing to certain vulnerable people experiencing homelessness.
Seniff said he was seriously considering moving out of Vermont entirely. Partly due to a revaluation of his home, he said, his property taxes have doubled in recent years.
“It’s just too expensive,” Seniff said.
