name: Michigan Advance
title: Vance makes final push for Rogers, James and Barrett in Michigan with continued attacks on El-Sayed
text:
U.S. Vice President JD Vance speaks to Republicans during a rally on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, at CHI Aviation in Howell, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)HOWELL — Vice President JD Vance was deployed once again to Michigan on Tuesday in a final push to boost the Republican Party ticket and to attack the Democratic ticket head-on, ahead of the Nov. 3 general election.
Both Vance and President Donald Trump have been barnstorming the state to shore up voter enthusiasm, with Trump pleading with his base to show up to the polls en masse and to vote as though he were on the ballot this year.
Vance continued that push for GOP enthusiasm in Howell during a rally at CHI Aviation, seeking to elevate the prospects of U.S. Senate nominee Mike Rogers, gubernatorial nominee John James of Shelby Township and U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte).SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“In one week, we have an opportunity to vote for three Michigan patriots who are fighting for you,” Vance said of the GOP candidates. “Next Tuesday, we’re going to remind the entire country exactly who it is that loves America.”
 Vance, like Trump did in Port Huron on Sunday, dedicated most of his address to attacking Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, but steered away from the same type of anti-Muslim rhetoric that Republicans have used to argue that voters should reject the former Wayne County health director. 
Vance did, however, claim that El-Sayed wanted to defund the police, cited his association with podcaster Hasan Piker, and invoked the scenes of violent protests coming out of France, which Vance has claimed had been brought on by that nation’s immigration policies, which the vice president believed El-Sayed would also advocate for.
“If sovereignty means anything to us, it means that the nation belongs to the people of America,” Vance said. “When you forget that, it’s how you get Paris. And unfortunately, it’s exactly what El-Sayed wants to bring to the shores of the United States of America.”
U.S. Vice President JD Vance speaks to Republicans during a rally on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, at CHI Aviation in Howell, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
A fact-check by the Associated Press determined that there was no evidence immigration policies were behind the unrest in France.
On Rogers, Vance said he believed the GOP candidate had shown courage in calling out El-Sayed’s alleged ties to the Muslim Brotherhood and not letting up.
“One of the most important jobs of a United States Senator, who gets to spend their lives around a bunch of politicians, is that you have to be able to fully and carefully deal with bulls**t,” Vance said. “That’s exactly what Mike showed you he was able to do. As much as the media and the El-Sayed campaign lied about Mike Rogers, he was born and bred in Michigan, who is a son of the state of Michigan.”
Michigan Public’s fact check of allegations that El-Sayed’s mother had ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, which have formed the basis of Rogers’ attacks, found that “those claims don’t match the evidence.”
The president and vice president’s campaign stops in Michigan followed a Saturday rally in Detroit featuring former President Barack Obama and the Democratic slate up for election in 2026, with a heavy emphasis on boosting the prospects of El-Sayed and gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson, Michigan’s secretary of state. El-Sayed has been working to shore up the Democratic coalition following struggles with Jewish and Black voters, and Obama’s visit aimed to bridge some of the lingering divisions within the party.
Trump and Vance’s visits also acted as a hedge against whatever boost Obama might have given them, with Vance working Tuesday to try and deflate the momentum the Democrats have running in the final leg of the 2026 race.
U.S. Vice President JD Vance speaks to Republicans during a rally on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, at CHI Aviation in Howell, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)Republican gubernatorial nominee and U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township) speaks during a rally with Vice President JD Vance on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026 at CHI Aviation in Howell, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte) speaks during a rally with Vice President JD Vance on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026 at CHI Aviation in Howell, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)Republicans gather at a rally featuring Vice President JD Vance on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026 at CHI Aviation in Howell, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)Michigan secretary of state nominee Anthony Forlini speaks with Republicans during a rally with Vice President JD Vance on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026 at CHI Aviation in Howell, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)Michigan attorney general nominee Doug Lloyd speaks with Republicans during a rally with Vice President JD Vance on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026 at CHI Aviation in Howell, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
Vance said that the current Republican platform, and the “Make America Great Again” movement it is based on, was about returning power to the people, again invoking American “sovereignty” and how that might be under attack from Democrats this cycle.
Vance claimed he and Trump have been delivering on that promise, helping to rein in inflation and high prices and have formed a government that has focused on cutting taxes, not raising them.
Trump’s war in Iran and his tariffs on U.S. trading partners, especially Canada, have nullified those assertions, with gas prices soaring and inflation hitting 3.7%.
Still, Vance spoke as if the economy under the Trump administration was the fault of Democrats who have not controlled the White House or Congress for nearly two years.
Rogers and James both spoke prior to Vance taking the stage, as did other key members of the Michigan Republican Party, including attorney general nominee Doug Lloyd, secretary of state nominee Anthony Forlini and U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte), the latter of which is in a tough reelection battle against challenger Will Lawrence in the 7th Congressional District.
Rogers said that through his own campaign outreach, it was his opinion that many Democrats have decided to vote against El-Sayed, which could give him a boost if stories about Democratic defections become a reality on election night.
“How many people is it going to take for us to start listening that this guy should never see through the threshold of the United States government?” Rogers said of El-Sayed. “If you can’t condemn terrorism you can’t be in the United States Senate. … Are we going to fall asleep at the switch over the next few days and allow someone who could not get a security clearance for any organization in the U.S. government to walk into the Senate representing us?
Republican U.S. Senate nominee and former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers and speaks during a rally with Vice President JD Vance on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026 at CHI Aviation in Howell, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
James said that all eyes appeared to be on Michigan, not just because of its contentious U.S. Senate race between Rogers and El-Sayed, but also key congressional races and his own race for governor.
“What happens here in one week will send shock rings around the world because of your effort, because you never quit,” James said in a pitch for Republicans to not sit the election out. “This will be a test of common sense versus crazy, and common sense will prevail. … There’s no such thing as patio patriots.”
Just after Vance’s remarks, Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel released a statement scorning the vice president’s message.
“Today, JD Vance came back to Michigan to brag about the very policies that have driven up costs and left Michigan families worse off. Mike Rogers, John James, Tom Barrett, and Michigan Republicans have fully enabled and endorsed Trump and Vance’s corrupt, cost-raising agenda—from reckless tariffs and the Iran war to devastating healthcare cuts that funded billionaire tax breaks,” Hertel said. “Michiganders are fed up with the higher costs and rampant corruption fueled by this administration, and a week from now, they will reject Trump and the Michigan Republicans who enabled him at the ballot box.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Trump administration awards Florida $193.7M for rural healthcare
text:
The rural health grant is $5 million-plus more than what the administration of Gov. Ron DeSantis said it hoped to receive from the Trump administration. (Getty Images)Florida has been awarded $193.7 million in federal funds to support telemedicine, remote patient monitoring, pharmacy services, diagnostic kiosks, and community paramedicine for rural areas in Florida, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services announced.
The grant is $5 million-plus more than the DeSantis administration had previously announced it was requesting. The money is made possible by the Rural Health Transformation Program, a five-year, $50 billion initiative included in the One Big Beautiful Act.
“President Trump understands that every American deserves high-quality healthcare, no matter where they live,” Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr said in a press release last week.
“We are putting resources directly into rural communities to strengthen the health workforce, modernize infrastructure, expand access, and bring care closer to home. We are giving states the flexibility to build solutions around the people they serve, while demanding accountability for results. That is how we strengthen rural health, improve the lives of patients and families, and Make America Healthy Again.”
The press release also contains quotes from Gov. Ron DeSantis, U.S. Sens. Rick Scott and Ashley Moody, Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds, and a bevy of others. The announcement cites the “Working Families Tax Cuts Act,” not the OBBBA, the name President Donald Trump assigned to the legislation.
Signed by Trump on July 4, 2025, the law cut about $1 trillion from Medicaid over a decade. Florida’s former Medicaid director, Brian Meyer, told state legislators late last year that the state would see about a $3.6 billion reduction for its state-directed payment programs — mechanisms the state uses to pay hospitals, physicians, and cancer hospitals that treat the poor, elderly, and disabled.
KFF projected the Medicaid losses for Florida from a low of $10 billion to a high of $17 billion, estimates that don’t take into consideration investments from the Rural Health Transformation Grant program.
OBBBA also made substantive changes to the Supplemental Nutrition and Assistance Program (SNAP), increasing the state’s share of administrative costs for the program and, moreover, putting states with high error rates, such as Florida, potentially on the hook for contributing to the costs of the food.
SNAP benefits help low-income, families and individuals who are food insecure
The CMS press release did not mention any of the reductions to the Medicaid program. It only included praise from Republican politicos for the rural grant money.
Praise and condemnation
Republican U.S. Rep. Jimmy Patronis, who represents CD 1 in the far western Panhandle, thanked the Trump administration in the release “for prioritizing rural health care and ensuring Northwest Florida gets the support our communities deserve.”
Republican Mike Haridopolos, who represents CD 8, which includes the Space Coast, said in the release that “every Florida family deserves access to quality health care.” He added: “This funding will help Florida build a stronger healthcare system for the future.”
The nonprofit group Protect Our Care issued a statement criticizing the announcement as misleading. Protect Our Care is dedicated to making affordable, high-quality, and equitable health care a right for every Floridian.
“Last year, Donald Trump and Republicans rammed through $1 trillion in cuts to Medicaid to pay for tax breaks for billionaires and big corporations. Florida alone will lose more than $13.5 billion from those Medicaid cuts — making the $193 million CMS announced a pittance by comparison,” the organization’s president, Brad Woodhouse, said in a written statement.
The group claims 16 hospitals, clinics, and nursing homes in Florida have already been forced to shut down, cut services, or are at risk of doing so due to the Medicaid reductions in the federal law.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: King endorses Dunlap in 2nd District House race
text:
Independent U.S. Sen. Angus King speaks to rallygoers on the bridge over the Kennebec River in Bath during the national No Kings day of action on October 17.  (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: How to register, key dates, who’s on the ballot and where the candidates stand on the top issues facing Maine.]Independent U.S. Sen. Angus King is endorsing Democrat Matt Dunlap in the 2nd Congressional District race.
In a video posted Tuesday, King, who served two terms as governor before joining the U.S. Senate, praised Dunlap for his time representing Old Town in the Maine Legislature.
“When you serve as governor, you get to know a lot of legislators, but one I particularly remember is Matt Dunlap. Why? because he was tough and smart and a strong advocate for his district,” King said.
Dunlap, who also served as Maine secretary of state and is currently the state auditor, is running against Republican former Gov. Paul LePage to replace U.S. Rep. Jared Golden, a Democrat. LePage is favored to win the conservative-leaning district, but the race is expected to be close. In September, the Cook Political Report shifted its rating in the Democrat’s favor, currently rating the district as leaning Republican. 
While Dunlap is known for his progressive position on many issues, such as Medicare for All, he’s also highlighted his support for gun rights, pointing to his previous post as executive director of the Sportsman’s Alliance of Maine.
King also touts Dunlap’s advocacy for the “sportsmen and women of Maine,” pointing out that the candidate has a hunting license. “He can represent the whole 2nd District in Congress, and that’s what we need,” King said.
King, who caucuses with Democrats, has also backed Democrat Hannah Pingree in the gubernatorial race, but has so far not weighed in on the U.S. Senate race between incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: What to expect in Pennsylvania at the polls a week from today
text:
A voter fills out his ballot at the Board of Elections office in Kittanning, Armstrong County, Pa. October 20, 2026. (Photo by John Beale/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)One week out from Election Day, Secretary of the Commonwealth Al Schmidt advised voters to be patient, both with those working the polls and those counting ballots as part of a high stakes midterm election. 
“I want to remind everyone that counting ballots takes time, and county election officials rightly prioritize accuracy over speed,” Schmidt said. “If a race is close, it may take time to know who the winner is, as provisional ballots and military ballots and overseas civilian absentee ballots are counted after Election Day.” 
Polls open at 7 a.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 3 and close at 8 p.m. — though any voter still in line at 8 p.m. will be allowed to cast a ballot. Volunteer poll workers will look up voters and direct them to sign next to their names in a poll book. 



First-time voters will need to show identification, such as a driver’s license or other state-issued photo IDs, before casting their vote on a paper ballot. The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.
Precincts will be busy places, Schmidt added, with election officials, poll workers, the judge of elections, majority and minority inspectors, appointed clerks and machine operators on hand. Additionally, a voter with a disability may request assistance voting from someone who isn’t their employer or union representative. 
Lastly, poll watchers — registered voters selected by local county-level parties — may observe proceedings alongside constables, who may be present to preserve the peace, Schmidt added. Some polls in four counties are expected to have election monitors from the U.S. Department of Justice.
[Voter Guide: 2026 Pennsylvania General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
“Voters have the right to vote without being harassed or intimidated. If a voter has reason to believe their rights are being violated, they should report it to the judge of elections at their polling place,” he advised.
The Department of State also offers a year-round hotline at 1-877-VOTESPA, or 1-877-868-3772.
Posted results will be available as they come in at the agency’s website, and Schmidt said his office will hold a press conference at 9 p.m. on Election Day. 
Voters who choose to use the mail-in option should drop off their completed ballot at an authorized drop box and not rely on the U.S. Postal Service. Ballots must be received by 8 p.m. on Election Day, and a postmark won’t be sufficient. 
Those who requested a mail-in ballot and changed their mind can still cast a provisional ballot at their precinct on Election Day. The deadline to request a ballot is 5 p.m., Oct. 27.

name: VTDigger
title: Proposal 3 protects the rights earlier generations fought for
text:
This commentary is by Larry Moquin Jr., president of the Vermont State Labor Council, AFL-CIO. 
I’ve heard people say that when we work, we’re selling our labor. But I think it’s more than that.  I think that when we work, we’re selling our most precious commodity: time. We can’t control how much of it we have and when it will be up, but it’s everything: time for family, friends, hobbies, passions and for yourself. All too often we spend it working until we die.  
This thought weighed heavily on me recently as I sat in a hospital room in Florida with my dad — a Marine, a Vietnam veteran and, at 79, a lifelong union laborer — who’s just beginning his fight with the cancer that will likely dictate what time he has left. His generation, and the generations before him, fought literally and figuratively for the rights that Americans and, specifically, American workers have relied on for decades. It was daunting to sit beside him, knowing that the sacrifices of his and past generations are being systematically dismantled and are at risk of being completely torn down. 
Our basic rights are under attack almost daily. Just two years ago, a billionaire sending pink slips to federal employees would have sounded like the beginning of a “Twilight Zone” episode. But, in reality, that was just the beginning of a concerted campaign by both politicians and corporations to get U.S. workers back under the thumb of the wealthiest people in the world. I never thought that future generations of Americans would have fewer rights than I did growing up. But it’s happening right before our eyes. Reproductive rights, civil rights, voting rights and workers’ rights are all up for auction to the highest corporate bidder. For decades, corporate money has been used to influence politicians who gut labor protections across our country. These groups that lobby to cut workers’ rights only care about maximizing profits for the companies they represent. 
Passing Proposal 3 is a guaranteed way to protect future generations of Vermont workers from out-of-state groups hoping to influence the Green Mountain State against working people.  There’s no rational argument against it, unless you stand to gain financially from the opportunities created when working people have fewer rights. 
But Vermonters can fight back. At a time when corporations and the billionaire class have bought politicians and are attempting to sow anti-worker sentiments into our collective consciousness, Vermonters can protect themselves and generations to come. 

READ MORE

Proposal 3 would amend the Vermont Constitution to establish that employees have the right to organize or join a labor organization and collectively bargain over wages, hours, working conditions, economic welfare and workplace safety. It would also prevent laws from interfering with or diminishing that right. 
This measure is about ensuring that workers who choose to organize have a fundamental right to do so and to have a voice in the workplace. It is about ensuring that a worker who believes their wages are unfair, their workplace is unsafe or their working conditions need to change can stand together with their co-workers and advocate for themselves. It protects the voice of workers on the job site and prevents rogue politicians from taking away workers’ rights. 
I can’t give my dad more time. And while it’s easy to dwell on the injustice of this, I choose to see a life’s work worth fighting for. He has what every Vermonter deserves: Because of the collective bargaining agreements negotiated on his behalf, and his many years of hard work and service, he earned a livable wage, had premium healthcare and has enjoyed a well-deserved and dignified retirement. 
When I was 20 and lacking any direction or anything resembling a life plan, my dad pulled up to our house in Winooski one afternoon and said, “Get in the truck, we’re going to work.” Now, more than 25 years later, as a proud second-generation member of the Laborers’ International Union of North America, I have the same protections he had. 
Proposal 3 would give these same protections to future generations.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska fights back against Trump-ordered elections lawsuit, seeks its dismissal
text:
U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, speaks at a rally featuring President Donald Trump on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, in Wasilla. On Oct. 22, Trump ordered the U.S. Department of Justice to file a lawsuit that would prohibit anyone but Sullivan from being certified as the winner of the U.S. Senate election. (James Brooks photo/Alaska Beacon)Attorneys representing the state of Alaska have asked a federal judge to dismiss a lawsuit by the U.S. Department of Justice that is seeking to halt the certification of the state’s ongoing U.S. Senate election.
The lawsuit, ordered by President Donald Trump and filed last week, asks the U.S. District Court for the District of Alaska to prevent the Alaska Division of Elections from declaring a winner in the election unless the winner is the incumbent, Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, an ally of the President. 
Attorneys representing the federal government have put forward a legally dubious argument stating that Alaska voters might be confused by the fact that one of Sen. Sullivan’s opponents is a man with the same first and last name — unaffiliated candidate Dan J. Sullivan of Petersburg.
Opposition grows to Trump lawsuit seeking to aid Sen. Dan Sullivan’s re-election bid

Late Monday, state assistant attorneys general Margaret Paton Walsh and Laura Fox said the complaint “has no legal basis” and, citing a September ruling by the U.S. Supreme Court, said “the United States lacks authority to intervene in state elections at all, much less in support of a favored candidate. This Court should follow the well established principle that ‘lower federal courts should not “alter the election rules” of a state “on the eve of an election,”’ and swiftly dismiss the complaint.”
They asked Judge Sharon Gleason, an Obama appointee who is presiding over the case, to rule no later than Monday, the day before Election Day. 
“This will ensure that Alaskans heading to the ballot box (as well as those who have already voted) have confidence that their votes will count and the U.S. Senate election result will be timely certified free from unlawful interference by the United States,” the attorneys wrote on behalf of the state.
If the federal government were to prevail in the lawsuit, the state would be unable to declare anyone but Sen. Sullivan the winner of the ongoing U.S. Senate election until a subsequent investigation is complete. 
That has implications not just for Alaska but for the United States as a whole. 
Cook Political Report, a leading expert on elections, says that in 13 of this year’s open Senate seats, Democrats are favored. If that holds true on and after Election Day, it would give them 47 seats. It rates seven other races as “toss-ups.” If Democrats win four of those races, they’ll control the chamber.
One of the seven toss-ups is Alaska’s race. 
Sabato’s Crystal Ball, a ranking of close races run by the nonpartisan Center for Politics, thinks Peltola is favored to win; its forecast gives Democrats 49 seats before toss-ups are considered.
Before the state’s filing late Monday, the DOJ lawsuit had already been challenged by two nonpartisan groups, as well as the campaign of Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola and a national Democratic group.
The nonpartisan groups and the Democratic groups also asked Gleason to dismiss the federal government’s case. On Monday, Gleason said the DOJ should be prepared to file rebuttal arguments against dismissal by 5 p.m. Thursday.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico utility regulators seek Legislature’s help with small water utilities
text:
New Mexico Public Regulation Commission Public Interest Advocacy Section Chief John Kreienkamp, left, and PRC Chief of Staff Cholla Khoury, right, speak before the interim Water and Natural Resources Committee on Oct. 27, 2026, about their proposal for the Legislature to make it easier for private water utilities to become regional or municipal entities. (Joshua Bowling/Source NM)New Mexico utility regulators on Tuesday told state lawmakers they’d like the Legislature’s help in tweaking the rules that govern the state’s small water utilities.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The New Mexico Public Regulation Commission oversees service and pricing issues for small, privately owned water utilities across the state. Often when problems with service arise, PRC leaders told lawmakers on the interim Water and Natural Resources Committee, the companies have too little money to correct course and regulators have too little time to intervene.
Small water utilities have presented plenty of problems in recent years. The New Mexico Environment Department last year sought a receivership for the troubled Camino Real Regional Utility Authority in Sunland Park after its water showed exceedingly high levels of arsenic. More recently, Timberon Water and Sanitation District near Alamogordo reported losing as much as 85% of its water to leaky pipes and the Melody Ranch Water Co. near Edgewood had a “complete disruption of water service.”
PRC Chief of Staff Cholla Khoury, on Tuesday said she hopes to see legislation in the upcoming lawmaking session that starts in January aimed at making it easier for utilities to access capital and streamlines the lengthy process by which a judge can place a utility under state receivership.
“Mostly what we will be looking for is to increase authority, so that when we do have a failing water system, we can move quickly,” Khoury told lawmakers.
Lawmakers were split, though, on support for facilitating state control of private companies — and on whether they had enough relevant data to begin crafting legislation.
“I understand the issue…but your solution is to take control, not to offer independent technical support for these entities,” Rep. Kathleen Cates (D-Rio Rancho) told Khoury. “I’d like to know why that is not on the table?”
Khoury responded and said that receivership is always “truly the last option” and said that streamlining the process would make it easier for the state to intervene in cases of emergencies.
Some lawmakers said they were eager to work on the PRC’s proposal.
Sen. Anthony Thornton (R-Sandia Park) referred back to the recent problems in his district, such as Melody Ranch, and said he wants to make sure utility regulators can swiftly intervene when needed.
“When people are out of water, that’s truly an emergency situation and we need to move quickly,” he said.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Report: Stratos Project’s emissions could cause up to 45 premature deaths, illnesses each year
text:
The sun rises over a part of Hansel Valley, in Box Elder County, near the proposed Stratos Project, a massive data center planned for 40,000 acres of land, on Thursday, May 28, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)An embattled data center campus project in Utah could emit “dangerous quantities” of air pollution linked to premature deaths, illness like asthma and heart attacks, and health-related economic damage, a new report from the firm EmPower Analytics Group says.
The vision for the Stratos Project, a massive data center planned for Box Elder County, has gotten smaller since its original concept, going from a 40,000-acre plan to 20,000 acres. Still, its full buildout would include the production of about 9 gigawatts of power, more than double what the whole state consumes.
If the plan to use mostly natural gas to power it goes through, the data center campus could emit up to 3,140 tons of fine particulate matter, which would impact not only Utahns, but also residents in Idaho, Wyoming and Colorado. It could even reach Illinois, according to the report commissioned by the Natural Resources Defense Council, an environmental nonprofit.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“If that demand were met entirely by gas, our highest estimates reach 45 additional premature deaths and $690 million in health damages each year, with effects extending far beyond Utah,” Michael Cork, CEO of EmPower Analytics Group said in a news release. That’s assuming a 9 gigawatt buildout operating at 90% of capacity.
‘I seek to do better,’ Cox says after heated comments on Box Elder County data center

The project has been explicitly tied to the Ruby natural gas pipeline, and according to presentations from former Military Installation Development Authority officers leading the project, the power plant envisioned for the site was meant to be solely fueled by natural gas. 
But, after facing explosive scrutiny over the data center project, Utah Gov. Spencer Cox said the developers, backed by “Shark Tank” celebrity investor Kevin O’Leary, have committed to pursue other energy resources, including renewables, energy storage and nuclear power generation in addition to natural gas.
A spokesperson for the Stratos Project developers didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on the report.
The first phase of the project is not to exceed 1.5 gigawatts of energy generation, Cox said in May. Future permits “must be contingent on meeting clear metrics and expectations during this initial phase,” the governor said. But, there haven’t been any specific commitments on the energy generation technology for the center.
Natural gas options
The EmPower Analytics Group evaluated two plausible methane-gas technologies of 3 gigawatts and 9 gigawatts. One of them, powered by gas-fired reciprocating internal combustion engines, also known as RICE, has already been permitted to power a Joule Capital Partners data center campus in Millard County, another data center in Utah, the report says.
That technology is estimated to cause about five to six times the premature deaths and economic damages of modern combined-cycle gas, a more efficient method that integrates a gas turbine with a heat recovery cycle to drive a steam turbine, analysts said.
Whichever route the developers decide to take, if it’s powered by natural gas, it would imply substantial public health costs, the study says.
“Although generating technology, pollution controls, and operating practices will shape the magnitude of these harms, all scenarios are estimated to cause premature deaths and illness both near Stratos and across a much wider region,” analysts wrote. “These estimates account only for air pollution from on-site power generation and do not include other potential environmental and community impacts, such as construction, water use, noise, and land use.”



Let us know what you think...


 


Over 30 years, Stratos’ natural gas power generation “could contribute to hundreds of premature deaths and billions of dollars in economic damages,” according to the study. At 9 gigawatts, “these harms could accumulate to approximately 856–1,350 premature deaths and $13.5–20.7 billion under gas-fired RICE, compared with 145–253 premature deaths and $2.3–3.8 billion under combined-cycle gas.”
It would also add pollution to a region already facing substantial air quality challenges since it’s prone to winter inversions and elevated summer ozone, the study says. The largest fine particulate matter increases would happen near the data center’s site, particularly in Box Elder and Cache counties, as well as southern Idaho.
Additionally, smaller increases of fine particulate matter would extend to the Wasatch Front and would extend to neighboring states, analysts said.
“Utah policymakers and regulators should consider the health and economic impacts identified in this analysis and account for them as they consider the future of large-scale off-grid, fossil fueled data centers in Utah, including the Stratos Project,” said Logan Mitchell, climate scientist and regulatory manager at Utah Clean Energy, who collaborated on the report. “Responsible off-grid data center developments should pursue the maximum amount of clean, emission-free generation resources ahead of fossil fuels.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: ‘Stop asking Jewish voters to sacrifice our values’ in midterm election, leaders urge
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippi Today Ideas is a platform for thoughtful ideas to be shared about our state’s past, present and future. Opinions expressed in guest essays are the author’s own and do not necessarily represent those of Mississippi Today. You can read more about the section here.   

During a recent appearance before the Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus, Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel offered a midterm election roadmap for Jewish voters. “We have a moral imperative to place the needs of the world above even our own self-interest and, yes, even our own survival,” she said. She urged “sacrific[ing] the comfort, safety and security and even the very future of our own people in exchange for the opportunity to save the rest of humanity.”
As the leader of a Jewish advocacy organization and former Jewish outreach director for a major presidential campaign, we were thunderstruck by Attorney General Nessel’s remarks. Her comments couldn’t be more wrong or offensive. But what disturbed us even more was just how commonplace those sentiments have become.
Never before in our careers have we experienced an election season in which Jews are so often asked to excuse antisemitic rhetoric and disregard actions that should have no place in American politics, all to serve somebody else’s definition of a greater good. Political leaders and candidates in both parties are routinely asking the Jewish community to overlook behavior from supposed allies that we would immediately condemn if it came from opponents.  
Here’s a simple message for our fellow Jewish voters: demand better than what we’re getting now from both parties.  
Democrats are trying desperately to flip the Senate. They have candidates like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, who summed up a Hezbollah terrorist sympathizer plowing his car into a synagogue full of preschool children as a case of “hurt people hurt people.” He only apologized months later after securing the nomination. They previously ran candidates like Graham Platner in Maine, whose Nazi tattoo was perfectly fine to party leaders until he was accused of rape—and whose successor, Troy Jackson, suggested that the Holocaust was clouding Jewish Mainers’ views of Israel’s actions in Gaza, before he too offered a politically convenient apology. 
Republicans, meanwhile, are trying desperately to hold Congress. They have incumbents like Randy Fine in Florida, who calls himself pro-Israel while comparing Muslims to dogs, backing the mass deportation of Muslims from the United States, and openinly rooting for Palestinians to starve in Gaza. They are also rallying around candidates like Brandon Herrera in Texas, who has admiringly referred to Nazi weapons as “ghetto blasters” and has spoken proudly of owning a copy of Hitler’s Mein Kampf, and Martin O’Donnell in Nevada, who hosted a Nazi sympathizer on his podcast and referred to the conversation as a “marriage made in heaven.”   
A marker that gives information about the 1967 firebombing of the Beth Israel Congregation synagogue is shown in Jackson on Monday, Jan. 12, 2026, shortly after the latest attack on the synagogue. Credit: Bashirah Mack/Mississippi Today
These individuals have little in common politically. What they share is excuse-making from their respective national parties. Jewish voters are being told repeatedly in this election cycle to forgive and forget offensive comments and dangerous worldviews because the stakes are too high to do otherwise. As each party warns of an existential threat to the country if the other side wins, the common message to Jews is that we need to just keep our mouths closed and fall in line. 
We reject that deal. 
We reject the idea that hate speech should have a home in our political discourse. We reject the notion that acquiescing to discrimination is simply the price of admission to our political system. We reject the principle that ‘anything goes’ in pursuit of control of Congress. 
As Jews, we know all too well the consequences of normalized bigotry. Jews comprise only 2% of America’s population, yet we were targeted in 64% of religion-based hate crimes in 2025. The Anti-Defamation League recorded more than 6,000 antisemitic incidents last year, including a record 203 incidents of physical assaults against Jews.
These numbers don’t exist in a vacuum. When lawmakers and political candidates routinely use hateful rhetoric, they inspire those who share those beliefs and are willing to act on them. Researchers who have examined this phenomenon call it “the emboldening effect.” Studies have found a significant association between hate speech from political leaders and subsequent hate crimes. There are consequences when the boundaries of proper political discourse shift to such a large degree. When political parties reward, excuse or ignore this behavior, they create room for even more of it. 
At a bare minimum, individuals running for office should be modeling respectful behavior. It should be a basic requirement for the job. Yet in too many cases, it appears too much to ask. 
With the midterm election just days away, we encourage our fellow Jewish voters to hold both parties and their candidates accountable for their words. Antisemitism should never be tolerated from anyone. No amount of hate speech is worth the price of victory.
In our system, voters should set the standards by which politicians abide. We Jews should not be expected to tolerate the hate being directed at us on the altar of political expediency. Our dignity will be respected, and our votes must be earned.    

Ron Halber is CEO of the Jewish Community Relations Council of Greater Washington. Joel Rubin is a former Obama Administration deputy assistant secretary of state who served as Jewish outreach director for Bernie Sanders’ 2020 presidential campaign.

text:

(Photo by Lori Kersey/West Virginia Watch)Democratic turnout exceeded Republican turnout in the first four days of early voting, according to numbers released by the West Virginia Secretary of State. 
A total of 66,855 West Virginians cast their ballots in the first four days of voting, according to a press announcement issued by Secretary of State Kris Warner on Monday. 
Registered Democrats cast 25,556 votes at an early polling location, while Republicans — which have a numerical advantage by registration — cast 24,191 votes. People with no party affiliation or are members of non-recognized third parties cast 12,332 votes. 
Recognized third party registrants — meaning members of the Mountain Party, Constitution and Libertarian parties — have cast a combined total of 287 votes. 
Absentee ballot returns show an even larger advantage. 
Democratic voters have returned 2,308 absentee ballots, while Republican voters returned 1,441 ballots. Non-party and members of non-recognized third parties have turned 725 ballots. Members of recognized third parties only consisted of 15 returned absentee ballots. 
Early voting concludes Oct. 31. Election Day is Nov. 3.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Candidates pledge to improve consumer advocacy at Oklahoma Insurance Department
text:
From left, Craig MacIntyre and Bob Sullivan are pictured. (Provided photos)OKLAHOMA CITY —  As he’s criss-crossed the state over the past few months, Craig MacIntyre said there’s a growing perception among Oklahomans that insurance feels like a scam.
About a decade ago, MacIntyre said about 1 in 100 people would have raised their hand when asked if insurance felt like a scam. Recently, when he spoke to a room of over 100 people while campaigning for insurance commissioner, every single person raised their hand.
MacIntyre said that’s concerning because “insurance is the backbone of the financial system of Oklahoma” and a requirement to drive a car or own a home.
“So we’re mandating that the consumer purchase a product that they have no faith in,” he said. “Nothing good is going to come out of that.”
The Tecumseh Democrat is running against Republican Bob Sullivan on the Nov. 3 ballot to become the state’s next insurance commissioner. Republican Glen Mulready, who has held the job for the past eight years, cannot run again due to term limits.
Amid soaring premiums, higher deductibles and issues with the insurance claims process, both Sullivan and MacIntyre are vowing to not only lower rates, which are the highest in the nation, but to fix the consumer advocacy division at the State Department of Insurance.
Both men agree the division, which is supposed to help Oklahomans address issues with their insurance policies, is not doing enough to advocate for insured consumers.
MacIntyre, 60, who has worked over half his life in a variety of insurance industry roles, said he’s dismayed at how bad rates and the claims process seem to be getting.
He said the Oklahoma Insurance Department has only two constitutionally mandated responsibilities — implement and enforce the state’s insurance laws and to advocate for consumers.
“I think that the department has done a poor job on recognizing poor claims service and bad acting on the part of insurance companies relative to policyholders,” MacIntyre said. “I think we need to beef up the consumer advocacy side, and when complaints are made, they need to be taken more seriously.”
He said insurance companies also need to be protected from bad actors. That includes providing more oversight of the roofing industry and investigating and prosecuting organized crime rings that are purposely causing vehicle accidents in the state to try to collect insurance payouts. 
MacIntyre said he believes all roofers doing business in the state should be required to be licensed and insured. He said some residential roofers are not required to be, but they should be held to the same standards as commercial ones. Oklahomans deserve to know that whoever is working on their roof is doing it properly and if something goes wrong, they’ll be covered, he said.
“Most people think that (the insurance department’s role is) only to advocate for consumers, but we also have to make sure insurance companies can stay in business and are not spending a ridiculous excess amount of money on fraudulent activity, so that the rates can be assisted to stay low,” MacIntyre said.
In addition to the need to lower insurance rates, Sullivan, 41, of Inola, said he’s heard “loud and clear” from Oklahomans that the consumer advocacy part of the Insurance Department is not working well. He said when people contact the consumer advocacy division, they feel like nothing ever gets accomplished. 
“You get one of two form letters to fill out and then it goes into some innocuous black hole, never to be heard from again,” Sullivan said.
The Oklahoma Insurance Department did not return an email seeking comment.
Sullivan, an independent agent and broker who works with clients in over a dozen states, said very few people compared to the number of disgruntled Oklahomans are filing complaints with the Insurance Department because they feel disenfranchised with the process. The most frequent complaint is claim denials, but they also include how long it takes for an adjuster to respond and poor communication from an insurer, he said.
Sullivan said there were efforts in the state Legislature to shorten the window insurance companies have to respond, but those didn’t advance. Despite that, Sullivan said he’ll press for faster responses.
He said the consumer advocacy division must have the vision that they work for the four million people of Oklahoma, not insurers, and if someone calls with a problem, they should find a solution.
“Without that type of aggressive advocacy, you leave consumers with no other reproach but to go lawyer up and sue the insurance company, and some people do that successfully, but ultimately it slows things down, it drives up costs,” Sullivan said.
He said if the agency can do a better job finding meaningful solutions for consumers, not only will that increase consumer confidence, but it will also result in a “dramatic improvement to the cost” of insurance, which will be reflected in better rates down the line.
“But we have to have that attitude of being there to protect the consumers,” he said. “That’s why we have an insurance commissioner to balance a very uneven playing field where the insurance companies are seemingly holding all the cards.”
The general election is Nov. 3. Polls open at 7 a.m. and close at 7 p.m. In-person early voting begins Wednesday and runs through Saturday.

name: VTDigger
title: Big Labor isn’t playing straight with Vermonters about Prop 3
text:
This commentary is by Mark Mix, president of the National Right to Work Committee.
For 233 years, the Vermont Constitution has done two essential things: set up the framework of state and local government, and safeguard the individual rights of every citizen — free speech, due process and more — often more comprehensively than the U.S. Constitution. Many Green Mountain Staters would agree that’s exactly what a constitution is for.
Unfortunately, Big Labor special interests strongly disagree. They want to use the Vermont Constitution to entrench coercive legal privileges already afforded by making it nearly impossible for future lawmakers and statewide executives to revoke them.
That’s what Proposal 3 is all about. Effectively, it has two core provisions. One would enshrine in the Vermont Constitution the power of government union officials, but no other private citizens, to co-determine with elected officials or their appointees how civil servants are compensated and managed.
The other would similarly constitutionalize the power of private-sector union officials to get workers fired for refusing to fork over money to a union they may not want and never asked for.
Poll after poll shows compulsory union financial support is extremely unpopular with Americans, regardless of age, race, education, marital status or political affiliation.

READ MORE

For example, a 2024 nationwide survey conducted by RMG Research showed that 82% of registered voters agree that workers “should never be forced to join a union or pay dues to a union as a condition of employment.” The survey also found support for the right-to-work principle is overwhelming among Republicans, Democrats and independents, as well as among employed union members and union-free workers.
The Teamsters and other union bigwigs funding the so-called Yes on 3 campaign clearly know compulsory dues are not what the vast majority of citizens want. That’s why their description of what the measure would do fails to acknowledge that one of its key purposes is to ensure that, even if Vermonters elect pro-right-to-work legislative majorities and a pro-right-to-work governor, Big Labor’s power to collect union dues and fees as a job condition won’t be jeopardized. 
There is simply no credible justification for forcing employees to bankroll a union if they choose not to belong to it. Even some academic apologists for organized labor make no bones about the fact that workers whose productivity is above average typically get paid less when they are unionized.
A case in point is Richard Rothstein, now a distinguished fellow with the Big Labor-funded Economic Policy Institute, whose board includes the heads of major unions. In a brief survey of union-friendly academic literature on the impact exclusive union bargaining has on the pay of employees with diverse levels of skill and industriousness, Rothstein acknowledged that in unionized firms, the wages of lower-paid workers are raised above the market rate, with the increase offset in part by reducing pay of the most productive workers. 
There is no moral justification for denying employees who oppose unionization the choice not to bankroll a union. Nor are there any economic grounds for doing so. Public opinion and the facts are lined up against Big Labor’s goal of enshrining forced union financial support, on pain of termination, in the Vermont Constitution.
It’s not so surprising, then, that the advocates of Proposal 3 aren’t candidly stating that’s what it would do. But that’s the reality.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Lawrence delivers campaign’s closing message as he preps for final election push
text:
Democratic Congressional candidate William Lawrence announces his final push to mobilize voters as he stands outside of U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett's (R-Charlotte) former office in Lansing on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)With one week left until Election Day, Democratic nominee William Lawrence gathered supporters outside of the building that previously held Rep. Tom Barrett’s (R-Charlotte) office as he announced his final push to reach voters within Michigan’s highly competitive 7th Congressional District.
“This campaign has always been about people, whereas Tom Barrett’s term in office has always been about doing the bidding of Donald Trump and the wealthiest few in this country,” Lawrence said, as he announced his plan to visit 24 towns across the district to talk with voters and share his campaign’s message in the final stretch of the race. 
Michigan’s 7th Congressional District encompasses Clinton, Shiawassee, Ingham, and Livingston counties and parts of Eaton, Genesee and Oakland counties, and has built a reputation as one of the most competitive U.S. House districts in the nation. The race is also the most expensive in the nation for advertising, with WKAR reporting $61 million in spending as of Oct. 21.
Reflecting on his campaign, Lawrence pointed to his efforts to meet with voters and help community members, including a 36-hour sit-in and food drive outside Barrett’s office, collecting donations for the Greater Lansing Food Bank and raising funds to eliminate $130,000 in local medical debt. 
“That set the tone from the very beginning on both sides,” Lawrence said. “He’s doing the bidding of Trump in D.C., I’m here strengthening our community and helping the helpers all across Mid Michigan.” 
Over the past two years, Lawrence said life has become harder for people in his community, while it’s become easier for the wealthy. 
“Already, 130,000 fewer Michiganders are insured than two years ago because of the cuts to the Affordable Care Act, and in January, hundreds of thousands more are at risk of losing their Medicaid,” Lawrence said in reference to work requirements for Medicaid recipients set to take effect in January.
Democratic Congressional candidate William Lawrence delivers his closing message of the race outside of U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett's (R-Charlotte) former office in Lansing on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)Democratic Congressional candidate William Lawrence discusses the contrast between his record of service and U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett's (R-Charlotte) while standing outside Barrett's former office on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)Kelly Kussmaul, who lives down the street from the site of a proposed hyperscale data center in Mason, shares support for Democratic Congressional candidate William Lawrence during a press conference on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)Jeff Breslin, president of the Professional Employee Council of Sparrow Hospital-Michigan Nurses Association shares how Republican healthcare policies will impact workers during a press conference held by Democratic Congressional candidate William Lawrence on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
“Meanwhile, over 160,000 people have lost their food assistance, and the cost of diesel and gas, of course, are squeezing us because of this outrageous war in Iran,” Lawrence said. “The rent, meanwhile, is still too damn high, as it has been. So I want to ask: Is your American dream nearer or farther away now than it was two years ago?”
Several community members also took to the podium to share their own concerns around data center development, the war in Iran and how Republican policies could harm healthcare workers and further increase the costs of care.
Kelly Kussmaul, who lives down the road from a proposed hyperscale data center in Mason, pointed to comments Trump made in an interview with Time Magazine stating “I would like to have data centers. It doesn’t mean I want them right next to my house, but certainly I like them in my county.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“The president might not want a data center next to his house, but he wants one next to mine, and someday maybe yours,” Kussmaul said. “That’s why we need representatives like Will Lawrence. Will understands that Michigan’s small towns – Mason, Leslie, Eaton Rapids, St. John’s, Charlotte, Howell, Williamston – are not for sale to giant corporations run by billionaires you’ll never meet.”
Jeff Breslin, president of the Professional Employee Council of Sparrow Hospital-Michigan Nurses Association, noted that one in four Michigan residents receives healthcare through Medicaid, while Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act reduces Medicaid spending by nearly $1trillion over the course of a decade.
“Michigan hospitals stand to lose billions,” Breslin said. “When hospitals lose money, they don’t cut from the executive level. They close units, then they cut staff, and in worst cases, they close hospitals. The staff are being asked to do more with less. This is not acceptable. These cuts will lead to worse patient outcomes.”
While Lawrence gathered supporters in Lansing, Barrett took the stage in Howell ahead of Vice President JD Vance, urging voters to come out in support of Republican candidates at the national and state level. 
U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte) speaks during a rally with Vice President JD Vance on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026 at CHI Aviation in Howell, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
Speaking with Michigan Advance, Barrett campaign strategist Jason Roe said the representative shares the frustrations residents have with Trump, noting Barrett’s opposition to the Iran War and legislation he has introduced to protect communities from AI and Data centers.
While Lawrence has proposed a yearlong moratorium on data center development to establish regulations, Barrett has introduced legislation to ban government officials from signing nondisclosure agreements concerning data centers as well as a bill to bar federal agencies from overriding local zoning and permitting for data centers, arguing that the decisions around whether to host a data center should be left up to the communities.
Roe also responded to Lawrence’s criticisms of Barrett’s constituent services, arguing that his record speaks for itself.
“In addition to the more than 1,000 constituent case issues resolved, Tom has personally met with more than 600 different people and organizations in the district in his two years,” Roe said. “He was able to secure $146 million in funding for the district, including Michigan State, the regional airport, public safety and infrastructure.”
Michigan Advance Senior Reporter Ben Solis contributed to this report.

name: Delaware
title: Walk to End Alzheimer’s brings renewed urgency to Wilmington Saturday
text:
As medical advances help more Americans survive cancer and heart disease, Delaware Alzheimer’s advocates call for greater attention to a disease that remains incurable.
By George D. Rotsch, Delaware LIVE News
WILMINGTON, Del. — As medical advances help more Americans survive cancer and heart disease, another major health challenge continues to confront families across Delaware: Alzheimer’s disease, a progressive and ultimately fatal illness for which there is still no cure.
That growing concern will bring families, caregivers, volunteers and supporters together Saturday, Oct. 31, for Wilmington’s annual Walk to End Alzheimer’s at Tubman-Garrett Riverfront Park.
Organized by the Alzheimer’s Association Delaware Chapter, the event is part of the world’s largest fundraising effort dedicated to Alzheimer’s care, support and research. But organizers say the walk also serves another important purpose: reminding the community that progress against other major diseases should be matched by a greater commitment to fighting Alzheimer’s.
For Glen Gray, board chair of the Alzheimer’s Association Delaware Chapter, the contrast between medical progress against other major diseases and the continuing challenge of Alzheimer’s underscores the importance of the annual walk.
“We have made tremendous progress in the fight against cancer and heart disease, and more Americans are surviving illnesses that once claimed so many lives,” Gray said. “But there is a heartbreaking reality. Too many people who have survived cancer or heart disease may be later diagnosed with Alzheimer’s. They have fought and won one battle, only to face a disease for which there is still no cure. That’s why this walk is becoming more important every year. We need to bring the same urgency, commitment and resources to Alzheimer’s that have helped us make such extraordinary progress against other major diseases.”
Medical progress highlights the Alzheimer’s challenge
There is evidence supporting the broader concern.
According to the American Cancer Society, the nation’s overall cancer death rate has declined dramatically since 1991, reflecting improvements in prevention, early detection and treatment. Five-year relative survival for cancer patients has reached approximately 70% for those diagnosed between 2015 and 2021.
Heart disease mortality has also declined over the longer term as advances in treatment, medications and prevention have helped more patients live longer.
Alzheimer’s presents a different challenge.
According to the Alzheimer’s Association’s 2026 Facts and Figures report, approximately 7.4 million Americans ages 65 and older are living with Alzheimer’s dementia. Between 2000 and 2024, reported Alzheimer’s deaths increased 134%, while deaths from heart disease and stroke declined.
New Alzheimer’s treatments offer hope by slowing disease progression in some patients, particularly in the earlier stages. However, there is still no treatment that cures the disease.
As more Americans live into their 70s, 80s and beyond, Alzheimer’s and other dementias present an increasingly significant challenge for families and the nation’s health care system.
More than 22,000 Delawareans living with Alzheimer’s
The Alzheimer’s Association estimates that approximately 22,300 Delaware residents are living with Alzheimer’s, while another 37,000 residents provide unpaid care for people with Alzheimer’s or other dementias.
The disease affects far more than memory. As Alzheimer’s progresses, patients can lose their ability to manage finances, drive, communicate, recognize loved ones and eventually perform basic daily activities.
For family caregivers, the responsibilities can last years and often require major changes to employment, household finances and personal schedules.
According to the association, Delaware dementia caregivers provide approximately 67 million hours of unpaid care annually, representing an estimated $1.7 billion in economic value.
Those figures underscore the importance of community resources, family education, respite services and continued medical research.
The Alzheimer’s Association provides educational programs, caregiver support and a 24-hour helpline to assist families confronting these challenges.
Promise Garden honors those affected by the disease
One of Saturday’s most meaningful traditions will be the Promise Garden ceremony, during which participants carry colorful flowers representing their personal connections to Alzheimer’s.
Blue flowers represent people living with Alzheimer’s or another dementia. Purple flowers honor individuals who have died from the disease. Yellow flowers recognize those caring for someone with Alzheimer’s, while orange flowers represent supporters of the cause.
Together, the flowers symbolize the different ways Alzheimer’s touches families and the shared determination to find effective treatments and ultimately a cure.
For participants who have lost loved ones, the ceremony offers an opportunity for remembrance. For those currently caring for someone with dementia, it provides a sense of community and reassurance that they are not facing the disease alone.
The event also brings together businesses, civic organizations, health care professionals and individuals who raise funds through teams and personal contributions.
Supporting research, treatment and families
Since its beginnings as Memory Walk in 1989, the Alzheimer’s Association’s nationwide walking initiative has mobilized millions of Americans in support of its mission.
Money raised helps advance research while supporting education, advocacy and assistance for patients and caregivers.
With an aging population and an increasing number of families affected by dementia, the work has taken on greater importance.
The association is encouraging Delaware residents to participate in Saturday’s Wilmington event by walking, forming a team, volunteering or contributing financially.
Residents who cannot participate in Wilmington will have another opportunity Saturday, Nov. 14, when the Southern Delaware Walk to End Alzheimer’s takes place. That event was rescheduled from its original fall date.
The two Delaware walks are part of the association’s broader national effort to turn public awareness into meaningful progress against the disease.
For families confronting Alzheimer’s today, that progress cannot come soon enough.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC Gov, AG call for data center owners to help pay for new power plants
text:
As power-hungry data centers proliferate, states are searching for ways to protect utility customers from the steep costs of upgrading the electrical grid, trying instead to shift the cost to AI-driven tech companies. (Photo: Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)North Carolina Gov. Josh Stein and Attorney General Jeff Jackson called on state regulators Tuesday to require prospective data center developers to shoulder more of the cost for the additional power they’ll need — or to produce more of it themselves through renewable energy.
The N.C. Utilities Commission has been working for months with Duke Energy and other stakeholders to iron out how data centers should be charged for the power they need. On Oct. 7, Duke announced the group had reached an agreement on a large-load tariff on data centers, as well as requirements that data centers pay for any grid upgrades needed, like transmission lines and substations.
According to the N.C. Department of Justice, Amazon, Meta affiliate Andale LLC, Google and Microsoft have all agreed to the deal, along with the United States Department of Defense and all other federal agencies.
The Utilities Commission still has to vote to approve the proposed agreement.
Stein called the proposal “a step in the right direction,” but said it’s inadequate because it doesn’t require data center owners to help pay for any new power plants the state will have to build to supply their needs.
“The overall rate of load growth projected in the next 15 years is at least five times what it was in the previous 20 years,” Stein said. ”Data centers make up about 80% of that future projected energy demand,” Stein said.
Stein said a new report produced by the state’s Energy Policy Task Force found that by 2050, the additional power that data centers will need is projected to cost North Carolina about $50 billion.
“If nothing changes, then we’re all going to end up having to pay for that in our electricity bills. It is absolutely unacceptable,” Stein said.
The governor also urged the commission to consider requiring data centers to “build or bring their own clean energy.” In other states, he said, tech giants like Meta, Google and Amazon have agreed to build or fund hundreds of megawatts of wind, solar and battery storage projects to offset their power needs.
Judge rules Chatham County data center can proceed despite moratorium

“If just half of the new large customers directly pay for or bring the clean energy that they need and operate that flexibly, it will save ratepayers $20 billion,” Stein said.  “There is no reason why the largest, wealthiest companies in the history of the world cannot be required to pay for the energy generation and transmission costs that they put onto the system.”
Jackson also urged the commission to approve the deal as a starting point. But he suggested that a large-load tariff might not be sufficient. He said regulators should consider creating an entirely new rate class for large data centers, which he said would better ensure they pay their share.
“We have residential, we have commercial, we have industrial, but really these data centers exist as a separate category because of the sheer amount of energy” they need, Jackson said.
“The Utilities Commission has not rendered a final judgment here yet. So while there is still time on the clock, the governor and I are making our case to the Utilities Commission to have strong defenses for families and your average ratepayer to make sure that costs are not shifted onto them,” Jackson said.
Asked for comment, Duke Energy spokesperson Bill Norton didn’t specifically address Stein’s and Jackson’s recommendations.
“Powering the demands of a growing state at the lowest possible cost requires balanced, diverse energy sources and is at the heart of the Carolinas Resource Plan and our recent settlement on a large load tariff,” Norton said in an email. “We look forward to continuing to work with Governor Stein, the North Carolina Utilities Commission, and other engaged partners on clean energy programs that can benefit all customers.”
No date has been set yet for the Utilities Commission to act on the proposed deal.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana unveils medical frailty exception to upcoming HIP work requirements
text:
Medicaid Chief Clinical Officer Katrina Etter speaks on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, at a quarterly financial review meeting. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)State officials on Tuesday revealed how they’ll apply a new federal definition for medical frailty, a key but contested exemption to fast-approaching work requirements for tens of thousands of Medicaid expansion enrollees.
The Healthy Indiana Program served roughly 475,000 Hoosiers as of Sept. 30, according to a quarterly financial presentation from the Family and Social Services Administration, with an “expansion” population of of 355,00 working-age adults who earn slightly too much for traditional Medicaid coverage.
Expansion enrollees face work requirements starting Jan. 1. They will need to demonstrate they’ve been working, volunteering or in school for 80 hours a month — for three months prior to their application or redetermination — to remain insured. Earning at least $580 a month — the equivalent of 80 hours at a minimum-wage job — would also count.
How will Indiana define medical frailty? State is still working out the details.

There will be exceptions for people considered medically frail, along with parents of younger children, participants in certain drug treatment programs, and more.
The state already uses the concept of medical frailty, but for a different purpose: a distinct benefit package within the HIP program. Now, it’ll be redefined for use as an exclusion from the work requirements.
A new federal framework narrows medical frailty to five statutory categories, like people considered blind or disabled under the Social Security Act. The other categories include physical, developmental or intellectual disabilities; disabling mental disorders; substance use disorders; and serious or complex medical conditions.
There’s another key change: someone who falls within one of the categories is only considered medically frail when their condition significantly impairs their ability to satisfy the work requirements.
The state will make decisions starting next year. Officials will use a new tool called Milliman Advanced Risk Adjusters, or MARA, which will sweep through all of the claims data available to the state.
“We have specifically customized it for the purpose of evaluating claims against the new federal definition,” Chief Clinical Officer Katrina Etter said of the tool. The frail will be excluded from work requirements for six months at a time.
New tool to determine frailty, with clinician team backup
Officials outlined three paths to the exemption.
Tier 1 is “diagnosis-based.” MARA will identify members with a medical diagnosis off a state list of conditions. Tier 2 is “evidence-based.” MARA will review qualifying conditions along with treatments, services or supports a member is receiving. Both will be reviewed continually.
A Sept. 30 run of the tool estimated nearly 140,000 people will qualify as medically frail under those mechanisms.
“If somebody does not hit medically frail through the use of that tool in one of those first two tiers, that’s when they can submit supplemental information for our clinical team to review,” Medicaid Chief Operating Officer Lindsey Lux said.
Under the third tier, a participant, provider, managed care organization or the state can make a recommendation or referral. State clinical staff will evaluate supporting documentation — medical records, treatments notes, medication lists, lab results — and make a decision.
Indiana officials outlined how they’ll determine who is “medically frail” and exempt from upcoming work requirements for the Healthy Indiana Plan’s Medicaid expansion members. (Screenshot from presentation)
The clinical team has just three full-time staff members for now.
“I do anticipate that we will need to build the team over time,” Etter said. “But I do think we want to see the volume of that tier three pathway, which will help inform what that looks like.”
Along with hiring, officials are working to refresh online guidance, create forms and more. They plan to run MARA again next month and send out mailers with medical frailty determinations by late November or early December, according to Etter.
“It’ll say: based on the information that we have today, we deem that you are meeting frail status, and then they won’t need to do anything,” she said. “If they get a notice that says, ‘Based on the information that we have today, we cannot determine that you are medically frail. If you believe that is an error, here’s your pathway to submit information.'”
The state estimates that nearly a quarter of the projected medically frail plan members will qualify through disabling mental disorders alone. There’s no tier 1 pathway for that category of conditions, meaning that MARA will need to capture those people under tier 2 or they’ll have to undergo manual review by the state’s clinical team.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: McKee names interim health and human services secretary
text:
Richard Charest, secretary of the Rhode Island Executive Office of Health and Human Services, left, attends an event at the State House in April 2025. Rhode Island Medicaid Director Kristin Sousa, right, will become interim secretary this week as Charest departs for a new role. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)Kristin Sousa, Rhode Island’s Medicaid program director, will serve as interim secretary of the Executive Office of Health and Human Services starting Oct. 29, Gov. Dan McKee announced Tuesday.
Sousa fills the opening left by Richard Charest, who is leaving the cabinet-level position at the end of the month to take a job as CEO of Roger Williams Medical Center and Our Lady of Fatima Hospital. 
McKee touted Sousa for her healthcare experience, including her current role overseeing all aspects of the state’s $5.2 billion Medicaid program covering one-third of Rhode Island residents.
“Director Sousa is an experienced state leader who has the knowledge and skills to step seamlessly into this role,” McKee said in a statement. “She understands the important work happening across EOHHS. I thank her for stepping up during this transition and for her continued commitment to serving the people of Rhode Island.” 
A graduate of Providence College with a bachelor’s degree in health services administration, Sousa has worked for the state since 2018, and as Medicaid program director since April 2022, according to her LinkedIn page. She previously worked as a senior program operations manager for Xerox State Healthcare, a subsidiary of the Xerox Corporation that managed government healthcare programs, according to her LinkedIn. A copy of Sousa’s resume was not immediately available.
As leader of the sweeping health and human services agency, Sousa will oversee nearly 200 employees and a $6.4 million budget encompassing public and mental health, hospitals, veterans services and those for children, families and people with disabilities. 
Both Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) are in the midst of major overhauls to eligibility and administration under the federal rescission package known as H.R. 1. Charest, who initially planned to retire on July 3, agreed to stay longer to help guide the state through the changes in Medicaid and SNAP, alongside spending of a $156 million federal grant for rural healthcare. His last day with the state will be Oct. 31.
There is no plan to search for a permanent health and human services secretary. McKee will be leaving office in January after losing his reelection bid in the Democratic primary. None of the gubernatorial candidates — Democrat Helena Buonanno Foulkes, Republican Aaron Guckian and independent Ken Block — have commented on their plans to hire a new agency leader.
“My priority is to maintain continuity and stability in the vital programs and services Rhode Islanders depend on while supporting a smooth and seamless transition to the next administration,” Sousa said in a statement. “I remain committed to serving individuals, families, and communities across our state and ensuring that EOHHS continues to deliver on its mission throughout this transition.” 
John Bonin, deputy Medicaid director, will assume Sousa’s previous role overseeing day-to-day operations of the state program.
