name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri appeals court rejects prison math that turned 23-year sentence into 40 years
text:
Deandre Pointer, serving four concurrent 23-year-sentences in the Missouri Department of Corrections, won a ruling Tuesday that he must get credit for all time he has served on all four counts of his conviction. If he had lost, Pointer would have been incarcerated for 40 years. He is shown in a 2025 interview (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).A Missouri man who should have been eligible for release in 2024 remains in prison because the state miscalculated his credit for time he had already served, the Missouri Western District Court of Appeals ruled Tuesday.
Deandre Pointer was sentenced to 23 years in the Department of Corrections on four counts, two of second-degree murder and two of armed criminal action, with the sentences to run concurrently. He received the sentence in 2023 after a Jackson County judge determined Pointer was abandoned by his public defender in a post-conviction case filed after his original sentence was handed down in 2005.
When the resentencing was finished, Pointer thought he would be out in about a year, when he had served the required 85% of the sentence. But when a Missouri Department of Corrections record clerk finished processing his paperwork, his projected release date was 2044.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The department misapplied the law on how to calculate his sentence, Judge Alok Ahuja wrote in the court’s unanimous opinion.
“The Missouri Supreme Court has held that, ‘in construing (state law), we are guided by the principle that criminal statutes must be ‘construed strictly against the (s)tate and liberally in favor of the defendant,’” Ahuja wrote.
The 2023 resentencing changed both the charge in one count, from first- to second-degree murder, and the way the sentences were imposed, from consecutive to concurrent.
“Pointer’s conviction and sentence for first-degree murder on Count 1 must be treated as if they never occurred,” Ahuja wrote.
In a 2025 interview with The Independent, Pointer said he pursued a new sentence because he was a victim of crime, forced to help the perpetrator out of fear for his own safety. 
The stress of having to fight for release after winning his resentencing has taken a severe toll, he said at the time.
Missouri math: How a 23-year sentence adds up to more than 40 years in prison

“I never took anxiety meds,” Pointer said. “Never in my life. Now, you know, I have to take anxiety meds just to have a functional day.”
Pointer’s attorney, Kent Gipson, said in an email that Pointer is pleased with the ruling but knows it will not result in his immediate release. The state can seek rehearing or transfer to the Missouri Supreme Court, and Gipson said he expects it to challenge the decision.
The Western District decision overturned a February ruling from Cole County Circuit Judge Brian Stumpe that found the department had calculated the sentence correctly.
“It should have never come to this,” Gipson said. “If the (corrections) officials had done this earlier, it would have likely resulted in my client receiving a parole hearing and an outdate three years ago.”
Pointer was arrested in June 2004 on one count of first-degree murder, one count of second-degree murder and two counts of armed criminal action. He was convicted the following year, sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole for first-degree murder and life in prison for second-degree murder and two counts of armed criminal action.
Those sentences were ordered to run consecutively
After his 2005 trial, Pointer said, prosecutors offered him a deal of 18 to 20 years in prison if he would testify against the person who committed the killings. But Pointer says he was forced at gunpoint to help dispose of the first body, and was tied to a chair during the second murder. 
He believed he was innocent and was unwilling to admit to committing a crime, he said.
“I told (the prosecutor) I would testify, but I do not want to take the plea for something I did not do,” Pointer said. “I testified, but I didn’t take the plea, because I wanted to keep my appeals open.”
After the resentencing, the department credited Pointer with 6,929 days on the changed first count but only 557 days on the other three.
In the opinion, Ahuja wrote that the court found the argument about the calculation mistake was enough to decide the case. The court did not address Pointer’s arguments that holding him constituted cruel and unusual punishment in violation of the Constitution and that the department violated his due process rights in its actions.
The case centered on Pointer’s prison “face sheet,” a document recording his sentence and parole eligibility dates. The department initially calculates those dates within 90 days of a person’s arrival in prison and recalculates them after resentencing.
The department tried to limit the credit after Pointer’s resentencing by arguing that while second-degree murder replaced first-degree murder as the first count of the charges, he was still convicted on that first count. 
But the department had no authority to disregard the new sentence, Ahuja wrote.
“Pointer’s June 2023 sentences are not subject to collateral attack in this proceeding,” Ahuja wrote, “and the department had no authority to disregard the sentencing court’s orders.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Pretti family: ‘We have not heard anything from the federal government’
text:
Alex Pretti’s parents, Susan and Michael Pretti, speak during a press conference Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026 in downtown Minneapolis alongside their attorney Steve Schleicher, calling for the federal government to release evidence and cooperate with state officials in the investigation into their son’s death at the hands of federal agents last January. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Nine months after Customs and Border Patrol agents shot and killed Alex Pretti in south Minneapolis, Pretti’s parents are publicly calling on the U.S. Justice Department to release information and evidence related to Pretti’s killing.
“We are here today begging for the Department of Justice to do what is right — to hold the men who killed our son accountable for what they did,” Alex’s mother Susan Pretti said at a press conference in Minneapolis Tuesday. 
Customs and Border Patrol agents tackled Alex Pretti to the ground, disarmed him, then shot him in the back several times on Jan. 24 during Operation Metro Surge. Six days later, Attorney General Todd Blanche announced the FBI was opening a civil rights investigation into the killing. But federal prosecutors have not charged any of the agents involved, and after much back-and-forth over evidence sharing, Minnesota law enforcement leaders said in a court filing last week that the feds are again refusing to hand over key pieces of evidence to local investigators. 
The federal government is also stonewalling the Pretti family, they said.
“We have not heard anything from the federal government,” Alex’s father Michael Pretti said. He called out the U.S. Attorney for the District of Minnesota, Daniel Rosen, by name: “(He) has stonewalled us for nine months, refusing to share a single update at any time. His only words have been, ‘I can’t tell.’”
Steve Schleicher, the family’s attorney, said he sent a letter to the Justice Department three months ago on behalf of the Pretti family, requesting information about the investigation, including the names of the shooters. (The shooters were independently identified by ProPublica, but not by the federal government.)
“We haven’t received a response,” Schleicher said. “We have not even received acknowledgement.”
The Pretti family, while pressuring the federal government to move forward with the investigation, also wanted to tell the public more about Alex. 
He researched molecular biology at the University of Minnesota before becoming a nurse in the intensive care unit at the Minneapolis VA Medical Center. He grew up in Wisconsin in a “in a tight and a blessed family,” his father said. 
“He understood right from wrong, and did not tolerate bullies,” Susan Pretti said. “He was intensely curious. He always wanted to do the right thing.”
Michael Pretti said the family has received more than 2,000 letters and cards from people mourning Alex. They brought some from their home in Colorado to display on the table in front of them as they spoke. 
“Thank you to the strangers who have written to us,” Susan Pretti said. “That has truly helped us with our grief.”
A portrait of Alex Pretti sits with some of his belongings and sympathy cards as his parents, Susan and Michael Pretti, speak at a press conference Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026 in downtown Minneapolis. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)

name: Source New Mexico
title: Commentary: A New Mexico political boss’ legacy lives on — in Maryland
text:
Brian Naranjo, a Democratic nominee for a seat on the Talbot County Council, is the grandson of the late New Mexico political patrón Emilio Naranjo -- whom the author covered early in his career. (Photo courtesy Naranjo campaign)

Over my 30 years writing about Maryland, I’ve invariably run into people in the political universe here who, like me, grew up in New York City. Or maybe went to school there. Or lived there at some point in their lives.
It’s been harder, though, to find people in Maryland politics who share a connection to another important time in my life – when I lived in New Mexico in the 1990s.
New Mexico is where I became a parent, so it will always be precious to me for that reason alone. I think about the jaw-dropping beauty of the state every day.
And I did some of my best professional work there, as a staff writer for the alt-weekly Santa Fe Reporter — exposing an oil and gas company’s attempts to rip off taxpayers, giving an insurgent candidate for mayor ammunition to topple the well-funded establishment favorite, and covering notable New Mexico politicians like Bill Richardson, Tom Udall and Gary Johnson fairly early in their careers.
Since I came to Maryland from New Mexico in late 1995, I learned that former Lt. Gov. Kathleen Kennedy Townsend (D) obtained her law degree at the University of New Mexico while her then-husband taught at the St. John’s College campus in Santa Fe (he later moved to the Annapolis campus, bringing KKT to Maryland). And I discovered that former Maryland Attorney General Brian Frosh (D) worked at the start of his career for the New Mexico attorney general’s office.
But those are the only two people I know who shared the Maryland-New Mexico political bond with me. Until now.
Just a few weeks ago, I was delighted and amazed to learn that Brian Naranjo, a retired foreign service officer and a Democratic candidate for the Talbot County Council, is the grandson of a Emilio Naranjo, who was the Democratic boss of Rio Arriba County, New Mexico, from the 1950s through the 1990s. He’s running with the support of Kathleen Kennedy Townsend – whose storied family had close ties with Emilio Naranjo.
The elder Naranjo, who died in 2008 at age 92, was a powerful and controversial figure who ruled the politics of Rio Arriba with an iron first. Over the years he was county sheriff, the chair of the Rio Arriba Democratic Party, a federal marshal in Albuquerque, and a state senator – which is where I got to see him in action.
But more importantly, he was the man to see for political favors in Rio Arriba County for over four decades, if you were looking for a government job, say, or a political appointment, or some kind of favorable decision from local government – or if you were running for higher office.
Famously, Emilio Naranjo campaigned with Ted Kennedy when Kennedy was stumping for his brother John F. Kennedy during the 1960 presidential campaign. Over the years, Naranjo campaigned again with Ted Kennedy, including in 1992, to support Bill Clinton’s White House bid, when I was out there.
Emilio Naranjo wasn’t beloved by everyone. He had political enemies. He was a patrón in the local parlance. Critics accused him of corruption. His deeds and misdeeds could fill a few books.
Brian Naranjo correctly calls his grandfather “the last boss in New Mexico.”
“I see the upside and the downside of that kind of political behavior,” he says.
Yet in a wide-ranging conversation with me, Brian Naranjo said he is running for Talbot County Council with many of the political lessons he learned from his grandfather and his father at the top of his mind.
“I do credit my grandfather for a lot of my instincts,” he said. “I translated it into diplomacy and now I’ve translated it into local politics.”
Brian Naranjo is hardly a political neophyte. He grew up in Montgomery County – his father, Emilio “Milo” Naranjo Jr., the eldest of the political leader’s nine children – came to Washington, D.C., to work for New Mexico Sen. Clinton Anderson (D) and later for NASA, all the while remaining an informal adviser to his father out in New Mexico.
Growing up, Brian Naranjo said, “We always talked politics. I can’t remember a day we didn’t.”
For 32 years, Naranjo applied what he learned to his work as a foreign service officer, through 16 postings on five continents, including stints in Venezuela, Canada, and Mexico.
On the campaign trail, he has talked about wanting to build bridges to poorer residents and communities – similar to the way Emilio Naranjo reached out to the economically impoverished Native American residents at the Santa Clara Pueblo in Rio Arriba County.
“My grandfather focused on Rio Arriba like a laser,” Naranjo said. “I see that as a model for Talbot, at a time when so many Republicans are focused on the MAGA side of the equation.”
Talbot County has become increasingly competitive politically. In 2020, Joe Biden became the first Democratic presidential contender to carry the county since 1964 – winning by 118 votes. Four years later, Donald Trump carried the county by just six votes.
Naranjo’s aggressive criticism of the status quo in Talbot County has brought him some harsh criticism. But he is unapologetic and argues that he’s helping to define the council race. And there too he sees some parallels with his grandfather.
Naranjo recalls his dad telling his grandfather that even with criticism from the local newspaper and some political opponents: “You are still driving the news here. They are reacting to you…Even your enemies can be useful to you under certain circumstances.”
But just as he’s critical of MAGA Republicans, Naranjo said he is also leery of Democrats who veer too far to the left or focus too heavily on national issues.
“When you grow up with Emilio Naranjo as your grandfather, you appreciate a politics that doesn’t exist anymore,” he said. “He grew up in the party of Roosevelt, Truman and JFK.”
Naranjo’s message to voters: “It’s more about pragmatism and solving problems and trying to meet people where they live.”
 
An extended version of this column appeared on Maryland Matters, which is part of States Newsroom, a nonprofit news network that includes Source New Mexico.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Gov. Lujan Grisham approves $8.25M for flooding, seeks additional federal assistance
text:
New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham on Oct. 26, 2026, announced she had approved $8.25 million in state funds to address widespread flooding, including in the Bloomfield area pictured above, and would push the federal government for more assistance to more areas. (Photo courtesy Elmer Ignacio)New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham’s office announced late Monday that she had approved $8.25 million in emergency funding for counties and pueblos recovering from severe floods and weather events. 
The governor’s office also noted the state intends to push the federal government for far more financial assistance than it has currently promised to the state as residents dig out from a disaster Lujan Grisham estimated this week will cost up to $300 million. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
President Donald Trump earlier Monday approved a federal disaster declaration due to the recent flooding that damaged thousands of homes in many northern New Mexico counties, as well as pueblos and the Navajo Nation. 
The declaration means the state can receive various forms of assistance from different federal agencies, including debris removal from the U.S. Army Corp of Engineers, flood monitoring from the U.S. Geological Survey and drinking water testing from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. 
But the declaration does not include assistance from the Federal Emergency Management Agency that the governor’s office and members of the state’s congressional declaration specifically requested. 
The declaration does not include funding from FEMA’s Public Assistance program, which reimburses local and tribal governments for up to 75% of costs they incur for debris cleanup and emergency protection. 
In a statement Monday evening, Lujan Grisham said she will continue to push for federal assistance beyond what Trump has agreed to provide so far. 
“New Mexico is facing its second major flood in a month, and our counties and Tribal nations have spent everything they have keeping people safe. They shouldn’t have to carry those costs alone,” she said. “I will keep pressing the federal government to do its part and get them the help they need.”
FEMA has agreed to provide assistance with mass shelters as needed, according to the governor’s office. FEMA officials did not respond to Source NM’s request for comment Tuesday on why the state will not receive Public Assistance funds. 
The federal declaration applies to San Juan, Rio Arriba, Cibola and Sandoval counties, as well as the San Ildefonso Pueblo, Zia Pueblo and Laguna Pueblo. 
But Lujan Grisham’s office has noted that storms and flooding have caused additional damage, namely in Santa Fe County — which experienced a rare tornado over the weekend — and Socorro County, where flooding has prompted evacuations and caused the death of a woman in the Rio Puerco, according to local officials.
New Mexico Gov. Lujan Grisham announces federal disaster aid for severe weather, flooding

Officials with the governor’s office said Monday they are preparing an additional disaster declaration request to the federal government that would include both counties, as well as reiterate the state’s case that local and tribal governments should receive reimbursement for debris cleanup and emergency response. 
While that federal request remains pending, the City of Santa Fe Mayor Michael Garcia on Monday issued an emergency proclamation that requests the governor also declare a state of emergency for the City of Santa Fe and make state resources available.
Michael Coleman, Lujan Grisham’s communications director, did not immediately respond to Source NM’s request for comment Tuesday about whether it had approved any state funding for Santa Fe. 
The governor’s office in late September approved $3.75 million in state funds to help with flooding across the state. It was not immediately clear Tuesday how the additional $8.25 million the governor approved will be apportioned among the communities dealing with the floods and other severe weather.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Wyandotte/Kansas City lawsuit settled, setting guidelines for local control on Chiefs project
text:
Gov. Laura Kelly, shown here at the December announcement that the Kansas City Chiefs will build a stadium in Kansas, says Kansas reached agreement to end a lawsuit filed by the Unified Government of Wyandotte/Kansas City. The local governments  objected to the way the deal was set up and could limit local power to make decisions. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — A lawsuit filed by local government officials challenging the state of Kansas over its deal with the Kansas City Chiefs to build a stadium was settled Friday. 
The Unified Government of Wyandotte County/Kansas City sued the state over concerns it was losing local control, specifically asking to stop implementation of House Bill 2466, or the Kansas Sports Facilities Authority Act. 
The act gave the state authority to make deals with the Chiefs and the Kansas City Royals to bring their stadiums across the state line. In its initial court filing, the local governments said they would lose “power to tax, to zone and plan, to set and collect local fees, and to provide utility service through the community’s own publicly-owned utility.”
Gov. Laura Kelly and Mayor Christal Watson said in a news release they “satisfactorily resolved concerns related to the Kansas City Chiefs Stadium project.”
The unified government agreed to dismiss the lawsuit without prejudice, the release said.
The agreement addresses concerns about the deal, including land use and utilities, the release said.  
The unified government and Wyandotte County Board of Public Utilities will retain jurisdiction on developments around the Chiefs stadium, including local planning and zoning and paying of the BPU payment in lieu of taxes, the release said. 
“The stadium and its parking areas will be State facilities owned by the Kansas Sports Facilities Authority (KSFA), not subject to local zoning or building codes, and leased to the Kansas City Chiefs for $7 million per year,” it said.
The unified government’s local pledge area will apply only within stadium, parking and ancillary development areas. 
“The collaboration in recent days has literally been a game changer,” Watson said in the release. 
The agreement includes a way for BPU to partner with Evergy regarding electric service for the stadium and outlines the way utilities will work, the news release said.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Federal government is again sending election monitors to New Hampshire next week
text:
The federal government is sending election observers to Manchester and Nashua as part of what it says will be the largest election obersvation effort in history. Shown here is an unoccupied observer area at a polling location in Nashua during November 2024's election. (Photo by Will Steinfeld/New Hampshire Bulletin)The U.S. Department of Justice will again be visiting polls in Manchester and Nashua during next week’s elections, the department told election officials.
Election monitoring is a longstanding practice that has attracted new partisan suspicion amid President Donald Trump’s rhetoric about elections and his attempts to insert the federal government into what has always been a state and local affair.
In emails to Deputy Secretary of State Brendan O’Donnell, Manchester City Clerk Mathew Normand and Nashua City Clerk Daniel Healey, the federal government said monitors will be at polling locations to verify that cities are abiding by the Voting Rights Act, the Voting Accessibility for the Elderly and Handicapped Act, the Help America Vote Act and other federal election laws.
The New Hampshire Secretary of State’s Office, photographed here on Feb. 11, 2026 in Concord, received an email last week from federal officials informing them of the election monitors. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
“The monitoring by the Civil Rights Division is done in the same way as in the past,” James Thomas Tucker, a trial attorney with the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division, wrote in the email. “Our monitors only observe and take notes. They do not intrude or interfere in any way in the voting process. Monitors will introduce themselves to the poll manager and present government ID (and a letter from the jurisdiction permitting entrance to the polls with the monitors’ names, if the jurisdiction wants each monitor identified).”
Tucker said monitors will wear “business casual clothing. No uniforms or pins identifying as DOJ are allowed.” They’ll “follow all rules of the state and jurisdiction,” are forbidden from carrying firearms and will not speak to voters, he said. And if they observe an issue, they’ll notify their team lead who may contact election officials.
Election monitors were also present during September’s primary elections in Manchester and Nashua. At the time, local election officials including Secretary of State David Scanlan said they were unconcerned and that election monitoring is standard.
Meanwhile, the DOJ sent a letter to Scanlan and other election officials across the country over the summer threatening him with “criminal liability” if he knowingly allows noncitizens to vote — something he has denied doing in interviews with the Bulletin. The Trump administration and Scanlan were also engaged in a monthslong legal battle until July over Trump’s unsuccessful attempts to force Scanlan to turn over confidential voter files.
In Tuesday’s election, the Trump administration is planning to send over 1,000 monitors across all 50 states in what Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon is calling “the biggest DOJ election observer effort in history.”
Harmeet Dhillon, shown here ahead of her April 2025 confirmation hearing in Washington, D.C., said the Department of Justice plans to send over 1,000 monitors in the department’s biggest election observation effort ever. (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
“They’re not going to be interfering in any way,” Dhillon said on cable network Real America’s Voice, “or running the election. They’re gonna be observing.”
However, election officials across the country are concerned about what the Trump administration may do and preparing for interference given the president’s recent actions.
Just last week, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit, seeking to preemptively block officials from certifying Alaska’s U.S. Senate results if the Republican doesn’t win over concerns that another candidates’ similar name will confuse voters.
Earlier this year, Trump called on Republicans to “nationalize” elections in some liberal-leaning states, ostensibly because those states allegedly allow undocumented immigrants to vote. Doing so would run counter to the U.S. Constitution, which specifies that states determine the “times, places, and manner” of elections in a purposefully decentralized system.
Additionally, in January, the FBI seized boxes of 2020 ballots from a Fulton County, Georgia, election center — a jurisdiction that’s at the heart of his false claims that the 2020 election was stolen from him.
On Tuesday, Democrats hope to take advantage of Trump’s low approval rating and the fact that the party in power typically does poorly in midterms to make big gains in the battle for Congress.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee blocks driver’s licenses for Dreamers, other immigrants with U.S. work permits
text:
The Department of Safety is blocking certain immigrants with valid federal work permits from obtaining drivers licenses, citing legislation enacted in 2025. Anti-immigrant legislation drew many protests that year including one pictured here in Nashville on February 3, 2025 . (John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee is rejecting applications for driver’s licenses from immigrants who are authorized by the federal government to work and live in the United States, a shift in policy that could strip thousands of longtime license-holders of the ability to legally drive, immigrant attorneys and advocates said.
The surprise change in Tennessee driver’s license rules, which lawyers and advocates said they first learned about through anxious client calls in recent weeks, could place immigrants permitted to work in the United States at risk for arrest, detention and subsequent deportation if caught driving to work, school or the grocery store without a license. 
Among those expected to be impacted are an estimated 6,000 “Dreamers” living in Tennessee. They are part of a federal immigration category known as DACA, or Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals for those brought here without legal status as children who are now protected from deportation. It is one of multiple categories of immigrants who are granted work permits by the government to live and work in the United States. 
Work permits do not denote permanent immigration status as a green card does, but they serve in many instances as the only official form of proof individuals receive from the government to show they are authorized to be in the country.
The credit-card sized permits contain detailed personal information, such as birth date, address and country of birth, a code signifying the individual’s specific authorized U.S. immigration status, immigration ID number and an expiration date.
Until now, the work permits have been accepted as sufficient proof that an individual is authorized to be in the country to obtain a Tennessee license. 



Quotation







“There were just a lot of feelings around not belonging in Tennessee, in a state that has been home for decades. Now the state is telling ‘you’re not welcome here, even though you have status. You don’t belong.'


– Jazmin Ramirez, Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition


State cites 2025 law change
A spokesperson for the Tennessee Department of Safety and Homeland Security confirmed last week the work permits are no longer accepted as proof of a valid immigration status for the purposes of obtaining a driver’s license. 
The spokesperson cited a portion of a 2025 state law that took effect Jan. 1 of this year, but does not appear to have been interpreted by state officials to deny licenses to DACA recipients and other immigrant work permit holders until recently. 
The law was sweeping in scope, with multiple provisions that included the creation of a new state immigration enforcement division and mandating local law enforcement collaboration with federal immigration agents. It was enacted as part of a slate of Tennessee Republican anti-immigration bills in 2025. 
Jason Pack, the spokesperson for the Department of Safety and Homeland Security, cited a provision of the state legislation that also requires applicants for temporary Tennessee driver’s licenses to provide documentation that establishes they have been “authorized by the federal government for a specific purpose and for a specified period of authorized stay.” 
Employment authorization documents do not provide  “sufficient information to verify an applicant’s lawful status and specified period of authorized stay,” he wrote via email.
A model for the nation? Tennessee GOP ushers in sweeping ‘Immigration 2026’ agenda

Hundreds of people have recently been denied a license renewal under the 2025 law cited by the spokesperson, according to advocates. Among them is a woman who has possessed a Tennessee license for 15 years.
Zavala is a Dreamer. She asked to be referred to only by her last name out of fear of retaliation from government authorities for speaking publicly.
The DACA program protects people from deportation who were brought to the country as children, and authorizes them to live and work in the United States. It is a temporary status that is periodically renewed by the federal government. DACA recipients have no direct route to becoming lawful permanent residents or citizens.
Zavala arrived in Tennessee from Mexico at age four and has held a valid Tennessee driver’s license since she was 18, she said. She is now 33.
Earlier this month, Zavala said she was blocked in two separate driver’s license stations from renewing her temporary license — a two-year, renewable license that has long been made available to immigrants in Tennessee with a federally-issued work permit.
Even as she presented the same paperwork she had each time she had previously renewed her license — the work permit, Social Security card and proof of home address — a state worker told her the papers were no longer acceptable proof she was legally authorized to be in the country, suggesting she provide other immigration paperwork instead. 
None of the other acceptable immigration documents listed for a Tennessee license are issued to DACA recipients.
‘I’m legally allowed to be in the States’
Without a license, Zavala cannot drive to her full-time job or take her daughter, who suffers from a chronic illness, to frequent medical and therapy appointments, Zavala said. 
“I have been on DACA since 2012,” she said. “I’ve never had an issue. My work permit is valid. I’m legally allowed to be in the States.”
“What concerns me the most is my little girl. I need to provide for her. How am I going to get her to the appointments she needs?”

Zavala has a partner she described as a devoted father, who also provides for their daughter and takes her to school and doctor’s appointments. “He has DACA, too,” she said.
Pack, the spokesperson for the Department of Safety and Homeland Security, did not specify when the department began interpreting the 2025 law to exclude immigrant work permits from a list of acceptable documents. The language of the law does not specify the types of documents necessary for authorized immigrants to obtain a license nor say that work permits are to be excluded. 
Peter McGraw, legal deputy director for the National Immigration Law Center, which tracks state legislation, disputed the state’s interpretation of the 2025 law’s language.

“Every state’s law is different,” he said. “Tennessee’s law makes clear that the federal government, not the state, determines whether an individual is authorized to be present in the United States. DACA recipients are authorized by the federal government to be present and work in the United States. I’m not aware of any other state denying driver’s licenses to DACA recipients contrary to its own laws.”
‘Acceptable documents’ exclude broad categories of immigrants
The employment card was listed as an acceptable document as late as August, according to an online website archive. By September, it had been erased from the state website.
Memphis immigration attorney Ari Sauer said he began getting calls two months ago from clients unable to complete routine temporary driver’s license renewals. 
None of the immigration documents now accepted for temporary Tennessee licenses are issued or available to DACA recipients, Sauer noted. The same is true for multiple other categories of immigrants whom the federal government has authorized to live and work legally in the country, he said.
“It’s a much bigger group than DACA,” who will not be able to get Tennessee licenses, said Sauer, a partner with the Siskind Susser law firm. 
The Tennessee Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights has asked the state to explain the rule changes, according to Jazmin Ramirez, director of advocacy. 
Ramirez said her organization has been receiving an uptick in calls from individuals across Tennessee who were unable to renew their licenses, especially DACA recipients, at the beginning of October. Other callers came from a “mix of categories” under immigration law, including certain people in the asylum process, she said. 
At a recent community meeting the organization held to hear from individuals denied licenses, Ramirez described a heavy atmosphere.
“There were just a lot of feelings around not belonging in Tennessee, in a state that has been home for decades,” Ramirez said. “Now the state is telling ‘you’re not welcome here, even though you have status. You don’t belong.’”
“This means in the practical sense people cannot get to work jobs they have been doing for many years. Parents aren’t able to drop off their kids or pick up their kids safely.” 
Ramirez also highlighted the risks for individuals who drive anyway, including getting pulled over, cited and taken into custody. “In the worst case scenario that means people could end up in the deportation pipeline,” she said.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Pillen requests federal aid for severe flooding in southeast Nebraska after early October storms
text:
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, front, is briefed on heavy rain and severe flooding in northern Lancaster County that occurred the night before on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Office of Gov. Jim Pillen)LINCOLN — Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen has requested a federal disaster declaration for severe flooding in eight counties in southeast Nebraska that occurred between Sept. 30 and Oct. 6.
Pillen had declared a state of emergency after the flooding on Oct. 1. At the time, the order did not specify the counties affected. His office announced the federal request to the Federal Emergency Management Agency on Tuesday and requested aid for Douglas, Fillmore, Lancaster, Saline, Sarpy, Saunders, Seward and Thayer counties.
A news release said the affected counties sustained damage to water control facilities, roadways, bridges, electrical infrastructure, schools, other public buildings and equipment.
Damage assessments have exceeded $23 million, Pillen’s office said. The estimate could rise.
“I have asked President Trump, through a request submitted to FEMA, to consider the extent of damage resulting from this extraordinary flooding event and to grant a request for public assistance, which will help cover the costs that communities, counties and our Natural Resource Districts will incur through repairs and recovery,” Pillen said in a statement.
President Donald Trump headlines a 2026 midterms rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds with thousands in attendance. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Pillen’s office said Lancaster, Thayer and Saunders counties had “extensive” debris to remove, and his office said rainfall was “particularly significant” in Douglas and Lancaster, the state’s most populous counties.
The governor has separately requested a disaster declaration from the U.S. Small Business Administration for Douglas County. Pillen’s office said at least 25 homes and/or businesses were damaged, exceeding uninsured losses of at least 40%. 
If the SBA disaster status is granted, affected property owners would have access to low-interest loans to assist with recovery.
When Trump visited Grand Island on Oct. 5, he said Pillen “calls me all the time, always looking for money for this state. I hate it, and I always give it to Jim Pillen.” The president said now-U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts, Pillen’s predecessor, also called frequently. 
Trump told the Grand Island crowd of a call with Ricketts, who had asked for $25 million after a flood. The president said he remarked, “Pete, that’s a lot of money,” but Trump explained to the crowd: “But you know, I won it three times. I say, ‘To hell with it. Give him the money.’”
Democratic senators pressed FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton during his confirmation hearing this summer on a perceived partisan tilt in which states get federal aid and how quickly.
Hamilton told senators that his focus would be to ensure FEMA “is objective, is fair and reasonable, follows the law, and is consistent in the approach to how we adjudicate and process claims and requests for disasters.” Hamilton was confirmed to the post in early August.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Asthma mortality rates in Jackson reach highest level in three years
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Jackson is among the most challenging cities in the United States if you’re living with asthma and has some of the highest rates of asthma-related deaths, says a 2026 report from the Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America.
Among the 100 largest metropolitan areas in the United States, Jackson ranks third in mortality rates linked to asthma. The common lung disease causes inflammation of the body’s airways, making it difficult to breathe.
Beyond counting the number of deaths, the nonprofit organization’s report looks at asthma prevalence and emergency department visits for asthma to rank the most challenging places in which to live with the chronic lung condition. Weighing these factors, researchers placed Jackson 36th on the list this year.  
These trends have worsened over recent years. In 2023, Jackson was the 63rd most challenging place to live with asthma out of the same 100 cities. By 2025, Jackson had moved up to 47th place. Previously lower asthma rates have gone up to be “average” with those cities, while deaths from asthma have declined below average.


“Not a lot of people know that (asthma) is life-threatening,” said Hannah Jaffee, research director at the foundation. During a severe asthma attack, the body’s airways narrow and can prevent enough oxygen from entering the bloodstream.
The most recent data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention shows that 239 Mississippians died from asthma between 2020 and 2024. While asthma deaths are rare, that number is likely an undercount, said Calandra Davis, the American Lung Association’s director of advocacy in Mississippi. When adjusted for population, Black Mississippians experienced a death rate twice as high as their white counterparts. Nationally, Black Americans are three times as likely to die from asthma as white Americans, and the rate is highest for Black women. 
“Structural and historical racism, at the systemic level, unfortunately has led to a lot of disparities that we see in terms of asthma prevalence, asthma-related emergency department visits and asthma related deaths,” said Jaffee.
While treatments for asthma have improved, racial and ethnic disparities have not, she said. She pointed to poverty from redlining, a practice where bankers denied investment in predominantly Black neighborhoods, and lack of health insurance as factors influencing the disparities. 
Research shows that many asthma-related deaths, especially for children and young adults, are preventable with better care and awareness of warning signs. One of the strongest indicators of a severe attack is extreme shortness of breath that may include audible wheezing and inability to speak. 


Dr. Joshua Phillips, an allergist at the Mississippi Asthma and Allergy Clinic in Jackson, said he considers almost all these deaths to be preventable. 
“This is, in 2026, a treatable disease,” he said, before listing a dozen medication types.  ”These drugs really lowered asthma mortality when they started coming out in the 1980s and 1990s.”
In addition to the daily and emergency rescue inhaler, he’s used injectable medicines, called biologics, that target specific antibodies to help manage severe cases of asthma. 
Phillips treats patients from around the state, and he’s seen the Mississippi State Fair in early October as the beginning of peak asthma season. Several factors come into play — the change in weather, the start of fall viruses, ragweed pollen season and people congregating at outdoor events. Being part of the southern United States, Mississippi experiences longer-than-average pollen seasons for trees and grasses. That exposure can bring out asthma symptoms in people who elsewhere would have experienced nasal allergies, Phillips said. 
“This is a multiple-issue crisis,” Davis said. When people lose access to healthcare, whether through not having health insurance or getting priced out of medications, she expects to see more asthma-related deaths.
Phillips noted that rural hospital closures have led some of his patients to drive into Jackson from the Delta, but lack of reliable transportation means they sometimes miss visits.
Meanwhile, air quality has gotten worse across Mississippi, which directly impacts people with lung conditions such as asthma. 
In April, the American Lung Association issued a “State of the Air” report that shows a decrease in air quality in and around Jackson since the previous year. The surrounding metro area received a B grade for ozone pollution, also known as smog. 
Other parts of Mississippi fared worse. One monitored area that includes DeSoto County received an F, while the Gulfport-Biloxi area was graded a C. Only 10 counties out of 82 in Mississippi have monitoring stations for air quality, limiting the geographic areas researchers are able to analyze. 
Factory gases, smokestacks, diesel engines and power plants can all contribute to poor air quality, said Davis. These pollutants are especially dangerous for youth and older adults, and are linked to health concerns, including heart disease, lung cancer and asthma.
“We are putting our children, our elders, those who are pregnant at risk because there’s an unsafe level of air quality,” Davis said. “So whether that’s a B grade or F grade, there is a level of unsafe air.”
Given the increase in asthma prevalence, Phillips encouraged Mississippians to think of asthma as a long-term, chronic disease rather than something that affects them temporarily. The best way to manage asthma, he said, is to be proactive. This can look like seeing a specialist twice a year and having a plan for how to handle sudden asthma attacks.
“A lot of patients just feel that, ‘Well, I feel better. My asthma went away.’” Phillips said. “No, your asthma did not go away. It may have gone to sleep, but it’s still very much there.”

name: California
title: Ponte al día rápidamente sobre las elecciones de California con nuestra guía para los indecisos
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Si aún no has enviado tu papeleta por correo, es hora de confirmar tu voto para el día de las elecciones.
 Los votantes de California están tomando decisiones importantes, entre ellas elegir al próximo líder del estado , quién ocupará un escaño en la Cámara de Representantes de Estados Unidos (y potencialmente qué partido controlará el Congreso) y si California se convierte en el primer estado en imponer un impuesto a los multimillonarios.
 Además, tenemos la asombrosa cantidad de 14 propuestas en las papeletas electorales estatales , incluidas algunas sobre temas complejos como el gasto en medio ambiente y atención médica.
El presidente Donald Trump y su administración llevan meses cuestionando el funcionamiento de las elecciones en California. Todo comenzó con una orden ejecutiva que pretendía limitar el voto por correo, método utilizado en California. Si bien este intento fracasó en los tribunales , avivó la preocupación de que las papeletas no se entregaran correctamente.
Ahora, la administración está demandando a California para obligar a los funcionarios electorales a apartar hasta 20,000 papeletas que, según el gobierno federal, podrían haber sido enviadas por correo a personas que no son ciudadanas. También acusó a 28 inmigrantes de votar o registrarse ilegalmente para votar. Los líderes demócratas del Congreso y grupos aliados han demandado a la administración en respuesta.
 Esto es lo que necesitas saber para estar al día y asegurarte de que tu voto cuente. 
 Cómo votar
La votación anticipada ya ha comenzado en algunos lugares de todos los condados, y aquí puedes consultar los centros de votación más cercanos donde puedes votar en persona o entregar tu papeleta.
También puedes enviar tu boleta por correo, la cual debe tener el matasellos del día de las elecciones o anterior y ser recibida por las oficinas electorales dentro de los siete días posteriores a dicho día. Las autoridades instan a los votantes a enviar sus boletas con anticipación en caso de que haya demoras en el servicio postal.
Después de enviar tu boleta, puedes consultar su estatus aquí . Los funcionarios electorales del condado deben comenzar a reportar los resultados al secretario de estado la noche de las elecciones, no más de dos horas después de comenzar el conteo de votos. Los funcionarios tienen 30 días para contar las boletas y finalizar los resultados para el estado. El secretario de estado tiene entonces 38 días para certificar los resultados. Puedes encontrar más información sobre el proceso de conteo de votos de California aquí .
 Elecciones a gobernador de California
 En un estado donde los demócratas superan en número a los republicanos en una proporción de dos a uno, el candidato demócrata Xavier Becerra es el que tiene más probabilidades de ganar. A diferencia de su oponente, el republicano Steve Hilton, Becerra se ha mantenido en silencio durante la campaña sobre las políticas específicas que implementaría como gobernador.
 Hijo de inmigrantes mexicanos de clase trabajadora, Becerra tiene una larga trayectoria en el servicio público: sirvió doce mandatos en el Congreso, se convirtió en el primer fiscal general latino de California y posteriormente en el primer secretario de Salud y Servicios Humanos latino de Estados Unidos.
 Becerra insta a los votantes a que revisen su trayectoria para saber cuál es su postura, como cuando demandó a la primera administración Trump para preservar el programa de Acción Diferida para los Llegados en la Infancia (DACA) o cuando presentó una demanda en Texas para preservar la Ley de Cuidado de Salud Asequible. También fue uno de los primeros defensores de los derechos LGBTQ+ y de la sanidad pública universal.
 Hilton, por su parte, aspira a ser el primer republicano en ocupar un cargo estatal en 20 años y cuenta con el respaldo de Trump. Nacido en el Reino Unido de padres inmigrantes húngaros, Hilton no se ajusta a una única ideología política. Mientras trabajaba en Londres para renovar la imagen del Partido Conservador británico, impulsó recortes en el gasto social, la reducción del empleo público y la privatización de los servicios gubernamentales. Pero también ha apoyado un salario mínimo nacional más alto en el Reino Unido y critica a la derecha por culpar a menudo a China y a la inmigración de la desigualdad en Estados Unidos.
 Ha llevado a cabo una campaña descarada, al tiempo que pregonaba promesas ambiciosas como la abolición del Departamento de Vehículos Motorizados de California , la reducción del precio de la gasolina a 3 dólares el galón y la reducción a la mitad de las facturas de electricidad.
 Los dos solo debatieron una vez, en septiembre , en la que Becerra vinculó repetidamente a Hilton con Trump y Hilton acusó a Becerra de eludir los verdaderos problemas de California.
 Para más información, consulte la postura de los candidatos sobre el clima , la atención médica , la regulación de la inteligencia artificial , la gestión del agua y la falta de vivienda . 
 Tantas propuestas
 A estas alturas, probablemente ya hayas oído hablar del impuesto propuesto para los multimillonarios . Pero hay más de una docena de otras propuestas que puedes considerar.
 Para facilitarte las cosas, tenemos un resumen aparte sobre las 14 propuestas electorales. También puedes consultar nuestras explicaciones sobre las cinco propuestas tributarias y otra que analiza las tres propuestas de bonos.
 Además de las explicaciones y los cuestionarios sobre las propuestas que ofrecemos en nuestra guía para votantes , nuestros reporteros dedicaron el último mes a analizar cada una de ellas en profundidad, repasando qué implicarían las medidas y quién está a favor o en contra.
Échale un vistazo:

 Propuesta 1: Bono para vivienda
 Propuesta 2: Fondo de reserva para imprevistos
 Propuesta 3: Impuesto a las personas de altos ingresos
 Propuesta 4: Recaudación de fondos públicos
 Propuesta 5: Reforma de la revocación del mandato
 Proposición 37: Préstamo para compradores de vivienda
 Propuesta 38: Bono para la investigación
 Proposición 39: Identificación del votante
 Proposición 40: Impuesto a los multimillonarios
 Proposición 41: Auditorías fiscales
 Propuesta 42: Impuesto sobre la propiedad
 Propuesta 43: Umbral impositivo
 Propuesta 44: Financiación de clínicas
 Propuesta 45: Revisión ambiental 

Elecciones congresionales de mitad de mandato
 Muchos californianos estarán pendientes de los resultados la noche de las elecciones para ver qué partido controlará el Congreso en los dos últimos años de la administración Trump. En California hay varias contiendas muy reñidas. Aquí las analizamos.

 El Distrito Congresional 4 , donde el veterano representante demócrata Mike Thompson se enfrenta al desafío del demócrata Eric Jones en la región vinícola de Napa y Sonoma.
 En el Distrito Congresional 7 , la representante demócrata Doris Matsui se enfrenta al desafío de la demócrata Mai Vang, quien compite por un escaño en el área de Sacramento.
 Distrito congresional 11 , donde el senador estatal demócrata Scott Wiener compite con la supervisora demócrata de San Francisco, Connie Chan, para obtener el escaño de la representante estadounidense Nancy Pelosi en San Francisco.
 El Distrito Congresional 13 , donde el representante demócrata Adam Gray se enfrenta al desafío del ex alcalde de Stockton, Kevin Lincoln, republicano, para representar al norte del Valle de San Joaquín.
 Distrito congresional 22 , donde el demócrata progresista Randy Villegas intenta desbancar al representante republicano David Valadao en el escaño del sur del Valle de San Joaquín.
 Distrito congresional 48 , donde la concejala demócrata de la ciudad de San Diego, Marnie von Wilpert, se enfrenta al supervisor republicano del condado de San Diego, Jim Desmond. 

 Comisionado de seguros y más elecciones estatales
 Los votantes también elegirán al jefe de seguros del estado, quien regula todo tipo de seguros. Los californianos pagan algunas de las primas de seguro más altas, por lo que quien esté al mando podría afectar su bolsillo. Si usted es inquilino, también deberá prestar atención, ya que la salud del mercado de seguros de propiedad del estado puede influir en el costo del alquiler, la oferta de vivienda y la capacidad de las comunidades para recuperarse de los desastres.
 Dos demócratas —el senador estatal Ben Allen de El Segundo y la ex supervisora de San Francisco, Jane Kim— compiten por el puesto.
 Si bien tienen mucho en común, ambas propuestas ofrecen soluciones diferentes para los problemas de seguros del estado. Kim propone ideas más progresistas , como un seguro público contra desastres y la ampliación del seguro de automóvil de bajo costo a todos los conductores de California.
 Mientras tanto, el plan de Allen para mitigar el riesgo de incendios forestales incluiría presionar a la industria aseguradora para que haga más por reducir dicho riesgo. Los comités de acción política han gastado la cifra récord de más de 6 millones de dólares en esta contienda . Más de la mitad de ese gasto, 3,2 millones de dólares, se ha destinado a apoyar al gobernador estatal Allen.
 Las demás contiendas siguen el tradicional enfrentamiento entre demócratas y republicanos. Para obtener más información sobre ellas, consulta nuestra guía para votantes.

name: National
title: Nearly half of AAPI women lack a reproductive health provider, survey finds
text:
Women with the National Asian Pacific American Women’s Forum walk down the streets of Washington, D.C., at a 2022 Unity March against anti-Asian racism. A recent survey led by the group found nearly half of Asian American, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander women don’t have a reproductive healthcare provider. (Photo courtesy of National Asian Pacific American Women’s Forum) A survey of Asian American, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander women and gender-expansive people found nearly half of respondents don’t have a reproductive healthcare provider and more than half don’t know how far they would need to travel for abortion care.
About 57% also said they are caregivers to a child or aging family member, and 23% said they themselves or someone they know have avoided travel, medical care, work or public spaces because of immigration status concerns. 
Fajer Saeed Ebrahim, vice president of policy and research at the National Asian Pacific American Women’s Forum, which commissioned the survey, said it’s the first of a five-year survey project the organization has planned to observe trends over time.
Early prenatal care declines across US, reversing years of progress

“I think our women face many of the same challenges as many other communities of color, but our experiences are often missing from policy discussions,” Saeed Ebrahim said.
Most of those who responded lived in states with legal access to abortion, while about 20% lived in states where it was illegal or heavily restricted. About 56% were unsure how far they would need to travel for an abortion, and 31% were unsure how far they’d need to go for general reproductive healthcare. Of those who did have an estimate, most said they would need to travel less than an hour for reproductive healthcare other than abortion. Japanese women and those with lower incomes were most likely to say they did not have a reproductive healthcare provider.
Saeed Ebrahim said some of those issues may connect back to cultural stigma. About 60% of AAPI women said it was difficult for people in their communities to talk about abortion, even though many of them are strongly in favor of abortion rights. But the survey also showed a lack of knowledge about state abortion laws.
“People are confused,” she said. “They often don’t know what their state has to say about abortion care, and many are surprised to learn their state is more restrictive than not. … A lot of our community members were surprised that providers could be punished.”
Saeed Ebrahim said having more health providers with training to provide culturally sensitive and responsive care for AAPI women would help bridge gaps in care, including expanded language access.
“We’ve heard from many of our community members and our past research has shown … providers just are not familiar with our communities and some of the cultural expectations that come with identifying this way,” she said.
The survey was offered in June in several languages besides English, including Korean, Chinese, Vietnamese, Hindi and Tagalog. About 45% of respondents were located in the Western U.S., 23% in the South, 20% in the Northeast and 11% in the Midwest, and represented more than 20 ethnic backgrounds. It was conducted on behalf of the National Asian Pacific American Women’s Forum by research and public opinion firms Lake Research Partners and Sprout Insight. 
Stateline reporter Kelcie Moseley-Morris can be reached at kmoseley@stateline.org.
