name: California
title: En la recta final: Entérate de lo que ha sucedido hasta ahora en la contienda por la gobernación de California
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
A una semana de las elecciones, la contienda de dos años para suceder al gobernador Gavin Newsom se acerca a un final predecible.
 Las encuestas publicadas durante el verano y el otoño muestran que el demócrata y ex fiscal general Xavier Becerra mantiene una ventaja dominante de dos dígitos sobre el republicano y ex presentador de Fox News, Steve Hilton, desde que ambos terminaron en los dos primeros puestos en las primarias de junio.
 La encuesta más reciente, realizada por Emerson College del 17 al 19 de octubre , sitúa a Becerra con una ventaja de 27 puntos porcentuales: el 60% de los votantes probables lo apoyaba, frente al 33% de Hilton. Al ser interrogados, casi dos tercios del pequeño porcentaje de votantes indecisos encuestados se inclinaron por Becerra.
 En Sacramento, los defensores de políticas públicas llevan semanas intentando desesperadamente conseguir una oportunidad para reunirse con el que se perfila como el próximo gobernador.
 Si los resultados se mantienen según lo previsto, no será por falta de esfuerzo por parte de Hilton.
 El candidato republicano, un novato en la política californiana, ha intentado de todo y más para impulsar su candidatura: recorrer el estado de punta a punta, inundar las redes sociales con anuncios provocativos , usar inteligencia artificial para representarse a sí mismo como un gladiador en el coliseo de Becerra y enviar vídeos selfie por mensaje de texto desde Skid Row en Los Ángeles.
 Propone una amplia y ecléctica gama de políticas, desde gasolina a 3 dólares y fuertes recortes de impuestos para todos los niveles de ingresos hasta la construcción de 10 nuevas ciudades y la creación de una “Oficina de Diversión y Libertad”. (Entre sus responsabilidades se incluirían la flexibilización de las regulaciones sobre la vida nocturna y la autorización de perros en más parques estatales). Su última propuesta exigiría que los refugios de animales notifiquen al público antes de sacrificar perros para que alguien pueda adoptarlos. Ha dicho poco sobre cómo conseguiría que las supermayorías demócratas en la Legislatura apoyen sus numerosos planes, que requerirían su aprobación.
El enfoque de probarlo todo ha tenido algunos tropiezos: su serie de anuncios dirigida a atraer a los liberales que deberían “simplemente intentar” votar por los republicanos provocó una fuerte reacción conservadora. Días después, acusó a Becerra de mentir sobre los antecedentes migratorios de sus padres, ya que su padre nació en Sacramento, fue llevado a México de niño y luego trabajó de joven a ambos lados de la frontera antes de establecerse nuevamente en California. Latinos dijeron que la acusación malinterpretaba la experiencia común de los mexicoamericanos de familias que se mudan constantemente a través de la frontera. Hilton, quien es británico-estadounidense, se mudó a California con su esposa, una ejecutiva de Silicon Valley, en 2012.
 El estratega republicano Mike Madrid dijo que esto hacía que Hilton, a quien por lo demás había elogiado como un candidato “sustancial”, pareciera desconectado de la realidad: “Literalmente está diciendo: ‘No soy uno de ustedes'”.
 El enfoque de Becerra no podría ser más diferente. Evitando cuidadosamente las promesas ostentosas, presentó pocas políticas específicas y, en cambio, habló en términos generales sobre cómo sus decisiones priorizarían a las familias de clase media y trabajadora.
 Algunas de sus propuestas representan ajustes graduales a lo que el estado ya está haciendo bajo la administración de Newsom, como la reducción de obstáculos burocráticos para que los promotores inmobiliarios obtengan la aprobación de sus proyectos de vivienda. Su promesa de campaña más ambiciosa es que California continúe brindando cobertura a todos aquellos que perderían la atención médica de Medi-Cal debido a los drásticos recortes federales de hasta 30 mil millones de dólares anuales; no ha revelado de dónde obtendrá el dinero, pero ha dicho que podría recortar algunos gastos superfluos y administrativos. También quiere proporcionar a ciertos hogares de bajos ingresos dos horas de electricidad gratuita durante las horas de menor consumo diurno y ampliar los programas de asistencia para el pago inicial.
Becerra se ha apoyado firmemente en su oposición a Donald Trump, quien es muy impopular en California . Trump respaldó a Hilton en las primarias; desde entonces, Hilton ha intentado ganarse el voto demócrata en las elecciones generales afirmando que no estaría de acuerdo con el presidente en todo.
El candidato demócrata se ha mostrado muy interesado en vincular a Hilton con el presidente en cada oportunidad. Esta táctica quedó patente durante un debate de CNN el mes pasado ; fue el único debate al que Becerra accedió y, al parecer, no cambió mucho el rumbo de la contienda.
 En un mitin en Bakersfield en apoyo del candidato demócrata a la Cámara de Representantes, Randy Villegas , Becerra declaró a la prensa que lideraría una demanda estatal contra las agencias federales de inmigración por su aplicación agresiva de la ley. Al ser preguntado por los periodistas sobre qué haría respecto a los precios de la gasolina, Becerra reconoció que las políticas estatales sobre la perforación y el refinado de petróleo podrían afectar los precios, pero señaló que el problema inmediato en cuanto a los costos era la guerra de Trump en Irán.
 “Lo primero que debemos hacer, obviamente, es lograr que Trump ponga fin a su guerra descabellada en el extranjero”, dijo. “Pero lo que sí podemos hacer en California es asegurarnos de que no se produzcan repuntes debido a ninguna medida que tomemos aquí”. 
 Becerra aparece en las últimas semanas
 Tras un verano con escasas apariciones públicas y entrevistas con los medios, Becerra ha vuelto a la campaña electoral en las últimas semanas, movilizando a votantes y voluntarios por todo el estado, aunque a menudo no en nombre propio. Con una cómoda ventaja en las encuestas, dedicó la mayor parte de su tiempo a celebrar ruedas de prensa con otros demócratas para oponerse a la Proposición 39 , la medida de identificación de votantes respaldada por los republicanos, y a impulsar a los demócratas que se postulan para cargos legislativos.
 Apareció junto a varios demócratas que se postulaban en distritos electorales competitivos para la Cámara de Representantes en el sur de California y el Valle Central, donde la campaña de Becerra cree que podría ayudar a movilizar a un importante grupo de votantes latinos.
 Quizás el mayor impacto de Hilton en la contienda ha sido obligar a Becerra a responder por las políticas demócratas a las que culpa del alto costo de vida, y a basar su campaña en el mensaje de cambiar “16 años de gobierno de un solo partido” en un intento por atraer a la mayoría de los votantes californianos que desean que el estado tome una dirección diferente.
 En Bakersfield, un condado republicano que apoyó a Hilton en las primarias, Becerra afirmó que su experiencia en el gobierno lo distingue. También se esforzó por diferenciarse de Newsom, quien goza de índices de aprobación generalmente favorables, haciendo hincapié tanto en su tiempo en el gabinete de Biden como en su trayectoria personal.
 “Soy diferente a todos los gobernadores que hemos visto, porque nadie tiene la experiencia ni las credenciales que yo tengo, y nadie tiene la experiencia de vida que yo tengo”, dijo.
 Tim Rosales, consultor republicano, afirmó que Hilton ha hecho todo lo posible dada la ventaja demócrata en California y ha demostrado que “una personalidad republicana singular puede influir en el debate político hasta cierto punto”. Ha recaudado 33,6 millones de dólares frente a los 40 millones de Becerra, el doble de lo que recaudó el principal candidato republicano en 2021 durante la fallida elección revocatoria de Newsom.
 “Ha hecho una buena campaña”, dijo Rosales. “Lo cierto es que los votantes demócratas de California, que son muchos, coinciden con Hilton en los temas importantes. Simplemente quieren que un demócrata intente resolverlos”.

name: California
title: Los californianos se rebelan contra los drones policiales tras su rápida adopción en todo el estado
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
El rechazo público al uso de drones por parte de la policía municipal está aumentando en toda California, convirtiendo las audiencias rutinarias sobre políticas locales en batallas de alto riesgo sobre los límites de la vigilancia vecinal.
Los debates públicos, cada vez más acalorados, se deben a un litigio histórico sobre privacidad y a una ley de 2021 que exige la aprobación explícita de las juntas locales para el uso de “equipos militares”, incluidos los drones. Estas revelaciones dejan claro que la policía esta considerando cada vez más a los drones como posibles “primeros intervinientes” en situaciones de emergencia en ciudades como San Francisco, Berkeley, Santa Ana y Stockton, lo que obliga a los líderes locales a enfrentarse al escepticismo de los residentes en las audiencias públicas necesarias antes de que se puedan ampliar los programas de drones.
 En estas circunstancias, los organismos encargados de hacer cumplir la ley están presionando para ampliar el uso de drones más allá de la respuesta exclusiva a emergencias, para que sirvan de ayuda en las patrullas cotidianas, mientras que los ciudadanos están preocupados por los drones que realizan registros sin orden judicial, por si los municipios están acaparando demasiados datos recopilados por drones y por si los fabricantes de drones tienen demasiado poder e información.
 Esas tensiones quedaron claramente de manifiesto a principios de este mes en San Francisco, cuando un debate político en una reunión de la comisión de policía congregó a un gran número de residentes con posturas opuestas.
 El Departamento de Policía de San Francisco solicitó a los comisionados que aprobaran una política que permitiera el uso de drones para una amplia gama de fines, incluyendo “respuesta a emergencias de seguridad pública”, investigaciones en curso, capacitación y “acercamiento a la comunidad”. Si bien el borrador prohibía la “vigilancia general” aleatoria o las actividades de seguimiento protegidas por la Primera Enmienda, estipulaba que las grabaciones públicas se conservarían durante 30 días a menos que estuvieran vinculadas a una investigación en curso. 
“Con los drones se puede volar a altitudes mucho más bajas, obtener imágenes térmicas y realizar seguimientos.”Katie Inman, abogada de Holland & Knight
 Los defensores argumentaron que la tecnología es vital para la lucha contra el crimen en la actualidad. “La seguridad pública y la privacidad personal no deberían ser intereses contrapuestos”, dijo Anna Carney, presidenta de Stop Crime SF, instando a los comisionados a brindar a los agentes todas las ventajas posibles para salvar vidas.
 Pero los defensores de la privacidad y los residentes escépticos vieron una pendiente resbaladiza hacia la vigilancia sin control, estableciendo paralelismos explícitos con la polémica implementación de lectores automáticos de matrículas en todo el estado. En los últimos años, ciudades como San Francisco y Stockton construyeron extensas redes de cámaras fijas suministradas por empresas como Flock Safety. Ahora, las comunidades temen que la incorporación de drones a esas mismas redes cree una red de vigilancia multidimensional e inescapable, que rastrea a los ciudadanos no solo en sus coches por la calle, sino también desde el aire sobre sus hogares.
 “Estamos todos aquí hoy porque estos drones están afectando a todas nuestras comunidades”, dijo Manny, miembro del grupo defensor de la privacidad DeFlock SF, quien instó a los comisionados a cancelar el contrato del departamento con el fabricante de drones Skydio. “Si al Departamento de Policía de San Francisco realmente le importara operar estos drones respetando la privacidad, lo mínimo que podría suceder es que alguno de ustedes proponga una enmienda para exigir una orden judicial”, agregó, refiriéndose al lenguaje utilizado en la política propuesta por el departamento.
 Aunque los comisionados votaron a favor de llevar la política a negociaciones laborales sin añadir un mandato de orden judicial, la fricción que se observa en San Francisco refleja un ajuste de cuentas a nivel estatal. 
 Incertidumbre jurídica y vacío político
 Las normas de 2021 que rigen el uso de equipos militares por parte de las fuerzas del orden aún dejan un vacío normativo al que se enfrentan los municipios de California: las agencias locales que despliegan drones se adentran en una zona gris legal donde la tecnología avanza mucho más rápido que la regulación estatal.
 Una demanda contra el condado de Sonoma pone de manifiesto la incertidumbre. Las preocupaciones sobre la privacidad persistieron durante años en el condado después de que las autoridades implementaran un programa de drones en 2019 para el cumplimiento de las normas urbanísticas. Sin embargo, investigadores de la Unión Estadounidense por las Libertades Civiles (ACLU) descubrieron posteriormente cientos de registros sin orden judicial en patios, viviendas y ventanas privadas, todos realizados sin una política publicada al respecto. En 2025, la ACLU del Norte de California demandó a Sonoma, y el mes pasado el condado llegó a un acuerdo. Sonoma se comprometió a limitar el uso de drones, obtener órdenes judiciales o el consentimiento antes de realizar inspecciones de cumplimiento de las normas urbanísticas en propiedades residenciales, restringir la retención de datos y notificar directamente a los residentes si su propiedad fue objeto de vigilancia aérea.
 Este caso puso de manifiesto la compleja maraña legal en la que deben desenvolverse los funcionarios al desplegar aeronaves no tripuladas.
 “Hay tres categorías principales”, explicó Katie Inman, experta en políticas de drones y abogada de Holland & Knight, quien anteriormente trabajó en la Administración Federal de Aviación (FAA). “Por un lado, están los principios generales del derecho constitucional; por otro, las leyes estatales; y, por último, las normas operativas de la FAA”.
 Inman señaló que California pertenece a una categoría de estados que carecen de una ley estatal integral que regule explícitamente el uso de drones por parte de las fuerzas del orden, lo que deja a los municipios la responsabilidad de interpretar y cumplir con la jurisprudencia constitucional de la Cuarta Enmienda, que protege contra los registros e incautaciones irrazonables.
 Según declaró, el Tribunal Supremo ha dictaminado que las aeronaves que vigilan zonas visibles a simple vista desde altitudes legales no violan las garantías constitucionales.
 «Pero esas eran aeronaves tripuladas; no son drones», dijo. «Con los drones, se puede volar a altitudes mucho más bajas, se pueden obtener imágenes térmicas, se puede rastrear, se puede mantener la aeronave en vuelo estacionario durante mucho tiempo; hay un gran potencial de vigilancia que normalmente no se tendría».
En todo el estado, casi 60 agencias policiales utilizan programas de drones, según el Departamento de Policía de Los Ángeles. La mayoría de las políticas fundamentales, incluidas las de Chula Vista, Fremont y la propuesta en San Francisco, prohíben la vigilancia aleatoria, pero los programas difieren en cuanto a los criterios de despliegue y la supervisión pública. Departamentos como el de Chula Vista despliegan unidades automatizadas de ” drones como Primeros Intervinientes ” generalmente antes que los agentes terrestres para las llamadas rutinarias al 911, mientras que marcos más recientes o sometidos a un escrutinio más riguroso, como la propuesta de San Francisco, intentan establecer límites más estrictos al restringir los vuelos a investigaciones criminales activas, persecuciones de vehículos o emergencias específicas basadas en incidentes.
Agentes del Departamento de Policía de Los Ángeles en la escena de un crimen en curso frente a un supermercado Superior Grocers, en la División Sur del LAPD en Los Ángeles, el 7 de diciembre de 2024. Foto de Mark Abramson para CalMatters.
Contratos multimillonarios y afirmaciones de seguridad no comprobadas
 Más allá de las cuestiones constitucionales y políticas, el rápido crecimiento de los programas de drones está estrechamente ligado a la agresiva presión ejercida por los proveedores de tecnología de defensa y vigilancia.
 Los departamentos de policía de San Francisco y Los Ángeles utilizan equipos fabricados por Skydio, con sede en San Mateo, mientras que otras empresas del sector, como Axon (fabricante de cámaras corporales) y Flock Safety (fabricante de lectores de matrículas), también se han expandido agresivamente en el mercado. Skydio se lanzó originalmente para ofrecer a los atletas de deportes extremos una forma de rastrear y filmarse practicando parkour o snowboard. Sin embargo, después de que el gobierno estadounidense calificara al fabricante chino de drones DJI como un riesgo para la seguridad nacional en 2020, Skydio reorientó su estrategia para cubrir la demanda de clientes militares, policiales y empresariales.
 En una reciente conferencia para clientes, Adam Bry, CEO de Skydio, presentó una ambiciosa hoja de ruta: pequeños drones para vuelos tácticos dentro de edificios, aeronaves de alcance medio para persecuciones de vehículos y modelos de alta velocidad capaces de alcanzar los 160 km/h en un radio de hasta 48 kilómetros. Bry también describió un futuro impulsado por la IA, imaginando un software que analiza las llamadas al 911 en tiempo real para recomendar automáticamente el envío de un dron autónomo al lugar de los hechos. 
 “El Departamento de Policía de San Francisco debería vincular los despliegues a incidentes específicos… Nada de patrullaje rutinario general. Nada de vigilancia general.”Jesús Gabriel Yáñez, comisionado de policía recientemente jubilado.
Para llevar a cabo esa visión se requieren grandes inversiones, tanto de los contribuyentes como de inversores multimillonarios. Santa Ana aprobó recientemente 682,900 dólares para su iniciativa de drones como primeros respondedores, en colaboración con Skydio, mientras que el Ayuntamiento de Stockton aprobó una ampliación de contrato de 3.15 millones de dólares con Flock Safety para integrar seis drones en su red existente de 120 cámaras lectoras de matrículas. En San Francisco, el año pasado, el departamento de policía recibió una donación de 9.4 millones de dólares del multimillonario de las criptomonedas y cofundador de Ripple, Chris Larsen, para ampliar su programa de drones y sistemas de vigilancia, según informó Mission Local.
 “La premisa de la Declaración de Derechos es el respeto a la libertad individual, y eso solía significar algo en esta ciudad”, dijo Ilona, residente de San Francisco, en la reunión de la Comisión del 14 de octubre, criticando duramente a los funcionarios por aceptar la donación de drones de Larsen. “Pero ya no, porque ahora nos hemos vendido a los multimillonarios de la tecnología… El Departamento de Policía de San Francisco ha sido negligente e imprudente con nuestra privacidad. ¿Cómo podemos confiarles estas herramientas?”.
 Los proveedores de drones respaldados por capital de riesgo han invertido grandes sumas de dinero para influir en los funcionarios locales y obtener su apoyo para su expansión. Por ejemplo, Flock Safety habría gastado millones de dólares en cabildeo a nivel local y federal , afirmando que su tecnología ayudó a “resolver” un millón de delitos solo el año pasado. Sin embargo, los investigadores se muestran cada vez más escépticos sobre lo que los proveedores y las fuerzas del orden afirman que esta tecnología puede lograr.
 La policía argumenta que los drones les ayudan a responder a incidentes con mayor rapidez, a reducir la tensión en situaciones potencialmente peligrosas y a mejorar los índices de resolución de delitos. Un estudio de febrero de 2026 del Centro de Derecho Penal y Justicia de la UC Berkeley concluyó que, si bien los drones de primera respuesta pueden mejorar los tiempos de respuesta, no hay evidencia de que reduzcan los tiroteos en los que participan agentes, disminuyan el uso general de la fuerza o mejoren los índices de resolución de casos.
 El rápido despliegue también ha intensificado la ansiedad de la comunidad sobre las redes de vigilancia interconectadas y ha avivado la creciente reacción en contra de la tecnología policial basada en inteligencia artificial.
 Jesús Gabriel Yáñez, comisionado de policía recientemente jubilado, intervino en la reunión de la comisión de San Francisco. Leyó brevemente un fragmento de la novela distópica “1984” de George Orwell antes de expresar su oposición a la política de uso de drones propuesta por sus antiguos compañeros.
 “El Departamento de Policía de San Francisco (SFPD) debería vincular el despliegue de drones a incidentes específicos que no puedan resolverse sin poner en riesgo la seguridad de los agentes, sin excepciones”, declaró Yanez. “Solo en esos casos deberíamos permitir el uso de drones. Nada de patrullaje rutinario ni vigilancia general”.
 Opositores como Yanez señalan casos anteriores en los que las agencias policiales de California compartieron ilegalmente datos de seguimiento de matrículas con las autoridades federales de inmigración , así como fallos técnicos como una reciente filtración que expuso en línea transmisiones de vídeo en directo de drones policiales debido a configuraciones incorrectas del proveedor. Esta preocupación por los abusos de los proveedores y la vigilancia mediante IA no se limita a California: una resistencia similar está surgiendo en todo el país. En Minneapolis, el ayuntamiento votó en contra de un contrato de drones policiales con Skydio tras las protestas de la comunidad por la privacidad y la tecnología militar de doble uso. En Nueva Orleans, el grupo activista Eye on Surveillance se movilizó con éxito contra una propuesta de política que habría permitido el uso de armas en drones policiales.
 Ya sea a través de debates públicos en los ayuntamientos, impulsados por la ley AB 481, o mediante acuerdos judiciales como el del condado de Sonoma, las comunidades californianas intentan dejar claro que la adopción de tecnología de seguridad pública de vanguardia no se logrará a costa de la privacidad. El sistema de vigilancia automatizado puede llegar en segundos, pero los ciudadanos exigen saber con exactitud quién los vigila y quién controla el sistema.
 Khari Johnson, reportero de tecnología de CalMatters, contribuyó a este informe.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Department of Justice election monitor deployment will include South Dakota’s Minnehaha County
text:
A voter fills out a ballot at a Sioux Falls polling place during the South Dakota primary election on June 2, 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)The South Dakota Secretary of State’s Office said this week that federal election monitors will be in Minnehaha County for the Nov. 3 election, as the Trump administration prepares to deploy 1,000 monitors nationwide. 
The state office said it received notice from the U.S. Department of Justice that monitors will go to the state’s most populous county, which includes Sioux Falls, to observe procedures and assess compliance with federal voting rights laws. The office did not specify how many federal monitors will be assigned to Minnehaha County or which polling locations they will visit.
Minnehaha County Auditor Leah Anderson said it’s routine to have Department of Justice monitors in the state, and she’s meeting with department officials Wednesday to learn more. 
“They usually just have observers to ensure federal civil rights are respected,” Anderson said.
Trump’s DOJ sends 1,000 election monitors to 50 states

Federal election monitoring is a longstanding practice. But the context of this year’s deployment has raised concerns among some voting rights advocates.
President Donald Trump attempted to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election, in which he refused to acknowledge defeat. Meanwhile, some state officials say they are preparing for chaos at the polls as Trump casts doubt on election security and advocates more federal involvement in states’ elections.
Voting rights groups have organized volunteers to observe polling locations and document potential problems. That includes the American Civil Liberties Union of South Dakota, which hosted four events this month to train volunteer observers. 
Samantha Chapman is the advocacy manager for the ACLU of South Dakota. She said President Joe Biden’s administration sent a few monitors to the state in 2024, and they were a “very neutral presence at the polls.” Chapman said she hopes this group is the same. 
“But with the Trump administration’s actions and rhetoric to almost try and federalize elections, it does read a little differently,” Chapman said. 
She said ACLU election observers will watch federal officials to see how they interact with voters and whether their presence is intimidating, intentionally or not.
Additionally, the Native American Rights Fund will send nearly 300 attorneys, law students and volunteers to polling places in seven states, including South Dakota. The volunteers will observe to ensure election rules are followed, and to document any barriers Native voters encounter. Organization attorneys can also provide legal counsel.
The U.S. Department of Justice has said its monitors will not interfere with voting and will report potential violations to the proper officials. The Secretary of State’s Office said the federal presence will not change any voting procedures established under state law.
“The DOJ has also stated that its monitors will not speak to voters inside polling places or carry firearms,” the Secretary of State’s Office said in a news release.
The office said voters should direct any concerns about activities at a polling location to the precinct superintendent or appropriate election officials. The ACLU has encouraged people to report problems to an Election Protection hotline, 866-OUR-VOTE.

name: California
title: ¿Bloquearán los republicanos el acceso de los demócratas al Congreso si ganan las elecciones de mitad de mandato? Les preguntamos
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
¿Intentarán los aliados republicanos MAGA del presidente Donald Trump en el Congreso impedir que los demócratas recién elegidos tomen posesión de sus escaños tras las elecciones de mitad de mandato, alegando que las elecciones fueron fraudulentas?
 Esa preocupación llevó a dos legisladores de ambos partidos a instar a sus colegas del Congreso a firmar un compromiso en el que se comprometían a aceptar los resultados de las elecciones de mitad de mandato.
 Mientras Trump y sus aliados impulsan agresivamente acusaciones de fraude electoral generalizado , sus autores esperan evitar un escenario similar a la presión que Trump ejerció sobre los republicanos del Congreso para que no certificaran la victoria presidencial de Joe Biden en 2020. Aquello desencadenó los disturbios mortales en el Capitolio de Estados Unidos el 6 de enero de 2021.
 La actual delegación del Congreso de California cuenta con ocho republicanos y un independiente que forma parte de su bancada. CalMatters se puso en contacto con sus oficinas para averiguar si habían firmado el compromiso.
 Solo uno, el representante Kevin Kiley, el republicano convertido en independiente que representa al área de Rocklin, dijo que lo había firmado.
 “Cuando terminen las elecciones, deberíamos certificar los resultados y comenzar con el importante trabajo que tiene que hacer el Congreso”, dijo Kiley, y agregó que aceptaría los resultados si perdiera la contienda contra el Dr. Richard Pan, un demócrata de Sacramento que se postula contra Kiley en un distrito de nueva creación con tendencia demócrata.
 La representante Young Kim, que representa la zona de Anaheim, no ha visto el juramento, pero “dará cabida a los nuevos miembros”, dijo su portavoz, Ellie Gilchrist.
 “No puedo responder a eso”, dijo Natalia Jovovich, portavoz del representante Jay Obernolte, cuando se le preguntó si el republicano que representa el área de Hesperia había firmado el compromiso. El representante Vince Fong, del área de Bakersfield, y su esposa tuvieron un bebé la semana pasada, por lo que Fong no estuvo disponible para comentar si nombraría a nuevos miembros del Congreso, según dijo su portavoz, Ryan Gardiner, en un mensaje de texto.
 Jonathan Wilcox, portavoz del representante de San Diego, Darrell Issa, respondió a la consulta de CalMatters, pero no especificó si Issa había firmado el compromiso.
 Los portavoces de los demás representantes republicanos de California en el Congreso de los Estados Unidos —Ken Calvert, James Gallagher, Tom McClintock y David Valadao— no respondieron a CalMatters.
 El Wall Street Journal fue el primero en informar sobre la promesa redactada por los representantes Don Bacon, republicano de Nebraska, y Josh Gottheimer, demócrata de Nueva Jersey. 
 ¿Qué dice el juramento?
 Los firmantes se comprometen a oponerse a “los intentos de socavar elecciones libres y justas o de anular la voluntad de los votantes, incluyendo cualquier intento de rechazar o retrasar la toma de posesión de cualquier miembro electo que presente un certificado electoral válidamente emitido”.
 Según el Wall Street Journal, los firmantes también acuerdan reconocer a “los ganadores de las elecciones certificados por cada estado de conformidad con la ley de ese estado”.
 No se han hecho públicos los nombres de los firmantes, y la oficina de Gottheimer no respondió a las solicitudes de CalMatters para saber qué otros miembros lo habían firmado. La oficina de Bacon remitió a CalMatters a la de Gottheimer. El viernes, Gottheimer anunció que 17 republicanos y demócratas habían firmado el compromiso, pero no especificó quiénes. La Cámara de Representantes de Estados Unidos cuenta con 433 miembros y dos escaños vacantes. 
 El representante Kevin Kiley, del área de Sacramento, firmó un compromiso para facilitar la entrada de los miembros recién elegidos al Congreso. Foto de Anne Wernikoff, CalMatters.
 Los republicanos cuentan con una mayoría mínima en la Cámara de Representantes de Estados Unidos de cara a noviembre, por lo que incluso un pequeño número de republicanos que mantengan el compromiso podría bloquear un intento de la ultraderecha de impedir que nuevos demócratas ocupen escaños tras las elecciones de mitad de mandato. El periódico informó a principios de este mes que dos republicanos —los representantes Mike Lawler de Nueva York y Brian Fitzpatrick de Pensilvania— lo habían firmado.
 La carta llega en un momento en que los investigadores federales han estado intentando activamente validar las afirmaciones de Trump sobre un fraude electoral generalizado en estados controlados por los demócratas, incluido California.
 En las últimas semanas, agentes federales han arrestado a varias decenas de personas en todo el país por supuestamente votar ilegalmente, pero hasta ahora no han encontrado pruebas de una conspiración generalizada que Trump ha afirmado durante años que consiste en manipular las elecciones a favor de los demócratas. 
 La Fundación Heritage presiona al Congreso
 La Heritage Foundation, un grupo de expertos influyente en el movimiento “Make America Great Again” de Trump, argumentó en abril que el Congreso tiene el poder de investigar las elecciones que sus miembros consideren fraudulentas. «El Congreso puede detectar todo tipo de votos fraudulentos, no solo los emitidos por personas que no son ciudadanas», escribió Scott Yenor, investigador principal de la fundación. «El Congreso puede entonces declarar inválidas las elecciones y ordenar la celebración de nuevas cuando considere que han sido fraudulentas».
 A principios de este mes, WNYC , una emisora de radio pública de Nueva York, preguntó a Rick Hasen, profesor de derecho de la UCLA, sobre un posible escenario en el que los líderes republicanos intentaran bloquear la incorporación de nuevos miembros el 3 de enero, fecha en la que se supone que deben prestar juramento.
 “Sería profundamente antidemocrático si sucediera”, dijo Hasen a la emisora, pero añadió que era poco probable.
 “Si los demócratas obtienen el control de la Cámara de Representantes y, de alguna manera, el 3 de enero alguien intenta este tipo de maniobra, provocará una reacción pública masiva”, dijo. “Esto parece muy descabellado”.
 En vista de lo ocurrido el 6 de enero de 2021, los autores del compromiso creen que es mejor prevenir que lamentar, según declaró Gottheimer a NPR en una entrevista a principios de este mes. “Como ya hemos pasado por eso”, dijo Gottheimer, “creo que es muy importante que, una vez más, eliminemos cualquier oportunidad para aquellos que quieren frenar la voluntad del pueblo”.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: U.S. Rep. Fleischmann says Hegseth could take Blackburn’s Senate seat if vacated
text:
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, photographed at the NRB International Christian Media Convention in Nashville, Tennessee on Feb. 19, 2026, could be in the running for a U.S. Senate seat. Hegseth moved to Tennessee in 2022.(Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)There’s a race going on in Tennessee that’s not on the ballot. If U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn wins her bid for governor, her vacated seat is up for grabs and open to an appointment by the governor. 
U.S. Rep. Chuck Fleischmann, a Republican,  is on the ballot for re-election in Tennessee’s 3rd Congressional District, but he is also vying for the Senate appointment, he said. 
But Fleischmann isn’t the only contender for the possible Senate vacancy. U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth could be interested in the appointment, Fleischmann told Tennessee Lookout on Sunday at a Republican get-out-the-vote rally in Hamilton County.
“I don’t know if this will come into fruition. Secretary Hegseth, should he decide to vacate that position — I don’t think he will, but if he did — as a Tennessean, he might be interested in that,” Fleischmann said. 
U.S. Rep. Tim Burchett of the 2nd Congressional District, who also spoke at Sunday’s event with Blackburn; Glenn Jacobs, the former mayor of Knox County; and Damon Hininger, the former CEO of Tennessee-based private prison operator CoreCivic, are the other names on the shortlist, said Fleischmann. 
The addition of Hegseth’s name to the list comes after House Democrats, including Minority House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries, have targeted Hegseth for impeachment if they secure a majority on Nov. 3. 
3rd Congressional District U.S. Rep. Chuck Fleischmann is interested in an appointment to the U.S. Senate seat that will be vacated by U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn if she wins the November 3 governor’s race. (Photo: Ruby Rayner for Tennessee Lookout)
Hegseth, a former Fox News contributor, moved to Sumner County in 2022.
Blackburn said that if she wins the race for governor, she plans to remain in her Senate seat until she is sworn in as governor and choose her own replacement. 
“I will be honored to have that,” Fleishmann said about the appointment to the Senate. “I think I bring a unique skill set to the job. But if not, I’ll stay in the House as a senior appropriator.”
With less than two weeks before election day, the state’s highest-ranking Republicans gathered to rally for support at Bo’s Bash hosted by state Sen. Bo Watson. 
Blackburn, Burchett and Hamilton County GOP chair Gail Greene hammered home that voting Republican is the only way to stave off what they characterized as socialists taking power. 
“A lot of people forget to go vote, so don’t let them forget,” Blackburn said to some 300 guests. “I have a Democrat socialist running. There is only one, only one Republican on the ballot for November 3. That Republican is me, and I need their vote.”
Fleischmann urged the sea of people sporting ‘Marsha, Marsha, Marsha,’ and ‘VOTE’ stickers to hit the polls in droves and prove the pundits wrong. 
“I’m predicting a surprise on November 3rd. Let’s make sure that Republicans come out in all 50 states, prove the pundits and the pollsters wrong, because we’ve got to keep the United States Senate, we’ve got to keep the United States House, because we have to make sure that our great President Donald J. Trump has a solid two years,” Fleischmann said.
Despite the polls predicting a blue wave, Fleischmann said he has no concerns about his Democratic challenger Anna Golladay.  
Golladay is a Chattanooga resident, small business owner, and former pastor for the United Methodist Church until she was dismissed in 2018 for officiating a same-sex wedding. 
“From a historical perspective, whether the 3rd district has had 10 or 11 counties every time without fail in the general election, I’ve carried every county. I don’t see any reason for that to change. We’ve polled. We’re up by large margins,” Fleischmann said. “We put a lot of money into campaigning this time, but I feel incredibly well.” 
Fleischmann said this is the first time in 10 years he has spent significant funds campaigning in a general election. The roughly $500,000 he spent was on targeting newcomers to the state and keeping his message out there, he said. 
Campaigning was targeted at the slightly redistricted 3rd Congressional District. Meigs and most of Rhea County are new to the district under the redrawn map.
Early voting across the state is up since 2022. Ten days into early voting, turnout is nearly 52% higher than at the same time for the Nov. 3 election in 2022, according to state data. The average turnout for the 3rd congressional district ten days into early voting is lower at about 41%. 
Early voting runs through Oct. 29.

name: WyoFile
title: With shrinking Freedom Caucus, is Wyoming positioned to create a ‘transformative’ Game and Fish trust fund?
text:
When the Wyoming Game and Fish Department anticipates a budget crunch, and one’s coming in the near future, it often asks state lawmakers to boost the cost of hunting or fishing licenses.
That’s just the reality of the wildlife management agency’s funding structure. There’s some diversification in Game and Fish’s budget: Federal excise taxes, for example, provide roughly 22% of revenues, grants cover about 8% and interest on savings another 5%. But license fees account for the majority, providing nearly 60% of the revenue Game and Fish uses to pay for its green trucks, red shirts and myriad other expenses. In an era of high inflation, it’s a formula that has its financial forecasts looking increasingly dim — “dire” has even been suggested — especially when the main commodity, huntable wildlife, is a finite resource. 
“We’re on a starvation diet, and things do not look good going forward,” Wyoming Game and Fish Commissioner John Masterson told state lawmakers in September. “I believe the department has proven itself to be prudent stewards of the money of its sportsmen. But it can only stretch dollars so far.” 
Masterson made those remarks to the Wyoming Legislature’s Travel, Recreation, Wildlife and Cultural Resources Committee at a Jackson meeting in September while advocating for a significant addition to Game and Fish’s revenue makeup. Specifically, he was recommending a funding tool — a trust account “of paramount importance” — that would potentially endow Wyoming wildlife managers for generations to come.
Wyoming Game and Fish Commissioners talks with members of the Wyoming Legislature’s Travel, Recreation, Wildlife and Cultural Resources Committee at a September 2026 meeting in Jackson. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
“The alternative is that we nickel and dime license fees … going through the entire bill process to raise the cost of a resident doe-fawn license from $22,” Masterson said. “I don’t feel that that’s efficient.”  
A bill is in the works that would make the Game and Fish trust fund a reality. It’s a top priority for the Travel, Recreation, Wildlife and Cultural Resources Committee, which is expected to finalize and ready the bill for introduction to the broader Legislature this coming general session at its Nov. 9-10 meeting in Cheyenne. 
When the budget-slashing Wyoming Freedom Caucus wielded significant power in the Legislature, the idea of a Game and Fish trust fund likely would have been farfetched. 
“It would have never passed the House, and it would have had a snowball’s chance in hell in the Senate,” said committee member Bob Wharff, a state representative from Evanston who often voted with the Freedom Caucus. “All that may change.” 

Rep. Bob Wharff, R-Evanston, during the 2026 Wyoming Legislature budget session in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata/WyoFile)

The change in outlook is due to the Freedom Caucus suffering a resounding statewide defeat during the August primary elections. Wharff, who was reelected to his old House seat in 2024, was among the casualties, losing to Kemmerer native David Walton by a 20% margin.   
With the more moderate faction of the Republican Party seizing control, passing a savings- and spending-centric bill that would create a Game and Fish trust fund becomes more feasible. Wharff didn’t divulge whether he’d vote to advance it during the upcoming committee meeting, but he spoke highly of a similar savings account, the Wyoming Wildlife and Natural Resources Trust, that he helped pass while working in an advocacy role two decades ago.  
“That’s a legacy that I’m very proud of,” he said. 
While a trust fund’s political palatability in modern Wyoming remains to be seen, wildlife advocacy groups are providing momentum and a strong push. The day before Wharff and fellow lawmakers met in Jackson, the Wyoming Wildlife Federation hosted a reception to build support for the idea. 
“Wyoming has a chance to make a generational investment in wildlife conservation, and that’s exciting,” said Craig Benjamin, the federation’s executive director. “Hunters and anglers have carried the system for decades, and Game and Fish’s responsibilities have grown. The question now is, ‘How do we build a durable funding model for the next generation?’ and it’s exciting that the Legislature is having that conversation.’” 
Wyoming Wildlife Federation Executive Director Craig Benjamin addresses a Jackson audience in an effort to build support for a Wyoming Game and Fish Department trust fund. (Chris Bancroft)
Exactly how much of a difference the trust fund would make to Game and Fish’s bottom line depends on the details, like the funding level required by the Legislature. At present the bill is structured similarly to the Wyoming Wildlife and Natural Resources Trust, which allows up to 4% of its market value to be expended annually (the rest of investment earnings go back into the account). 
Pushing for the trust at the commission’s September meeting, the Theodore Roosevelt Conservation Partnership’s Alex Aguirre told lawmakers that he’d love for Wyoming to “shoot for the stars.” 
“We stand in full support of the proposal to increase funding for our Wyoming Game and Fish Department,” Aguirre said, “with an ask of at least $500 million.”
Other groups echoed the ask. 
Trout Unlimited Wyoming State Director Leslie Steen suggested the same dollar amount for a fund that she called an “incredible opportunity” at giving Game and Fish a “stable, long-term foundation.” Muley Fanatic Foundation President Joey Faigl also uttered $500 million, while pointing out that the cost of habitat work needed to help arrest the decline of struggling mule deer is estimated at $300 million alone. 
The degree to which a hypothetical trust provides Game and Fish with a financial lifeline for the long-term depends “100%” on the size of the account, Game and Fish CFO Meredith Wood told WyoFile. 
A “major influx” in contributions could be “transformative in perpetuity,” Wood said. 
Although the half-billion-dollar funding level may sound astronomical — the figure is roughly 15% of Wyoming’s general fund expenses — only a fraction of that amount would be available annually. If lawmakers limit withdrawals from the trust account to 4% annually, that would generate about $20 million a year from a $500 million corpus. 
The agency’s projected fiscal year 2027 revenues are about $112 million. A $500 million trust would provide about an 18% revenue bump. 
Nevertheless, many wildlife advocates and lawmakers are excited about the prospect. Sen. Bill Landen, who chairs the wildlife panel, chose not to run again after a two-decade-long stint representing Casper and Natrona County. As he prepares to leave the Legislature, he’ll go out pushing for a trust account to diversify Game and Fish’s funding structure and alleviate pressure on hunting and fishing license sales. 

Sen. Bill Landen, R-Casper, listens to testimony during a meeting of the Senate Travel, Recreation, Wildlife and Cultural Resources Committee in February 2024. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)

“It just didn’t seem reasonable and right that we say, ‘Well, it’s all up to the hunters and fishermen,” Landen told WyoFile. “I think we all need to be a part of this. That’s one of the underlying principles of the bill.”
Landen didn’t hazard a guess about the likelihood of the Wyoming Legislature creating such a trust fund during the 2027 general session, though he hopes it gets some traction.
“It’s one of those issues that you may not be able to get done in one year,” Landen said. “You might just need to keep working on it. But I can’t think of a better thing for Wyoming to be investing in than what we’re talking about.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Denny Hoskins denies whistleblower lawsuit allegations from former employee
text:
Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins speaks to reporters following Missouri Supreme Court arguments Sept. 2 (Annelise Hanshaw/MissouriIndependent).Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins responded on last week to a lawsuit filed by his former director of election integrity alleging he was fired after reporting allegedly illegal and unethical conduct.
The secretary denied many of the accusations from former director Nicholas La Strada, a Republican who was hired by Hoskins, according to court documents.
In his lawsuit, La Strada claims Hoskins’ staff conspired to create a false whistleblower submission to use as evidence in a federal trial.
He also alleged Hoskins ordered a retabulation of write-in votes in Marshall after a complaint about this year’s April election.
Hoskins’ response states that La Strada’s disclosures are “materially false and a reasonable person would know they are false.”
He said La Strada had his administrative rights revoked to the Missouri Centralized Voter Registration system because he was allegedly making changes to voter audit logs.
Further, he said La Strada’s concerns about an affidavit in a federal trial were unprompted, as it was materially accurate and the plaintiff had no way of knowing what was inside it before he was terminated.
Former elections official accuses Missouri secretary of state of altering results, misleading judge

Hoskins said La Strada was terminated after he was told to meet with the deputy general counsel to prepare for the hearing and allegedly refused, among other reasons.
“Plaintiff by then had a history of not showing up to work, poor communication, unprofessional conduct, insubordination, and other misconduct to include refusing to go to meetings when he had disagreements with senior staff and Secretary Hoskins,” lawyers for Hoskins said in their response to the lawsuit.
The Secretary of State also disagreed with La Strada’s naming of him and the state of Missouri as defendants. Hoskins’ lawsuit claims only the Office of the Secretary of State is the correct party to sue.
His lawyers moved to strike his name from the litigation, according to court documents.
This story originally appeared on KOMU. It can be republished in print or online.

name: California
title: Get up to speed fast on the California election with our guide for the still undecided
text:
In summary
Californians have a full ballot for the November 2026 election, including a governor’s race, congressional seats and 14 propositions. Don’t miss your chance to make your ballot count.


It’s time to lock in on Election Day if you haven’t already mailed in your ballot. 
California voters are making some big decisions, including choosing the next leader of the state, who will serve in the U.S. House (and potentially what party controls Congress) and whether California becomes the first state to impose a billionaire tax. 
Plus we have a dizzying 14 propositions on our statewide ballots, including ones on complicated topics like environmental and healthcare spending.
On top of that, President Donald Trump and his administration have been contesting the mechanics of California elections for months. It began with an executive order that was meant to limit mail-in voting, which California uses. That effort failed in court but fueled worries that ballots would not be delivered.
Now, the administration is suing California to force elections officials to set aside up to 20,000 ballots that the feds claim could have been mailed to noncitizens. It also charged 28 immigrants with illegally voting or registering to vote. Democratic congressional leaders and allied groups have sued the administration in return.
Here’s what you need to know to get up to speed and make sure your vote counts.
How to vote
Early voting has already begun in some locations across all counties, and you can look up nearby voting centers here where you can vote in person or drop off your ballot. 
You can also mail your ballot, which must be postmarked on or before Election Day and received by election offices within seven days after Election Day. Officials are urging voters to mail ballots early in case there’s any post office delays. 
After you submit your ballot, you can track its status here. County elections officials must begin reporting results to the secretary of state on Election night, no more than two hours after they begin counting votes. The officials have 30 days to count ballots and finalize their results to the state. The secretary of state then has 38 days to certify the results. More information about California’s vote-counting process can be found here.
California governor’s race
In a state where Democrats outnumber Republicans two-to-one, Democratic candidate Xavier Becerra is the likeliest to win. Unlike his opponent, Republican Steve Hilton, Becerra has remained mum during the race about specific policies he’d enact as governor.
The son of working-class Mexican immigrants, Becerra has had a long history of public service: He served a dozen terms in Congress, became California’s first Latino attorney general and went on to become the first Latino U.S. secretary of Health and Human Services.
Becerra urges voters to look at his record to see where he stands, like when he sued the first Trump administration to preserve the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals immigration program or filed a lawsuit with Texas to preserve the Affordable Care Act. He was also an early supporter of LGBTQ+ rights and universal public healthcare.
Hilton, meanwhile, hopes to be the first Republican to hold statewide office in 20 years and is endorsed by Trump. Born in the U.K. to Hungarian immigrants, Hilton doesn’t fall neatly into one singular political ideology. While working in London to refresh the British Conservative Party’s image, he pushed to slash welfare, cut government employment and privatize government services. But he’s also endorsed a higher national living wage in the U.K. and is critical of the right for oftentimes blaming China and immigration for inequality in the U.S.
He’s run a cheeky campaign while touting lofty pledges such as abolishing the California DMV, lowering gas to $3 a gallon and halving electricity bills.
The two only debated each other once, in September, in which Becerra linked Hilton repeatedly to Trump and Hilton accused Becerra of dodging California’s real problems. 
For more, see where the candidates stand on climate, healthcare, artificial intelligence regulation, water management and homelessness.
So many propositions
At this point you’ve probably heard about the proposed billionaire tax. But there are more than a dozen other propositions for you to consider.
To make it easier, we have a separate rundown on just the 14 ballot measures. You can also check out our explainers on just the five tax measures on the ballot, and another examining the three bond measures.
Besides our voter guide explanations and quizzes of the propositions, our reporters spent the past month digging into each one, going over what the measures would do and who’s for or against it. 
Take a look:

Prop. 1: Housing bond
Prop. 2: Rainy day fund
Prop. 3: High-income tax
Prop. 4: Public fundraising
Prop. 5: Recall reform
Prop. 37: Homebuyers loan
Prop. 38: Research bond
Prop. 39: Voter ID
Prop. 40: Billionaire tax
Prop. 41: Tax audits
Prop. 42: Property tax
Prop. 43: Tax threshold
Prop. 44: Clinic funding
Prop. 45: Environmental review

Midterm congressional races
Many Californians will be watching results on Election Night just to see which party controls Congress in the final two years of the Trump administration. California has several hot races. Here’s a look at them.

Congressional District 4, where longtime Democratic Rep. Mike Thompson faces a challenge from Democrat Eric Jones in Napa and Sonoma wine country.
Congressional District 7, where Democratic Rep. Doris Matsui faces a challenge from the left by Democrat Mai Vang. They’re competing for a Sacramento-area district. 
Congressional District 11, where Democratic state Sen. Scott Wiener is competing with Democratic San Francisco Supervisor. Connie Chan to claim U.S. Rep. Nancy Pelosi’s San Francisco seat.
Congressional District 13, where Democratic Rep. Adam Gray faces a challenge from former Stockton Mayor Kevin Lincoln, a Republican, to represent the Northern San Joaquin Valley.
Congressional District 22, where progressive Democrat Randy Villegas is trying to unseat Republican Rep. David Valadao in the Southern San Joaquin Valley seat. 
Congressional District 48, where Democratic San Diego City councilmember Marnie von Wilpert is facing Republican San Diego County Supervisor Jim Desmond.

Insurance commissioner and more statewide races
Voters will also choose the state’s insurance chief, who regulates all kinds of insurance. Californians pay some of the highest insurance premiums, so who’s in charge could affect your wallet. If you’re a renter, you’ll also want to pay attention because the health of the state’s property insurance market can influence the cost of rent, housing supply and how well communities can bounce back from disasters.
Two Democrats — state Sen. Ben Allen of El Segundo and former San Francisco Supervisor Jane Kim — are vying for the position. 
While they have a lot in common, both offer different ways to solve the state’s insurance problems. Kim is proposing more progressive ideas, including public disaster insurance and expanding low-cost auto insurance to all California drivers. 
Allen’s plan for wildfire risk mitigation, meanwhile, would include pushing the insurance industry to do more to reduce fire risk. Political action committees have spent a record-high of more than $6 million on this race. More than half of that spending, $3.2 million, has been in support of state Allen.
The other races take on the traditional Democrat vs. Republican matchup. For more info on them, check out our voter guide:

Lieutenant governor
Secretary of state
Attorney general 
Controller
Treasurer
Superintendent of public instruction

CalMatters reporter Maya C. Miller contributed to this story.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Commentary: The League of Women Voters is testing election processes. You can, too.
text:
Election officials perform an accuracy test on voting machines ahead of the August primaries Wednesday, July 8, 2026. (Photo by Ria Gupta/Minnesota Reformer)From testing voting equipment to reviewing election results, nonpartisan League of Women Voters volunteers are observing firsthand how Minnesota’s election safeguards work.
Voters need more than assurances. They need to know safeguards are in place, procedures can be observed, and problems can be identified and corrected. That’s why the League of Women Voters of Minnesota is working across the state to make election administration more transparent and accessible.
Since 1920, the League has worked to empower voters and defend democracy. Today, more than 3,300 members across 36 local Leagues help Minnesotans participate in our democracy. This election season, volunteers are observing, documenting and reporting on the processes that help ensure votes are counted accurately.
Volunteers are documenting how Minnesota’s election safeguards work — from pre-election equipment testing to post-election reviews — and sharing what they learn with their communities.
Before voting begins, the equipment is tested
Before every election, local officials conduct public accuracy tests to demonstrate that voting equipment accurately counts ballots with known results.
In 2026, the League organized a statewide effort to expand public observation. More than 200 trained volunteers observed tests across Minnesota, watching officials run ballots through tabulators and comparing the results with expected totals.
One League volunteer described the experience: “The results matched the ballots perfectly in every case, and the officials were happy to answer any and all questions about the process.”
These observations let community members see equipment testing firsthand, ask questions and learn how officials verify that voting equipment works as intended.
After Election Day, Minnesota checks the results
Minnesota conducts a post-election review after every statewide election. During these reviews, county canvassing boards randomly select precincts where officials hand-count ballots and compare the results with voting equipment totals.
In 2024, the League trained 160 nonpartisan observers who watched post-election reviews in 43 of Minnesota’s 87 counties. More than 250 people signed up for training, demonstrating strong public interest in seeing how election results are verified. League observers reported that officials conducted reviews fairly and followed state law and guidance from the Minnesota Secretary of State’s Office.
The League is continuing this work in 2026, training and coordinating more than 200 nonpartisan observers to watch post-election reviews across Minnesota, Nov. 12–17.
Oversight also helps identify and address errors. The League’s reporting on election certification in Scott and Sherburne counties in 2024 documented administrative errors that led to recounts, court review and subsequent legislative changes. These cases illustrate why established procedures matter: Concerns can be examined, errors addressed and improvements made.
Getting the facts matters
Through its “Trusted Elections: Stronger Together” tour, the League has partnered with the Reformer, the Minnesota Secretary of State’s Office, and local election officials to host discussions in five Minnesota cities about election security, safeguards and common questions about how our elections work. Topics included voter registration, vouching, noncitizen voting, voting equipment and post-election reviews. Watch a recording of the St. Paul event here.
Melanie Hazelip of the Minnesota Secretary of State’s Office has emphasized the seriousness of election fraud: “When you commit voter fraud you are committing a felony offense, which is punishable by $5,000, 10 years in prison and permanent deportation”.
Kari Tyson, city clerk in Detroit Lakes, has similarly stressed the importance of election rules and safeguards, noting that violations can be detected through subsequent checks and may result in criminal charges.
In 2024, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s Election Performance Index ranked Minnesota first among states for overall election performance. The index evaluates election administration across multiple measures.
As Hazelip put it, “Not only are we number one in voter turnout, but we do election administration really well.”
See for yourself. Make your voice heard.
The best way to build trust in our elections is to let people see how they work. When Minnesotans can observe election safeguards firsthand and get reliable information about the process, they can distinguish facts from misinformation. The League’s trained volunteers are helping make election transparency real by showing people not just that safeguards exist, but how they work.
Explore the process, ask questions and seek reliable information. Every eligible voter should have the information they need to participate with confidence.
Visit VOTE411.org for nonpartisan information about candidates and elections. To learn more about the League of Women Voters of Minnesota or find a local League, visit LWVMN.org.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Over 56,000 absentee ballots cast so far in Mississippi midterm election
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippi voters have returned more than twice as many absentee ballots as they had done at this point in the 2022 midterms.
But there was no Senate race on the ballot in 2022, and the numbers remain below the last presidential race.
As of Monday, circuit clerks’ offices had received 56,049 absentee ballots, according to the Secretary of State’s office. At roughly the same point in 2022, they had received 22,221.

The jump comes in a year when a U.S. Senate seat is on the ballot, with Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith facing Democrat Scott Colom and independent Ty Pinkins. 
VOTER GUIDE: Mississippi 2026 midterm elections guide: Who’s running? What are the issues?
The absentee ballot count this year is still far below the 2024 federal election cycle, but voter turnout usually increases in presidential election years.  At this point in 2024, 119,818 absentee ballots had been received, so this year’s count is a little under half of that.
DeSoto County currently has the most returned absentee ballots at 4,588, followed by Hinds County at 4,240 and Harrison County at 4,183.
Voters with a qualifying excuse can vote absentee in person at their circuit clerk’s office until noon Saturday, Oct. 31. Mail-in absentee ballots must be postmarked by Election Day, Nov. 3, and received within five business days, by Nov. 10.
Mississippi does not offer no-excuse early voting. Voters must have a legal excuse to vote absentee, such as being 65 or older, having a disability, working during polling hours or being away from their home county on Election Day. Eligibility is narrower for mail-in ballots than for in-person absentee voting.
For more information on how to vote absentee in person or by mail, go to this secretary of state’s web page.

title: Hadley Kistler is gearing up for a career as an early childhood educator
text:
Hadley Kistler is committed to working with kids, now and in the future. A senior at St. Johnsbury Academy, she’s already employed per diem at a local childcare center in her free time. As she develops her college applications, she’s narrowed her sights to early childhood education and set a goal to get into a competitive academic program that’s also close to home. 
Hadley describes herself as “a bit of a homebody.” She lives with her mom and stepdad in St. Johnsbury and she likes spending time at home and with her family. Those facts influenced the schools she is considering as well. All have great early childhood education programs and are a “doable” drive home for a weekend. 
Staying on top of deadlines and applications with help from VSAC
“I always knew I wanted to go to college,” Hadley said. “And my family is really supportive of that.” The hardest part of the process for Hadley is keeping on top of the various deadlines for each piece of the puzzle. That’s where her VSAC outreach counselor, Trish Turner, comes in. “Trish is keeping me on track,” Hadley added. “With her help, I’m able to focus on school at the same time I’m doing all my applications and financial aid paperwork.”
Trish works in VSAC’s GEAR UP college and career readiness program. Together, Hadley and Trish have worked through the Vermont Grant application, the FAFSA federal financial aid form, and most of Hadley’s college applications. Hadley’s working on her essay this week. Trish, Hadley shared, “is always there to help.” 
Hadley started working with VSAC a few years ago. At the time, she was a student at Oxbow High School in Bradford. Last year, her family moved to St. Johnsbury and she transferred to the Academy. She’s been working with Trish ever since. 
“She’s helped me understand when deadlines are, when grants are open, what scholarships might be good for me. Sometimes I struggle with deadlines and she’s great about helping me with remembering them,” Hadley noted. 
Hadley is setting her sights on the education that leads to her goal: being the best person and teacher she can be in her field 
Hadley knows she wants to earn her bachelor’s degree. It’s not only a requirement for early childhood education, but an opportunity for her to be the best person and teacher she can be in the field. If finances, life, and time allow, she’d like to go further to her master’s degree or beyond. “If more education gets me to my goal, that’s what I’ll do,” she said. 
Financial aid is a big part of the calculation. Hadley describes financial support as a “necessity” and is staying on top of the dates and deadlines with Trish’s help. “Trish will text me with reminders because all the scholarships and grants and things have different deadlines,” she added. “Some are first-come, first-served and so it’s important to get them done fast.” 
Beyond her schoolwork, college applications, and part-time job, Hadley has been involved in theater in high school and was part of bringing Her Education Required, a student-led initiative to bring more women’s history into the high school curriculum, to the Academy. The movement was founded at a Vermont high school, and Hadley is proud of her role in starting it at the Academy. 
That same commitment to making a difference in others’ lives shapes her plans for the future. Hadley describes early childhood education as having the potential to influence some of the most important years in a child’s life. She’s drawn to the role early childhood educators have, helping people build fundamental skills that they will use their entire life, and she likes the idea of helping kids learn them. “Kids can get overlooked and being a constant and positive presence means a lot to them,” she said. “My goal would be to be that constant and great adult presence.”
She’s already getting a feel for what it’s like to work in a classroom at her per diem job. It solidified her passion for early childhood education and confirmed for her that she’s on the right path. Right now, Hadley said, “it feels great to be at the end of high school and ready to take the next step!”  

The Vermont Student Assistance Corp. was created by the Vermont Legislature in 1965 as a public nonprofit agency. We advocate for Vermont students and their families to ensure that they have the tools they need to achieve their education and training goals. We create opportunities for all Vermont students, but particularly for those—of any age—who believe that the doors to education are closed to them. Growing families save for education with VT529, Vermont’s official 529 savings program. To help Vermonters plan and pay for college or job training, our counselors work with students in nearly every Vermont middle school and high school, and are also available to work with adults. Our grant, scholarship, and workforce development programs create opportunity, help students re-skill or learn new skills, and grow the economy. VSAC’s loan, loan refinance, and loan forgiveness programs provide competitive education financing to students and families. Find us at www.vsac.org or visit Facebook, Instagram, or LinkedIn.
