name: Alaska Beacon
title: Calls for higher voting participation pervade Alaska Federation of Natives convention
text:
Michelle Sparck, director of Get Out the Native Vote, holds a promotional sign and several Division fo Elections pamphlets in the upper lobby at the Dena'ina Civic and Convention Center during the Alaska Federation of Natives convention on Oct. 22, 2026. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)From the opening to the closing of the Alaska Federation of Natives convention, speaker after speaker, information booth after information booth and placard after placard had the same message: a call for Alaska’s Indigenous people to vote.
Michelle Sparck, leader of the Get Out the Native Vote, held up four fingers during her brief remarks on Thursday, the convention’s first day, to emphasize that Alaska Natives make up about a quarter of the electorate.
“If my four fingers represented all the voters in Alaska, we’re one whole finger. That’s how important we are,” she said.
Yet voter participation has nosedived since the 1980s, when almost all Native adults in villages voted, she said. In 2024, only 11% of qualified Alaska Natives cast ballots, she said.
“That’s not showing our power. That’s not owning our power,” she said. “If we’re only voting 11% out of 25%, we are not sending a clear message to politicians.”
 

Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, and outdoing Alaska Federation of Natives Co-Chair Joe Nelson share smiles on Oct. 22, 2026, at the organization’s annual convention. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	U.S. Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, made an impassioned plea for more voter participation and fewer logistical roadblocks to ballot-casting in rural areas, where residents are predominantly Native.
“We have to be attuned to this, because where you live should not determine whether your voice is heard and whether your vote is counted,” she said in her speech, delivered Thursday.
Outgoing AFN Co-chair Joe Nelson, who closed the convention on Saturday with a speech of gratitude, said he had one request of everyone attending or watching the convention: Vote.
Alaska Native people “take care of everybody. We give, give, give, give, and that’s OK,” he said. “And my only ask here tonight is that every one of you take your whole clan and go give your vote. Vote for the next U.S. senator. Vote for the next U.S. congressperson. Vote for our new governor. And bring your kids along with you.”
 

Former Gov. Tony Knowles, the last Democrat to hold the office, mingles with well-wishers at the Alaska Federation of Natives arts fair on Oct. 24, 2026. Knowles was an early supporter of Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, and he is wearing a campaign button promoting the Democratic candidate. Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	Boosting voting participation is a high priority for AFN. The federation, the largest Native organization in the state, scheduled its convention a week later than normal so that it and the adjacent, Native-led Elders and Youth Conference held earlier in the week could coincide with early voting opportunities. In-person early voting in Alaska opened on Oct. 19.
At the convention, speakers exhorted conference attendees to walk from the Dena’ina Civic and Convention Center, site of the AFN event, across the street to Anchorage City Hall, where the Alaska Division of Elections operates an early voting site. Volunteers with Native Get Out the Vote even provided escorts for early voters.
“We’re not going to tell you who to vote for, but we can get you comfortable and confident enough to walk across the street and vote in person,” Sparck said in her speech.
They promoted other early voting sites as well: the busy Midtown Mall site just south of downtown and the Curtis D. Menard Memorial Sports Arena in Wasilla.
 

Sirahna Dragicevich, whose family is from Southeast Alaska, collar with traditional designs as she walks through the artists mart at the Alaska Federation of Natives convention on Oct. 22, 2026. THe collar was made by her grandmother. Her family is Áak’w Kwáan Wooshkeetaan, Eagle Shark, from Auke Bay in the Juneau area. The collar depicts the raven and eagle lovebirds. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	Visitors from rural areas can avoid a lot of logistical challenges by voting early in the state’s largest city, speaker after speaker reminded the AFN audience.
Sparck and her organization have been doing special outreach to the hundreds of Yukon-Kuskokwim region residents who are still living in Anchorage and other unfamiliar urban locations a year after they were evacuated from villages wrecked by ex-Typhoon Halong, Sparck said.
More than 1,500 people were airlifted from the region after the storm hit, mostly from the Yup’ik villages of Kipnuk and Kwigillingok.
As the evacuees navigate housing problems, contend with transportation difficulties and make other adjustments to city life, evacuated residents might not consider voting to be a top priority, Sparck said in an interview. That was apparent during the Aug. 18 primary, when only eight total votes, all by absentee, were counted from the two hardest-hit villages, she said.
In her AFN address, Sparck spoke directly to the displaced Yukon-Kuskokwim residents.
“For the Halong evacuees, we care about what you’re going through, and we want you to turn out the vote in the midterms,” she said.
For the general election, Native Get Out the Vote is providing rides to polls for the evacuees, she said – and also rides to the Alaska Native Heritage Center on the east side of Anchorage, where there is a stockpile of donated traditional foods that the displaced Yukon-Kuskokwim residents can use to make their lives easier.
More broadly, the voting problems that have plagued voting in rural Alaska, such as unopened or late-opening polling sites, erratic and undependable plane service and mail delivery, continue.
At least 18 rural sites designated as places to cast ballots early had failed to open during the first week of early voting, which started on Oct. 19, state Sen. Bill Wielechowski, D-Anchorage, told the Division of Elections.
Most of the sites he listed were in Western Alaska. “There is no legal excuse for the failure to open these sites,” he said in a letter he sent Friday to the division.
Alaska lawmakers passed a bill that would have eased some of the logistical challenges for rural voters, but Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, vetoed the bill. The measure, Senate Bill 64, would have ensured that the state provide postage-paid envelopes for mailed ballots, set up a ballot-tracking system and allowed voters to correct technical mistakes and make other changes.
Despite those ongoing impediments to voting for Alaska Natives from rural communities, there is one positive change that should make it easier for rural Native residents to cast their ballots, Sparck said.
The Division of Elections has agreed to set up an early voting site on the Alaska Native Tribal Health Consortium campus, allowing more access for voters who are patients using services at the Alaska Native Medical Center or other facilities.
It took a long time to win that service, which had been available at the hospital in the past, Sparck said.
“It took 10 years for us to argue with the Division of Elections to bring voting back onto the ANMC campus,” she said.
That voting site, at a Southcentral Foundation facility on the ANTHC campus, is set to open on Tuesday and continue operating until Nov. 2, the day before Election Day, according to the Division of Elections.
Buttons promoting the Get Out the Native Vote initative are displayed on a table on Oct. 22, 2026, at the Alaska Federation of Natives convention in Anchorage. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Political Notebook: Question 8 surpasses Question 3 as most expensive ballot question
authors: Hallie Claflin, Chris Lisinski, and Jordan Wolman
text:
FOR ALL OF THE money wealthy donors from private equity and the investment world have splashed on changing how Massachusetts elections work, Question 3 is, at least for now, no longer the most expensive ballot question. 
An early-October burst of spending by opponents of an attempt to eliminate the recreational marijuana industry has pushed the total amount spent on that measure (Question 8) to nearly $6.5 million. That’s a good chunk more than the $5.9 million spent for and against the all-party primary question so far. 
Facing the prospect of their business being deemed illegal, the marijuana industry has mustered the financial cavalry. Opponents have already spent more than $2.8 million urging voters to reject the measure, more than twice as much as both sides have spent arguing their cases for whether to keep or spike a 2024 gun control law. 
The campaign pushing the anti-pot question is far more centralized. More than $3.7 million so far, almost all of the money behind the effort, came from a single source: SAM Action Inc., a Virginia-based nonprofit that exists primarily to oppose the recreational marijuana industry. 
That’s nearly twice as much as any other entity has put behind a single Massachusetts question this cycle. The second-largest contributor so far is the Massachusetts Opportunity Alliance, a coalition of business groups that has so far provided $1.9 million in in-kind contributions, mostly to kick-start the campaign to overhaul the state’s tax cap and rebate formula.  
Altogether, campaigns supporting or opposing the nine statewide questions on the ballot spent more than $25 million, including in-kind contributions, through October 15, the end of the most recent reporting period. The total is still well short of the record $70 million spent on the four questions on the ballot in 2022, but spending tends to be backloaded heavily to the weeks immediately before the election, so it’s still possible 2026 breaks into new territory. 
DOJ’s federal election monitors to be in Lowell, Boston again on Nov. 3 
The US Department of Justice is planning to send election monitors to polling sites in two Massachusetts cities — Boston and Lowell — on November 3, just as they did on primary election day in September, according to state election officials.  
DOJ officials say it’s a routine practice meant to ensure voting rights laws are being followed, particularly in places with high volumes of non-English speakers and voters with disabilities. 
“They typically go to those two cities for federal elections because they have probably the most complicated language requirements in the state,” Deb O’Malley, a spokeswoman for Secretary of State William Galvin, told CommonWealth Beacon. “In Lowell, there’s a trilingual ballot — English, Spanish, and Khmer. In Boston, there are bilingual ballots, but they have three different versions — Spanish, Chinese, and Vietnamese.”  
The move comes as the DOJ announced their goal of dispatching 1,000 election monitors to all 50 states on election day this year — an effort that would more than double the number of federal monitors deployed during the 2022 midterms, when the DOJ under President Joe Biden sent out less than 400 monitors to polling sites. The Trump administration has made unfounded claims that a significant number of noncitizens cast votes or are on voter rolls.   
The DOJ’s nonpartisan election monitoring program has spanned multiple presidential administrations, though it made headlines during the 2026 midterm primaries mainly because of an incident in Wyoming in which a local official witnessed a pair of election monitors seeking access to tabulators and asking questions about poll worker training and newly acquired election equipment — behavior Gov. Mark Gordon described as “aggressive” and “irregular.”  
O’Malley said the monitors, by law, are allowed to listen, take notes, and watch the general polling process from a designated area like anyone else, but they cannot look at anyone’s ballot or talk to poll workers or voters.  
During the September 1 primaries, the DOJ dispatched monitors to six states, including Massachusetts and New Hampshire.  
The monitors were sent to polls in Boston, Lowell, and New Bedford, a move Gov. Maura Healey called voter intimidation, State House News Service reported. The DOJ had sent a letter to New Bedford’s election commissioner in July stating that the city was selected due to “a significant population of limited-English proficient United States citizens of voting-age in New Bedford.”  
Harmeet Dhillon, assistant US attorney general for civil rights, has said that monitors are often sent into cities and counties “where there might have been some problems in the recent elections.” The state, for instance, investigated Boston’s election department after several city polling locations ran out of ballots during the 2024 election. 
Greens are spending their green 
For all the attention paid to what sort of influence utility companies and fossil fuel interests are able to wield this campaign season in light of Gov. Maura Healey’s evolution on natural gas, environmental groups in the Bay State are reminding us that they have plenty of cash to throw around, too. 
The Environmental League of Massachusetts’s action fund, which endorsed the governor earlier this year, has spent $25,000 this year in support of Healey’s reelection bid, according to filings with the Office of Campaign and Political Finance. The group also spent $175,000 last year to boost Boston Mayor Michelle Wu’s successful campaign for a second term. 
Separately, a coalition of environmental groups has raised a total of $4.3 million so far to pass a ballot question aimed at increasing financial support for nature conservation and water projects in the state, according to OCPF data, though ELM isn’t involved in that effort. 
The donations from ELM’s action fund come as some environmental advocates have grown concerned with Healey’s commitment to the fight against climate change as she confronts soaring energy costs that are weighing on voters’ minds — and were withholding financial support for the governor earlier this year. Healey even petitioned the Trump administration for help fast-tracking federal approvals for a small gas expansion project that she supports and left the door open for a much larger pipeline expansion proposal.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Fairfield County Dems push to flip state senate seat for first time in over 50 years
text:
The last time voters in Connecticut’s 28th state senate district elected a Democrat as their state senator was in 1974, as a wave of Democrats across Connecticut and the country were swept into office in the aftermath of the Watergate Scandal.
Democratic State Sen. Joseph Schwartz, only held the 28th district seat for two years from 1974 to 1976. Voters in the district which includes the towns of Fairfield, Bethel, Easton, and Newtown, have since only elected Republicans.
Republican State Sen. Tony Hwang, represented the district for five terms after first being elected to the position in 2014. Hwang announced his retirement last March.
Democratic state senate candidate Rob Blanchard, ran against Hwang for the 28th state senate district seat in 2024 and lost.
Blanchard said he’s in a better position now, especially a year after Democrats flipped nearly 30 municipal seats across the state.
“It certainly helps,” Blanchard said. The atmosphere has shown that the choices being made by the president and the federal government are impacting our everyday costs, and that’s undeniable.”
Blanchard and Democrats see a better chance of winning as anger mounts over cost of living issues.
A recent Quinnipiac University poll surrounding the gubernatorial race between Governor Ned Lamont and Republican challenger Ryan Fazio of Greenwich shows 24% of likely voters said cost of living was most important to them when compared to other issues such as the economy, taxes, health care, and immigration.
Blanchard’s Republican challenger, Amybeth Laroche, has attacked Blanchard for focusing his campaign on President Donald Trump’s impacts on Connecticut while ignoring statewide cost of living issues under Democratic control.
“Don’t get me wrong,” Laroche said. “Washington does have an impact in Connecticut, I’m not going to pretend that otherwise. But Hartford has its own responsibility to its taxpayers…we have the highest costs in the country for electricity,” Laroche said.
Laroche and Blanchard both say they’re focusing their campaigns on affordability, but differ sharply on their approaches towards tackling the issue.
Blanchard said he wants to let municipalities buy electric power in bulk, and strengthen regulation for utility providers among others.
Laroche said she wants to do away with Connecticut’s Public Benefits Charge on utility bills. She also said she would send quarterly questionnaires to constituents to gauge district reactions to state spending.
“At the end of the day, if I’m working hard every single day to just pay my bills, why should I have to be paying other people’s bills,” Laroche said.
Blanchard, who also works as Lamont’s campaign spokesperson, said Laroche’s attacks on Democrats rings hollow. He mentioned Lamont’s efforts at cutting state income taxes, the Democratic-controlled legislature passing legislation on child care and criticized Laroche’s performance during a recent debate where Laroche appeared to struggle with answering a question regarding the UI Monopoles, a hot topic for Fairfield residents.
“If you want to just say no to everything the governor’s done, then what’s your alternative,“ Blanchard said. “What ideas do you have.”
Laroche has attacked municipal car taxes, which have also been criticized by both Democratic and Republican legislators over the years. Yet she herself faced criticism in a recent CT Insider article over nonpayment of car taxes over the last few years.
Laroche said the article was retracted, but an editor’s note shows the article had been updated to show that two separate checks for the car tax were received by Newtown shortly after the article was originally published.
Blanchard expressed guarded optimism he could win and he’s not alone.
Fairfield University Political Science Professor, Gayle Alberda, says Blanchard is in a good position to win this time around.
“If the election were held today, Blanchard would likely win because there is, in particular, this national sentiment that is really disadvantaging Republican candidates at large, not just candidates at the federal level, and we’re seeing that kind of trickle down into state and local races as well,” Alberda said.
Alberda correctly predicted Trump would win during the 2024 presidential election.
This story was first published Oct. 26, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa State University research team works to scale bio-based carbon fiber production
text:
Rise Energy co-founder Tannon Daugaard, Iowa State University research assistant Abdulrahman A. B. A. Mohammed and Iowa State University Professor Xianglan Bai are working with bio-waste materials to create carbon fiber. (Photo courtesy of Iowa State University)As American politicians and industries look to bring manufacturing to U.S. soil, Iowa State University researchers and their partners are working to scale a method of carbon fiber development using cheap, readily available materials.
ISU mechanical engineering professor and Bioeconomy Institute associate director Xianglan Bai, joined by other bioeconomy institute leaders and researchers, has received a four-year, $2 million grant from the U.S. National Science Foundation to bring carbon fiber made from waste products from the lab to commercial markets.
The study into bio-based carbon fiber began more than 60 years ago by Japanese researchers, Bai said, and her own work in the area has spanned more than a decade. However, new methods of development established by Bai’s team and the addition of bio-oil from a different ISU-connected group is allowing the researchers to create high-quality carbon fiber at a lower cost.
“Everyone knows carbon fiber is a good material, but a lot of people cannot use it because the cost is too high,” Bai said. “If we can offer very cheap carbon fiber and enlarged production, then people will adopt carbon fiber in the application that originally they couldn’t dare to use the stuff.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Softwood kraft lignin — a component of plants that waterproofs cell walls and keeps them strong — is good for protecting the plants against environmental damage, Bai said. It’s not as useful for product applications despite its high carbon content, she said, because it’s difficult to break down. It’s also a byproduct of the paper and pulp industry, used as boiler fluid to recover chemicals from pulp.
This is the polymer that Bai, and others, have focused on in their research when it comes to carbon fiber production. She said her team needed to “bridge the chemistry and the material science,” and did so in one way through “thermo-mechanochemistry,” where they heat lignin and put it under tension to cause changes in its material structure.
Bai said there are several patents or patent-pending projects that have come from her team’s study of lignin carbon fiber development. Another component unique to ISU’s work is a type of bio-oil also patented by ISU and developed by Rise Energy, an Ames-based startup company run by leaders in the university’s bioeconomy institute.
“Right now, we are trying to create the carbon fiber that is lower than $5 per pound, because … our precursors are all bio-based and all the byproducts are low cost, and the byproducts basically have very limited use, and then our process is also very simple,” Bai said.
From left: Lignin and bio-oil are being used by Iowa State University researchers to create carbon fiber. (Photo courtesy of Iowa State University)
Rise Energy co-founder and bioeconomy institute engineer and faculty member Tannon Daugaard said his company takes waste from agriculture and other areas and converts it into bio-oil and bio-char, which can act as a fertilizer. The addition of bio-oil to the lignin shortens the time it needs to stabilize, and now the team is trying to figure out if any feedstock can work for the bio-oil they’re using or if specific kinds must be used.
Carbon fiber has applications in all kinds of industries, the researchers said, from agriculture to automotive, aerospace and infrastructure. Both Bai and Daugaard say they hope that by the end of the grant period, they’ll have the resources to establish manufacturing plants for bio-oil and bio-based carbon fiber production.
“Much like the Bioeconomy Institute has that collaboration, that network, all of those sources exist in Iowa, right, so it’s the feedstock to the final use of the product and the manufacturing along the way,” Daugaard said. “So we want to have that infrastructure here in Iowa.”
While in-state infrastructure is Daugaard’s hope, other partners in the project also hope to bring those kinds of benefits to their own states. Latis Materials, an advanced materials manufacturing company in Maine, is acting as “industry adviser” to the ISU team and is focused on customer and funding research, as well as figuring out the details of scaling the new carbon fiber production.
Will Salisbury, co-founder of Latis Materials and co-principal investigator for the grant-funded project, said his company is working to reproduce what the ISU researchers developed to gather scalable data and use it to develop a full-scale, continuous system for carbon fiber production.
Companies in the fields of agriculture, fuel storage and outdoor products have expressed interest in the new type of carbon fiber, Salisbury said, and his goal is to generate enough material for them to use in prototype parts. He hopes they would then sign a contract to buy a certain amount of the material, giving them a stronger start in getting financed to build a real factory.
“I think it has huge potential, you know, bringing jobs back into forested communities like Maine, like where we are, but also in the Pacific Northwest and in the Southeast, and even into Canada and northern Europe too,” Salisbury said.

title: After Dobbs, 900+ women have been criminally charged for conduct during pregnancy
text:
In the first three years after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the constitutional right to an abortion in June 2022, more than 900 women faced criminal charges for conduct related to their pregnancies, according to a new report.
Most state laws that prohibit or regulate abortion seek to penalize those who provide abortions, not the women who undergo them. Nevertheless, researchers from Pregnancy Justice, a nonprofit group that supports abortion rights, found 13 specific allegations related to obtaining, seeking to obtain, or researching how to get an abortion. The group would not provide additional details on those cases, saying it is still collecting data and hopes to publish a full analysis in 2028.
The vast majority of the charges — 876 of 955 — were for child abuse, neglect or endangerment, most related to substance use during pregnancy. Researchers found 871 separate allegations of substance use and 77 allegations that a woman had failed to obtain prenatal care.
The most prominent anti-abortion groups have long argued against prosecuting women for having abortions, a punishment that remains broadly unpopular. But the new report comes as a growing number of state legislators are pushing to enact such penalties: In the past two years, lawmakers have introduced bills in about a dozen states, and supporters expect that number to grow next year.
Members of the so-called abortion abolition movement believe that embryos and fetuses should have the same legal protections as people, and that women who have abortions should be criminally prosecuted to the furthest extent of the law — up to and including the death penalty.
“It sure sucks that someone who’s had a miscarriage has to be investigated, but that’s not the fault of the abolitionist legislation,” said T. Russell Hunter, founder of Oklahoma-based Abolitionists Rising. “That’s the fault of the people who would willfully break the law to abort babies. They would be the ones causing that situation.”
Hunter credits groups like his with pushing anti-abortion bills to be “a little more radical.”
Some prominent anti-abortion leaders are concerned that groups like Abolitionists Rising are gaining ground.
“It’s impossible to prosecute those abortions without enacting a police state,” said Eric Scheidler, president of the Pro-Life Action League. Scheidler and two prominent anti-abortion attorneys penned articles arguing against such prosecutions in the summer issue of Human Life Review.
“Every miscarriage would have to be investigated in order to treat these embryonic and fetal dead bodies the same way that we would treat a dead body at a hospital or in an old folks home or out in the street where a crime took place,” he said.
Most cases in three states
The Pregnancy Justice report found that 902 women faced a total of 955 charges in 23 states, but the vast majority of cases were in South Carolina (381), Oklahoma (222) and Alabama (204).
Those three states are among the 13 that have enacted near-total abortion bans since the high court dismantled the federal right to an abortion in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization.
And in all three states, courts have supported the concept of fetal personhood, or the idea that a fetus, embryo or fertilized egg has the same legal rights as a person who has been born.
South Carolina, which bans abortion after six weeks, explicitly prohibits prosecuting women for seeking or getting abortions. But lawmakers in South Carolina and at least eight other states (Georgia, Idaho, Indiana, Kentucky, Missouri, North Dakota, Oklahoma and Texas) have introduced bills in recent years that would classify abortion as homicide, making violators in those states (except for North Dakota) eligible for the death penalty.
In South Carolina this year, a Senate committee approved a bill that included a penalty of up to two years in prison for a woman convicted of inducing her own abortion, but the legislation did not advance further.
South Carolina lobbyist Hayden Laye of Pro-Life Greenville said his group opposes penalizing women for abortion. But his group ended up backing the bill when the punishment was reduced to a misdemeanor and it appeared likely that the state Senate would remove the provision.
Laye said he expects the legislation to be reintroduced next year. He noted that the abolitionist groups have lobbied against anti-abortion legislation that does not penalize the pregnant person.
“The abolitionist groups put up just as much opposition to these bills as groups like Planned Parenthood and the ACLU does,” Laye said. “We are really having to fight both sides of this — the side that wants no abortion laws, and the side that wants all or nothing, which isn’t happening. It’s not happening here in South Carolina. It’s not happening anywhere.”
Since 2022, several states including California, Colorado, Minnesota and New Jersey have enacted laws protecting women from criminal or civil penalties for their conduct during a pregnancy or while receiving reproductive healthcare.
The only state where a woman can be charged for inducing her own abortion is Nevada, which enacted its law in 1911. A Winnemucca woman who miscarried in 2018 and was charged under the law pleaded guilty to manslaughter in 2019, but her conviction was vacated in 2021 for ineffective assistance of counsel. Earlier this month, Humboldt County, Nevada, paid $1.6 million to settle her claim that it violated her state and federal constitutional rights.
Next month, voters in Nevada will consider codifying abortion rights in their state constitution after voters initially approved the amendment in 2024.
Dissuaded from seeking care
Madalyn Wasilczuk, a law professor at the University of South Carolina and one of the authors of the ongoing Pregnancy Justice study, said the Dobbs decision “really has affected how willing law enforcement and prosecutors are to treat miscarriages and stillbirths and other newborn deaths immediately after delivery as culpable acts and as crimes rather than as medical tragedies.”
Wasilczuk said that even the fear of criminal charges can dissuade pregnant women from seeking care, especially if they are substance users.
“Seeking care becomes a place where they expect to be criminalized, and so people avoid healthcare, which really underscores why it’s so dangerous to treat the criminal legal system as if it can solve a public health problem,” she said. “These instances are times when women need healthcare, not handcuffs.”
Jennifer Girdish, communications director for If/When/How, an abortion rights organization, said women who live in states with abortion bans often call the group’s helpline because they are scared to go to the emergency room after they have a miscarriage or experience complications after taking abortion pills.
“You shouldn’t need a lawyer to stop the police from investigating you after pregnancy loss,” Girdish said. “You shouldn’t need a lawyer to convince the doctor that you need emergency abortion care. But more and more you do.”
In addition to South Carolina, Oklahoma and Alabama, the Pregnancy Justice report found that prosecutors also initiated pregnancy-related cases in Arizona, Arkansas, California, Florida, Idaho, Kentucky, Michigan, Missouri, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Mexico, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, South Dakota, Texas, Utah, Washington, Wisconsin, and Wyoming.
This story was first published Oct. 27, 2026 by Stateline.

name: California
title: What if Dems win, but Congress ignores the result?
text:
U.S. Rep. Kevin Kiley during a hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 22, 2026. Photo by Al Drago, Getty Images




Democrats are ahead in the polls and appear to be on track to flip at least one branch of Congress next week. But if they win, would Republicans refuse to accept the results?
That may sound impossible, but memories of Jan. 6 led a bipartisan pair of federal lawmakers to urge their colleagues in Congress to sign a pledge promising to accept the outcome of the midterms.
Out of California’s current congressional delegation — which includes eight Republicans and one independent who caucuses with them — only one congressmember has signed it, reports CalMatters’ Ryan Sabalow.
The pledge by GOP U.S. Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska and Democratic Rep. Josh Gottheimer of New Jersey commits lawmakers to opposing “efforts to undermine free and fair elections or override the will of the voters, including any attempt to refuse or delay the seating of any Member-elect who presents a validly issued election certificate.”
Out of the House’s 433 current members, Gottheimer said on Friday that seven Republicans and Democrats had signed the pledge. And so far, the only one from California to say they had is Rep. Kevin Kiley, the Republican-turned-independent representing Sacramento’s eastern suburbs. 

Kiley: “When the election’s over, we should get things certified and get started on the important work Congress has to do.”

On Jan. 6, 2021, deadly riots at the U.S. Capitol broke out when supporters of President Donald Trump attempted to stop the certification of Joe Biden’s 2020 presidential victory. At the time, Trump and his allies pushed unsubstantiated claims of widespread election fraud — which is exceedingly rare — as the reason he didn’t win. 
This year his administration is suing multiple states to secure sensitive voter roll information. The administration is also suing California to force elections officials to separate 20,000 ballots from alleged non-citizens. 
Read more.



We’re bringing our voter guide to life through VotingMatters events across California, in collaboration with on-the-ground partners. We’re holding three events today: In Stockton at Cal State Stanislaus, in Thousand Oaks at California Lutheran University’s Lundring Event Center and in San Fernando at Bodevi Wine & Espresso Bar.

Other Stories You Should Know


Revolt against police drones


A Skydio X10 drone, which is commonly used by several police agencies in California. Photo via Skydio




In some California cities, tension is growing between local police departments that want to expand their use of drones and residents who view the devices as portents of harmful police surveillance.
As CalMatters’ Katherine Ortiz explains, police departments are pushing to expand their drone use from emergency-only responses to potentially aid in everyday patrols or serve as “first responders.” Police say drones help them respond to incidents faster, assist in deescalating potentially dangerous situations and improve crime clearance rates.
But privacy advocates and skeptical residents argue that drones can lead to unchecked surveillance. They raise concerns about drones conducting warrantless searches and collecting data. A February study by UC Berkeley also found no evidence that drones lower overall use of force or improve crime clearance rates.
Last year, the American Civil Liberties Union of Northern California sued Sonoma County after it uncovered hundreds of warrantless searches over private yards, homes and windows conducted by the county’s drone program. The county settled last month and pledged to rein in its drone use, including notifying residents if their property was subjected to aerial surveillance.
Read more.



Who’s in charge of schools? The next governor


Students play during recess at Loma Vista Elementary School in Salinas on Aug. 8, 2023. Photo by Semantha Norris, CalMatters




California’s next governor will have a bigger say in how schools are run through a new commissioner tasked with overseeing the California Department of Education.
For those keeping score, that means the next elected state superintendent will have less power to set policy.
While the change is intended to streamline California’s complex education bureaucracy, experts say that having a commissioner is only the first step toward improving the state’s education system, writes CalMatters’ Carolyn Jones.
Once appointed, the commissioner needs to simplify and clearly communicate goals for schools, provide stricter oversight and offer more direct assistance for struggling schools, according to researchers of a recent report backed by a state agency on what the state needs to do next. 
But the two candidates for governor have offered only a handful of hints about their plans for commissioner or K-12 schools. Democrat Xavier Becerra said in a debate that he thinks schools are mired in too much bureaucracy, and schools should hold back failing students. Republican Steve Hilton, meanwhile, said he favors an education savings account that would allow parents to use public funds to pay for private school.
Read more.



And lastly: Does Hilton have a chance?


Gubernatorial candidates Becerra (left) and Hilton. Photos by Zoë Meyers and Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters




We’re in the final sprint before Election Day, and California’s gubernatorial race appears to be reaching its anticipated end, with Becerra maintaining a double-digit lead over Hilton. Nevertheless, the GOP former Fox News host continues to be on a campaign warpath, flooding social media with provocative ads and texting selfie videos from Los Angeles’ Skid Row. Read more from CalMatters’ Jeanne Kuang.






California Voices
CalMatters columnist Dan Walters: With his time as governor drawing to a close, there has been some speculation that Gov. Gavin Newsom might call a special session to take another swipe at holding utilities liable for wildfires, or seek a deal after the Legislature convenes in December.
Many kids go online to access communities where they truly feel comfortable, and while blanket bans sound protective, we should instead design better platforms that accommodate everyone, writes Gillian Hayes, a professor and computer scientist at UC Irvine.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Here’s why you should view polling results on ballot questions differently than those on races between candidates
text:
NINE BALLOT QUESTIONS have turned voters’ ballots into booklets this fall, with questions ranging from marijuana policy to voting rules to zoning reform. Not since 1994 have Massachusetts voters had the opportunity (or burden) to decide so many questions. In recent months, we’ve seen some or all of the nine questions appearing in pre-election polls, including the poll that CommonWealth Beacon released earlier this month.   
So what to make of these polls? At one level, 8 of the 9 questions have shown a clear edge for the “yes” side at this stage, which would seem to suggest they are favored to pass. If these were polls of candidate races, it would be reasonable to conclude that the candidates favored by more respondents have a better chance of winning than their opponents.  
While we’ve been conditioned for years to read “horse race” polling in that way, we should not apply the same lens used in candidate races to ballot question polls. Doing so gives a far too rosy a picture of each question’s likelihood of passing. 
That’s because undecided voters break late and toward the “no” side when it comes to ballot questions, meaning an ostensible lead in the polls for the yes side is more tenuous than it might appear, especially when that lead involves less than majority support. The current “lead” for the yes side is actually far less predictive than just looking at the percentage who say they will vote “yes.” Viewed this way, the outcomes for questions 2 through 7 are much less clear based on polling from MPG and Suffolk University. Each shows an ostensible lead for the “yes” side, but “yes” vote also are hovering in the danger zone of the 40s or low 50s.  



Political consultants and others have noticed and noted this dynamic, and cautioned ballot question proponents against becoming overconfident unless polling shows their side is favored by a healthy majority, though that advice is often lost when ballot question polls are discussed in public.  
The precise statistics to support this view, however, have not been available before now. To provide a more rigorous test of this bit of conventional wisdom, we plumbed the depths of the Massachusetts polling archives, compiling a database of publicly released poll results from every ballot question survey we could find from the last eight cycles of even-year elections (2010-2024).  
Our search turned up 129 instances of ballot questions included in a public survey. In building the list, if the same poll had 2 or 3 (or 9) questions on it, each result is entered separately. 
Using this newly created database, we put the insider knowledge to the test, with very clear results. First and foremost, the level of the “yes” vote in a poll is indeed much more predictive of the ultimate result than the “yes” versus “no” gap.  
The results of ballot question polling typically include three main numbers: the percentage who say they would vote support the question or vote “yes,” the percentage who say they would vote “no,” and the percentage of undecided voters.   
In our analysis of these three responses in ballot question polling over these eight election cycles, the percentage who say they will vote “yes” is the most closely related to the actual election results. Put another way, if a group of polls finds about 45 percent say they will vote yes, the actual yes vote is generally close to that estimate, regardless of whether the pre-election poll showed the yes side leading or trailing the no side.  
One way to look at this is measuring the size of the “error” in each poll, or how different the poll was from what ended up happening. Using that approach, as shown in the table below, polls taken at any point in the pre-election cycle were, on average, 4.6 points from the final “yes” vote, but a whopping 11.6 points away from the final yes-versus-no gap. This includes all polls done anytime from January of an election year up through Election Day. The gap improves somewhat as a predictor of the actual outcome as Election Day draws nearer but never comes close to the “yes” percentage in terms of accuracy.



These error figures also allow us to look at the polls to see if they are skewed, or biased, in a specific direction. Accuracy tells us how far the polls were from what they were trying to measure. Bias tells us if they are consistently off in one direction, or if the direction of the errors are more or less random.  
Applying this lens shows the margin in ballot question polls tends to be both large and biased toward the “yes” side. In other words, analyzing the gap between the “yes” and “no” side would give you an overly rosy view of the “yes” side’s prospects by an average of 8.5 points.  



The reasons for this bias is that voters who report being undecided earlier in the election cycle move overwhelmingly to the “no” side when they actually cast their ballots. So polls undercount the “no” voters who just haven’t made their minds up yet. This bias persists in polls taken right up until Election Day, though it does get smaller in the last few weeks of a campaign. 
This late break is because voting “no” on a ballot question almost always preserves the status quo, making no change to current law. Ballot questions often cover arcane or esoteric topics, which can be difficult or impossible for the average voter to become expert on with the time they allot to deciding how to vote. For these voters, “no” often becomes the default choice, and “no” campaigns are often built around introducing a variety of specific doubts – just enough to make voters nervous about the proposed change.  
So what does this mean about this year and the record-tying nine ballot questions voters are being asked to decide? Looking at the MPG and Suffolk polls shows which questions seem to be on the bubble and which offer a clearer picture of what outcome is most likely.  
We’re now right in the middle of the time when voters are making up their mind. If history is any guide, we’ll see more and more “no” voters as Election Day approaches.  
Steve Koczela is president of the MassINC Polling Group. Janice Hagerman is a research associate at MPG.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Fort Hays State’s Sternberg Museum will remain open after outpouring of support
text:
Tisa Mason, president of Fort Hays State University, shown here during an Oct. 29, 2024, podcast interview with Kansas Reflector, told the Legislative Budget Committee the university will be able to keep Sternberg Museum of Natural History open after donations flooded in. Mason initially said the museum would close in December because of state budget cuts. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — The Sternberg Museum of Natural History will remain open after fear of its closure pushed donors to gift $1.2 million toward its operating expenses, the president of Fort Hays State University told a legislative committee Monday. 
Despite the museum’s reprieve, legislators challenged the way Tisa Mason, who has led the university since 2017, managed the recent announcement the museum would close and also her reasoning for deciding to cut the facility from FHSU’s budget. 
Mason told the Legislative Budget Committee that the announcement was mishandled through no ill intent. She had planned to let the museum staff know the museum would close in December before the message was publicly released, but someone posted the information online. 
Although apologizing about the way the decision was communicated, Mason declined to apologize for the reasoning behind it. The most recent legislative budget cut was $2.4 million, she said.
“We’ve run lean for years, and when you’re cutting funding from the leanest operation, you’re not trimming fat. You’re cutting into the muscle,” she said. “I want to be clear that announcing the museum’s closure wasn’t our first move. It was indeed our last resort.”
Fort Hays State cut its budget by $7.4 million over the past five years, which included reducing 55 faculty and staff positions, Mason said. In budget year 2027, the university cut activities, suspended men’s and women’s golf and cut an additional 12 positions, she said.
“I leaned into one framing question: Does this activity clearly, indirectly benefit students?” Mason said. “And if we stopped it tomorrow, would students be less likely to enroll, persist, graduate, or find meaningful employment? The museum’s beneficiaries are statewide and community-wide, but the cost sits entirely in our university budget.”
Mason’s explanation about the decision to close the museum wasn’t received well by several committee members, at least two of whom were upset they weren’t told about the decision before it was publicly announced.
Vice chair Rep.Troy Waymaster, a Bunker Hill Republican, said he would have considered alternative funding for the museum if he had known it might close.
“We could have found action to not even have this discussion right now,” he told Mason. “I mean, in your testimony, you had that you talked to the executive team, university leadership, Senate presidents, and then the cabinet and broader university community. I wish we would have been part of that as well.”
Mason said she didn’t know the museum closure was on the table when originally talking about budget challenges with Waymaster and others in the Statehouse. Fort Hays State has to make budget decisions a priority because it lags behind other universities in full-time equivalency funding from the Legislature, she said. 
Full-time equivalent metrics convert student credit hours to full-time academic year students and are used to determine base funding from the state.
“After the (budget) decision was made, we had to get back into the books and see what we could do,” she said. “I mean, the other scenario is that you have a great Sternberg and no Fort Hays State University. That’s not helpful either. In the ideal world, we have both, and we have a path forward for both now.”
Rep. Kristey Williams, an Augusta Republican, was critical of the data Mason presented about the university budget and asked for additional information. 
Mason told the committee that the Sternberg museum budget is about $1.3 million annually and that it brings in about $470,000, leaving a gap of about $830,000 for the university to fill.
“This was a 1% cut of an operating expense when your enrollment in the last five years has declined about 18.9% FTE. Headcount is down 14.6, and I don’t know out of that what percentage is online versus in person,” Williams said. “So we’re paying more per pupil.”
Williams said the state fulfilled its obligation by increasing expenditures over the past five years by 35.9%, even as FHSU’s enrollment dropped.
“The state of Kansas has really been there for you,” she said. “When the state of Kansas has fulfilled its obligation, 10% over (Consumer Price Index for all Urban Consumers), has given more and more money to Fort Hays State, even when you have a declining enrollment, and yet you say you can’t even manage a 1% cut of operating budget. Then I’m kind of stunned.”
Mason said the university had growing enrollment for 20 years before the COVID-19 pandemic hit, and is now recovering that growth trajectory. The university is managing its money responsibly, she said. 
“The amount of resources that we get for FTE is substantially less than the other institutions,” Mason said. “When you give one person $5, one person $10, and one person $15, and you said, ‘Everybody, we need $1 back,’ it’s much more difficult for the person with $5 than $10, $15, $20, and that’s that’s how we’re feeling.”
Mason listed growing expenses, including $400,000 of a $785,000 increase in health insurance and the 1% increase in Legislature-approved salary increases for employees, for which the university’s share was $381,000.
“We’re managing responsibly,” she said. “We’re going to get there, but we just couldn’t get there without making this big cut, which now has been helped by community partners.”

Williams asked Mason to submit more data about university enrollment online and in-person, and staffing levels, saying she wants to ensure the university is being responsive to enrollment changes.

name: Delaware
title: Delaware composer’s 9/11 requiem to honor victims, support Claymont memorial
text:
Music with a Mission is a Wilmington-based nonprofit established to support the creative work of Somers, a Delaware native, composer, conductor and performer whose career has combined classical music, jazz, sacred compositions and charitable service.
Music with a Mission continues its tradition of combining musical performances with charitable giving as Newark Symphony Orchestra marks the 25th anniversary of Sept. 11.
NEWARK, Del. — Twenty-five years after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, a Delaware composer and a nonprofit organization built around the power of music are bringing the community together to remember those lost, honor those who served and support a lasting memorial in Claymont.
The Newark Symphony Orchestra will perform Wilson Gault Somers’ “Requiem for 9/11” at 3 p.m. Sunday, Nov. 8, at The Independence School in Newark.
The anniversary performance, presented in partnership with Music with a Mission, will benefit the Guardian of Defenders Memorial in Claymont, which honors those who died in the Sept. 11 attacks and the military service and sacrifices that followed.
For Music with a Mission, the performance continues a decades-long Delaware tradition of using music not simply for entertainment, but as a way to bring attention and financial support to important community causes.
A Delaware organization where music serves a greater purpose
Music with a Mission is a Wilmington-based nonprofit established to support the creative work of Somers, a Delaware native, composer, conductor and performer whose career has combined classical music, jazz, sacred compositions and charitable service.
The organization operates on the belief that artistic expression can do more than entertain audiences. Through concerts and collaborations with other musicians, it seeks to connect the emotional impact of music with the needs of people and organizations serving the community.
Music with a Mission helps organize performances, raise financial support, develop partnerships and promote original compositions. A portion of proceeds from its events is directed to charitable causes.
According to the organization’s website, it operates as a 501(c)(3) nonprofit governed by a volunteer board of directors, with no paid employees. Pete Booker serves as interim president.
Its charitable work has touched numerous Delaware organizations over the years, including the Ministry of Caring, Salvation Army, Catholic Charities of the Diocese of Wilmington, Family Promise of Northern New Castle County and Sojourners’ Place.
The organization reports contributing $14,000 to the Ministry of Caring, $11,000 to the Salvation Army, $11,000 to Sojourners’ Place and $2,500 to Catholic Charities through its musical activities over the years.
Other concerts have supported Lutheran Community Services, Friendship House and organizations working to address homelessness and hunger.
Those contributions reflect a central theme of Music with a Mission: Audiences can enjoy outstanding musical performances while knowing that their attendance helps support people facing difficult circumstances.
From helping the homeless to honoring 9/11 victims
The organization’s roots are closely connected to one of Somers’ most significant compositions, “Mass for the Homeless,” created with his wife, Joan.
The work, developed over several years, was inspired by the need to recognize the dignity of people experiencing poverty and homelessness.
Its 1997 premiere at Wilmington’s Grand Opera House featured the Delaware Symphony Orchestra and sold out before the performance. All proceeds from that premiere benefited five Delaware organizations serving people experiencing homelessness.
An encore performance followed in 1999, further establishing the connection between Somers’ music and community service.
Somers, who began his musical education at the former Wilmington Music School in 1962, has also composed film scores, jazz works and music exploring historical and spiritual themes.
He spent 30 years as choral director at The Tatnall School and has maintained a career as a church musician, conductor and jazz pianist.
His work on a documentary about Delaware artist Edward Loper earned him an Emmy Award for his original jazz score.
The same philosophy that inspired “Mass for the Homeless” also shaped “Requiem for 9/11.”
The composition premiered in 2012 at the Grand Opera House, bringing together orchestra, chorus, soloists and spoken text drawn from the Jewish, Christian and Islamic traditions.
Rather than focusing exclusively on the tragedy, Somers designed the work to explore grief, remembrance and the eventual restoration of hope.
A smaller chamber orchestra arrangement was subsequently developed to make the composition accessible to more community and school ensembles.
That version was performed at St. Helena’s Roman Catholic Church in Wilmington in September 2021, marking the 20th anniversary of the attacks.
The upcoming performance by the Newark Symphony Orchestra will bring the work to audiences again during the 25th anniversary year, under the direction of conductor Simeone Tartaglione.
Supporting a memorial born from military service
This year’s beneficiary, the Guardian of Defenders Memorial, provides a direct connection between the musical tribute and the sacrifices made by Americans following Sept. 11, 2001.
Located at 1300 Philadelphia Pike in Claymont, the memorial was envisioned by two retired military chaplains, the Rev. John Gayton, a Navy commander, and the Rev. Donald Van Alstyne, an Army major.
Both served in Iraq and Afghanistan, and each received a Bronze Star for his military service.
Their experiences counseling service members and families affected by combat helped inspire a permanent place dedicated to remembrance, reflection and healing.
The memorial features an angel carrying a fallen service member above a battlefield cross, symbolizing sacrifice and the spiritual care of those who served.
According to the organizers, Gayton mortgaged his home to help begin financing the project. Donations continue to support the memorial and its long-term maintenance through the Guardian of Defenders Foundation.
The site has become a place for public remembrance, including a Veterans Day visit by then-President Joe Biden in 2024, when a plaque honoring his late son, Beau Biden, was unveiled.
For Somers and Music with a Mission, the connection between the concert and the memorial is especially meaningful.
“I can’t think of a more fitting beneficiary to join us in remembering the sacrifices, the heroes and the ultimate triumph of the human spirit that arose from that terrible, momentous day,” Somers said. “We are so very honored to offer support to this effort.”
Continuing a tradition of music and giving
Music with a Mission’s work extends beyond its major orchestral compositions.
The organization has presented jazz concerts, holiday programs and smaller performances that bring together local musicians while supporting charitable organizations.
Its annual “A Jazz Christmas” performances have supported Delaware nonprofits, including those providing food, shelter and assistance to struggling families.
The organization has also presented Jazz Vespers programs combining sacred themes, original music and jazz performances.
In March 2026, Somers introduced “The Lincoln Legacy,” a composition examining President Abraham Lincoln’s leadership during the Civil War and the continuing relevance of his words during periods of national division.
A performance of “A Jazz Christmas” is scheduled for Dec. 6 at The Tatnall School in Wilmington.
These events reflect the organization’s continuing efforts to make music a vehicle for community engagement, charitable giving and reflection on issues that extend beyond the concert hall.
For the upcoming “Requiem for 9/11,” those goals come together in a particularly meaningful way.
The performance will offer an opportunity to remember the thousands of Americans killed on Sept. 11, honor those who responded and served in the years that followed, and support a Delaware memorial dedicated to ensuring those sacrifices are not forgotten.
Twenty-five years later, Music with a Mission is continuing its commitment to using the power of music to connect remembrance with hope and charitable service.
TO GO: Requiem for 9/11 — 25th anniversary performance

What: Newark Symphony Orchestra performance of Wilson Gault Somers’ “Requiem for 9/11”
When: Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026, at 3 p.m.
Where: The Independence School, 1300 Paper Mill Road, Newark
Conductor: Simeone Tartaglione
Beneficiary: A portion of the proceeds will support the Guardian of Defenders Memorial in Claymont.
Tickets: musicwithamission.org or newarksymphony.org
Learn more: guardianofdefenders.com
Contact: Pete Booker, Music with a Mission, 302-740-3220

name: Michigan Advance
title: Commentary: Michiganders in manufactured housing deserve protection from corporate exploitation
text:
Photo by Jon King/Michigan AdvanceThis past summer, a Canadian private equity firm became Michigan’s third-largest landlord to little fanfare. On an earnings call, Brookfield Asset Management disclosed that it had deployed its first investment to purchase YES! Communities, one of the largest manufactured housing owners in the country, with over 80,000 home sites in 23 states, including 21,574 home sites in Michigan.
This acquisition shows just how quickly a single investment firm can expand its control over Michigan’s housing market with little to no input from the thousands of Michiganders now paying rent to a new landlord. While the recently-passed federal ROAD to Housing Act attempts to rein in corporate landlords in the single-family housing market, residents of manufactured housing were largely overlooked. That leaves Michigan lawmakers with an important opportunity to establish protections before further consolidation puts even more residents at risk.
As a Michigander who works to uncover the impacts of private equity on our state and beyond, I have seen firsthand the pressing need for protections for manufactured housing residents against mistreatment by corporate landlords like Brookfield, especially in Michigan. Michigan has one of the highest concentrations of private equity-owned manufactured housing in the country, with more than one in four manufactured homes owned by PE firms as of January 2026. Given the gap in federal protections for manufactured housing residents, the Michigan legislature should take action to protect the tens of thousands of Michiganders living in private equity-owned manufactured housing.
In recent years, Brookfield has come under scrutiny for their profits-at-all-costs approach to property management, with reports of tenants enduring neglected maintenance and exorbitant junk fees at Brookfield properties. Residents of a Brookfield-owned apartment building in Washington, DC, accused the private equity firm of overbilling for utilities and charging variable fees for trash for different tenants. In Spain, where an affordable housing crisis has triggered an early election, members of the Sindicatos de Inquilinos de Madrid tenant union have organized protests against Brookfield’s attempts to sell off their apartments, potentially displacing residents.
Renters at a Brookfield-owned luxury apartment building in New York City complained of recurring flooding and other water issues in their building. And in San Francisco, tenants at a Brookfield and Ballast Investments-owned building received notices of eviction following a rent strike over habitability issues including a rodent infestation and a broken elevator.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Corporate-owned manufactured housing communities have experienced similar issues – and residents are even more vulnerable to such profit-maximizing tactics as a result of the unique business model of manufactured housing. Despite commonly being referred to as mobile homes, manufactured homes are almost never moved once placed in a park. In most cases, residents own their home but not the land beneath it, and must pay lot rent to the owners of the park. As a result, when lot rent and fees go up, or other maintenance issues arise in a manufactured housing community, homeowners are typically forced to endure it.
Manufactured housing residents across Michigan are already experiencing the worst impacts of corporate ownership of their communities. In early 2025, residents of TIR Equities-owned Kristana Estates in Dewitt Township were told they had only three days to move out so its owner could overhaul the park, with water being shut off just days later. In 2022, residents of Open Door Capital’s Landmark Estates in Warren reported that management did not respond to complaints of raw sewage spills, severe rat infestations, and unsafe electrical boxes.
Protest in front of North Morris Estates in Thetford Township, Mich. on Aug. 5, 2026. (Photo provided courtesy of MHAction)
At Kingsley Management-owned Oakland Estates in Auburn Hills, residents were hit with a $10,000 collective water bill, which residents claimed was due to a neglected leak. And in Thetford Township, Alden Global Capital affiliate Homes of America was the first-ever operator to be criminally convicted of operating a mobile home community without a license under Michigan’s nearly 40 year-old Mobile Home Commission Act. Residents of the community had endured foul, brown water coming from their taps and severely neglected maintenance under private equity ownership.
Even before YES! Communities was acquired by Brookfield, residents across the country reported extreme rent hikes, mold and mildew issues, and wastewater issues. Karen Anderson, a homeowner at Avon on the Lake in Rochester Hills, told Pennsylvania pension officials in August that her lot rent had increased nearly one-third since 2021. She described additional fees, restrictions on window A/C units, and difficulty selling her home despite investing more than $12,000 in improvements. Residents and advocates are eager to learn what Brookfield plans to do to address these longstanding issues at YES! Communities in Michigan and beyond.
Currently, the Michigan House is considering a set of bipartisan bills that would provide essential protections for manufactured housing residents and promote transparency and accountability among corporate owners of manufactured housing like Brookfield. These bills would limit excessive fees and utility billing; create a database of ownership information for manufactured housing communities; enforce licensing regulations more stringently; and create more opportunities for residents to purchase their parks if they go up for sale.
Michiganders living in YES! Communities can’t wait any longer for Brookfield to decide to make the changes they need. As our state endures punishing fuel prices, skyrocketing groceries, and unsustainable healthcare costs, it is essential that manufactured housing be protected as a key source of unsubsidized affordable housing. Michiganders living in manufactured homes deserve clean water, affordable lot rent, and well-maintained communities. If corporations can’t be counted on to be responsible stewards of manufactured housing, our lawmakers must act.
