name: Mississippi Today
title: Rural communities push back on school consolidation efforts: ‘They’re just looking at numbers on the paper’
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippi has lost thousands of public school students over the past decade, leaving fewer children enrolled in the state’s 138 school districts and less money to go around. 
State leaders think they’ve found a solution: School consolidation. 
House Speaker Jason White has formed a select committee to examine how merging districts in Mississippi could benefit students. Lawmakers say the state has too many small, underperforming school districts that spend too much on administration.
Representatives have identified several counties as potential candidates for consolidation, including Tallahatchie, Copiah, Washington and Bolivar. But state leaders are struggling to articulate a cohesive vision. It’s not clear if their intent is to merge staff, close schools or both.
House Education Chairman Rob Roberson, a Republican from Starkville, says the push is primarily about improving education while acknowledging that saving money is another factor. 
Rep. Rob Roberson, R-Starkville, speaks during a meeting of the House Select Committee on Consolidation at the Capitol in Jackson on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“It’s unfortunate, and it makes me sound like a bad guy, but I’ve got to look at it realistically,” he said, admitting that administrators’ jobs may be on the chopping block. “Adults matter to me, but the kids matter more.”
But people in communities across Mississippi worry that state leaders are only concerned about saving money without considering how school closures will affect their small towns.
In Tallahatchie, locals fear consolidation will stall progress while Copiah residents fret about deeper dysfunction.
“I don’t think it’s about the kids,” said Bernard Berryhill, a former West Tallahatchie teacher. “I think it’s about dollar bills.”
Shrinking populations, shrinking budgets
The stakes are different for school districts that may be forced to merge. In Copiah County, consolidation could bring Wesson schools in closer proximity with communities with a history of low academic performance and administrative turnover. Hazlehurst schools would lose local control, including the ability to direct their spending and hire school staff. 


“They’re just looking at numbers on the paper,” said Hazlehurst school board President Paul Rhodes. “And there’s going to be some other costs that may go along with it that they’re not even considering.”
The move comes as Hazlehurst schools face a possible state takeover. School leadership has made the kind of progress in recent months that might put off a state takeover, but a key question they still face is: Are your dysfunctional days behind you?
In some ways, the consolidation makes financial sense. 
The Copiah County School District’s central office is less than a mile away from Hazlehurst City Schools’ in downtown Hazlehurst. Both districts’ bus barns are in the county seat. 
Copiah County School District map with different school zones displayed in the district office in Hazlehurst on Sept. 3, 2025. Credit: Leonardo Bevilacqua/Mississippi Today
But for local communities, the possible savings seem meager compared to losing representation on the school board and mixing district finances and instructional planning for student populations with different needs.
“We want what’s best for the kids,” said Barbara Higgins, whose nonprofit Empowering Doves helps connect Hazlehurst seniors with scholarships. “If they’re afraid of progress, make sure the students have what they need first. We want the chance to grow. And we have been.”
‘The raw end of the deal’
The eastern side of Tallahatchie County is anchored by Charleston, a town of about 1,900 people with a bustling downtown square. The other end of the county is a constellation of four-way stops, rural communities with little more than town halls and gas stations. 
There’s already a sense of inequity between the two ends of the county, said Stephanie Kassem, leader of the Boys & Girls Club in Tutwiler.
The east side has “a stronger tax base, so of course they get more money,” she said. “That’s led to this feeling that they get better things than they would over here.”
Berryhill, the former teacher, said he’s concerned that funds would not be fairly divided between the county’s two districts, East Tallahatchie and West Tallahatchie, after a consolidation. 
Crystal Morgan, whose children attend Wesson Attendance Center in the Copiah County School District, is pictured at Wesson Public Library, Aug. 27, 2026. She is an alumna of Crystal Springs schools. Credit: Leonardo Bevilacqua/Mississippi Today
Superintendent Tony Young’s perspective, West Tallahatchie School District is doing well on its own, financially and academically. He is already concerned about losing money next year because of a new school funding formula that’s tied more closely to student enrollment. A clause that protects districts from losing funding because of declining enrollment expires next summer.
Almost 70,000 students have left Mississippi public schools since 2013. In that time, West Tallahatchie schools have lost more than 300 students, nearly half of its student body. East Tallahatchie has lost a third.
Opposition to consolidation in Copiah County is centered in Wesson and Hazlehurst, where parents and community leaders fear the change would provide few benefits while deepening disparities in resources.
Crystal Morgan, whose three children attend Wesson schools, fears consolidation will overwhelm teachers and crowd classrooms. The consolidation proposed by the legislature last session redrew boundaries to coincide with board of supervisor lines, which would mean some Hazlehurst students would be zoned into Wesson schools. 
She said she hopes her kids don’t end up getting “the raw end of the deal with extra students in their already small classroom,” and worries about adding poorly-performing schools to the district.
Tanya Marsaw, whose daughter is a senior at Crystal Springs High School in the Copiah County School District, and Dwayne Thompson, a bail bondsman in Copiah County, discuss the prospect of school consolidation over lunch at Brando’s Steakhouse and Buffet in Crystal Springs, August 21, 2026 Credit: Leonardo Bevilacqua/Mississippi Today
“Wesson thrives because it’s a small and tight knit community,” she said. 
Tanya Marsaw, a mother of a Crystal Springs High senior, said the district’s students learn and play in subpar facilities. She’s not sure if that would change in a consolidation, but wonders if new leadership after a merger could pave the way for some improvements. 
“My daughter plays volleyball,” she said. “She goes into the Wesson locker room… It’s like going somewhere else. They don’t have rats, they don’t have roaches, they don’t have paint chipping off the wall, none of those things.”
Fears of violence
For many Tallahatchie County locals, who are proud of the academic growth of both districts, the first question about consolidation is, “Why?” The immediate second question is, “How?”
Lorenzo Pimpton, a West Tallahatchie teacher and coach, said busing a student from Tutwiler, in the western part of the county, to Charleston in the east could take hours if there are multiple stops. 
Lorenzo Pimpton, a teacher and coach, talks about potential consolidation in Tallahatchie County on Aug. 21, 2026.  Credit: Devna Bose
The idea, a possible reality of consolidation, is “outlandish” unless lawmakers find the funding for the community to build a centralized school, said Rep. Tracey Rosebud, a West Tallahatchie graduate who now represents the whole county.
“Otherwise, it’s going to be ugly to transfer kids across the region like that,” he said. 
And those long bus rides could lead to fights, he said. Rosebud is particularly concerned about violence between older students if they’re forced together unexpectedly. The two schools have long had a friendly rivalry that sometimes turns hostile, he said.
From her work at the Boys & Girls Club, Kassem worries a merger could destabilize already-struggling students. She knows the trauma many Tallahatchie students are living with: unable to depend on regular meals at home, unreliable transportation and other issues.
Stephanie Kassem, unit director of the Boys & Girls Club in Tutwiler,  pictured on Aug. 21, 2026, in her office. Credit: Devna Bose
“You’re in that kind of awkward age and then you are self-conscious, and this is a huge change to be going through,” she said. “I think it would be too much … and would add to some of their trauma.”
A seat at the table
Whatever lawmakers decide on an administrative or school consolidation, Berryhill hopes they consider locals’ voices and make slow, intentional changes.
“If the state is going to make a change, I’d prefer it’s gradual,” he said. “Where can we meet in the middle? A new campus or a new building, maybe.”
When Hazlehurst students exited their buses on the first day of school in August, they were met with landscaped lawns and planters outfitted with red mulch, repainted buildings and glossy gym floors.
Bernard Berryhill, an alumnus and former West Tallahatchie teacher, talks about consolidation with his mother, Lucinda Berryhill, who serves on the school board.  Credit: Devna Bose
The upgrades were the brainchild of Nonya Thrasher, the superintendent appointed in September. She fielded donations and volunteers from local businesses as part of a beautification project. Thrasher brought local leaders into the schools, and cleared the majority of outstanding accreditation violations that kept the district on the state’s radar. 
To many in the community, she has brought something that has eluded the district in recent years: hope. 
For Higgins, a girl scout leader in Hazlehurst for over 30 years, her support for consolidation hinged on the school board’s decision to hire Thrasher, who she says is the most qualified and effective superintendent the district has had in years.
As they discuss consolidating Hazlehurst and Copiah County schools, state lawmakers may also be lingering on a painful and chaotic state takeover of the city district that lasted from 2008 to 2014. The district was out of compliance with nearly every accreditation standard and has struggled to run a functional special education department. 
State lawmakers listen as John Ellison, former Chickasaw County School District superintendent, speaks during a meeting of the House Select Committee on Consolidation at the Capitol in Jackson on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
For now, Thrasher is part of the conversation. She is expected to address the subcommittee on school consolidation in October.
Roberson wants the communities to be involved in the discussion, he said, which also requires admitting there’s a problem.
“Leadership shows up trying to protect what they have,” he said. “What you currently have will not exist over the course of the next few years, because it’s not working. If it was, we wouldn’t be having this conversation.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: 8 key questions about school district (and college) consolidation in Mississippi
authors: Devna Bose, Leonardo Bevilacqua, and Candice Wilder
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
School consolidation, a perennial topic in Mississippi, is poised to be a top education policy debate during the 2027 legislative session.
Mississippi has 138 school districts, 15 community colleges and eight public universities. State leaders want to shrink those numbers by merging students, administrators and — in some cases — closing schools. 
School districts are set to receive $3 billion in state funding next school year. Community colleges and public universities are set to receive more than $1.26 billion.
Mississippi Today talked to legislators, educators and residents across communities that have experienced school district consolidation or may be targeted for consolidation next year. The reporting reveals fears, successes and other insights. 
Below, we address key questions about school and district consolidation. We also break down how consolidation might affect public education. 
What is school or district consolidation?
Consolidation refers to merging schools (K-12 or college) or districts under centralized management, according to the National Education Policy Center at the University of Colorado. 
It can involve two or more school districts merging central offices, which is an administrative consolidation, or combining multiple schools or districts into one, including staff and students. The same goes for consolidations that involve colleges.
Is consolidation the same as closure?
No. Closing a school or district means to permanently shut down a school — ending operations, closing the building and letting staff go. A consolidation combines multiple schools — its staff, students and resources — into one. 
Still, people might use the term “closure” over “consolidation” because of the loss they’ve experienced, said Carrie Hahnel, a senior associate with Bellwether, a national nonprofit that works to improve education outcomes. 
What are Mississippi lawmakers planning around consolidation?
Almost immediately after this year’s legislative session wrapped, lawmakers indicated they are interested in merging K-12 school districts in a number of counties next year, including Tallahatchie, Copiah, Bolivar and Washington, Mississippi Today confirmed. They are focusing on underperforming districts with declining student enrollment.
Members of the House Select Committee on Consolidation meet at the Capitol in Jackson on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Legislators say they have no immediate plans to close any colleges and universities but are weighing factors like population loss, enrollment declines and concerns over whether taxpayer money is being used efficiently.
This isn’t the first time lawmakers have explored consolidating schools in Mississippi. A bill that would’ve consolidated Copiah and Hazlehurst schools died earlier this year. 
Why are lawmakers focusing on consolidation now?
Lawmakers have mentioned shrinking student enrollment, administrative costs and student performance as reasons for their consolidation talks. 
House Speaker Jason White formed a select committee in May to investigate how consolidating schools, districts and colleges in Mississippi could benefit students. 
“My number one goal is to improve academic performance,” said House Education Chairman Rob Roberson, a Republican from Starkville. “Obviously, if you have money savings and efficiency, that would be a secondary benefit of that.”
What are some pros and cons of consolidation?
Some positive outcomes could include enhanced academic and extracurricular offerings for students, better facilities and less spending. 
However, communities can lose a sense of identity when local school buildings close, and students may have to travel farther for school. There tends to be local pushback to consolidation plans because of fears of violence between students from rival communities coming together and the economic impact because of the loss of jobs. 
Also, it doesn’t always result in improved academics. In fact, merging low-performing districts can exacerbate existing dysfunctions. 
Do lawmakers have the power to consolidate K-12 schools and merge colleges in Mississippi?
Local K-12 school boards can initiate school or district consolidations, but the Legislature tends to do the initiating.
The Mississippi Legislature holds the ultimate power in determining which colleges and universities merge or close.
Do consolidated school districts save money?
In Mississippi, generally, yes. But not much.
On average, districts saved a quarter of a million dollars on administrative costs, a fraction of most school districts’ budgets, according to Mississippi Today’s analysis of school superintendents’ spending reports.
One district didn’t save any money. Greenwood-Leflore Consolidated, the product of Leflore and Greenwood school districts, ended up spending $16,070 more on administrative costs in 2020, the year after the districts merged, compared to administrative costs for the two individual districts in the year prior.
In 2012, lawmakers mentioned large savings on administrative costs as part of efforts to sell a school district consolidation to hesitant Bolivar County. Then-state Sen. Gray Tollison, a Republican who represented Oxford, told the Clarion Ledger that the county’s school districts could save $1.6 million if they consolidated their six districts into two. The consolidated districts saved $718,000, according to an analysis of the districts’ administrative spending reports. 
But to make these big savings, school districts have to make tough decisions, former Winona-Montgomery Superintendent Teresa Jackson told state representatives in August at one of the school consolidation select committee’s meetings. 
“If we had not closed schools, we would have saved very little,” she said. 
How strong is consolidated districts’ academic performance?
It varies. 
In Mississippi, most of the mandated consolidations since 2014 involved low-performing districts. 
The Starkville-Oktibbeha district merger in 2015 is considered a bright spot. The consolidated district’s enrollment grew. Community members now say students have access to more academic and extracurricular opportunities. The combined district is now rated an A.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Washington 9th graders perform better with new program, but funding isn’t guaranteed
text:
(Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)Across Washington state, schools rolled out a support system designed to help high school freshmen over the last few years. 
In the Ninth Grade Success initiative, teachers and other school support staff pair up with students dealing with low grades, truancy, poor behavior and more. 
A recent state evaluation shows it’s working: More students pass their classes and stay on track to graduate, a report for the Office of Superintendent of Public Instruction shows.
“It’s really a student-centered approach,” said Kimberly Tennant, assistant principal at River Ridge High School, part of the North Thurston Public Schools. “We do empathy talks, we talk to their parents, we talk to their teachers. We kind of get a whole picture of the kid and then we think about what the student needs.” 
Around 60 schools participate in the program. Those that do typically see a 6 percentage point boost in freshman students passing their classes, according to the evaluation.
Ninth grade is a critical year for students, and studies show that those who pass their freshman year classes are more likely to graduate high school on time. 
In schools with 250 enrolled ninth graders, about 15 more students stayed on track to graduate.
“This evaluation confirms what educators across Washington have seen firsthand: when we strengthen educators’ routines and data practices, students receive the right support during their first year of high school, more of them succeed,” said Superintendent of Public Instruction Chris Reykdal.
Last year, Ninth Grade Success served 50 schools across 32 districts, but there are more schools that have sustained the program without additional funding, said Katy Payne, chief strategy officer for OSPI. 
Ninth Grade Success is particularly helpful for low-income and multilingual students where on-track graduation rates increased by 6.75 percentage points and 10.96 percentage points, respectively. 
“Ninth grade is a make-or-break year,” said Henterson Carlisle, Northwest regional director for the Center for High School Success, a nonprofit educational organization that partnered with OSPI to help get the program started. 
“This approach has been working for kids, regardless of what school, community, where you live … As long as we can continue to have the partnership with OSPI and the state of Washington, I see a future — a bright future — for our ninth graders.”
The program is comparatively cheap, but with the state of Washington’s budgetary affairs, it’s longevity isn’t promised. 
Those involved with the program are “gravely concerned” about funding.
“Every year, until we have multi-year funding or funding that is guaranteed, there’s always a worry,” Carlisle said. “I’m not comfortable saying, oh yeah, we’re going to be here next year.” 
OSPI will be requesting $1.5 million each year over the next four years to keep the program running and to expand it to more schools, said Payne. 
North Thurston Public Schools received $6,000 in the 2025-2026 school year to kickstart the program.  
In its first year, 65.8% of ninth graders at North Thurston passed all their courses. In the 2024-2025 school year, that figure jumped to 75.4%. Last year, it was 72.8%, according to data from OSPI. 
Ninth Grade Success operates in 15 states. Washington launched a pilot program in five high schools in the 2019-2020 and 2020-2021 school years. Over the next seven years, it expanded to 78 schools, according to the OSPI evaluation.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Issue Spotlight: What candidates in Arkansas’ US Senate race say about AI, data centers
text:
A server room in a data center.  A recent poll found more than 70% of Americans don't want a data center built near them. (Getty Images)Voters’ concerns about artificial intelligence and the data centers that keep it running have gained prominence during the midterm election cycle, prompting questions about how the federal government could regulate the industry.
AI’s rapid growth over the past few years has generated policy debates in all levels of government. A Pew Research Center poll in August found that 71% of people surveyed are worried AI will replace jobs done by humans over the next 20 years.
‘Dumbfounds us all’: Congress struggles with policies rippling from AI development

AI chatbots have sparked safety concerns, including a recent lawsuit from Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin against OpenAI, alleging it hid ChatGPT’s risks from users. Some states have passed laws preventing ChatGPT and other chatbots from giving mental health advice in light of young users’ suicides.
Data centers’ water and electricity usage has sparked local backlash nationwide, including in several Arkansas communities where officials have butted heads over regulations.
Potential AI and data center regulations have been floated in Congress, though President Donald Trump has dismissed the call for new guardrails. One of Arkansas’ Republican U.S. senators, Tom Cotton, is up for reelection in November.
Cotton faces two challengers, Democrat Hallie Shoffner and Libertarian Jeff Wadlin. All three have said in interviews that they support giving Arkansans a vote on whether a data center is built near them.
Hallie Shoffner, a Democratic candidate for the U.S. Senate race in Arkansas, answers questions during the debate against Libertarian Jeff Wadlin on Monday, October 12, 2026 at the Arkansas TV studios in Conway, Arkansas. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)
Here’s what else they had to say about AI and data centers:
 Shoffner calls for more transparency

Shoffner said Arkansans have asked her questions about data centers at every event she’s held since launching her campaign last year. Arkansans are curious about new forms of industry that might affect their daily lives, and current officeholders aren’t answering their questions, she said.
“They want industry that comes in and provides jobs, but they want transparency about what those industries are, the impacts that they’ll have on the community, and whether or not they have a say in whether something is built in their own backyard or not,” Shoffner said.
She said city and county residents should be able to vote on the construction of a nearby data center.
Shoffner also said she also would support the creation of a federal agency to monitor and regulate the AI industry. She compared the idea to how the Environmental Protection Agency regulates fertilizers that introduce chemicals into the food supply when sprayed on crops.
“I don’t think it’s unreasonable to ask to have that same kind of administration when it comes to AI,” she said.

Arkansas Explained: Understanding the data center boom and debate

 

 Cotton calls for ‘targeted’ regulation

Cotton did not respond to a list of emailed questions from the Advocate. Cotton, who chairs the Senate Intelligence Committee, told 40/29 News in September that he has discussed “both the promise and the risk” of AI with the White House, the Pentagon and the CIA.
Arkansas Republican U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton (Photo by John Sykes Jr./Arkansas Advocate)
He said he’s spoken to Arkansans about how they use AI in their daily lives, “whether it’s a routine to help them get over an achy knee or an achy back, or maybe developing a summer reading or math plan for their kids.”
Cotton has introduced a bill that would allow data centers to build their own power grid so their construction and use doesn’t siphon power from local communities and increase residents’ utility bills. He supported another measure by fellow Republican U.S. Jon Husted of Ohio that proposed standards for regulators to enforce when connecting data centers to the grid, but that measure was blocked by Senate Democrats who called the measure toothless. 
Like Shoffner, Cotton said AI companies should be transparent about the uses of their products and data centers’ impacts on communities. He also said local residents should have the power to choose whether a data center is built near them.
Unlike Shoffner, Cotton said he doesn’t believe the federal government needs a “Department of Artificial Intelligence” or for “big government bureaucracy” to oversee the AI industry.

Data center backlash set to sway midterm elections

 

“If we’re going to pass legislation [in Congress], it needs to be targeted and straightforward, and provide some clear guardrails, like protecting children from misuse of AI chatbots, making sure that we’re not exploiting some of the most vulnerable people, [or] making sure it’s not being used for fraud,” Cotton told 40/29 News.
 Wadlin: ‘Regulation needs to develop with the industry’

Wadlin said he would support prohibiting the use of AI in the public safety and transportation industries. 
He said the use of agentic AI, a type of semi- or fully autonomous artificial intelligence which companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are developing, requires more stringent regulations.
“[It’s] not just asking the AI to do something and produce something for you, but you’re giving it the keys to the car,” Wadlin said.
Jeff Wadlin, a Libertarian candidate for U.S. Senate for Arkansas, answers questions during the debate with opponent Democrat Hallie Shoffner at the Arkansas TV studios in Conway, Arkansas on Monday, October 12, 2026. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)
He also said he would be open to a government agency or a commercial auditing entity monitoring AI companies, as long as there is some nationwide oversight because “the regulation needs to develop with the industry.”
Regarding data centers, Wadlin said the companies behind them should be required to pay for their own electricity and water use. He also agreed with his opponents that local control should be crucial to whether a data center is built.
“There should be town halls [where] these things should be discussed,” Wadlin said. “It should not be backroom deals where the state government is signing an NDA, or some county judge is making a decision without consulting their local constituents.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri congressional map fight reaches voters as Republican campaign goes quiet
text:
Supporters of a referendum on Missouri's gerrymandered redistricting map rally at the state Capitol Building Tuesday, May 12 after the Missouri Supreme Court heard arguments on two cases involving the redistricting map (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).Missouri Republicans spent more than a year fighting to put a new congressional map into effect, including a costly campaign to prevent voters from having the final say.
Now that voters have that say, the organized Republican campaign to defend the map has all but vanished.
On Nov. 3, Missourians will decide Proposition A, a referendum on a redistricting plan passed last year at President Donald Trump’s urging to improve Republicans’ chances of winning seven of Missouri’s eight seats in the U.S. House. A “yes” vote approves the new map; a “no” vote rejects it and keeps the boundaries adopted in 2022.
Neither outcome will change the congressional districts used in this year’s election. After a prolonged legal fight, the U.S. Supreme Court ordered Missouri to use its 2022 map in November. Proposition A will instead determine which boundaries apply beginning with the 2028 election, barring another redistricting effort.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The campaign to defeat Proposition A is pouring money into advertising and voter outreach. People Not Politicians, which collected the signatures that forced the referendum, has reported $5.4 million in contributions of at least $5,000 each since mid September.
Put Missouri First, meanwhile, spent about $2.9 million trying to block the referendum but has reported no large donations since July.
Michael Hafner, a spokesman for Put Missouri First, said the hope is that “Missourians will tune out the noise and look beyond the millions of dollars in advertising” and support the map drawn by lawmakers last year.
“Prop A deserves Missourians’ support because it delivers a practical, commonsense map that respects more community boundaries throughout our state,” he told The Independent.
But while Republicans continue hoping voters will approve the map, Hafner told St. Louis Public Radio there is currently no organized effort to support the passage of Proposition A. Instead, the GOP is investing money and resources in other races.
“The left has allocated significant funds into defeating the map,” he said, “and Republicans nationally have other fish to fry.”
Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, who fought unsuccessfully to keep the referendum off the ballot, said he remains firmly behind the new congressional boundaries. He acknowledged the competition for campaign dollars and public attention but said he believes supporters of the map are organizing at the grassroots level.
“While they might not be the loudest or most well funded,” he said, “I believe they are a formidable force and their efforts will be worthwhile on election night.”
 A fight over Kansas City

At the center of the dispute is Kansas City and the 5th Congressional District, represented since 2005 by Democrat Emanuel Cleaver.
Under the 2022 map, most of Kansas City lies in a district contained within Jackson and Clay counties. The 2025 boundaries would divide much of the city among three districts, combining its neighborhoods with Republican-leaning communities stretching into northern and central Missouri and the Ozarks.
The result would change the 5th District from one Kamala Harris carried with about 61% of the vote in 2024 to one Trump carried with about 58% — potentially converting one of Missouri’s two Democratic congressional seats into a seventh Republican seat.
Richard von Glahn, executive director of People Not Politicians, argues the proposal would weaken the voices of Kansas City residents while tying rural voters to distant urban neighborhoods for partisan gain. He noted that one dividing line follows Troost Avenue, long associated with racial segregation in Kansas City.
“It targets Kansas City,” von Glahn said during an interview on The Independent’s Missouri on the Record podcast. “But the harm is really statewide when politicians start manipulating elections and rearranging voters on the map.”
Republican supporters counter that the map improves on several traditional redistricting measures. In May, the Missouri Supreme Court upheld the map against a separate constitutional challenge concerning compactness and population equality.
Prop A and the fight over Missouri’s congressional map

 
Ordinarily, states redraw congressional districts once every decade after the federal census. Missouri Republicans undertook a second redraw in September 2025 amid a national partisan battle over control of the U.S. House. Republicans pushed new boundaries in states including Texas, while Democrats sought advantages elsewhere, including California.
People Not Politicians responded with more than 300,000 petition signatures. Hoskins refused to certify the referendum, arguing the congressional map could not be subjected to a statewide vote.
The Missouri Supreme Court unanimously rejected that position Sept. 3, ordering the referendum onto the ballot and ruling that the new districts had never legally taken effect. After additional litigation, the U.S. Supreme Court concluded Sept. 25 that the 2022 districts must govern November’s election.
 Millions spent on both sides

The money battle began long before the referendum qualified. National groups aligned with both parties supplied millions of dollars, including contributions through political nonprofits that do not disclose their underlying donors.
Von Glahn said volunteers and anger over an unusual mid-decade redraw propelled the petition drive, though he acknowledged the campaign could not operate without substantial financial backing.
An August Saint Louis University/YouGov survey illustrated the challenge of explaining the vote. With ballot wording presented to respondents, 35% favored Proposition A, 32% opposed it and 33% were unsure.
The official ballot description emphasizes that the new map would keep more counties intact. It does not mention the plan’s potential to give Republicans another congressional seat.
Von Glahn said his campaign has to explain the referendum’s unusual mechanics: People Not Politicians sponsored the petition, but it is asking voters to mark “no.”
 Another redistricting fight ahead?

Even if voters reject Proposition A, the battle over Missouri’s congressional districts may not be over.
Minutes after the Missouri Supreme Court ruled against the new map, Republican state Sen. Nick Schroer posted “8-0 2027” on social media, signaling interest in a map that could give the GOP all eight congressional seats. Hoskins has said he could “most certainly” see lawmakers revisiting redistricting next year.
Whether Republicans could succeed may depend on another Nov. 3 ballot measure. Amendment 6 would prohibit lawmakers from passing legislation “similar in effect” to a law rejected by referendum unless at least 80% of both the House and Senate agree to send it back to voters for approval.
Travis Crum, a Washington University law professor who studies election law, said another Republican redraw before the 2030 census would likely trigger that restriction if voters reject Proposition A and approve Amendment 6. But the amendment does not define “similar in effect,” meaning another redistricting effort could end up back in court.
Even without Amendment 6, the state Supreme Court’s ruling means voters could use the referendum process again to suspend a new congressional map. Von Glahn said he hopes lawmakers instead take a rejection of Proposition A as a signal to move on to other issues.
“Unfortunately, we can’t stop legislators from bringing up bad ideas,” he said.
For now, von Glahn said, the argument against the new map is one that should resonate across party lines.
“People should pick our politicians,” he said. “Politicians shouldn’t pick their voters.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska’s 1st Congressional District race could be one to watch
text:
U.S. Rep. Mike Flood, R-Neb., left, and Democrat Chris Backemeyer will face off for Nebraska's 1st Congressional District in November 2026. (Candidate photos courtesy of respective campaigns | U.S. Capitol photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)LINCOLN — As the political environment has worsened for Republicans, Nebraska’s 1st Congressional District is now viewed as more competitive than earlier in the cycle.
Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Flood represents a district that spans 12 counties, including Lancaster County, home to heavily Democratic Lincoln, a city whose blue voters are often drowned out by the region’s more conservative smaller cities and rural areas. He has won his past two U.S. House elections by 20 and 16 percentage points. But Cook Political Report and Inside Elections have recently shifted Flood’s race from safe — or solid — Republican to likely Republican. 
Chris Backemeyer, the Democratic challenger, has stayed under the radar throughout the cycle with few national outlets mentioning Backemeyer’s bid against Flood. If Backemeyer pulls off an upset, it would likely signal a historic night for Democrats nationally.  
Nebraska State Treasurer Joey Spellerberg of Fremont and U.S. Rep. Mike Flood, R-Neb., at a 2026 midterms rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds featuring President Donald Trump. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Flood downplayed the rating changes, saying they likely reflect the political environment rather than the polling data. The former legislative speaker said he’d been in a race like this before, pointing to a 2022 special election against Patty Pansing Brooks. 
“I think the message is I’m a proven entity,” Flood told the Examiner. “I am rooted in this state, and I know its people, and I’ve delivered results. I’m not trying to get on TV every day or, you know, be a showboat. I’m trying to deliver for the people of my home state.”  
Backemeyer said he believed this race was winnable from the start because he appeals to “the part of the electorate that’s sort of center left (and) center right.” 
Chris Backemeyer in his Lincoln campaign office on Oct. 21, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
“The last thing we needed was the National Democratic Party telling us what to do in Nebraska’s 1st District, and so we’ve been able to run our own race,” Backemeyer said. “They finally have woken up and said, ‘Oh, holy cow! There’s actually a race here.” 
Backemeyer is a former diplomat who launched his bid shortly after he asked a question at one of Flood’s rowdy town halls last year. After winning his Democratic primary, Backemeyer then faced a brief month’s spat with Austin Ahlam, who joined the race as a nonpartisan before suspending his campaign over concerns about his father’s health. 
One recurring issue in this House race has been the Iran war. During the only debate in this race, Backemeyer emphasized his work on the 2015 Iran nuclear deal under then-President Barack Obama, saying the deal would have prevented the current war but was torn up for “partisan political purposes.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The war in the Middle East has been ongoing since February. The war has caused high gas prices and skyrocketed farmers’ fertilizer costs. Flood, much like other Republicans in the midterm races, has acknowledged the increased prices. Flood has pointed to tax cuts from Trump’s tax and spending law and his role in passing a landmark housing law earlier this year as examples of his delivering for constituents. 
Flood has defended his votes for the war, saying the United States can’t pull out of Iran as it did in Afghanistan during the Biden administration. Flood has criticized the 2015 nuclear deal, calling it a “failed” deal.  
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
He recently told ABC’s affiliate KETV that he doesn’t want to undermine the president during the current conflict. 
Backemeyer has also attacked Flood over Trump’s tariffs. He has a campaign ad playing on Flood’s last name, saying people are getting “flooded” with high prices because he voted for the tariffs. 
Tariffs have been a key tool for the Trump administration, which has used them as a bargaining chip with other countries. While the U.S. Supreme Court dealt a major blow to Trump’s trade agenda earlier this year, some tariffs are still in place. 
Flood has said the Trump administration has made progress in trade relationships with countries across the globe, but “it takes time to dig out of the hole,” referring to earlier trade deals. Flood has attacked Backemeyer for being an “outsider” — pointing to his career in D.C. and a Plains Sentinel story about Backemeyer’s residency in Nebraska. 
“I believe strongly that Nebraskans want a representative who is invested in this district, someone whose roots are here and whose future is here,” Flood said in a Sunday press call. “That’s the difference in this race; Chris Backemeyer still has a lot of Washington in him.” 
Backemeyer told the Examiner that if Flood thinks his time in D.C. is a “negative, then that’s up to him.” 
He has worked for the State Department for 20 years in Washington, D.C., focusing on counterterrorism, economic policy and the Middle East. 
“As I’ve talked to people around this district, they think experience is valuable,” Backemeyer said. “They think that having somebody that understands Iran and how we could have stayed out of this war would have been useful to have in Congress instead of a rubber stamp.” 
The former diplomat said his final message isn’t about Flood’s character but his “failure” to push back against decisions from the Trump administration that have “hurt every single person in this district economically.” 
Two other candidates are in the race: Libertarian Nik Sandman and America First Party’s Dan Hartong. Their answers are in the Examiner’s voter guide.
The general election is Nov. 3. Early voting has already begun.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Commentary: Want to end redistricting wars? Start by uncapping the US House.
text:
The U.S. Capitol on April 9 (Ashley Murray/States Newsroom).Missouri’s congressional redistricting battle has taken voters on a dizzying tour of the court system leading up to the midterms. After trips to the Missouri Supreme Court and federal district court resulted in different rulings, the state took not one but two trips to the U.S. Supreme Court, which held – twice – that the state should use its 2022 congressional map for the November 2026 election.  Voters will decide the fate of the new map through Proposition A.
The legal question that dominated these disputes was about whether Missouri could use a newly drawn map despite a valid referendum petition.  But the process invokes a larger and more important question about our representation: why has control of a single congressional seat become so consequential that politicians are willing to fight over it in multiple court rooms instead of trusting voters to decide?
One way voters can take matters into their own hands is to support uncapping the U.S. House of Representatives.  From our nation’s founding until the passage of the Permanent Apportionment Act of 1929, the House grew alongside the national population.  The cap at 435 members created an artificial scarcityaround representation, and that scarcity is one of the drivers fueling the current gerrymandering wars, in Missouri and beyond.
With the same number of House seats representing a population that has more than tripled since 1929, each individual district has become larger, and political control of each one has become more consequential.
Missouri’s congressional delegation provides a particularly striking example.  When the House was capped in 1929, Missouri had 16 seats in the House, representing a population of 3.6 million residents, or approximately 225,000 constituents per representative.  By contrast, today Missouri has only eight House seats, representing a population of nearly 6.3 million, meaning that each representative has approximately 783,000 constituents.  In other words, Missouri’s population has nearly doubled yet its House delegation has been cut in half.
The average Missourian now experiences a much lower quality of representation as a result, because even the most conscientious representatives struggle to serve such large districts.  For example, Missouri’s 6thCongressional District, spanning all of northern Missouri from the Kansas border to the Mississippi River, includes 39 counties and is so large that it covers more square miles than nine U.S. states.
To be clear, uncapping the House is not a panacea for partisan gerrymandering.  The process will always be political, and the parties will always compete to control the process.  But expanding the House would reduce the artificial scarcity problem that has made each individual seat such an extraordinarily valuable political asset.  More representation is also consistent with what the Founders intended – in Federalist No. 55, Madison warned against making the House too small, arguing that it must be large enough to secure “a full knowledge of the interest of its constituents,” and ensure “that its members are not lifted too far aloft from the mass of the citizens.”
 Smaller districts would also mean more opportunities for voters to elect someone responsive to their communities and less political power concentrated in each individual seat.
And that is where Missouri’s recent redistricting battle intersects with the debate over the size of the House. We should be asking not only how to stop politicians from manipulating district lines, or which court is most likely to stop them when they do.  We should also be asking why control of a single congressional seat has become so consequential in the first place.
Instead of endlessly searching for another favorable courtroom or a more clever way to control the limited number or seats, maybe the way out of our redistricting wars is simply more seats at the table.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Commentary: Proposed census changes could worsen childcare shortage
text:
Child care that is high quality and affordable is vital to Nebraska's economy. (Stock photo by Lourdes Balduque/Getty Images)Every year, as part of my job at Voices for Children in Nebraska, I gather the most up-to-date information on thousands of key child wellbeing indicators in the state of Nebraska. To take one example, we produce a map featuring the childcare capacity of all 93 counties in Nebraska. So, for instance, if a county has a score of 50, it means there are 50 licensed childcare spots available for every 100 children in need of care in that county. By tracking this information, it is possible to pinpoint where in Nebraska there are critical shortages of childcare.
 To determine this requires full and accurate information from the U.S. Census regarding the number of children living in Nebraska’s communities. I have witnessed how such information was key to convincing state lawmakers to raise the income cap on families eligible for childcare subsidies from 130% of the federal poverty level to 185%, as well as reduce administrative barriers associated with running a childcare business. I have also seen the power of this information used by nonprofit organizations and community members to address shortages in their communities.
Yet the Trump Administration has proposed changes to the upcoming decennial census that would limit the count to U.S. citizens and “lawful permanent residents,” such as immigrants with green cards. Such rule changes are not only unconstitutional but would negatively impact the ability of communities to plan and direct resources toward solving public problems such as childcare, housing, schooling, traffic congestion and healthcare services.
As stated by the U.S. Constitution in Article 1, Sections 2 and 9, the government is to conduct a census every 10 years. Furthermore, the 14th Amendment states that the “whole number of persons in each state” are to be counted, a distinction that has long been understood to mean all people residing in the U.S. The census is the most important tool we have for accurately determining how many people are living in the U.S. and where they reside within the country, critical knowledge used to determine the number of congressional seats and Electoral College votes each state gets for the next 10 years, as well as where to distribute trillions of dollars in federal funding.
The rule changes proposed by the Trump administration would exclude work-visa holders, refugees, asylees and other residents who would be dropped from the apportionment count for the first time. Without a full and accurate picture, the childcare capacity maps we make every year will be less reliable and could show that there is adequate childcare capacity in counties where families are struggling to find care. And this will not just impact the “big cities” of Omaha and Lincoln. According to current numbers from the Census Bureau, with 10% of its population being foreign born, Hall County will be particularly vulnerable to having incomplete information.
If the proposed changes go into effect, a growing number of residents will disappear from the census counts, but they will not disappear from our community’s childcare facilities, roads, workplaces, schools, neighborhoods and hospitals. We will not just be hurting those who are not counted but lessening the quality of services for all community members. It will mean, among other things, more severe shortages in childcare and housing, longer traffic lines, overcrowded schools, and longer waits for critical health care services. It will mean less effective public systems and weaker communities.
Luckily these changes have not gone into effect and the Census Bureau is accepting comments regarding the proposed rule changes until Nov. 2. Tens of thousands of comments have already been submitted by community members concerned about the integrity and accuracy of the census count. I encourage you to join the fight to save the census and submit your own comment to the Federal Register here.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Commentary: Americans over 60 lose billions to cybercrime. Here’s what to do if a loved one has been scammed.
text:
In 2025, South Carolinians reported about 14,700 cybercrimes to the FBI that robbed them of $264 million. The total numbers are likely much higher, since many scams aren't reported. (File/Getty Images)
As a cybersecurity educator, I’m used to being the unofficial IT support for my friends, family and neighbors. Forgotten passwords, suspicious emails, how-to’s — I’m the person they turn to because I “know about computers.”
So when I received a text from one of my neighbors, a woman in her early 70s, saying she had been scammed, I did not immediately think the worst. I texted her with the usual advice: Change your passwords, contact your financial institution, file an identity theft report, and perhaps make a police report if the situation was serious.
Then she replied: “I think you better come down here and let’s talk.”
When I arrived at her house, I immediately knew this was different. She greeted me with a mixture of embarrassment, shame, fear and confusion. Over the next hour, she frantically told me how a series of events over the course of three days had resulted in scammers stealing approximately $100,000 from her.
Her ordeal began when she discovered that she was locked out of her bank account. Naturally, she called her bank for help. During the process, she believed she was transferred to technical support, but somewhere along the way she ended up communicating with scammers.
Then another crisis appeared.
Her computer displayed an alarming warning claiming that the computer was being hacked and that she needed to contact Microsoft immediately.
The scammers effectively isolated her and persuaded her not to communicate with anyone who might have interrupted the scheme. They convinced her that her money was in danger and instructed her to move it into cryptocurrency, supposedly to protect her assets from being stolen or seized.
Unfortunately, that money was now long gone.

The scope of the problem
Before this incident, I understood that fraud targeting older adults was a serious problem. But I didn’t fully appreciate its scale until I saw its impact sitting across from me.
The FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center received more than 1 million complaints in 2025, representing nearly $21 billion in reported losses.
Across all age groups in 2025, investment fraud accounted for approximately $8.6 billion in reported losses, while tech/customer-support scams accounted for another $2.1 billion. Romance and confidence scams, where the scammer psychologically manipulates the victim, added up to approximately $929 million in reported losses.
But the numbers for older Americans are particularly troubling.
People age 60 and older submitted about 20% of all complaints to the center and accounted for more than 37% of financial losses, totaling about $7.75 billion. That’s more complaints and more reported losses than any other age group. The average reported loss among complainants 60 and older was approximately $38,500, and nearly 12,500 people in that age group reported losing more than $100,000.
Reasons for the higher losses for the elderly range from access to a nest egg and a lack of comfort with newer technology to loneliness and declining cognitive abilities.


Internet crimes reported in SC
A look at South Carolinians’ complaints in 2025 to the FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center:

14,699 cybercrimes reported
$264 million total loss, ranking 20th
3,136 complaints from people 60 and over
$97.3 stolen from people 60 and over

Source: FBI Internet Crime Report 2025


A cloud over the Sunshine State
This issue has particular significance in Florida. About 23% of Floridians – 5.3 million people – are 65 or older.
In 2025, Florida generated 71,843 complaints to the Internet Crime Complaint Center for a total of nearly $1.6 billion in reported losses.
This is the third-highest number of complaints and total losses in the country, which is unsurprising, given that Florida is the third-largest state. But Florida came in second in both total cybercrime complaints and total financial losses for residents over 60, with more than 17,000 complaints and nearly $710 million lost.
So, protecting older Floridians from fraud is more than simply a cybersecurity awareness issue. It is a significant financial and community issue. Operation Senior Shield is a program through the Florida Department of Elder Affairs that provides free alerts via email, text or phone about scams targeting older adults and their caregivers.
Scams on the rise
In 2026, the Global Anti-Scam Alliance, an international organization that brings together governments and private institutions to understand and stop online scams, surveyed 3,110 U.S. adults and found that 82% had encountered a scam during the previous year.
Despite 86% saying they were confident they could recognize scams, 43% still interacted with a scammer, and 9% experienced financial or data loss as a result.
Perhaps most concerning, only 40% of the victims who said they lost money reported the incident to authorities. Among those who didn’t lose money in their interaction with the scammer, only 4% reported it to authorities. In addition, 59% reported an impact on their mental well-being, and more than half experienced repeat scams.
That reporting gap matters: A report that appears insignificant by itself may contain the phone number, email address, cryptocurrency wallet, domain name, bank account, IP address or other piece of infrastructure that investigators can use to connect multiple victims to the same criminal network.
It may help identify the scammer.
What to do if you or a loved one has been scammed online
After listening to my neighbor’s story, she and I began to document what had happened and contacted our local U.S. Secret Service office.
The response was swift.
Within about a week, one of the scammers involved was arrested. It turns out her scammer was already on law enforcement’s radar in connection with other crimes.
The case ultimately resulted in a restitution order, meaning my neighbor will get her money back eventually. This is the best possible outcome, but this incident permanently changed the way I think about cybercrime.
If you or a loved one has been scammed, here’s what you can do:
1. Contact your financial institution immediately.
2. Document everything. Save emails, text messages, phone numbers, screenshots, receipts, transaction records, cryptocurrency wallet addresses, websites, usernames and correspondence.
3. Report the crime to the appropriate authorities. Start with the local police and the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center at IC3.gov. If your driver’s license or identity was impacted, visit identitytheft.gov.
Depending on the nature of the scheme, it may also be appropriate to report to state regulators, the Federal Trade Commission, the Securities and Exchange Commission or other agencies.
4. Secure all of your accounts. That includes social media, banks and email accounts. Reset passwords wherever possible and enable multifactor authentication.
5. Watch for the second scam. Scammers may contact previous victims claiming to be investigators, attorneys, cybersecurity companies, cryptocurrency experts, or “recovery specialists” who can supposedly retrieve stolen cryptocurrency or money for a fee.
6. Do not overlook the emotional impact. Being scammed can be traumatic. Seeking care from a mental health professional may help the victim process their feelings and recover from this experience.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Commentary: A Talbot County candidate, his grandfather the political patrón, and my front-row seat
text:
Brian Naranjo, a Democratic nominee for a seat on the Talbot County Council, is the grandson of the late New Mexico political patrón Emilio Naranjo -- whom the author covered early in his career. (Photo courtesy Naranjo campaign)Over my 30 years writing about Maryland, I’ve invariably run into people in the political universe here who, like me, grew up in New York City.  Or lived there at some point in their lives.
Heck, former state Sen. Roger Manno (D-Montgomery) even went to my junior high school, JHS 104, on East 21st Street in Manhattan. We weren’t in the building at the same time, but we had many of the same teachers and experiences, growing up in gritty 1970s New York.
It’s been harder, though, to find people in Maryland politics who share a connection to another important time in my life – when I lived in New Mexico in the 1990s.
New Mexico is where I became a parent, so it will always be precious to me for that reason alone. I think about the jaw-dropping beauty of the state every day.
And I did some of my best professional work there, as a staff writer for the alt-weekly Santa Fe Reporter – exposing an oil and gas company’s attempts to rip off taxpayers, giving an insurgent mayoral candidate ammunition to topple the well-funded establishment favorite, and covering notable New Mexico politicians like Bill Richardson, Tom Udall and Gary Johnson fairly early in their careers.
Since coming to Maryland from New Mexico in late 1995, I learned that former Lt. Gov. Kathleen Kennedy Townsend (D) obtained her law degree at the University of New Mexico while her then-husband taught at the St. John’s College campus in Santa Fe. (His move to the Annapolis campus, brought KKT to Maryland). And I discovered that former Maryland Attorney General Brian Frosh (D) worked at the start of his career for the New Mexico attorney general’s office.
But those are the only two people I know who shared the Maryland-New Mexico political bond with me. Until now.
Just a few weeks ago, I was delighted and amazed to learn that Brian Naranjo, a retired foreign service officer and a Democratic candidate for the Talbot County Council, is the grandson of a Emilio Naranjo, who was the Democratic boss of Rio Arriba County, New Mexico, from the 1950s through the 1990s.
The elder Naranjo, who died in 2008 at age 92, was a powerful and controversial figure who ruled the politics of Rio Arriba, a rural, overwhelmingly Hispanic county wedged between Santa Fe and Taos, with an iron first. Over the years he was county sheriff, the chair of the Rio Arriba Democratic Party, a federal marshal in Albuquerque and a state senator, which is where I got to see him in action.
But more importantly, he was the man to see for political favors in Rio Arriba County for over four decades, if you were looking for a government job, say, or a political appointment, or some kind of favorable decision from local government – or if you were running for higher office.
Famously, Emilio Naranjo campaigned with Ted Kennedy when Kennedy was stumping for his brother John during the 1960 presidential campaign. Over the years, Naranjo campaigned again with Ted Kennedy, including in 1992, to support Bill Clinton’s White House bid, when I was out there.
Emilio Naranjo wasn’t beloved by everyone. He had political enemies. He was a patrón in the local parlance. Critics accused him of corruption. His deeds and misdeeds could fill a few books.
Brian Naranjo correctly calls his grandfather “the last boss in New Mexico.”
“I see the upside and the downside of that kind of political behavior,” he says.
Yet in a wide-ranging conversation with me, Brian Naranjo said he is running for Talbot County Council with many of the political lessons he learned from his grandfather and his father at the top of his mind.
“I do credit my grandfather for a lot of my instincts,” he said. “I translated it into diplomacy and now I’ve translated it into local politics.”
Brian Naranjo is hardly a political neophyte. He grew up in Montgomery County – his father, Emilio “Milo” Naranjo Jr., the eldest of the political leader’s nine children – came to Washington to work for New Mexico Sen. Clinton Anderson (D) and later for NASA, while remaining an informal adviser to his father out in New Mexico.
Growing up, Brian Naranjo said, “We always talked politics. I can’t remember a day we didn’t.”
For 32 years, Naranjo applied what he learned to his work as a foreign service officer, through 16 postings on five continents, including stints in Venezuela, Canada and Mexico. Naranjo and his family bought a home in St. Michael’s in 2011, and it was the place they came to between assignments overseas. After his retirement from the federal government, it became their permanent home.
As he became more enmeshed in local politics, Naranjo said he didn’t like everything he saw. He felt some Talbot leaders were capitulating to developers and that several Republicans had become full-on MAGA supporters, coarsening the political discourse. He was also troubled by the economic disparities in the county.
“What surprised me is no one paid attention to that,” Naranjo said. “The whole county is not just St. Michael’s or Oxford or big houses along the water.”
On the campaign trail, he has talked about wanting to build bridges to poorer residents and communities – similar to the way Emilio Naranjo reached out to the economically impoverished Native American residents at the Santa Clara Pueblo in Rio Arriba County.
“My grandfather focused on Rio Arriba like a laser,” Naranjo said. “I see that as a model for Talbot, at a time when so many Republicans are focused on the MAGA side of the equation.”
Talbot County has become increasingly competitive politically. In 2020, Joe Biden became the first Democratic presidential contender to carry the county since 1964 – winning by 118 votes. Four years later, Donald Trump carried the county by just six votes.
The County Council currently has three Republicans and two Democrats, but many Democrats believe they have an opportunity to capture the majority this year. Five Republican nominees and five Democratic nominees are on the ballot.
“So you don’t have to be the fastest runner,” Naranjo observes. “You just have to be faster than the sixth guy.”
Naranjo’s aggressive criticism of the status quo in Talbot County has brought some harsh criticism. But he is unapologetic and argues that he’s helping to define the council race. And there, too, he sees some parallels with his grandfather.
Naranjo recalls his dad telling his grandfather that even with criticism from the local newspaper and some political opponents: “You are still driving the news here. They are reacting to you … Even your enemies can be useful to you under certain circumstances.”
But just as he’s critical of MAGA Republicans, Naranjo said he is also leery of Democrats who veer too far to the left or focus too heavily on national issues.
“When you grow up with Emilio Naranjo as your grandfather, you appreciate a politics that doesn’t exist anymore,” he said. “He grew up in the party of Roosevelt, Truman and JFK.”
Naranjo’s message to voters: “It’s more about pragmatism and solving problems and trying to meet people where they live.”

name: WyoFile
title: No victory lap for Wyoming GOP after rejecting Medicaid expansion
text:
I gazed into my Wyoming legislative crystal ball after setting it for Jan. 12, 2027, when the next session begins. I couldn’t believe what I saw.

Opinion

A miniature Sen. Charlie Scott, R-Casper, was jogging from desk to desk, playfully getting high-fives from almost everyone in the chamber. In the gallery former senators I hadn’t seen in years were locked arm-in-arm, singing a terribly off-key version of “For He’s a Jolly Good Fellow.”
“What would they be celebrating?” I wondered.
Then someone wheeled in a cake. I squinted to read the tiny message in bright red frosting: “Charlie Was Right About Medicaid Expansion.”
“Oh no you don’t,” I said. “I knew this day would come, Sen. Scott, and I’m not going to let you get away with it!”
Please forgive the above silliness. It was my rather childish way to try to trick you, dear reader, into spending at least a few minutes thinking about Medicaid expansion. 
You’ll see a lot of headlines soon about a subject few Wyomingites seem to have much interest in anymore. But when you learn about billions of dollars in Medicaid cuts in other states, you should know what to expect here.



A bit of foreshadowing: What you’re about to read will be comforting, if your top concern is keeping state costs down. But you may be surprised about where that leads.
Do you remember the summer of 2025, when President Donald Trump and his “One Big Beautiful Bill” promised to cut $880 billion from Medicaid over the next decade? The huge number didn’t even seem real, because no one offered an explanation about who would be affected.
Well, we’re finding out that the answer is different depending on many factors, but one that looms large is whether a state expanded Medicaid. Wyoming is one of 10 that did not.
The state of Washington, an expansion state, recently ran the numbers to get a head start on Jan. 1, when the cuts start to kick in.
The news in Washington isn’t good, according to the Seattle Times, which reported that hospitals will lose nearly $6 billion over the next seven years because of federal Medicaid cuts.
Much of that expected loss is due to hospitals absorbing “uncompensated care,” when patients can’t afford to pay hospital bills. U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., said the losses “will likely lead to clinic closures, longer ER wait times and other challenges for patients.”
There could be up to 200,000 Medicaid recipients in Washington who no longer qualify if they don’t meet the federal work requirements that take effect Jan. 1.
That $880 billion in Medicaid cuts has been revised to $625 billion. Still, it’s estimated that 7.5 million people will lose their benefits over the next 10 years.
But what about Wyoming? To find out the expected impact here, I asked Eric Boley, president of the Wyoming Hospital Association.
“Medicaid cuts will affect each state differently,” Boley said. “We’re not an expansion state. Some of the huge cuts that they’re seeing in the disenrollment come from changes in the federal match that’s taking place.”
Because the Wyoming Legislature didn’t expand Medicaid, Wyoming still splits the cost 50-50 with the federal government. In states that did expand the program to more people, the feds picked up all costs for three years and 90% after that.
Now, after a Republican president and Congress united to pass a huge tax cut for the wealthy and help pay for it by taking health insurance from low-income people, expansion states must pay 10% more of program expenses each year until they get back to the 50-50 match.
“We won’t see that,” Boley said. “But some of the expansion states are really going to see decreases in their funding as it ratchets down to a lower matching rate.”
The other way states will spend more for Medicaid is from state-directed plans, which allow them to make additional payments to healthcare providers under managed care programs. But Wyoming doesn’t have a state-directed plan, Boley said, so it doesn’t lose any money there, either.
Some states will have to spend more to make sure people on Medicaid are complying with new federal work requirements that begin Jan. 1.
But Wyoming joins Alabama, Florida, Kansas, Mississippi and Texas as the non-expansion states that don’t have to meet those work requirements.
While other states are looking at huge cuts, Wyoming and South Dakota — because of their low population and number of Medicaid recipients — may actually receive an increase in federal payments. RAND Health says the pair will benefit substantially percentage-wise from the Rural Health Transformation Program from the One Big Beautiful Bill “and see little to no impact from other provisions.”
So why did the fantasy version of me looking into my crystal ball get so ticked off at the thought of Scott — by far the most vocal anti-Medicaid expansion legislator — taking a victory lap? Doesn’t this show that the Legislature was right to reject Medicaid expansion year after year?
Sen. Charlie Scott (R-Casper) during the 2024 Wyoming Legislature. (Ashton J. Hacke/WyoFile) 
No, it only seems good if you look at the issue from this point forward. To view the big picture we must go back to 2012, when the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that the Affordable Care Act’s mandate that all states expand Medicaid was unconstitutional. 
The court allowed states to voluntarily expand the program, which 40 did because it was so obviously beneficial to their respective economies and the low-income workers who desperately needed health insurance.
In the 14 years since, Wyoming flushed an estimated $1.6 billion in federal Medicaid funds down the drain. How is that not the most boneheaded move in the state’s history?
In addition, approving Medicaid expansion would have led to adding more medical providers and related jobs and businesses, plus giving about 20,000 low-income Wyomingites — our families, friends and neighbors — health insurance.
Any workforce is more efficient if it’s healthy. But a majority of Wyoming legislators acted like anyone receiving Medicaid was a leech who didn’t want to work, despite the fact 20% of low-income Americans are helped by Medicaid. 
Some Republicans, particularly in later years, did want to expand Medicaid. But a majority opposed it, even though they kept saying they wanted a “Wyoming solution” to healthcare problems. Did it occur to them that $1.6 billion since 2012 might have helped them find one?
Scott’s chief concern about Medicaid expansion was that the feds could stop paying 90% of the cost, and they did, but only after 14 years and at the direction of the senator’s own party.
Year after year I watched Democrats and some Republicans implore GOP leaders to expand the program, if only for a year or two, to help people get off welfare and become healthier by getting regular care from a doctor, and not wait to go to the emergency room when their conditions became worse and more expensive.
I’ve read quite a bit about how expansion states will cope with the drastic increases they’ll be paying for Medicaid. Most involve three unacceptable options: raise taxes, cut education, and reduce benefits for at-home and community-based health programs, mental health and patients with disabilities.
If Republicans want to celebrate the biggest federal Medicaid cut in history, go ahead. But don’t expect anyone to believe that you did it to be fiscally responsible or whatever BS you try to sell voters on Nov. 3.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee subterranean authority member won’t take first Boring Company tunnel ride
text:
An August 2026 aerial shot of the Boring Company's Music City Tunnel station under construction at the Tennessee State Capitol.
A recent report from the Southern Evironmentatl Law Center cautions construction of the tunnel for Tesla vehicles could trigger the creation of sinkholes. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)A member of the Tennessee board overseeing construction of a Nashville tunnel isn’t worried yet about the potential for sinkholes detailed in a new study, but even he is leery it could be flooded by the Cumberland River.
Former state Sen. Bill Ketron of Murfreesboro, a member of the newly-formed Subterranean Transportation Infrastructure Coordinator Authority, said Monday he’s aware of a report by the Southern Environmental Law Center that the Boring Company’s tunnel from downtown Nashville to the airport could cause sinkholes, groundwater contamination and a litany of problems. He hasn’t spoken with anyone from Elon Musk’s Boring Company about the report and isn’t overly concerned yet about the potential for damage.
Ketron said he toured the section of the tunnel that’s been completed and was told the limestone under Nashville is extremely hard. The company told him concrete for the underground structure is prefabricated in Nevada.
Asked whether he feels the concrete barriers will be able to prevent flooding in the tunnel from the Cumberland River, Ketron quipped, “They say that they will, but I don’t think I want to be one of the first ones riding through it.”
A 9.5-mile tunnel that will ferry passengers in all-electric Tesla vehicles is supposed to be 13 feet in diameter and dug 30 to 60 feet underground to provide transportation between downtown Nashville near the state Capitol and the Nashville International Airport. Republican lawmakers have called the project a good method for reducing traffic on Nashville interstates.
Ketron made the comment as he recalled posing questions to former Nashville Mayor Megan Barry and a consulting firm in 2017 about the potential for massive leaking when her administration proposed a nearly $1 billion tunnel under the downtown area from Music City Central to Fifth and Broad. 
“I raised concerns about (if) you get too close to the Cumberland River you might fill the whole thing with water,” Ketron said.
The project failed to get off the ground as Barry stepped down from office amid scandal and the $5.2 billion transportation plan fizzled.
The Southern Environmental Law Center’s analysis shows the Music City Loop route will be forced to go through layers of bedrock prone to sinkholes and caves, known as karst geology, a threat to cause more sinkholes, groundwater contamination and the settling or sinking of rock. 
The Boring Company has said in an environmental impact assessment it will “avoid tunnel boring in areas where karst development is identified.” 
The Southern Environmental Law Center, though, said in its report that the route won’t be able to avoid karst regions with caves and underground streams in the area because it runs under Browns Creek, Mill Creek and the Cumberland River. 
The Southern Environment Law Center report
REPORT - Hydrogeology of Nashville and Implications for the Music City Loop
The Southern Environmental Law Center report details a “karst mitigation plan” obtained through a public records request describing methods the company would use to find karst features, including drilling wells into rock to see whether it’s solid and testing called “multichannel analysis of surface waves,” which uses vibrations to determine whether underground structures are present.
The report also points toward the possibility of groundwater pollution caused by the disturbance of areas such as the former Aladdin Industries site on Murfreesboro Road near the airport, which has a history of contamination caused by hazardous solvents and metals. 
Democratic state Sen. Heidi Campbell of Nashville said Nashville sits on limestone that’s riddled with caves and sinkholes and pointed out the report by an independent hydrogeologist warns that the tunnel could push toxic materials into the groundwater.
“Instead of demanding answers, the state handed Elon Musk our public right-of-way, cut Nashville out of the decision and took the company’s own paid-for report at its word,” Campbell said in a statement to the Lookout.
She called the state’s actions “reckless” and said taxpayers will wind up paying to fix any sinkhole that opens on Murfreesboro Road.
Tennessee donated the underground right-of-way to the Boring company for its project and set up the subterranean authority to oversee it.
Gov. Bill Lee has said the state gave the right-of-way because the Boring Company is making an “enormous investment” on the state’s behalf.
A Department of Transportation spokesperson did not respond immediately Monday to questions for Commissioner Will Reid.
