name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Outgoing Tennessee lottery head optimistic that revenue for college scholarships won’t keep dropping
text:
The Tennessee Education Lottery has funded college scholarships since its launch in 2003. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout) 
Tennessee’s outgoing chief executive of the lottery education corporation told state officials she was optimistic revenue designated for college scholarships won’t keep falling.
“I don’t think you’ll see the same level of growth,” said Rebecca Paul, the Tennessee Education Lottery CEO, to the state funding board on Oct. 19. “But I think we’ve stemmed the decline.”
Lottery officials project revenue will remain flat for the next several years, but not fall as it has over the past five years. 
Tennessee legalized lottery and scratch-off tickets in the early 2000s, earmarking the revenue for college scholarships. For years, the lottery generated hundreds of millions of dollars and grew consistently, allowing officials to expand grants to nearly 170,000 students.
Last year, Tennessee awarded about $500 million in college scholarships while the lottery generated roughly $420 million, creating a structural deficit after Tennessee legalized online-only sports betting in 2019.
“Most people who do sports betting have bought a lottery ticket or two,” Paul said. “Take $5 billion out of the market, and it has to come from somewhere.”
State lawmakers have been playing a more active role in the lottery and its revenues since legalizing sports betting. Initially, sports gambling money went to the lottery education fund and the lottery corporation regulated it.
But in 2025, lawmakers diverted that revenue to schools as part of the deal to pass private school vouchers, creating the structural deficit.
How Tennessee’s House speaker helped keep a payday lender’s struggling sports gambling company alive

 
Tennessee House Speaker Cameron Sexton, a Crossville Republican, led a successful effort earlier this year to pass legislation to reset the lottery board and make Paul’s compensation package a public record.
Paul has led the state’s education lottery since its founding and is one of the state’s highest-paid employees, earning $650,000 a year, a salary that lawmakers have scrutinized since she was first hired. She is stepping down at the end of the year, and the state has not yet chosen her replacement. 
Sexton has played an active role in wrestling sports betting regulation away from the lottery, amid complaints about the suspension of a company owned by a prominent financial donor to his political campaigns.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama Democrats highlight decades-long effort to repeal grocery tax
text:
Former House Ways and Means General Fund Committee John Knight, D-Montgomery, speaks to reporters on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026, at the Alabama Capital to urge lawmakers to repeal the state’s grocery tax. Knight, who served in the Alabama House from 1993 to 2018, led efforts over several decades to repeal the state's grocery tax. (Ralph Chapoco/Alabama Reflector) Democratic candidates for state office Monday highlighted their party’s decades-long efforts to repeal the state sales tax at a press conference where they pushed their affordability message a week before the general election.
The press conference featured former Rep. John Knight, D-Montgomery, a former chair of the House Ways and Means General Fund committee, who for decades sponsored legislation to repeal the tax.
“I think more people are coming together to realize that they are suffering,” Knight said during the news conference. “Even though you may try to hurt a certain segment of the population, when you pass taxes that are not fair and unequal across the board, you are hurting more than just the Democrats in the state of Alabama.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The conference came as the eight-decade tax has come under fire as the cost of living dominates political campaigns in Alabama and around the country.
“Everywhere I have been, Alabamians are hurting,” said Rep. Phillip Ensler, D-Montgomery, the Democratic nominee for lieutenant governor. “They are struggling to pay their grocery bills, they are struggling to pay for their prescription drugs, they are struggling to pay for health insurance, they are struggling to pay for these high gas prices that have been caused by (President) Donald Trump’s war overseas.”
Alabama until 2023 imposed a 4% state tax on groceries. Combined with local levies, it could amount to a 10% tax on food in some areas. The state was one of only three states to tax groceries fully, and remains one of only eight states to impose the tax.
Efforts to repeal the tax languished because of arguments over whether and how to replace the lost revenue, which could add hundreds of millions of dollars to the Education Trust Fund, which pays for most public education in the state. Knight for years sought to repeal the grocery tax and make up the revenue by repealing a 1965 constitutional amendment allowing residents to deduct federal taxes paid from their state income taxes, an arrangement that tends to favor the wealthy. The proposals did not move.
In the 2023 session, the Republican-controlled Legislature passed legislation to reduce the grocery tax from 4% to 3%.
In 2025, lawmakers passed legislation to cut the state tax to 2%. The Legislature this spring also approved a two-month grocery tax break in May and June, coinciding with primary elections and runoffs.
“Don’t misunderstand me, I am glad families got a break,” said Rep. Penni McClammy, D-Montgomery, who has sponsored legislation to eliminate the grocery tax. “But why didn’t we get a break when the election ended, when families are getting out of school with their kids, when they have summer food and programs to pay, and then the tax increases?”
Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones has also called for a repeal of the grocery tax. U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville, R-Alabama, the Republican nominee for governor, and Republican legislative leaders have said elimination of the state grocery tax would be the first priority of the 2027 legislative session.
The grocery tax was one element of the platform on affordability that Democrats unveiled at the news conference. They also proposed a $15-an-hour minimum wage; expanding Medicaid to improve public health and address the solvency of rural hospitals; and reducing the sales tax on farm equipment.
“There are ways to look at the tax structure and look at where there are exemptions and handouts being given to big corporations and big companies who can afford to do it,” said Ensler. “We are also big proponents of a state lottery and the lottery revenue. We are missing out on hundreds of millions of dollars that would come into the state so we can cut expenses for working people while bringing in revenue without raising their taxes.”
Corey Hill, the Republican nominee for Commissioner of Agriculture and Industries, and Ron Sparks, the Democratic nominee for the office, both support elimination of the 1.5% sales tax on farm equipment.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Millions in ‘dark money’ spent to influence votes on Colorado ballot measures
text:
Ballots are seen at the Weld County Elections office in Greeley on June 25, 2024. (Andrew Fraieli/Colorado Newsline)Colorado’s most expensive ballot-measure showdown in the 2026 midterms is an overlapping series of fights over several high-stakes tax questions, with a mishmash of left- and right-leaning groups spending a combined total of more than $14 million to influence Colorado voters on the measures ahead of Election Day.
Among the dozens of issue committees registered to support or oppose the 14 measures appearing on the 2026 statewide ballot, none is better-funded than Yes for Kids Colorado, a teachers-union-funded group that has spent more than $6.8 million to support Proposition NN.
That measure, referred to the ballot by the Legislature, would increase funding for K-12 education by about $500 million a year by raising the state’s constitutionally-mandated revenue growth cap. Most of Yes for Kids Colorado’s funding comes from the National Education Association.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Protect Colorado’s Future Coalition, meanwhile, has spent a little less than $2 million to support Amendment 87, a proposal to establish a graduated state income tax. The coalition’s top donors include philanthropist Merle Chambers; Colorado WINS, the state employees’ union; and progressive advocacy groups like the Bell Policy Center and the Colorado Fiscal Institute.
Two conservative issue committees, Brighter Colorado and Let’s Go Colorado, are registered in opposition to both Amendment 87 and Proposition NN. Brighter Colorado has received more than $2.6 million in funding from donors including Advance Colorado, a conservative “dark money” group that does not disclose its donors; the Republican-affiliated group GOPAC; and Common Sense America, a separate dark-money group based in Maryland. Let’s Go Colorado is funded entirely by the Denver Metro Chamber of Commerce.
Brighter Colorado is also registered in support of six other Colorado ballot measures backed by Advance Colorado, including Proposition 136, which aims to neutralize Amendment 87 by setting a cap on state income tax rates. Issue committees aren’t required to separate their expenditures for different ballot measures in the disclosure reports they file with the Colorado secretary of state’s office.
Another group, Don’t Price Us Out, has reported spending just under $2 million to oppose Amendment 87 only, most of which came from the dark-money American Prosperity Coalition, according to campaign finance disclosures. An issue committee affiliated with Americans for Prosperity, the network founded by conservative megadonor Charles Koch, has also spent $350,000 to oppose Amendment 87.
Statewide, more than $47 million had been spent on issue campaigns in Colorado in 2026 — a figure that includes dozens of campaigns at the local level, as well as spending on some statewide campaigns, like a Democratic-backed redistricting proposal or an effort to increase state funding for roads, that were withdrawn or blocked from the ballot. The total spending puts the state on pace to see more money spent on ballot measures this year than in any election since 2020.
Millions backing Proposition 137
Colorado’s most lopsided 2026 ballot contest involves Proposition 137, which would boost state funding for conservation and wildfire mitigation projects by exempting tax revenue from sporting goods sales from constitutional limits set by the Taxpayer’s Bill of Rights.
A campaign in support of the measure reported spending more than $5 million through Oct. 14. Most of the campaign’s funding comes from two environmental groups, The Nature Conservancy and Western Resource Advocates.
Some grassroots environmental groups are critical of the measure and its funding for wildfire mitigation, which can involve “fuel reduction” projects that they say harm forest ecosystems. A campaign opposing Proposition 137 has reported $6,295 in expenditures, mostly on digital advertising.
Dark-money voter ID push
Spending figures for most of the rest of the 14 measures appearing on Colorado’s 2026 ballot show either proponents or the opposition with a major financial advantage.
More than $5.7 million in dark money has been spent to convince voters to back Amendment 84, which would require Colorado voters to provide the last four digits of their Social Security number or driver’s license number, in addition to their signature, to ensure their mail ballot is counted.
The sources of that money are entirely undisclosed. The Colorado Voter Trust Initiative, the committee supporting Amendment 84, has received all of its funding from four entities: the Texas-based American Prosperity Caucus, which contributed $2.4 million; the Coalition for American Prosperity and Growth, which contributed $2.2 million and is based in Colorado Springs; and the American Jobs and Growth Fund and A Public Voice, two Virginia-based groups that gave $1 million each. None of the four groups has a public presence, and all four list their addresses as P.O. boxes.
Defend Our Ballots, an issue committee registered to oppose Amendment 84, reported spending $75,000 as of Oct. 14. Its largest donor is a Denver-based dark-money nonprofit of the same name. Vote Common Sense, a committee funded by a wide range of left-leaning advocacy groups, has also spent $130,112 to oppose a slate of nine conservative ballot measures than includes Amendment 84.
Opposition to anti-trans measures
Protect Kids Colorado, a conservative group backing a pair of ballot measures targeting the transgender community, has reported just under $400,000 in expenditures since it launched its campaigns last year. Proposition 134 aims to prevent transgender children from participating in school sports, while Proposition 135 would prohibit health care professionals from knowingly performing any surgery on a minor “for the purpose of altering biological sex characteristics.”
The group’s top donors include a dark-money nonprofit also named Protect Kids Colorado, which has contributed about 60% of its funding; brewing scion Jeff Coors; and two groups associated with far-right Woodland Park pastor Andrew Wommack, the Truth and Liberty Coalition and Andrew Wommack Ministries.
Families Not Politics, the campaign opposing Propositions 134 and 135, has outspent Protect Kids Colorado by a 5-to-1 margin since it was registered in February. The group has received funding from liberal advocacy groups including LGBTQ+ rights organization One Colorado; reproductive rights groups Cobalt and Planned Parenthood; and the American Civil Liberties Union.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: GOP House candidate Clagett remains on ballot in Berkeley County after racist social media posts
text:
Chris Clagett is the Republican candidate in the 91st District for the House of Delegates. He faces Democratic challenger David Michaels. (Source: Sample ballot from the West Virginia Secretary of State’s Office)A Republican House of Delegates candidate in Berkeley County remains on the ballot after authoring several racist posts on social media that targeted Black women and Muslims. He reportedly called the Confederate flag “beautiful.”
Chris Clagett’s social media activity, first reported by West Virginia Watch in September, drew ire from House Speaker Roger Hanshaw, R-Clay.
“If the voters of Berkeley County choose to send that attitude to the House of Delegates, it will be a lonely place,” Hansshaw told MetroNews in an interview last month. 
Chris Clagett is the Republican candidate for House of Delegates District 91, which represents southern Berkeley County. (Photo courtesy of Chris Clagett’s campaign website)
If elected, Clagett could be left off House committees, giving him little input in the legislative process.
Early voting is underway across West Virginia and continues through Oct. 31. Clagett faces Democratic challenger David Michaels in the race. 
State law prohibits the West Virginia Republican Party from replacing him at this point if Clagett had chosen to resign.
“The West Virginia Republican Party condemns the language used on social media. It is not reflective of the values of our party nor the values of our candidates running for office,” said Josh Holstein, chair of the West Virginia GOP. 
The West Virginia Democratic Party called for Clagett to withdraw from the race “because he is unfit to serve the people of this district.”
Clagett did not return an email for this story nor has he responded to previous interview requests about his social media activity. He confirmed he authored the posts during a radio interview with Eastern Panhandle station WRNR about the social media posts. 
In January, Clagett posted on X, “Maybe because black women are the most ill-mannered, ill-behaved, loud-mouthed demographics on the face of the Earth. Does that clarify it for you … ?”  He responded to a post that said, “They always think saying I’m not doing anything means they’re not resisting arrest.”
He told WRNR radio hosts that, “context is everything,” then later said the post he responded to with the words “ill-mannered” included Black women “behaving in exactly the manner I described.”
Clagett is running to represent the 91st District in the House, which covers mostly southern Berkeley County. He ran unopposed in the May primary election. 
The district is heavily Red. 
Clagett’s political platform focuses on medical freedom from vaccinations, immigration enforcement and curriculum reform in public schools.
His fundraising activity has been light, with the latest campaign filing showing he has about $2,800 in cash on hand.
(Photo courtesy of David Michaels)
Michaels has $10,307 cash on hand with about a week to go until Nov. 3 Election Day. He has focused his campaign on locality pay for teachers and improving infrastructure in Berkeley County during its population increase. 
No candidates with the Constitution Party, Libertarian Party or Mountain Party filed to run in the race.
Joseph de Soto (West Virginia Division of Corrections and Rehabilitation)
The 91st district has seen a string of controversies involving its Republican House candidates. Previous candidate Joseph de Soto was arrested after making terrorist threats against sitting lawmakers.
House Republicans in January voted to vacate the seat instead of expelling de Soto, saying it was the correct way to deal with the seat since de Soto was on house arrest and never sworn in.
Del. Ian T. Masters, R-Berkeley, sits in a meeting of the House Public Heath subcommittee on March 5, 2025 in Charleston, W.Va. (Perry Bennett | West Virginia Legislative Photography)
De Soto switched his party affiliation to Democrat before his arrest, prompting an ongoing legal challenge from the state Democratic Party that the seat should have been filled by a Democratic candidate under state law.
Gov. Patrick Morrisey appointed Ian Masters to the House seat after Republican delegate-elect Joseph de Soto, who won the November 2024 election. 
Last summer, Masters denied allegations that he was responsible for an antisemitic comment made by a private Instagram account that used his name and is linked to an organization he recently led.
Masters is not seeking reelection.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Six West Virginia state house races to watch next week
text:
The West Virginia State Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia. (West Virginia Legislative Photography)With polling heavily in Democrats’ favor throughout the nation, even ruby red West Virginia is seeing some healthy competition in the 2026 midterm election. 
While Democrats and Republicans aren’t known for agreement, their respective party chairs both believe there are at least six races to keep an eye on in the election on Nov. 3. 
With 91% of the state Legislature controlled by Republicans, West Virginia has one of the most solid GOP supermajorities in the country. But this year, Democrats aren’t taking it laying down — they’ve fielded their largest slate of candidates since 2020. 
Democratic Party State Chair Mike Pushkin said he thinks if trends seen in the spring primary — where Democratic votes outnumbered Republican votes in some counties — hold, it could bode well for his party. 
“We defeated Patrick Morrissey’s handpicked Supreme Court justices and elected a dyed-in-the-wool Democrat in Jim Douglas in a statewide race to the Intermediate Court of Appeals,” Pushkin said. “We’re feeling cautiously optimistic.” 
Republican Party State Chair Josh Holstein said 80 out of the 91 seats held by the GOP in the House of Delegates are safe, as are 29 out of the 32 seats held in the state senate. 
“We don’t expect to lose the majority of the remainder. We feel like we’re in a very good spot,” Holstein said. 
Holstein said the GOP’s gains in party registration and past elections show his party’s track record is resonating with voters. 
“We’ve done the vast majority of what we said we would do, and we’re still working to accomplish the rest of it,” Holstein said. “ On the economic front, we’ve been able to cut taxes over and over and over on a bunch of different things: Social Security, income tax, motor vehicles.” 
Pushkin said the West Virginia Democratic Party is keying in on issues that have energized voters, like data centers and inflation.  
“They are upset with the Republicans for taking away local control in regards to regulating these big AI data centers. People are suspicious of Flock cameras. They value their right to privacy,” Pushkin said. “But most importantly, the biggest issue is the cost of living is incredibly high, and the Republicans who control every aspect of our government here in West Virginia have done absolutely nothing to address rising gas prices, rising grocery prices and out-of-control utility bills.” 
Here are the six races both Pushkin and Holstein said people should watch on election night. 
Democrat Lucia Valentine is challenging incumbent Republican Chris Anders for House of Delegates District 97. (Submitted photo and West Virginia Legislative photography photo)
House of Delegates District 97 (Berkeley and Jefferson counties): 
In a rematch from the 2024 election, Democrat Lucia Valentine is challenging incumbent Republican Chris Anders for a delegate seat in the growing and bustling Eastern Panhandle. In the 2024 election, despite outraising Anders in campaign donations, she lost the district by 700 votes. 
This election season, she’s done it again, raising double what Anders did. Both are out knocking on doors and campaigning hard in the final stretch — Valentine estimates her campaign has knocked on 4,000 doors, while Anders said his campaign has been to 3,800 homes. 
Valentine is running on a message of affordability and focusing on infrastructure in the Eastern Panhandle, where the growth in population is outstripping the roads and schools. 
“I think part of that is having a strong delegate in Charleston advocating for our region and bringing those infrastructure dollars and our tax dollars back home to work on the projects that we need to keep up with with our pace of growth,” she said. 
Anders is the chair of the Freedom Caucus in the House of Delegates and has advocated for outlawing county rain taxes — a tax on landowners for runoff from storms most notably used in Berkeley County — eliminating property tax and expanding gun rights. 
“I’ve been in communication with my constituents since I’ve been elected,” Anders said. “They’ve been receiving letters and mail from me nonstop because I work for them and the Constitution. That’s the two responsibilities that I have.” 
House Bill 2014, the controversial law that strips counties and towns of any say in a high-impact data center project, could also play a role in the election, where the Penzance data center is being built just on the border of the district. 
Both candidates have said they want to restore local control over data centers in the future. In the 2026 legislative session, Anders backed an amendment that would’ve put those projects up to a vote. 
In Senate District 13, Sen. Mike Oliverio, R-Monogalia, (right) is defending his seat against Del. John Williams, D-Monongalia.
Senate District 13 (Monongalia and Marion counties): 
The 13th Senate District is seeing a showdown between two seasoned politicians, and a libertarian candidate, in one of West Virginia’s last Democratic strongholds. 
Sen. Mike Oliverio, R-Monogalia, is defending his seat against Del. John Williams, D-Monongalia. Oliverio has served in the House and Senate on and off since the 1990s, while Williams was first elected to the House of Delegates in 2016. 
Oliverio said his long record of getting legislation passed will return to the state senate in January, invoking the wisdom of a long-serving speaker of the U.S. House. 
“Tip O’Neil taught everybody that ever served in public office that all politics are local, and when people look at Mike Oliverio, they know they have someone who they can trust, who has been a champion for West Virginia University, Fairmont State, WM Medicine, Vandalia, our economic development efforts here in the area are roads, our bridges, and I think that’s what will be most important to people,” Oliverio said. 
Williams said he represents a change up, citing data centers and inflation as the top concerns he’s hearing from voters. 
“The electorate and I have kind of been in tune with one another in terms of what we think needs to happen in Charleston,” he said. “And typically, when there’s that synergy between voters and candidate, it can lead to a big win.” 
Both Oliverio and Williams have been raising big dollars in the final stretch, with more than $200,000 spent between the two. 
Former mayor of Huntington Steve Williams is challenging two-term Republican incumbent Patrick Lucas for his House of Delegates seat. (West Virginia Legislative photoes)
House of Delegates District 24 (Cabell County) 
In district 24, which includes parts of Huntington and outlying areas, Steve Williams is challenging two-term Republican incumbent Patrick Lucas for his House of Delegates seat. 
Williams, a Democrat, served several terms in the House of Delegates in the 1980s and 1990s, before being elected Mayor of Huntington in 2012. After serving an unprecedented three terms as the mayor of the state’s second-largest city, he ran and lost against Patrick Morrisey for governor in 2024. 
Williams said if he is elected, he wants to focus on economic issues in his district. 
“I am going to use a four-letter word, and it’s going to define everything that we’re trying to do,” Williams said. “J-O-B-S Jobs. Creating jobs, taking advantage of what we have right here in Cabell County.” 
Lucas, a local relator, said he’s heard a litany of issues on the campaign trail. 
“I’ve heard questions about energy, questions about potable water and also a little bit about data centers,” he said. “And that’s really about it. And of course, all those are things that we are working on and have more work to do in the upcoming session.” 
Both men said their performance in the race is part of a larger picture for the way politics is heading in the state. 
“If I and all the other delegates that are currently in the house survive this year, then that’ll say something about the landscape,” Lucas said. “ That will tell you that not only has the state over the last 10, 15 years moved substantially to the right, but that they’re going to come out and make their voice heard in every election, no matter when that election happened.”
“The big question is going to be how many will be how many of the Democrats will come in with me,” Williams said. “It’s going to send a message that folks aren’t happy with the way the administration is going.” 
In District 1, incumbent Sen. Laura Chapman, R-Ohio, faces a challenge from Democratic candidate Shawn Fluharty, who currently serves in the House of Delegates. (West Virginia Legislative Photography photos)
Senate District 1 (Hancock, Brooke, Ohio, Marshall) 
State Sen. Laura Chapman, R-Ohio, is being challenged by Del. Shawn Fluharty, D-Ohio, in what is becoming one of the most expensive races this year. 
This is Chapman’s first reelection campaign for her seat. So far, she’s raised about $145,000. Mountaineer Conservative Action, an independent political action committee with ties to state Senate President Randy Smith, has spent nearly $200,000 to attack Fluhuarty. 
Fluharty has raised about $165,000, taking the race to a grand total of almost $510,000 so far. 
Chapman said the big numbers are nothing unusual for a state senate race. 
“I’ve never seen a political race where there wasn’t (outside spending)” she said. “Of course, in the state senate there’s more money involved because there are fewer seats.” 
Fluharty said the big spending against him shows he’s working hard for the seat. 
“They’re spending more against me than anyone else in the state,” he said. “I wear that as a badge of honor.” 
Chapman said during her time in office, she supported legislation to freeze power rates, expand testing for COVID and flu at pharmacies and help improve access to childcare. If reelected, she wants to keep working on issues surrounding energy costs and flooding. 
“I am the only person in this race who is effective,” Chapman said. 
Elected to the House of Delegates in 2014, Fluharty is now the House minority whip. During his time in the House, he has become well-known for championing Raylee’s law, regulating sports betting and his bombastic antics on the chamber floor. 
He said his campaign is focusing on the economy. 
“People don’t care about the manufactured outrage you hear from leadership in Charleston. They care about real issues, and that issue is the economy,” he said. “Under the current leadership, West Virginia is dead last in economic development.”
In House District 82, Republican Del. David McCormick (right) is facing Democrat Eddie Wagoner (left). (Courtesy photo/ West Virginia Legislative Photography photo)
House District 82 (Monongalia County) 
Del. David McCormick, R-Monongalia, is facing his first reelection bid after winning the seat in one of the closer contests two years ago. 
McCormick won the seat by less than 700 votes in 2024. This year, McCormick said he’s not going to rest on his laurels.  
“I’m expecting a close race, and not taking anything for granted,” he said. “We’re working hard and getting our message out.” 
McCormick faces Democrat Eddie Wagoner, who dipped his toe into politics about a decade ago when ran for the House as a Libertarian. He too anticipates a narrow margin. 
“I’m not going to prognosticate,” he said. “ It’ll be a close race. That’s why you’re calling me.” 
McCormick said the two issues he hears coming up the most in his district are roads and trash. 
“The number one thing is that trash service all over the state is terrible, and talking with other delegates, that it’s not something that’s exclusive to Mon County, but these trash haulers are not being held accountable for poor service,” he said. “This is a basic service to citizens in West Virginia, and it may take some legislation to fix it-that’s one thing.” 
Wagoner said he’s hearing concerns about data centers, even though there’s not one currently slated for his district. 
“I think the bill they had, (House Bill) 2014 a couple years ago, was a bad bill,” Wagoner said. “One, I don’t think we need to roll out the red carpet for these things. Two, the control that they shouldn’t strip the counties of any control over them. And then the biggest one, the one that irritates me the most, is the sending the bulk of the tax money down to Charleston.” 
Democratic candidate DuRon Jackson (left) and Republican Chris Miller (rigth) are vying for Sen. Mike Woelfel’s seat in the West Virginia Senate. (Photos by Ryan Fischer/The Herald Dispatch and submitted)
Senate District 5 (Cabell and Wayne counties): 
Senate District 5, which includes Huntington and parts of northern Wayne County, became an open seat this year after long-serving state Sen. Mike Woefel, a Democrat, declined to run again. 
Now two men are vying for the seat, Chris Miller and DuRon Jackson.
Miller, a Republican, is the son of U.S. Rep. Carol Miller, and ran an acrimonious campaign against Gov. Patrick Morrisey in the 2024 gubernatorial primary. 
So far, he’s raised nearly $100,000 for his bid. Jackson, on the other hand, has reported raising $2,500 — enough for a clunker on Facebook Marketplace. 
Jackson is a former Huntington City Councilman and owns a restaurant and catering business. 
Miller said he wants to focus on energy, harnessing West Virginia’s current energy for the betterment of the state if elected.  
“I think the absolute best play to grow West Virginia’s economy is to turn our state into a battery, and literally become the battery of the East Coast, and export all of our power, and then create a sovereign wealth fund similar to what Alaska did, and put a portion of all those proceeds into a sovereign wealth fund to dramatically wipe down our power costs and become the state in the country with the cheapest power,” he said. 
Jackson did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: The Democrat daring to defy the odds and flip Tennessee’s 3rd District blue
text:
Anna Golladay, left, the Democratic nominee for the 3rd Congressional District, is challenging GOP U.S. Rep. Chuck Fleischmann, who has held the seat since 2010. (Photos: Golladay from annagolladay.com; Fleischmann from Congressman Chuck Fleischmann Facebook)Anna Golladay, the Democratic candidate for Tennessee’s 3rd Congressional District, is no stranger to politics. She first ran for elected office in 2025 for a seat on the Chattanooga City Council, losing in a runoff by 256 votes.
Beyond politics, Golladay, a United Methodist pastor, has a history of using her faith to advocate for social justice — at a personal cost. In 2018, she was fired from Chattanooga’s St. Marks United Methodist Church for officiating a same-sex wedding.
From preaching in the pulpit to running for local office, Golladay is now vying to take her message to the U.S. House.
“When I lost in that runoff, I knew I would run again,” Golladay said in an interview. “I did not know for what, and I certainly did not expect it to be for federal office.”
For Golladay to win, it will be no easy task. Republican incumbent Chuck Fleischmann has represented the district since 2011, winning with a commanding 67.5% of the vote in 2024. Holding the seat for over three consecutive decades, the GOP has maintained margins well over 20 percentage points each election cycle since the turn of the century.



Quotation







It would really take a lot of Republicans staying home or changing their minds for that district to do anything but go Republican. However, it’ll be a closer race than I think the congressperson in that district is used to.


– Samuel Wang, The Gerrymandering Project


Fleischmann also has a significant financial advantage, outraising Golladay, per the latest Federal Election Commission filings from mid-October, $2.7 million to $165,000 — a difference by a factor of over 16.
Still, in a midterm projected to be favorable for Democrats, Golladay sees an opportunity to overcome the odds.
“It’s the perfect storm of things colliding at the same time,” Golladay said. “We are watching not only the dismantling of democracy and the norms we have seen in Washington, but we’re also watching a radically corrupt administration and a Congress that has absolutely no backbone to do anything to mitigate it.”
Golladay sees an inactive and absent Fleischmann as part of the problem.
“We’ve got a significant number of people in this district who want more out of Fleischmann,” said Golladay, whose website has a ticking counter since Fleischmann last held a town hall — over 5,500 days dating back to 2011 during his inaugural term. “He is not accessible. He is hiding from his constituents.”
Fleischmann, who told the Chattanooga Times Free Press last year that he would “never” hold a town hall, calling them “left-wing bait,” did not agree to an interview with the Tennessee Lookout, but his office did email some written answers to questions.
“Woke Democrats can accuse me of whatever they want, but the fact of the matter is that East Tennesseans know what I stand for and the results that I deliver,” Fleischmann said in an email. “That is why they continue to elect me to fight for their families in Congress year after year.”

Golladay’s pitch versus Fleischmann’s record
Golladay’s campaign focuses on lowering the cost of living, especially when it comes to high gas prices induced by the war in Iran and President Donald Trump’s tariff policy upending global trade and raising the cost of general goods and services.
Since late February, when the war began, the price at the pump has shot up, sitting at, according to AAA, an average $3.81 a gallon as of this week in Tennessee — well above the sub-$3 before the fighting started.
According to a joint congressional committee, the average U.S. household paid more than $1,700 in tariff costs over Trump’s first year in office.
“This district is in shambles and really does not know how they are going to feed their families and put gas in their car,” Golladay said. “Chuck Fleischmann has voted against the provisions that would assist District Three residents.”
The representative has continually voted against a war powers resolution that would rein in the president’s authority in Iran. Fleischmann voted against blocking Trump’s tariffs on Canadian imports; he told the Chattanooga Times Free Press that he “wanted to give President Trump as much support as possible in his overall negotiations on tariffs.”
The representative voted for the president’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which made massive cuts to Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act, spiking health care costs for millions.
The bill also gave U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, ICE, $75 billion, making it now the highest-funded law enforcement agency in the country with a budget at its disposal higher than that of many industrialized nations’ militaries.
The administration’s immigration policy, particularly in Minneapolis earlier this year when federal agents shot and killed two Americans, is what led Golladay to run for Congress.
“I watched Alex Pretti and Renee Good be murdered in the streets of Minneapolis, and it all changed for me,” Golladay said. “We have a representative that is consenting to this kind of terror and is not speaking out against it.”
To remedy an inactive Congress, Golladay is part of the Take BAC Congress initiative, a group of over 150 candidates across 40 states pushing for political reforms such as instituting congressional term limits and overturning Citizens United, among others.
Despite Fleischmann’s loyalty to an unpopular president — one of his only notable breaks from the president was his vote against the administration’s cuts to federally-funded cancer research — the representative sees his record as supporting East Tennesseans.
WASHINGTON, DC – AUGUST 31: U.S. Rep. Chuck Fleischmann (R-TN) departs the office of Speaker of the House Mike Johnson (R-LA) on August 31, 2026 in Washington, DC. The House is expected to try to pass the short-term funding bill to prevent a pre-midterm shutdown. (Photo by Finn Gomez/Getty Images)
“As a conservative, I will continue working to curb our government’s massive unproductive spending, cut taxes, uphold the values that we were founded on, and champion America’s energy dominance,” Fleischmann said in an email. “I have had the privilege to live the American dream, and I want every Tennessean to have that same opportunity.”
The representative, chair of the Energy and Water Development subcommittee, often touts the amount of federal dollars he brings into his district, such as the $213 million that recently went to the ongoing lock replacement at the Chickamauga Dam on the Tennessee River in Chattanooga.
That earmark Fleischmann secured for the lock project, the largest nationwide, is part of its ballooning costs over the past 20 years, something Golladay said voters should keep in mind as the representative cites it as a positive mark of his record in Congress.
Starting in 2004 to replace the deteriorating lock, which is used to safely manage water levels, the project had an initial estimated cost of $267 million.That amount has risen to over $1.5 billion.
“Quite frankly, if I were the congressman, I’d be embarrassed that it’s taken this long to still make nothing happen,” Golladay said.
Even with any shortfalls voters may see in the GOP, Fleischmann said his party is better than the alternative.
“The radical left has gone too far, and Republicans offer a clear vision for an America that is free, safe, and strong,” Fleischmann said in an email.
The odds of a Democratic victory
Back in May, given clearance to do so by the U.S. Supreme Court’s Louisiana v. Callais decision, the GOP supermajority in the statehouse split the lone Democratic, Black-majority district centered around Memphis three ways — a gerrymander meant to produce a completely Republican congressional delegation in Tennessee.
The redistricting required Republicans to redraw the state’s entire map, including the 3rd District. Portions of Campbell, Scott and Morgan counties near the Kentucky border were cut and replaced with Rhea and Meigs closer to Chattanooga.
With the new map, Golladay said the district, with the campaign based in Chattanooga, is “more accessible for us.”
“That will, I think, shift the tone of this race, and we believe will shift in a way that accelerates our possibility to win and make this race much closer than any Republican is going to tell you,” Golladay said.
While the redrawn district does consolidate more around Chattanooga, the broader picture of the electorate remains almost exactly the same.



Quotation







We’ve got a significant number of people in this district who want more out of Fleischmann. He is not accessible. He is hiding from his constituents.


– Anna Golladay, Democratic candidate for Congress


In 2024, Trump won the 3rd District — in either the old or new map — with over 65% of the vote. It’s similar for the state’s other districts; Trump would have won every district by at least 20 points.
But in a year where the national environment is favorable for Democrats, the party in each of these races, even if it doesn’t win outright, could pull much closer than expected.
“It would really take a lot of Republicans staying home or changing their minds for that district to do anything but go Republican,” Samuel Wang, part of the Gerrymandering Project team at Princeton University, said of the 3rd District. “However, it’ll be a closer race than I think the congressperson in that district is used to.”
Golladay is concerned that many will chalk up any Democratic success next week, particularly in the South, to a short-term reaction to the Trump administration and not the start of a more long-term shift.
“I think that there will be a tendency to say we won because things are so out of control,” Golladay said. “They also need to be saying we won and we’ve gained momentum and we made some races really close that have not been close in a generation because we recruited candidates and we had people doing this hard work in the South.”

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota families can face debt collections if they can’t afford school lunch
text:
Students eat lunch at Carl Ben Eielson Middle School in Fargo on Jan. 22, 2025. School districts statewide reported student meal debt of about $2 million at the end of the 2025-26 school year, according to the Department of Public Instruction. (Photo by Dan Koeck/For the North Dakota Monitor)Every K-12 student has the legal right to receive a lunch at school in North Dakota without any stigma or shaming. But students and families who can’t afford to pay can still have long-term consequences, and some students may choose to go hungry to avoid them. 
There are more than two dozen school districts that reported referring parents to debt collection agencies for unpaid lunch debt, according to a state survey. At least one district withholds transcripts from students who haven’t paid off their account balance. 
Both types of policies are legal in North Dakota.
State law requires school districts to provide a meal to any student who requests one even if they lack the funds to pay for it. Legislation passed in 2023 known as the anti-lunch shaming bill prohibits schools from identifying or stigmatizing students for unpaid meal debts, and bans certain consequences such as limiting participating in graduation or other school activities.
Michelle Wagner, legislative chair for the North Dakota School Nutrition Association, said the 2023 law did not solve the problem. 
“I think the legislators had good intentions when they developed that anti-lunch shaming bill. But then there’s like no funding to help support it. So it’s really put us as districts and families in a tough situation,” said Wagner, who is also the child nutrition program director for Bismarck Public Schools.
Bismarck is among school districts that refer parents to debt collections for unpaid meal account balances. Wagner said it is used as a last resort. 
Lynelle Johnson, director of the Office of Child Nutrition and Food Distribution for the Department of Public Instruction, said lawmakers did not ban the practice in the 2023 law.
“They felt like that was one last thing they could do,” Johnson said. 
Being referred to debt collections can have significant financial consequences. The existence of the debt can be placed on a person’s credit report and lower their credit score. It can stay on a credit report for up to seven years from the date of the debt, even if it is paid off, according to credit agencies Experian and TransUnion.
“That will stay on because it shows your history on your ability to pay your debt,” said Lise Kruse, commissioner of the Department of Financial Institutions, which regulates collection agencies in North Dakota. 
That note on a credit report can make it more difficult for a person to get approved for a loan from a bank, among other things. 
“The credit score isn’t everything when they make a decision, but it definitely helps to have clean credit,” Kruse said. 
School districts statewide reported student meal debt of about $2 million at the end of the 2025-26 school year, Johnson reported to lawmakers last month. That does not include donations of nearly $46,000 that helped some districts pay down their debt, or transfers of nearly $500,000 from districts’ general fund budgets to reduce the debt. 
Lynelle Johnson, director of child nutrition and food distribution for the Department of Public Instruction, speaks during a committee hearing on June 11, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Sen. Scott Meyer, R-Grand Forks, said it is up to each school district to determine what the appropriate penalty for an unpaid meal account is. He said he doesn’t have a problem with debt collection referrals because the likely alternative is taxpayers will bear the cost, either through the state or an increase in property taxes. 
“If you’re not paying it, it’s going to get paid some way, and now you’re possibly putting it on the backs of your neighbors,” Meyer said.
Transcript trouble
Collection agencies are not the only way school districts have been trying to recoup unpaid meal debts accrued by students. The Elgin New Leipzig School District, in southwest North Dakota, will withhold transcripts from college applications or when a student wishes to volunteer for the military. 
“When they request a transcript, we won’t release one if they have an outstanding bill from lunch, and that usually gets people’s attention enough that they take care of it,” said Sherlock Hirning, superintendent of Elgin New Leipzig in Grant County. 
Hirning said the tactic has been successful in helping the district collect outstanding meal debt, and added that if a student requests a transcript a second time, the district would relent. 
“I would say that those are still very shaming tactics,” said Amy Jacobson, a member of the Together for School Meals coalition. “That’s terrible.”
Elgin is in compliance with North Dakota’s anti-lunch shaming law. But there could be long-term consequences of withholding a transcript if the student or family is unable to pay the debt. 
It’s unclear how many school districts use similar strategies. Elgin New Leipzig was one of three school districts that indicated transcripts or permanent records are affected by meal debt in a February survey by the state. The survey did not include a space for a district to elaborate on the details of the policy. 
The other public school respondent was Garrison Public Schools. But Superintendent Nick Klemisch said that was likely an error, and he is not aware of any policy that would withhold transcripts, or place information about a meal debt on a transcript or permanent record. 
Klemisch said the district rarely has issues with unpaid meal debts, is successful in fundraising private donations to cover debt that isn’t paid off and is often willing to work with parents on payment plans. 
“We’ve continued to allow families to charge, even if their balances are negative or in the hole,” Klemisch said. He said he can only recall one family in 12 years that refused to pay for meals entirely. 
The survey was not exhaustive, as it included responses from 79 of the 193 school districts in the state that participate in the National School Lunch Program. 
Stigma is hard to measure
It’s difficult to know whether every student who wants a lunch actually ends up being fed at school, advocates of free school meals say. 
Johnson said it can be true that all students have the opportunity to receive a school lunch while many do not take advantage of that option because they or their families do not want to accumulate debt. 
“Students know that they have a large negative balance, or they don’t have money, and they know that they will accumulate debt if they take the meal, even though they can’t be refused it,” Johnson said. 
She and others have heard anecdotes about students who choose not to go through the lunch line to avoid building up debt, who will visit the restroom during lunch to avoid the stigma, or older students who leave school premises so nobody knows their family can’t afford to pay for lunch. 
Meyer said there needs to be a conversation in the Legislature about the lack of funding provided in the 2023 bill, which mandates schools provide a meal to students who request one even if they have a negative account balance. 
But the lawmaker emphasized that students have access to meals in school, regardless of their account status, if they want it. It’s up to the kid if they choose to take advantage of that meal option or not. 
“We can’t force them to eat. But we do have to have access to lunch,” Meyer said. “That’s the important thing here.”
Some schools in North Dakota already provide free lunch and breakfast to all students through the Community Eligibility Provision program, because more than one-fourth of the students qualify for free or reduced lunch from the federal government. 
Turtle Mountain Community School, also known as Belcourt School District, is one. Earl Demery, one of the district’s administrators, said it has a positive impact on students’ academic performance because a kid thinks better and works harder when they are well fed. 
Wagner said there are six elementary schools and one alternative high school in Bismarck that qualify for the Community Eligibility Provision program. Staff have observed significant positive impacts in recent years as a result, including better student effort during the day and fewer visits to the nurse for stomach aches, likely caused by hunger, in the morning. 
“Feeding kids is the right thing,” said Wagner, one of the sponsors of a ballot measure to provide free school meals. “If families or parents are struggling financially, should that come back to the student? Probably not. It’s not fair to that student. I think it puts a lot of burden on that student, knowing that their family is struggling to pay that.”
Sen. Paul Thomas, R-Velva, speaks during a legislative committee meeting on Sept. 2, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Sen. Paul Thomas, R-Velva, said he has heard anecdotes of his own about students showing up to school hungry on Monday mornings because they didn’t have enough to eat at home over the weekend. He said he views that scenario, where a parent isn’t providing sufficient food at home, to be of greater concern and needs to be addressed. 
“To me, that’s a big concern. We need to take care of our youth,” Thomas said.
Policy solutions
A coalition of school meals advocates is asking voters to approve an amendment to North Dakota’s constitution on the general election ballot next week that would guarantee all K-12 students receive a free breakfast and lunch, and require the state to reimburse schools. 
Sen. Chuck Walen, R-New Town, is one of the lawmakers who oppose the measure. He prefers a legislative solution. 
But he also condemned the practice of referring parents to collection agencies for unpaid meal debt. And while he had heard of that happening, Walen said he was unaware transcripts were being withheld. The lawmaker said he would support strengthening the anti-shaming law to put a stop to both tactics.
“Any student is supposed to get their meal, period, without any stigma attached to it,” Walen said. “Your student record shouldn’t be held because that’s a student stigma in my mind.”
Walen said if Measure 2 fails, he plans to introduce legislation requiring the state to pay off all outstanding meal debt once a year. He said the more targeted approach would achieve a similar outcome and represent a far smaller cost to the state. 
Thomas is another opponent of Measure 2 who favors similar legislation.
“That debt is borne by the state, not by the student, not by the parent, not by the taxpayers of that individual school district,” Thomas said. “The state would take care of those balances.”
Thomas said he plans to introduce legislation in 2027 that would refocus the debate on school meals regardless of whether Measure 2 passes. He wants to take a closer look at students who aren’t receiving enough to eat at home and looking at “meal enhancements,” including the option for larger portion sizes and more nutritious meals, when they are in school. 
“That’s where our resources need to be allocated to in taking care of those students and making sure our youth in this state are receiving good, nutritious meals,” Thomas said.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Jacob Orledge can be reached at jorledge@northdakotamonitor.com.
