name: Alabama Reflector
title: Commentary: The specter of the midterms haunts us all
text:
Campaign signs for the Democratic nominees for Alabama's constitutional offices on display inside the Doug Jones for Governor headquarters in Birmingham, Alabama, as seen on Sept. 30, 2026. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)The most spine-tingling event of the year creeps ever closer, casting its long shadow over October’s brilliant blue days. 
The evidence is everywhere: Loud yard decor. Groups traipsing through neighborhoods, knocking door to door. Bloodcurdling stories about imaginary terrors, like furry airline pilots and hordes of invading communists. 
As the calendar ticks toward the month’s end, this most electrifying of days inches inexorably closer, cloaked in a shroud of fear and anticipation. Though we may shrink away from it, there’s nowhere to hide. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Election Day is coming for us all. 
Some Alabamians, uninterested in the circus or unimpressed by their options, might be tempted to close their eyes and wish away the specter of the political season. There’s recent precedent: More than 40% of registered voters in Alabama did not cast a ballot in the 2024 general election.
But the results of this election will haunt every person who lives in the state, whether they brave the ballot box or not. The ghosts of elections past already lurk within Alabama’s most persistent challenges: crime, healthcare, education, prisons. Pick your poison; there’s plenty to choose from. 
This year’s election cycle has become especially unignorable, as formerly safe Republicans have faced new, serious challenges from reanimated Alabama Democrats. 
Leading the pack, Democratic gubernatorial candidate Doug Jones has returned from beyond the political grave to chase Republican contender Tommy Tuberville across the state, forcing Coach to fight for the job he’s gunning for. Of late, this year’s race for governor has more closely resembled a real contest than a lazy cruise to victory, a change of pace that I hope we repeat in future cycles. Politicians should, after all, earn every vote instead of becoming entitled to them.
Jones recently acknowledged that it’s been an ‘uphill chug,’ but his Sisyphean efforts appear to have cracked the armor of Alabama conservatism. With less than two weeks remaining before Election Day, election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball shifted the Jones/Tuberville contest from “Safe Republican” to “Likely Republican.”
That is one heck of a plot twist.
The last time Jones and Tuberville faced off, during their 2020 battle for the U.S. Senate, Tuberville beat Jones by about 20 points. Now, two recent polls measured their gap at around 10 points. Jones has closed the distance by half. 
His inroads with voters match the national trend. 
One of the starkest examples: Kansas hasn’t elected a Democratic senator since the 1930s, but this year’s race between incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall and Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton has, against all odds, suddenly become a toss-up.
Even in Mississippi—a political kindred spirit to Alabama if ever there was one—a GOP-aligned super PAC this month abruptly decided to spend $160,000 to defend incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, with more cash to follow.
Republicans have become increasingly concerned about the potential depth and breadth of this year’s anticipated blue wave. In an Oct. 21 story, reporters at Axios quoted a national Republican political operative as saying: “The wall has broken. The enemy is inside the fort. We are now fighting hand to hand.” 
Some political insiders have decided to project that fear outward and dial up the fright factor all the way to 11 during this final stretch of the campaign, an attempt to drive disaffected voters to the polls.
Fox News host Jesse Watters earlier this month told his fellow hosts on “The Five” that touting accomplishments is all well and good, but the key to galvanizing voters is to ratchet up so-called “fear porn” (his words, not mine).
“You have to say, these people are going to take your healthcare, they’re going to let in the Third World, they’re going to jack up your taxes, and that’s what’s going to get people to come out to vote,” he said. “You have to say, these people are scary and dangerous.”
That strategy may raise blood pressures among the electorate, but the “fear porn” (it’s gross even to type it out) will have to be truly terrifying if it’s going to overpower the foundational truth that’s driving current voter sentiment: It’s the economy, stupid. 
People vote with their wallets. And right now, as price tags remain stubbornly high for everything from gas to housing to Halloween candy, people’s wallets are telling one of the scariest stories of all. 
Who knows how the push and pull of all these competing forces will shake out when voters head to the polls on Nov. 3? But regardless of who wins, one thing is certain: Within a matter of weeks, the smoke and mirrors of the campaign trail will dissipate. And in the cold light of day, our new crop of elected officials will be expected to trade fairy tales for real-life results.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: A homeowner’s last stand against Alabama Power
text:
Fenn Church, center, is flanked by supporters at the gate of his property in Shelby County, Alabama. (Lee Hedgepeth/ Inside Climate News)This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here.
CALERA — Fenn Church knew what he had to do.
“I’m going to stand in front of that gate and say, ‘This is my home, and I’m not letting you drive through that gate,’” Church said on Thursday morning. “And then if they want to arrest me, they can handcuff me and take me to jail or run me over. But this is where I take my stand.”
For months, Church had fought Alabama Power’s effort to use eminent domain to secure access to his property in Alabama’s lower courts, arguing that the utility could easily use alternative routes to build a transmission line that would not be as disruptive to homeowners like himself in rural Shelby County, about a 45-minute drive south of Birmingham.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In September, that legal battle resulted in a victory for Church when Circuit Court Judge Jonathan Spann issued a temporary injunction preventing Alabama Power from accessing Church’s property. In his ruling, Spann found that Alabama Power, one of the state’s most powerful companies, had failed to follow the necessary procedures for condemnation of Church’s land outlined in state law.
Church was likely to succeed on the merits of his case, and without a preliminary injunction, he would be irreparably harmed, the judge wrote.
Spann also noted that an Alabama Power employee had testified in court that the route for the planned transmission line crossing Church’s property had been finalized with “no consideration” to zoning plans or the “development potential or suitability” of properties it would cross.
That unrebutted testimony made it likely that Church would be able to prove that Alabama Power’s siting of the transmission line was illegally arbitrary and capricious, Spann ruled.
Church’s victory would be short-lived. On Wednesday, in a 5-1 ruling, the Alabama Supreme Court issued an order granting Alabama Power’s motion to stay Spann’s injunction against it. The state’s highest court did not provide reasons for its decision.
“Alabama Power understands that property is personal, and we remain committed to treating property owners fairly and respectfully,” the electric utility said in a statement after the state Supreme Court ruling. “The Alabama Supreme Court’s decision allows work on this section of the transmission line to move forward, supporting a project that is an important investment in the security and reliability of the electric grid for the customers and communities we serve.”
Desperate in the wake of the high court decision, Church called his federal lawmakers—U.S. Sens. Katie Britt and Tommy Tuberville and U.S. Rep. Barry Moore. He wouldn’t hear back before the trucks were scheduled to arrive.
John Rich, a country music star and a Trump-appointed, so-called Special Envoy for American Homeowners, had also pledged support for Church’s cause.
“We can build out our energy infrastructure and treat landowners with respect simultaneously, and that’s what I intend on doing in this case,” Rich had initially said publicly. “About 200 yards away, there’s a wide open, clear-cut path that doesn’t involve driving bulldozers and trucks and 18-wheelers for the rest of eternity through this man’s property, right through his front driveway.”
But it wasn’t long before Church said he felt that Rich was hitting a roadblock somewhere in the administration.
“Somebody must’ve got to Trump and told him to back down,” Church said.
Hours after the Supreme Court ruling against Church on Wednesday afternoon, representatives of Alabama Power notified Church’s lawyers that its crews would arrive at the property between 7 and 8 a.m. to begin the work to which he’d long objected.
With few options left, and on Rich’s advice, Church turned to social media, calling on supporters to show up the next day.
“Tree cutting crews are coming to my front gate in the morning,” he posted. “Appreciate any support that anyone can give me standing at my gate in the morning!”
Within hours, the post had been viewed more than 100,000 times on the social media platform, eliciting dozens of comments from across the country.
Rep. Phillip Ensler, a Democrat running to become the state’s lieutenant governor, showed up Thursday morning to stand alongside Church. It wasn’t the first time he’d visited Church’s property in solidarity—the only public official to do so, according to Church.
Fenn Church, left, speaks with Rep. Phillip Ensler, center, and lawyer Jay Welborn. (Lee Hedgepeth/ Inside Climate News)
“Alabama Power thinks they can just walk over anyone and everyone,” Ensler said. “They’re just trying to flex their muscles and intimidate people, and if they can do that to him and do it here, they can do it anywhere.”
Ensler and Church talked more as the nippy morning began to slowly warm. One by one, cars and pickup trucks rolled up Church’s driveway. Whenever the hum of an engine could be heard coming down Township Road toward Church’s front gate, the group would crane their necks toward the gravel entrance.
Each time, one of the men, this time Church himself, would approach the vehicle stopped just outside the gate.
“Hey there,” Church said, a smile stretched across his face. The driver of the truck rolled down his window.
“You’re not here to cut down my trees are you?” Church asked.
The man in the truck laughed. “No. I’m here to help you stop them if I can,” the driver said.
Church waved the man through, instructing him to park wherever he’d like and make sure he grabbed himself a Hardee’s biscuit. Soon, Church and the newcomer would rejoin the growing group ready to resist Alabama Power, and the wait would continue.
The Alabama Power trucks never came.
Instead, close to 8 a.m., Church and others looked to the sky. A faint buzz overhead had drawn their attention. Just above the towering pines, a drone strafed into view, pausing briefly around a hundred feet above Church’s driveway before flying away.
“I wonder if they liked what they saw,” one man said. Church and the others laughed.
A couple hours later, cameras on the southern side of Church’s property showed crews surveying and marking trees, having accessed the property via another route.
“It was sneaky,” Church said of the move. “They knew we were here, so they snuck around back. It’s just a dirty way of doing business.”
Alabama Power did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
But now, Church said he knows the power company’s playbook. He’s got one, too.
Church said he heard from Tuberville around 11:30 a.m. on Thursday. The senator said he would make a call to Alabama Power in an effort to resolve the conflict, according to Church, a gesture he appreciates.
“His father had property lost to eminent domain in Arkansas and died of a heart attack a few months later,” Church said. “He has a personal attachment to my battle seeing what his father went through.”
Tuberville’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Tuberville’s action, Church said, gives him some hope that the senator will actually try his best to mediate with the electric utility.
Alabama Power’s crews are gone for now, but Church knows they’ll be back. And while he may not be able to keep them off his land forever, he’s certainly going to try.
“If I catch them trying to come onto my property, I’ll get on the phone and get everybody back up here,” Church said. “We’ve got no choice.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: (Most) Democrats at Question 3 rally, Harbeson heads out, more in political notes
authors: Bryan P. Sears, William J. Ford, Christine Condon
text:
Supporters hold signs Monday at a rally in Bowie attended by top state Democrats backing the passage of Question 3, the constitutional amendment on congressional redistricting. (Photo By Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)Democrats are making their closing push for Question 3, the proposed amendment to the Maryland Constitution that will establish new standards for redrawing the state’s eight congressional districts.
At a rally in Bowie Monday — following the release of an ad for Question 3 featuring former President Barack Obama — focused their arguments on the issue as one of standing up to Republican President Donald Trump. Rep. Glenn F. Ivey (D-4th) said passage was needed because “Donald Trump has been attempting to find any way he can to steal this election, and we got to fight fire with fire.”
Maryland’s entry into hyperpartisan redistricting was prompted by Trump’s calls for Republican-led states to redraw lines to increase the number of Republican seats in the current mid-term election, Ivey told the crowd.
“We’re trying to fight back, and we have to fight back here in Maryland by redrawing our lines too. And that’s what Question 3 is all about,” Ivey said. “Because helping to control the House of Representatives is the way we put some guardrails on the Trump administration, and Lord knows if there’s an administration that ever needed it, it’s this one.”
This despite a predicted national blue wave in next week’s midterm elections. Most analysts predict Democrats will pick up enough seats to take control of the House, and that control of the Senate may also be within reach for Democrats.
The ballot question in Maryland will have no effect on the partisan makeup of Congress after the Nov. 3 election. There is no new map with the ballot question, just permission for legislators to make changes in the future. No new congressional maps could be drawn before 2027, and would not take effect until the 2028 elections, as Trump’s second and final term comes to a close.
Rep. Steny Hoyer (D-5th) calls for the passage of Question 3, an constitutional amendment that would lift state standards regarding the drawing of congressional districts. (Photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
Rep. Steny Hoyer (D-5th), following the rally in Bowie said passage of the proposed amendment is needed to allow a redistricting process that could make it easier for Democrats to secure all eight of Maryland’s House seats. Rep. Andy Harris (R-1st) is the only Republican in the state delegation, the seven other seats are held by Democrats.
Hoyer noted that a 2022 decision by Judge Lynne Battaglia made that redistricting effort more difficult. Passage would make it clear that nothing in the Maryland Constitution or state Declaration of Rights would set standards for redrawing the state’s congressional districts. It would eliminate almost any opportunity for a group to legally challenge a map in a Maryland court.
“We could [draw new maps], but this clarifies the court’s decision as to what was meant,” Hoyer said. “We all believe that the court made a mistake. In fact, the Supreme Court of Maryland suggested that in a subsequent opinion. The real answer to the question is, can’t we do the second [draw a map] without the first [passing the ballot question].”
Doug Mayer, a spokesman for the opposition group Protect Maryland Votes, said Hoyer “has been a beneficiary of extreme partisan gerrymandering for nearly 30 years, so it’s hardly surprising he is unwilling to admit the truth about Question 3.”
“But he did say some of the quiet part out loud – they are angry that a Democrat-appointed judge thought there should be controls around politicians picking their own voters and they want to get rid of those controls,” Mayer said. “This is about total power and nothing more.”
Ferguson’s focus
Absent from the Question 3 rallies and commercials is a key Maryland Democratic leader: Senate President Bill Ferguson.
Aside from an email that went out from the Fight Back Maryland campaign, the Baltimore City senator has been largely absent from the ballot question push. A Question 3 commercial features Democrats including Gov. Wes Moore, Hoyer, House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk and U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, but not Ferguson.
All five favor a new House map that would favor a Democratic sweep, but Ferguson has not favored redrawing the districts before the 2030 Census.  And the relationship between Moore and Ferguson remains frayed from a bruising fight over redistricting earlier this year and Moore’s decision to not endorse the Senate leader.
When asked about Ferguson’s absences, a spokesperson for Fight Back Maryland shrugged but offered no comment.
A Ferguson spokesperson offered a different explanation.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“The Senate president’s primary focus has been on retaining and growing our Democratic majority in the state Senate including going after a potential seat flip in places like District 42,” said David Schuhlein. The retirement of Sen. Chris West (R-Baltimore and Carroll) has left the District 42 seat open.
Want to vote by mail? You’d better get cracking
There’s still time to vote by mail in next Tuesday’s general election — but not much, said the Maryland State Board of Elections, which continues to remind voters of looming deadlines.
Tuesday is the last day to ask that a mail-in ballot be mailed or faxed to you to fill out and return. If you miss that deadline, you have until Friday to ask for an emailed link to your ballot, which you will then be responsible for printing and providing an envelope in which to return it. In either case, the request must be done online and include your name, address and driver’s license or identification number.
Early voting began Thursday and continues through 8 p.m. this Thursday at voting centers — which may be different than your normal polling place — around the state.
The Board of Elections said it had sent out 642,901 mail-in ballots so far this year, and had 290,990 returned as of 6 p.m. Sunday. Of those, 151,709 had been “accepted,” or counted by local election offices. Local elections officials in every county have had ballots returned, but officials in Caroline, Cecil, Dorchester, Garett, Kent and Somerset counties had not reported any had been accepted as of Sunday evening.
Democrats, who account for half the registered voters in the state, have asked for 66.3% of mail-in ballots so far, and were responsible for about 69% of the returned and accepted ballots. Republicans asked for 15.5% of mail-in ballots and other voters requested 18%, according to state officials. So far, 151,709 have been accepted, or counted. Amongst those, 105,615, or 70%, have been come from registered Democrats.
In the 2022 gubernatorial election, a total of 541,201 mail-in ballots were received.
You can find more voting deadlines and how-to information in our voter’s guide, along with information on statewide races, legislative elections and questions on proposed constitutional amendments.
Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3, when polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m.
Harbeson leaves LCV for Gally
After 11 years as political director for the Maryland League of Conservation Voters, Kristen Harbeson will be departing for Annapolis lobbying firm Gally Public Affairs next month.
Kristen Harbeson, political director for the Maryland League of Conservation Voters. (Photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
“It has been an honor and a privilege to work with the talented team at Maryland LCV for more than a decade, and I look forward continuing to supporting them in advancing their mission from my new post,” Harbeson wrote in a post on LinkedIn, adding that she will start in her new role Nov. 15.
Gally Public Affairs, the firm started by Eric Gally in 1997, has represented the League of Conservation Voters, according to the state’s online lobbying database, along with other environmental organizations such as the Chesapeake Bay Foundation, Earthjustice and the Nature Conservancy.
Before she joined the League in 2015, Harbeson was a senior staffer to Del. Maggie McIntosh (D-Baltimore City), and she worked for the legislature’s former Environmental Matters Committee.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Commentary: A tale of a law, a lawsuit and many missed opportunities for Kentucky children
text:
The Kentucky Court of Appeals in Frankfort, Kentucky, on Oct. 23, 2026. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Sarah Ladd)At 2:30 Saturday morning, I woke up troubled by the October 23 hearing in the Kentucky Court of Appeals that I had attended.
One thought kept returning: We shouldn’t have been in that courtroom at all.
I had listened as attorneys debated subpoenas, funding, the State Auditor’s authority and whether the dispute was moot. How had a kinship care law intended to protect vulnerable children brought us to this point?
My thoughts returned to a conversation with a grandmother in 2019.
When her grandson was removed from his home, she took him in. She signed paperwork without fully understanding how that decision could affect financial assistance for his care.
She later realized she had potentially waived access to thousands of dollars of assistance. 
I shared her concerns with a senior Cabinet for Health and Family Services official, who acknowledged communication could improve, but maintained the process was legal.
In my view, communication fell short. And something can be legal and still need to change.
That experience helped lead to Senate Bill (SB) 151, unanimously passed by Kentucky’s General Assembly in 2024 and signed by Governor Andy Beshear.
The law established a 120-day window for relatives and fictive kin to understand their options and pursue approval as kinship foster parents. It allowed caregivers experiencing qualifying events to seek reconsideration for foster care approval—potentially keeping children in the same home with support.
It also strengthened opportunities for children to identify relatives or trusted adults they wanted considered for placement.
Then implementation stalled.
The administration cited Fletcher v. Commonwealth, a Kentucky Supreme Court decision concerning legislative appropriations, to justify waiting for additional funding.
CHFS initially estimated implementation at $20 million, later revising that figure to $14.6 million annually. Both estimates relied entirely on state General Fund dollars, despite SB 151’s direction to maximize available federal funding.
I believed Kentucky had other funding options and that portions of the law could have moved forward while financial questions were resolved.
Instead, families waited.
That’s why I asked State Auditor Allison Ball in 2024 to independently examine the funding assumptions behind the delay.
What followed was a legal battle over the Auditor’s authority to obtain information.
Ball sued Governor Beshear and CHFS. The Cabinet maintained it had cooperated with her investigation; Ball argued she lacked information necessary to complete it.
Franklin Circuit Court Judge Thomas Wingate dismissed the lawsuit as premature, citing, in part, the Auditor’s failure to use subpoenas.
On appeal, Ball argued that routinely requiring subpoenas could undermine independent oversight. She cited KRS 43.080, requiring agencies to permit access to records upon the Auditor’s request.
After nearly 30 years in government, I understand what may feel like burdensome information requests. But genuine cooperation means providing what you can and establishing reasonable timelines—avoiding the appearance of a standoff.
If agencies decide what information is sufficient for an independent audit, how independent is that oversight?
Ball warned that without meaningful access to information, her office could become an “empty shell.”  There are implications far beyond SB 151.
In July 2026, CHFS began implementing SB 151 after the General Assembly appropriated $12 million over two years.
The Cabinet now argues that implementation makes the appeal moot.
Really? Moot to whom?
Beginning implementation two years later doesn’t answer whether the original funding estimates were accurate, whether federal funding opportunities and alternative approaches were adequately explored, or whether portions of the law could have been implemented sooner.  
Nor does it restore opportunities lost by families in 2024 and 2025.  
These are questions, not accusations, but answers matter—especially when the full implementation of a law intended to protect vulnerable children was delayed for two years.
In March 2026, a proposed administrative regulation was found deficient following legislative review. I testified, raising concerns about the approach and absence of federal funding.
Then HB 500, the 2026 budget legislation, incorporated language from the proposed regulation, and CHFS proceeded through internal policy.
Questions remain about whether that approach fulfills SB 151’s intent and whether state funding is sustainable. To my knowledge, there is still no approved implementing regulation. I continue working with legislators, CHFS and the Auditor’s office to seek answers.
Meanwhile, children still need their voices heard.
Days before the appeal, I advocated for a teenage foster youth who was in three homes in five days. Although his social worker reportedly had arranged his latest placement days earlier, I was told he learned about the last move when transportation arrived after football practice to take him there. 
SB 151 was intended to strengthen children’s voices in placement decisions.
Was that promise moot to him?
We cannot always change what brings children into the child welfare system. But we can change how government responds.
And that brings me back to the courtroom.
There I sat, a kinship caregiver and advocate, watching State Auditor Allison Ball herself stand at the podium, defending her authority to obtain information.
Our fight began with children and families who deserved better. But it had grown beyond SB 151. The independence of an office responsible for government oversight was now at stake.
The court will decide the legal questions. But the consequences of government decisions don’t disappear when a lawsuit ends.
We don’t need empty shells. We need laws that deliver on all their promises and independent oversight to ensure accountability.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Even with a GOP supermajority, some of KY’s legislative races have competitive spice
text:
Kentucky's General Assembly will have plenty of races on Election Day on Nov. 3, 2026.  (Kentucky Lantern photo by Arden Barnes)Kentuckians won’t just vote on who to replace the outgoing U.S. Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell in the general election on Nov. 3. 
In addition to a constitutional amendment and local races, voters will decide who will represent them in the Kentucky General Assembly for the next two- and six- year terms.
While all 100 in the state House seats are up for grabs in the November election, only half of the state Senate’s 38 seats are up for election. And in the last few weeks heading into the general election, there’s plenty of storylines to follow. 
In one state House race, for example, the self-proclaimed MAGA Republican dropped out last week, citing a job promotion as the reason, leaving Democratic Rep. Anne Donworth running unopposed for the 76th Kentucky House District seat. 
Republicans in the General Assembly have a supermajority in both chambers. Still, there are a handful of legislative races expected to be competitive, and Democrats are hoping to gain a few more seats in Frankfort during the upcoming midterm election. 
Here are some of the races to watch. 
State House District 45: Incumbent Adam Moore versus Republican Killian Timoney 
Former Republican Rep. Killian Timoney is hoping to represent the 45th district again. Timoney, who has often been viewed as a moderate, served in the House from January 2021 through December 2025. 
In 2024, Liberty Republican candidate Thomas Jefferson ousted Timoney in the Republican primary. During that election cycle, campaign mailers slammed Timoney for voting against an anti-transgender law affecting medical treatment for youth and public schools, which was a key issue among GOP voters. 
But Jefferson lost to then-Democrat candidate Adam Moore in the general election. 
Timoney said he wants to represent the district again because he wasn’t done with his work in Frankfort when he left. 
“(I felt like) my departure was abrupt and it was premature,” Timoney said. “Anybody that starts something wants to finish it, and that’s one of the tough things about being a legislator, is that your clients can be interrupted by the voter, and that’s part of it.”
Timoney said he has received positive feedback while door-knocking, and he believes voters are looking for someone like himself who will work across the aisle and build bridges instead of burning them. 
He also believes being a Republican gives him an advantage to get things accomplished in Frankfort. 
“If you’re in the supermajority, you get bills passed and you get projects, and if you’re not, you don’t,” Timoney said. “I don’t make the rules. It’s just the way that they are, and that’s something that is an unmistakable, undeniable advantage, and that’s what a lot of the people in the 45th want.” 
The district, which is made up of parts of Jessamine County and and Fayette County, has been seen as purple, which could end up resulting in a close race between Moore and a more moderate Republican like Timoney. 
Moore said while he believes he has every opportunity to win again, he’s not going to “count his chickens before they hatch.” 
“I know he’s a real candidate,” Moore said. “I’m sure he’s working hard, and that’s why I just have to keep working hard.” 
Issues and campaign priorities for Moore include creating good-paying jobs, access to affordable healthcare and fully investing in public schools. 
Moore said that he’s received positive feedback from voters and thinks he has been an effective legislator for the district, which is why he should be reelected. 
“I’ve been someone who has been very bipartisan, someone who’s worked across the aisle, who’s focused on things like affordable health care and strong public schools and trying to put guardrails on data centers,” Moore said. “I’m not someone who’s out there throwing bombs or trying to be a culture warrior, but just trying to actually, I think, restore faith in politics and government, and I think that’s been received very well.” 
State House District 95: Democrat Johnny Ray Turner versus Republican Tanner Hesterberg 
Timoney isn’t the only former legislator running for office.
Democrat Johnny Ray Turner, who represented state Senate District 29 from 2001 to 2021, is hoping to make a comeback in Frankfort next year too. In 2020, Johnny Ray Turner lost in the general election to then-Republican candidate Johnnie Turner, who died in October 2024 from injuries in an accident. 
Johnny Ray Turner said he’s running because he enjoyed helping people as a state senator, and the race has an open seat. Democrat Rep. Ashley Tackett Laferty, who has represented the district since 2019, is not seeking reelection and running for Floyd District Judge. 
“When an opportunity came about for me to run for the House of Representatives, which is a smaller district and what I call more my people…I thought I would like to try it and be in a position to help my people in Eastern Kentucky, especially in Floyd and Pike Counties,” Turner said. 
While Democrats in the General Assembly represented the urban areas, including Louisville and Lexington, Tackett Laferty was the sole Democrat who represented rural Kentucky. 
Turner said it’s important for the district to have someone like himself to work across party lines. If elected, Turner wants to use the contacts he made as state senator to help improve Eastern Kentucky. 
Tanner Hesterberg, an attorney who is running as the Republican nominee in the race, did not respond to an interview request at the time of publication. 
State Senate District 36: Incumbent Julie Raque Adams versus Democrat Sarah Cole McIntosh 
When Democratic candidate Sarah Cole McIntosh served on the Jefferson County School Board, she said she became aware that community problems were a result of “bad policy coming out of Frankfort.” 
That prompted her to launch a campaign for state Senate District 36, which Sen. Julie Raque Adams, R-Louisville, currently represents. 
McIntosh doesn’t consider herself a “career politician,” which is a perspective she thinks would help her represent the district.
“I’m living the same issues and problems and struggles as all the other Kentuckians, from figuring out how to pay bills, hoping that my husband and I get to retire someday, (and) taking care of my loved ones through illness to the end of life,” McIntosh said. 
In early October, the Kentucky Lantern reported Republican outside groups have spent more than $620,000 to help reelect Adams. 
These donations follow a Lantern story from April that reported that Adams was paid $80,500 since 2023 by an inactive political committee, called Kentucky Strong, that she headed and has been funded exclusively by lobbying interests in recent years. 
McIntosh said she would represent her constituents instead of “corporate lobbyists,” and work ethic is just as important as fundraising in a campaign. 
“I always knew that I was going to be outspent, but I will never be outworked, and so that’s the same kind of work ethic that I think voters can expect from me once I’m representing them in Frankfort,” McIntosh said. 
Adams did not respond to an interview request at the time of publication. 
State Senate District 6: Incumbent Lindsey Tichenor versus Democrat Christian Furman 
Republican Sen. Lindsey Tichenor, a legislator who has become notable in the far-right “Liberty” faction of the General Assembly, will face a Democrat challenger for the first time in the state Senate District 6 race. The district includes part of Jefferson County, which tends to learn blue, Oldham and Trimble County. 
Democrat Christian Furman, a Prospect City Council member and physician, is challenging Tichenor on the November ballot, who has served in office since 2023. 
Furman said her experience as a doctor has helped her acquire listening and collaboration skills, which she said are essential for someone who is in public office to have. 
“I listen to the patient first of all. I listen to other doctors. I listen to their family,” Furman said. “I collaborate with the whole healthcare team, and together we come up with a care plan, and that same skill set of being a doctor translates to being a senator. 
She added that she’s willing to work with Republicans to pass legislation. 
“If I have a good idea, some people say you have to kind of turn it over to the Republican to get across the finish line,” Furman said. “That’s fine. I don’t have an ego. It’s not like it has to be my way or the highway. 
Issues important to Furman include making Kentucky more affordable, safer and healthier. 
Throughout Tichenor’s tenure, she has pushed for legislation that would limit diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives in K-12 public schools, banning minors from “explicit” drag performances and require public school districts to increase transparency on how public dollars are spent. 
Tichenor did not respond to an interview request at the time of publication.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: As living costs rise, more people need assistance to obtain abortions, Va. fund reports
text:
A sign outside a clinic that provides abortions in Richmond, Va. (Photo by Sarah Vogelsong/Virginia Mercury) As Virginians prepare to reject or approve an amendment to enshrine reproductive rights into the state’s constitution on Election Day next week, new data shows more people inside and outside the state are relying on assistance to obtain abortions. 
The Virginia-based Blue Ridge Abortion Fund on Monday reported an uptick in patients requesting their help to obtain the procedure amid bans in surrounding areas and rising costs of living. 
Over the past year, from June 2025 to June 2026, BRAF supported 1,920 abortion seekers. According to their latest report, roughly $1.2 million in funding was disbursed among people who needed assistance to cover costs for the procedure itself and expenses like lodging or transportation. 
More than one in four callers supported by BRAF stem from out of state — with most coming from North Carolina, Georgia and Florida, which have 6-week and 12-week limits. 
BRAF director April Greene emphasized that people typically need to sort out time off from work, childcare or finances before they can obtain an abortion. 
Rising costs of fuel, other goods squeeze already strained abortion funds

For those living in states with deep restrictions, sometimes time-strapped patients have to travel to less-restrictive states like Virginia. That process comes with a cost. 
“The longer someone has to wait to access care, the more expensive and logistically complex that care becomes,” Greene explained. 
Since the fund’s 1989 founding, BRAF has helped more than 15,000 people and committed $6.3 million in financial support. Over $4 million of that has been spent in the four years since federal abortion protections were overturned. 
The overall cost of getting an abortion has also gone up, and fuel costs and inflation are also rising.  With costlier plane tickets or strain at the pump for patients traveling in and out of state, BRAF also reports a downtick in some donor bases. 
“The economy is hitting everyone, and our donors aren’t immune from that,” Greene said. 
A surge of donations in the summer of 2022 immediately following the Dobbs v. Jackson ruling — the U.S. Supreme Court case that overturned abortion protections — has helped sustain BRAF. 
“Because of that post-Dobbs support, we were able to build up a bit of a reserve fund,” Greene said. 
But with about $10,000 to $15,000 less donations per month, Greene shared, the organization is grappling with less in its coffers to offer to people. 
“If we aren’t able to kind of rebuild that individual donation momentum, we probably will be looking at needing to decrease our weekly funding budget in the new year for sure,” she said.
Constitutional: The amendment that could permanently protect reproductive rights in Virginia

While most nearby states have restrictions or bans, Maryland has permanently protected reproductive rights, similar to the proposition Virginia voters are deciding this year.
Greene said BRAF is watching to see if Virginians will approve the ballot referendum and noted that both states are critical access points for abortion care. 
“We are really trying to remind folks that being able to access that legal right is just as important,” Greene said. “We need them to kind of stick with us for the long haul and make sure we can get people to those appointments after Election Day, too.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginia lawmakers approve plan to advance new K-12 school funding formula
text:
A cup of pencils sit on top of a classroom desk in a Virginia school. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)A state legislative subcommittee on Monday approved a plan to hire an expert to study a new school funding formula for Virginia, with up to 24 months to complete the work.
The decision continues lawmakers’ work to update the state’s 52-year-old funding formula, which determines the Standards of Quality, or funding level for public schools. A December 2023 study showed that Virginia local governments spend far more on K-12 education than the state, underscoring the need for a clearer approach.
Virginia Dept. of Ed projects K-12 schools will need $1.2 billion over next two years

Researchers from the Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission, which studied the formula, said lawmakers could partially replace the SOQ formula by using student-based calculations for special education and English learner funding. Another option would be to fully replace the entire staffing-based formula with a new student-based formula, researchers said.
Sen. Mamie Locke, D-Hampton, who was re-elected chair of the Joint Subcommittee to Study Elementary and Secondary Education Funding on Monday, said that although the group has 24 months, it would be “optimal” to complete the work when Gov. Abigail Spanberger presents her biennium budget requests in December 2027.
“I don’t think it’s going to take us 24 months to get this work done, and that would be better and in the best interest of our school districts and our kids if we can move this as quickly as possible,” Locke said.
The scope of work requires the consultant to give lawmakers a data-driven tool to evaluate alternative K–12 funding formulas and understand their fiscal and distributional impacts before implementing changes.
Holly Coy, chief of staff for the Virginia Department of Education, said that once the agency finalizes the draft Request for Proposal, or formal service request, it will publish the proposal and accept bids for 30 days. 
The agency expects to select a consultant and begin work during the upcoming General Assembly session in January.
Coy said lawmakers will have an opportunity after the session to provide further input to the consultant on the policy factors that will be built into the funding model. 
Factors include base funding per student, extra weights for student needs, class sizes, operating costs, transition provisions, and the Local Composite Index, which determines what each locality can pay for its schools.
Virginia has increased ongoing K–12 education funding by just over $4 billion, or 50%, from fiscal year 2023 to fiscal year 2028, according to a staff report for the subcommittee, highlighted by $1.5 billion in teacher salaries, plus $375.4 million in one-time educator bonuses.
Other investments include $273.2 million in additional funding for at-risk students, $537.5 million in additional funding for school support staff, $126.8 million to establish and expand dedicated funding for special education, and $106.9 million for additional English language learner teachers and reading specialists positions.
The state has also contributed to additional funding for school construction, early childhood education, and updates to school funding calculations.
Del. Cia Price, D-Newport News, a committee member, expressed support for moving the matter forward without further delay.
“I think this is overdue, and so anything that we can do one time thoughtfully and expeditiously… I think just to put on the record our desire for this to go aggressively, thoughtfully, quickly,” she said.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Lawmakers say push from public, governor behind new batch of proposed data center guardrails
text:
A former coal power plant in Bow is one site under preliminary consideration for a potential data center development, according to town officials. Multiple state legislators and New Hampshire Governor Kelly Ayotte have said they will pursue a statewide moratorium on data center developments. (File photo by Dave Cummings/New Hampshire Bulletin)Although a mash of proposed restrictions and protections for AI data centers raised debate in the New Hampshire Legislature earlier this year, they largely failed to progress. Now, as early filings for the 2027 session show, some lawmakers are hoping to do more.
With some preliminary bill requests tentatively filed ahead of the next legislative session, at least three incumbent lawmakers — only one of whom has a challenger — have so far submitted requests to the state’s Office of Legislative Services for help drafting bills pertaining to data centers. (If a lawmaker is not reelected, their early-filed proposal could be taken on by another legislator or, otherwise, fail to advance.)
The early proposals reflect two visions for a statewide moratorium on data centers. It’s a move more than a dozen states are considering, with New York becoming the first to adopt a one-year ban this summer. Early versions of the proposals floated in New Hampshire differ in their lengths, requirements, and the expectations shared by the legislators who authored them for New Hampshire’s role in a post-moratorium future.
A call from the Executive Branch
One person pushing for a moratorium on data centers in New Hampshire is Gov. Kelly Ayotte, who said in September she would support such a pause after proposals floated for Nottingham and Bow were met with public opposition. 
The governor indicated she would propose a moratorium on the centers in the next biennial budget, which will be finalized in summer 2027. She said she would support a “years” long pause, according to reporting by New Hampshire Public Radio.
Ayotte, who is up for reelection, has taken criticism from some Democrats, including her challenger,  Cinde Warmington, for not acting sooner. 
In an Oct. 22 debate co-hosted by New Hampshire Public Radio, Manchester Ink Link, and the Granite State News Collaborative, Warmington said Ayotte had previously acted favorably to developers by signing a bill allowing off-grid power generation in the state.
“Be clear about what her position is; it has only changed now because it’s politically convenient,” Warmington said.
Ayotte said that was “absolutely false,” adding that New Hampshire could not sustain a data center. She cited concerns over “energy costs, also the water costs, the environmental costs” of data centers. 
“I oppose data centers… and I will work to get this moratorium done,” she said.
Proposals from the Legislature
Sen. Daniel Innis, a Bradford Republican, is another member of New Hampshire’s majority party calling for a pause on data centers ahead of the 2027 session.
From left: Sens. Donovan Fenton, Dan Innis, Denise Ricciardi, and Keith Murphy debate cryptocurrency legislation on Oct. 30, 2025. Innis, who is running for reelection, has filed a proposal for a statewide moratorium on data center construction for the Legislature to consider during the 2027 session. (File photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)
 
He is running for reelection against Rebecca Harned, a Democrat, who has previously called for regulation of artificial intelligence and data centers; in a September op-ed in the Concord Monitor, Harned called for a “temporary moratorium” on large-scale data centers.
Innis is behind one of two early-phase proposals for a data center moratorium filed so far this fall. In an interview, he acknowledged a shift within his party toward data center skepticism.
“As we’ve learned more, you know, we’ve taken a different position,” he said.
The other early-filed moratorium proposal comes from Rep. Thomas Cormen, a Lebanon Democrat, who is running unopposed for reelection.
Only the titles of the proposals are currently published, but in interviews, Cormen and Innis outlined different visions for the length and details of a potential pause. Both said Ayotte’s request for a moratorium had motivated their proposals.
Innis said he envisions a pause that would expire at the end of 2027. As legislation cannot be acted upon until the upcoming session, this would see the moratorium lasting less than one year. But that would be long enough, Innis said, to allow legislators to map out a way to ensure data centers do not contribute to rising electric rates or environmental disruptions like noise pollution.
Cormen said a draft version of his proposed moratorium would last through the end of 2028, and apply to any data center using 20 megawatts or more of electricity at its peak.
“I think it’s going to take a while to get the guardrails through and get them right,” he said in an interview. 
Other protective measures
As for what those guardrails must look like, proposals are forthcoming, Cormen said, including in another proposal he has filed early to regulate facilities — like data centers — that use large amounts of energy.
Both Cormen and Innis identified finding ways to prevent the cost of delivering large amounts of power to data centers being shifted onto ratepayers as a priority. Cormen envisions protections applying to facilities with peak loads of 30 megawatts — a threshold he chose in an attempt to exclude New Hampshire’s existing large-power-use customers, like universities and hospitals. 
Rep. Thomas Cormen, a Lebanon Democrat, and Rep. Kat McGhee, a Hollis Democrat, prepare to deliver testimony before the New Hampshire House of Representatives in March 2026. Cormen, who is running for reelection, said he hoped to introduce multiple AI- and data-center-focused guardrails in the 2027 session if reelected. He has filed preliminary requests for bills including a moratorium on data center construction and clean energy requirements for facilities using large amounts of power. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Cormen’s draft proposal would require large power users to use entirely “clean” sources if they are generating power on-site to fire their servers, he said, meaning they may not use any greenhouse gas-emitting source of energy. The bill would also seek to require the Public Utilities Commission or utilities to give projects using clean power preference in the queue for interconnecting to the grid, he said. 
Data center developers are increasingly turning to diesel fuel as a power source, including at a site in Lowell, where neighbors have raised air quality concerns as they attempt to stop the development from expanding further.
Cormen said the draft also sought to encourage large power users to reduce demand during peak periods, when electricity is most expensive.
Rep. Laurel Stavis, a Lebanon Democrat who is also running unopposed for reelection, said she was motivated by the failure of proposed AI regulations last session to reintroduce multiple measures this fall, including through her work on an AI working group within the House Democratic caucus. 
One proposal Stavis has filed early would define different scales of data centers in New Hampshire’s statutes, which she said would allow communities to regulate data centers differently depending on their size. 
Data centers exist in a range of sizes, from server clusters found in office buildings to vast complexes used to train artificial intelligence. 
Within Stavis’ proposal is the requirement that any action to repurpose a building for use as a large-load data center — which she defines as a facility with a peak load of 50 megawatts, about the amount of energy used to power about 25,000 homes — would trigger review by the local zoning board. Stavis also intends, she added, to propose a prohibition on the use of non-disclosure agreements between developers and municipal officials during the proposal and permitting process.
These ideas are only the earliest of those filed by lawmakers this session, Stavis said. She and Cormen said they were confident the state will see numerous other proposed regulations in the coming session.
In addition to trepidation, in interviews, Stavis, Cormen, and Innis expressed a mix of cautious optimism about the future of artificial intelligence and data centers in New Hampshire.
Innis said he believes New Hampshire could benefit from the facilities if the right protections are adopted for ratepayers and the environment.
“We’ve got to work with these companies, and we’ve got to work among ourselves and figure out how it is that we want it done in New Hampshire,” Innis said. “I think once we do that, we’ll be able to green-light some of these things.”
Stavis said the developments could become smaller and less obtrusive, while Cormen, a retired computer science professor, said he hoped the technology would lead to new frontiers. 
“I’m worried about AI … I am very concerned about the misuse of it, and it getting out of control,” he said. “But I also see that it’s going to open up many possibilities for many people, and I also believe that it’s going to create industries and careers that we have no idea, right now, what they are.”
But for now, the legislators agreed that a moratorium was warranted and expressed confidence that one would pass through the Legislature in 2027.
While Innis says he believes the tide of public opinion will change, at present, it is clear that public opinion is strongly against the developments and the technology they power, he said. 
“It’s almost universal,” he said.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Community solar bills languish as Michigan debates energy affordability
text:
Rooftop solar panels on the Bryant Community Center in Ann Arbor on Oct. 20, 2026. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)Since 2021, Michigan lawmakers have drafted six community solar bills in the House and Senate under both Republican and Democratic leadership, but no bill has been passed into law. Two separate House bills and two tie-barred Senate bills are currently languishing in committee with no hearings scheduled. 
Polling shows strong support for community solar among Democrats, Republicans and independents alike. Yet despite that bipartisan appeal, Michigan lawmakers have struggled to advance legislation that supporters say could improve energy affordability and reliability in a state facing high energy rates and persistent power outages.
Community solar allows municipalities to develop small-scale solar projects that supply electricity to subscribers who cannot install their own panels because they rent, cannot afford the upfront costs or have unsuitable roofs. Subscribers receive credits on their utility bills for the energy generated, and some programs offer battery backup during grid outages. 
Senate Bills 518 and 519 were introduced by state Sens. Jeff Irwin (D-Ann Arbor) and Ed McBroom (R-Waucedah) in 2025, with seven Democratic and two Republican co-sponsors. It was the second set of bills introduced by the senators since 2023. 
The legislation would require 60% of capacity to come from projects smaller than 40 kilowatts, and no project larger than 5 megawatts of solar. The bills contain broad language about energy affordability for ratepayers and labor equity for solar project workers.  SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
State Rep. Greg Markkanen (R-Hancock) introduced HB 4590 in June 2025 with 22 Republican co-sponsors. The bill directs the MPSC to establish rules and credits for community solar projects, including for low-income participants. 
House Bill 6041 was introduced this year by state Rep. Donavan McKinney (D-Detroit) and co-sponsored by 27 Democrats. The bill contains more specifics about environmental justice and prevailing wage protections, including a 40% set-aside for low-income households. Subscriptions must provide at least a 10% utility bill savings for standard residential subscribers and at least a 20% savings for low-income households.  
Neither the House nor Senate community solar proposals would override local zoning rules. 
McKinney represents Michigan’s 11th district, which includes northeast Detroit. In a phone interview with Michigan Advance, McKinney said he has personally experienced fifty power outages since 2022. 
“This community solar legislation provides opportunities for everyone, in particular to target underserved populations and over burdened populations when it comes to energy shutoffs and power outages. It provides more opportunities for people to produce their own energy in a clean, responsible way, and get some tax credits for it,” McKinney said. 
Michigan remains one of roughly two dozen states without a community solar program. 
A 2023 statewide poll of registered Michigan voters commissioned by Data for Progress found that 73% of respondents supported increasing the share of electricity produced from renewable energy sources. Rather than political ideology, the differences between lawmakers appear to center on who pays for the community solar assets, and concerns that these costs could be shifted onto nonparticipating customers. 
Michigan State Rep. Donavan McKinney (D-Detroit) speaks at a news conference detailing a Democrat-led effort to create a utility ratepayer’s bill of rights on Sept. 9, 2025. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
Bipartisan bills face utility opposition
DTE and Consumers Energy contend that community solar programs would force nonparticipating ratepayers to bear the costs of community solar assets, although they declined to provide details on how this would be the case. 
In a statement to Michigan Advance, DTE spokesperson Ryan Lowry points to the utility’s own solar program MIGreenPower, which allows customers to support solar and wind energy “without having to spend tens of thousands of dollars on solar panels for their homes and businesses.” 
Subscribers of the MIGreenPower program can pay as little as $1 to access 21% clean energy. To achieve 100% clean energy, the average household would pay $155.52 annually. 
“It is important community solar proposals do not have the opposite effect of its intended purposes – raising costs for all customers,” says Lowry.
Katie Carey, director of media relations for Consumers Energy, echoed DTE’s concerns in a statement to the Advance. 
 “We support community solar policies that benefit customers, but we cannot support legislation that shifts costs onto customers who do not participate, particularly those who can least afford higher bills. Our existing community solar programs are designed so participating customers pay the full costs of the program.”
Consumers Energy has two community solar programs. Based on its published 2024 solar credits, the average household would pay approximately $578 annually to subscribe to enough Solar Gardens Community Solar Program capacity to match its electricity consumption.  
While subscribers of the utility-run programs do bear the full cost of the programs, they do not benefit from the lower cost of renewable energy. According to Lazard Inc.’s 2025 report, Levelized Cost of Energy+, unsubsidized utility-scale solar and onshore wind have been the lowest-cost sources of new electricity generation in the United States for a decade. 
Supporters of community solar claim that energy generated in small solar fields close to end users is less expensive than utility-scale solar because it does not rely on expensive grid infrastructure for delivery.
Dr. Laura Sherman, president of the Michigan Energy Innovation Business Council, believes that utility bias toward owning energy infrastructure is baked in. “Investor-owned utilities in Michigan earn ~10% return on equity for their capital investments, so they have a strong bias to own as much infrastructure as possible.”
Home in Ann Arbor’s Bryant neighborhood with rooftop solar panels on Oct. 20, 2026. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)
Who pays for community solar?
Rep. McKinney believes that HB 6041 can’t get a hearing because elected officials take campaign contributions from utilities.
“I have to say, a lot of people’s decisions come down to who’s giving the money. It’s politics, and that’s why the utilities hate our legislation. That’s why they blocked it from a hearing,” he said. 
State Rep. Pauline Wendzel (R-Watervliet) chairs the House Energy Committee. In an email to the Advance, she denied that utilities had lobbied her to hold the bill. “I haven’t taken up the bill because I oppose the policy,” she writes.
Wendzel’s concerns about HB 6041 focus on who covers the costs of maintaining the electrical grid. If community solar customers are paid credits that are greater than the cost of generating the power, then the costs of maintaining the grid would be passed on to customers that do not participate in the program. Wendzel says that would be unfair because community solar subscribers also utilize the grid to deliver power.
HB 6041 proposes minimum savings for subscribers, including greater savings for low-income participants. Wendzel argues that requiring those discounts doesn’t establish whether the underlying solar generation is economical or who absorbs any shortfall. 
“Whatever the credit pays beyond what a facility saves the system has to be recovered somewhere. The bill doesn’t say who pays it, and it bars charging subscribers in a way that cuts into their savings. That leaves general rates, which every customer pays,” Wendzel said.
McKinney responds that the MPSC is responsible for ensuring that costs of the law would not be shifted onto nonparticipating ratepayers, and he plans to work with the commission to ensure the law is applied equitably. 
States offer different approaches to cost shifting
Community solar programs in other states demonstrate that cost shifting is a risk but is not inevitable, and depends on program design and on how the full value of electricity and grid benefits is calculated. 
A study commissioned by the state of Massachusetts found that its distributed solar incentive program, which includes community solar, delivered $1.49 in direct ratepayer benefits for every dollar spent, including savings for nonparticipating households, while Minnesota found that credits in its original community solar program exceeded the value of the electricity generated and redesigned the program to address cost shifting.
In 2020, the City of Ann Arbor adopted A2Zero, a $1 billion plan to achieve community-wide carbon neutrality by 2030. To help reach its goal, Ann Arbor voters authorized the creation of the Sustainable Energy Utility, also known as A2SEU, in 2024, the nation’s first renewable, supplemental energy utility. 
Rather than support the creation of off-site community solar facilities, the program finances, owns, installs, and maintains custom-built solar and battery systems at customers’ own homes and businesses. Customers remain connected to the DTE grid for any power needs that exceed the A2SEU system. 
Missy Stults is the director of Ann Arbor’s Office of Sustainability Innovations, which led the creation of A2SEU. She would like it to serve as a model for other cities that do not have state laws that support community solar.  
“I don’t want to just solve this for Ann Arbor,” she said. “Climate change does not care if Ann Arbor solves this problem and we do it in a way that’s not replicable or transferable to anyone else.”
Passing community solar legislation in Michigan will depend on whether lawmakers can agree on a bill credit formula that saves subscribers money without shifting the burdens of maintaining the electrical grid onto ratepayers who do not participate. 
According to Sherman, customers will continue to pay a premium for renewable energy if utilities own the assets. 
“Utility-owned resources are often more expensive and slower to construct than third-party-owned resources,” she explains. “Allowing for third-party owned community solar with a guaranteed bill savings would correct that problem by removing utility profits and high costs from the equation.”

name: National
title: 900+ women criminally charged for their conduct during pregnancies
text:
In the first three years after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the constitutional right to an abortion in June 2022, more than 900 women faced criminal charges for conduct related to their pregnancies, according to a new report. (Photo by Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder)In the first three years after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the constitutional right to an abortion in June 2022, more than 900 women faced criminal charges for conduct related to their pregnancies, according to a new report.
Most state laws that prohibit or regulate abortion seek to penalize those who provide abortions, not the women who undergo them. Nevertheless, researchers from Pregnancy Justice, a nonprofit group that supports abortion rights, found 13 specific allegations related to obtaining, seeking to obtain, or researching how to get an abortion. The group would not provide additional details on those cases, saying it is still collecting data and hopes to publish a full analysis in 2028.
The vast majority of the charges — 876 of 955 — were for child abuse, neglect or endangerment, most related to substance use during pregnancy. Researchers found 871 separate allegations of substance use and 77 allegations that a woman had failed to obtain prenatal care.
The most prominent anti-abortion groups have long argued against prosecuting women for having abortions, a punishment that remains broadly unpopular. But the new report comes as a growing number of state legislators are pushing to enact such penalties: In the past two years, lawmakers have introduced bills in about a dozen states, and supporters expect that number to grow next year.
Members of the so-called abortion abolition movement believe that embryos and fetuses should have the same legal protections as people, and that women who have abortions should be criminally prosecuted to the furthest extent of the law — up to and including the death penalty.
“It sure sucks that someone who’s had a miscarriage has to be investigated, but that’s not the fault of the abolitionist legislation,” said T. Russell Hunter, founder of Oklahoma-based Abolitionists Rising. “That’s the fault of the people who would willfully break the law to abort babies. They would be the ones causing that situation.”
Hunter credits groups like his with pushing anti-abortion bills to be “a little more radical.”
Some prominent anti-abortion leaders are concerned that groups like Abolitionists Rising are gaining ground.
“It’s impossible to prosecute those abortions without enacting a police state,” said Eric Scheidler, president of the Pro-Life Action League. Scheidler and two prominent anti-abortion attorneys penned articles arguing against such prosecutions in the summer issue of Human Life Review.
“Every miscarriage would have to be investigated in order to treat these embryonic and fetal dead bodies the same way that we would treat a dead body at a hospital or in an old folks home or out in the street where a crime took place,” he said.
Most cases in three states
The Pregnancy Justice report found that 902 women faced a total of 955 charges in 23 states, but the vast majority of cases were in South Carolina (381), Oklahoma (222) and Alabama (204).
Those three states are among the 13 that have enacted near-total abortion bans since the high court dismantled the federal right to an abortion in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization.
And in all three states, courts have supported the concept of fetal personhood, or the idea that a fetus, embryo or fertilized egg has the same legal rights as a person who has been born.


South Carolina, which bans abortion after six weeks, explicitly prohibits prosecuting women for seeking or getting abortions. But lawmakers in South Carolina and at least eight other states (Georgia, Idaho, Indiana, Kentucky, Missouri, North Dakota, Oklahoma and Texas) have introduced bills in recent years that would classify abortion as homicide, making violators in those states (except for North Dakota) eligible for the death penalty.
In South Carolina this year, a Senate committee approved a bill that included a penalty of up to two years in prison for a woman convicted of inducing her own abortion, but the legislation did not advance further.
South Carolina lobbyist Hayden Laye of Pro-Life Greenville said his group opposes penalizing women for abortion. But his group ended up backing the bill when the punishment was reduced to a misdemeanor and it appeared likely that the state Senate would remove the provision.
2 states, 2 abortion ballot measures, and the effort to win over Gen Z voters

Laye said he expects the legislation to be reintroduced next year. He noted that the abolitionist groups have lobbied against anti-abortion legislation that does not penalize the pregnant person.
“The abolitionist groups put up just as much opposition to these bills as groups like Planned Parenthood and the ACLU does,” Laye said. “We are really having to fight both sides of this — the side that wants no abortion laws, and the side that wants all or nothing, which isn’t happening. It’s not happening here in South Carolina. It’s not happening anywhere.”
Since 2022, several states including California, Colorado, Minnesota and New Jersey have enacted laws protecting women from criminal or civil penalties for their conduct during a pregnancy or while receiving reproductive healthcare.
The only state where a woman can be charged for inducing her own abortion is Nevada, which enacted its law in 1911. A Winnemucca woman who miscarried in 2018 and was charged under the law pleaded guilty to manslaughter in 2019, but her conviction was vacated in 2021 for ineffective assistance of counsel. Earlier this month, Humboldt County, Nevada, paid $1.6 million to settle her claim that it violated her state and federal constitutional rights.
Next month, voters in Nevada will consider codifying abortion rights in their state constitution after voters initially approved the amendment in 2024.
Dissuaded from seeking care
Madalyn Wasilczuk, a law professor at the University of South Carolina and one of the authors of the ongoing Pregnancy Justice study, said the Dobbs decision “really has affected how willing law enforcement and prosecutors are to treat miscarriages and stillbirths and other newborn deaths immediately after delivery as culpable acts and as crimes rather than as medical tragedies.”
Wasilczuk said that even the fear of criminal charges can dissuade pregnant women from seeking care, especially if they are substance users.
“Seeking care becomes a place where they expect to be criminalized, and so people avoid healthcare, which really underscores why it’s so dangerous to treat the criminal legal system as if it can solve a public health problem,” she said. “These instances are times when women need healthcare, not handcuffs.”
Republican AGs sue abortion ‘shield law’ states in US Supreme Court

Jennifer Girdish, communications director for If/When/How, an abortion rights organization, said women who live in states with abortion bans often call the group’s helpline because they are scared to go to the emergency room after they have a miscarriage or experience complications after taking abortion pills.
“You shouldn’t need a lawyer to stop the police from investigating you after pregnancy loss,” Girdish said. “You shouldn’t need a lawyer to convince the doctor that you need emergency abortion care. But more and more you do.”
In addition to South Carolina, Oklahoma and Alabama, the Pregnancy Justice report found that prosecutors also initiated pregnancy-related cases in Arizona, Arkansas, California, Florida, Idaho, Kentucky, Michigan, Missouri, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Mexico, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, South Dakota, Texas, Utah, Washington, Wisconsin, and Wyoming.
Stateline reporter Sofia Resnick can be reached at sresnick@stateline.org.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Republican cash advantage showing up with late spending in Indiana legislative races
text:
Indiana House Speaker Todd Huston, left, watches as Rep. Chris Jeter, R-Fishers, speaks during a January 2025 news conference in the House chamber. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Republicans are making big money drops in a handful of Indiana legislative races as they aim to secure their full General Assembly supermajority for an eighth straight election.
The October spending surge that is approaching $2 million ahead of the Nov. 3 Election Day is centered on a cluster of House and Senate districts across the northern suburbs of Indianapolis, while also reaching into northwest Indiana and a perpetually close Bloomington-area House race.
Republicans are following the playbook they’ve used in recent election cycles of tapping their sizable fundraising advantage to pour money into hotly contested races during the final weeks.
The GOP enters this year’s elections with a 70-30 House margin, with Democrats needing to gain at least four seats to break the two-thirds supermajority Republicans have held since the 2012 election that allows them to take action even without any Democrats present.
“We really feel good about our team and the members and want to support them and are doing everything we can to support them,” Republican House Speaker Todd Huston told the Capital Chronicle. “We’re giving them the resources that they need to get their message to the voters in their district.” 
Cash infusions for Republican incumbents
Terri Austin, a former longtime Democratic state legislator from Anderson, sees the late flood of Republican money differently.
“They don’t spend money unless they think they’re in trouble,” Austin said.
October funding infusions from state Republican committees reported to the Indiana Election Division as of Monday include boosts for:

Rep. Chris Jeter of Fishers, with about $250,000 in his bid for a fourth term against Democrat Stephanie Jo Yocum, whom Jeter defeated with 58% of the vote two years ago.
Rep. Danny Lopez of Carmel, receiving more than $220,000 as he seeks a second term against Democrat Lindsay Gramlich.
Rep. Dave Hall of Norman, getting about $220,000 in his run for a third term from a Bloomington-area district against Democrat Amy Huffman Oliver.
Rep. Becky Cash of Zionsville, with about $140,000 in her race for a third term against Democrat Tiffany Stoner.

Republicans have parlayed their supermajority status into big fundraising hauls. For this fall’s elections, for example, the House Republican campaign arm reported raising about $6.5 million as of early October, while the House Democrats raised about $2.5 million.
The Democratic candidates in those House races had largely similar fundraising to the Republican incumbents before the latest money moves began.
Could data center opposition boost Democrats in Indiana House races?

Democrats have responded from their smaller state bank accounts, giving about $180,000 to Gramlich for her race against Lopez; about $130,000 to Yocum’s challenge to Jeter, and a $45,000 boost to Stoner in her bid against Cash.
Democrats have also invested in a couple other suburban Indianapolis House races, sending about $225,000 to Racheal Bleicher’s campaign against Republican Rep. Hunter Smith of Zionsville — and $75,000 to Lauren Cole for her challenge to Huston in his district that runs from Fishers into rural northern Hamilton County.
Huston was unopposed in his 2022 and 2024 reelection runs but said he knew the national mood of voters could turn against Republicans. Both Huston and Cole have been running TV ads in recent days, with Cole’s commercials targeting Huston for his support of data center tax breaks and increases to the state’s gasoline tax.
“I’ve been knocking doors since July, recognizing that this year could be challenging,” Huston said. “This is the type of year you just don’t take anything for granted and you go out there and you work really hard.”
Austin is the Democratic chair in the 5th Congressional District, which includes much of the contested suburban Indianapolis area.
Democrats have targeted those legislative districts for the last three or four election cycles, only to have Republicans largely hold onto the seats.
Austin said she believed voters “not only are frustrated by the national economy, but they’re very unhappy with the direction of the state.”
“After 20 years of Republican rule, there’s only one place to look if you want to make some change,” she said.
“Working hard” to keep Republican supermajority
Republicans hold an even stronger advantage in the state Senate, with a current 40-10 margin for the supermajority they’ve had in that chamber since the 2010 election.
Senate Republicans are looking to hold — or even build — that majority with their October spending moves.
So far this month, state reports of spending by Republican committees show:

Republican candidate Trevor De Vries receiving $450,000 in bid to hold an open Lake County seat for the GOP against Democrat Scott Houldieson.
Republican Nate Uldricks getting $315,000 for his run against Democratic Sen. Rodney Pol of Chesterton.
Republican John Ruckelshaus being boosted by $215,000 in his bid to flip an open district in suburban Indianapolis against Democrat Kristina Moorhead.
Republican Juanita Albright getting $110,000 as she seeks to hold another suburban Indianapolis district for the GOP against Democrat Kerry Forestal, the Marion County sheriff.

Senate Democrats, meanwhile, have only responded with $25,000 to Pol — whose $210,000 in fundraising by early October was more than three times the $65,000 Uldricks had raised.
State Senate control likely safe for Republicans but Democrats aim to make gains

Democrats argue that breaking the supermajority would give them additional influence over legislation.
A recent Republican-paid mailer in the Lopez-Gramlich race in Hamilton County highlights the 2011 boycott by House Democrats against right-to-work legislation that lasted for 36 days.
The mailer argues that Democrats want the power to “not show up for work to stop legislation they don’t like.”
Huston, the House speaker, said Republicans “are doing everything we can” to hold the supermajority.
“I have no idea what, if any, impact it would be if it wasn’t the case,” he said. “Certainly, we want it to be the case and are working hard to keep it.”
