name: Michigan Advance
title: Incumbency gives Democrats an edge in Michigan Supreme Court races
text:
Michigan Supreme Court / Hall of Justice | Photo by Jon KingOn Nov. 3, Michigan voters will elect two justices to the Michigan Supreme Court. Though those races are listed as nonpartisan on the ballot, all six candidates on the ballot were nominated by political parties. 
Michigan Supreme Court Chief Justice Megan Cavanagh and Justice Noah Hood, both nominated by the Democratic Party, are up for reelection. They face four challengers: Republicans Casandra Morse-Bills and Michael Warren, and U.S. Taxpayers Party nominees Thomas Howe and Jody White. 
Because the elections are nonpartisan, explained Mitchel Sollenberger, a professor of political science at the University of Michigan-Dearborn, candidates tend to be less well-known or advertised to the public. Sollenberger noted, however, that in recent election cycles, both the Democratic and Republican parties have done a much more effective job of sending out mailers and putting out ads for their nominated candidates. 
But though both parties have worked to inform voters which candidates on the ballot belong to their party, Sollenberger explained that, across states with judicial elections like Michigan’s, incumbents tend to have a significant advantage.
“Typically what you see is the voter, if they don’t know if it’s a Republican or Democrat, the voter is picking the incumbent,” he said. “You typically see the candidate being retained. You don’t see the challenger winning.”
Currently, Democratic justices hold a 6-1 majority on the state’s highest court. Justice Brian Zahra is the court’s only Republican and with a decisive liberal majority, he is often the sole dissenter on important court decisions. 
Even if both Democratic incumbents lose in November, Democrats would retain a majority on the court, but with a narrower margin. In a 4-3 court, a single justice’s vote could determine the outcome of a decision. 
Sollenberger highlighted a number of such decisions in recent years, in which having a slimmer majority might have flipped the decision entirely.
That includes Attorney General v. Eli Lilly and Company, which defined the application of the Michigan Consumer Protection Act, as well as People v. Parks, which considered the “cruel and unusual punishment” statute in the state constitution in relation to life sentences without parole for young adults. 
All six candidates recently participated on a virtual candidate forum hosted by the League of Women Voters of Michigan.


Cavanagh, a graduate of Wayne State University Law School, has served as chief justice since early 2025 and has been a justice since 2019.
Hood is the newest justice on the Supreme Court, having been appointed by Gov. Gretchen Whitmer in 2025 after then-Chief Justice Elizabeth Clement, a Republican, left the court. He is the only current justice on the court who has not yet been elected or reelected following an appointment to the court. 
Prior to joining the Supreme Court, Hood — a graduate of Harvard Law School — served as a judge of the Michigan Court of Appeals for three years, and before that was a circuit court judge on the Third Judicial Circuit of Michigan. 
Both Republican nominees, Morse-Bills and Warren, are circuit court judges.
Warren has been a judge in Michigan’s Sixth Judicial Circuit Court in Oakland County since 2002. He is a graduate of the University of Michigan Law School and served on the state Board of Education prior to his time as a judge.
Morse-Bills, a graduate of Cooley Law School, is currently the presiding judge in Michigan’s 23rd Judicial Circuit Court, which covers Alcona, Arenac, Iosco and Oscoda counties in rural northern Michigan. She was elected to that court in 2018 and reelected in 2024.
Howe and White, the nominees from the U.S. Taxpayers Party, have a unique obstacle — they would not be eligible to serve as Supreme Court justices under Michigan law if elected in November, as neither is licensed to practice law in Michigan. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Under Michigan state law, any justice or judge in a state court “must be persons who are licensed to practice law in this state,” and “To be qualified to serve as a judge of a trial court, a judge of the court of appeals, or a justice of the supreme court, a person shall have been admitted to the practice of law for at least 5 years.”
That requirement does not prevent them from campaigning or from their names appearing on the ballot, but would prevent them from assuming the office.
Sollenberger noted that, especially in a race where candidates are not labeled by party affiliation — and where the ballot will not note that these candidates are ineligible to hold the office for which they are listed — it is likely that some voters will cast their ballots in support of Howe or White without knowing this. 
That means that those candidates would split the non-incumbent vote with the Republican candidates, making it an even further uphill climb to unseat the Democrats in a race that already heavily favors incumbents.
Sollenberger also noted the important context of the gubernatorial race in the balance of the state Supreme Court — in the event of any vacancy, the governor is able to appoint a replacement in a process that generally moves quickly. When Hood was appointed, for example, he assumed office on May 27, 2025, just over a month after Clement officially resigned from the court.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Georgia Republicans are trying to court Latino voters. National politics are complicating things.
text:
Dalton resident Roberto Paramo holds a campaign pamphlet in Spanish given to him by a Democratic canvasser. Ignacio Perez/Georgia RecorderDALTON, Ga. – Mary Dennard canvassed alone through one of Dalton’s neighborhoods on the eve of Hurricane Isaias. The other canvassers, who speak Spanish, canceled due to the weather. Her blue shirt peeked out from under her windbreaker, reading “Somos vecinos, we are neighbors,” and Dennard carried Spanish language pamphlets to leave with Latino voters or at unanswered doors.
Nearly a quarter of registered voters in Dalton’s Whitfield County are Latino, according to data from the secretary of state office. And the northwest Georgia county had the seventh most Latino voters in the state as of 2024, according to a report from GALEO, a nonprofit working to increase civic engagement among Hispanics in Georgia.
Today, Republicans and Democrats are making a play for Latino support in the midsize city of Dalton. Grassroots engagement and targeted campaigning are part of an effort on both sides of the aisle to boost Latino turnout and win Hispanic votes ahead of the midterms.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In a battleground state with tightening margins, Georgia’s Latino voters have the potential to affect the outcome of the governor’s race in November. With polls showing the two candidates, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Rick Jackson, within striking distance of each other, a two or three percentage point swing in either direction could make all the difference. 
About 5% of Georgia’s more than 8 million registered voters are Latino, according to the most recent data from the Georgia Secretary of State’s office. Over the past decade the number of active Hispanic voters has grown by 210%, or 267,614. 
Healthcare businessman Rick Jackson, the Republican candidate for governor, speaks at a press conference in Marietta on Sept. 16, 2026. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
Jackson and Bottoms have made attempts to reach this growing voter bloc in Whitfield County and across the state alongside efforts from local political parties. 
In August, Jackson hosted an event in Dalton at a restaurant owned by former Latino city council member Nicky Lama before a rally in town. Earlier that month he attended Cumming’s yearly Latin festival. 
“He understands that American dream, the reason that a lot of Latinos come here, and he will protect that American dream. And so that’s a message that is resonating a lot with the Hispanic voters we’ve been talking to,” Stefanie Zaenker, advisor to the Libre PAC, a conservative-leaning Latino group that endorsed Jackson. 
That same week, Bottoms arrived in Dalton with a slew of other candidates running on the Democratic ticket. In a speech she spoke about making Georgia a welcoming state for immigrants and said that, as governor, she would be a check on federal immigration enforcement activity. Bottoms later spoke directly to Hispanic voters in an interview with Univision Atlanta, stressing her plans to address affordability.
Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms speaks to reporters at an early childhood education event in Atlanta Sept. 29. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder.
“The Latino community is one of the fastest-growing communities in the state of Georgia. So we can’t think about Georgia without thinking about our Latino community,” Bottoms said. “All of our communities should feel that they have a buy-in and feel that the American dream is within reach for their families as well.”
Bottoms held a campaign event Thursday in Atlanta with Latino leaders, reiterating her commitment to push back on the Trump administration’s immigration policies. 
What impact will Trump’s immigration policies have on the midterms? 
At the local level, county political parties table at Latino community events, host panels, sponsor a local soccer team and send out bilingual canvassers, placing Hispanics in the middle of a tug-of-war of talking points and cultural appeals. 
But while Republican President Donald Trump made gains with Latino voters in 2024, there are signs that this support could be unraveled as his administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement. In Georgia, immigration enforcement agents have arrested thousands of people. 
A Republican state lawmaker who represents Dalton, Kasey Carpenter, said he fears the increased immigration enforcement could turn away formerly Republican-voting Hispanics in the area. Carpenter’s state House district has the most registered Latino voters of any state house district.
Republican state Rep. Kasey Carpenter (center) at a Georgia Chamber event in Athens on Aug. 5, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
“I always tell people, even though they are checking nine out of 10 boxes with our party, that one box, if you take somebody’s aunt or uncle or cousin or grandmother and haul them off to a country they haven’t seen in 25 years, it’s hard pressed to worry about kitchen table issues and private property rights and all the things Republicans hold near and dear,” Carpenter said in an interview. 
The state Republican party, Carpenter said, should decouple itself from Washington and the increase in federal immigration enforcement and instead stress their accomplishments in the state. Otherwise, he said the gap between Democratic and Republican support among Latinos stands to widen.
One of Dalton’s voters who supported Democrats in 2024 is Bryan Aguilar. The politically active 26-year-old said his biggest concern lies with the country’s immigration system. The state needs to stop local law enforcement cooperation with federal immigration officials, Aguilar said. At the federal level, Aguilar would like to see lawmakers streamline new pathways to citizenship. 
Aguilar said he believes candidates who don’t try to understand Latinos make blanket statements about immigrants to justify their views.
“It’s coming from a place without facts to back up their claims,” Aguilar said. “It’s rather incendiary language about immigration they use.”
Representatives of both major parties are attempting to win over Latinos, often through proposals to curb the cost of living and even cultural appeals.
“I don’t know why any Spanish person or any Hispanic person would ever be a Democrat because their policies do not align with most Hispanic’s morals that they have and their religious beliefs,” Jackie Harling, chair of Northwest Georgia’s 14th Congressional District GOP, said after a panel discussion in Dalton in August that was hosted in part by the Libre Initiative.
Dennard, vice chair of the Whitfield County Democrats and canvas organizer, strongly disagrees.
“What this administration is doing to the community of Latinos and people of color is just reprehensible in my opinion. I think that’s going to help the Democrats and hurt the Republicans in the election,” she said in an interview.
Energizing a growing minority 
Georgia’s Hispanic population may be growing, but that doesn’t translate into greater political influence automatically.  
A little more than half of registered Latinos turned out to vote in Georgia in 2024 and 2020 according to GALEO’s voter report. According to data from the Georgia Secretary of State’s office, 72.9% of all registered voters participated in the 2024 election. 
“In local elections here, few Hispanics vote despite Dalton’s population being majority Latino,” Rod Miller, first vice chairman of the Whitfield County Republican Party who has led the local party’s attempts to reach Latino voters, said by phone. 
Latinos’ lower turnout rate can have several causes. Those who didn’t grow up in the U.S. may be unfamiliar with the voting process. Because most counties in Georgia do not have election materials in Spanish, others might not feel confident enough in their English to go to the polls. Finally, Hispanics as a whole are generally younger than non-Hispanics, says  Charles Bullock, a political science professor at the University of Georgia. 
“We know the older you are the more likely you are to vote. That low turnout is endemic among young voters whatever their ethnicity or background,” Bullock said. “Voting is habit forming. If you start voting, vote consistently, then you’re probably doing it the rest of your life.”
At the city and county level, a lack of Hispanic representation among elected officials doesn’t help either. Despite the fact that more than half of the population in Dalton is Hispanic, currently no one in office is Latino, a statistic local groups want to change. 
“We are hoping to develop Hispanic Republican candidates who will energize their community to greater levels of participation,” Miller said.
America Gruner, president of the Coalition of Latino Leaders in Dalton, a nonpartisan civic organization, said the outreach to Hispanic voters needs to extend beyond election season. Her group, for example, works year round to increase civic participation through information sessions, candidate forums, canvassing and vote together walks, Gruner said. 
Gruner said when she speaks with Hispanics in the area, many don’t know what offices are up for election or the names of candidates. Candidates only seek out Latino residents when there are elections, she said, and they want their vote. 
“They aren’t going to motivate me to get out to vote because there isn’t anything I can relate to, right?” Gruner said, “They should get to know our needs and at least include something that says, ‘yes they listen to us, yes they know us, yes this is a thing I’m interested in fighting for.’”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio’s Kroger gets $3 million ‘MAHA’ grant. Critics call it taxpayer-funded marketing.
text:
A Kroger store in Columbus, Ohio. (Photo by Marty Schladen/Ohio Capital Journal)Cincinnati, Ohio-based Kroger has received a $3 million Make America Healthy Again federal grant. Critics say it appears to be a taxpayer gift to market the company and do more customer surveillance.
The award was made by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services on Sept. 30. 
The program is explicitly intended to create a “statistically significant sales lift” in Kroger stores as the company buys out its competitors. 
Progress toward those goals will be monitored by Kroger’s data-gathering subsidiary, 84.51°. That operation is already generating more than a third of corporate profits by surveilling customers and selling their information to other businesses.
The award to Kroger is part of the Make America Healthy Healthy Again program spearheaded by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a lawyer and vaccine skeptic — not a health professional. 
Kennedy’s MAHA program says it will “build a healthier, stronger America.”
Kroger and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services didn’t respond to questions for this story. 
The taxpayer grant to Kroger is part of MAHA’s Eat Real Food campaign.
By encouraging consumption of whole foods such as fruits and vegetables, it purports to address what is a real health crisis in the United States. 
The Stanford University School of Medicine reports that 60% of calories consumed by U.S. adults and 70% of those eaten by children are ultraprocessed, or non-whole foods.
Nutritionists and doctors report that high intake of ultraprocessed foods is associated with a 32% higher risk of obesity, a 37% higher risk of type 2 diabetes, a 32% higher risk of hypertension, and a 23% higher risk of pulmonary heart disease.
The produce section at an Ohio Kroger store. (Photo by Marty Schladen/Ohio Capital Journal)
Kennedy’s MAHA movement has its critics. The independent, nonprofit Center for Science in the Public Interest said MAHA’s initial assessment of public health “selectively picks from the scientific literature to support Kennedy’s predetermined biases in favor of specific diets and products such as animal fats, and against vaccines and exposure to electromagnetic radiation — anti-scientific beliefs that Kennedy has raged about for years.”
When it spotted the Kroger grant, the nonpartisan Center for Responsible Food Business saw what it thought was another problem — that the taxpayer grant seemed aimed at as much increasing the grocery giant’s sales as at promoting healthy eating. It also appeared to feed Kroger’s lucrative data-gathering operation.
“Kroger will not only have more of its sales boosted, it will be getting more of that customer data funneled through 84.51°,” Taylor Warren of the Center for Responsible Food Business said in an interview. “I don’t think taxpayers want to be funding Kroger’s customer-surveillance program.”
That the taxpayer grant seeks to boost the Kroger sales is undeniable.
It lays out program activities such as vouchers for whole foods and in-store cooking classes. It also describes local and social media outreach. But among the goals it lists is a “statistically significant sales lift in featured whole foods categories at participating stores.”
Success in meeting that and other goals will be determined through “post-event measuring and reporting via Kroger’s 84.51° data platform,” it said.
Warren sees conflicts in the arrangement.
“So Kroger gets the $3 million and it’s grading its own homework,” he said. “When (the department of Health and Human Services) goes to determine the success of the program, it’s determined by Kroger.”
He added, “Why are we subsidizing any part of what Kroger is doing when they have profits in the billions?” 
Kroger turned a $1.25 billion profit in the fourth quarter of 2025 alone. While rising input costs are responsible for much of customers’ sticker shock, in at least some instances, company profits rose even faster. 
In a 2024 trial to block a proposed merger with Albertson’s, the Federal Trade Commission presented testimony from a Kroger executive who said the company hiked the price of milk and eggs above the rate of inflation.
The compensation of the company’s top executive also raises questions from critics in an era of sky-high grocery prices: Kroger CEO Greg Foran’s pay is more than $17 million a year.
“For a company as large as Kroger and the profits they’re already making, when they learn they’re taking taxpayer money, people don’t like it,” Warren said. “It just feels so unfair.” 
Warren and his group find another use to which the federal grant money might be put to be particularly nefarious. 
It has to do with “dynamic pricing” — the ability to use electronic price tags to quickly change prices, similar to the electronic signs used by gas stations.
“We believe there’s a machine built around dynamic pricing that they are putting together and this has implications for that because this grant going to Kroger will be measured by none other than their own data subsidiary 84.51°,” Warren said. 
“They’re using this data on us to determine the highest prices we would be willing to pay through things like dynamic pricing, which is very enabled by things like digital price tags that can change at a moment’s notice.”
Kroger has said the labels would allow it to save employee labor and rapidly update prices to reflect changes in supply and demand. But skeptics, including U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and then-Sen. Bob Casey, D-Penna., in 2024 expressed suspicions.
“Widespread adoption of digital price tags appears poised to enable large grocery stores to squeeze consumers to increase profits,” they wrote in a letter to the company.
Warren, of the Center for Responsible Food Business, said Kroger’s data subsidiary already hoovers up information from 63 million loyalty members every time they scan their Kroger card. 
From that, the platform builds customer profiles estimating income, family size and things like whether they have pets. It can also monitor customer behavior and make educated guesses about what the maximum amount one is willing to spend on an item and dynamically price it accordingly, Taylor Warren said.
As it is, Kroger’s 84.51° subsidiary sells the data it gathers from customers to other businesses. In 2025, those sales accounted for 35% of Kroger profits, according to Consumer Reports.
The $3 million taxpayer grant Kroger received envisions engagement with between 1.2 million and 1.8 million customers. Warren said their data likely will be sucked into Kroger’s data operation and commodified along with all the rest.
“This is very unsavory,” he said. “It’s very concerning.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio’s Tandanda Foundation on a humanitarian mission in Mali
text:
Mayor Garibou Yalcouye (in purple) with Hamidou Yalcouye of Tandana. (Photo provided by Alan Johnson)With wars and violence erupting in hot spots around the world, Mali is easy to overlook although the West African nation of 26 million has been embroiled non-stop in coups and armed conflicts for more than a decade.
Helping Malians has been the focus of an Ohio-based non-profit group, The Tandana Foundation, for all its 20-year history. The group helped build schools, dig wells and plant community gardens, while providing education and training programs for women.
But in recent years the foundation’s work was forced to shift dramatically from improving people’s lives to helping them survive as rural villages and townships were overrun by insurgent forces, forcing residents to flee their homes and become refugees to Mali’s larger cities.
Anna Taft, Tandana’s founding director and daughter of former Ohio Gov. Bob and Hope Taft, quickly had to come to grips with the transition from empowering communities to helping survivors.
“It’s heart wrenching to see this happening to our friends,” she said. “It’s a challenging, horrible situation. It doesn’t make me feel like all our work is lost … but it hits me in the heart.”
With support from her parents, and dozens of others, Anna Taft created the foundation in 2006 to help communities in Mali in Africa and Ecuador in South America. The foundation’s home base is the Taft’s residence in Spring Valley, Ohio, in Greene County.
Joyce Johnson of Columbus visited Mali in 2011 in what she said was a life-changing trip with Tandana. Johnson, a retired schoolteacher and spouse of Tom Johnson, a former state lawmaker, had traveled to Europe previously but was unprepared for what she experienced in Mali.
“I had no idea what to expect. The territory was so raw. It was almost shocking.”
She remembers carrying stones on her head, helping local people dig wells, building a school and plant gardens. Johnson said she was amazed that children walked up to nine miles each way just to get to school each day.
While she has not been back – there currently is a travel ban in effect for Mali – Johnson said she “can’t image how everything is gone and burned and the people had to leave everything behind. They have to start their lives all over again.”
“But work is still being done,” Johnson said. “Tandana is providing tents and food and supplies and schools and training people to start earning some income.”
An impoverished country comprised two-thirds by the Sahara Desert, Mali was a French colony until 1960. It is home to Timbuktu, a faraway place many have heard of but could not locate on a map. The country’s per capita annual income is $1,137 in U.S. dollars; the leading cause of death is malaria. Mali flirted with democracy, but for years has been battered by military coups and armed conflicts triggered by religious, ethnic and economic tensions. Violence resulted in wholesale murders and purges of dozens of rural communities.
Kessia Kouriba (on the right holding a baby), a Tandana employee, with refugees. (Photo provided by Alan Johnson)
The unrest and suffering in Mali were exacerbated last year by dramatic cuts – as much as 90 percent – made by the Trump administration to allocations from the U.S. Agency for International Development. One program eliminated had trained thousands of young people to read and write in their own language.
Another Columbus woman, Mary Maloney, pitched in to help Mali in the early years of Tandana. Among other things, she purchased a computer system, a gift celebrated with great pomp and local flourishes when she visited Kansongo in central Mali visited in 2009. A new-born baby was named Mary to honor her gift.
“Now that place is filled with refugees, people are usually live and die in the same village, are fleeing violence,” Maloney said. “It is so sad. My heart is with Mali. It was life-changing for me to be able to spend time there.”
While Johnson and Maloney were visitors, the Mali situation is personal to Moussa Tembine, a native and Tandana’s country director. He started working with the Ohio group in 2006 after researching organizations to help his native country.
Tandana’s work has focused on an area in the Sahara region with little rainfall and a scattered population of about 90,000. When violent rebels burned their villages, many people fled to Bandiagara, the closest large city. Tandana has been working there to help displaced people, providing food and shelter, schools for children, and teaching job skills to adults who have no experience living and working in cities. They show the new city-dwellers simple things such as how to set up a bank account, something they never dreamed of needing.
The villages “suffered many attacks,” Tembine said. “These groups are very violent and spare no one. They rob, burn the village, and chase the population out … They attack the trucks transporting food and fuel and take everything.”
Tembine estimated 2,000 people from destroyed townships and villages fled to cities.
 “We spend sleepless nights. It was hard to see the work of years disappear. I do hope, little by little, peace is doing to come back,” he said. “In any case, we’re in it for the long haul … Without support from the U.S. people, we wouldn’t be able to do this.”
Garibou Yalcouye, a local mayor who worked with Tandana, said his township suffering terrorist attacks four straight months resulting in “great losses of human lives and material damage. I ask the Tandana Foundation and other partners to come to our support. It is a cry of my heart in this crisis.”
Aissa Seguepire, a refugee aided by Tandana, said when people fled the village they had no news of family for weeks. “They killed many people and took all our belongings.” She lost four brothers. As refugees fled, several young women gave birth, including her daughter who had twins.
Tandana will commemorate two decades of humanitarian efforts in Ecuador and Mali with a Nov. 21 celebration at St. Charles Prepatory School, 2110 E. Broad St. in Bexley. Information is at tandanafoundation/20th.

title: Commentary: For Ohio voters, here’s what the law says regarding federal interference in state elections
text:
A voter casts a ballot. (Photo by Jim Neuger/States Newsroom)At a time when the stakes could not be higher, it is essential for Ohio voters to know exactly what the law states about the many threats that are appearing in regard to the federal government interfering in elections which are administered at the state and local level. 
These threats have been manifesting in regard to all states as well as here in Ohio. The University of Wisconsin Law School has performed a great public service by surveying the entire body of both federal and state law and publishing a report on which laws would come into play in the event that the threats being anticipated are actually implemented.
The entire report is too lengthy to reproduce, but it is possible to highlight the most relevant excerpts. 
In the interest of creating an informed citizenry, this writer has undertaken to do so for the readers of the Ohio Capital Journal.
The format is to identify a specific issue, and then quote directly from the law school report in regard to what the law states.
[Voter Guide: 2026 Ohio General Election Voter Guide: Races, deadlines, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
THE ELECTORAL AUTHORITY OF THE EXECUTIVE BRANCH –
“The Executive Branch, including the President, has no unilateral authority with respect to election administration or voting.”
THE DEPLOYMENT OF FEDERAL TROOPS OR NATIONAL GUARD TO POLLING PLACES – 
“Several federal laws prohibit the deployment of federal troops or armed officers to the polls and bar military disruption of elections. Under 18 U.S.C. § 592, federal officers may not send “troops or armed men” to “any place where a general or special election is held, unless such force be necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States.” Under 18 U.S.C. § 593, officers or members of the Armed Forces of the United States may not, among other things, interfere with election officials’ duties or prevent by force, threat, or intimidation any qualified voter of any State from fully exercising the right of suffrage. Those who violate either law can face fines, imprisonment, and disqualification from office.” 
THE POTENTIAL USE OF ICE AGENTS TO INTERVENE IN STATE AND LOCAL ELECTIONS –
“18 U.S.C. § 595 prohibits any federal administrative employee from using his official authority for the purpose of interfering with, or affecting, the nomination or the election of any candidate for federal office.”
INTERFERENCE IN THE DELIVERY OF MAIL-IN BALLOTS – 
“Any postal worker who unlawfully secretes, destroys, detains, delays, or opens mail and anyone who knowingly and willfully obstructs or retards the passage of the mail can face fines and/or imprisonment.” 
POTENTIAL REFUSAL TO ABIDE FEDERAL LAW – 
“Some federal officials have suggested that they may not abide by these prohibitions, and there are concerns that federal prosecutors will look the other way…..If federal officials decline to enforce federal law, then state criminal laws could provide a necessary backstop for holding them accountable…….States uniformly have some regulations that are intended to protect the sanctity of the voting process and ensure that voters may cast a ballot free from any intimidating presence.  State election codes throughout the country criminalize conduct related to intimidating voters, interfering with the delivery of ballots, and inappropriately possessing ballots or accessing voting equipment.” 
Another resource for Ohioans to be aware of is the American Civil Liberties Union. The ACLU is an officially non-partisan organization, so it does not favor a political party, but it has prepared a concise guide for how to deal with the appearance of any federal agents at the polls. 
The transcendent issue that rises above all partisan politics in this election is the question of whether fundamental election law is going to be enforced. 
Every citizen — no matter what political stripe — has the right to ask any government official related in any way to the election process in Ohio — from the County Board of Elections right up to the Secretary of State and the governor — whether there is a commitment to follow electoral law and administer the upcoming election in a fair, transparent, and legal manner. 
It is exceedingly important for such officials to go on the record as to where they stand.

title: Commentary: Trying to decipher the Ramaswamy-McColley ticket’s seemingly contradictory stance on energy
text:
(Photo by Marga Buschbell-Steeger/Getty Images)While it is not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy and Amy Acton have different views on energy policy for Ohio, what is confusing are the diametrically opposed views that Ramaswamy and his running mate Robert McColley seem to have on the subject.
Ramaswamy has called for the rapid expansion of the number of generating plants, gas, coal, nuclear, and renewables in Ohio, and the streamlining of the permitting process to both facilitate and accelerate the construction of more generating assets in the state. 
Indeed, that is the centerpiece of his agenda for reducing the price Ohioans pay for electricity. His plans, of course, rely heavily on the legal powers  of the Power Siting Board to override any adverse, perhaps parochial, decisions by local governments in regard to permitting. 
He is calling for am increased supply of diverse energy resources that would both better assure reliable energy production  for the state, an approach that might also enable open competition in the market place as a means of disciplining prices, as opposed to excessive government interference in the marketplace.   
That is where, at least in regard to large scale wind and solar plants, McColley deviates substantially from his running mate’s position.
McColley co-sponsored Ohio Senate Bill 52, signed into law in 2021, which gives county commissioners the authority to restrict or prohibit the permitting of large-scale wind and solar generating plants within their jurisdictions. 
Instead of streamlining the process for permitting new plants, as called for by Ramaswamy, McColley has enabled increased government intervention in the marketplace to not only reduce the supply of energy resources, but also to limit the very type of robust competition in the marketplace that Republicans have could called for, and which could serve both consumers and the public interest more broadly. 
Where Ramaswamy wants streamlined permitting, McColley has put in place a far more burdensome permitting process for wind and solar plants, so much more difficult that there is little prospect that such facilities can be built in Ohio.  
Clearly the running mates have diametrically opposed views on how to facilitate additional generation, on government intervention in the marketplace, and on the benefits of a diverse portfolio of resources to Ohio’s supply.
There is are additional and very important aspects to the differences between Ramaswamy and McColley. 
Ramaswamy’s position has been formulated as part of an effort to reduce Ohio’s electric bills. Whether his plan is effective, or even sufficient, for doing so or not is debatable; the objective of the plan Ramaswamy has called for is that Ohioans are to be assured of reliable energy supply at an affordable price.
McColley has taken action to do the exact opposite, to make reliable supply less certain  more and less affordable.  
McColley’s sponsorship of Senate Bill 52 will inevitably result in higher electric bills for consumers in the state. 
Of all the generating options Ramaswamy has called for, the ones with the lowest marginal cost of producing energy are wind and solar, yet those are the very resources McColley sponsored legislation designed to discourage, if not actually exclude from the state’s energy portfolio. 
Because of the dispatching protocols on the PJM regional grid, wind and solar, with their zero marginal cost of production, will inevitably drive down the prices of other, more costly, sources of energy, the very objective that Ramasawmy says he wants seeks to accomplish, but which  McColley by sponsoring S.B. 52 was making almost impossible to accomplish. 
Moreover, wind and solar generation combined with batteries provide Ohio with protection against interruptions in the supply of fossil fuels that occasionally occur, thereby assuring the state with greater reliability of supply.
There is an additional aspect of McColley’s legislation that has a notable adverse impact on Toledo and Northwest Ohio, an ironic effect, given that the McColley hails from Northwest Ohio. 
That adverse consequence is its impact on Toledo’s efforts to use its traditional role in the glass market to become a center for the production of solar panels, a product which McColley has attempted to keep out of the Ohio market, a result that, presumably, Ramaswamy is not endorsing.
Ohioans deserve to know which of the highly divergent, indeed, quite contrary plans, the two running mates will follow if they are elected. 
Ramaswamy’s stated desire for a more competitive, less costly, and more reliable supply of energy, or McColley’s plan for government to intervene to make energy less affordable and less reliable? 
To support Toledo’s efforts to produce solar panels to improve the region’s economy, or to set back if not foreclose that option, as McColley’s S.B. 52, is likely to do?
Ashley C. Brown is a former PUCO Commissioner, and retired Executive Director of the Harvard Electricity Policy Group of Harvard University’s Kennedy School.

As campaigns for governor are headed into the last week before the election, Democratic candidate for governor Amy Acton is on the offensive, launching a new ad about where her opponent stands on data centers. But a political action committee (PAC) supporting Republican Vivek Ramaswamy is also putting a new ad out on his behalf that goes after Acton on data centers.
• Tax cuts for weapons manufacturer take away from schools. Taylor Barnes of Inkstick Media reports, “An Ohio school needs funds. It voted to cut Anduril’s tax bill, anyway.”
On the afternoon of Jan. 16, 2025, just hours after Ohio’s governor announced that the autonomous weapons manufacturer Anduril was setting up a mega-factory near Columbus, the treasurer of a rural school district sent an urgent email to school board members.
He asked them to convene at 8 a.m. the following day and vote on whether to grant Anduril more than 30 years of property tax breaks. In Ohio, school boards are allowed to review and veto such deals when the tax abatement is more than 75% of what the company would have otherwise paid to public schools, which rely heavily on property taxes for their funding.
Records obtained from the school district indicate that the local government agreed to cut Anduril’s property taxes by at least $60 million. However, a calculation by Inkstick using figures in separate county records suggests the value is far higher.
• Oil and gas incidents. The Athens County Independent’s Dani Kington and Eric Boll report, “Report finds increase in Ohio oil and gas incidents.”
A new report from regional environmental groups claims that the Ohio Department of Natural Resources failed to properly investigate, enforce regulations and record data on oil and gas wells.
The report, authored by the FracTracker Alliance and the Buckeye Environmental Network, looked at ODNR incident reports over a 10-year period, 2015–2025.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT can help student loan borrowers before they fall behind
text:
A student loan crisis is brewing in Connecticut, and recent federal policy changes are making it considerably worse. 
The good news is that the state can still help residents before missed payments become defaults and those defaults lead to their wages and tax refunds being seized. Statewide guidance can help families secure relief before the damage deepens.

Richard Cordray

The governor’s office reported last month that approximately 521,400 Connecticut residents hold $19.8 billion in federal student debt. The state has the nation’s fifth-highest student loan average per person and an above-average delinquency rate. For families already juggling housing, groceries, and childcare, that debt adds pressure to budgets with little room to spare.
Consider Jon Coffin, a Bridgeport teacher who recently told Connecticut Public that he owed more than $160,000 in student loans. Despite keeping up with his monthly payments, he’s struggling to weigh everyday purchases for his family against his heavy student loan bill.
For borrowers who fall behind, the consequences are even more severe. Recent reports indicate that the federal government plans to start seizing wages and tax refunds from defaulted borrowers this winter.
For a Connecticut resident with $50,000 in student loans and a disposable income of $60,000, this will mean up to $11,000 in lost cash in 2027 through federal seizures. At scale, the federal government can use these tools to forcibly take an estimated $300 million next year from the 91,000 Connecticut residents who are already in default. That money will entirely disappear from the state’s economy.
Borrowers need reliable assistance as federal support weakens. With the most affordable federal income-driven repayment option (known as the SAVE plan) ending, borrowers must now choose a new repayment plan. Those who don’t will be moved into a standard repayment plan that will result in significantly higher payments for many. Meanwhile, the GAO found that the U.S. Department of Education’s Office of Federal Student Aid lost nearly half its staff during 2025. This attrition places borrowers at risk, as the agency is unable to assess the accuracy of loan servicer records and their call quality, which will increase the frequency of costly errors.
Having led both the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and Federal Student Aid, I saw essential relief that existed only on paper without reaching borrowers in need. Federal benefits offer no real help if people cannot successfully claim them.
Income-driven repayment can lower payments for eligible borrowers. Public Service Loan Forgiveness offers another path for qualifying public servants and non-profit employees who can see their debt entirely eliminated. Borrowers in default need more help to understand how second-chance programs such as rehabilitation or consolidation can help them exit default. Each option involves paperwork, deadlines, and servicer processes that are intricate and easy to get wrong. Borrowers shouldn’t have to navigate them alone.
Gov. Ned Lamont and the legislature have established the Office of the Student Loan Ombudsperson. Michelle Jarvis-Lettman is a great resource to help borrowers and make sure they understand their rights. But even the best firefighters need reinforcements. Connecticut should give her office the tools and resources to match this crisis.
Connecticut’s next step should be a statewide service that helps residents secure relief. Working in coordination with the Ombudsperson, it should combine easy-to-use digital enrollment tools with qualified specialists who help borrowers complete applications for federal relief and resolve obstacles. A coordinated campaign among colleges, employers, unions and community organizations can effectively connect residents to the service, extending the office’s reach and impact.
Helping residents claim federal assistance also helps the state. Lower payments leave families more money for rent, food, and childcare —money that is spent on local businesses. Instead of Washington forcibly seizing up to $300 million next year from Connecticut borrowers, these federal programs ––when properly accessed–– can mitigate defaults and create hundreds of millions of dollars in savings to boost the local economy.
Connecticut has already recognized the problem and built a foundation for action. Now it can help residents claim the federal benefits they need and deserve before federal garnishments of wages and benefits put more household income at risk.
Richard Cordray served as the first director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and later as chief of Federal Student Aid, overseeing the federal student loan program.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Trump rallies for Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi: ‘You like me’
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
CORINTH – President Donald Trump rallied for Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi on Monday, urging his supporters not to take chances by staying home and allowing a potential midterm upset in a state he won handily.
As Trump’s approval ratings have cratered amid backlash to soaring consumer prices and an unpopular war in Iran, Democrats have grown hopeful that their nominee in Mississippi, Scott Colom, might flip a seat in what has been a Republican stronghold. Both national parties are sinking money and resources into the race in the homestretch, and national Democratic players have filed into Mississippi to campaign for Colom.
President Donald Trump takes the stage during his rally at the Crossroads Arena in Corinth on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Trump arrived in the state three days after his 2024 presidential campaign opponent, former Vice President Kamala Harris, hosted a rally for Colom in Columbus.
At Crossroads Arena in the rural northeast Mississippi town of Corinth, Trump told an energized crowd that he had taken notice of the state’s heated Senate race.
“I’m here because Cindy is doing great, but I just have to make sure,” Trump said. “I can’t take a chance.”

The event marks Trump’s first rally in Mississippi since 2019, when he came to Tupelo, a town just over 50 miles away whose name and location the president couldn’t remember on Monday.
“We did a rally in the north or the south, I don’t know where the hell it was,” Trump said.
Trump has won the state three times, but with the midterm elections eight days away, he acknowledged that Republicans could be in for a rough night. The president asked voters to pretend he was on the ballot, hoping to turn out his loyal supporters who don’t always bother to vote in non-presidential elections.
President Donald Trump embraces Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith during his rally at the Crossroads Arena in Corinth on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodaySupporters gather for President Donald Trump’s rally at the Crossroads Arena in Corinth on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayTyson Robinson, 10, adjusts his hat as he prepares for President Donald Trump’s rally at the Crossroads Arena in Corinth on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayPresident Donald Trump speaks during his rally at the Crossroads Arena in Corinth on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodaySen. Cindy Hyde-Smith waves to supporters during President Donald Trump’s rally at the Crossroads Arena in Corinth on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayMississippi Republican Party Chairman Mike Hurst speaks during President Donald Trump’s rally at the Crossroads Arena in Corinth on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodaySupporters gather for President Donald Trump’s rally at the Crossroads Arena in Corinth on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodaySupporters cheer during President Donald Trump’s rally at the Crossroads Arena in Corinth on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayGov. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodaySecretary of State Michael Watson, center, takes a photo with supporters during President Donald Trump’s rally at the Crossroads Arena in Corinth on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayState Sen. Kevin Blackwell, right, waves at someone in the crowd during President Donald Trump’s rally at the Crossroads Arena in Corinth on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayState leaders are recognized during President Donald Trump’s rally at the Crossroads Arena in Corinth on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Hyde-Smith said she has fought to support Trump’s agenda and that voters face a binary choice between herself and an opponent she called “radical.”
“The control of the Senate is at stake on Nov. 3,” Hyde-Smith said. “I want you to send me back to be that fighter with the president.”
In a scattered speech that lasted just over 80 minutes, Trump called Colom, a district attorney in north Mississippi, a “Democrat communist” and accused him of being soft on crime and overly supportive of transgender rights. He called Hyde-Smith a “great friend” and “unbelievable, frankly.” 
He said his administration has protected American jobs through tariffs, deported large numbers of immigrants and reduced crime. He also launched into commentary on Mississippi’s “beautiful women” and the allegedly poor state of the White House’s crown molding when he arrived back in office two years ago.
Trump was preceded on stage by Republican U.S. Rep. Trent Kelly, Mississippi Republican Party Chairman Mike Hurst and Gov. Tate Reeves. 
Reeves said Mississippi is faced with a choice between the rule of “conservative rural America” and the “socialist coast.” Other Republican officials in attendance included U.S. Rep. Michael Guest, Secretary of State Michael Watson, State Auditor Shad White and multiple state lawmakers. 
Supporters gather for President Donald Trump’s rally at the Crossroads Arena in Corinth on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
According to many polls, Trump’s support has plummeted as prices have risen for essential goods such as groceries and gasoline. Colom has responded by labeling Hyde-Smith “Cindy High Prices” and has hammered her for advising Mississippians to “pick another protein” amid the rising cost of beef.
Hyde-Smith has responded by calling Colom a “transgender defender” and has said his campaign has been buoyed by liberal out-of-state donors such as billionaire George Soros. 
In a statement ahead of the rally, the Democratic aligned Super PAC American Bridge 21st Century announced it had spent $2.1 million on Mississippi’s Senate race. 
“Cindy Hyde-Smith is a weak candidate and one of the most hated GOP senators in Congress who is on record voting for legislation that has hurt her constituents,” said American Bridge 21st Century President Pat Dennis. “Mississippians want a Senator who will fight to lower their costs, not one who will vote to let beef prices soar, then shrug them off and suggest finding another protein.”
As Trump’s supporters lined up outside to get into the rally, many said rising costs across the economy have hit their pocketbooks hard. But they also said their support for Trump hadn’t wavered, citing potential long-term benefits of his policies. 
Lori Lawson, the mayor of Burnsville, owns Subway franchises and a convenience store that sells gasoline and diesel. She said rising prices have hit everybody hard, but people are fixating too much on gas in particular. 
“Yes, the price of gasoline has gone up, and it’s affected everybody,” Lawson said. “People want to complain about the price of gas and diesel, but they don’t have a problem giving $5 per gallon of water. That water doesn’t make anything go.” 
Lawson came to the rally with Lance Heavener, a Burnsville city alderman who owns a lawn servicing company and a funeral home. He said rising prices have cost him an additional $58,000 this year to do business, but he was still willing to take the financial hit if it meant winning a war with Iran.
President Donald Trump speaks during his rally at the Crossroads Arena in Corinth on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“If Trump can get those folks under control, I’m willing to bear the expense. I don’t know how long we can do it, but hopefully it’ll be short enough.”
Colom traveled to Corinth on Monday to hold a press conference before the rally. He criticized Hyde-Smith for refusing to debate him and campaigning with Trump instead. 
“We’ve got a message we want to send to President Trump and our junior senator,” Colom said. “President Trump and our junior senator, they’ve been doing too much talking and not enough listening.”
In a possible overture to Trump’s base, Colom said Hyde-Smith hasn’t done enough to urge Trump to release the Epstein files, accusing her of being more willing to “protect pedophiles over people.”
After the press conference, Colom went to the Crossroads Arena, where he spoke with attendees outside waiting in line. 
The vast majority of those who attended the rally showered Trump with praise and said they had no reservations about voting for Hyde-Smith. 
On stage Monday, the president didn’t hesitate to highlight the adoration.
“You like me, I like you,” Trump told the crowd. “That’s just the way it is.” 
Referring to his efforts to rename the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America, Trump also promised to never do the same with the Mississippi River, apparently because Mississippi is a Republican-led state. 
“Boy that would be terrible. Can you imagine that,” Trump said. “I promise I will never change the name of the Mississippi. Cindy Hyde (Smith) and Roger (Wicker) would have a little problem with me if I did that.”

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Conservative lender accused of Ponzi scheme sentenced to 15 years in prison
text:
First Liberty Building and Loan the day after the Securities and Exchange Commission filed its complaint against the Newnan-based lender. Jill Nolin/Georgia RecorderEdwin Brant Frost IV, the founder of a conservative lending firm in Georgia, was sentenced on Monday to 15 years in prison for his role in running a Ponzi scheme that defrauded investors out of millions of dollars.
Frost, a 69-year-old and founder of the now-defunct First Liberty Building & Loan, was accused of leading a $140 million Ponzi scheme that officials say started around 2021 and scammed about 300 investors. Frost, who was convicted of wire fraud in May after he pleaded guilty, will also have to pay back over $76 million in restitution to victims. After he serves his sentence, he will have three additional years of supervised release.
At Frost’s sentencing hearing Monday in Newnan, Frost took responsibility for his role in scamming these investors, including many people who handed over their savings for retirement to Frost and believed those funds would be used to provide “bridge loans” to small businesses seeking long-term Small Business Administration loans. Frost offered annual returns ranging from 8% to 18%. Federal officials alleged that Frost and his entities did not use investor funds as represented and most of the bridge loans ultimately defaulted.
Assistant U. S. Attorney Angela Adams, who prosecuted the case, argued that Frost’s crimes were not a result of a “passive mistake” but rather a “calculated deception” that he repeated over several years. Adams pointed to how he used politics and religion to defraud his victims, saying that “he used those personal convictions to get into the hearts and the pockets of his victims.”
“He did that and caused victims to lose everything,” Adams said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Frost said at the hearing that he “was wrong” and took “full responsibility” for his actions. U.S. District Court Judge Leigh Martin May said that she took all sides into consideration and called it a “complicated situation,” but concluded that anything less than a 15-year sentence would not be sufficient for “such a serious crime.”
“It wasn’t just a little bit of money for some people. This was a large portion of their money,” May said, adding that for some victims, it was “a lifetime of savings” and that “some people won’t retire” as a result. May also pointed to other consequences, such as the mental health toll this scam has had on families.
Marc Mukasey, a lawyer for Frost, had asked the court to consider a five-year sentence, pointing to his age and repeatedly saying that issuing Frost to a longer sentence would be equal to death sentence. He said that a 14-year sentence, which Frost’s counsel agreed to in a plea agreement, would “lock Brant up for the rest of his days” and that the sentence was “too severe for the life he lived.” Mukasey argued that Frost had “no malice” when he defrauded those hundreds of people, adding that the only reason he kept the scam going was because “he was desperate not to hurt anyone” and needed even more money to pay back returns on the bridge loans.
May wasn’t convinced that Frost had no ill intention, saying that “this level of delusion is not believable.” She said that she also believed the numerous letters friends and family of Frost wrote defending his character but that she was “still concerned (Frost) is in a bit of denial” about what he has done. 
“I don’t believe the narrative that you weren’t trying to hurt people,” May said.
Prosecutors say Frost diverted at least $5 million of the investor funds for his own personal uses, including for a $230,000 vacation home rental in Maine, $2 million in credit card payments and $570,000 in political contributions to conservative candidates. 
She also heard emotional testimony from victims, many who said they were fooled by Frost’s charisma and apparent kindness. Jordan Baldwin, one of the witnesses who testified and said that because of Frost’s actions his “family will be financially insecure longer than (Frost) will be incarcerated,” said he fell for the scam because Frost appeared to him “as Godsent.”
“Brant’s charisma makes him a psychopath,” Baldwin said.
Other victims used other words to describe Frost to the judge, such as “sociopath,” “master of deception” and “slick.”
Frost will have 30 days to surrender himself to authorities. His counsel asked the court if he could serve his time at a federal prison in Montgomery.
Before concluding the hearing, May offered some consolidation to Frost’s victims. She said that while she couldn’t guarantee their money would be fully recovered and that the judicial system may not right every wrong, she hopes that they are able to find some peace.
“You have to find a way to put this behind you,” she said.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Josh Turek ad on transgender issues draws bipartisan criticism
text:
Democrat Josh Turek, running for U.S. Senate in 2026, spoke to Democrats gathered for state Rep. Sean Bagniewski's annual Fish Fry dinner in Des Moines Oct. 11, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Josh Turek, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate, is facing criticism from both LGBTQ+ advocates and Republicans for a recent ad in which he said he opposed allowing transgender women to compete in women’s sports, and supported blocking Medicaid funding going to gender-affirming care for transgender Iowans.
Turek, a state representative from Council Bluffs who faces Republican U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson in the general election, released an ad Sunday titled “Stop the Nonsense,” about issues related to transgender Iowans. Hinson and other Republicans argued Monday that Turek’s ad was misrepresenting his record on transgender issues while LGBTQ+ advocates said his position was a “dramatic” departure from that of other Democratic candidates.
“As a kid in a wheelchair, I faced my share of bullying,” Turek said in the ad. “That’s why I believe that no Iowan should face discrimination. As a Paralympian, I also know it’s important to have rules. It’s why I oppose males competing in female sports, something that is already illegal in Iowa. I’m against taxpayers paying for sex changes too. Anyone tells you any different is lying.”
Turek said, “it’s time to stop the nonsense from both extremes and start to focus on lowering costs for Iowans.”
This is not the first ad in which Turek has emphasized his willingness to take a more conservative approach to issues if elected to the U.S. Senate. He has also spoken about his support for increasing border security efforts, saying he would work with President Donald Trump to make changes to the U.S. immigration system if elected. Other ads by the Turek campaign — including two released Monday — focus on issues like diesel prices and high healthcare costs.
He is not also not the only Iowa Democrat to make statements and release advertisements about transgender issues this election cycle. Rob Sand, running for governor, has repeatedly said he does not support allowing transgender women to compete in women’s sports, and Democratic congressional candidates including  Sarah Trone Garriott, Lindsay James, and Christina Bohannan have all released ads discussing the issue.
While advocates and others have criticized these ads from other Democratic candidates in recent months, the LGBTQ+ advocacy organization One Iowa Action, released a statement Monday condemning Turek’s ad. The organization has not released statements criticizing other ads.
In a statement, One Iowa Action Executive Director Max Mowitz said, “we unequivocally condemn Josh Turek’s recently released campaign ad and the policy shift it represents.”
Keenan Crow, director of policy and advocacy for One Iowa, said though other Democratic candidates have put out political advertisements referencing transgender Iowans, the organization chose to issue a statement condemning Turek’s advertisement because it directly called for a policy change to ban coverage of gender-affirming healthcare for individuals on public programs like Medicaid.
“This ad is advocating a policy change that would be a dramatic departure from what anybody else in the Democratic Party is saying right now,” Crow said.
The ad is not the first time Turek has said he opposes public funding for gender-affirming surgeries. In an article from American Journal News, Turek said he does not endorse using taxpayer funds for these medical procedures. He also explained his 2025 vote against an Iowa Health and Human Services appropriations bill, which included this restriction, by saying his “no” vote was because the budget did not address Medicaid waitlists and provider shortages.
Turek’s statement that he opposed “taxpayers paying for sex changes” comes after Iowa Republicans have repeatedly attempted to pass a state-level ban on Medicaid coverage for gender-confirming surgeries. In 2019, the Iowa Legislature passed a law to this effect that was struck down by a court decision which found the measure violated the Iowa Constitution and the Iowa Civil Rights Act. This was a decision Gov. Kim Reynolds and other Republicans referenced when the state removed “gender identity” as a protected class in the state’s civil rights code in 2025.
Turek voted against this measure, Senate File 418. The law not only impacted Medicaid coverage — it also ended state civil rights protections for people facing discrimination in areas like employment, housing, public accommodations and education because of their gender identity.
Though One Iowa condemned Turek’s ad, Mowitz said in the statement the organization was not supportive of Hinson, who has also regularly spoken and voted against transgender athletes competing in women’s sports, alongside other restrictions on transgender medical care.
“Make no mistake, Ashley Hinson is no friend to LGBTQ+ Iowans, and that is not our claim,” Mowitz said. “Hinson has taken every opportunity she has had to strip the rights of transgender Iowans, and we believe she would continue that record in the US Senate. But on the specific policy of Medicaid coverage for gender affirming surgical care, there is no light between Hinson and Turek. Their policies on this issue are the same, and that is a dangerous escalation. This places Josh Turek as the most trans exclusionary federal Democrat on the ballot anywhere in the country. We cannot and will not let this go unaddressed.”
Adam Peters, director of operations of Clock, Inc. LGBT+ Community Center in the Quad Cities and the Democratic nominee for Iowa House of Representatives District 97 in 2026, said he believed there was still a sizable difference between Turek’s and Hinson’s records on transgender rights.
“I voted on the first day of early in-person voting, but if I were filling out my ballot today, I would still vote for Josh Turek,” Peters said. “While I disagree with his ad, I know I can talk to him and make my concerns heard. You can too. I can’t say the same for Ashley Hinson. I know what it feels like to support candidates, including President Obama, while still waiting for them to fully support my rights. I also know Josh voted against stripping gender identity from Iowa’s civil rights protections last year. That record matters, even as we ask him to do better.”
Iowa Rep. Aime Wichtendahl, D-Hiawatha, said the ad was disappointing in an interview with Gray Media Iowa Monday. Wichtendahl, who serves with Turek as a member of the minority party in the Iowa House, was the first transgender Iowan elected to the state Legislature.
“These talking points aren’t going to gain you anything with the voters,” Wichtendahl said.
But Rep. Adam Zabner, another Democratic colleague of Turek in the Iowa House, said in a statement that he believes Turek will continue to fight against discrimination if elected to Congress.
“I have worked alongside Josh for years and saw firsthand how committed he is to ensuring the rights of all Iowans and fighting against discrimination,” Zabner said. “With Ashley Hinson, Iowans would get just another corrupt D.C. politician who would continue to cut health care and food assistance to give tax breaks to billionaires.”
At a campaign rally with fellow Republicans including U.S. Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks in Coralville Monday, Hinson also criticized Turek’s ad — claiming he was misrepresenting his voting record.
“You may have seen he just launched a new trans ad last night, I think it was, saying he does not support boys and girls bathrooms,” Hinson said. “Well, sorry to say this, but again he’s lying about his record. His record shows otherwise.”
Hinson referenced Turek’s votes on several pieces of legislation, including votes against GOP-led law banning transgender students from using school restrooms that conflict with their assigned sex at birth. A Turek campaign spokesperson said he opposed because that bill because it “puts disabled Iowans and their caregivers, particularly caregivers of the opposite sex, at risk of legal consequences for entering a public restroom.”
Hinson also cited Turek’s vote against a law requiring parental consent if a child requests gender-related accommodations like the use of different name or pronouns at school. That law, currently being challenged in court, also banned books containing depictions of sexual acts from being available in K-12 school libraries and restricted gender identity and sexuality from being in any instructions or material for K-6 students.
“He is trying to act like a Republican to win this election here in Iowa, and he has to run away from his liberal record,” Hinson said.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: UVU fills new top safety position after Charlie Kirk shooting
text:
Law enforcement responds after conservative political commentator Charlie Kirk was shot and killed during an event at Utah Valley University in Orem on Wednesday, Sept. 10, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Utah Valley University is bringing on a past leader of the state’s highway patrol to fill a new safety post after the assassination of Charlie Kirk on the campus last year. 
The announcement comes a month after an outside review identified gaps in the university’s planning and protocols. The report recommended Utah Valley create a top administrative role to oversee safety operations and emergency management, and the university said in response it was already doing so. 
Michael Rapich is taking the job at the university in Orem after 33 years with the Utah Highway Patrol, where he served at the helm for nine years before retiring in November 2025. 
UVU didn’t act in ‘wanton disregard’ leading up to Charlie Kirk shooting, independent review says

Utah Valley University President Jon Anderson said in a prepared statement that Rapich “brings decades of public safety leadership, sound judgment, and trusted relationships across Utah. His experience and collaborative approach will strengthen how UVU prepares, responds, and works together to serve our campus community.”
The university has faced criticism for failing to secure each rooftop and assigning just six police officers to staff the event attended by some 3,000 people. Kirk’s family blames lapses in event security for his death and has taken a first step toward suing the school by sending a notice of claim. 
Rapich’s longtime relationships with law enforcers throughout the state will help enhance emergency response and coordination with other agencies, the university said.  
Rapich said in a statement that he’s honored and looks forward to working with students, employees, and others in public safety at the university and surrounding communities “to identify every opportunity to ensure that UVU Campus is a trusted place for learning, growth, and engagement.” 
Rapich became a state trooper in 1992 after serving in the U.S. Coast Guard and working as a 911 dispatcher, the university said. 
Kirk, a founder of the student organization Turning Point USA and a close ally of President Donald Trump, was shot and killed just minutes into an outdoor speaking event in a courtyard on Sept. 10, 2025. 
The 23-year-old Tyler Robinson is accused of using his grandfather’s hunting rifle to fatally shoot Kirk from a rooftop on the campus. He has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder. 
A judge last month ordered Robinson to stand trial. If he’s convicted, prosecutors have said they’ll seek the death penalty. They expect a trial to take place in 2028, while Robinson’s defense team says they will need until 2029 to adequately prepare for a trial.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Vice President JD Vance renews call for Kansas GOP voters to back US Sen. Roger Marshall
text:
Vice President JD Vance speaks to a Topeka crowd on Monday urging voters to re-elect U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall. (Photo by Thad Allton for Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Vice President JD Vance returned to the state Monday for a second time since mid-September to rally voters on behalf of Republican Roger Marshall and try to prevent the first Kansas victory by a Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate since the 1930s.
Vance’s visit to a steel fabrication business came days after President Donald Trump headlined an arena rally in Park City and six weeks since the vice president was in Olathe to deliver a shot of adrenaline for Marshall in the race against Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton, founder of the largest United Methodist congregation in the United States.
Despite Trump’s endorsement, Marshall has struggled to break away from Hamilton in a state the president carried three times and won by 16 percentage points in 2024. In 2020, with Trump on the ballot, Marshall won his first campaign for U.S. Senate by 11 points.
“Next week’s election, ladies and gentlemen, it’s not just red team versus blue team,” said Vance, who lauded Marshall’s leadership. “It’s about whether we stand for a fighter who’s always stood for the normal, everyday Americans who keep this country running.”
The vice president urged Kansas voters to reject Hamilton. He claimed the Democrat’s candidacy was given shape by Washington political gurus tied to U.S. Sen. Chuck Schumer of New York.
“Adam Hamilton says he’s a pastor and, I don’t know, I can’t possibly know what is in the man’s heart, but I do know the lawgiver in Adam Hamilton’s world. It isn’t Moses. It’s not Jesus. It’s Chuck Schumer,” Vance said. “Here’s the deal. If elected, Adam Hamilton would use our faith and your vote as Kansas senator to launder a political ideology that despises the way that Kansas lives. This man is a lab creation of Washington operatives and far-left activists who don’t now a thing about you or what you care about.”
From left: Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall and U.S. Sen. Derek Schmidt attend a Topeka rally featuring Vice President JD Vance on Monday. (Photo by Thad Allton for Kansas Reflector)
 
The vocal protesters
During the speech, Vance noted when a heckler was escorted out of the rally.
“The thing I’ve realized after having these rallies for the last couple of weeks is the only chance the Democrats have is to interrupt and shut down the debate, because when we have a free and open debate, the American people will realize that all the Democrats are selling is a fat load of bulls***,” Vance said.
A couple of minutes later, the vice president celebrated the exit of another vocal protester. He said that the “bulls*** artist, excuse my language for the kids. He’s out of here.”
The unexpectedly close race in Kansas emerged as Republicans battled Democrats for control the U.S. House and and U.S. Senate. MS NOW’s polling data partner FiftyPlusOne indicated the Kansas Senate contest was essentially a tie, with Hamilton at 45.9% and Marshall at 45.7%. The race has been pegged as a toss-up by other polling platforms, although advance voting in Kansas has been more robust among Democrats.
“Democrats are coming out like it’s a presidential year. Republicans, we’ve got to match that excitement, that enthusiasm,” Marshall told the Topeka crowd in a warm-up speech. “Send me back for one more term — for six more years. We sure can’t send back a woke radical liberal Democrat. That’s for sure.”
Marshall’s campaign has been hobbled by Trump’s declining approval ratings and voter anxiety about the economy, fuel costs, tariffs and the Iran war.
Marshall, a physician who practiced medicine for more than 20 years in Great Bend, has been dogged by reports that his attempt to collect unpaid medical debt led his attorney to file 700 lawsuits that and resulted in the arrests of 80 people. The Kansas senator responded to negative news coverage with attacks on Hamilton’s character. He also doubled down on his dedication and allegiance to Trump and Vance.
U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kansas, waves to a line of people waiting to attend a rally on Oct. 26, 2026, in Topeka, where Vice President JD Vance campaigned for Marshall. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)
 
Vance’s attack
Vance said that with the assistance of lawmakers including Marshall the Trump administration had taken on the “tyranny of DEI and racial discrimination.”
He said “we happen to believe that no individual and no person can be truly free when their government or their employer cares more about so-called ‘white privilege’ than it does about promoting the American dream for everybody.”
During the speech, Vance said Hamilton was masquerading as a moderate and should be viewed as a component of  the “radical left” within the Democratic Party.
Drawing upon Hamilton’s archive of sermons, Vance claimed the pastor said Kansans ought to apologize for consuming meat. He was also critical of Hamilton’s congregation supporting a community LGBTQ pride festival.
The vice president echoed criticism shared by Marshall that the pastor didn’t do enough to circumvent misconduct by a church volunteer who abused children at a summer camp in Kansas. Hamilton said church staff conducted an inconclusive internal inquiry before turning information over to police a year later. During the Senate campaign, Hamilton said he should have contacted authorities immediately.
Marshall has had to respond to a barrage of campaign commercials that he voted in 2025 to table a bipartisan measure to compel the U.S. Department of Justice to release files related to convicted sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein. At that time, Marshall said it was improper to link Epstein to a defense bill.
Before Vance arrived in Kansas, Hamilton issued a statement that said he appreciated how politicians in Washington, D.C., were taking an interest in the welfare of Kansans. Hamilton has presented himself as a centrist concerned about the escalating cost of living, fuel and healthcare, as well as U.S. tariffs and the war with Iran, to draw votes from moderate Republicans and swing-vote independents.
“Folks in Kansas have been getting hurt by policies out of Washington for too long,” Hamilton said.
Hamilton’s campaign invited the vice president to attend a service at Church of the Resurrection, the nation’s largest United Methodist congregation, to get a better sense of economic challenges faced by Kansans.
“Our congregation is roughly equal parts Republicans, Democrats and independents,” said Hamilton, founder of the 24,000-member church. “We sit in the same pews and worship together every Sunday. Then we go out and serve our community. I believe Washington could learn something from us.”
Vice President JD Vance made his second visit to Kansas this campaign cycle to rally support for U.S. Sen Roger Marshall. (Photo by Thad Allton for Kansas Reflector)
