name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: When we have the chance to prevent tragedy, why would we take it away?
text:
NEXT WEEK, Massachusetts voters will decide the future of a law that gives licensed clinicians an important tool to intervene before a crisis becomes a tragedy. For those of us working at the intersection of firearm injury prevention, suicide prevention, and public policy, the stakes extend far beyond the political debate surrounding gun ownership. They concern a fundamental question: What should we do when we recognize that someone is at serious risk of harming themselves or others, but still have an opportunity to prevent it? 
In 2024, Massachusetts enacted H.4885, An Act Modernizing Firearm Laws, which made several important updates to the Commonwealth’s firearm safety framework. Among them was an expansion of extreme risk protection orders (ERPOs), allowing licensed health care professionals and certain educational personnel to petition courts for temporary firearm restrictions when an individual poses a significant risk of harm to themselves or others. 
This change addressed a critical gap in our approach to firearm injury and suicide prevention. ERPOs, sometimes referred to as red flag laws, are civil court orders that temporarily restrict firearm and ammunition access when evidence indicates an individual presents a danger to themselves or others.  
It is important to emphasize that they are not criminal convictions, nor are they permanent firearm prohibitions. Rather, they provide a legal mechanism to intervene during periods of elevated risk, when access to a firearm can turn a temporary crisis into an irreversible outcome. This distinction is extremely important for suicide prevention. 
In 2024, 64 percent of firearm deaths in Massachusetts were due to suicide. Suicidal crises can be acute and time-sensitive, and firearms make these crises exceptionally lethal. Creating time and distance between an individual in crisis and a firearm provides a critical opportunity for intervention, treatment, and recovery. 
Health care professionals are often among the first to recognize these warning signs. Emergency physicians, psychiatrists, primary care providers, and other licensed clinicians routinely encounter patients experiencing suicidal ideation, psychiatric emergencies, or circumstances involving a heightened risk of violence or harm. Before the 2024 law was passed, these clinicians lacked the legal authority to petition directly for an ERPO, even when their clinical assessment and expertise identified an immediate concern. This critical legislation bridged that gap. 
As a firearm injury and suicide prevention researcher working with Boston Medical Center and Boston University, I have studied the implementation of this expansion, including the challenges clinicians face in translating new legal authority into practice. My research has reinforced an important reality: effective prevention requires strong, evidence-based policies that set the stage for training, institutional infrastructure, and meaningful collaboration between health care, legal systems, and community partners.  
These systems take time to build. In just one year, more than 480 clinicians across all 14 Massachusetts counties have participated in ERPO training, demonstrating the statewide reach and importance of the expansion this legislation provided. The clinician expansion has been in effect for just over two years, and its long-term impact remains an important subject for evaluation.  
Opponents of ERPOs frequently argue that these laws violate constitutional protections and deprive individuals of their property without due process. I agree that constitutional rights and procedural fairness are legitimate concerns that deserve careful examination. But describing ERPOs as firearm confiscation without due process ignores the judicial safeguards that have been carefully written into Massachusetts law.  
An ERPO requires court involvement and evidence of risk. Although emergency orders may initially be issued without the respondent present, they are temporary, and a subsequent hearing must occur within a defined period. Individuals have the opportunity to appear, contest the allegations, and present their case. Longer-term orders require judicial findings and are subject to expiration or extension. These safeguards matter. They reflect the principle that protecting public safety and respecting individual rights are not inherently competing objectives. Both must inform how preventative policies are designed and implemented. 
Question 9 places this framework before voters. A yes vote would retain Massachusetts’s 2024 gun violence prevention law, including the expanded authority for licensed clinicians and educational personnel to petition for ERPOs. A no vote would repeal the legislation, removing that expansion while leaving the earlier, more limited ERPO framework in place. 
This decision is consequential. Repeal would not eliminate ERPOs altogether, but it would significantly shrink who can initiate these potentially lifesaving interventions. 
No single law can eliminate firearm violence or suicide. Nor should ERPOs be viewed as substitutes for accessible mental health care, community-based violence prevention, or comprehensive suicide prevention services. ERPOs are one component of a broader public health approach that recognizes the importance of identifying risk early and responding with appropriate, evidence-based interventions. 
The question before Massachusetts voters cannot be reduced to whether firearm regulations should be more or less restrictive—it is whether the Commonwealth should preserve an additional pathway for intervention when credible warning signs are present. In public health, we often measure success by the tragedies that never occur: the injury prevented, the crisis resolved, the life that continues, the community that does not have to grieve. 
As Massachusetts approaches Election Day, I encourage voters to look beyond political rhetoric, examine what the 2024 legislation actually changed, consider the consequences of preserving or removing these preventive tools, and ultimately vote yes on question 9. The choices we make about firearm policy should be informed by evidence, constitutional safeguards, and a shared commitment to preventing avoidable loss of life. If we knowingly dismantle legislation designed to prevent violence and suicide, we cannot pretend the consequences are out of our control. 
Annie Buck, PhD, MS, is a firearm injury and suicide prevention researcher at Boston Medical Center and Boston University.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Feds allege over 400 noncitizens vote in WA; Hobbs disputes data
text:
A drop box at the Ballard branch of the Seattle Public Library in King County. (Photo by Laurel Demkovich/Washington State Standard)The top federal prosecutor in Seattle claimed on Monday that more than 400 noncitizens have been voting in Washington, as the Trump administration’s crusade against alleged voter fraud intensifies in the Evergreen State.
Acting U.S. Attorney Charles Neil Floyd said in a press conference Monday that prosecutors haven’t charged any of the alleged fraudulent voters with a crime, but “I do anticipate that we will.” He’s asking the state to set aside their ballots for next week’s midterm election pending confirmation that they’re voting legally.
Secretary of State Steve Hobbs said his office is “carefully reviewing the request and assessing the information sought to ensure that our response complies with applicable state and federal laws.” Voter fraud is incredibly rare in Washington, he said, and when these cases are found, they’re forwarded to local authorities for prosecution.
He argued the timing just a week before the election is “no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results.”
Floyd sent a letter to Hobbs on Monday with information about the alleged 405 noncitizen voters. He claimed those voters, many of whom are lawful permanent residents, have cast upward of 1,500 ballots in past state and federal elections, and said this was “only the tip of the iceberg.” Some have voted for over a decade, according to the letter.
Hobbs said one of the 405 records shared by federal authorities was from 1994. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The allegations come as President Donald Trump has escalated the federal government’s search for voting by noncitizen immigrants who are not legally eligible to vote. Trump has falsely complained of widespread fraud for years since his 2020 election loss to Joe Biden. Trump said Monday he’d give $1 million to anyone who reports such fraud that leads to a conviction.
In California, his administration is seeking a judge’s order requiring state election officials not count the ballots of 20,000 voters who are suspected to be noncitizens. Estimates from federal officials in other states have been determined to be overblown.
“We take our responsibility to protect voter information seriously and will only respond to requests that follow due process. We saw what happened in California and don’t want Washingtonians to be harassed,” Hobbs, a Democrat, said in a statement. 
The U.S. Department of Justice has for over a year been trying to get ahold of Washington’s voter rolls, including sensitive information contained there. Like elsewhere, a federal judge here tossed the Justice Department’s lawsuit trying to force the state to hand over the voter data. Floyd said that the state withholding this information made it harder to investigate the alleged noncitizen voting. 
In July, federal authorities threatened to criminally prosecute state election officials if they failed to prevent noncitizens from voting in next month’s federal elections. And more recently, federal authorities have filed more than 60 subpoenas for individual voter records, Hobbs said.
Floyd’s letter, also signed by First Assistant U.S. Attorney Pete Serrano for the Eastern District of Washington, said federal authorities expect to get another list of noncitizen voters registered in the state from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security before next Tuesday’s election.
Floyd, a Trump appointee, alleged Washington doesn’t have the capacity to confirm noncitizens are barred from voting.
“Who is checking to make sure that the people registered to vote are United States citizens? Who is checking to see if noncitizens are voting in Washington?” Floyd said. “Sadly, the answer to those questions in Washington is no one.”
April Miller, the acting special agent in charge for Homeland Security Investigations in Seattle, told reporters “we take these allegations seriously and investigate them within the scope of our federal criminal authorities.”
Midterm voting is underway in  Washington, which has more than 5.1 million registered voters and uses a mail-in ballot system. Voters attest to their eligibility when returning their ballot.
Federal authorities will have a presence in Washington’s most populous county on Election Day. King County is one of numerous jurisdictions nationwide where election monitors from the Justice Department will be on hand to ensure election officials comply with federal voting rights laws. The department says this is routine.
Gov. Bob Ferguson is also offering to deploy members of the Washington National Guard to help counties protect ballot drop boxes. At least half a dozen counties have taken him up on the offer.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho conservative policy center, opponents of Prop 1 sue to stop TV ads
text:
Blaine Conzatti is the president of the Idaho Family Policy Center. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Family Policy Center)Opponents of the proposed abortion rights initiative Proposition 1 filed a lawsuit Monday seeking to pull TV ads paid for by the Idaho Democratic Party in favor of the initiative. 
The conservative, Christian advocacy organization, the Idaho Family Policy Center, and leaders with a political action committee that opposes the initiative, Too Extreme for Idaho PAC, brought the lawsuit. 
The ballot initiative Prop 1 would repeal Idaho’s abortion ban, allowing the procedure up to viability or after in cases of emergency, enumerate rates related to a range of reproductive healthcare, and provide legal liability protections for healthcare providers who provide that type of care. The initiative will be before Idaho voters in the Nov. 3 general election. 
The lawsuit, filed in Canyon County court, alleges that the supporters and authors of Prop 1, a group called Idahoans United for Women and Families, paid the Idaho Democratic Party to run ads in favor of the initiative in order to pay the more favorable rates that broadcasters are required to charge to political candidates ahead of elections. The ads were run on behalf of Democratic gubernatorial candidate Terri Pickens. 
“Pro-abortion activists cheated their way into cheaper television advertisements to stump for their radical abortion ballot initiative,” Idaho Family Policy Center President Blaine Conzatti said in a written statement. “Instead of playing by the rules of the game as outlined in our state campaign finance laws, Idahoans United for Women and Families colluded with the Idaho Democratic Party to mislead  voters and gain an unfair advantage. Idaho voters deserve transparency — not shell games and dirty tricks.” 
Idaho Democratic Party spokesperson Avery Roberts called the lawsuit “frivolous” in an email to the Idaho Capital Sun. She said it was “another attempt by opponents of Prop 1 to distract from the devastating consequences of Idaho’s extreme abortion ban.” 
“Women are being forced to leave the state for lifesaving medical care, and the politicians responsible have done nothing to fix it,” Roberts said. “Instead of addressing the harm this ban has caused, opponents are trying to silence the families speaking out, even after the Secretary of State’s Office confirmed our advertising complies with Idaho campaign finance laws. We won’t be intimidated into silence. Idahoans deserve to hear these families’ stories and make up their own minds on November 3.”
The family policy center helped author Idaho’s law allowing family members of an aborted fetus to sue the abortion provider for a minimum of $20,000. It has also been a supporter of Idaho’s criminal abortion ban, which includes felony prison penalties for abortion providers. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Idaho Secretary of State’s Office says office isn’t investigating ad, never received a complaint about it

Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane at the State Capitol building on Jan. 8, 2024. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun)
The Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane’s office, which oversees statewide elections, told Boise State Public Radio Friday that the ads did not violate campaign finance laws. 
Secretary of State’s Office spokesperson Joe Parris told the Sun Monday that the office was not investigating an ad about Prop 1 paid for by the Idaho Democrats because it had not received a complaint about it. 
The lawsuit includes a complaint to the office about financial reporting related to ads paid for by the Pickens campaign, but does not mention Prop 1 or a contribution from Idahoans United.
“Our office has not received a complaint on the ad that is at the center of this lawsuit,” Parris said. 
 What does the lawsuit say? 

Attorneys from the Idaho Family Policy Center argued that a donation from the Idahoans United for Women and Families PAC to the Idaho State Democratic Party was an attempt to “conceal” the source the funding and pay lower rates for TV ads. 
Within 60 days of a general election, Federal Communications Commission, or FCC, rules require TV broadcast stations to charge qualified political candidates the lowest rate they’ve charged for the same type of ad, length and time of day. 
These lower rates only apply to political candidate ads, and not “issue ads,” which are “political ads that are paid for and sponsored by non-candidate persons and entities,” according to the FCC. 
The lawsuit alleges that the rates paid by Idaho Democrats for the ads were much lower than ads paid for by Too Extreme for Idaho in opposition to Prop 1. It also argues that the party and candidate campaigns purchasing the ads after a large donation from Idahoans United violated Idaho campaign finance laws requiring disclosure of who pays for political ads. The attorney argued the move violated laws against attempts to conceal the funders of political ads. 
Family Policy Center spokesperson Edward Clark told the Sun in an email the organization had not yet filed a complaint with the FCC, “but we are considering all of our options to ensure the integrity of this campaign.” 
A letter from legal counsel for the Idaho Democrats to TV stations that received complaints from the Stop Prop 1 leaders argued that the ads complied with laws. 
“… note that both the IDP and Ms. Pickens strongly support Proposition 1, the Reproductive
Freedom and Privacy Act Initiative,” legal counsel Jessica Robinson wrote. “Ms. Pickens has repeatedly announced her support in public on the campaign trail.” 
She also noted that the U.S. Supreme Court recently ruled that limits cannot be placed on how much political parties may spend in coordination with a candidate for office. 
“As a result, IDP may lawfully spend unlimited amounts of its own funds on communications coordinated with Idaho Democratic candidates, including Ms. Pickens,” Robinson wrote.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Justice Department sending election monitors to 2 Arkansas counties on Election Day
text:
Signs for several candidates line the street outside the Pulaski County Regional Building in Little Rock, Arkansas on the first day of early voting on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)The U.S. Department of Justice will send election monitors to Arkansas’ two most populous counties on Election Day, prompting one of the counties to vote to not allow them inside polling places.
The decision to send monitors to Washington and Pulaski counties comes several days after the start of early voting. The Washington County Election Commission cited a lack of timely notification from the federal government as its reason for not allowing the monitors inside polling places.
The Pulaski County Election Commission will meet at 7 p.m. Thursday to consider the same decision, election coordinator Amanda Dickens said.
Washington County’s commissioners said there was no reason to monitor its elections, citing the accuracy of the recount it conducted in April’s Republican secretary of state primary runoff.
Commissioner Matt Mendenhall said he was frustrated that the Justice Department did not tell the commission how many monitors it will send until nearly a week after first announcing the plan.
“I think that some of those people from the Justice Department could learn something if they would come here and do it, but it’s got to be done right,” Mendenhall said. “It’s got to be planned, and your lack of planning is not our emergency.”
DOJ confirms it’s sending election monitors to Louisiana — and all 50 states

The federal government has the authority to monitor polling places, with permission from local election officials, to ensure compliance with election laws and procedures. The Justice Department confirmed Friday that it will send monitors to all 50 states.
Dickens said Justice Department officials told her they will send four to six election monitors, who will be in plainclothes and stationed 100 feet outside the polling place. If they speak to voters at all, they will do so only to ask about their experience voting, Dickens said.
“They said that they’re not going to be intervening at all,” she said. “They’re just going to be like a fly on the wall.”
Republican President Donald Trump’s administration has spent the past week trying to assert authority over election officials in multiple states. 
In 2024, when Democrat Joe Biden was president, Arkansas Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders’ spokesperson, Sam Dubke, told ABC News that Sanders would “not permit the Department of Justice to improperly intimidate or unduly influence Arkansas voters.”
On Monday, Dubke said Sanders’ administration “will continue to work with state and federal partners to make it easy to vote and hard to cheat in the upcoming elections.”
Republican Secretary of State Cole Jester said through a spokesperson that his office has “no objection” to federal officials observing Arkansas’ elections.
“Transparency and accountability are essential to maintaining public trust,” Jester said.
Nearly 280,000 Arkansans have cast a ballot since early voting began.
 Projected Democratic gains

The Trump administration’s actions come on the heels of projections that Democrats will flip at least one chamber of Congress, and some Republican-held U.S. House seats are considered competitive. 
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee is directing fundraising efforts toward central Arkansas’ 2nd Congressional District, and the Almanac of American Politics moved Arkansas’ U.S. Senate race from safe to “likely” Republican.

Arkansas Democrats look to make election gains in fast-changing Washington County

 

The move also comes as Democrats say they’re hopeful they can make gains in Washington County. 
The Justice Department has not disclosed why it chose the two counties it did, prompting concerns from Wendell Griffen and Dana Deree, the Democratic nominees for county judge in Pulaski and Washington counties, respectively.
The two candidates released a joint statement Sunday on Facebook, noting that their counties are among Arkansas’ most politically and racially diverse. Little Rock and Fayetteville are home to large populations of Spanish speakers, and Washington County has a significant Marshallese population.
“We are aware of no credible evidence of irregularities in either county that explains this deployment,” Griffen and Deree said. “The Justice Department should disclose its selection criteria and explain whether it applies the same standards to predominantly Republican-voting areas and predominantly white communities elsewhere in Arkansas. Neither a community’s racial composition nor its political preferences should invite selective scrutiny or intimidation.”
 Public feedback

The Washington County Election Commission’s decision to keep election monitors out of polling places came after half an hour of county residents urging them to take this stand.
Herschel Hartford, who uses a wheelchair, said the county has always given him the proper accommodations to vote.
“We do this because all of us are neighbors, not because federal overseers are watching over our shoulders,” Hartford said.
Beth Coger, who represents northeastern Fayetteville on the Washington County Quorum Court, said the area’s immigrant families have been afraid to go out in public due to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity in the area and nationwide for months.

Trump administration faces second lawsuit to block ICE agents at polls

 

“Against that backdrop, imagine how the presence of federal officials at polling places might be perceived by some voters, particularly Black and Brown voters, naturalized citizens, and members of immigrant families,” Coger said.
The Trump administration faced two lawsuits in September from civil rights groups opposing a federal policy to allow ICE agents to enter polling locations in certain circumstances.
For AR People, a progressive political organizing group, issued a call Monday afternoon for Pulaski County residents to “help defend local democracy” by attending Thursday’s election commission meeting and signing up for public comment.
“Respectfully ask the Commission to protect Arkansas’s Constitutional right to conduct its own elections, free from government overreach and interference,” For AR People said in a news release.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Vance visits Belgrade, stumps for Alme and Flint
text:
United States Vice President JD Vance stands during an event at the Bozeman International Airport in Belgrade, MT, on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. (Jordan Hansen/Daily Montanan)BELGRADE — Vice President JD Vance headlined a group of Republican state and federal officials stumping for Congressional candidates Aaron Flint and Kurt Alme at the Bozeman International Airport on Monday morning.
The stop by Vance is part of Trump 47 Committee events — an effort by Republicans to stump for their candidates in battleground states. President Donald Trump came to Kalispell on Oct. 14. Flint is running in a tightly contested race for Montana’s western Congressional seat, while Alme faces three challengers in Montana’s open U.S. Senate seat. 
About 500 people packed into the hanger, though organizers did not immediately have a crowd estimate.
Vance spoke for about a half-hour with a large flag displayed by two cranes behind him. He focused on giving “sovereignty” back to the American people. 
“If the Trump movement is about anything, it’s not just about beating Democrats,” Vance said. “As fun as that is, our movement is about restoring sovereignty to you, to the people who make this country.”
Vance’s remarks ranged from farmland to DEI. He also touched on race, the economy and his time in the military. 
“Sovereignty means that American homes and American farmland ought by right belong to the American people,” Vance said. “We have ended the tyranny of DEI and racial discrimination in jobs and in universities because I happen to believe that real sovereignty starts with the individual, and no person can be truly free when their government or their employer cares more about so-called white privilege than about promoting the American dream.”
He added: “You have a rare opportunity to vote for Montana Patriots who believe in real sovereignty.”
That message resonated with some, including Laura Doucette, an attendee at the event.
“Amazing experience,” Doucette said. “Just made me proud to be an American to be in a small setting like that, and just hear the values we believe in.”
Republican U.S. Senate candidate Kurt Alme holds an anti-fraud pledge during an event at the Bozeman International Airport in Belgrade, MT, on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. (Jordan Hansen/Daily Montanan)
Many speakers’ remarks also focused heavily on the border with Mexico, with Montana’s junior Sen. Tim Sheehy, a Republican, claimed there hadn’t been any “border crossings” since Trump took office. 
While the Pew Research organization has said that border crossings are at an historic low, between October 2024 and September 2025, there were 237,538 crossings according to the U.S. Border Patrol. 
Sheehy also pointed to protests in Paris, which he blamed on migrants moving to Europe.
“They literally have taken over a culture, they’ve taken over economies, and they don’t answer to anybody except themselves,” Sheehy said. “And that’s what can happen here.”
Flint, running in the state’s western district, is in a competitive race with Sam Forstag, which two analysts have recently moved to a toss-up race. Alme, meanwhile, is favored in the U.S. Senate election against independent Seth Bodnar, Democrat Alani Bankhead, and Libertarian Kyle Austin.
Bodnar was not mentioned by name during the event, though Vance did say that in the Senate race, Montanans “have not one, but two Democrats on the ballot.”
Both Flint and Alme gave their last-minute campaign pitches, which hit issues of law and justice.
“In Montana, we don’t defund the police. We back the blue, and that’s not just a promise,” Alme said. “That’s my record.”
Flint also highlighted his military experience, which has been common among Montana politicians — Sheehy and Rep. Ryan Zinke are both veterans as well. 
“I watched my daughter born over a computer screen while I was deployed over in the Horn of Africa,” Flint said. “And then came back home and got to fight behind the microphone,” referring to his time as a conservative talk-show radio host.
Republican U.S. House candidate Aaron Flint speaks during an event at the Bozeman International Airport in Belgrade, MT, on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. (Jordan Hansen/Daily Montanan)
Montana Gov. Greg Gianforte, state Attorney General Austin Knudsen, outgoing U.S. Sen. Steve Daines and Zinke all spoke during the event as well.
Gianforte, Knudsen and Zinke criticized Forstag for his time working for the ACLU and moving to Montana from Portland. Forstag moved to Montana in 2012.
“He’s a friend of Bernie Sanders and AOC (Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-New York), he’s for Medicare for all, the Green New Deal, and free higher education for everybody,” Zinke said. “Is that common sense or crazy?”
In the middle of Vance’s address, a woman briefly interrupted by yelling “liars,” and officers escorted her out of the hangar without further incident, said Koula Black, a spokesperson for Gallatin County. Black said the woman was not cited.



 Forstag holds flurry of events in Flathead as VP stumps in Belgrade

Flint’s Democratic opponent, Forstag, spent Monday in the Flathead Valley hosting a small business roundtable in Whitefish, touring a wood products manufacturing plant and meeting with faith leaders in Columbia Falls before heading to Browning for another event.
Forstag said Vance’s visit, coming on the heels of rallies with President Donald Trump and Speaker of the House Mike Johnson, showed that Republicans are “pretty desperate.”
“They’re desperate because they see the same numbers we’re seeing,” Forstag said Monday morning. “The campaign that I’m trying to build is something that actually builds community.
Forstag also said national Republican groups, including a Trump-aligned political action committee, are pouring millions of dollars into the race “to buy a congressional seat.”
“Aaron Flint bringing in his party bosses to bail him out does not tell me that he’s going to do anything to actually make life better for working people,” Forstag added.
At his stop in Whitefish, Montana state Sen. Dave Fern, a centrist Democrat, said the federal government has reached several forks in the road and chosen policies of “insanity,” and that Democrats can win the election if they are aligned with the needs of small businesses.
Forstag has promised to make working-class Montanans the priority in all his policies if elected.
“The federal government should supply stability, not chaos,” Forstag said. “And that’s not what we’re seeing right now.” 





 Yelling interrupts Vance

In the middle of Vance’s address, a woman interrupted by yelling, and officers escorted her out of the hangar without further incident, said Koula Black, a spokesperson for Gallatin County.
“She didn’t fight,” Black said. “She obviously was just there to I guess have her voice heard, and she left, and that was that.”
Black, who attended the event, said the person who yelled was a white female who appeared to be in her late 20s. The woman yelled “liars,” interrupting for less than 30 seconds, Black said.
Three of four law enforcement officers escorted the woman out of the hangar, and Secret Service officers flanked the sides in case she tried to flee or head towards the stage, Black said. She said the woman was told she could not be at the event anymore, but she was not cited or arrested. 
She said another female walked with the woman when she was leaving, but she didn’t appear to be part of a group, and the incident didn’t escalate.
“This was just one moment that occurred, and it was handled quickly and, I think, correctly,” Black said.



Keila Szpaller and Micah Drew contributed to this report.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Forstag holds flurry of events in Flathead as VP stumps in Belgrade
text:
Sam Forstag, Democratic candidate for Montana's western congressional district, seen during a primary season rally in May, 2026. (Micah Drew/Daily Montana)Before the sun crested the Swan Mountains on Monday, Democratic candidate Sam Forstag was meeting with a group of small business owners in a Whitefish bagel shop.
Sesame seeds, a topping of one of the best selling bagels, are more expensive these days, said Dan Moe, owner of Cutthroat Bagel Company, as are paper products and “all of the things” needed to run his business. 
Forstag, listened to concerns that global tariffs, the war in Iran and federal rhetoric against Canada — which has led to a decline in tourism in Montana — will continue affecting Montana businesses.
Afterwards, Forstag toured the SmartLam mass timber manufacturing facility in Columbia Falls, met with local faith leaders and then headed across the Continental Divide for an event in Browning. 
Forstag, running for the state’s western U.S. House seat that is considered competitive by political analysts, has kept a packed schedule of events every day in recent weeks as Nov. 3 looms. 
His opponent, Republican Aaron Flint, has drawn several VIP visits on the stump — President Donald Trump in Kalispell two weeks ago, Speaker of the House Mike Johnson last week in Bozeman, and Monday in Belgrade, Vice President J.D. Vance.
“What it says to me is that they’re pretty desperate,” Forstag said on Monday morning. “They’re desperate because they see the same numbers we’re seeing.”
In the last two weeks, three political analyses — Fox News, the Cook Political Report and Inside Elections — all upgraded the race in favor of Forstag, with two moving the race to “toss up” status. 
A Libertarian, Nick Sheedy, is also running.
Forstag said the presence of high-profile “party bosses” stumping for Flint is an attempt to “bail him out” and rely on spectacle, and that more and more political rhetoric in stump speeches, ads, and his opponent’s campaign, is leaning into fear and anger. 
“You’re not seeing any attempt from (Flint) — or frankly, a lot of people nationally in either party — to try to get past this politics of anger,” Forstag, 32, said. “That seems like it has been most of what I have known in my adult life, where most politicians are all too happy to … scream about everything that’s wrong with the other guy, but they don’t actually tell you how they’re going to make our life better, and then our life doesn’t get better.”
In Whitefish, an hour south of the Canadian border, business owners from around the Flathead Valley talked about rising costs due to tariffs, the effect of decreased tourism from Canada on their businesses, and a lack of constituent services from the state’s current federal delegation. 
Moe said as a food business, labor is his biggest cost, and the lack of affordable housing in the Flathead makes it hard to find full-time workers. 
Forstag said if elected he would push for affordable housing solutions to be part of H.R. 1, the first bill introduced under the new Congress next year. 
“This campaign is about getting back to the absolute basics,” Forstag said. “The simple notion that you should be able to work one good job in this country and afford a roof over your head and health coverage that actually gets you healthcare when you need it, childcare if you’re somebody like me who would like to stick around and raise a family and doesn’t want us to get run out of town because you can’t afford it, and a good retirement on the back end that you spent your whole life paying into. These are the things that 80% of us can agree on.”
Montana’s western congressional district is an open seat due to incumbent Republican Rep. Ryan Zinke’s decision to retire.

name: VTDigger
title: Local Fairlee developers want to build an apartment block. Their neighbors are standing in the way.
text:
Réal Hazen Construction co-owner Jonah Richard, center, talks to carpenters Larry Hatch, left, and Randy Welch about the finishing touches remaining on a building rehabilitation project that will create four units of workforce housing inside a home built in 1836 in Bradford, Vt., on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026. Richard hopes to build a new mixed-use project in Fairlee, but several residents have been vocal about their opposition to the project and to the Community and Housing Infrastructure Program that would provide necessary funding for it. Photo by Alex Driehaus/Valley News

This story by Sophie Levenson was first published in the Valley News on Oct. 20, 2026.
FAIRLEE — Deecie Denison approached her seat at the small square table in the middle of the Fairlee Town Hall meeting room. She kept her eyes, framed in red glasses, on a script she had printed out for the occasion — out of character for a self-proclaimed “adrenaline junkie” who has spoken at public meetings for most of her career.
From the 23 chairs arranged to face her, nearly two dozen stern expressions stared back.
“It’s painful to sit someplace and know that your neighbors hate you for what you’re doing,” Denison said recently in her Thetford home, which borders Fairlee and has a Fairlee address.
What Denison is doing is investing in a development named after herself. The Denison would consist of two three-story buildings in the center of town, with four commercial spaces and 22 market-rate rental apartments. 
The selectboard approved the project last fall. But to build it, Denison and her partners need a state financing tool called the Community and Housing Infrastructure Program, or CHIP, and the selectboard has promised residents a town vote on whether Fairlee can use CHIP at all.
Across from Denison, selectboard Chair Miranda Clemson leaned back in her own chair, one sparkly silver slip-on shoe resting against a leg of the table she shared with fellow selectboard members Lance Mills and Peter Berger. White-bearded Town Administrator Gene Craft sat diagonally across from her, monitoring his laptop screen as remote participants flooded the Zoom meeting.
“I know, it looks intimidating,” Clemson said to Denison.
Denison started her speech. She said Fairlee, which highly values tourist revenue, could benefit from a more year-round local economy. She mentioned the town plan, approved by Fairlee residents in 2020 to foster “a greater sense of community.” The plan’s specific goals include building housing and encouraging a diverse local economy. She stressed that The Denison needs CHIP to finance the septic system it would require.
“Without CHIP, The Denison does not get built,” Jonah Richard, the Fairlee native steering the project, told the room on Oct. 13.
Richard, 35, founded the development company Village Ventures, responsible for several new and renovated buildings in Fairlee. He leads the Denison project alongside Barrett Brown and Travis Noyes, co-owners of Chapman’s General Store and Richard’s second cousins. The three of them, along with Denison, formed Appleseed Development to focus on The Denison.
The Town Hall, an old white building, sits in the middle of Fairlee behind a gazebo and the town commons. To its right stands the dark red Chapman’s General Store, selling groceries, toys and local knickknacks. The next building over, 501 Main — another one of Richard’s projects — houses Sunnyside Coffee Company. Across the street, a marijuana dispensary occupies the old Citgo station, which Village Ventures renovated into a retail space a few years ago.
The lot next to the dispensary used to be home to the Colby Block, a two-story building that housed apartments and commercial spaces, just as The Denison would. In 2007, the Colby Block burned down, and nothing has since taken its place. As Denison and Richard see it, building The Denison will revitalize what was once the liveliest part of the town center.
Generally, Richard’s projects have been met with approval in his hometown. This time is different. A vocal group of residents has emerged with complaints about both The Denison and CHIP. Selectboard members and CHIP proponents worry that townspeople who oppose The Denison will vote against the financing program entirely, limiting the other projects Fairlee can afford for the foreseeable future.
“People don’t want to see change,” Denison said after the meeting.
Berger is now trying to persuade his fellow selectboard members to make CHIP a board vote, not a townwide vote, following precedent set by Burlington and Middlebury, which have both used CHIP for development. He said Vermont has been adamant about municipalities expanding their grand lists — the total value of all taxable property in a town — and that CHIP could be key to such expansion in Fairlee.
After Denison’s introductory speech Oct. 13, Richard delivered a presentation addressing the concerns he has heard time and again about his development. Until he, Denison and their partners get access to CHIP, they are stuck in limbo, unable to start construction and pessimistic about securing investors.
Defending The Denison
Old road signs plaster the Fairlee Town Hall’s blue-and-yellow walls. Faded red and green paint spells out “Titus Takes Tourists” on a dark wooden panel, the relic of a Fairlee bed-and-breakfast that closed two decades ago. 
All evening, residents introduced themselves by saying, “I’ve lived in Fairlee for a very long time.” One of them, Gary O’Donnell, piped up from the corner: “I don’t see why we need all this development.” Mary and Don Davenport, owners of the Wings Market on Route 5, shouted their assent from the front row.
Those frustrated with the project lobbed accusations at Richard from every angle. They insisted the building would require a level of police presence the town couldn’t provide, that the ladder on the fire department’s truck wouldn’t reach the third floor, and that Denison tenants might cram the town commons with their pets’ waste.
Richard lifted his hands and shrugged. “We’ll just have no pets,” he said.
“Everyone has an emotional support animal these days,” Dan Ludwig, whose wife, Georgette, is the town clerk, said later outside the Town Hall.
When Craft, the town administrator, started explaining that neither The Denison nor CHIP would increase local taxes, Bob Maddock practically burst out of his chair.
“That’s a false statement,” he said.
He accused Richard of turning a multimillion-dollar profit from The Denison while Maddock’s own property taxes keep rising. Then he brought up the fire truck once again, insisting its ladder only extends 24 feet.
Berger’s patience snapped then. He looked at Maddock.
“You were budgeted for a 40-foot,” he said. “If you didn’t purchase it and you don’t spend your budget, I can’t help you.”
Constance Geoghan challenged Richard’s claim that building The Denison would add only three or four new police incidents each year. Geoghan lives in New York and can’t vote on CHIP; she said her mother, who has a summer home on Lake Morey, can. The town, however, said Geoghan’s mother is not on the voting list. 
Geoghan’s family is also in a zoning dispute with a neighbor who hired Richard’s construction company for renovations.
“Your numbers are going to go up,” Geoghan told Richard at the selectboard meeting, her voice emanating from a black rectangle on the Zoom screen.
“We’re taking it from 1,000 residents to 1,035,” Richard said, his tone incredulous.
Geoghan told the Valley News a few days later that the four commercial spaces on The Denison’s ground floor would make the town busier, which might require Fairlee to hire another police officer. Fairlee Police Chief Wayne Briggs said last week that he’s concerned about the town’s population growing. As the town’s only officer, he’s already stretched thin, responding to about 600 calls a year.
“Anything like that’s a concern, when you add a big jump to any community,” Briggs said. “It’s my job to think of the what-ifs.”
Twenty-two apartments may not seem like a “big jump” in population, but The Denison isn’t the only development project in town, and even 50 people means big growth in Fairlee.
More than police presence, however, Geoghan has questioned CHIP’s significance.
“I don’t believe that a $6 million project dies on the vine of a $500,000 grant,” she said by phone recently. CHIP, however, is not a grant, but a financing tool. 
Richard is equally adamant about its necessity. CHIP covers infrastructure costs, and the Denison team wants about $550,000 to build the new septic system behind Chapman’s General Store, since the space zoned for The Denison lacks the septic capacity needed for any serious development. While that amount will finance less than 10% of the project’s total estimated cost, Richard considers it key to attracting other investors.
“From a funder standpoint, usually the riskier sources need to come in first,” he told the Valley News. “So this is the first step of the puzzle.”
Understanding CHIP
CHIP has a built-in “but for” approval policy, meaning applicants can use the tool only if they can prove that their developments could not be built “but for” CHIP. So it’s not just Richard’s word that he needs CHIP to move forward with The Denison: It’s up to the state.
According to Denison, wariness of CHIP mostly comes from confusion. CHIP is neither a grant nor a loan: It lets developers either go into debt or take out a bank loan. Appleseed would opt for the latter. Once the development starts to generate tax revenue, a share of the incremental revenue — not including the original tax value — goes to the lender to repay the debt over up to 20 years.
The share paid to the bank would come only from new tax growth. Right now, the empty lot where Richard wants to build The Denison has a property tax value of about $3,000. Appleseed would continue to pay that amount in full during the loan repayment period, as well as 100% of its taxes on The Denison’s new, much higher value. All of the original tax value plus 0% to 15% of the incremental municipal tax value would go to the town, while the rest of the tax bill would go toward repaying Appleseed’s loan.
During the repayment period, the town receives less revenue from the property than it would if it were built without CHIP, which is the essence of Geoghan’s argument against it. Nobody, however, has proposed an alternative plan; developers aren’t exactly waiting in the wings to jump on the empty lot.
“No one’s getting rich on this project,” Richard said in the selectboard meeting.
Fairlee would also get more out of the project even during the repayment period than it does now from the empty lot, with up to 15% of the municipal tax increment going to the town. Once The Denison is debt-free, Appleseed would direct all of its municipal taxes to the town. Richard has estimated he will pay around $79,000 a year in property tax.
The developers, not taxpayers, repay the loan to the bank. CHIP does not raise property taxes or municipal tax rates.
“It’s a win-win,” Denison told the Valley News.
‘The center of the world’
Denison could draw lines between almost everybody who showed up to the selectboard meeting earlier this month.
Having lived full-time in the area since the late 1970s, Denison knew most of the people at the meeting and counts several as her friends. She was at the Ludwigs’ wedding. Noyes and Brown are related to her godson. Berger had to recuse himself from selectboard votes related to The Denison because he and Denison are in a relationship. Fairlee is the kind of place where everybody knows their neighbors’ business.
The few full-time residents who have stuck around Fairlee care deeply for their town. For some, that means they never want it to change. For others, like Denison, loving Fairlee means pushing it toward a better version of itself.
“I’m headed to 80 now, and I realize that there’s not a whole lot I can do to make an impact on anything, except take care of the people around me as best as I possibly can,” Denison said. “And that means providing housing and community where I can.”
Denison lives with two fluffy corgis in a large house that smells like dogs and a bonfire. It perches on a hill above Fin and Feather Pond, part of her 40-acre property in the woods. Before her husband, John, died in 2020, he sold the house he had long kept in California and put the money into an account for his wife. Denison has used that money to invest in real estate in and around Fairlee.
“I am doing this purely” — Denison emphasized the latter word — “out of my passion for community.”
To her, “West Fairlee Center is the center of the world.” 
Since the controversy over the development began, Denison has felt that many of her friends and neighbors see her as a rich woman trying to rack up income by investing in real estate. She said it’s a feeling that has cost her hours of sleep.
In the past, harsh comments at a town meeting would have bounced right off her, but now they can bring her to tears, as they did at one meeting earlier this month. Denison is sure that plenty of people in the town support CHIP and The Denison, but said those in favor need to speak up. If she and Richard can’t apply for CHIP soon, they will lose momentum on the whole project.
Lisa Avery was one of the few positive voices at the Oct. 13 selectboard meeting. She stood up toward the end of the discussion, her bright mane of curly red hair grabbing the room’s attention. She said her husband, Mark, often complains that the people who work for him at the Lake Morey Resort cannot find anywhere to live in Fairlee. Avery is a social worker at Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center and works daily with families in need of housing. She also believes in the team behind The Denison.
“I’ve spoken with Deecie Denison on multiple occasions, and she has this vision. How phenomenal is that?” Avery told the Valley News after another selectboard meeting last week. “Sometimes you have to take those chances, and you have to hop off that cliff a little bit, and have a little faith to make these things move forward.”
Avery turned and walked out of the Town Hall. Across the street, the lot Richard and his partners have bought for The Denison sat quietly in the dark. A mini gazebo with a sign reading “Chapman’s Place” keeps it from total abandonment. 
Denison also commissioned murals by local artists to line its edge: Turtles crawl in one, and an owl tilts its head at the onlooker in another. Crop beds dot the grassy lot, another attempt by Denison to turn Chapman’s Place into a community hub. All of them are empty.
A previous version of this story said that Constance Geoghan’s mother could vote on a CHIP decision; a representative from the town of Fairlee clarified, however, that she cannot.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Opposition grows to Trump lawsuit seeking to aid Sen. Dan Sullivan’s re-election bid
text:
Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, speaks as Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, listens at the conclusion of a May 5, 2026, roundtable on Missing and Murdered Indigenous People held at the Cook Inlet Tribal Council office in Anchorage. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)One of the most prominent figures backing Sen. Dan Sullivan’s re-election campaign is speaking out against a Department of Justice lawsuit intended to aid him.
Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, said on Friday that the DOJ should have never filed a lawsuit asking a federal judge to pause certification of the ongoing U.S. Senate election if another candidate defeats Sullivan.
“Alaskans don’t need any help voting for their preferred candidates, and the State of Alaska has already handled this by clearly distinguishing the candidates on this year’s ballot,” Murkowski said in a post on social media. 
Sullivan is being challenged by Democratic candidate Mary Peltola, undeclared candidate Dan J. Sullivan and Republican candidate Gerald Heikes. Murkowski backed Peltola in a 2022 race for U.S. House but endorsed Sen. Sullivan for re-election this year.[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Dan J. Sullivan is listed on the ballot as “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.,” while Sen. Sullivan is listed as “Dan S. Sullivan (Registered Republican) Incumbent.”
In a complaint against the Alaska Division of Elections last week, the DOJ said that because Alaskans could be confused by the fact that there are two Dan Sullivans on the ballot, it would be appropriate to pause certification of the election results if Peltola wins. 
Legal experts say the lawsuit — and the federal government’s authority on voting issues in Alaska — is dubious. 
“I believe that this lawsuit is abusive in its intentions and borders on frivolous in its arguments, and that it is destined for defeat in the courts should it reach the merits,” said Walter Olson, a senior fellow at the Cato Institute, a libertarian think-tank.
President Donald Trump, who has endorsed Sen. Sullivan and visited Alaska to campaign for him earlier this month, said he ordered the DOJ to file the lawsuit.
On the day Murkowski criticized the lawsuit, Peltola’s campaign and the national Democratic Senate Campaign Committee asked to intervene on the side of the defense, alongside the Division of Elections.
Immediately afterward, they filed a motion to dismiss the case. 
“DOJ’s claim is lawless and utterly unsupported by precedent or statute,” wrote attorneys for the two groups, noting that the Alaska Supreme Court already ruled in June that Dan J. Sullivan’s candidacy did not harm the election.
The Division of Elections, represented by the Alaska Department of Law, has yet to respond to the federal government’s claims, and Judge Sharon Gleason, an appointee of former President Barack Obama, has not yet ruled on any outstanding motions.
Attorneys for the Peltola campaign and the DSCC have asked Gleason to set an expedited schedule of arguments and decisions that could have the case resolved by the end of the week. 
Legal experts have said that unless Gleason dismisses the case outright, it is unlikely to be ripe for argument until after the election. If Sen. Sullivan wins outright or Peltola wins by a margin larger than the number of votes received by Dan J. Sullivan, the federal government’s arguments would be moot.     
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

That’s because the DOJ has argued that some voters for Sen. Sullivan may accidentally vote for Dan J. Sullivan as well. 
If Peltola wins by more votes than Dan J. Sullivan receives, it would show that even if every Dan J. Sullivan voter was a confused backer of Sen. Sullivan, that confusion was not enough to change the result of the election. 
Two nonpartisan groups represented by attorneys from the American Civil Liberties Union also filed motions to intervene on Friday.
The League of Women Voters of Alaska, and Common Cause, a national group, said they are interested in having a free and fair election, and that the DOJ case “risks disenfranchising Alaska residents entirely.”
By email, Dan J. Sullivan said on Monday that “this experience has been beyond anything I could have ever imagined. To say that it has now become overwhelming and intimidating is an understatement. It is unending stress, at times paralyzing and I am looking forward to it being over.”
“I ran because I was unhappy with the status quo and wanted to be a voice for common sense, Alaska values and change.  With the litigation and threats, I was never really able to get up and running like I wanted, but I did the best I could under the circumstances,” he said. 
“As for the DOJ lawsuit against the state, it seems a gross misuse of the Justice Department for a situation that has already been litigated and resolved by the Alaska Supreme Court. I think the Division of Elections did a notable job of differentiating two candidates on the ballot with similar names and the primary showed there was little if any confusion. Alaskan voters are smart and I have faith in their ability to make an informed decision on their ballots.”

title: Wyoming teams with Trump admin to expedite energy, industrial projects
text:
Wyoming will partner with the Trump administration on an initiative to streamline and expedite permitting for large energy and other industrial projects such as data centers, representatives from both groups announced Monday.
Gov. Mark Gordon joined Federal Permitting Improvement Steering Council Executive Director Emily Domenech during a press conference Monday afternoon to sign a memorandum of understanding “to prevent unnecessarily long reviews for critical infrastructure projects.” The agreement promises to align Wyoming with the administration’s expedited permitting efforts, which have included shortened environmental reviews and public commenting periods.
“I’m really excited because I think the relationship that we’re going to put together today will prove mutually beneficial, because it will help make sure that our environmental reviews [and] federal environmental reviews are done expeditiously,” Gordon said.
Some federally expedited environmental reviews in Wyoming, however, have already caused heartache among residents and local officials, like the Seminoe pumped water storage hydroelectric project that has raised concerns about a prized trout fishery downstream and a bighorn sheep herd.
But the governor noted that some large energy projects in the state have endured years — and more than a decade, in some cases — of permitting reviews before final approval. The process can take so long that markets often change the economic viability and scope of a project.
From left to right, Siemens Energy North America President Rich Voorberg, Utah Office of Energy Director Gregory Todd, Colorado Energy Office Advisor James Lester, Interior Secretary Deb Haaland, Gov. Mark Gordon and Nevada Office of Energy Director Dwyane McClinton participate in a groundbreaking ceremony June 20, 2023 for the TransWest Express transmission line in Carbon County. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)
“If it takes us eight years just to get through scoping [the initial federal, state and public reviews], and things can change as dramatically as they have, then it really slows things down,” he said.
The Federal Permitting Improvement Steering Council, created in President Barack Obama’s second term, has been instrumental in implementing the Trump administration’s efforts to accelerate permitting reviews for energy and other large projects such as artificial intelligence computing centers. The agency, Domenech said, expedites permitting timelines while providing more transparency, including via its permitting dashboard — a tool that will now include information about Wyoming’s permitting agency actions on particular projects.
“We can help to make the environmental permitting process more transparent, more predictable and more accessible to developers who are trying to develop the incredible natural resources and grow the economies of the states across the country,” Domenech said. “This agreement we’re signing today is a cornerstone of what I think the president has really brought to every governor in the country, which is, ‘We want to help you grow your economy, create more jobs, bring more industry to your state.'”
The agency has helped the Trump administration reduce the average time it took the federal permitting review process from 1,500 days to 400, Domenech added. 
“I want to stress we’ve done that by following the law,” she said. “We’re meeting every single standard that’s set in the law. We’re finishing reviews on time and we’re making sure projects can move forward faster.”
Permitting heartache
Prospective developers, including many Wyoming-based companies planning to serve them, are not the only ones with heartache over the permitting process. 
Gov. Mark Gordon, Interior Secretary Deb Haaland and Department of Energy Secretary Jennifer Granholm speak at a TransWest Express groundbreaking celebration June 20, 2023 in Carbon County. The project took some 15 years to permit and gain approval from landowners. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)
Many industrial projects in the state have raised the ire of local communities that say they either don’t have enough time to keep up with the permitting process or that their efforts to tailor fit a project gets a cold response.
The Seminoe pumped water storage hydroelectric project in Carbon County spurred residents and local officials alike to plead for more time and local input, for example. Residents in Crook County say they were caught off guard by the federally expedited Bear Lodge rare earth mining project. Both projects were granted FAST-41 status — an expedited federal permitting review.
Asked by WyoFile how Wyoming’s cooperation with the federal permitting council might address those concerns, Gordon said, “The MOU will allow for better coordination with the state to make sure that we really do give those communities an opportunity to participate in the process.
“Being a FAST-41 project doesn’t guarantee you get a permit,” Gordon added. “There’s nothing in the law that says you get it. You still have to do all of the things that are required in order to finish the permitting process. But what it does require is that we have a transparent forum for anyone in the community to go and see that work.”
Domenech has made rounds in the national media recently to bolster support for a bipartisan bill now before Congress. It would galvanize the Trump administration’s efforts to speed up permitting, in part, by limiting state authority and litigation powers over approved projects, she told Bloomberg this month. 
“So how do we stop frivolous lawsuits from taking down projects and how do we reform the Clean Water Act so we don’t have a system where states can really veto any project?” Domenech told Bloomberg. “Those things have to stay in this bill in order for it to get to a place where it gets to the president’s desk and he’s ready to sign it.”
Is that in Wyoming’s best interest, WyoFile asked the governor.
“If all you want to do is stop stuff,” Gordon responded, “then [courts are a] really a great process. But on the other hand, you want to make sure things are done correctly, according to law and done in a timely fashion, we do need to have some permitting reform.”
Domenech said her agency, empowered by the Trump administration and the potential of further Congressional permitting reform, should provide a cleaner process to ensure projects don’t face court challenges.
“When we think about the best way for permitting to move forward, it’s more work on the front end to be more transparent and better coordinated across agencies so that you can have confidence in your permit going forward,” Domenech told WyoFile. “That’s the core of the permitting certainty argument, is you do your work right the first time and then it should be harder to sue that project.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Ringleader of $1.2B healthcare scheme to spend 20 years in prison, SC judge decides
text:
Prosecutor Samantha Usher and U.S. Attorney Bryan Stirling talk to reporters outside the federal courthouse in Columbia, S.C., on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — A U.S. citizen who pleaded guilty to running an international healthcare scam, then fleeing to the Philippines for two years, will spend 20 years in prison, a federal judge decided Monday.
Herb Kimble, 60, was the ringleader of the operation, which prosecutors believe to be among the largest in the nation’s history. His company swindled $1.2 billion from taxpayers. More than 80 people have been charged in the scheme, prosecutors said.
Kimble will have to pay back more than $199 million to the Medicare program. That’s the amount investigators believe he earned running the operation, U.S. District Judge Joseph Anderson said during a sentencing hearing Monday.
It’s unclear how he can pay that back.
“He was the architect; he was the engine; and he was the fuel that preyed upon elderly, disabled and the infirm,” state U.S. Attorney Bryan Stirling told reporters.
The scheme dates back at least a decade, prosecutors said. Beginning in at least 2016, Kimble’s company ran advertisements offering back, shoulder, wrist and knee braces at low prices to elderly and disabled people covered by Medicare. His company also bought contact information of people enrolled in the government-funded healthcare system to reach out directly.
At a call center in the Philippines, employees took down identifying information about callers, who often had cognitive impairments such as dementia, and attempted to sell them multiple medical braces, according to court documents.
Information on buyers was sent to a network of doctors and nurses who accepted kickbacks to sign off on prescriptions for medical equipment without examining, testing or even meeting the patient. The medical professionals prescribed only the braces offered through Kimble’s company, which were mass produced and not medically necessary or fitted to the people receiving them.
Kimble’s company then sold those prescriptions and customers’ information to fraudulent medical equipment companies, which fraudulently billed Medicare, according to court filings.
In 2019, Kimble brokered a deal with investigators to help gather evidence against fellow fraudsters involved in the scheme in exchange for a shorter sentence. Kimble’s attorneys and prosecutors agreed he could serve out his time on probation instead of in prison and pay back $40 million, which was the amount he was estimated to have in money and real estate, attorneys said.
For years, Kimble held wiretapped interviews with business partners that helped investigators nail down other cases. He turned over all of his company’s financial records and contact information.
In the meantime, though, Kimble, who was released on bond, made bad investments with his money, including giving $10 million to a concert promoter who promised to give him back $17 million and instead gave him nothing, said Jim Griffin, Kimble’s defense attorney. By the time Kimble’s sentencing hearing came around in 2024, he had no way of paying the agreed upon amount, he said.
Kimble instead fled to the Philippines, where he evaded authorities for two years. In June 2026, days after placing Kimble on the nation’s “most wanted fraudsters” list, law enforcement arrested him in a casino, said Samantha Usher, the lead prosecutor for the U.S. Attorney’s Office.
Prosecutors struck Kimble’s previous plea agreement, which had required him to show up for court hearings, and charged him with three counts of failing to appear.
“Kimble was promised an extraordinary benefit for his cooperation,” prosecutors wrote in court filings. “Bafflingly, he breached that plea, fled, and remained at large for nearly two years. There is no one to blame for these changes in circumstances but Kimble.”
Although Kimble was from Chicago and lived in the Philippines, he did business in South Carolina, which was where investigators first connected him to crimes. That led to the charges in the Palmetto State, prosecutors said.
With AI at their disposal, financial scammers are on the rise

Kimble apologized through tears for his actions Monday.
When he realized he couldn’t pay the amount he owed, he panicked and ran, hoping to make back the money, he said.
He also struggled with an opioid addiction after his doctors prescribed him painkillers following a rotator cuff surgery, he said.
“I’ve asked myself countless times why I made the decisions I did,” Kimble said.
Kimble and Griffin both pointed to years of cooperation with investigators as a reason for a reduced sentence. Kimble has repaid $9 million toward his total restitution and another $5 million in bond, Griffin said, acknowledging that’s a small fraction of what he owes.
But cooperation has to come with accountability, which Kimble tried to escape when he went on the lam, Usher said, adding that Kimble was motivated “not by desperation but by greed.”
Kimble’s crime was not victimless, she said. He exploited thousands of elderly and disabled people, including selling their information, and stole from taxpayers, said.
The 20-year sentence, which was the longest possible under Kimble’s new plea agreement, sent a message to fellow fraudsters that they can’t get away with their crimes, Stirling said.
“Healthcare fraud is just not acceptable,” he said. “You’re literally taking from the elderly, you’re taking from people in need, you’re taking resources that could have been used for someone’s grandmother that needed it or someone else. I mean, it’s just a terrible thing to do.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: U.S. Navy veteran, retired manufacturing executive face off in Legislative District 36
text:
The 2026 candidates for  Legislative District 36, from left: State Sen. Rick Holdcroft of Bellevue and Darin Tompkins of Papillion. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)GRETNA — Voters of Legislative District 36 will choose between a retired U.S. naval officer and a retired manufacturing executive to represent one of the fastest-growing areas of the state.
State Sen. Rick Holdcroft of Bellevue, a 2026 candidate for Legislative District 36, outside a Gretna coffee shop in the district on Oct. 9, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
State Sen. Rick Holdcroft, the Republican incumbent with a 28-year military career, wants to resume a quest for a safe haven “baby box” law, while challenger Darin Tompkins, a Democrat, wants to “protect” public education and raise the bar on business incentives. Both want to rein in property taxes.
“Service is really my forte,” said Holdcroft, 72, who has a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and a master’s in computer science. He touts fiscal and social conservative values and a pro-life stance, and he says his distaste for marijuana is based on the negative impact he saw on young sailors.
On the side, Holdcroft, who lives in Bellevue, is a beekeeper — an interest over the past six years that helped inform recent proposed legislation that didn’t quite get off the ground but that he hopes to resuscitate if reelected.
Darin Tompkins, candidate for Legislative District 36, campaigns in his district. (Photo courtesy of Tompkins campaign)
Tompkins, 56, lives in Papillion and said his political debut stems from wanting more affordability and less “brain drain” of workforce talent. That includes his blended family of six kids, ages 24 to 34, five of whom live in Nebraska and another who’s studying in Iowa.
“One of the biggest things I’ve seen that has impacted my kids, future employees and people who want to retire here is our property tax,”  Tompkins said, adding that reclaiming Nebraska’s financial stability is a top priority for him.  
The South Dakota native was attracted to Nebraska 27 years ago by a position in the animal health products industry and now has a “hobby job” that involves testing water quality and improving aquarium displays for fish, coral and plants. 
Holdcroft and Tompkins are vying to represent a district that covers parts of western and southern Sarpy County, including Gretna, Springfield and portions of Papillion and Bellevue.
 High income, good life districts

Of Nebraska’s 49 legislative districts, District 36 has the second-highest median income, ranks fourth in educational attainment and is among the bottom three for childbirth rates, according to Nebraska’s Legislative Research Office. 
It contains two of the state’s five “good life districts,” a designation established by lawmakers in 2023 to spur tourism-magnet campuses. Under that law, the state gave up half of the state sales tax within approved boundaries for up to 30 years, with that revenue to be steered toward developing the district.
Boundaries of Legislative District 36 in Sarpy Count. (Courtesy of Nebraska Legislative Research Office)
About 31,300 of the 41,000 or so residents in District 36 are eligible to vote. The Legislature and its races officially are nonpartisan, and political affiliations are not included on the ballot. According to state records, Republicans are more than double the number of Democrats in the district, 16,113 compared to 6,590; 8,230 voters are registered nonpartisan.
Tompkins is not deterred, saying his history includes being a registered Republican and a nonpartisan. In the primary election, Tompkins garnered about 53% of the vote. 
He turned to his past supervisory approach, saying that in the workplace he didn’t ask about party affiliation. Tompkins noted conversations initially driven by a Ph.D.-status manager that “completely flipped” when an employee doing the work weighed in.
“I don’t care where the idea comes from, I’m looking to make progress,” Tompkins said.
He said knocking on doors reinforced voter frustration that lawmakers aren’t “listening to them.” Tompkins cited pushback in the Legislature on voter-approved measures regarding medical marijuana, private school vouchers, minimum-wage increases and paid sick leave.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Two years have passed since a majority of voters spoke in favor of medical cannabis, for example, and he said he hasn’t seen a sign of a product. Tompkins  noted the Legislature’s resistance to immunity for doctors recommending medical cannabis. 
Holdcroft, as chair of the General Affairs Committee, favored a more restrictive approach in 2025 to defining qualifying conditions for medical marijuana. He said overly broad guidelines lead to recreational use. That wide-ranging proposal, which included provider protections, did not pass. 
Earlier this year, when the Legislature again considered immunity for practitioners recommending the medicine, Holdcroft was present but did not vote on the bill. That bill did not pass.
Despite his opinion that marijuana generally is an “addictive, terrible drug,” Holdcroft noted that 70% of Nebraska voters approved of cannabis for medical use. He said he respects the voters’ decision and looks forward to guidelines from the regulatory Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission.
“I don’t have a dog in the fight,” Holdcroft said. “I’m not planning on using medical cannabis or cannabis.”
 Safe haven 

Holdcroft and his wife of 50 years have five children, four who served in the military and one who still lives in Nebraska. 
He highlighted the expansion of Nebraska’s safe haven law as among his legislative accomplishments. That 2024 measure gave Nebraska parents and caregivers more places and time (90 days from birth instead of 30 days) to surrender a child they’re unable to care for without facing prosecution.
State Sen. Rick Holdcroft of Bellevue applauds an announced guest during Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen’s State of the State address on Wednesday, Jan. 25, 2023, in Lincoln, Neb. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
If re-elected, Holdcroft said he’ll resurrect a related effort that would allow a more anonymous method of surrender — in temperature-controlled, wall-mounted safety devices some refer to as baby boxes. He said he found a funding source to pay for four fire station spots across Nebraska: unclaimed dollars from personalized “choose life” license plates. 
“Most of my bills have to do with law enforcement and pro-life,” Holdcroft said. 
After retiring from active duty, Holdcroft, a California native, said that for a decade he worked for an aerospace and defense company, building a Bellevue operation to support StratCom and later directing nationwide field offices. He wants to grow Nebraska’s economy, citing agriculture, biofuels and power production as areas of potential investment.
Holdcroft expects to continue working with counties to find a resolution to unfunded mandates, which are rules imposed by the state that can drive up local property tax bills. 
Of the projected deficit, Holdcroft said he is concerned but believes that the state can find savings in administration and that the financial situation is “manageable.” 
Nebraska’s current projected deficit is about $208 million by the end of the budget period that wraps up next June. If that is not closed, the deficit would grow to $846 million through the next biennium, which ends in June 2029.
 Incentive check

Tompkins, who has degrees in microbiology and biology, said his work in the Legislature would be shaped by experience in private business. He grew from production manager to site executive director at Merck Animal Health, where he said he helped secure a $200 million facility built around 2020 that led new jobs into the Elkhorn area.
Darin Tompkins, candidate for District 36 in the Nebraska Legislature. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
“If you see the projections of what’s going on, from a business standpoint … would you believe what promises have been told to you and invest here? Those are discussions that happen in the boardroom about stability,” he said.  
Tompkins favors more state scrutiny on corporations receiving tax breaks and questions whether certain economic development incentives have delivered enough benefit to Nebraskans. He said he is wary of increasing sales taxes if it hurts working families. 
Tompkins and Holdcroft diverge on state vouchers for private education. Holdcroft is supportive. Tompkins said his wife works in a private-school setting, his kids went to Gretna Public Schools and he does not support public vouchers for private education. 
The general election is Nov. 3. Early voting is underway.
