name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Nearly half of Iowa corn acres harvested
text:
A corn field in Johnston, Iowa on Oct. 20, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Soybean harvest across Iowa has picked up after a slow start to harvest season and is now 6 percentage points behind the five-year average harvest, according to the latest crop progress and condition report from the U.S. Department of Agriculture.
Seventy-eight percent of soybeans have been harvested and slightly less than half, 47%, of corn acres have been harvested in Iowa, which is about 20 percentage points behind the five-year average. According to the report for the Oct. 19 through Oct. 25 reporting period, corn condition rated 73% good to excellent.
Farmers had 6.4 days suitable for field work during the reporting period as conditions were mostly dry throughout the week. State Climatologist Justin Glisan said portions of northwest and southwest Iowa were the only regions to report any measurable rainfall during the reporting period. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
While the statewide average precipitation for the week, at 0.02 inch, was significantly below the normal precipitation average, the statewide average temperature for the period, at 59.7 degrees Fahrenheit, was more than 5 degrees above the normal. 
According to Glisan, northern Iowa had temperatures nearly 15 degrees above the normal during the reporting period. 
Soil temperature guidelines for fall fertilizer
As the temperatures remain warmer than normal, Iowa Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig and the Iowa Department of Natural Resources are reminding farmers to wait for soil temperatures that are below 50 degrees before applying fall fertilizers. 
Research has shown that waiting for cooler soil temperatures can help to limit nitrification in the soil and therefore reduce the amount of nitrate that can run off of agricultural fields. 
“Iowa has experienced unseasonably warm temperatures this fall,” Naig said in a statement. “As farmers continue fall field work, it’s important to time nutrient applications based on ’50-and-falling’ best practices instead of dates on the calendar, especially with a warmer and wetter weather pattern setting up as we head into November.”
Agronomists with Iowa State University have predicted that the super El Niño weather pattern and wetter soil will cause warmer soil temperatures to persist longer than normal. 
According to the Iowa Environmental Mesonet, 4-inch soil temperatures across the state were in the upper 50s and lower 60s as of Sunday. Soil temperature forecasts from the mesonet predict soil temperatures will drop to the low 50s and below around Nov. 3. 
A news release from DNR also reminded producers to “monitor soil temperatures rather than calendar dates” as they plan applications. DNR and ISU agronomists have promoted the use of nitrification inhibitors to help limit nutrient run off from fall fertilizers.
DNR also urged producers and manure applicators to reduce the risk of spilling into streams by slowing down, being diligent and avoiding water. The department has reported multiple manure spills this month.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: DOJ to send election monitors to six Georgia counties
text:
Election workers process absentee ballots at the Fulton County Elections Hub and Operations Center in Union City, Georgia. Maya Homan/Georgia RecorderThe U.S. Department of Justice will send Election Day monitors to six Georgia counties, all of which are considered Democratic strongholds. But election officials so far say they do not see the move as unusual. 
Last month, Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon announced that roughly 1,000 monitors would be deployed across the country in what she called “the biggest DOJ election observer effort in history.” In Georgia, those monitors will be dispatched to Bibb, Chatham, Cobb, DeKalb, Fulton and Gwinnett counties. 
Their job, she said, would be to observe the elections process alongside other poll monitors.
“They’re not going to be interfering in any way or running the election,” she said. “They’re going to be observing, making notes, making sure that language accessibility is there, that disability accessibility is there, that nothing funky is happening and that people are able to vote.”
The Department of Justice did not respond to a request for comment Monday.
Outgoing Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger, a Republican, said that Georgia’s election process will be open and transparent, and he said that poll watchers from both major political parties and the Carter Center will be monitoring elections alongside DOJ officials. 
“It’s a transparent process, and we’re not concerned at all,” he told reporters on Monday.
Three Georgia counties flagged by Trump administration for using non-English election materials

This is also not the first year that Department of Justice lawyers have monitored Georgia’s elections. Many of the same counties that are receiving monitors this year were also observed during the presidential election in 2024. However, the prospect of federal monitoring may be raising more concerns this year in the wake of the Trump administration’s attempts to exert greater influence over election administration. Just this year, federal officials have seized 2020 election materials from Fulton County, attempted to gain unrestricted access to sensitive voter data and compiled a report of counties that offer election materials in multiple languages.
All six of the selected counties are also counties that presidential candidate Kamala Harris won in 2024. 
But county election workers, including Fulton County Elections Board Chair Sherri Allen, have not raised concerns about the prospect of federal officials monitoring the election. In a press conference Monday, Allen said that the county has scheduled a meeting with federal officials to discuss the monitoring.
“We are planning to meet with them about the nature of their observation, but we are not surprised by it and it’s not unusual,” Allen said.
Thomas Gillon, the Bibb county elections supervisor, also appeared unfazed by the prospect of federal monitoring.
“The DOJ sent a similar team to monitor our November 2024 election, and nothing interesting happened,” he said. “I suspect nothing interesting will happen again this year.”

name: VTDigger
title: Judge extends anti-stalking order for Burlington mayor’s protection
text:
Burlington Mayor Emma Mulvaney-Stanak speaks at a press conference in August 2024. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

A Chittenden Superior criminal court judge extended the anti-stalking order designed to protect Burlington Mayor Emma Mulvaney-Stanak — the latest development in a case that encompasses both First Amendment rights and the safety of politicians in the current political environment.
Aryeh “Ari” Moskowitz was criminally charged with stalking and harassment in June after Mulvaney-Stanak reported that he had accosted her on multiple occasions, causing her to fear for her and her family’s safety. The defense, led by attorney Robert Kaplan, argued that Moskowitz’s actions were protected under free speech.
Mulvaney-Stanak and other witnesses described multiple interactions with Moskowitz, according to court documents, but Judge Colin Owyang’s Oct. 15 decision hinged on two incidents. Although the court could have considered the other incidents as well, Owyang wrote that the court decided to exercise extreme caution to prevent any incursions on First Amendment rights.
Mulvaney-Stanak’s request to extend the order and Owyang’s ultimate decision were narrowly focused on Moskowitz’s actions, according to court documents.
“She nowhere requested any abridgement of defendant’s speech, only limitations on his unprotected ‘expression,’” Owyang wrote.
This ruling will extend the anti-stalking order for one year, requiring Moskowitz, a past critic of Mulvaney-Stanak, to stay 6 feet away from her at all times, according to court documents.
The first incident the court considered occurred after a Ward 5 meeting at the Department of Public Works building in January, according to court documents. Mulvaney-Stanak said Moskowitz blocked her exit from the building and demanded to meet one-on-one. She recognized a neighbor, Paul Fleckenstein, in the area and asked him to escort her to her car.
Moskowitz appeared to be agitated and “ramped up,” according to Fleckenstein’s testimony cited in the decision, and Fleckenstein said he felt it necessary to step between the two of them. 
After Fleckenstein walked with Mulvaney-Stanak to her car, Mulvaney-Stanak said, she took an unusual route home and felt the need to repeatedly check to make sure Moskowitz was not following her.
The second incident was in June, when Mulvaney-Stanak entered a Burlington restaurant with her executive assistant Penny Powers for a lunch meeting. Mulvaney-Stanak saw Moskowitz sitting inside the restaurant and continued toward a nearby bakery, while Powers stayed.
Shortly after, Powers and Mulvaney-Stanak said, they saw Moskowitz heading quickly toward the bakery, according to court documents. Mulvaney-Stanak searched for a back exit to the bakery and, finding none, hid inside the bathroom. Powers found her there and told her to stay in the bathroom and lock the door.
After Moskowitz left, Powers returned to the bathroom to fetch Mulvaney-Stanak, where she reported that Mulvaney-Stanak hugged her and started to cry.
Powers then called a security service, who escorted them back to City Hall.
After Moskowitz left, he encountered Shawn Burke, the interim chief of the Burlington Police Department, according to court documents. Moskowitz told Burke that Mulvaney-Stanak had looked afraid and had run away. Moskowitz laughed in a “sinister way” while recounting the incident, Burke reported, according to court documents.
After Burke told Moskowitz that his actions may have been a crime, Burke said, Moskowitz’s demeanor shifted and he asked to retract his previous comment, according to court documents.
The temporary order was issued in Chittenden Superior Court on June 12. Owyang extended that order for one year after deciding that Moskowitz’s actions were sufficient to cause fear for a reasonable person.
Moskowitz’s defense has focused on the issue of freedom of expression, with Kaplan arguing in a past interview with VTDigger that Mulvaney-Stanak is “weaponizing the criminal justice system in order to insulate herself from having to answer uncomfortable questions.” 
“She elected to be mayor, she put herself in that position by asking the public to put her in that position,” he said in the interview.
Kaplan did not respond to requests for updated comments in time for publication.
Mulvaney-Stanak issued a press release Oct. 9 after the latest ruling, framing this case as another example of attacks against politicians nationwide, particularly female politicians. She declined to comment further on the matter.
“We can choose the community we want to be — by naming this as unacceptable and refusing to accept it,” she wrote. “No political figure should ever have to experience this as the price for public service. And I stand here today to say enough is enough.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana 5th District candidates share views on abortion, redistricting
text:
Most candidates at a Louisiana 5th Congressional District election forum in Baton Rouge Monday said they were opposed to abortion rights. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)Four out of five candidates at a 5th Congressional District election forum Monday said they were opposed to abortion rights, while only one said he would oppose a national abortion ban if elected to the U.S. House of Representatives. 

“I’m a devout Christian who believes in the Bible, and I believe that life starts at conception,” state Rep. Gabe Firment, R-Pollock, said at a midday event the Baton Rouge Press Club hosted at Drusilla Seafood Restaurant. 
Firment appeared with fellow Republicans state Rep. Michael Echols of Monroe and welding business owner Austin Magee of Franklin as well as Democrats Dan McKay, a Bunkie attorney, and state Rep. Pat Moore of Monroe. 
Echols, Firment, Magee and Moore said they oppose abortion, while McKay said he supports access to what he considers part of reproductive care. 

“The Bible does not prohibit abortion. That is healthcare. It’s good healthcare, and it is for a woman to decide in conversation with her healthcare professionals,” said McKay, who added that he attends an independent Baptist church. 

Moore, who lost the Democratic Party nomination over her abortion stance, has a personal connection to the issue. Moore’s mother gave birth to her after being raped at the age of 14, she said. 

“Life is not in the hands of us,” Moore told the lunchtime crowd. 

But Moore said Republicans need to do more to help children born into difficult circumstances. In previous interviews, she has mentioned her pro-life stance includes supporting a robust safety net with Medicaid, food assistance and other government assistance. 
“[Republicans] want the baby to come into the world and after that, that’s it. That’s hypocritical,” she said. 

Echols and Magee said they both support continued access to birth control as anti-abortion candidates. 

“I believe that we should also make birth control as available as possible to also reduce the unwanted pregnancies because you can’t have your cake and eat it too,” Magee said. “If we’re going to take a hard stance on abortion, then we also need to take a hard stance on preventing pregnancies.” 
Candidates in the field who chose not to participate in Monday’s forum were state Sen. Stewart Cathey, R-Monroe, Board of Regents chair Misti Cordell, Hammond bail bondsman and retired police officer Omar Dantzler and Tallulah licensed contractor Antonio Wilson.  
Redistricting divide
The candidates also diverged on how political districts should be drawn in the future. 

The U.S. Supreme Court upended the process of drawing district lines nationwide earlier this year when it removed protections offered in the Voting Rights Act. In Louisiana, the decision led Republican state lawmakers to approve a new U.S. House map that dropped the number of majority-Black seats from two to one out of six total. 

Moore, the only Black candidate at Monday’s forum, said she strongly disagreed with the legislature’s decision to overturn Louisiana’s previous map with two majority-Black districts. 

McKay, the other Democrat, said he thought the Supreme Court went “too far” with its redistricting ruling but also that “race-based districting” has its own problems. It results in Black voters being packed into fewer districts, which dilutes their voting power, he said. 

Firment said he found the suggestion that he, as a white Republican, couldn’t represent a Black constituent personally offensive. 

“The idea that people in my district somehow don’t have a voice because they’re different colors than me — that’s ridiculous,” he said. 
Magee, also a white Republican, said he thought GOP candidates need to do a better job of reaching out to Black voters. 

“I have been to five forums where the crowd was a majority that had a different skin color than me, and I was the only Republican candidate who showed up,” he said. 

In order to use a new U.S. House map this year, Gov. Jeff Landry canceled a May party primary election after thousands of absentee ballots had already been cast. Candidates in Louisiana’s six district races were forced to sign up again to run for office, some in a different district after the new congressional map was put in place. 

Echols and Firment said they agreed with the governor’s decision to cancel the May primary election, even though voting was already underway. 

“I do think the governor was justified in that because the court decision was out … We had to do something to make sure our election was fair,” Echols said. 
McKay and Moore said the U.S. House race should have been held under the old map — with one more majority-Black seat — because the election was already underway when the court decision came down.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Chrissy Teigen will meet with Idaho mothers, speak in favor of Prop 1 at Boise rally
text:
Volunteers pass boxes full of signed ballot initiative petitions through the Idaho Capitol on July 2, 2026. The Reproductive Freedom and Privacy Act would restore abortion access “without government interference” until fetal viability, and would protect fertility treatments and other reproductive care such as contraception. (Photo by Kelcie Moseley-Morris/Stateline)Chrissy Teigen will be in Boise on Wednesday to campaign in favor of Proposition 1, which would repeal Idaho’s strict abortion ban laws and provide protections for the procedure.
Proposition 1, also called the Reproductive Freedom and Privacy Act, also provides protections for access to birth control, in vitro fertilization and privacy in healthcare decisions.
Chrissy Teigen (Photo courtesy of Chrissy Teigen)
Teigen, who is a New York Times #1 bestselling cookbook author, model, entrepreneur and advocate for maternal health, will meet privately with Idaho mothers to talk with them about how the state’s abortion ban laws have affected them.
She’ll then speak at a “Yes on Prop 1” rally, to be held from noon to 1 p.m. Wednesday at Treefort Music Hall, to encourage Idahoans to cast their ballots during the final days of early voting. The Treefort Music Hall is located at 722 W. Broad St. in Downtown Boise, and the rally is open to the public.
Idahoans will decide the outcome of Proposition 1 during the Nov. 3 general election. It would take a simple majority of “yes” votes across the state to approve Prop 1.
Under Idaho’s abortion ban laws, it is a felony to perform nearly any abortion, except to prevent the death of the mother, or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester with a police report. Doctors in Idaho can be sued for a minimum of $20,000 and be criminally prosecuted for performing an abortion.
“In September 2020, Teigen underwent a medically necessary abortion at 20 weeks after experiencing a partial placental abruption, a serious pregnancy complication that put her health at risk,” a press release announcing Teigen’s appearance said. “The pregnancy was deeply wanted, but the baby was not expected to survive, and continuing the pregnancy posed serious risks to Teigen’s health.”
Idaho’s abortion ban laws do not carve out an exception to protect a mother’s health, and instead only has an exception to prevent her death.
Teigen, who lived in Idaho Falls as a teen, is married to singer and pianist John Legend. They have four children.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ GOP ‘a little nervous’ as Democrats open wide preelection edge
text:
People line up for early voting at the Watsessing Park Community Center in Bloomfield on Oct. 24, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)[2026 election Voter Guide: Who is running in this November’s midterm elections?]New Jersey Democrats are voting in droves ahead of Election Day, outpacing turnout in last year’s gubernatorial race in all but two counties as the number of Republicans casting mail ballots or early machine votes declines statewide.
Republican Party officials acknowledged the declines and said they have spurred worries among GOP chairs in some counties over what the early returns presaged for Election Day, but they insisted traditional Republican areas would see GOP candidates through to victory in the Nov. 3 elections.
“You see what’s happening. It’s good for the Democrats, but I think it’s like calling a game in the second inning,” said Cape May GOP Chairman Mike Donohue. “You don’t have enough data to conclude that it’s really this massive thing.”
Early in-person voting in New Jersey began on Saturday, while mail-in ballots went to voters more than a month ago.
All 12 of New Jersey’s House seats are on the ballot this year, as is Sen. Cory Booker (D).
New Jersey’s three House Republicans — Reps. Jeff Van Drew, Chris Smith, and Tom Kean Jr. — are defending their seats in a tough environment for Republicans. Recent polls have put President Donald Trump’s job approval rating at an average of 38%.
As of Monday morning, 385,626 registered Democrats had cast ballots in the Nov. 3 Elections, dwarfing the 124,813 Republican votes made so far, according to a New Jersey Monitor analysis of preelection data.
Perhaps more concerning for the GOP is that, as of Monday morning, 19,529 more Democrats have voted than did so at this point in the cycle last year. Republicans have seen the reverse trend, and their pre-Election Day turnout is down by 38,618.
“In speaking with some other Republican chairs throughout the state, there’s a concern about it,” said Ocean County GOP Chair George Gilmore. “People are a little nervous.”
Gilmore expressed confidence that Van Drew and Smith, incumbents who represent Ocean County, would prevail in their races, a sentiment echoed by Donohue and GOP State Chair Christine Hanlon.
Republican voters have historically been likelier to cast ballots on Election Day.
Democratic State Chairman LeRoy Jones said his party had ramped up activity in Van Drew’s district “because the signs are giving us a good reason to make some investments there as well.” Van Drew faces a challenge from Cape May City Mayor Zack Mullock (D).
Kean, meanwhile, faces a competitive challenge from former U.S. Navy helicopter pilot Rebecca Bennett (D). Race raters say the contest leans in Bennett’s direction.
Though significantly more Democratic voters request mail-in ballots, voters belonging to both major parties have historically returned them at similar rates.
In 2025, Democrats’ return rate was only 1.1 percentage points higher than Republicans’ eight days out from Election Day, though it would expand to about 3.5 points once all mail ballots were counted.
This year, Democrats’ mail return rate is already 7.2 points higher than Republicans, and though the GOP has historically relied on stronger Election Day turnout, it’s possible the gap has already opened too wide.
New Jersey Dem chair LeRoy Jones speaks at Gov.-elect Mikie Sherrill’s victory party at the Hilton East Brunswick on Nov. 4, 2025. (Photo by Amanda Brown/New Jersey Monitor)
“It’s a full-court press all the way. We don’t see ourselves letting up on the gas at all. Every day is going to be better than the day before,” said Jones, who also chairs Essex County’s Democratic Committee. “I don’t want to get ahead of my skis here. I’m cautiously optimistic.”
Republicans lost last year’s gubernatorial race and a handful of Assembly races, defeats that blindsided Republicans and could have sapped enthusiasm for Republican voters and campaigners, Donohue and Hanlon suggested.
“We’re facing headwinds, and we all have to — as Republicans — work together to get the vote out and try to get our voters enthusiastic about coming out,” said Hanlon, who is also Monmouth County’s clerk.
Enthusiasm in midterm elections historically has flowed away from the party in power in Washington, Hanlon added.
It’s possible Democrats’ preelection voting gap only appears so wide because of distortions. For one thing, Democrats this year are significantly likelier to cast their ballots by depositing them in a drop box.
A little more than half, 53%, of Democratic mail voters who’ve cast ballots so far used a drop box, compared to 39% of Republican mail voters. Ballots cast by drop box reach election officials faster than ballots turned over to the U.S. Postal Service.
While election data shows far more registered Democrats have voted at this point in the race, the data does not say who those voters actually backed on the ballot. Mail ballots won’t be counted until after polls close on Election Day.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Analysis: 75 Iowa nursing homes qualify for abbreviated state inspections
text:
In September 2026, Waterloo’s Friendship Village Retirement Community was awarded “gold trophy” status by CMS and deemed eligible for abbreviated, risk-based inspections. That same month, state inspectors fined the home $5,000 for violations that resulted in a resident’s hospitalization for a broken hip. Friendship Village was also cited for failing to make a good-faith effort at identifying and correcting regulatory violations. As of Monday, the home still displayed "gold trophy" status on the CMS website. (Photo via Google Earth)Seventy-five of Iowa’s 393 nursing facilities are now subject to a reduced form of government inspection, a new analysis of federal data shows.
The National Consumer Voice for Quality Long-Term Care, a nonprofit advocacy group, has analyzed, on a state-by-state basis, the federal government’s new, shorter inspection process for nursing homes that’s based on the facilities’ perceived risk to residents.
Beginning on Sept. 8, 2026, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services began using the new Risk-Based Survey process for selected nursing homes across the country, replacing the traditional, more thorough process at those facilities that CMS considers “lower risk.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The homes deemed eligible for the abbreviated inspections are now flagged with a “gold trophy” icon on CMS’ Care Compare website, where consumers are encouraged to look for information on nursing homes and hospitals.
In deciding which homes qualify for the reduced level of oversight and scrutiny by inspectors, CMS says that each quarter it will be measuring every care facility’s performance using 11 separate criteria. A care facility must meet all 11 standards to qualify for the shorter inspections, which are carried out by state-employed inspectors on behalf of CMS.
Despite the criteria emphasizing favorable outcomes for infection control and staffing levels, a review of the Iowa homes awarded “gold trophy” status and currently deemed eligible for the abbreviated inspections shows some of those facilities have been cited for violating both standards.
In June 2026, for example, inspectors visited the Good Samaritan Home in St. Ansgar, and cited the facility for insufficient staffing and for infection-control issues. The home, inspectors found, had failed on four separate days in one two-week period to meet the federal mandate of having at least one registered nurse on duty for eight consecutive hours each day.
In November 2025, inspectors conducted an annual inspection at Wapello Specialty Care and cited the home for infection control issues. Today, CMS’ website shows the home is deemed eligible for risk-based inspections.
In September 2026, Waterloo’s Friendship Village Retirement Community was awarded “gold trophy” status by CMS and deemed eligible for the abbreviated, risk-based inspections. That month, state inspectors fined the home $5,000 for violations that resulted in a resident’s hospitalization for a broken hip. Friendship Village was also cited for failing to make a good-faith effort at identifying and correcting regulatory violations.
As a result, CMS temporarily suspended Medicaid-Medicare payments for new admissions to the home — although, as of Monday, the home still displayed “gold trophy” status on the CMS website.
No reviews of abuse history
According to CMS, only 12% of all nursing homes in the nation qualify for the risk-based inspection process. The agency says the new process will result in shorter inspections that are more focused on specific issues and are conducted with fewer state inspectors, freeing up resources to focus on problem care providers.
Some of the criteria homes must meet to be eligible for risk-based inspections are secondary in nature in that they’re based on other forms of recognition already measured by CMS, such as having at least a three-star rating for staffing levels on CMS’s Care Compare site.
Other criteria are based on a curve, such as a health-inspection score from CMS that falls within the better half of all facilities within that state.
Criteria that would disqualify a home from the abbreviated inspections include citations for causing residents actual harm or placing residents in immediate jeopardy during the previous 15 months, a failure to pass the most recent audit of the home’s self-reported staffing data, and a change in ownership since the last full inspection.
Also, homes that are already deemed to be repeat offenders and designated Special Focus Facilities are ineligible for risk-based inspections.
The differences between the traditional inspection process and the new risk-based inspection process include:
— Fewer interviews: Fewer residents are contacted and interviewed by inspectors. Traditionally, about eight residents’ care is reviewed, depending on a home’s overall population. The new process calls for about three residents to be interviewed, regardless of the home’s population. Inspectors will not be required to visit every resident room, but only to observe residents in a manner CMS calls “efficient.”
— Fewer investigations: Inspectors will only check in on residents who fall into specific “red flag” categories — such as those with serious pressure sores, or a recent fall resulting in an injury. According to the coalition, this means “an inspection can end with no investigation of anyone’s care.” Records for residents who died, were hospitalized, or were discharged are not automatically reviewed.
— Fewer procedural checks: In a traditional inspection, inspectors review medication handling, staffing levels, meal assistance, and kitchen sanitation at each 15-month visit. Under the risk-based process, infection control is the only regulatory requirement checked automatically. Everything else is investigated only if a specific problem happens to surface.
— Abuse history unchecked: Under a risk-based inspection, a facility’s history of abuse complaints is not reviewed prior to the inspectors’ arrival on site. According to the coalition, state inspectors preparing for such a visit are “specifically told not to look at whether the facility has a history of abuse allegations.”
The coalition has opposed the new risk-based process, arguing that the quality of care in nursing homes can change quickly. Using CMS’ publicly reported data from January 2024 through February 2025, the coalition found that nearly half of all homes that would have qualified for the abbreviated inspection process at that time were no longer eligible one year later.
A similar examination of the 1,699 homes currently considered eligible shows that only 54% would have been considered eligible a year ago, the coalition says.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: South Dakota task force recommends bills to move toward ambulance service regions
text:
A Humboldt, South Dakota, ambulance in November 2022. (Photo by John Hult/South Dakota Searchlight)Creating eight to 14 ambulance service regions might help preserve sustainable access to emergency medical care in South Dakota, according to lawmakers on a legislative study group.
The group’s members cautioned, however, that it will take years to hash out where those regions might be, how large they’d be, and how much the state would pitch in to keep them viable.
“It’s so important that we make everybody understand that we’re heading towards a funding model where there will be state aid,” said Sen. Tim Reed, R-Brookings, chairman of the Emergency Medical Services Funding Task Force. 
Task force: Regional ambulance hubs for South Dakota will take years to establish

The task force was created after the 2026 Legislature punted on a bill that would have designated ambulance care as an essential service. Instead of voting to do that — which would’ve created an expectation that the government ensure access to the services — lawmakers opted to convene the task force. 
It’s the second in as many years to have spent the months between legislative sessions studying the future of ambulance service. South Dakota has an aging, often volunteer workforce laboring on behalf of agencies that struggle financially due to Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement rates that are too low to cover the cost of operations.
On Monday in Pierre, the task force voted to endorse two bills that would open up access to more reimbursements and lay the groundwork for a new approach to ambulance service organization throughout the state.
The endgame remains the same, according to Rosebud Democratic Rep. Eric Emery, the vice chair of the task force: ensuring the long-term future of emergency medical services within the state’s borders.
“That’s what we’re really aiming for,” Emery said. “That when 911 is called and somebody needs an ambulance, that ambulance is going to be able to respond.”
Ambulance regions
The group voted to endorse the two pieces of model legislation in its final meeting. The group’s findings, as well as the model bills, will be included in a report offered to the Legislature’s Executive Board.
One of the bills would create an emergency medical services advisory council to study ways to regionalize service with state oversight and, eventually, state funding. 
The council would include four emergency medical services personnel, a city manager or mayor, a county commissioner or auditor, a medical director, a representative of a critical access hospital and a representative of a 911 dispatch center.
‘I have no reason to quit’: South Dakota EMTs still lending a hand in their 80s

The group’s discussions would center on how to divide the state into “at least eight but no more than fourteen emergency medical services regions.”
As they work to carve out regions, the group would consider the location of current services, how many emergency medical personnel are licensed in each region, population density, call volume, response times and the locations of hospitals and other care facilities.
The group’s findings and recommendations would be delivered to the Department of Health, along with recommendations on how ambulance services could apply for state aid. That department would then, in consultation with the council, set standards for response time, geographic areas, staffing and equipment, and work to figure out how much money the state and, to a lesser extent, counties and municipalities, ought to offer to support the new ambulance regions.
“On or before” June 1, 2028, the bill says, the department and council would deliver their recommendations to the Legislature and the Governor’s Office.
Eric Erickson, a lobbyist who represents South Dakota counties, testified that they would have concerns about any additional financial burden.
“We see additional costs every year, and this looks like a big one,” Erickson said.
Rep. Keri Weems, R-Sioux Falls, told Erickson it’s too soon to be concerned about local costs, because it would be years before a regionalization plan is ready to implement.
“This is a state issue, and this is where we need to have state funding available,” Weems said. “But we want the counties and cities to be players in that.”
Treatment-in-place
The other bill would require Medicare, Medicaid and private insurance companies to cover a wider range of treatment-in-place, meaning services rendered on-site by responding ambulance personnel.
When an emergency medical technician hooks up an intravenous flow of glucose for a diabetic patient in their home and thereby undoes the need for a trip to a clinic, ambulance services often go unpaid because there was no transport to bill. 
Medicare and Medicaid can be billed for such services, but the services are reimbursed at a “basic life support” rate, even if the services rendered count as “advanced life support” and as such would be reimbursed at a higher rate.
At a previous task force meeting, lawmakers learned that many rural ambulance service leaders were unaware they could be reimbursed for treatment-in-place at either rate.

The committee’s bill would require Medicare and Medicaid to reimburse at the advanced life support level if such services are rendered on-site, and require private insurance companies to do the same.
The bill would also require those entities to reimburse ambulance services for trips to places that aren’t hospitals. Currently, trips to places like acute care or a mental health clinic aren’t reimbursed.
Sen. Sue Peterson, R-Sioux Falls, expressed some concern about the appropriateness of trips to places like mental health centers, saying there are other options. 
“Would there be an alternate source of transportation, other than an ambulance?” Peterson said.
Reed pointed to language in the bill that would require any trips in an ambulance to be deemed medically necessary by an ambulance service’s medical director or program director.
“It has to be medically necessary to really transport them, where there’s no alternate way of getting them to the detox,” Reed said.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico off track for 2030 greenhouse gas goal, environment official says
text:
Claudia Borchert, chief of the New Mexico Environment Department's Climate Change Bureau, speaks to lawmakers on the interim Water and Natural Resources Committee on Oct. 26, 2026, about the state's progress toward meeting its greenhouse gas reduction goals. (Joshua Bowling/Source NM)At its current rate, New Mexico won’t meet its 2030 goals for reducing greenhouse gas emissions, a New Mexico Environment Department official told state lawmakers Monday.
A 2019 executive order from Democratic Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham charged New Mexico environment officials with reducing the state’s greenhouse gas emissions by 45% in 2030, relative to 2005 levels. The New Mexico Environment Department late last year published a “Climate Action Plan” that outlined more than three dozen steps for New Mexico to not only meet that goal but to also achieve carbon neutrality by 2050.
NM Environment Department unveils ‘Climate Action Plan’ to reach net-zero emissions by 2050

Claudia Borchert, chief of NMED’s Climate Change Bureau, on Monday told lawmakers on the interim Water and Natural Resources Committee that the state’s greenhouse gas emissions declined by 21% between 2005 and 2023.
While that’s a substantial cut, she and several lawmakers noted that it’s far short of the 45% goal.
“Current policies don’t have us getting to our desired outcome,” she said.
Her department’s plan outlines 45 steps the state can take to meet those goals, including decarbonizing electric grids; promoting energy-efficient building codes; and enhancing forest health and expanding post-fire recovery programs.
While state leaders in the Environment Department and the New Mexico State Land Office have spent recent years prioritizing efforts to curb oil and gas spills, plug abandoned wells and embrace renewable energy sources, some proposed developments could impact the state’s ability to hit its climate goals. Earlier this year, energy experts spoke before the Water and Natural Resources Committee and said that hyperscale data center proposals in New Mexico threaten to undo more than 20 years of progress on air quality, largely because of proposed “microgrid” energy sources that would power the data centers with fuel cell systems, natural gas pipelines and more.
The state’s shortcomings at meeting its reduction goal prompted concern from state Rep. Tara Lujan (D-Santa Fe).
“We really need to buckle down,” she said, citing New Mexico’s recent major weather events — including catastrophic flooding in San Juan County and a tornado in Santa Fe — as evidence that climate change is an urgent threat to the state. “It’s beyond critical. It’s a crisis.”
Lujan Grisham’s administration has prioritized regulations that tamp down on pollution in a number of industries. Last year, for example, she credited the state’s strict methane rules for bringing New Mexico’s emission levels down to half of those in neighboring Texas.
The state’s largest industrial sources of emissions still include the oil and gas industry, Borchert said Monday. They also include transportation and agriculture. About 83% of transportation emissions come from on-road vehicles, she said, noting that large trucks make up the biggest share of vehicles contributing to that total. In fact, passenger vehicles account for just 12% of the industry’s emissions, according to Borchert’s presentation.
New Mexico leaders have also heavily invested in renewable energy projects in recent years, including the SunZia wind project, which is the largest wind farm in the nation.
However, Rep. Randall Pettigrew (R-Lovington) questioned whether it’s prudent for renewable energy projects in New Mexico, such as the SunZia wind farm, to sell their power to other states. He also questioned whether keeping energy from that project would help New Mexico offset the emissions of other energy sources, he said.
“Let’s go back and do some course correction,” Pettigrew said.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Dan J. Sullivan switches from Republican to ‘undeclared’ ahead of general election
text:
Dan J. Sullivan Jr. is running for U.S. Senate in the 2026 election. (Photo courtesy of Dan J. Sullivan Jr.)Alaska U.S. Senate candidate Dan J. Sullivan is heading into the general election as an undeclared voter, a type of independent.
According to records kept by the Alaska Division of Elections, Sullivan switched from a Republican to an undeclared party affiliation when he requested an absentee ballot for the August primary election.
Sullivan’s status as a Republican was one of the reasons the division initially rejected his candidacy, claiming that he was not running in good faith. The division’s decision was reversed upon appeal to the Alaska Supreme Court. 
Polling indicates incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan and Democratic challenger Mary Peltola are well ahead of Dan J. Sullivan and Republican challenger Gerald Heikes. 
On the general election ballot, Dan J. Sullivan is listed as “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.,” without any party label. Dan S. Sullivan is listed as “Dan S. Sullivan (Registered Republican) Incumbent.”
Last week, the U.S. Department of Justice filed a lawsuit against the Alaska Division of Elections, seeking to pause the certification of the Senate election unless Dan S. Sullivan wins re-election. 
The department has made a legally dubious claim that the federal government has the ability to intervene in the election because voters could be confused by the two similarly named candidates.
President Donald Trump and other Republicans have repeatedly lambasted Dan J. Sullivan by name, accusing him of running a sham campaign in order to harm the incumbent’s chances of re-election. 
Dan J. Sullivan has said he is dissatisfied with the incumbent and is running to offer Alaskans a different option.
A former member of the Alaska Independence Party, Dan J. Sullivan became a political independent after that party voted to dissolve earlier this year. He changed his registration to Republican when he filed to become a U.S. Senate candidate in June.
When he requested an absentee ballot in August, ahead of that month’s primary election, he listed his political affiliation as ‘undeclared,’ an act that switched him from Republican to undeclared.
When initially contacted by email last week about the change, Sullivan said he hadn’t requested it.
On Monday, Division of Elections spokesman Steve Kirch said he had and provided a copy of Sullivan’s absentee ballot request form.
Informed about that, Sullivan said by email, “holy cow … I did! – I can only guess I was thinking that since they didn’t affiliate me on the ballot, I should go with that, but to be honest with you, I am frazzled by all of this.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Early voting in SC sets new midterm record
text:
(Illustration by Hill Street Studios/Getty Images)COLUMBIA — Early voting in South Carolina hit a new record Monday for a gubernatorial election, according to state Election Commission data.
Nearly 564,000 South Carolinians had voted as of 3 p.m., topping the total ballots cast ahead of Election Day in 2022 by more than 2,000 votes. That year marked the first election cycle under the state law that standardized no-excuse-needed early voting statewide.
The tally is still well below the all-time record. Two years ago, almost 1.5 million people voted early in the contest with presidential nominees on the ballot. Early voting accounted for more than 57% of all ballots cast in the election won by President Donald Trump.
Four years ago, early voting made up one-third of all ballots cast, according to state elections data.
Early voting continues through Saturday. By law, each county must offer at least one early voting location from 8:30 a.m. to 6 p.m. daily. Counties can open up to seven locations.
Prior to 2020, South Carolinians could vote absentee either by mail or at county offices ahead of the election, but they had to select a reason for being unable to vote on Election Day. Legislators temporarily changed that in 2020 amid the pandemic, allowing every registered voter to cast a ballot early in person without needing an excuse — or being forced to lie. But each county sets its own rules for opening hours and days.
The November 2020 election represented the first time in state history that more people voted absentee — about 53% — than on Election Day. But those changes died with that election.
The law signed in May 2022 that established two weeks of true early voting also changed rules for absentee ballots. It remains an option by mail, but only for voters who can’t show up in person either on Election Day or during the entire early voting window. The deadline for requesting an absentee ballot passed last week.

name: VTDigger
title: Voter voices from the Upper Valley
text:
Shoppers at the Norwich Farmers Market on Oct. 17, 2026 react to sudden snow flurries. Photo by Olivia Gieger/VTDigger

VTDigger reporters visited a variety of sites across Vermont in recent weeks, asking voters directly about the issues they care most about this election season. This week we’ll bring you those voices as we approach Election Day on Nov. 3.
NORWICH — Between snow showers on an otherwise sunny Saturday, tourists, locals and hordes of Dartmouth College students filtered through the Norwich Farmers’ Market on one of its final days before winter.  
An Oct. 17 snapshot of voters in Norwich, a reliably blue town that has nevertheless voted for Republican Gov. Phil Scott in his bid for Vermont’s top office in years past, revealed a desire for a change in leadership. 
Heather Daniels, a self-employed consultant from Hartford, voted for Scott in each of his previous races but is now ready to cast her ballot for the Democratic nominee, Amanda Janoo. 
“It might be time for a change at this point,” she said. 
As a remote worker herself, she takes particular issue with Scott’s mandate for state employees to return to in-person work. She said she worried it will limit the talent and geographical diversity the state can draw on, excluding many potential workers from places like Windsor County. “I feel like that was harsh, and I feel like that was a little short-sighted for the state of Vermont,” Daniels said. 
Marilyn Syme, a Pomfret artist, is supporting Janoo after years of voting for Scott. Syme said her vote is motivated by a national perspective, as she watches a Republican-led Congress and presidential administration with horror. She doesn’t want to see influences like that take root in Vermont.
“I think (Democrats) need to make a stand on every level and not take a chance that there’s any wiggle room,” she said.

Shoppers at the Norwich Farmers Market on Oct. 17, 2026 react to sudden snow flurries. Photo by Olivia Gieger/VTDigger

Jim Smith, a Thetford software engineer, was undecided. He said he was waiting to hear what both Janoo and Scott had to say in the gubernatorial debate that Vermont Public would be hosting a few days later, on Oct. 21. He’s voted for Scott in the past and suspected he may again.
“I don’t vote party line, that’s for sure,” he said, describing himself as a conservative Democrat. 
Smith said he appreciates the work the Scott administration is doing to consolidate school districts. Also, “land use is definitely important,” he added. 
Chris Gray, who runs the long-embattled Norwich Creamery, also said he’s undecided, but his convictions are clearer when it comes to the loss of small farms and working lands. 
“From a farmer’s perspective, when you look at the land, you see a lot of it being unused,” he said. “We’ve essentially turned southern Vermont into a land museum for the rich.”
And he said the wealthy should have to pay an entrance fee for that museum, or at least stop in the gift shop. “They should be taxed for their second homes,” he said, describing a vision for a wealth tax not unlike Janoo’s.
But he said more of that income collected could go toward support such as a universal basic income for Vermont farmers. “One percent of our population feeds 100% of us,” he said. 
“It’s a good industry,” Gray said. “We’ve got to eat. We make the best milk in the world. We should be making more of it. So I want a leader who’s going to reach down to us directly, solve problems on a one-on-one basis.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Voter voices from the Upper Valley.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Annual Kansas Speaks survey shows distrust in politics but support for Gov. Laura Kelly
text:
Gov. Laura Kelly answers a reporter's questions during a Feb. 24, 2026, interview in her office at the Statehouse in Topeka. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Gov. Laura Kelly remains the most-liked politician in Kansas, as public support crumbles for U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall, President Donald Trump, the Republican and Democratic parties, and politics at large.
The Docking Institute of Public Affairs at Fort Hays State University released its annual Kansas Speaks survey on Monday, which examines public opinions about politicians and a wide range of topics.
The survey found found unwavering support for Kelly, the two-term Democratic governor who will leave office in January, with 46.9% of state residents satisfied with her performance. That level and consistency of support makes her an outlier when compared with Republicans such as Marshall, whose approval fell from 34% in 2024 to 26% this year, and Trump, whose approved dropped from 43% last year to 33% in this year’s survey.
Alex Middlewood, who chairs the political science department at Wichita State University, and Michael Smith, a political science professor at Emporia State University, provide questions for the survey and analyze the results. Middlewood said she was surprised by Kelly’s approval rating, especially after Sen. Ethan Corson, the candidate she endorsed for the Democratic nomination for governor, lost the primary.
At the same time, the survey found high levels of distrust in Congress and national politics. Even 26% of Republicans say they aren’t happy with Marshall, and 21% of Republicans don’t like Trump.
“It is certainly not a good result for a democracy,” Middlewood said. “As a political scientist, of course, I would hope that that spurs people to actually participate in this election. But there is so much voter apathy, and when you have high levels of corruption, or perceptions of corruption, like that, and you have high levels of dissatisfaction, what often happens is that people just don’t participate because they don’t think that their voice matters. They don’t think that voting is going to change anything. Where, again, as a political scientist, that is not true.”
She said those who participate in politics see how they can make change and have higher levels of trust in government.
“When voters have distrust, they’re less likely to participate,” she said. “And so, it’s really this mutually reinforcing cycle where people don’t participate because they don’t have trust. But then they have lower levels of trust because they’re not participating and they’re not seeing any change.”
 
On the issues
The weighted online survey results are based on 603 adults who answered 57 questions between Sept. 23 and Oct. 16. They survey examined attitudes on quality of life, economy, sin taxes, Medicaid expansion, family and medical leave, marijuana, abortion, immigration, education, homelessness, guns, petition initiatives, and data centers.
“Ours is one of the first honest-to-goodness public opinion surveys I’ve ever seen asking people about data centers in a way that’s not clearly meant to lead toward a preferred answer for an interest group, pro or con, and I think that’s kind of a big deal. I’m kind of proud of that,” said Emporia State’s Smith.
The survey shows most people are wary of data centers.
A little more than a third said they were aware of a proposal to put a data center in their community.  Most were concerned about energy and water usage and the AI made possible by data centers. More than 40% were concerned about data centers being targeted by terrorists or foreign governments, as well as the heat they generate, land use and noise. About one-third were concerned about new solar installations to power data centers.
About 40% said they thought data centers would have a negative impact on the economy in the community where they were located, while 30.5% anticipated a positive impact.
“In communities like Emporia and others, there are people organizing against the data centers,” Smith said. “And the argument you’re always going to get is, well, that represents the activists. You get a couple hundred people at a town hall meeting in a town with a population of 20,000 … it’s a tiny percentage of the population. Now we have data about just regular folks, not activists, and overwhelmingly, it’s showing they’re pretty concerned about data centers.”
On other issues:

About two-thirds support Medicaid expansion, but only about one-third say they think about it a lot as a political issue.
About two-thirds support legalizing medical marijuana, and nearly 60% support recreational use.
Most people had favorable views of “legal immigrants,” while 42.8% believe “illegal” immigrants are a danger to public safety.
About 75% were comfortable with supporting K-12 schools with their tax dollars, and 53.8% said funding education was more important than cutting taxes. About 37% preferred to cut taxes.
Most Kansans don’t think people should be able to carry a handgun without a license or permit. They also don’t want guns on college campuses. Wide majorities support keeping guns from people who are dangerous to themselves or others. They also support background checks on sales at gun shows. About 42% said there was a gun in their houses.
Nearly 69% support paid family and medical leave, while 11.4% oppose.
A little more than 51% support giving Kansans the ability to place questions on the ballot through petition initiatives, while 12.2% oppose the idea. When informed that bordering states have petition initiatives, 58.4% supported the idea while 7.7% were opposed.

 
Kansas life
About half of the survey respondents said Kansas is a good or excellent place to live, a less favorable view than in past years, while 14.4% said they plan to leave the state.
Few people think the state’s economy is good. About half think it is getting worse. And when asked to rank the most important issues, 45% said the economy was No. 1.
“We wanted to ask, are people actually feeling the economy in their cost of living and what they are paying week to week,” Middlewood said.
The answer: “Kansans are feeling higher cost of living, and so we can make the assumption” that it will influence their votes, she said.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont officials raise concerns over ‘heated’ confrontations between voters, town clerks ahead of Election Day
text:
Vermont’s Democratic Secretary of State Sarah Copeland Hanzas and Republican Gov. Phil Scott speak at a press conference on Monday in Montpelier about the upcoming 2026 general election. Photo by Shaun Robinson/VTDigger

MONTPELIER — Top state officials on Monday urged Vermonters to turn down the temperature amid an uptick in what one called “heated” confrontations between voters and local city and town clerks about the integrity of next week’s general election.
The rhetoric from people who are “agitated” and unsure of the process is fueled by “a lot of misinformation that’s coming out of Washington, D.C. — daily, nightly social media posts from the president — about how elections work,” said Sarah Copeland Hanzas, Vermont’s Democratic secretary of state, at a press conference in Montpelier.
She was joined by Gov. Phil Scott, a Republican. Scott said the state government and Vermont law enforcement will “do whatever we have to do” to help town and city officials run the Nov. 3 election safely and securely. That could include preventing federal officials from exerting undue influence over the voting process, which is run by the state, he said.
President Donald Trump’s administration has taken unprecedented steps to assert more control over elections during Trump’s second term. Last week, for example, the federal government moved to preemptively challenge the certification of Alaska’s U.S. Senate election if the Republican candidate there narrowly loses.
“The (U.S.) Constitution is clear on this: The elections are the responsibility of the states. We take that very seriously,” Scott told reporters. “So, from our standpoint, we will do everything within our power to protect the process — and we will counter anything that comes up.”
Copeland Hanzas, who is Vermont’s top election official, said she was not aware of any specific threats to polling places in the state as of Monday and added that the heated rhetoric she described was not centered on any one geographic area.
The press conference came as about 101,400 people had already cast a Vermont general election ballot as of Monday morning, according to Copeland Hanzas’ office. That’s about a fifth of the 500,700 total registered voters in the state. 
The number of people who’ve voted early is down from recent years, though. At this point in 2024, about 141,500 ballots had been cast; at this point in 2022, that figure was just shy of 113,400, Copeland Hanzas said. Turnout is consistently higher in years with a presidential election, like 2024, than in midterm years, like 2022 and 2026. 
Copeland Hanzas said it’s also possible people have less confidence in the security of mail-in voting this year than in the past because Trump has tried to curtail people’s access to mail-in voting, plans that have so far been struck down in court. 
Scott, meanwhile, said the well-documented mail delivery delays around Vermont have meant some voters still have not received their ballots. Anyone who has not received a ballot by this point, and who wants to vote early, should go to their local clerk’s office and fill one out there, Copeland Hanzas said. 
She and Scott said the state is planning for “any number of contingencies” during next week’s voting, including power outages, internet outages or other communications disruptions, physical threats to election workers and the appearance of federal immigration agents at polling locations.
The Trump administration said earlier this month that it would not send U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to polling locations around the country en masse, but it would not rule out their presence entirely. Vermont officials would be unlikely to get much if any heads up about such activity from the feds, Copeland Hanzas said. 
Scott said the state Agency of Digital Services has taken additional steps this year to protect the secretary of state’s website and online election management system out of a concern for cyberattacks. State officials have also been meeting with city and town clerks, as well as local law enforcement and the Vermont State Police, to make sure there’s a shared understanding of the rules governing where and how people can observe the voting process and what activities are permitted at the polls. 
Federal law prohibits the military or federal officials from stationing “troops or armed men” at polling locations, according to the secretary of state’s office, though federal agents are generally allowed to operate in any public place that’s near a polling station. 
The goal, Copeland Hanzas said, is that “our law enforcement partners will be able to respond and be prepared to uphold Vermont law.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Salt Lake County to hold early voting for the 1st time on a Saturday — Halloween day
text:
Voters wait in line on primary Election Day at the Salt Lake County Government Center on Tuesday, June 23, 2026. (Photo by Marco Lozzi for Utah News Dispatch)Salt Lake County Clerk Lannie Chapman has announced that her office will offer early in-person voting for the first time on a Saturday, Halloween day. 
“We’re excited to offer early voting on a Saturday for the first time,” said Chapman said in a news release announcing the new early voting option. “We hope this makes it even more convenient for voters to cast their ballot and make their voice heard.”
The Salt Lake County Clerk’s Office will be open for early voting on Saturday from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. in the South Building of the Salt Lake County Government Center, at 2001 South State Street in Salt Lake City. 
Voter Guide: 2026 General Election

By default, Utah clerks automatically send by-mail ballots to all eligible registered voters, but voters who prefer to vote in person have the option to do so at their local county clerks’ offices. 
Early in-person voting began last week, Oct. 20, at the Salt Lake County Government Center, but starting Tuesday, county officials will expand that option to seven additional locations. 
It’s the first time that early voting will be available on a Saturday in Salt Lake County. 
To vote in person, the clerk’s office encouraged voters to bring valid voter identification. Any eligible Salt Lake County voter can choose to vote in person on Saturday or other days leading up to the Nov. 3 election. 
“Because the day falls on Halloween, voters are welcome to celebrate, but costumes that cover the face should be left at home,” the clerk’s office said in Friday’s news release. 
For those who have their by-mail ballots in hand, they can choose to mail them back to the clerk’s office through the postal service. Voters can also drop off their ballots at early voting locations, including on Saturday, or at designated drop boxes located throughout the county and state. 
More information about how to vote in the election, including voting locations and hours, ballot drop box locations, and ID requirements is available on the county’s website. 
Election Day is on Tuesday next week. Polls will close that day at 8 p.m.

name: VTDigger
title: Burlington mayor picks new chief of police
text:
The Burlington Police Department on North Avenue in Burlington on Thursday, August 13, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Burlington’s mayor has selected a longtime New York police official to be the city’s next police chief. 
Anthony Geraci served in various New York police departments throughout his career, beginning with the New York City Police Department in 1998. He later moved upstate to Albany, and served as police chief in Watervliet and Newburgh, according to Seven Days and Vermont News First. Most recently, Geraci worked for Strategic Government Resources, a Texas-based recruitment firm.
“He is an exceptional candidate with the experience, character, and values to meet our community safety challenges, and I am confident he will be a strong leader to bring the Burlington Police Department into its next chapter,” Mayor Emma Mulvaney-Stanak wrote in a statement Monday. 
Mulvaney-Stanak had yet to publicly announce her decision when the selection was first reported by Vermont News First on Sunday. His appointment follows a months-long selection process which began in July. 
Geraci will replace Burlington’s interim Police Chief Shawn Burke. Burke stepped down as South Burlington’s police chief to take on the interim role beginning in March 2025. 
Former Police Chief Jon Murad did not seek reappointment in 2025 after he and Mulvaney-Stanak, a Progressive, clashed over their approaches to public safety, as Burlington has debated reducing its police force by 30% since 2020. The city has struggled to manage homelessness and drug use, asking Gov. Phil Scott for help in August.
Geraci, leaves behind several controversies from his time in New York. Efforts to reach him for comment on Monday were unsuccessful.
The city of Watervliet placed Geraci on leave after 10 months, claiming it was facing budget constraints related to the Covid-19 pandemic. Watervliet’s police union backed him when he was asked not to return, telling a local news outlet that Geraci’s firing was “personal in nature.” The union said they believed his dismissal was a result of changes he made in the department which deprioritized profit from ticketing motorists, The Times Union reported.
Geraci then served as chief for Newburgh between 2021 and 2024. He left the department amid accusations of misconduct by three women, according to Hudson Valley News 12. Geraci told the news outlet that an independent investigator cleared him of any official wrongdoing, and moved to serve as the director of security for Newburgh schools between May 2024 and February 2025. Geraci said he left that position after changes in district leadership “no longer aligned with my personal values,” Westchester News 12 reported.
Burlington’s city council is expected to vote on Geraci’s appointment at a meeting on Nov. 9.

name: VTDigger
title: Inside the confidential contest to lead Vermont’s most powerful healthcare regulator
text:
Emily Brown, the executive director of the Green Mountain Care Board, leads the work of the regulator, under the direction of the chair. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger.
A confidential contest to see who will assume one of the most powerful seats in Vermont’s healthcare landscape is now taking shape.  
When Green Mountain Care Board chair Owen Foster announced in July that he would be stepping down, it kicked off the formal process to find his replacement. 
Vermont law stipulates that a nine-person nominating committee — composed of senators, representatives and healthcare experts appointed by the governor and legislative leaders — submit a list of qualified applicants to the governor. Then the governor picks their preferred candidate, who is subject to approval by the Senate, much like the judicial appointment process. 
The process is confidential, but that does not mean it escapes public scrutiny, especially as the board’s role has seen a “seismic shift” under Foster’s tenure, as one observer put it. And the soil is fertile for change under new leadership: At the end of September a healthcare watchdog group gave a broad overview for how the Green Mountain Care Board can expand the metrics and processes it uses to set hospital budgets and insurance premium increases. 
Gov. Phil Scott is advocating for ways to “reform (Vermont’s) regulatory system away from the legacy architecture” of single payer, as a representative for his campaign wrote to VTDigger earlier this month. The care board is the main regulatory body that still exists in the wake of the single-payer effort. 
The board’s role in Vermont’s healthcare system has evolved since its 2011 creation as part of a push for single-payer. Now, the board’s chief responsibilities include approving hospital budgets and health insurance premium increases for plans sold on Vermont’s Affordable Care Act marketplace. Under Foster, the board has taken that authority seriously, slashing the revenue hospitals are allowed to collect from commercial insurers year after year in an effort to force lower prices for insurers and their patients. 
The stakes are high for consumers, with the cost of premiums for individual marketplace plans compounding to increase 74.6% between 2021-2025, according to the office of the Health Care Advocate. The care board has tried to curtail that drastically, approving increases between 1% and 6% for those individual and small group plans for 2027, even as the rest of the nation sees median increases of 15%.
Foster described the chair as wearing two hats. In one, the chair has equal voting power to any of the other four board members. But wearing the other, the chair has the unique authority to direct the care board office and staff of nearly 30. The chair sets the care board’s policy priorities, the research its analysts do, its legislative stance, and relationships with other agencies, the governor’s administration and the federal delegation.
“By being able to task the office with what work to take on, you can decide what problems get understood and they get addressed,” Foster, who remains as the care board’s interim chair until his replacement is selected, told VTDigger in an interview. 
Foster will leave Vermont’s hospitals in a different place from where he found them when he joined the board in 2022. After a tenure defined by an effort to shrink hospital budgets and move care to lower-cost settings, Foster ended by supporting less aggressive budget cuts for the state’s largest hospital, University of Vermont Medical Center.
“I hope that the next chair continues that trajectory,” said Chris Pearson, who now leads the healthcare advocacy group VT Healthcare 911. He previously sat on the care board nominating committee.  
Pearson described the change in the healthcare landscape from one where “spending at hospitals had really ballooned and our premiums were top in the nation,” to one where hospitals, insurers and regulators alike are working towards a shared goal of keeping costs low. 
“Frankly, now we are centering Vermonters and the affordability question in the process, which had been missing for a long time,” he said. “I think our state owes (Foster) tremendous gratitude for being willing to tackle just a massive industry.” 
But the decision on how the next chair might continue, complement or counteract Foster’s legacy is entirely up to the governor. It’s not the selection committee’s job to prioritize any specific philosophy on regulating, Pearson said. It’s really just a vetting body to send the governor qualified candidates.
“In some ways it’s dull. I didn’t get to inject my politics into the process,” Pearson said.
To Sen. Ginny Lyons, D-Chittenden Southeast, who chairs the Senate’s healthcare committee and also previously sat on the selection committee, an apolitical approach is the point. 
The committee should look for someone with “the capacity to understand and distinguish what really needs to happen without taking one’s prejudice or bias into that decision making,” she said. 
Still, she said, it’s important to listen to the ways a candidate articulates ideas for how the board may be improved and which parts of the healthcare system need better regulation. 

READ MORE

Specifically, she is curious to see how the new chair will approach costs embedded in the healthcare system beyond the board’s regulatory scope — things such as primary care or self-employed and employer-sponsored insurance plans.
In a written statement to VTDigger, Scott’s press secretary Amanda Wheeler said that the governor has encouraged the nominating committee to seek qualified candidates, including those with “a proven ability to improve organizational performance.”
“As Vermont works to improve access, increase affordable choices, and reduce costs, the next Chair of the Green Mountain Care Board will play a critical role in helping build a healthcare system that is more affordable, transparent and accountable to the people it serves,” Wheeler wrote.
Foster advised the new chair to look broadly at the healthcare system. 
“The Green Mountain Care Board’s biggest lever, by far, is hospital budgets,” he said. “But it’s not unlimited.”
Now the areas with the biggest potential to reduce costs lie in sectors the board has no authority over, according to Foster. Savings need to come from the ongoing work of redesigning the hospital system, addressing pharmaceutical costs or regulating other insurance plans, he said. 
“As a state we need to get together and determine what the affordability goals actually are and define them and say what they are, and then come up with a plan as a state as to where to get there,” Foster said.

name: VTDigger
title: Can we trust the polls?
text:
This commentary is by Geoffrey Skelley, chief elections analyst for Decision Desk HQ, which provides independent results and analysis for U.S. elections.
Can we trust the polls? As an election analyst, I often get this question. That’s understandable. Polls underestimated Donald Trump’s support in the 2016, 2020 and 2024 presidential elections. This November, Democrats are clearly favored to capture the U.S. House of Representatives and have a realistic shot at flipping the U.S. Senate.
The answer? Yes, we can trust the polls — but only if we allow for uncertainty. That means not relying on one poll, but looking at them in aggregate, which usually means looking at a polling average. After all, polls are snapshots in time, so one poll alone can only gauge support at a particular moment.
Every poll will have some degree of polling error, some larger, some smaller. Surveys are statistical instruments that measure public opinion, so they come with mathematical uncertainty. If a poll were fielded 100 times, a candidate’s support would fall within a certain range — say, plus or minus 3 percentage points — in 95 cases. Yet in a close race, that could mean a candidate is leading or losing by a small amount.
By aggregating polls into averages, we can get a better sense of what the universe of polls says about a given race. This reduces the sway of a single survey, particularly an outlier, on our understanding of a race. That’s not to say averages are perfect: They rely on the quality of their inputs, and as we’ve seen with Trump, particularly in 2016 and 2020, a systematic polling error can consistently underrate one candidate. But averages still give us a better sense of the broad electoral picture, including trends regarding who may be gaining or losing support.
However, averaging polls is less helpful when you only have a few surveys, as in Vermont. How do we make sense of Vermont’s gubernatorial contest when we only have three publicly released polls conducted since mid-September? 
With so little polling data, we should be even more cautious about drawing conclusions. But we can also consider other data, such as past election results, and other important factors, including national political conditions and incumbency. This can be done quantitatively with a forecast model that gives a win probability for a candidate, or by a more qualitative approach that relies on categorical ratings such as “tossup” or “lean Republican.”

READ MORE

The polls suggest an edge for the Republican incumbent, Gov. Phil Scott, but one small enough that his Democratic challenger, Amanda Janoo, could win. The most recent poll, an early-October survey by State Navigate, found Scott ahead by just 3 points among likely voters, 46% to 43%. This finding was well inside the poll’s margin of error and fell between two earlier surveys, each conducted in September. Most strikingly, a University of New Hampshire Survey Center poll found Janoo up by 6 points, 49% to 43%. Around the same time, a Braun Research poll for Vermont Public found Scott ahead by about 10 points, 44% to 34%.
A simple average of these polls gives Scott about a 2-point edge, 44% to 42%, while an approach that fits the data based on each survey’s date, weighting recent data more heavily, would have Scott up by closer to 5 points, 43% to 38%. Either way, that’s a fairly close race, but again, based on limited data.
Although Vermont is a reliably Democratic state in federal elections, Scott has an impressive electoral record, having won at least 70% of the vote in back-to-back races. All in all, the 2026 electoral environment is very good for Democrats. But it remains unclear if things are so pro-Democratic that a fairly popular incumbent like Scott could lose.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Newberry hospital picked for free federal cybersecurity pilot program
text:
U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Chief Counselor Chris Klomp speaks at the launch of Project Lifeline 250 at Newberry Health Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)NEWBERRY — A group of private cybersecurity companies will offer their services, free of charge, to a Newberry hospital as part of a federal pilot project aimed at better protecting rural healthcare from virtual attacks.
White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross and U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Chief Counselor Chris Klomp were on hand Monday at Newberry Health, located 40 miles northwest of downtown Columbia, for the launch of Project Lifeline 250.
