“Thanks to the commitment of the world-leading American industry here today, we’re deploying the greatest American tools and capabilities to defend hospital networks, deploy physical backup devices after an initial incident to ensure an impacted hospital can still provide critical care and identify high-risk devices and replace them,” Cairncross said. “We’ll find what works and we’ll scale it. America’s rural communities and hospitals, they rely on it, and we’ll get it done.”
“We have an opportunity to build a model that every rural hospital across the entire country can rely upon,” Cairncross added.
The announcement was light on details. Officials did not say when the six-month pilot period would start, how it would be maintained and expanded after the pilot period or how that expansion might be paid for. Nor did they say why they selected South Carolina for this initial trial.
White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross speaks at the launch of Project Lifeline 250 at Newberry Health Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. (Photo by Jessica Holdman)
The Office of the National Cyber Director and the South Carolina State Law Enforcement Division’s cybersecurity arm will oversee the program.
Technology companies including Cisco, Cyera, Microsoft, Trellix, Zscaler, Rilian, Dispel, Abnormal AI and Becton, Dickinson and Company, Palo Alto Networks, ServiceNow, Infoblox Security Solutions and Forescout Technologies will provide their services.
The average hospital has more than 26,000 internet-connected devices, all of which could be subject to a cyber attack, Klomp said. And his agency tracked more than 2,200 health-related cyber incidents just last year.
And unlike larger hospital systems, rural providers don’t have the same financial resources to shore up its technological defenses.
“When a family walks through the doors of a hospital, they’re counting on a nurse, they’re counting on a doctor, someone to be there and to help them,” Klomp said. “Those professionals are depending on systems to share the medical records, the labs, the radiology communications, and others to give them the information to coordinate care appropriately. When those systems fail, the consequences can reach the bedside. They impact real lives. They impact the patient, impact their family.”
Klomp told the story of St. Margaret’s Health, a Catholic hospital system in Illinois, which closed in 2023. In their filings to the state, hospital officials cited a cyberattack as one of the reasons behind their closure.
“They couldn’t generate revenue and they couldn’t keep their doors open,” Klomp said.
Closer to home, AnMed in the Upstate saw its operations interrupted for months by a cybersecurity attack in which CEO William Kinley said cybercriminals accessed patients’ health information.
AnMed, with its 461-bed hospital in Anderson and more than 60 physician practices across South Carolina and Georgia, kept its urgent care and emergency services locations open following the July 26 attack. But doctors and patients had limited access to medical records.
It wasn’t until mid-September that the hospital system returned to normal operations.
“Cybersecurity is no longer just an IT issue,” SC Law Enforcement Division Chief Mark Keel said. “It is a public safety issue. It’s an economic issue. And in a healthcare environment, it can be the difference between life and death.”
“South Carolina is not waiting for a next cyber incident to happen,” Keel added. “We are identifying risks, bringing partners together, and putting practical solutions in place to better protect the citizens of our state.”
SC rural hospitals, doctors’ offices receive share of $200M in federal funding amid Medicaid cuts

One of the technologies the Newberry hospital will test out is called Project Code Cart, Cairncross said.
Researchers at the University of California San Diego developed Code Cart, which Cairncross described as an IT system in a box, using a U.S. Department of Health and Human Services grant.
“It’s designed, in the event of a full shutdown of systems in a hospital for a ransomware attack, to completely restore essential functionality within two hours, so that all operations can be maintained,” Cairncross said. “Think essential communications. Think radiology labs, access to critical electronic health records.”
Project Lifeline follows a similar White House-led cyber effort: Project Watershed 250, a pilot project to protect water infrastructure from a cyber attack in Texas. The Office of the National Cyber Director announced that pilot in August.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Struggling Canton school loses its charter
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
SR1 College Preparatory and STEM Academy has lost its charter and must halt instruction by the end of the year — a first-time penalty for a Mississippi charter school.  
The Mississippi Charter School Authorizer Board voted unanimously on Monday to revoke the Canton school’s charter. Two board members, Candace Robbins and Marcy Scoggins, were absent. 
While other charter schools have been cited for breaking federal education law and violating the terms of their contract, no other school has been ordered to effectively shut its doors.
Hearing officer Kim Turner asks questions during a hearing about SR1 on Thursday, May 14, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Kim Turner, an assistant attorney general who serves as state agencies director in the attorney general’s office, recommended the board revoke the school’s charter because of numerous instances of noncompliance with federal law, state law and the terms of its 2020 contract.
The authorizer board had waited four months, since a related May 14 hearing Turner presided over, to take action.
The evidence presented during that hearing affirmed a “statutory and contractual basis” for revoking the school’s charter, Turner concluded in her recommendation. “Such a decision would be neither arbitrary nor capricious.”
Earlier in the meeting, Dorlisa Hutton, an SR1 administrator and wife of Chief Executive Officer Tamu Green, made a final plea before board members moved to vote on the fate of the school. 
READ MORE: Charter school in Canton opened with a STEM focus but no full-time STEM teachers. It has had many more problems
Hutton asked the board to hold off on a final decision until the school’s latest audit was available —  an alternative action Turner had suggested. Hutton also asked the board to return the school to good standing. She asked the board to release $300,000 in charter school start-up funding, which had been frozen pending the vote on the school’s fate.
Dorlisa Hutton, vanguard ambassador for SR1 College Preparatory and STEM Academy, speaks at the Dec. 8, 2025 meeting of the Mississippi Charter School Authorizer Board Meeting in Jackson. Credit: Leonardo Bevilacqua/Mississippi Today
Returning the school to good standing would mean “we can build the facilities our students deserve and bring to the table the bankers and partners who are ready to invest in Canton,” Hutton said. “And it means the chance for Mississippi’s first college prep and STEM [science, technology, engineering and math] charter school serving children of whom nearly nine and 10 are economically disadvantaged to become the first charter school in this state to earn an A.”
Hutton did not respond to questions from Mississippi Today about whether the school planned to appeal.
Jamie Travis, an attorney for the charter school, suggested in May he would pursue an appeal process if the authorizer board voted to revoke the school’s charter. The appeal should be directed to the Hinds County Chancery Court, Turner said, which is where the board is based.
The board’s vote ends a process that began in December, when the authorizer board reviewed the school’s financial statements, which showed SR1 CPSA had one day’s cash on hand. The school had also over projected its enrollment each year since it opened in 2023.
SR1 CPSA was the only charter to face revocation twice. The authorizer board first cited the school for requesting money to serve 150 students, but enrolling 12. The school spent $816,725 that year, which would break down to about $68,060 per student — five times what the average Mississippi school district spends.
“The record established this revocation proceeding did not arise from one isolated event. Rather, these proceedings were initiated following years of notice, monitoring intervention, corrective action, and requests for and production of documents,” Turner found.
Students head to waiting vehicles and school buses after classes end for the day at SR1 College Preparatory and Stem Academy, Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026, in Canton. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Since then, the school’s fate has been in limbo, which also affected its funding. 
The board could not act without a recommendation from Turner. That board received that recommendation on Oct. 6.
Regulators had reason to worry about the school’s future. A disorganized business office and an allegedly unsafe cafeteria were just some red flags that came up during inspections by authorizer board employees. Visits from other agency inspectors soon followed.
Green severely mismanaged the school, charter board attorney Dillon Pitts argued at the May hearing. Also at the hearing, Green said his “unwritten rule” of  management was: “we just spent.” He claimed to not know that school records had to present the best financial snapshot by the end of the fiscal year. 
Tamu Green, CEO of SR1, confers with Dorlisa Hutton, chief operations officer and vice president for SR1 College Preparatory and STEM Academy, during a hearing about SR1 on Thursday, May 14, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
The school was also out of compliance with federal food safety and nutrition guidelines. 
A Mississippi Today investigation found school leadership tried to deceive regulators before inspections by moving furniture and other supplies on site and retagging them. Former employees accused SR1 leadership of deceptive business practices.
The school has experienced significant turnover as well. The school’s top administrator resigned at the end of September, after starting in August. The school is on its third business manager in less than a year. 
SR1 CPSA could still reopen as a private school.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Regulators eye in-state path for out-of-state medical marijuana patients
authors: Katie Castellani | State House News Service
text:
CANNABIS REGULATORS ARE EYEING rules to eliminate residency requirements for purchasing medical marijuana in an attempt to make the product easier for out-of-state patients to buy.
“Simply put, it is a really effective way and a thoughtful way for us to give medical patients across the country more access to treatment for any of the reasons that they’re using marijuana for medicinal purposes,” Cannabis Control Commissioner Xiomara DeLobato told the News Service.
Under a regulatory proposal introduced at an October 22 CCC meeting, individuals 18 and over – regardless of what state they live in – diagnosed with a “debilitating medical condition” by a certified health care provider in Massachusetts can register to purchase medical marijuana. Those under 18 who have been diagnosed with a debilitating condition that is also considered a “life-limiting illness” and certified by two health care providers can get medical marijuana.
Forty-one states and the District of Columbia allow medical marijuana use, as of June 2025, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. And if the regulations are passed, the Bay State would join many others including New Hampshire, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York and Maine, that allow non-residents to get medical marijuana. Massachusetts and Vermont are the only New England states that don’t allow non-residents to access medical marijuana.
Jeremiah MacKinnon, president and executive director of the Massachusetts Patient Advocacy Alliance, said the proposed regulations mark “a step in the right direction to modernize our medical program.”
“We have such a robust health care system here in Massachusetts that people travel from other states to get surgeries, and whether it’s tourism or visiting family or other situations, if an individual wants to seek continuity of their care, accessing medical marijuana, this is a great pathway because it allows them to continue to access medical marijuana tax-free,” MacKinnon told the News Service. 
Also, he said proposal could help get more needed dollars flowing to the state’s medical marijuana industry.
“For the past few years, the medical marijuana market has been struggling, and so to expand the pool of patients that are able to access medical marijuana in the state, I think is a positive thing for the health and long-term stability of the industry,” MacKinnon said.
Medical marijuana products are not taxed in Massachusetts and adult-use cannabis products are available to anyone, from any state, over 21. Recreational cannabis products are subject to a 6.25 percent state sales tax and a 10.75 percent excise tax while municipalities that host licensees can receive a local option tax of up to 3 percent. As of September, the industry has generated $2 billion in state and local taxes since it was enacted in 2016.
According to CCC data, year-to-date medical marijuana sales to patients and caregivers have fallen from $17.9 million in September 2023 to $11.2 million last month.
Ryan Dominguez, executive director of the Massachusetts Cannabis Coalition, said the regulations would create an avenue for out-of-state patients to get marijuana products they may need in Massachusetts if voters here next month support Question 8 repealing the state’s recreational cannabis market. 
Patrick Nestor, a spokesperson for the campaign supporting the ballot question, declined to comment on the proposed regulations.
The proposed regulations are similar to a Senate-approved measure recognizing patient registrations in other states for medical marijuana prescriptions. After talks with the House, that provision was dropped from the bill (H 5350) lawmakers sent to Gov. Maura Healey, which she signed into law in April. 
DeLobato said that commissioners plan to take an initial vote on the regulations on December 10. Then, the commission will take public comments on the regulations from January 1 to February 2 before making any changes and taking a final vote.

name: VTDigger
title: Guard families deserve an answer
text:
Dear Editor,
As a veteran of the Vermont Air National Guard, I understand that military service is not simply about following orders. It also involves sacrifices by those who serve and the families who stand behind them.
I served four years in the Guard. My husband also served while we were raising our family. I chose to leave because I did not want to risk an overseas deployment and its impact on our family. My husband continued to serve.
That experience is one reason I am concerned about Gov. Phil Scott’s apparent lack of response to a letter signed by 27 Vermont veterans, retired military officers and Guard family members calling on him and state legislators to support the Defend the Guard Act. The letter raised concerns about deploying Vermont National Guard members into overseas combat without prior congressional authorization and called for a public legislative hearing. It was publicly reported on Aug. 20. To date, as far as I know, there has been no response from the governor.
Reasonable people can disagree about the legislation, and a governor is entitled to explain his position. But when veterans and military families raise serious concerns, they deserve more than silence.

READ MORE

Leadership does not require agreement. It requires listening. It requires responding. It requires being willing to explain decisions to those affected by them.
I served in the Vermont Air National Guard. I know that service comes with obligations. Our elected leaders have obligations, too.
Lonnie PolandMilton, Vt.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: No indication of targeted attack behind Peltola car crash in Anchorage
text:
Former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola, D-Alaska, speaks at a campaign gathering in Anchorage on Oct. 21, 2026. Peltola is running for U.S. Senate. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)An official with the Anchorage Police Department said Monday that there is no evidence that Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola was deliberately targeted in a weekend car accident that injured her and members of her family.
“There is nothing new to share and at this time, there are no indications that this was a targeted attack,” said Gina Romero, director of the department’s community relations unit.
Australian lawmaker Helen Haines was critically injured after someone repeatedly rammed her with a car earlier this month. 
Public polling indicates Peltola may have a small lead over incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan in the ongoing election. Alaska’s U.S. Senate race is one of a handful that could determine whether Democrats or Republicans control the Senate. 
According to a weekend bulletin from the Anchorage Police Department, a vehicle containing Peltola and members of her family was hit from the rear shortly before 7 p.m. Saturday while stopped at the intersection of O’Malley Road and Lake Otis Parkway. 
The crash was severe enough that it pushed Peltola’s vehicle into another car ahead of it.
“The occupants of vehicle 2, which included U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola, were transported to a local hospital with non-life threatening injuries. The driver and sole occupant of the first vehicle was also transported to a local hospital with non-life threatening injuries,” the department said on Saturday.
The Beacon submitted public records requests Monday for video, audio and documents about the crash.
In a statement Sunday, Peltola’s campaign manager said events scheduled Sunday and Monday were being postponed.
“Mary and her family sustained minor injuries but are in good spirits. Unfortunately, per the advice of medical professionals, Mary’s upcoming events in Fairbanks and Bethel will be rescheduled for later in the week as she takes time to recover,” said campaign manager Cheryl Bruce by email.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Rhode Island is first state to sue Meta over alleged profits from scam ads
text:
A laptop displays a Ninjabot AI ad promoting trading technology and a website offering a license for $397, with a graphic suggesting continuous profits. The ad is among the examples of deceptive ads cited in Rhode Island’s lawsuit against Meta. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)A fake investment opportunity, a phony Social Security benefit or a dubious health product might seem like just another random ad on Meta’s platforms. 
But Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha claims the tech giant allows the same advertising machinery that helps legitimate businesses find customers to be used by scammers to target victims, allowing Meta to reap in billions of dollars of revenue.
That’s the central allegation in a lawsuit Neronha’s office filed Oct. 22 in Providence County Superior Court, making Rhode Island the first state in the nation to sue Meta over its alleged role in profiting from scam ads. The 85-page complaint accuses the California-based Meta, which owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, of violating Rhode Island’s consumer protection laws.
“For a company that engages so many Rhode Islanders and Americans, maintaining high standards for consumer safety should be of the utmost importance,” Neronha said in a statement.
A Meta spokesperson called the state’s claims “unfounded,” noting that the company ​regularly partners with law enforcement to disrupt scam networks.
“The Attorney General refused to engage with us on ways we protect Rhode Islanders from scams, and has instead hired an out-of-state private law firm to concoct a lawsuit that ignores the full range of actions we take to combat scams every day,” the spokesperson said in a statement to Rhode Island Current. “We fight scams because they’re not good for us or the people and businesses that rely on our services.”
Rhode Island is the first state to sue Meta over its alleged role in profiting from scam ads, but not the first government to do so. Santa Clara County in California filed a similar lawsuit in May, accusing the company of violating state laws against false advertising and unfair business practices.
The state’s case adds to a wave of legal challenges Meta has faced over the harms its platforms allegedly cause, from child safety to consumer privacy.
In August, Meta agreed to pay 47 states, including Rhode Island, along with the District of Columbia and several U.S. territories, up to $17.1 billion to settle claims that its social media platforms are addictive and endanger children.
Just a day before Rhode Island filed suit, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay the state $25 billion after finding the company liable for violating consumer protection laws in a case involving its handling of users’ data.
Can Rhode Island hold Meta liable?
Neronha’s office filed the case under the state’s Deceptive Trade Practices Act, which prohibits unfair or deceptive business practices. The law allows the attorney general to sue companies in Rhode Island Superior Court and ask a judge to order them to stop, restore money or property obtained through unlawful conduct, or face other penalties.
Michael Yelnosky, a professor at Roger Williams University School of Law, said Meta may consider moving the case to Providence’s federal court, where defendants in complex litigation often prefer the closer pretrial oversight. But the optics wouldn’t look good for the tech giant, he warned.
“I would also imagine Meta would prefer not to be the big bad out-of-state defendant litigating against the AG on his home turf,” Yelnosky wrote in an email Monday to Rhode Island Current.
A more consequential legal question posed by Yelnosky is whether Section 230 of the federal Communications Decency Act shields the company from liability for scam ads posted by third parties.
“The complaint alleges conduct by Meta that takes it out of the role of passive poster, but a court will need to make that call and the AG will need to factually support those allegations,” he wrote.
Rhode Island’s lawsuit cites reporting by Reuters from 2025 on internal Meta documents detailing the scale of fraudulent advertising on the company’s platforms — and its estimates that revenue from scam ads and other prohibited advertising far exceeded the fines it expected to pay for failing to stop them.
The state alleges the company’s advertising tools help scammers create and refine ads, identify audiences likely to respond and use automated systems to reach potential victims.
“Meta knew that fraud was rampant on its platforms but not only developed and applied policies that protected fraudulent actors and reined in its own enforcement efforts, but misled consumers about the prevalence of such fraud and its efforts to address it,” the lawsuit states.
The complaint points to ads promoting supposed miracle cures, including one that promised to reverse Alzheimer’s disease in 45 days. More than 2,000 versions of the ad were active in Meta’s public advertising library, according to the lawsuit.
“Meta left Rhode Island consumers without the ability to protect themselves from bad actors on its platforms,” the lawsuit states.
The complaint also cites ads for AI tools that generate sexually explicit images. One example shows a fully clothed woman in a coffee shop before depicting her in a sexual act in the next frame, which is blacked out in the lawsuit.
Much of the 85-page complaint is redacted, including Meta’s internal communications surrounding its ads.
In a motion filed Monday, Neronha’s office asked the court to allow it to file a complete, unredacted version of the complaint under seal while the parties work to determine which information should remain confidential. The motion proposes resolving those disputes by Nov. 19.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Election 2026: Your Ballot Questions, Explained
text:
ELECTION 2026 · EDITION 2
Your Ballot Questions, Explained

Welcome back to CommonWealth Beacon‘s Election 2026 newsletter run.
There is a lot to sort through before you head to the polls on November 3, and much of the space on your ballot will be dedicated to eight initiative petitions and one repeal referendum. 
For more than 100 years, voters have been able to make law at the ballot box, but eagerness to bypass the Legislature was extremely high this cycle. Many campaign organizers say they pursued questions because they’re frustrated at Beacon Hill’s slow pace, and the frequency with which popular ideas die without a vote.
For those who don’t have the time to read an 88-page state-issued voter guide or need help parsing the record-tying number of ballot questions, CommonWealth Beacon’s 2026 special ballot section — in partnership with The Bay State Banner and El Planeta — is aimed at making the lift more manageable.  
Here’s what you’ll be deciding at the voting booth: 


Question 1 · Public records
Extend the public records law to the Legislature and governor’s office
Read More →


Question 2 · CPCS union
Allow Committee for Public Counsel Services staff to form a union 
Read More →


Question 3 · All-party primaries
Replace partisan primary elections with a single “all-party primary”
Read More →


Question 4 · Election Day registration
Allow prospective voters to register and cast a ballot on Election Day
Read More →


Question 5 · Tax cap reform
Recalculate the formula for the limit on state tax collections
Read More →


Question 6 · Conservation funding
Direct existing sales tax to a state fund for conservation
Read More →


Question 7 · Starter homes
Reduce minimum lot-size requirements in many communities
Read More →


Question 8 · Recreational marijuana
Repeal the legalization of the sale and use of recreational marijuana
Read More →


Question 9 · Gun law repeal
Uphold Massachusetts’s updated firearms law
Read More →


The cycle began with one question locked in: a proposal to repeal the state’s 2024 gun law. Another 11 cleared the 74,574 certified signatures needed to make it over the first hurdle. 
A dozen ballot questions would have smashed the state record. But the state’s highest court introduced another wrinkle, tossing two of the highest profile questions of the cycle — one that sought to impose statewide rent control and one that sought to slash the income tax — on what were essentially technicalities. Based on an advisory opinion from the Supreme Judicial Court, the attorney general’s office withdrew its certification of another question that would have created a new stipend system for lawmakers who chair committees. 
The nine ballot questions that are left range from the esoteric — voters are being asked to decide whether to change the formulation of Massachusetts’s tax cap — to the aim of making Beacon Hill more transparent and transforming the state’s primary system. 
Legislators have decried the number of ballot questions as proof that deep-pocketed donors are out to buy new laws, a claim not entirely without merit. Heading into October, campaign filings showed more than $21 million raised and almost $17 million spent on the various ballot questions.  
Ballot measure backers say initiative petitions are some of the more effective ways to advocate for policies that the Legislature could back-burner indefinitely.  
Organized labor is out in force this cycle, at this point mostly looking to fight a proposal to repeal the 2024 gun law that created a host of new firearm regulations and a proposal that would create an all-party primary system. But just as in 2024, organizing itself is on the ballot — this time for employees of the state’s public defender agency. 


Dive into the data

The tension around ballot measures is often Beacon Hill versus everyone else, but this cycle features a sequel to one of the uglier recent battles at the ballot box.  
Two years ago, voters overwhelmingly approved a question that explicitly gave Auditor Diana DiZoglio the power to probe the Legislature. Democratic legislative leaders have pushed back, arguing it violates the separation of powers clause in the state constitution. In a follow-up this year, as the fight over the audit continues, DiZoglio and a coalition of transparency advocates have put forward a ballot question seeking to subject the Legislature and governor’s office to the state’s public records law.  
In response, House and Senate lawmakers have passed different bills that would create a new, more limited public records law than the ballot question envisions. A final draft of that bill could emerge from a conference committee at any point before the end of the year, including after the election — possibly superseding what voters just decided.  
But Question 1 isn’t the only measure that could be disrupted by lawmakers this cycle. Senators also included language in their version of the economic development bill, currently under negotiation, that could take the wind out of Question 5 — the proposal to trigger more frequent rebates to taxpayers. That legislation would introduce a new eligibility criterion that would essentially make refunds less frequent if the ballot question passes. 
While lawmakers are defending the moves as sensible options to protect state revenues and make sure that public records law and the audit pass constitutional muster, advocates across political lines are seething. 
Scotia Hille, executive director of the Act on Mass group supporting a measure to expand the public records law, told CommonWealth Beacon that the possibility of late-emerging legislation on ballot question subjects is troubling. 
“The fact that the Legislature can try everything to fight a ballot question, and then, in the last few days of the legislative session, pass legislation that would essentially nullify the impact of the ballot question — I think it absolutely sets an alarming precedent about our right as citizens to make laws by initiative petition,” Hille said.

title: University of New Mexico Hospital diverting ambulance traffic due to ‘cybersecurity’ issue
text:
University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center officials on Oct. 26, 2026, announced that a “cybersecurity issue” required them to divert all ambulances and cancel appointments. (Photo courtesy UNM)Officials at the University of New Mexico Health System on Monday announced that they were diverting all ambulances and canceling all appointments due to a “cybersecurity issue” that is impacting patients at one of the state’s largest hospitals and at dozens of clinics across the state. 
In an emailed statement Monday afternoon, UNM Health Sciences Center Communications Director Chris Ramirez said that patients should not show up to any UNM Health facilities Monday while UNM officials are “actively working to resolve the issue.”

The statement did not give more details about the nature of the cybersecurity issue or provide an estimate as to when the hospital and clinics would reopen to patients.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Money flows to South Dakota US Senate race as independent challenges Republican incumbent
text:
Republican U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota, left, faces independent Brian Bengs in the Nov. 3 election. (Rounds photo by South Dakota Searchlight; Bengs photo courtesy of South Dakota Public Broadcasting; illustration by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)Money is pouring into South Dakota’s U.S. Senate race as people and groups across the country sense a rare chance to support a potentially competitive challenger against a Republican incumbent.
Both candidates have raised a majority of their campaign contributions from outside the state and have spent a combined $6.1 million, according to data compiled by the nonpartisan, nonprofit money-in-politics website OpenSecrets. Additional spending by federally registered political action committees to influence the race has topped $3 million, pushing the total cost of the race near $10 million and counting.
In a race with no Democratic candidate, about 40% of the spending has been in support of independent Brian Bengs or against Republican Sen. Mike Rounds.
Independent US Senate candidate in South Dakota backed by Forward Party

Bengs trailed Rounds by 8 points in an Emerson College/KELO-TV poll released last week, with 8% of respondents undecided. Another poll released last week, from Mason-Dixon Polling and Strategy and South Dakota News Watch, showed Rounds with a larger lead of 19 points, 56% to 37%.
Nationally, Bengs is one of four independent candidates for U.S. Senate in the Nov. 3 election who are the main opponents of Republican senators. All of them are in states where Trump has won and Democrats struggle in statewide elections. The other states are Nebraska, Montana and Idaho.
In South Dakota, Democrats are outnumbered more than 2-to-1 by Republicans. South Dakota Democrats have also been surpassed in recent years by the number of voters who register as independent or leave their political affiliation blank on the voter registration form.
Federal committees and nonprofits
Much of the advertising in the campaign’s final weeks has been funded by groups immune from state-level contribution limits, with varying levels of disclosure about their donors. That includes $1.7 million spent to promote Bengs or oppose Rounds by the federally registered political action committees Retire Career Politicians and Freedom from Politics.
Retire Career Politicians has received large recent contributions including $890,000 from the Western Futures Fund, a nonprofit that says it promotes “responsible leadership in the Western United States” and is not required to disclose its donors; $500,000 from the Way Back PAC, which has received much of its own funding from the Western Futures Fund; $200,000 from Scott Shenker, an internationally known computer scientist from California; and $100,000 from Brennan Bilberry, a political and communications strategist from Massachusetts.
[Voter Guide: 2026 general election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Freedom from Politics Inc. has received all of its $1.2 million from Stephen Pajcic, a Florida lawyer, Democratic politician and philanthropist. The committee’s stated mission is to “support independent-minded leaders who answer to the people they represent, not to a political party.”
On the other side, the South Dakota Conservative PAC has spent nearly $1 million while Defend American Jobs has spent about $400,000 to support Rounds or oppose Bengs.
South Dakota Conservative PAC received $200,000 from the late South Dakota billionaire-philanthropist T. Denny Sanford before he died, among other large individual contributions. Recently, the committee received an infusion of $521,000 from South Dakota First Action Inc., an entity that divulges little about itself publicly but describes itself as a nonprofit dedicated to “promoting policies that promote free enterprise, strong national security, and individual liberty.”
Defend American Jobs’ contributions include a recent $70 million surge of funding from Fairshake, a Minnesota-based political action committee that says it “supports candidates committed to securing the United States as the home to innovators building the next generation of the internet.” Contributors to Fairshake include the California-based tech company Ripple Labs Inc. and Marc Andreesen, a leader of a Silicon Valley venture capital firm and co-founder of the early web browser Netscape.

name: California
title: ¿Por qué hay tantos bonos en la boleta electoral de California? Esto es lo que se podría comprar con 44 mil millones de dólares.
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
La papeleta electoral de noviembre te invita a hacer que «llueva el dinero»… en forma de bonos.
Si se aprueban, se verá un conjunto de propuestas de la magnitud de El Niño que podrían inundar los sectores de la construcción de viviendas y la investigación científica de la economía californiana con 44,000 millones de dólares en gasto mediante bonos.
 Dos de esas propuestas de bonos —la Proposición 1 para vivienda y la Proposición 38 para investigación inmunológica— son los típicos acuerdos de préstamo a plazos que añaden varios miles de millones de dólares al costo total de las propuestas. Una tercera, la Proposición 37 , es una medida atípica que equivale a un experimento radical de bajo riesgo que probablemente no recaerá sobre los contribuyentes, al menos no directamente.
 Históricamente, las propuestas de bonos obtienen la aprobación de los votantes en mayor proporción que otras medidas. Desde el año 2000, los votantes aprobaron 23 de los 26 bonos estatales presentados, lo que representa un 88% de votos a favor. En los últimos años, los votantes aprobaron miles de millones en deuda pública para la construcción de escuelas, la lucha contra los efectos del cambio climático y la vivienda para veteranos.




Los bonos son una forma de deuda que el estado debe pagar a lo largo del tiempo, lo que implica pagos anuales con intereses . El estado gasta 6 mil millones de dólares anuales para amortizar unos 80 mil millones de dólares en bonos. Además, los votantes y legisladores han aprobado 40 mil millones de dólares en bonos que aún no se han vendido.
 Afortunadamente, para facilitarle el estudio de su papeleta electoral, la siguiente guía rápida le ofrece una introducción a los tres bonos que tiene ante usted. 
 Propuesta 1: Vivienda asequible
Si los votantes dan su aprobación, la Propuesta 1 permitiría al tesorero de California vender bonos de obligación general por valor de 11,250 millones de dólares. Ese dinero se destinaría a diversos tipos de vivienda, incluyendo a veteranos, personas sin hogar en California, inquilinos, propietarios, trabajadores agrícolas, estudiantes y miembros de tribus indígenas.
La medida destina 7,000 millones de dólares a la construcción, renovación o adquisición de complejos de apartamentos, principalmente mediante préstamos a promotores de vivienda asequible. Estos proyectos deben estar destinados a residentes de bajos ingresos, reservando al menos el 10 % de las unidades para hogares con ingresos extremadamente bajos. Más de 1,000 millones de dólares de este total se destinan a viviendas permanentes y temporales para personas sin hogar.Según la Oficina del Analista Legislativo, que es el grupo de expertos no partidista de la Legislatura, si se aprueba, la emisión de bonos daría como resultado unas 40,000 nuevas viviendas de alquiler.
 Esta es la única propuesta de bonos presentada por los legisladores que figura en la boleta electoral. Las otras dos consiguieron las firmas suficientes de los votantes para asegurarse un lugar en las elecciones de noviembre.
La oposición a este bono es mínima. El Partido Republicano estatal se mantiene oficialmente neutral respecto a la medida. Varios legisladores republicanos votaron en junio en contra del proyecto de ley que posteriormente se convirtió en este bono. Argumentaron que el título del proyecto de ley —Ley de Bonos para Veteranos y Vivienda Asequible— engañó a la opinión pública sobre la cantidad exacta de los ingresos procedentes de los bonos que se destinaría a los veteranos. ¿La solución? 1,250 millones de dólares para que los veteranos obtengan préstamos para vivienda. Otros 350 millones de dólares se destinarían a los dos sistemas universitarios públicos del estado para ayudar a financiar la construcción de residencias estudiantiles. Pero dado que el costo por cama suele superar los 250,000 dólares, todos esos millones de dólares solo alcanzarían para dar cabida a unos 1,300 estudiantes.
 El apoyo a la Propuesta 1 es enorme, e incluye al gobernador Gavin Newsom, el partido demócrata estatal, la empresa de alquiler de viviendas AirBnB, los principales sindicatos y muchos más.
 ¿Quieres saber más? Lee la guía de Marisa Kendall de CalMatters sobre la Propuesta 1 . 
 Propuesta 37: Ayuda para el pago inicial
 Esta medida de emisión de bonos es extraña , novedosa e introduce una gran cantidad de incógnitas.
 ¿Confundido? Todos lo estamos, por eso Ben Christopher, reportero de CalMatters especializado en vivienda, describió esta propuesta poco convencional como “simplemente extraña”.
 La Proposición 37 debe considerarse una forma de ayudar a los compradores de viviendas nuevas a obtener el pago inicial. Esta disposición permite solicitar hasta el 17% del precio de compra de una casa, condominio o casa adosada nueva. Esto cubre gran parte del pago inicial típico del 20%.
¿Quiénes pueden optar a este programa? Aproximadamente el 90% de todos los inquilinos de California. Los límites de ingresos varían según el condado: alrededor de 115,000 dólares en Imperial y más de 400,000 dólares en San Mateo para una familia de tres personas.
Las viviendas que cumplan los requisitos deben satisfacer varias condiciones: deben ser nuevas o haber sido recientemente reformadas y no costar más de aproximadamente 1.5 millones de dólares en el Área de la Bahía o 1 millón de dólares en Riverside; de nuevo, esto se basa en una fórmula imprecisa que varía según el condado. ¿Qué no hará? Aumentar la deuda estatal. No se trata de un bono que los contribuyentes pagarán; en cambio, los prestamistas privados que otorgan este bono recibirán el reembolso de los compradores de vivienda en forma de intereses.
 Es imposible predecir cuántas viviendas se podrían comprar con ese dinero. Esa cifra depende del precio de las nuevas viviendas, de los ingresos de los compradores y de si los promotores construyen nuevas viviendas.
 La mayoría de los inquilinos hoy en día no podrían permitirse ni siquiera las viviendas nuevas más baratas, dijo Eric McGhee, analista del Instituto de Políticas Públicas de California, una organización sin fines de lucro que ha escrito sobre la Proposición 37.
Estimó que entre 60,000 y más de 1.8 millones de compradores podrían beneficiarse de la ayuda para el pago inicial que ofrece esta medida de bonos. El límite inferior supone un pago inicial del 20% para las viviendas más caras, mientras que el límite superior supone un pago inicial del 5% para las viviendas menos caras.
 Proposición 38: Investigación en inmunología
Esta propuesta de bonos destinaría 4,200 millones de dólares a un único instituto sin ánimo de lucro, cuyo nombre no se ha revelado, centrado en la investigación inmunológica y en la búsqueda de curas para enfermedades importantes como el Alzheimer, el cáncer y las enfermedades cardíacas.
 La misma cantidad se distribuiría a un comité que identificaría a un número limitado de investigadores de universidades públicas y organizaciones sin ánimo de lucro que estudian la inmunología y las inmunoterapias.
 Según informes previos de CalMatters, solo un instituto en California cumple actualmente con los criterios de la Proposición 38 para recibir la mitad de los fondos: el Instituto de Inmunología e Inmunoterapia de California. El principal financiador del instituto es el multimillonario Gary K. Michelson, autor de la Proposición 38 y, con diferencia, el mayor donante de su campaña política.
 Información adicional de CalMatters plantea la cuestión de cuán preparado está el instituto para implementar la enorme cantidad de dinero proveniente del bono. El instituto contaba con solo tres empleados el mes pasado, muchos menos que los 51 que planeaba tener en plantilla el año pasado.
 La campaña a favor de la Proposición 38 afirma que los ingresos de los bonos son necesarios para contrarrestar los continuos esfuerzos de la administración Trump por recortar la investigación científica federal o limitar los temas de estudio. Argumentan que cualquier restricción en los ensayos clínicos y otras terapias puede provocar sufrimiento y muerte evitables a pacientes con enfermedades debilitantes. Los opositores a la medida la critican por concentrar la mitad del dinero en un solo instituto y limitar qué otros investigadores pueden recibir financiación. Argumentan que la investigación científica se realiza mejor en un entorno competitivo abierto a todos los científicos de las universidades públicas y sin fines de lucro de California.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Democrats ask TV stations to take down James ad amid campaign finance allegations
text:
Republican gubernatorial nominee and U.S. Rep. John James talks to reporters following a debate in Grand Rapids on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026. (Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel is asking television stations around Michigan to stop airing an ad from John James’ gubernatorial campaign paid for by the Michigan Republican Party — using funds that a campaign finance complaint from Hertel and the Democrats say violate campaign finance laws. 
The money in question comes from a $1.8 million in-kind donation from the Michigan Republican Party, which was listed in James’ pre-election campaign finance filing as for “media placement media production.”
The donation far exceeds the contribution limits cited in both the complaint and on the Department of State’s website. 
But the James campaign argues that a June 2026 U.S. Supreme Court decision, NRSC v. FEC, allows the spending after the court struck down a federal law that limited the amount of money that national political parties are able to spend in coordination with a candidate for office.
“The United States Supreme Court made clear in the NRSC decision that political parties have the constitutional right to spend unlimited funds in coordination with their candidates,” Alyvia Bailey, a James campaign spokesperson, wrote to the Michigan Advance. “No scare tactic is going to stop our momentum. Support across Michigan for John James is surging at the right time and we look forward to victory come November 3rd.”
Screenshot of ad in question as submitted in the complaint filed by the Michigan Democratic Party.
Asked in a press conference if he believed the NRSC decision made it so decisions like these would be legal, Hertel said that Michigan law is currently clear and does not permit this.
“Michigan law is clear: anyone who’s running for governor in the state should follow it, and they are obviously not doing that,” he said. “If this was legal, this is what they’re trying to claim is now legal, it would create a completely Wild West situation where any one person could contribute unlimited dollars and get the issue ad rate afterwards. There is no way that that is a reasonable interpretation of what the Supreme Court said, and this should be adjudicated in the courts before we ever get to this point.”
The ad contains three written disclosures — “Paid for with regulated funds by Michigan Republican Party,” “Authorized by John James for MI” and “Approved by John James.”
The campaign finance complaint from the Michigan Democratic Party, filed on Friday with the Michigan Department of State, says that those three statements indicate that the ad was paid for with money governed by the Michigan Campaign Finance Act, and it was run in coordination with and authorization by the James campaign.
The Michigan Democratic State Central Committee and election lawyer Mark Brewer, a former Michigan Democratic Party chair, are asking TV stations across Michigan to stop running the ad, given that it is a part of an active Michigan Campaign Finance Act complaint. 
If stations will not remove the ad entirely, the letter sent by Brewer asks that stations stop giving it the “preferential candidate rate treatment,” a lower amount charged for candidate ads, and instead charge them the rate for “non-candidate political advertisements.” SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“This course of action ensures that the station’s treatment of the advertisement is consistent with the facts presently known and avoids preferential candidate rate treatment to James where entitlement to that treatment is, at best, uncertain, and more likely illegal,” Brewer writes in the letter, which was sent on Monday morning.
Hertel told reporters Monday afternoon that no station had yet indicated that it would stop airing the ad or change the rate for it.
A decision on the campaign finance complaint is unlikely to come before the Nov. 3 election. But Hertel said the likelihood of a post-election decision is precisely why stations should act on Monday’s letter, instead of waiting for an official decision.
“What I would argue is that that’s why the station should take this seriously,” he said. “They are literally giving preferential treatment under something that is a violation of Michigan campaign finance law, and there is nothing that’s been done in the courts that would suggest that what they’re doing is correct. So each of them are making a decision right now to honor this rate, even though it is patently illegal under Michigan law.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Judge rejects bid by secretary of state candidate Ballard to force Election Commission meeting
text:
Lincoln Party candidate Greg Ballard, center, speaks during an Indiana secretary of state debate alongside Republican Max Engling, left, and Democrat Beau Bayh. (Photo by Doug McSchooler for Indiana Debate Commission)The Indiana Election Commission doesn’t have to consider the validity of campaign misconduct allegations ahead of Election Day on Nov. 3, a Marion County judge ruled Monday.
The decision was made following a lawsuit filed by Lincoln Party secretary of state candidate Greg Ballard, who asked the judge to order that the commission hold a meeting regarding campaign finance complaints against Republican candidate Max Engling and Democrat Beau Bayh.
Marion County Superior Court Judge Jennifer Harrison said in her decision that Ballard had “failed to identify any concrete, actual harm” from the commission waiting until its scheduled Nov. 20 meeting.
“He instead presents hypothetical harm with no support that if Defendants meet before November 3, it will affect voter decision-making in the Secretary of State race,” Harrison wrote. 
Ballard said in a statement that he was “exploring our legal options to compel the commission to perform its statutory duty to meet.”
“Might makes right. The laws are intended to protect those in power,” Ballard’s statement said. “Not so long ago, the Election Commission acted in a more ethical, nonpartisan manner. However, the law does not protect voters from blatant political maneuvering if the commission decides to act to protect political parties over people.”
Election commission suit decision
The state attorney general’s office argued during a court hearing Friday that state law does not set a time frame for the commission to review campaign finance complaints and that Ballard was trying “to use the commission to influence voters before Election Day.”
The most prominent of the pending complaints was filed in July alleging that Engling’s campaign improperly accepted $60,000 from Hoosier Leadership for America, a dark money political group associated with Republican U.S. Sen. Jim Banks.
Engling’s campaign has reported it refunded the money a week before the complaint was filed by Knox County Clerk David Shelton, who finished second to Engling in seeking the Republican nomination during June’s state party convention.
The pending complaints also include allegations that Bayh attended several events sponsored by county Democratic parties but reported no in-kind donations from those organizations.
State law gives Election Commission Chair Beth Boyce, who is also the Johnson County Republican chair, authority over calling meetings of the panel, which is made up of two Republicans and two Democrats.
