name: California
title: Los barrios latinos de Los Ángeles respaldaron a Karen Bass en junio. ¿Seguirán apoyándola en noviembre?
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
En las elecciones a la alcaldía de Los Ángeles hay una pregunta clave que quizás solo el recuento de votos pueda responder: ¿A qué candidato prefieren los latinos de la ciudad, el grupo étnico más numeroso de esta metrópolis multicultural?
 Las encuestas apuntan en todas direcciones. Justo antes de que se enviaran las papeletas por correo este mes, una encuesta del Instituto de Estudios Gubernamentales de la UC Berkeley reveló que la concejala Nithya Raman tenía una ventaja aplastante de 24 puntos entre los latinos en su intento por desbancar a la alcaldesa Karen Bass.
 Eso sorprendió a ambos bandos. La campaña de Bass lo desestimó por completo, e incluso algunos colaboradores de Raman reconocieron que el margen era mayor de lo que indicaban sus propias encuestas. El panorama se complicó aún más una semana después, cuando una encuesta respaldada por Bass informó que los latinos la favorecían por 12 puntos. Esto también parece improbable, ya que las encuestas a nivel de la ciudad muestran consistentemente a Raman a la cabeza, y sería difícil obtener una ventaja significativa en Los Ángeles sin un apoyo considerable de los latinos, que representan más de un tercio del electorado de la ciudad.
 Esto obliga a los analistas a buscar otras maneras de medir las preferencias de los latinos en esta campaña. Un buen punto de partida son los resultados reales.
 Un análisis realizado por CalMatters de los votos emitidos en junio, cuando Bass, Raman y Spencer Pratt figuraban en la boleta electoral, reveló que Bass superó ampliamente a sus oponentes en los distritos donde los latinos representaban al menos la mitad del voto. Aproximadamente uno de cada cinco distritos electorales de la ciudad tiene una mayoría latina, según datos de la base de datos oficial de redistribución de distritos del estado.


Bass se impuso en 120 de estos 144 distritos electorales, frente a solo 16 para Raman. En conjunto, Bass ganó en esos distritos al obtener el 37.5% de los votos, superando el porcentaje de votos de Raman y Pratt en 11 y 16 puntos porcentuales, respectivamente.
 La distribución geográfica de esos distritos electorales también es significativa. Los distritos que ganó Bass se extienden desde las zonas residenciales predominantemente latinas del sur de la Bahía, pasando por el centro de la ciudad y llegando hasta el noreste del Valle, donde los barrios de casas unifamiliares en Sunland y Pacoima incluyen a muchos residentes y propietarios de larga data.
 Mientras tanto, los votos que Raman obtuvo se concentraron en las comunidades dentro y alrededor de su distrito del consejo municipal: Hollywood, Silver Lake, Los Feliz, Highland Park, hogar de jóvenes angelinos y muchos otros que son nuevos en Los Ángeles. Se trata de comunidades densamente pobladas, con menos casas unifamiliares y más apartamentos.
 El apoyo latino a Pratt fue mínimo y disperso, un recordatorio pasajero de por qué un republicano respaldado por Trump no tenía ninguna posibilidad en una ciudad liberal.
 Lo que ilustran las votaciones de junio es que los votantes latinos reflejan la composición del electorado en general: los propietarios de viviendas y los residentes de larga data están más inclinados a apoyar a Bass, mientras que los inquilinos y los recién llegados encuentran a Raman más atractivo.
 La fortaleza de estos datos radica en que no están sujetos a las ideas preconcebidas ni a las interpretaciones de los encuestadores. Representan votos reales emitidos, y es poco probable que los simpatizantes de un candidato que votan por él cambien de bando en una segunda vuelta. En consecuencia, demuestran que Bass inicia la campaña de otoño con un amplio respaldo latino, proveniente principalmente de comunidades de clase media donde el electorado latino es numeroso.
 Dicho esto, esto no garantiza en absoluto la victoria de Bass entre los latinos, como tampoco sugiere su reelección. El apoyo a Raman puede estar menos concentrado, pero ser mayor en general; menos visible en un mapa, pero más poderoso a la larga. La sorprendente encuesta del IGS de Berkeley de principios de este mes indica que esto podría estar sucediendo. 
 De izquierda a derecha: la alcaldesa de Los Ángeles, Karen Bass, y la candidata a la alcaldía y concejala Nithya Raman. Fotografías de Damian Dovarganes, AP Photo y Vivien Killilea, Getty Images.
 Esto quedó patente cuando revisé el análisis de CalMatters con los estrategas de ambas campañas. Un representante del equipo de Raman, por ejemplo, afirmó que las características de los distritos electorales de mayoría latina de Bass no reflejan al electorado latino en general, que está disperso por toda la ciudad y se inclina más hacia los recién llegados y los inquilinos, el núcleo del apoyo a Raman.
 “Muchos latinos viven en comunidades jóvenes, con una alta proporción de inquilinos, donde Nithya ha logrado un fuerte apoyo”, dijo la portavoz de la campaña, Lauren Perez-Rangel. “Están listos para el cambio y están eligiendo a Nithya”.
 Las encuestas a nivel de toda la ciudad refuerzan este argumento. Todas las encuestas fiables muestran a Raman con al menos una ventaja moderada, y dado que los latinos constituyen el mayor grupo demográfico votante de la ciudad, es difícil imaginar cómo Raman podría estar por delante sin ellos, señaló Pérez-Rangel. La encuesta del LA Times, añadió, mostró a Raman con una ventaja abrumadora entre los latinos menores de 50 años.
 La campaña de Bass, por el contrario, considera que esos distritos con mayoría latina constituyen un núcleo de apoyo confiable y una base sólida para construir su futuro. Julie Rodríguez, quien dirige la campaña de Bass, afirmó que considera a los propietarios de viviendas como un electorado natural para la alcaldesa en una contienda contra una oponente que ha contado con el respaldo de los Socialistas Democráticos de América. Los propietarios de viviendas tienden a priorizar la seguridad pública, y el historial de Bass le brinda importantes ventajas, con índices de delitos violentos y contra la propiedad en mínimos históricos.
 Ambas campañas coinciden en que ganarse el apoyo de los recién llegados a la ciudad —aquellos que han vivido aquí durante cinco años o menos— probablemente dependerá de qué candidato pueda hacer que la ciudad sea más asequible.
 En este aspecto, Raman tiene ventaja. Su reputación en cuanto a la asequibilidad comienza con su trayectoria como concejal que impulsó la ordenanza de estabilización de alquileres de la ciudad, una medida que limita los aumentos anuales de alquileres por parte de los propietarios de Los Ángeles. Bass firmó dicha ordenanza, por lo que ambos candidatos pueden atribuirse parte del mérito, aunque, con razón, se asocia más a Raman.
 Además, Bass ha propuesto ampliar las guarderías municipales, y Raman ha ofrecido diversas ideas para acelerar la construcción de viviendas de alquiler, confiando en que un aumento de la oferta generará una presión a la baja perceptible sobre los alquileres. Ambos candidatos prometen reducir los obstáculos que impone el Ayuntamiento a la construcción de nuevas viviendas.
 La asequibilidad no solo es popular entre los latinos, por supuesto, sino que encabeza la lista de la mayoría de las encuestas que preguntan a los inquilinos qué es lo más importante para ellos. Dado que muchos latinos son inquilinos, estos dos grupos demográficos se superponen.
 Otra dinámica que subyace en los resultados de las elecciones de junio y en la información que ofrecen sobre las inclinaciones de los votantes latinos en Los Ángeles es la siguiente: si bien ambas campañas reconocen la importancia de atraer a los votantes latinos en general, están intentando llegar a diferentes sectores de la comunidad.
 La campaña de Raman cuenta con un elenco joven, presentándola como un soplo de aire fresco frente a las prácticas asfixiantes del Ayuntamiento. Habla español con fluidez y su mensaje busca atraer a la comunidad latina a una coalición multiétnica que una a jóvenes y a inquilinos, superando las antiguas divisiones raciales. En su coalición, importa menos si el votante es blanco, negro o latino, y más que esté harto de la política tradicional de Los Ángeles.
 Por su parte, Bass cuenta con bases de apoyo más institucionales. Demócrata liberal de larga trayectoria y oriunda de la ciudad, Bass goza del respaldo de importantes grupos de derechos civiles y de los inmigrantes, sindicatos y líderes respetados como la senadora estatal María Elena Durazo , una figura clave del movimiento obrero de la ciudad.
 En definitiva, las elecciones dependen de la participación electoral. La combinación de los resultados de las elecciones de junio y las encuestas realizadas desde entonces sugiere que Raman probablemente cuenta con un respaldo más amplio entre los latinos de Los Ángeles, pero Bass probablemente tiene un apoyo más sólido entre los votantes más habituales.
 ¿Acudirán los latinos más jóvenes a votar por Raman en número suficiente para contrarrestar la fuerza de Bass entre los latinos propietarios de viviendas y residentes de larga data? Las elecciones de junio reflejan un momento específico y muestran el comportamiento real de los votantes, pero las de noviembre atraerán a nuevos electores y reflejarán la campaña en sí.
 Al final, esos son los resultados que importarán.
 Los periodistas de datos Mohamed Al Elew y Jeremia Kimelman contribuyeron a este artículo.

name: WyoFile
title: How will Wyoming spend $205M in federal healthcare money? On rural hospitals, first responders and workforce programs.
text:
Spanning 8,000 square miles of sparsely populated southern Wyoming infamous  for its brutal weather, Carbon County is a tough place to provide healthcare. 
Memorial Hospital of Carbon County faces challenges experienced in much of Wyoming: low patient volume, high costs involved in 24/7 emergency care and difficulty recruiting and retaining a workforce. The Rawlins hospital in 2022 closed its labor and delivery services, and today local residents routinely drive 100 miles to Laramie for obstetrics. 
Given these realities, Memorial Hospital CEO Kerry Ashmant said Friday, $5.8 million in Rural Health Transformation Program funds will have a significant impact. The federal dollars will bolster the hospital’s EMS services and help it deliver critical hemodialysis to patients with chronic illnesses, he said. 
“For a rural hospital like ours, funding of this kind represents much more than financial assistance,” he said. “It represents a commitment to the people who call rural Wyoming home, to the families who depend on local healthcare and to the principle that access to essential medical services should not be determined by zip code.”
The hospital is among the clinics, ambulance services and workforce development programs that will benefit from the new federal program. Gov. Mark Gordon, U.S. Sen. John Barrasso and healthcare officials on Friday celebrated Wyoming’s $205 million in year-one awards, which were finalized barely a year after the state began to put together its application. 
“I can’t believe the level of teamwork and thoughtfulness that’s gone into this in a super tight timeline,” said Matt Dammeyer, CEO of Memorial Hospital of Converse County in Douglas. His facility will receive more than $5 million for hospital and EMS services. 

U.S. Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyoming, speaks to an audience before the antler auction begins at Elk Fest in Jackson May 20, 2023. (Natalie Behring/WyoFile)

Given the tasks involved for Wyoming — including collecting public input, negotiating with federal administrators, getting legislation passed, publishing requests for proposals and assessing provider applications — it’s an impressive feat. It’s one that has required agility from the Wyoming Department of Health and others, Gov. Gordon said. 
“We’ve moved very expeditiously,” he said.
Wyoming stands to receive up to $1 billion over the program’s five-year funding period, which advocates like Barrasso, an orthopedic surgeon who practiced in Casper, say will truly transform the state’s fragile rural health system. “We’re going to be able to work to improve high-quality care, close to home,” said Barrasso, who was a major champion of President Donald Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” that created this initiative. 
The Rural Health Transformation Program aims to offset some of the federal healthcare dollars cut by the act, which is expected to result in more uninsured Americans.
An additional challenge for Wyoming is finding ways to deploy program funds that will sustain beyond the five-year funding window. That is why Wyoming didn’t produce a wish list of shiny products and new buildings, said Department of Health Director Stefan Johansson, but focused on innovating around the basics. 
“It’s very Wyoming,” he said. “Balance the ideal with the practical.”
Breaking down the awards
In its approval, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services gave the Wyoming $5 million more than it requested — the second-largest award per capita, behind Alaska.
Wyoming’s original vision for how it could spend the federal dollars has evolved to fit federal rules as well as state lawmaker appetite. Notably, the state removed two core proposals: a system of “perpetuity” investments that could generate revenue for Wyoming healthcare programs indefinitely and a state-operated public catastrophic insurance plan.
Of the award pie, Wyoming is serving the largest piece to initiatives under the category of “improving access to emergency medical care.” The $91.8 million slice aims to incentivize hospitals to provide essential basic services and to regionalize and strengthen EMS services. 
Warm Valley Health Care in Fort Washakie, North Lincoln County Hospital District in Star Valley and Cody Regional Health are among significant award winners in that category.
The second-largest pie piece, $56.3 million, will support programs that increase rural workforce supply. These range from individual awards for education boosts to grants given to education organizations for expanding programs. 
(Office of Gov. Mark Gordon)
The Wyoming Innovation Partnership, a workforce development program Gordon launched in 2021, will act as the fiscal agent for the majority of this section. The partnership will invest more than $35 million into workforce projects. In addition, the University of Wyoming will receive $6.2 million for graduate medical education and the University of Utah will receive $9.3 million for a similar program. 
The third-biggest pie slice, $38.6 million, will go to the “Make Wyoming Healthy Again” category. These programs aim to improve physical and behavioral health with interventions including integrated primary care, diet and exercise. 
The final pie chunk, $16.9 million, will go toward transforming health technology. This will entail updating systems and employing telehealth to improve access. Along with individual awards to places like Evanston Regional Hospital and Powell Valley Health Care, the state will fund a statewide telehealth specialist program with $3.5 million. 
Once a state advisory committee finished first-round award recommendations in August, there was $17.6 million leftover. The panel earmarked those to support targeted EMS and labor and delivery efforts, and Wyoming is partnering with the Wyoming Hospital Association to deploy the money.
Health department administrative costs will use 0.7% of the total award, which amounts to $1.3 million. 
What’s next
Now that Wyoming has finalized its year-one funding obligations, it will move on to  next steps in the program, which has unfolded with rapid and aggressive deadlines. 
In year-two, Wyoming hopes to continue the work, officials said, with some expansion. The health department is also tasked with monitoring the deployment and reporting on outcomes to the federal government.
Recipients, meanwhile, are preparing to implement their awards. 
The emergency room entrance at St. John’s Health in Jackson. (Angus M. Thuermer Jr./WyoFile)
Johnson County Hospital District will receive $4.8 million for technology. 
“It’s going to be super meaningful for us,” Luke Senden, CEO at Johnson County Healthcare Center in Buffalo, said of the award. The facility currently functions by patching together three separate medical record systems, he said, which creates many inefficiencies. 
“No one joins healthcare because they like paperwork and they like cumbersome processes,” Senden said. “The ability for our providers to have a unified system for each one of our patients, no matter what setting they’re in, is going to do so much for transforming the way that we deliver care inside of our community.”
The post How will Wyoming spend $205M in federal healthcare money? On rural hospitals, first responders and workforce programs. appeared first on WyoFile .

name: Mississippi Today
title: Jackson seeks $125 million under controversial federal policing grant
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippi’s capital city is a finalist for a U.S. Department of Justice grant that could pump tens of millions of dollars into its police department, a surge of funding that Jackson officials have said would be used to rebuild the city’s forensic laboratory, hire more officers and expand surveillance of violent crime, including using artificial intelligence to track potential criminals.
Other Democratic-led cities, including Charlotte and New Orleans, declined to apply for the grant, which will require participating municipalities to cooperate with certain Trump administration priorities, including immigration enforcement and a ban on public sleeping. 
In Jackson, which has some of the highest homicide rates in the nation, Mayor John Horhn said he had not heard from any constituents who are concerned the grant could result in a federal takeover of the Jackson Police Department.
Jackson Mayor John Horhn delivers his State of the City address at the Jackson Convention Complex on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“I haven’t seen one bit of concern or criticism about our going after this grant,” Horhn told Mississippi Today. “In fact, most people are happy to hear that we might be able to get a tremendous amount of resources that can help with crime fighting.” 
Jackson is requesting $125 million over three years.
Unlike other federal law enforcement grants, the Model Cities Initiative will be administered through a “cooperative agreement,” giving the DOJ a more active role in implementation. 
In a statement, the ACLU of Mississippi called on the city to be transparent with residents about the grant before any agreement is finalized, adding that it was concerned the funding would require JPD to adopt an aggressive approach to policing that could jeopardize Jacksonians’ civil liberties. 
“Jackson deserves investments in public safety that build trust, address the root causes of violence, and protect the rights of all residents,” said Lydia Grizzell, the advocacy manager of the ACLU of Mississippi.
Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney, who did not respond to an interview request, was invited to brief federal officials on the city’s application on Oct. 1. The DOJ has not yet announced which two to four cities will receive the new Model Cities Initiative grant, part of a federal initiative to “Make America Safe Again.” 
In the city’s grant application, which Mississippi Today obtained through a public records request, JPD argued that Jackson’s “violent-crime problem is fundamentally a lack of system capacity.” 
The department noted that its officers frequently work in silos. In one example, JPD wrote that even though officers have access to federal ballistics data, the department’s case-management system shows no “leads formally linked to an arrest or conviction,” according to the grant application. 
“This reflects a tracking gap, not an absence of investigative value.” 
The department proposed spending much of the potential $125 million award on solving these gaps, including creating a specialized gun crimes unit focused on “repeat shooters,” expanding JPD’s network of cameras housed at the Real Time Command Center, and creating a database that would link 911 calls to the addresses of burned-out homes, illegal dumping sites and other code enforcement complaints. 
“It is the infrastructure behind Jackson’s vision of becoming ‘The City That Responds Before It Arrives’: seeing the threat, understanding the condition, directing the right resource, and intervening before it becomes the next crime, emergency, or community crisis,” the department wrote. 
JPD also proposed using $10 million to fund a victim advocate unit that would “connect victims to advocacy from the first 911 calls,” $10 million to create a reentry council that would monitor “high-risk reentry cases,” and $22 million on rebuilding the forensic center. 
“Its current capability is limited to testing green leafy substances,” the city wrote. 
The Jackson City Council gave Brackney the authority to apply for the grant earlier this year. The agenda item passed with no discussion. 
The city’s grant application was supported by letters from state and local law enforcement officials, including Hinds County Sheriff Tyree Jones, then-Capitol Police Chief Bo Luckey, Mississippi Department of Public Safety Commissioner Sean Tindell, and Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch. 
Jackson “provides an opportunity that no other city can replicate to demonstrate that surging personnel and resources and working in partnership across federal, state and local levels can reduce criminal activity, restore law and order, and positively impact the quality of life for residents in high crime jurisdictions,” Fitch wrote in an Aug. 13 letter. “Simply put, Jackson, Mississippi is the best opportunity to provide the underlying hypothesis of the Model Cities Initiative.”

name: California
title: Guía de última hora para los votantes sobre las 14 propuestas en la boleta electoral de California
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Sí, el tan comentado impuesto a los multimillonarios estará en la boleta electoral de noviembre, pero es solo una de las 14 propuestas a nivel estatal.
 Si no eres un experto en políticas públicas ni conoces a fondo las leyes estatales sobre elecciones, impuestos o medio ambiente, no te preocupes: no estás solo y estamos aquí para ayudarte. La guía electoral de CalMatters incluye explicaciones completas, videos e incluso cuestionarios para ayudarte a decidir si estas medidas se alinean con tus valores y prioridades.
 Pero si lo que quieres es un resumen conciso sobre quién apoya a qué, aquí tienes un resumen aún más breve y de última hora. 
 Impuestos: Propuestas 2, 3, 40, 41, 42 y 43
Si te parece que la boleta electoral de este año tiene una cantidad inusualmente alta de propuestas relacionadas con impuestos , pues tienes razón. Así es.
La Propuesta 2 permitiría al estado depositar más dinero en sus reservas , también conocidas como el fondo de reserva para tiempos difíciles. El estado tiene normas estrictas sobre la cantidad de dinero que puede ahorrar para épocas de crisis, en parte debido a las limitaciones impuestas durante la revuelta de contribuyentes de la década de 1970. Sin embargo, California también tiene un sistema tributario bastante volátil que fluctúa según los ingresos de sus contribuyentes más ricos. Los demócratas buscan mayor flexibilidad para ahorrar dinero para épocas de recesión. Muchos republicanos afirman que el dinero sobrante debería destinarse a los contribuyentes, en lugar de permanecer en las arcas estatales.
La Proposición 3 convertiría un impuesto temporal sobre la renta para las personas con mayores ingresos en una ley permanente. Este impuesto, que afecta a quienes tienen ingresos individuales superiores a 360,000 dólares, se promulgó como una solución rápida en 2012, y la mayor parte de los fondos se destinaron a la educación primaria y secundaria y a los colegios comunitarios. Ahora, el sindicato de maestros más grande del estado quiere que el impuesto sea permanente , pero los opositores afirman que California ya tiene algunos de los impuestos más altos del país.
 La Proposición 40, también conocida como el impuesto a los multimillonarios, es sin duda la campaña electoral más destacada y costosa de este año. Establecería un impuesto único del 5% sobre el patrimonio neto de los multimillonarios, recaudando aproximadamente 100 mil millones de dólares en cinco años, según el sindicato de trabajadores de la salud que impulsó la medida. Los defensores argumentan que estos californianos ultrarricos ya reciben recortes de impuestos federales y que el dinero ayudará a los programas de salud que enfrentan recortes de financiación estatales y federales . Sin embargo, los líderes empresariales señalan que California depende de estos multimillonarios para sus ingresos fiscales , y si se marchan, el estado podría sufrir. Incluso algunas organizaciones de salud, como Planned Parenthood, se oponen a la Proposición 40, porque les preocupa que el dinero no ayude realmente a evitar los recortes de financiación estatales y federales.
 La Proposición 40 es tan controvertida que sus opositores han presentado dos propuestas rivales, la Proposición 41 y la Proposición 42 , que, de ser aprobadas, anularían el impuesto a los multimillonarios. Un voto afirmativo a cualquiera de estas dos propuestas invalidaría dicho impuesto.
 La Proposición 43 dificultaría la aprobación de referendos tributarios locales impulsados por los ciudadanos. Actualmente, estas medidas tributarias locales solo requieren una mayoría simple para ser aprobadas. Si la Proposición 43 se aprueba, necesitarían dos tercios de los votos. Sus defensores afirman que la Proposición 43 subsana una laguna legal en la legislación sobre impuestos electorales. Sus detractores la consideran antidemocrática. 
 ¿Debería California endeudarse para financiar vivienda e investigación médica?
 El estado puede recaudar rápidamente grandes cantidades de efectivo mediante la venta de bonos a inversores, pero vender demasiados bonos conlleva el riesgo de endeudar al estado.
 La Propuesta 1 autorizaría al estado a endeudarse hasta por $11.25 mil millones para la construcción y renovación de viviendas, principalmente para unidades de alquiler. Muchos promotores inmobiliarios y gobiernos locales que reciban el dinero tendrían que reservar una parte para viviendas asequibles para inquilinos de bajos ingresos o para viviendas especializadas para personas sin hogar. Parte del dinero también se destinaría a apoyar a quienes compran una vivienda por primera vez, veteranos, trabajadores agrícolas, estudiantes y las comunidades indígenas de California.
 La Proposición 37 crearía un fondo de préstamos para ayudar a los compradores de vivienda de clase media con el pago inicial. Técnicamente, se trata de un bono de 25 mil millones de dólares, aunque el dinero sería reembolsado gradualmente por los compradores de vivienda en lugar de por los contribuyentes. De aprobarse, la mayoría de los inquilinos de California cumplirían los requisitos. Los defensores, incluidos sindicatos, promotores inmobiliarios y el Partido Demócrata, afirman que la proposición podría facilitar el acceso a la vivienda, pero los opositores señalan que presenta varios problemas que podrían impedir su implementación o, peor aún, que podría endeudar aún más a los compradores.
La Proposición 38 destinaría 8,400 millones de dólares en fondos estatales a la investigación inmunológica, pero con una condición. Aproximadamente la mitad del dinero se destinaría a una organización sin fines de lucro , muy probablemente el Instituto de Inmunología e Inmunoterapia de California. Gary K. Michelson, cofundador del instituto, impulsó esta propuesta para que se incluyera en la boleta electoral.
 Modificación de las leyes electorales
 Estas propuestas electorales podrían influir en la forma en que los candidatos recaudan fondos y en el funcionamiento de las elecciones revocatorias. Los votantes también se pronunciarán sobre una propuesta de identificación de votantes.
 La Proposición 4 permitiría a los gobiernos estatales y locales crear financiamiento público para campañas políticas. Sus defensores, incluido el Partido Demócrata de California, argumentan que podría ayudar a limitar el gasto político, ya que los candidatos generalmente deben aceptar ciertos límites de gasto a cambio de acceso a fondos públicos. Los opositores afirman que la propuesta podría obligar a los contribuyentes a aportar dinero para candidatos que no apoyan. Los estudios sobre la efectividad del financiamiento público para campañas políticas presentan resultados contradictorios.
 La Proposición 5 modificaría las reglas que rigen las elecciones revocatorias en California. Actualmente, en una elección revocatoria se pregunta a los votantes si desean destituir al funcionario electo y a quién prefieren en su lugar. Un voto afirmativo a la Proposición 5 establecería que las elecciones revocatorias solo preguntarían si los votantes desean destituir al funcionario electo. Si se produce la revocación, se celebrarían otras elecciones para determinar quién debería reemplazarlo. El Partido Demócrata apoya esta propuesta. Los republicanos se oponen.
 La Proposición 39 aumentaría los requisitos de identificación para los votantes de California. Para registrarse, los votantes ya deben declarar por escrito que son ciudadanos estadounidenses. Esta proposición exigiría que los votantes presenten prueba de ciudadanía antes de emitir su voto. Los republicanos argumentan que la proposición alinearía a California con muchos otros estados y que combatiría el fraude electoral, que es poco común. Han gastado más de 36 millones de dólares en apoyo de la proposición, casi la mitad provenientes del multimillonario de Illinois Richard Uihlein . Los demócratas afirman que la Proposición 39 podría crear “barreras innecesarias”, especialmente para los inmigrantes y los californianos de bajos ingresos que carecen de licencia de conducir. 
Otros temas: La sanidad y el medio ambiente
 Cualquiera puede incluir una propuesta en las papeletas electorales de California si sigue los procedimientos correctos y consigue suficientes firmas, pero los grupos de interés especiales, como los sindicatos y las organizaciones a favor de las empresas, lo hacen con más frecuencia que la mayoría.
 La Proposición 44 proviene del mismo sindicato de trabajadores de la salud que impulsó el impuesto a los multimillonarios. Obligaría a las clínicas a destinar al menos el 90% de sus ingresos anuales a la atención al paciente. El sindicato, Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, argumenta que la Proposición 44 es necesaria para controlar los salarios de los directores ejecutivos y garantizar que las clínicas inviertan en la atención al paciente. El Partido Demócrata y las asociaciones de salud se oponen, afirmando que creará una regulación innecesaria en un momento en que las clínicas ya enfrentan presiones financieras debido a los recortes presupuestarios federales.
 La Proposición 45 , patrocinada por la Cámara de Comercio de California, una organización que defiende los intereses empresariales, podría debilitar la emblemática ley de evaluación ambiental de California, conocida como CEQA. Esta ley de 1970 exige que las agencias consideren el daño ambiental antes de construir, pero los promotores inmobiliarios afirman que a menudo se utiliza para retrasar proyectos de infraestructura y vivienda asequible muy necesarios . Los ambientalistas advierten que la aprobación de la Proposición 45 podría ser desastrosa para las comunidades que viven cerca de zonas contaminadas por industrias.
 Si desea obtener más información, recuerde que toda esta información, y mucho más, está disponible en la guía para votantes de CalMatters.

name: Delaware
title: Milford’s Lulu Ross school fire closes classes for week, disrupts neighboring campus and moves polling place
text:
Photo is Courtesy of the Georgetown Fire Department on 10/25
More than 600 Milford students face an uncertain return after Sunday’s three-alarm fire, while investigators work to determine the cause and the district develops a longer-term education plan.
MILFORD — The fallout from a major fire at Lulu M. Ross Elementary School expanded Monday, with classes canceled for the entire week, neighboring Mispillion Elementary temporarily affected and election officials moving a polling place ahead of the Nov. 3 general election.
The developments come one day after a three-alarm fire heavily damaged portions of Lulu Ross, a Milford School District elementary school serving more than 600 students.
Students at Lulu Ross will have no in-person or remote instruction from Monday, Oct. 26, through Friday, Oct. 30, while district officials assess the building and determine how and where instruction can resume.
The Milford School District has not yet announced whether students will eventually return to portions of the building, be temporarily relocated to other facilities or use another arrangement.
The uncertainty represents one of the most significant immediate challenges facing the district following the fire.
Fire began in Kent wing
The Delaware State Fire Marshal’s Office said investigators determined the fire originated in the Kent wing of the school.
The cause remains under investigation, but officials said they have found no evidence at this point that criminal activity was involved.
Firefighters were dispatched shortly after 4 a.m. Sunday after an automatic fire alarm activated at the school on Lovers Lane.
When crews arrived, fire was coming through the roof.
Firefighters initially attempted to attack the fire from inside the building, but deteriorating conditions forced crews to evacuate and shift their response. The blaze eventually grew to three alarms, bringing firefighters and equipment from departments throughout the area.
It took crews about three hours to bring the fire under control.
No students or employees were inside the school when the fire started, and no injuries were reported.
The fire caused extensive damage to the Kent wing and spread into central portions of the school, including the front lobby, administrative offices and library. Classrooms in the Kent and New Castle hallways were also heavily damaged.
The State Fire Marshal’s Office has not released a damage estimate.
Fire crews returned to Lulu Ross Monday morning, according to Carlisle Fire Company response records, as investigators and emergency personnel continued work at the property.
Neighboring school also affected
The fire also disrupted operations at nearby Mispillion Elementary School, which shares the campus area and infrastructure with Lulu Ross.
Mispillion was closed Monday because the fire damaged fiber-optic infrastructure serving the schools, leaving the building without working internet and telephone service.
District officials said operating without those communication systems presented a safety concern.
State agencies and repair crews were working to restore the service.
The district initially announced the Mispillion closure for Monday only. Other Milford School District schools were operating on their normal schedules.
Polling place moved
The effects of the fire will also reach beyond the school district.
The Delaware Department of Elections announced Monday that voters in Sussex County Election District 36-01 who normally vote at Lulu Ross will instead vote at Mispillion Elementary School for the Nov. 3 general election.
Mispillion Elementary is located at 311 Lovers Lane in Milford, adjacent to the Lulu Ross campus.
The Department of Elections said notification letters were mailed to voters affected by the change.
Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. on Election Day.
Early voting is already underway and continues through Sunday, Nov. 1.
Focus turns to students
Beyond the physical damage, district leaders now face the challenge of determining how to continue educating hundreds of elementary students if Lulu Ross cannot reopen quickly.
The school enrolled 614 students during the 2025-26 school year, according to Delaware Department of Education enrollment figures.
The district’s crisis response team has been working on both short-term and longer-term plans for students and employees.
District officials are also coordinating with state agencies to provide resources for families and staff members affected by the fire and its aftermath.
Community organizations and school systems around Delaware have begun offering assistance.
For parents, however, the immediate question remains what happens after Friday.
District officials have not yet announced plans for the week beginning Nov. 2 or provided a timetable for determining how much of Lulu Ross can eventually be returned to service.
Officials are asking members of the public to stay away from the Lulu Ross property while investigators, emergency crews and district personnel continue their work.
The fire investigation remains active, and additional announcements are expected as the district evaluates the condition of the school and develops a plan for returning Lulu Ross students to instruction.
TO GO BOX:  Lulu M. Ross Elementary School fire

What happened: A three-alarm fire heavily damaged Lulu Ross Elementary School early Sunday, Oct. 25.
School closure: Lulu Ross students will have no in-person or remote classes through Friday, Oct. 30.
Students affected: More than 600.
Cause: Under investigation by the Delaware State Fire Marshal’s Office. Investigators have reported no evidence of criminal activity at this time.
Mispillion Elementary: Closed Monday because fire damage interrupted internet and telephone service. Families should monitor Milford School District updates for additional schedule information.
Election change: Sussex County Election District 36-01 voters will vote Nov. 3 at Mispillion Elementary School, 311 Lovers Lane, Milford, instead of Lulu Ross.
Where to follow updates: Milford School District, Delaware Department of Elections and Delaware LIVE/Milford LIVE.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Pressure mounting in courts to deal with WV school funding as Berkeley County prepares lawsuit
text:
A classroom at Woodrow Wilson Elementary School in South Salt Lake is pictured on Tuesday, March 12, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Berkeley County Schools plans to sue state officials over public school funding as pressure mounts in the courts to deal with the issue. Families, school officials and their lawyers are turning to the judicial system for help after lawmakers didn’t make any changes to the school funding formula this year.
The state’s school funding formula is largely tied to school enrollment numbers, complicating school’s budgets due to the state’s overall shrinking population. The student population is also declining — 8,200 fewer students are in the public school system compared to last year.
The school funding issues coupled with one-time COVID-era money drying out has led to a wave of school closures across West Virginia, where most students attend public schools.
Lawyers for American Civil Liberties of West Virginia last month said it will sue over the decades-old funding formula on behalf of a Lincoln County sixth grader. The group is asking the state Supreme Court to determine whether West Virginia’s school funding formula is inadequate and force state lawmakers to address it.
The West Virginia Supreme Court has given state officials named in their lawsuit until Nov. 20 to submit their positions in writing.
Berkeley County Schools Superintendent Ryan Saxe (Photo: Berkeley County Schools)
On Monday, Berkeley County Schools Superintendent Ryan Saxe said the county will move forward with its own school funding lawsuit.
“It’s about ensuring that the resources provided to the school district reflect the responsibilities that we’re expected to fulfill … to ensure that we have a funding system that reflects what it actually costs to provide the education our students are entitled to receive under the Constitution,” Saxe said in a phone interview.
Berkeley County is a bit of an anomaly compared to other West Virginia counties rapidly losing student population. While their headcount has dipped a bit, Saxe said, the county is one of the few parts of the state that is growing.
But there are other issues straining the school budget, Saxe explained. The district is facing significant challenges recruiting and retaining teachers in the border county due to the state’s low teacher pay.
For each of the past three school years, Berkeley County Schools has relied on approximately 200 to 250 permanent substitutes annually across 33 school sites after being unable to recruit enough certified teachers.
Along with serving the state’s highest rate of English language learners, which bring additional costs, the district also services a significant number of special education students.
“The costs are not optional,” Saxe said. “Last year alone, Berkeley County’s special education costs exceeded the funding provided to us by the state for those students by $38 million. That is something that the district obviously was required to pay for from our general fund.”
The county is required to give a 30-day notice to state officials and entities about litigation.
Other West Virginia counties have reported consequential financial strain providing services to the state’s 46,000 special education students. The issue has pushed multiple school systems into millions of dollars of debt.
The current student aid formula largely doesn’t account for increased funds needed for federally and state-level required special education accommodations, like one-on-one aids or technology.
School funding formula debate in Legislature
The legislative session concluded in March without lawmakers making any changes to the school funding formula after debate on multiple bills to deal with the issue. Roadblocks often centered on funding concerns; a House bill updating the funding formula would have cost $214 million.
Senate Education Chair Amy Grady, R-Mason, and House Education Chair Joe Statler, R-Monongalia, have spent the summer and fall working on school funding legislation, though neither has vowed it will make it through the GOP-controlled legislature.
The West Virginia Board of Education recently shared its own proposed school funding formula overhaul for lawmakers to consider. It would restructure the funding formula to address declining enrollment along with needs in special education, high poverty areas, rural schools and more.
Board members also voted to side with the ACLU-WV in their school funding lawsuit; all but one board member acknowledged that the funding formula is insufficient.
There was no overall price tag yet for the school board’s proposed funding changes, but state school officials estimated that the special education funding changes alone would cost $190 million.
Saxe said he will continue to work with local lawmakers to address the school funding issue while his district’s lawsuit moves forward.
“I think that they see the needs and and the challenges that are facing the school systems here in the Eastern Panhandle, and I think they they’ve been huge advocates for what we need as it relates to looking at regional labor market pay, to looking at the need for special education funding,” Saxe said.
“We want to continue to work with them, but we also recognize that if something is not done this legislative session, we want to be able to have a have some assurance that in the future it may be that the courts are going to have to decide that this is actually not constitutional, and the legislature is going to have to do something,” he added.

name: VTDigger
title: Supporters raise offer for Rice Memorial High in hopes of spurring court approval of sale
text:
The football field at the grade 9-12 Rice Memorial High School in South Burlington. Photo by Kevin O’Connor/VTDigger

Supporters wanting to save the Vermont Roman Catholic Diocese’s flagship Rice Memorial High School from potential liquidation in the church’s ongoing Chapter 11 financial reorganization case have upped their offer from $4.3 million to $5.9 million.
The state’s largest religious denomination asked a U.S. Bankruptcy Court judge this summer for permission to privately offer the grade 9-12 South Burlington campus to the new nonprofit entity RMHS Inc., whose principal officers are the nine members of the Rice School Board.
But a creditors’ committee representing more than 100 people who have filed clergy abuse claims against the diocese contested the plan’s initial price tag — spurring all sides to hold mediation talks this fall and supporters to raise their bid.
“The diocese has discussed the purchaser’s offer with the official committee,” church lawyers have written in court papers filed this month in advance of a scheduled Nov. 20 hearing on the issue. “The committee consents to the proposed sale.”

READ MORE

An attorney for the creditors’ committee confirmed that consent to VTDigger, although the group has yet to formally affirm its approval in a court filing.
Any sale during the Chapter 11 process also requires a judge’s sign-off. That could come just weeks before the diocese is set to ask to withdraw its financial reorganization case at a Dec. 8 hearing, although an affirmative ruling on the latter request isn’t guaranteed and could take time.
The diocese asked the bankruptcy court for help in the fall of 2024, saying a past series of nearly 70 priest misconduct settlements had reduced its bank-and-building holdings by half — to about $35 million — with more than 100 other abuse claims dating as far back as 1950 yet to be resolved.
As part of the process, the church asked the court in July for approval to sell Rice’s 42-classroom building and surrounding 27 acres to a group of unnamed “dedicated donors.”
Supporters said their initial $4.3 million offer came after White + Burke Real Estate Advisors of Burlington issued a seven-page estimate of the school’s market value at between $4 million and $6 million.
In response, the creditors’ committee questioned why the proposed price wasn’t closer to a more comprehensive 31-page church-commissioned appraisal by Champlain Valley Appraisal Services of Waterbury that valued the campus at $30.5 million. Abuse claimants called for higher bids in hopes of raising more money for settlements.
Rice began in 1917 as Cathedral High School in downtown Burlington before moving to a new name and its current South Burlington location in 1959, according to its online history.
The 400-student Rice campus is one of three Catholic high schools in Vermont, alongside Mount St. Joseph Academy in Rutland and St. Michael School in Brattleboro. The diocese hasn’t announced any plans for the latter two institutions or its 10 schools for elementary and middle grades.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Gov. Lujan Grisham announces federal disaster aid for severe weather, flooding
text:
Flooding in San Juan County damaged thousands of homes, particularly along the banks of the San Juan and Animas rivers. Amateur drone photographer Elmer Ignacio posted the above footage of Bloomfield on Oct. 23, 2026. (Photo courtesy Elmer Ignacio)New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham on Monday announced that President Donald Trump had approved a federal disaster declaration following widespread flooding afflicting many northern New Mexico counties and pueblos. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The governor, at a news conference Monday from San Juan County, said she is awaiting specifics on the disaster declaration’s scope. But she said the state needs all the assistance it can get to help pay for a flooding disaster that has damaged thousands of homes and that the governor estimated could ultimately cost up to $300 million.
“The environmental issues and the road issues and the infrastructure issues alone really are expensive, and they are very hidden costs,” Lujan Grisham said. 
San Juan County, and particularly between Bloomfield and Farmington, has borne the brunt of the recent flooding. Approximately 1,500 homes in that area suffered some damage, according to the National Weather Service, and swiftwater crews conducted at least 60 rescues. Helicopter crews rescued additional homeowners who were stranded on their rooftops, officials have said. 
State officials have estimated that emergency response costs following floods and other weather-related havoc have already grown to at least $4.5 million, with an additional $13.7 million expected through Tuesday. 
State officials told Source NM on Friday that full damage estimates aren’t possible until floodwaters recede, but initial estimates are that as many as 18,000 homes sustained flooding damage in San Juan County alone, according to a letter New Mexico’s delegation sent Sunday to President Donald Trump. 
The delegation asked Trump to provide $13.8 million in relief efforts, plus additional funding for ongoing environmental remediation, to San Juan, Rio Arriba, Cibola and Sandoval counties, as well as Acoma Pueblo, the Jicarilla Apache Nation, San Ildefonso Pueblo, Zia Pueblo and Laguna Pueblo.

“It is imperative that the federal government provides direct and immediate assistance to support local and state efforts to respond to the historic and ongoing flooding,” the lawmakers wrote.
Officials with the Federal Emergency Management Agency, which would spearhead any federal response if a federal declaration is declared, did not immediately respond to Source NM’s request for comment Monday on the status of the delegation’s request. 
Lujan Grisham and state Sen. Steve Lanier (R-Farmington), in the news conference Monday announced that Trump had signed a disaster declaration, but it was not immediately clear what the declaration would cover. 
FEMA can cover a range of costs related to infrastructure and debris removal and can also provide direct assistance to families, depending on what a president authorizes. 
The agency also requires local governments to pay 25% of costs, with the federal government paying the remaining 75% on a reimbursement. Lujan Grisham on Monday urged residents and local elected officials to pressure FEMA to waive that cost-share. 
“I need everyone in the community to bolster that request and to get your own letters ready to go,” she said. 
At the same news conference Monday, San Juan County officials said that rescue operations had largely ceased, but that crews were still in the early stages of assessing potential hazards residents might face upon return to flooded homes.
In the meantime, they urged residents not to return to their homes until those inspections occur over the coming days. They also stressed that lingering floodwaters pose an array of health risks, so they urged residents to avoid them. 
In addition to San Juan County, severe weather has impacted much of northern New Mexico in recent days. Floods, hail, wind gusts and even a tornado prompted calls from the state’s congressional delegation for a federal disaster declaration that would bring additional resources to communities as floodwaters begin to recede.
A National Weather Service database recorded nearly 50 major weather events across the state since Friday, including 15 flash floods, 10 hail storms, 10 floods and seven severe thunderstorm-related wind gusts. 
The severe weather over the weekend included a tornado on a neighborhood street in Santa Fe that NWS officials said damaged 10 homes. The tornado — which NWS officials designated as an EF-1, meaning wind gusts up to 110 mph — broke power poles, uprooted trees and caused at least two roof collapses, according to city officials, though no injuries were reported as of Monday. 
Much of the Navajo Nation, including its eastern edge in New Mexico, was also digging out from heavy floods Monday. The Navajo Nation Police Department shared drone video showing swathes of the Shiprock area underwater and San Juan River water rising to just underneath one of the town’s main bridges. 
Navajo Nation Chief of Staff Sharen Sandoval on Monday said that as many as 500 homes in the Shiprock area were damaged.
Navajo Nation President Buu Nygren on Sunday said flooding and power outages continue to affect Shiprock. Nygren predicted in a news conference at 2:30 a.m. Sunday that additional flooding was expected to occur on tribal land in Utah and thanked crews for working around the clock across the vast Navajo Nation.
“Not enough thank yous can go out to our first responders,” he said.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: State: Fridley Public Schools risks ‘debt spiral’
text:
Fridley Public Schools' students on the first day of school this year. (Courtesy photo)The Minnesota Department of Education is hiring an outside auditor to examine Fridley Public Schools, according to a letter sent to the district Oct. 20, signed by Commissioner Willie Jett and obtained by the Reformer. The letter details significant concerns about financial management and the potential for the district — whose bonds were downgraded to junk level earlier this year — to “continue into a debt spiral,” of issuing new debt to pay off old debt.
Fridley Public Schools was placed on the state’s list of school districts in financial distress in March, called statutory operating debt under Minnesota law. Despite warnings in 2024 by its then budget director and its auditor, Superintendent Brenda Lewis told the Reformer in an interview last month that the district was surprised in December when the state informed the district that the designation was coming.
At the same time, district leadership notified the school board that its fiscal year 2025 audit would not be completed in time to meet the Dec. 31 state deadline. Nearly ten months later, that audit is still incomplete, and may cause the district to miss its 2026 audit deadline, too.
Under statute, school districts in statutory operating debt, or SOD, must submit a plan for state approval that shows how they will rebuild their financial reserves. If the plan is not approved, the state can withhold aid payments to the school district. In the letter, MDE says it cannot approve the district’s current plan “because the draft is not based on concrete financial information due to the missing [2025] audit” and late and incomplete financial data the district is required to submit to the state.
The letter also says, “the plan does not show a realistic or committed effort to move the school district out of SOD.”
When Lewis was asked about the state’s letter, she responded with an emailed statement, which reads in part: “Fridley Public Schools recognizes the seriousness of our financial challenges and remains fully committed to working cooperatively with the Minnesota Department of Education. We welcome the opportunity for a thorough review of the district’s financial records and practices as we continue our work toward long-term financial stability.” 
Board Chair Jake Karnopp referred questions to district administration.
The Minnesota Department of Education declined multiple requests in September and October for interviews about Fridley Public Schools and did not respond to emailed questions as of publication. It is not clear what recourse the state has to require changes in the district. Minnesota is one of 15 states without a legal framework for state takeover or intervention in school districts.
The fallout from the district’s financial woes has been accumulating all year. In January, the district borrowed $11.5 million in short-term bonds, called aid anticipation credits, to make sure it had enough cash available to pay its bills. 
To pay back the $11.5 million, and to cover its cash flow for the current school year, the district issued $23.4 million in new bonds in September. Cash flow projections from its financial advisor indicate that the district will need to borrow again next fall, to repay the $23.4 million and to borrow more for the following school year. Under state law, those bonds are capped at 75% of a district’s expected state aid.
Moody’s downgraded the district’s bond rating to junk status in January, lowered the rating again in July and then withdrew its rating in September due to insufficient financial information. Most institutional investors, including mutual funds and pension funds, cannot buy bonds that are unrated. Fridley currently participates in the state’s credit enhancement program, which extends the state’s bond rating to participating school districts to lower their cost of borrowing.
The state says that in May Fridley’s bond paying agent notified the state it had concerns that the district would not be able to make future debt service payments.
The state says it made numerous attempts to work with Fridley to address its issues. In May, the state asked the district for a completed audit no later than July 13, recommending the district hire an auditor or accountant “well-versed in Minnesota school district accounting.” 
After missing the July 13 deadline, the state and district met again in July, when the state expressed concerns about the possibility of a “debt spiral.” At that point, the state scheduled monthly meetings with the district related to its finances, operations, the unapproved SOD plan and the unfinished 2025 audit.
According to the state, at the September meeting the district said the staff working on the 2025 audit had changed. “The lack of experienced and consistent staffing has contributed to the district’s challenges completing the overdue audit, as well as the district identifying issues to solve for future audits,” according to the Oct. 20 letter.
Fridley’s financial situation isn’t unique in Minnesota or nationally. It has faced cost increases that exceed its revenue increases in recent years. And, its enrollment has declined in recent years because of a combination of lower birth rates and competition from open enrollment and charter schools. State aid is determined by enrollment — fewer students means fewer dollars. 
The district’s financial outlook is worsening with time, according to Fridley’s own SOD plan to get out of statutory operating debt, which was approved by the school board in January. The district’s unreserved fund balance, a measure of its financial reserves, is estimated to be -16% at the end of fiscal year 2025. This is an estimate because the 2025 audit isn’t completed yet. Projecting out to 2029, the district’s plan estimates that -16% exploding to -81%.
Fridley’s operating revenue is currently around $50 million per year, and is expected to grow at around 1% per year. Its operating expenses are around $60 million per year. According to the district’s SOD plan, expenses would remain flat, but it’s unclear how they’ll achieve this given a contract with educators that granted a roughly 5% raise last year, and again this year. The result is a projected annual deficit of around 20% of its budget.
The district was required to submit additional details as part of its SOD plan to the state. A public spreadsheet outlines $2.9 million in budget cuts for the current school year, with $600,000 of the proposed cuts coming from school-level staff. 
Lewis attributes the district’s financial challenges to a range of issues. She told the Reformer the district has had significant turnover in its finance department since 2017, which led to numerous errors in how the district codes its expenses and counts students. Those errors have been responsible for Fridley losing out on potentially millions of dollars in funding, according to Lewis. 
During the 2024-25 school year — the year with the incomplete audit — Fridley hired the Center for Effective School Operations to run its finance operations. Lewis said at a May 2026 school board meeting that the district was dissatisfied with the services and did not renew the contract. 
In response to questions from the Reformer, Lewis did not explain why numerous financial errors occurred during the 2024-25 school year while CESO was running finance operations. Nor did she explain why the audit was delayed, even though one of CESO’s responsibilities was supporting the audit process.
CESO is currently providing support to Minneapolis Public Schools finance operations. Its CEO, Stephanie Burrage, previously served as a deputy commissioner of education and as chief equity officer to Gov. Tim Walz.
In recent public updates, Lewis has pointed specifically to errors in coding special education expenses and missing out on subsequent state reimbursements for these expenses. It is not clear whether the district will be able to recoup any missed reimbursements from prior years, but Lewis has said this should improve the district’s finances in the future. Lewis has not provided an exact dollar amount for any potential new funding, however.

name: Delaware
title: Delaware looks to expand power supply as electric bills continue to climb
text:
Public Advocate Jameson Tweedie says rising regional demand, higher grid costs, and uncertainty over new generation are pressuring Delaware consumers.
By Delaware LIVE Staff
DOVER, Del. — Delaware faces a growing challenge: finding enough affordable electricity to meet future demand while protecting residents and businesses from rising utility bills.
Delaware Energy Advocate, Jameson Tweddie, spoke with Jane Brady, from A Better Delaware this morning on her weekly podcast.
New power plants, including natural-gas facilities, could be part of the answer. But uncertainty surrounding proposed projects, increasing regional electricity costs and a pending Delmarva Power rate increase leave consumers facing continued financial pressure.
That was the central message from Delaware Public Advocate Jameson Tweedie, who joined Jane Brady on Monday’s A Better Discussion, a public policy podcast presented by A Better Delaware.
Tweedie said Delaware needs additional electricity generation, but the problem extends well beyond the state’s borders. The regional power system is struggling to keep new generation in line with growing demand, particularly from large data centers.
At the same time, the three major components of consumers’ electric bills — generation, transmission and distribution — have been increasing.
New generation could help meet demand
One of the more significant developments discussed was the potential expansion of electricity generation in Delaware.
Tweedie cited a PJM Interconnection study showing nearly 1.8 gigawatts of proposed generating capacity under review in Delaware, most of it natural gas.
PJM’s August 2026 information identified nine proposed projects, including three natural-gas facilities, four solar projects and two energy-storage projects.
However, the proposed projects are not guaranteed to be built.
An independent review of PJM’s interconnection queue reported that a proposed natural-gas project of approximately 1.5 gigawatts in Sussex County had been withdrawn. The withdrawal raises questions about how much of the generation identified in earlier PJM reports remains under active consideration.
A project entering PJM’s study process must undergo technical and financial review before it can move toward construction.
The uncertainty makes it difficult to predict how much additional electricity Delaware will produce in the coming years.
Delaware produces less electricity than it consumes
Although Delaware has substantial installed generating capacity, the state continues to rely heavily on electricity produced elsewhere.
According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, Delaware had approximately 3,303 megawatts of net summer generating capacity in 2024.
The state generated approximately 4.8 million megawatt-hours of electricity that year, while retail customers purchased approximately 11.4 million megawatt-hours.
Those figures illustrate Delaware’s dependence on electricity supplied through the regional power system.
During Monday’s discussion, Brady questioned whether Delaware could better utilize existing generating facilities before encouraging the construction of additional plants.
Tweedie explained that installed capacity does not necessarily translate into actual electricity production.
Power plants operate according to demand, operating costs, transmission limitations and conditions within the regional electricity market. Some facilities generate power continuously, while others operate primarily during periods of high demand.
Delaware is part of PJM Interconnection, which coordinates electricity markets and transmission across 13 states and Washington, D.C.
That means Delaware policymakers can influence which generating facilities are developed in the state, but they cannot independently determine the price or availability of electricity throughout the regional market.
Electric bills have increased dramatically
The financial consequences are already evident in Delaware households.
An April 2026 report from the Delaware Division of the Public Advocate examined 20 years of Delmarva Power electric rates and documented substantial increases.
Among the findings:

Residential distribution rates have more than doubled since 2006.
Transmission rates increased 93.5% between 2020 and 2025.
Residential summer electricity supply rates increased 114.1% between 2021 and 2026.

For years, declining electricity supply costs helped offset increases in transmission and distribution charges.
That trend has reversed.
Tweedie explained that all three components are now rising, putting additional pressure on household budgets.
One particularly troubling development involves PJM’s capacity market, which pays electricity generators to ensure enough power will be available in future years.
Tweedie said capacity-market prices have increased approximately 1,000% over three years.
Although those charges account for only part of a typical electric bill, the increases reflect growing concern that electricity demand is rising faster than new generating capacity can be brought online.
Delmarva seeks another major rate increase
Delaware consumers also face a significant rate case involving Delmarva Power.
The utility initially requested a $67.8 million annual increase in base-rate revenue in December 2025. That amount included approximately $23.2 million already being collected through a separate infrastructure charge.
Delmarva subsequently updated its request to approximately $75.8 million.
The Delaware Public Service Commission allowed an interim increase of approximately $34.3 million to take effect in July while the full request remains under review.
Delmarva appealed the interim decision, arguing that the commission improperly accounted for an existing infrastructure charge and that the company must recover investments necessary to maintain reliable electric service.
Company officials have pointed to improvements in system reliability resulting from infrastructure spending.
Tweedie said his office is reviewing the proposed increase and will challenge expenses it determines are unjust or unreasonable.
The Public Advocate represents residential and small-business customers of regulated utilities before the Public Service Commission and in regional and federal proceedings.
Data centers could substantially increase demand
Another major concern is the rapid growth of large data centers, particularly facilities supporting artificial intelligence.
Tweedie said Delmarva previously examined several potential data-center projects that, if developed together, could have roughly doubled Delaware’s peak electricity demand.
These facilities can require enormous amounts of electricity, creating potential costs for new generation, transmission lines and other infrastructure.
In August, Gov. Matt Meyer signed legislation designed to prevent large electricity users from shifting those costs onto existing consumers.
House Bill 233 established a separate utility rate classification for major electricity users, including data centers, while House Bill 445 requires qualifying large energy facilities to produce or secure enough new generation to meet their power needs.
The legislation also contains provisions intended to prevent additional infrastructure costs from being passed along to residential and small-business customers.
Tweedie acknowledged that data centers can bring significant construction investment and employment opportunities, although permanent employment may be more limited.
His primary concern is ensuring that existing utility customers are not required to subsidize those developments.
Natural gas, nuclear and batteries offer different possibilities
The discussion also examined which energy technologies could help Delaware meet future electricity needs.
Natural gas remains an important part of the regional electricity system and has attracted substantial interest from developers proposing new generation.
However, Tweedie noted that a large natural-gas generating facility could take five to seven years or longer to develop.
Solar generation can generally be developed more quickly, although its output depends on available sunlight.
Nuclear power offers another possibility.
Tweedie served on Delaware’s Nuclear Energy Task Force, which recommended continued examination of nuclear generation.
He emphasized nuclear power’s ability to produce large quantities of dependable, carbon-free electricity around the clock.
But the substantial construction costs and lengthy development process remain obstacles.
Small modular reactors could eventually provide additional options, although Tweedie said their projected costs remain high and the technology has not yet achieved widespread commercial deployment.
Battery storage could offer benefits by capturing electricity when supplies are plentiful and releasing it during periods of peak demand.
Tweedie pointed to large-scale battery deployment in other states as evidence of the technology’s potential to reduce peak electricity costs and avoid some additional infrastructure investments.
The challenge: reliable power at a price consumers can afford
The discussion highlighted two related challenges for Delaware policymakers.
The first is ensuring that sufficient electricity will be available to serve existing customers and support economic growth.
The second is determining how that electricity and the infrastructure needed to deliver it will be paid for.
Generating more electricity within Delaware could improve the state’s available supply, but additional in-state capacity would not automatically lower electric bills because wholesale electricity prices are determined through regional markets.
Tweedie said his office is continuing to advocate for consumers before the Public Service Commission, PJM and federal regulators.
For Delaware households and small businesses, the larger question remains whether policymakers, regulators and energy providers can expand reliable electricity supplies without placing an even greater financial burden on customers.



TO GO: Delaware electricity costs and consumer assistance

Public Advocate: Jameson Tweedie, Delaware Division of the Public Advocate.
What the office does: Represents residential and small-business customers of regulated utilities, challenges unreasonable rate requests and helps resolve utility complaints.
Consumer assistance: Customers experiencing billing disputes, threatened disconnections or other utility problems can contact the office.
Website: publicadvocate.delaware.gov
Phone: 302-241-2555
Related research: Historical Review of Delmarva Power Electric Residential Rates, April 6, 2026, available through the Public Advocate’s website.
Podcast: A Better Discussion, hosted by Jane Brady, chair of A Better Delaware.
Broadcast: Monday, Oct. 26, 2026.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa Food System Coalition studies economic impact of raising livestock on pasture
text:
A small herd of cattle graze in a western Iowa pasture. (Photo by Jared Strong/Iowa Capital Dispatch)The Iowa Food System Coalition is embarking on a 12-month project studying pasture-based livestock systems in Iowa to examine the community and economic benefits of the practices. 
The coalition received a $40,000 grant from the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, or ASPCA, to support the study as part of the animal welfare group’s initiative to end “factory farming” practices. 
Tommy Hexter, Iowa Food System Coalition’s executive director, said the practice of pasture-based livestock operations “presents opportunities” for land stewardship, animal welfare and rural economic development. 
“But we have limited information about the scope of this industry in Iowa,” Hexter said in a news release. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Pasture-based livestock systems allow animals to graze freely — as opposed to being fed in a confined system. For beef operations, that might mean a grass fed or grass finished system, or a free-range operation for chickens. Hexter said part of the research will be to determine what Iowa producers consider pasture-based. 
“We’re casting a really wide net to start to allow people to self-identify pasture-based livestock farming, and then we’ll kind of get a holistic picture of what people in the state view as pasture-based livestock farming,” Hexter said. 
The coalition is working with Iowa State University Extension and Outreach and Practical Farmers of Iowa to disseminate a survey to Iowa livestock farmers to gather information about their operations, size, livestock types, equipment, land, staffing, budgets and profits. 
The project also plans to develop a statewide map of these operations, which Hexter said would help build consumer awareness of pasture-based livestock farms. 
The 2026 Food & Farm Index survey from Iowa Farm Bureau found that a growing number of Iowans are interested in buying protein directly from farmers. According to the index, 84% of Iowa grocery shoppers had purchased directly from farmers, meat lockers or farmer networks and nearly 80% of respondents said they review labels for information about how products were raised or processed. 
Hexter said that while the Iowa Farm Bureau survey doesn’t translate directly to a consumer desire for more pasture-raised protein, it indicates a growing consumer awareness of the “health benefits and the ecological benefits of pasture-based farming.” 
“We want to make a specific opportunity for people to locate those pasture-based farmers, so they can support them,” Hexter said. 
Hexter said the map would also help to identify gaps in local processing facilities across the state. 
In addition to the interactive map and economic analysis, the study will also present case studies from farmers running pasture-based livestock operations. 
Iowa Food System Coalition was one of five projects across the country awarded ASPCA funding through the organization’s Fund to End Factory Farming grants program. 
Hexter said farmers who participate in the survey will be eligible for a stipend for their time.
