name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Trump’s DOJ to send election monitors to Kentucky’s two largest counties on Nov. 3
text:
An election observer monitors two poll workers processing absentee ballots in the Milwaukee Election Commission warehouse on Aug. 13. Discrepancies in the count could be used by county canvassing boards in swing states as a reason not to certify elections. (Photo by Matt Vasilogambros/Stateline)
Kentucky election officials say they have been alerted by the U.S. Department of Justice that election monitors will head to the state’s largest cities for next week’s general election. 
A DOJ attorney sent an emailed letter to Republican Secretary of State Michael Adams and Kentucky State Board of Elections Executive Director Karen Sellers about the election monitors on Wednesday. 
The Kentucky effort comes as the DOJ plans to send 1,000 election monitors to polls across the nation during a heated midterm election. The DOJ has sent election monitors to review activities in past elections, including during the Biden administration, but this fall is expected to be the DOJ’s largest endeavor. 
A copy of the letter reviewed by the Kentucky Lantern says the Civil Rights Division of the DOJ “intends to send election monitors to two counties (Jefferson and Fayette) in your state on November 3, 2026.” The counties are home to Louisville and Lexington, the state’s largest cities, and both are Democratic strongholds. 
“The monitoring by the Civil Rights Division is done in the same way as in the past.  Our monitors only observe and take notes. They do not intrude or interfere in any way in the voting process,” the letter said, adding that monitors will introduce themselves to poll managers.
The monitors are not supposed to speak to voters inside the polling places, the letter says. Adams’ office did not have a public comment as of Monday afternoon. 
Quin Welch, a spokesperson for the Fayette County Clerk’s Office, said in a statement that FCCO officials met with DOJ representatives Monday afternoon to discuss the plans. 
“DOJ representatives said on the call that election monitors in groups of two to three will visit polling places in Fayette County to check for ADA compliance, provisional ballot distribution and required language assistance,” Welch added. “Election monitors are required to follow state law and FCCO will continue to work with its partners at the state and federal levels to ensure election monitors’ compliance with Kentucky election law.”
Jefferson County Clerk David Yates’ office also said the DOJ plans to focus on language assistance for voters, accessibility at polling locations and provision ballot use in a press release. Yates’ office added that “the Clerk’s Office has informed the DOJ that routine federal monitoring inside polling locations is not authorized under Kentucky law absent other applicable legal authority” and the county clerk provided “alternative ways for DOJ representatives to raise concerns, access public election information, and report potential voting-rights issues for prompt review.”
“While no formal documentation has been received, the DOJ has indicated that approximately a dozen federal monitors are expected to visit Louisville,” Yates said. “These individuals are DOJ employees serving as civil election monitors. They are not federal law enforcement officers and will not be serving in a law enforcement capacity.”
Josh Douglas, a law professor at the University of Kentucky said the DOJ election monitors are a “normal” part of an election.
“The federal government often sends federal monitors to polling places,” he added.
The Lantern sent an email seeking additional information to the DOJ Monday afternoon, such as why Fayette and Jefferson were selected out of 120 counties. A DOJ spokesperson said that election monitors will be in “all 50 states, including Kentucky, doing the routine election monitoring the department has done for decades.”
“We will have around 1,000 monitors in counties throughout the United States, but we will not share the full list until Election Day,” the spokesperson added. “Every monitor will merely observe and report any potential violations of federal law to the Department, which will be reviewed after Election Day.”
When the president held a rally in Northern Kentucky earlier this month, signs with a QR directed attendees to protectthevote.com, paid for by the Republican National Committee, to sign up to become an “election integrity volunteer,” and offer to watch polls. 
Kentucky Democratic Party Chairman Colmon Elridge said in a statement: “With his own popularity plummeting, it’s no coincidence Trump is singling out areas ready to elect and reelect Democrats like Zach Dembo and Congressman Morgan McGarvey.” Dembo is the Democratic candidate in the 6th Congressional District, which includes Fayette County. McGarvey is the incumbent in the 3rd Congressional District in Jefferson County.
“As part of our commitment to full and fair elections in Kentucky, we will not tolerate any interference,” Elridge said. “We expect and demand that federal monitors follow all rules.”
This story has been updated with additional comments.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Uthmeier: Property risk-assessment company ‘is marketing fear to advance a climate activism agenda’
text:
Florida's lawsuit against First Street Technology Inc. alleges a pattern of "climate chicanery" in its assessment of risks to homeowners from floods and other factors under the state's Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.Florida has sued a company that issues climate change assessments of property risks including flooding that the state alleges are deceptive, deviate from the federal flood insurance assessments, and are depressing home sales.
First Street Technology Inc., the complaint filed Friday alleges, posts “alarmist” risk data and “is marketing fear to advance a climate activism agenda while exploiting the same fear to line their pockets.” The venue is state trial court in Polk County.
First Street promises “validated and proven methodologies to ensure model accuracy. We measure and predict the impact of a peril based on the underlying physics of how an actual event would transpire.”
However, Uthmeier says in a video posted to X, “First Street rates certain properties as major flood risk. The FEMA rates the same properties as minimal flood hazard, the lowest federal classification. Those inflated scores have real consequences. Homes take longer to sell. They sell for less, insurance costs rise, and when homeowners try to correct obvious errors, First Street refuses.
“Their models are speculative, based on undisclosed choices, and frequently contradict official data. They claim transparency and peer review, yet underlying details are hidden behind a paywall, and independent analysis shows major discrepancies,” he says.
He demands “clear disclosure that the reports are subjective, uncertain, and may be contradicted by other credible sources. Florida homeowners deserve facts, not alarmist scores that hit their property values and their wallets. We are holding First Street accountable.”
The company’s risk assessments cover floods, fires, wind, air quality, and heat.
The Phoenix sought comment from First Street but has not heard back. Uthmeier, a former Gov. Ron DeSantis aide appointed to his position by the governor last year, is running for election in his own right.



Quotation







First Street is entitled to monetize and treat its data as proprietary and withhold it from public view. However, it is deceptive for First Street to claim transparency while cloaking its data behind a paywall.


– Uthmeier lawsuit


“Deciding to buy a home these days is hard enough without dealing with fake flood risk. Yet that is exactly what First Street forces on Florida homebuyers. Sellers suffer, too — stuck with perfectly good homes tainted with First Street’s climate chicanery,” the complaint says.
“First Street seeks to add alarming climate risk factors to the homebuying decision and to profit from risk scores that use faulty models to exaggerate the risk. These faulty risk factors unnecessarily intimidate buyers and increase their insurance costs, resulting in lost sales for sellers or at least the ability to sell for full value,” the document continues.
Deceptive acts alleged
Uthmeier’s office alleges two counts under the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act for “unfair and unconscionable practices” plus deceptive practices, punishable by disgorgement of ill-gotten gains, civil penalties of $10,000 for each violation, and $15,000 for each violation that victimized or attempted to victimize a senior citizen or person with a disability, plus the state’s attorney fees.
“CEO Matthew Eby wants to personalize the threat of climate change by quantifying the risk to the individual’s wallet,” the complaint alleges. “Eby sees climate change activism as a marketing problem. As Eby described in 2023, ‘If we can make it personal for them, if we make the impacts here and now, that’s what we’ve found as marketers is the best way to convey the impact of something as big as this.’”
The complaint points to a sample evaluation warning that the county involved had experienced flooding, hurricane, or tornado winds, and that a facility nearby emitted toxic pollution.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.“Not only is the information provided by First Street vague; it is also misleading. A key insight provided for this specific property is ‘this county has flooded in the past.’ The property is in Pinellas County, which indeed had extensive flooding in 2024 due to back-to-back hurricane impacts. The devastation in the Tampa Bay area was national news, “ the complaint says.
“However, this property is located inland, approximately three miles from the coast, and did not experience flooding in 2024. Nor has it ever flooded. A person from New York looking to purchase the property may not be familiar with the exact geographical area and assume that First Street’s county-wide assessment of prior flooding impacts this property.”
The complaint alleges the company’s claims its weather models had been peer-reviewed were false. As for the company’s claim to transparency, the complaint alleges it has refused to let independent third parties view data necessary to review site-specific findings.
“First Street is entitled to monetize and treat its data as proprietary and withhold it from public view. However, it is deceptive for First Street to claim transparency while cloaking its data behind a paywall,” the document says.
Analyses’ uses
Sites including Realtor.com, Redfin, and Zillow have used First Street scores in its property listings, the complaint says. Zillow stopped including them after real estate agents in California complained they deterred property purchases but they’re still used by mortgage lenders and insurers, it notes.
“Zillow’s study found that only 52 percent of homes given a high flood risk assessment eventually sold, whereas 71 percent of homes given a low flood risk eventually sold. Though that gap between sales has existed ‘since our analysis began in 2018, the gap has widened in recent years,’ Indeed, ‘Zillow’s analysis shows that high flood-risk homes have had a consistently lower chance of selling since at least 2018, the earliest data available,’” the complaint says.
“However, Zillow listings still contain a ‘climate risks’ category that directs users to First Street ‘flood, wildfire, and other predictive climate risk information,’” it continues.
Furthermore, in Florida First Street’s analyses differ from FEMA’s national flood hazard evaluations, the document alleges, as well as with the company’s competitors. Its data place Orlando at risk for coastal flooding and Lake City for poor air quality, although the latter city in May “received national recognition from the American Lung Association for low ozone and particle pollution.”
Orlando sits about 45 to 60 miles from the nearest coastline, of the Atlantic.
Homes rated by the company with a high flood risk linger on the market, the complaint says, noting a 1.5 % slowdown in sales over the year ending in August. Sellers have posted FEMA floodplain maps on their listings to counter the First Street analyses, it adds.
“A property owner can pay First Street for purportedly better data for their own use but cannot fix the score that prospective buyers, lenders, and insurers see,” it asserts.
“Florida has the highest home insurance premiums in the nation — an average of $8,292. Floridians cannot afford increased insurance premiums based on conjecture and speculation without appropriately robust scientific backing,” the document asserts.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Would Demuth pardon Derek Chauvin? She won’t say
text:
House Speaker Lisa Demuth, the Republican nominee for Minnesota governor, and her running mate, Ryan Wilson, spoke at a Capitol press conference on Oct. 26, 2026. (Photo by Michelle Griffith/Minnesota Reformer)House Speaker Lisa Demuth declined to say Monday whether she would pardon convicted murderer Derek Chauvin if she’s elected governor.
Demuth, the Republican nominee for Minnesota governor, convened the Capitol press conference Monday to again criticize Sen. Amy Klobuchar’s response to fraud in Minnesota’s social safety net programs, arguing that Klobuchar’s claim of working to hire more prosecutors in the U.S. Attorney’s Office was not enough.
Demuth was asked if she is open to voting in favor of clemency for Chauvin, who was convicted in 2021 of murdering George Floyd.
“I have never stated that,” Demuth replied.
“Are you open to (a) pardon?” the reporter asked.
Ryan Wilson, Demuth’s running mate, jumped in and changed the subject to Gov. Tim Walz’s “yes” vote earlier this year on a pardon for Tou Lue Vang, who was convicted in 2006 of sexually assaulting a 10-year-old girl. The victim wrote in favor of the pardon, but the Ramsey County attorney recommended against it. Vang has since been deported.
“The speaker, from day one, said no child rapist would be pardoned under her watch. Hold Amy Klobuchar to her words. Is she taking off the table any child rapist ever being pardoned ever? The speaker has. So I think that’s what matters,” Wilson said.
(Klobuchar has said the pardon of Vang was a mistake.)
The reporter again asked about a Chauvin pardon.
“Well, back to Chauvin. What is your position then?” the reporter asked Demuth.
“So are there any more questions to do with the fraud or anything that we brought forward?” Demuth interrupted. Demuth then told reporters that they should ask Klobuchar more questions about Minnesota’s fraud scandal and what she did to address it.
Minnesota’s governor, attorney general and chief justice of the Supreme Court sit on a pardon board, which meets twice a year to make determinations on pardon and commutation applications. If two of the three members vote in favor of a pardon — one of whom must be the governor — the pardon will be granted. If the governor votes no or is the only member to vote yes, then the application is denied.
At the Minnesota Republican Party’s statewide convention back in May, delegates held a moment of silence for Chauvin, even though Chauvin is still alive.
Reporters asked Demuth days after the convention whether she supported the moment of silence or would vote to pardon Chauvin if elected governor. She said moments of silence are typically reserved for fallen police officers, but she didn’t rule out the possibility of a pardon.
“There’s a lot that goes into any type of decision,” Demuth said.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: $9M renewable electricity project coming to Smith Hill next year
text:
Workers install rooftop photovoltaic solar arrays on the Capitol Hill Campus in Providence in 2018. (Photo courtesy of Rhode Island Office of Energy Resources website)A pair of solar carports, a battery storage system and an electric vehicle charging station will increase the renewable energy capacity of Rhode Island’s Capitol Hill campus to 1 megawatt in total, the state Office of Energy Resources announced Monday.
The $9.3 million project is funded through a $4.5 million federal earmark and will be matched with state funds through revenue from the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative, said Robert Beadle, a spokesperson for the energy department.
The state has also secured an immediate federal tax credit deduction equal to 5% of the project costs, with the promise of additional federal tax credits equal to between 30% and 40% of total costs in tax year 2028.
“By leveraging federal funding and tax credits, we’re bringing innovative solar, battery storage and electric vehicle charging technologies to state facilities while making smart investments in Rhode Island’s energy future,” Gov. Dan McKee said in a statement.
Construction is expected to begin in the first quarter of 2027. The parking lot solar panels, battery storage and charging station must be operational by the end of the year to secure the federal tax credits administered through the Internal Revenue Service.  Once complete, the projects, together with existing rooftop solar panels on state buildings, will provide enough solar-powered electricity to power roughly 190 homes per year while helping meet state decarbonization mandates.
“This is a forward-looking project that is both economically and environmentally responsible,” said U.S. Sen. Jack Reed, who secured the $4.5 million federal earmark.
The projects also advance the state’s Lead by Example program, which aims to spur private investments in renewable energy infrastructure by starting with solar panels, battery storage, and charging stations on state and municipal-owned buildings and public schools. Since the 2015 executive order establishing the state-led program, the Office of Energy Resources has invested more than $48 million into 185 projects, said Chris Kearns, the state’s acting energy commissioner.
Kearns hailed the upcoming projects for the parking lots of the Rhode Island Department of Administration and Department of Health as among the largest to date.  The work will also help to reduce energy costs, Kearn said in a statement.
There are already 900 rooftop solar panel on Smith Hill buildings, including on the departments of transportation, health and administration buildings, as well as energy-efficient lighting upgrades at the State House and Department of Transportation buildings. 
Rising energy bills remain a top concern among residents, despite seasonal bill credits meant to offset the seasonal spike in electricity prices. Two of the three gubernatorial candidates, independent Ken Block and Republican Aaron Guckian, have called for delaying the deadlines for state climate change mandates to reduce costs for customers, a move which Gov. Dan McKee tried unsuccessfully to incorporate in the state’s fiscal 2027 budget. 
Democrat Helena Buonanno Foulkes, who defeated McKee in the Sept. 9 primary, has insisted the state should “lean in” to renewables as a more stable and cost-effective energy solution, without changing decarbonization deadlines in state law. 
The new Capitol Hill project is expected to save $3.3 million in avoided energy costs, reducing carbon emissions by 12,700 metric tons over the lifetime of the project, according to state analysis. 
Since 2021, state agencies have produced or purchased credits to offset 100% of electricity needs across state facilities.
Retail electricity suppliers must purchase or produce 38% of total electricity needs statewide this year under the state’s Renewable Energy Standard law, which sets a 2033 deadline for zero-net electricity emissions.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma retains declining share of its college graduates
text:
A sign outside of Troutt Hall on the University of Science and Arts of Oklahoma campus congratulates graduates on July 10, 2024, in Chickasha. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Graduates of Oklahoma public colleges are remaining in the state’s workforce at a declining rate, a new report shows.
A year after graduation, 76.5% of graduates from all fields of study and degree levels were still working in Oklahoma, according to a 2025 Employment Outcomes Report the state Regents for Higher Education released Monday.
That number has fallen from 83% in 2024 and 87% in 2023, previous editions of the report show.
Even fewer remained five years after graduation. In 2025, 70.8% of graduates were still part of Oklahoma’s workforce after five years, similarly showing a steady decline from 2024 and 2023. 
After 10 years, 65.8% remained.
Sean Burrage speaks to the Oklahoma State Regents for Higher Education after he was named the chancellor for higher education with a unanimous vote on Oct. 9, 2024, at the regents’ offices in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
Those who were Oklahoma residents before college tend to stay at a higher rate, according to the report. The latest report shows 87.5% of Oklahomans who graduated in-state remained after one year. That dropped to 81% after five years and 75% after 10 years.
“This report demonstrates the lasting impact of public higher education on Oklahoma’s future,” the state regents’ chair Courtney Warmington said in a statement. “When graduates of our state system colleges and universities choose to build their lives and careers here, they strengthen our labor force and boost our economy, which secures a brighter future for generations of Oklahomans to come.”
The report also tracks remaining graduates of fields the Oklahoma Employment Security Commission deemed critical to economic growth. That includes degree programs in science, technology, engineering and math, as well as teaching and nursing.
About 73% of all STEM graduates, from associate to doctoral degrees, stayed in Oklahoma a year after graduation. Their numbers fell to 63.6% after five years and to 59.6% after 10 years.
After completing a bachelor’s degree, 85% of teachers continued working in Oklahoma a year later and 77.3% remained five years later, the 2025 report shows.
Nursing programs show the highest rate of graduate retention among all “critical occupations,” according to the data. Eighty-nine percent of all nursing graduates were employed in the state a year after graduation, followed by 81% after five years and 76% after 10 years.
Strong retention rates among critical workforce fields “indicate that our institutions are preparing students for career success while helping meet our state’s most pressing employment needs,” Oklahoma Higher Education Chancellor Sean Burrage said.

name: WyoFile
title: Lawmakers sponsor bill to bar lawsuits intended to silence free speech in Wyoming
text:
Wyoming lawmakers sponsored a bill Monday that aims to block lawsuits intended to silence free speech. The full Legislature will consider the proposed measure during the legislative session in January. 
Wyoming remains one of a handful of states without a law to prevent “strategic lawsuits against public participation,” known as an anti-SLAPP statute. SLAPPs are usually civil complaints brought by powerful people to silence critics through the stress and high costs of lawsuits regardless of their legal merits. Anti-SLAPP laws are meant to protect people who face such retaliatory litigation.
State lawmakers are trying again to get an anti-SLAPP measure on the books after similar legislation died two years in a row. Legislators argued that previous bill proposals had too many holes. They suggested taking a deeper dive and crafting a different anti-SLAPP bill for the 2027 legislative session. 
The new bill draft is based on the Uniform Public Expression Protection Act, a model anti-SLAPP law made by the Uniform Law Commission, a nonprofit organization of state-based commissioners who aim to craft laws that offer consistency across states.
The bill might still be fine-tuned. Beth Lance, an attorney speaking on behalf of the Wyoming Trial Lawyers Association, asked lawmakers on the Joint Judiciary Committee to add an exception to the bill for bodily injury, wrongful death or survival actions, as well as statements made about such legal action, unless those statements could fall under defamation. 
If someone files a medical malpractice lawsuit, Lance explained as an example, the bill might allow a doctor to have the complaint dismissed. The complaint then wouldn’t be able to move forward “on the actual grounds to analyze whether or not there was a negligence claim,” Lance said. 
The Joint Judiciary Committee didn’t add these suggestions Monday, with lawmakers noting that the draft bill includes a broad exemption for bringing complaints against people who sell or lease goods or services, with some exceptions. But there’s still time for lawmakers to take a closer look at those concerns during the legislative session. 
“I don’t have the language in mind today, but I do think it’s something we continue to look at, because I understand the points, and I think there’s merit in some of those points,” said Sen. Barry Crago, an attorney and Republican lawmaker representing Johnson and Sheridan counties.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Hope Scholarship report released for 2025-2026 school year; program cost $68M
text:
The West Virginia  State Treasurer’s Office released the 2025-2026 annual Hope Scholarship on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. (Screenshot of report)Kanawha County leads the state in the amount of students participating in the Hope Scholarship during the 2025-26 school year, according to an annual report released Monday by the West Virginia State Treasurer’s Office. 
A little more than 1,600 students took the Hope Scholarship, an increase of nearly 300 students from the prior school year. Berkeley County saw an increase of nearly 500 students taking the scholarship. 
The data also shows incoming kindergartens make up the biggest portion of students, with 2,100 students listed in the school year. 
The 2025-26 school year is the last the Hope Scholarship had restrictions on eligibility. In the current school year, any resident student can receive the scholarship, regardless of whether or not they have ever participated in public schools. In prior years, it was only open to students in public school or in-coming kindergarteners. 
The report showed the Hope Scholarship cost $68 million in 2025-26, with $45 million of it going to non-public schools. 
Faith Christian Academy, located outside of Martinsburg, received the most payments, at $1.5 million. 
Microschools, a highly unregulated form of private education, received $5 million. The biggest recipient was City on a Hill Christian Academy Inc in Fairmont, at $674,000. 
Computer purchases ranked number one for educational supplies, coming in at $2.3 million, followed by instructional materials and curriculum at $1.8 million.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Many Medicare patients could lose access to remote monitoring devices
text:
Dianne Williams takes her blood pressure at home in rural Georgia. The device transmits her data to her local doctor and a remote nurse who checks in with her each month. (Matt Odom for KFF Health News)Dianne Williams said she lost weight and lowered her blood pressure thanks to quarterly doctor appointments, monthly phone calls with a nurse, and a blood pressure cuff she uses at home that transmits data to her care team.
“It’s good to have somebody talk to you and tell you what your progress is like. And she’s a very nice person,” Williams said of her nurse.
Williams, who lives in rural Georgia, said these services — referred to as remote patient monitoring — encourage her to take her medication and inspired her to revamp her diet and exercise.
But many Medicare patients, especially those in rural areas like Williams, soon may no longer be able to use devices and receive coaching from the comfort of their homes.
That’s because a proposed federal rule would halt Medicare reimbursements for providers who use health technology companies to administer remote monitoring for their patients. Medicare would pay clinicians only when the service is provided by someone at the facility where they work.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services’ proposed rule is a response to reports on remote monitoring from the Department of Health and Human Services’ Office of Inspector General, an independent federal oversight agency. The 2024 and 2025 reports raised concerns about fraud, a lack of data collection, and patients’ not receiving treatment from the clinician who prescribed the device.
But Caroline Pearson, executive director of the nonprofit Peterson Center on Healthcare, said “the rule would virtually eliminate the use of remote monitoring services, or dramatically reduce the use,” for many Medicare patients.
“I think the rural communities will be some of the hardest hit,” said Pearson, whose organization focuses on healthcare affordability.
She said remote monitoring programs can be especially helpful in rural areas, where it can be difficult for patients to travel to in-person appointments. Most rural healthcare facilities that offer these programs use third-party vendors since they don’t have the capacity to launch and oversee their own, she said.
CMS spokesperson Timothy Foster said the agency “recognizes the important role that technology-enabled care can play in improving access to care, including in rural communities.” But more safeguards are needed, he said.
The proposed rule says outside vendors may “have little to no established relationship” with patients and their clinicians, which it says can “fragment care.” It also says the clinicians may not be involved enough to warrant being paid by Medicare. Pearson, other health policy experts, and vendors agree with the Trump administration that these programs need further regulation. But public comments show widespread strong disagreement with CMS’ approach.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The proposal “took us by such surprise,” said Andrew Van Ostrand, senior vice president at the Alliance for Connected Care, a group that advocates for wider adoption of health tech, including remote monitoring, on behalf of healthcare organizations and tech companies.
Van Ostrand said many vendors have already made changes inspired by the “very well-reasoned recommendations” from HHS’ Office of Inspector General and were surprised that the proposed Medicare rule didn’t mandate all its suggestions.
The proposed rule would apply only to patients enrolled in traditional Medicare, not those with privately run Medicare Advantage plans, which cover more than half of Medicare participants. But Van Ostrand and Pearson said Medicare Advantage plans, Medicaid programs, and private insurers could end up adopting the same change, further limiting access.
Van Ostrand said the vendor rule and other proposed changes — including a “draconian” cut in reimbursement rates — are in “deep misalignment” with one of President Donald Trump’s signature initiatives: the five-year, $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program, which encourages states to adopt tech solutions to improve rural healthcare.
States have earmarked at least $240 million from their first-year rural health funding for remote monitoring, according to a report by the Alliance for Connected Care, which also wrote to CMS to oppose the rule change.
More than 230 health tech vendors, healthcare systems, and patient and medical advocacy groups had signed the opposition letter as of Sept. 14.
A few organizations largely support the proposed rule, including major health industry players Humana, Blue Cross Blue Shield Association, and Sutter Health, a large health system that offers its own remote monitoring program.
Remote patient monitoring 101
Remote monitoring can be used for patients who are in physical therapy, recovering from surgery or hospitalization, or living with a chronic condition such as diabetes or heart disease.
The idea is to help patients manage their health and prevent dangerous complications or pricey emergency room visits. Remote monitoring can also make it easier to obtain care for patients who struggle to travel to in-person appointments — such as those with disabilities, without cars, or from rural areas far from hospitals.
To track her blood pressure, Williams straps a cuff to her arm and presses a button. The device automatically sends her data to CoachCare, a private company whose staff monitor patients.
“I don’t have to wait until I go to the doctor’s office when I can do it every day,” Williams said.
Other patients are given devices such as scales, blood glucose monitors, and fitness bands that transmit data that’s monitored by nurses or other staffers, and, increasingly, with the help of artificial intelligence.
Some large academic health systems create their own devices or use their own employees to review data and check in with patients. But most health facilities contract with health tech companies.
If staff notice — or are alerted by AI to — patient data trending in the wrong direction, they can call patients to offer advice or schedule a follow-up appointment with their doctor. If vitals indicate life-threatening problems, staff urge patients to call 911.
Williams said she was frustrated when her medication wasn’t lowering her blood pressure. She said that’s when her CoachCare nurse suggested she start exercising and eating healthier.
“That made me feel better, because they gave me encouragement,” she said. “They just didn’t just take my blood pressure and that was it.”
Williams said she now walks at a local track each day and made diet changes, such as switching from fried to baked fish.
Edward Vance is the chief medical officer of Albany Area Primary Health Care, which includes Williams’ clinic. He said the health system, which serves many rural and low-income patients, couldn’t offer remote monitoring without an outside vendor.
“We already run at a borderline understaffed situation,” and many community health centers operate with “shoestring budgets,” Vance said.
Growing pains
The federal government created Medicare billing codes for remote patient monitoring during Trump’s first presidency. That allowed providers to be reimbursed for initiating and overseeing such services. Health facilities often use part of that revenue to pay vendors for their devices and monitoring.
Only 1% of patients on traditional Medicare use remote physiologic monitoring, the more common type of remote monitoring, and the cost is a small fraction of overall spending. But both measures are rapidly growing.
The number of traditional Medicare patients enrolled in such programs grew tenfold from 2019 to 2023, while program spending on them increased from just under $7 million to more than $194 million, according to an April 2025 report from the Peterson Center on Healthcare.
Pearson said evidence shows remote monitoring is most helpful when providers use the data to inform how they treat patients — such as adjusting medications — and only until the patient is stabilized.
“We shouldn’t be paying for doctors to be reviewing huge numbers of readings, for years on end, for patients that have controlled blood pressure,” Pearson said.
“That doesn’t feel like a clinically driven decision. That feels like a revenue decision,” she said, adding that some vendors explicitly pitch their services as an opportunity for health facilities to generate income.
But traditional Medicare patients are enrolling in remote physiologic monitoring programs for longer periods of time. From 2019 to 2023, average duration increased from 1.7 months to 5.2 months, the Peterson report found.
Pearson said Medicare should limit how long patients can be prescribed remote monitoring unless there’s proof treatment is still needed. The agency also should require clinicians to report more data, including outcomes, she said.
She said Medicare should eventually transition to a reimbursement system that pays based on whether programs improve patients’ health. Pearson said CMS has already begun to do so through its new ACCESS program, which pays not only clinicians but also vendors.
But Pearson said the program, which launched in July, reimburses less than traditional models.
Williams said the government should keep remote monitoring accessible.
“It looks like they’re cutting off everybody, and that’s not right,” she said.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico lawmakers revisit funding proposal to pay for improving state’s poor roads
text:
At an Oct. 23, 2026, interim legislative subcommittee hearing, New Mexico lawmakers expressed enthusiasm at a proposal to pay for road repairs and maintenance — and frustration at how such proposals have typically stalled in recent years. (Danielle Prokop/Source NM)A majority of New Mexico voters think road construction and maintenance should be a priority for state leaders, according to a new poll presented to state lawmakers Friday, but they lack a consensus on how to pay for it.
Franklin Garcia, a lobbyist for the trade organization Asphalt Pavement Association of New Mexico, presented the new poll to lawmakers on the Transportation Infrastructure Revenue Subcommittee in Albuquerque on Friday. The poll, conducted by Albuquerque-based Research and Polling Inc., found that 83% of voters statewide believe road construction and maintenance should be a top priority for state leaders and 42% rated New Mexico’s road conditions as poor or very poor.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
When asked how to finance road projects, though, there was less agreement — 54% said they would support a legislative proposal to redirect how the state collects sales tax on car sales to pay for it.
Currently, the state imposes a 4% tax on car sales, minus the value of a trade-in. About 60% of that tax goes into the state’s general funds, while the rest goes toward road projects.
Sen. Roberto “Bobby” Gonzales (D-Ranchos de Taos) last month introduced a proposal during a different interim legislative committee hearing to greatly reduce the general fund’s share and instead funnel the revenue into road and transportation projects. At the September hearing, he also proposed raising the state’s gas tax, to much opposition.
“This is not a Democrat thing or a Republican thing,” Gonzales said at Friday’s subcommittee hearing. “Everyone wants the potholes to be filled…But they don’t want to pay for it.”
Advocates for local leaders across the state, such as the New Mexico Municipal League, have backed similar proposals in recent years to no avail.
Garcia, the trade organization lobbyist, told lawmakers he particularly supports the pitch to redistribute the tax on car sales, as it wouldn’t raise taxes.
“That additional revenue…over a five-year period would generate about $850 million,” Garcia said.
He pointed to a January report from the Washington, D.C.-based transportation research nonprofit TRIP, which identified a $7.5 billion funding shortfall in New Mexico’s transportation projects. It also found that the state’s poor road conditions cost the average New Mexico commuter more than $1,000 annually in repairs and wasted fuel.
Lawmakers on the subcommittee discussed the particular importance of these issues in a state as rural and spread-out as New Mexico.
Rep. Randall Pettigrew (R-Lovington), who represents such an area, agreed with Gonzales’ assertion that fixing the state’s roads should be an easy agreement for lawmakers on opposite sides of the aisle. Despite that, the effort typically stalls when the legislative session comes around.
“We bring this up every year,” he said, “and we fail to do anything about it.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: After a series of drug thefts in four states, nurse wins back Iowa license
text:
(Photo courtesy of the Iowa Board of Nursing)Iowa regulators have reinstated the license of a nurse previously sanctioned for alleged drug thefts in four different states.
State records indicate the Iowa Board of Nursing first licensed Krystal Bauer of Omaha as a registered nurse in 1993.
Board records indicate that in 2003, Bauer was working at an unspecified hospital when it was reported that she was disposing of a high volume of Nubain, an opioid painkiller, and was also seeking prescriptions for Stadol NS, another opioid painkiller, from a resident physician.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Bauer later admitted that in 2003 she had been using numerous physicians to obtain prescriptions for the two drugs, according to board records. The board charged her with unethical conduct for obtaining prescription medications under false pretenses, and suspended her license indefinitely pending the completion of a chemical dependency evaluation. Her license was later reinstated subject to probation.
In 2008, Bauer was charged by the board with failing to report action taken against her license in another state. The board alleged Bauer had been working as a travel nurse in Wisconsin when she allegedly stole morphine from a dispensing device while on duty at a hospital, and later that same day tested positive for morphine.
According to the board, Bauer admitted to a medical review officer that she had given herself an injection of morphine that had been intended for a patient. Wisconsin regulators then revoked Bauer’s nursing privileges in that state, which Bauer allegedly failed to report to the Iowa Board of Nursing.
Bauer subsequently agreed to surrender her Iowa license.
Also in 2008, the North Carolina Board of Nursing revoked Bauer’s practice privileges in that state after alleging there were discrepancies in the documentation of her handling of controlled substances while working in North Carolina. Bauser was accused of stealing drugs from Greenville, N.C., hospital.
A few weeks later, the Arizona State Board of Nursing issued an order revoking Bauer’s privileges to practice there, citing narcotics discrepancies in audited charts while Bauer was working in that state. Bauer had been accused of stealing drugs while working at a Glendale, Ariz., hospital.
In 2009, Bauer was criminally charged in the state of Wisconsin for the theft of drugs in that state and, according to the Iowa Board of Nursing, she pleaded no contest to one felony charge of possession of narcotics.
In 2014, Bauer sought reinstatement of her Iowa nursing license, expressing what the board called “deep remorse for the actions that led to the surrender of her nursing licenses.”  The board agreed to reinstate her license subject to one year of probation.
In 2017, Bauer entered into a chemical dependency agreement the Iowa Nurse Assistance Program. The same year, the board alleges, she “relapsed from sobriety” and in October 2017 stole hydromorphone, an opioid painkeller, from the hospital where she was working.
According to the board, Bauer failed to notify the Iowa Nurse Assistance Program of her employment at the hospital, the drug theft, and her relapse. After the board charged Bauer with failing to comply with the terms of her agreement with the program, Bauer surrendered her Iowa nursing license a second time.
In 2019, the board charged Bauer with continuing to practice nursing through December 2018 despite having surrendered her license. That case was resolved when Bauer agreed to pay a civil penalty $600.
In April 2026, Bauer submitted a letter to the Board of Nursing requesting reinstatement of her Iowa license.
Earlier this month, the board agreed to reinstate the license pending Bauer’s completion of a nurse refresher course and satisfaction of the still-unpaid $600 fine that was imposed in 2019.
Bauer’s license will be on probationary status for two years, during which she will be required to submit to chemical screening and monitoring, according to board records.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Bauer for comment on her case.
In 2010, Bauer told ProPublica that the time-consuming process surrounding the various state licensing boards’ disciplinary proceedings and their need to give licensees due process was what allowed her to keep moving and landing nursing jobs even while investigations in other states were pending.
“Until an investigation is closed,” Bauer reportedly told ProPublica, “it’s not going to look like there’s anything going on.”

title: No write-in candidates for Congress, governor, Legislature, Nebraska state education boards in 2026
text:
Four candidates are running unopposed for the Nebraska Legislature and one is running unopposed for the State Board of Education. Teresa Ibach of Sumner (Legislative District 44). At bottom left is state Sen. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — In a year of twists and turns for some of Nebraska’s highest elected positions, there are no declared write-in candidates for congressional offices or for constitutional officers, the Legislature and state education boards.
Under state law, candidates must file a written affidavit and the respective filing fee no later than the second Friday before an election for their votes to be counted. That was Friday, Oct. 23. On election night, write-in votes will be grouped collectively. If an affidavit has been filed, votes for that candidate will be separated in the immediate days after the election.

By Friday’s 5 p.m. deadline, no one had filed a write-in candidacy for:

U.S. Senate
U.S. House of Representatives, Districts 1-3
Governor
Secretary of state
Attorney general
Auditor of public accounts
State treasurer
Public Service Commission District 2
Nebraska Legislature, even-numbered districts and District 41 for a two-year term.
State Board of Education, Districts 5-8
University of Nebraska Board of Regents, Districts 1-2 and District 4, for a four-year term

name: Source New Mexico
title: Commentary: New Mexico guarded its drivers’ data. Border Patrol is watching anyway.
text:
Surveillance equipment on the border wall between the United States and Mexico in Nogales, Arizona. (Photo by Jerod MacDonald-Evoy/Arizona Mirror)Last week, the New York Times documented what a Border Patrol surveillance tower can see from a hillside in Sunland Park. It sees children on an elementary school playground, neighbors entering and leaving their homes, and cars on the town’s main road. At least 10 such AI-powered towers ring the city, and no one in New Mexico agreed to them.
New Mexicans should weigh these towers against the Driver Privacy and Safety Act, Senate Bill 40, which took effect July 1. It bars police and others from sharing license plate reader data when they reasonably believe it will be used for immigration enforcement, investigating reproductive or gender-affirming care, or punishing protected speech. Lawmakers acted after reporting showed out-of-state agencies searching New Mexico camera networks for immigration cases.
The law matters, but the new federal AI towers expose the state law’s own limits. New Mexico can tell the Las Cruces police what to do with their cameras. It cannot tell U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), Border Patrol’s parent agency, what to do with its towers.
That limit is not a drafting error. Federal law is supreme, and states may not directly regulate federal operations. SB 40 binds New Mexico agencies and their vendors. It cannot bind the federal agency that watches Sunland Park around the clock.
The gap runs deeper. SB 40 controls data leaving New Mexico agencies, not data flowing in. CBP told the Times that tower footage can be shared with local, state and federal police, and even foreign governments. So a local department barred from feeding license plate hits to immigration agents may still receive federal video of residents’ front doors, their license plates, or of parents picking up their children from school.
Scale matters too. The administration has secured more than $1 billion for 1,500 new towers. The Times found that more than a million people on both sides of the border already live within the network’s view. Most residents the Times interviewed thought the towers were cell towers. CBP concedes that people near the border cannot opt out.
Defenders will say the border is different. In part, it is. Courts give federal agents wide latitude at the border, particularly when inspecting people at an airport or land port of entry. But Sunland Park is not a port of entry. It is a town with schools, churches and backyards.
Courts have eroded some constitutional protections near the border, such as allowing Mexican ancestry to be used as a factor in roving patrol stops. But federal agents remain bound by the Fourth Amendment’s bar on unreasonable searches, even near the border. In 2018, the Supreme Court required a warrant for long-term cellphone location records because they reveal “the privacies of life.” A federal appeals court later held that Baltimore’s persistent aerial surveillance program violated the Fourth Amendment. A camera that watches the same homes every day raises the same concern.
What can New Mexico do? More than it might think.
First, the Legislature could close the inbound gap. It can bar state and local agencies from using federal surveillance footage for purposes SB 40 already forbids and require them to report when they receive such footage.
Second, New Mexico’s federal congressional delegation can demand transparency. CBP should disclose where each tower stands, what it sees, how long it keeps footage and who receives it. SB 40 already requires New Mexico agencies to report yearly how many cameras they run and who can access the data. Federal agencies watching New Mexicans should meet at least that standard.
Third, state and local officials can carry residents’ concerns to Washington. Communities across the state have begun to question surveillance cameras. The Bernalillo County Sheriff’s Office ended its Flock contracts. Cibola County scheduled its cameras for removal. Sunland Park residents deserve a say over cameras aimed at their homes.
As an ACLU lawyer, I litigated in federal court and worked on Border Patrol accountability. I have watched enforcement tools built for the border move inland. Technology tested on border towns rarely stays there.
New Mexico drew a line this year: Its data will not become a pipeline for immigration enforcement. That line means little if the federal government can build its own pipeline, mount it on a hillside, and point it at a playground.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: DOJ election monitors to be deployed in four Pennsylvania counties on election day
text:
Voting booths at a polling place at the Armagh & East Wheatfield Volunteer Fire Department in Armagh, Indiana County on Election Day May 19, 2026. (Photo by John Beale for the Pennsylvania Capital-Star)The U.S. Department of Justice notified Secretary of the Commonwealth Al Schmidt last week that it plans to send federal election monitors to observe polling places in four Pennsylvania counties on election day. The counties are Allegheny, Lehigh, Luzerne and Philadelphia.
The deployment is part of a nationwide effort. Harmeet Dhillon, assistant attorney general for DOJ’s Civil Rights Division, has said the department intends to send out 1,000 election monitors across all 50 states on Nov. 3, a larger number than typical. 
Election monitors’ roles are purely observational. They are not allowed to interfere with voting and receive no greater access to polling places than members of the general public.
“Our monitors only observe and take notes,” the letter to Schmidt said. “They do not intrude or interfere in any way in the voting process … Monitors follow all rules of the state and jurisdiction.”
The DOJ has deployed election monitors in virtually all past elections under Democratic and Republican administrations. Historically, their goal has primarily been to observe compliance with the Voting Rights Act, such as ensuring access to non-English language services in places where that’s required.
The letter to Schmidt added that monitors will introduce themselves to poll managers, but will not wear uniforms or pins identifying themselves as working for the DOJ. It also said they do not speak with voters inside polling places and are forbidden from carrying firearms.
If monitors observe issues at a polling place, they can notify someone at the Justice Department, who may then contact the affected jurisdiction.
“The Pennsylvania Department of State expects everyone working in, voting in, and observing polling places to follow all applicable state and federal laws,” spokesperson Matt Heckel said in a statement. “We encourage [DOJ monitors] to coordinate with local election offices where they will be present to ensure that their activities do not disrupt the voting process.”
Luzerne County Manager Romilda Crocamo said at a virtual press conference with the nonpartisan elections education group Keep Our Republic that the DOJ sent election monitors to her county in the 2022 and 2024 elections as well.

She also noted that other groups, such as the American Civil Liberties Union, have intend to send observers to polling places as well. They are similarly not allowed to interfere with the voting process.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Vantage points: The view from where NC county election directors sit
text:
Gay Ferguson, right, speaks with election official Carter Blaisdell prior to voting at the First Baptist Church of Black Mountain polling place on March 3, 2020, in Buncombe County. (Photo: Colby Rabon / Carolina Public Press)In the first eight days of early voting, Wake County Election Director Olivia McCall has seen 70% higher turnout than in the 2022 midterm election.
It’s “unprecedented,” she said. But it’s too early to tell whether the higher turnout foreshadows record-breaking overall turnout or excitement around early voting, she added.
That’s the story across the state. In Mecklenburg County, turnout is about 45% higher than at the same point in the 2022 election, according to Election Director Michael Dickerson. He said he expects Election Day voting to go down as a result.
In Cabarrus County, turnout is up “significantly,” said Election Director Carol Soles. There’s record-breaking turnout in Buncombe County — a nearly 60% increase from 2022 and a 23% increase from the previous 2018 record, as of Friday, Oct. 23.
In Jackson County, turnout topped 15% by Friday.
“Everybody seems to be pretty steady,” Election Director Amanda Allen said. “Not in a presidential kind of year where we would have lines of people waiting back to back, but it has been pretty consistent at most of our sites.”
According to State Board of Elections data, it’s not just the raw numbers that are up. Through the second Sunday of early voting in 2022, 15.7% of registered voters had cast ballots. This cycle, it’s increased to 20.1%.
Election directors on absentee voting 
While early voting numbers are high across North Carolina, absentee voting is down 34%.
In Buncombe County, there were only 6,700 absentee ballot requests; in 2022, about 7,500 voters returned ballots. Election Director Corinne Duncan attributed the shift to getting further away from the COVID pandemic years.
“2020 was gigantic,” she said. “Everyone figured out that absentee was an option, and then it’s been kind of dropping since then.”
While President Donald Trump’s calls to change the mail-in voting process have failed thus far, some voters may be avoiding absentee voting because of the resulting uncertainty. Absentee votes also may take longer to get from voters to their county election boards due to the USPS’ transition to centralized regional processing and distribution centers. North Carolina does not have a grace period; all non-military and overseas ballots must be returned by 7:30 p.m. on Election Day to count.
Another factor potentially contributing to lower absentee voting may be new North Carolina State Board of Elections guidance concerning how to count mail-in ballots.
When voters get an absentee ballot, there are two envelopes. They are supposed to place their ballot in an inner, container return envelope, attach their photo ID photocopy to an attached sleeve, and place that all in an outer return envelope. Both envelopes should be sealed. Before this year, the State Board advised county boards to count ballots when only one of these envelopes was sealed, as long as the ballot was inside a sealed envelope.
But after a lawsuit and much debate, the State Board changed its guidance this cycle. Now, if either envelope is unsealed, regardless of whether the ballot is inside a sealed envelope, the absentee ballot must be spoiled and reissued.
McCall said they’ve spoiled 277 ballots, or 3.5% of all absentee ballots, as of their last board meeting on Tuesday, Oct. 20. Of those spoiled ballots, 147 were related to the new guidance, and 53 of those voters either decided to vote in person instead or already returned their replacement ballots.
Dickerson said they’ve spoiled 260 ballots based on envelope sealing, and about 60 have returned replacement ballots or voted in person. Duncan said the Buncombe County election board has spoiled 24 ballots based on envelope issues. In other, smaller counties, election directors reported that the envelope sealing guidance change had little to no effect.
Early voting drama
State and county election boards made several changes to early voting plans this cycle, following the mid-2025 shift of election boards from majority Democratic to majority Republican. Many counties axed Sunday voting, shifted weekend hours to Saturdays and moved around early voting sites.
Under current North Carolina law, the state auditor appoints members of the State Board of Elections and the chairs of county election boards. He also hired an election liaison, Dallas Woodhouse, to communicate with local boards.
However, Woodhouse caught flack for allegedly pressuring election officials in several counties to select certain early voting plans, according to public records. Woodhouse resigned after the issue got widespread news media attention.
In Jackson County, Republican board member Jay Pavey spoke out about pressure from “Raleigh” during an early voting planning meeting. Fellow Republican board member Wes Hanemayer resigned over the issue. During the primary, the board removed a long-standing early voting site from Western Carolina University. Pavey said he was pressured to also exclude a WCU site from the general election, but he did not agree with that plan.
The county board ultimately voted 3-1 to keep an early voting site on WCU’s campus, with Republican chair Bill Thompson preferring a plan using the Cullowhee Recreational Center instead of the WCU site. The State Board ultimately found a middle ground, and included both sites in Jackson County’s final plan.
Director Allen said they were anticipating four sites, not five sites, but that they always leave a little budgeting room for unexpected changes.
“You never know if those plans will change, if things will get more expensive,” she said. “We’ve had years where we’ve had to reprint ballots, so there is some flexibility in our budget.”
The WCU site — which is located on the outskirts of campus at the Health and Human Services building, compared to the more centrally located WCU early voting site in 2022 — has been widely popular, according to an analysis by WCU political scientist Chris Cooper.
In 2022, the WCU site had 448 voters through the first week of early voting; this year, it had 1,200. The county’s other early voting sites have only small shifts from the last midterm election, including the Cullowhee Recreation Center, whose turnout numbers are slightly down from 2022.
While Wake County had a unanimous early voting plan, board members disagreed over where to place a North Carolina State University early voting site. Democrats wanted the site to remain at the NC State Talley Student Union, in the center of campus, while Republicans preferred the Western Boulevard Business Services site, which is further away from central campus but has more parking.
According to Wake County election data, the new site has had higher turnout than the student union site, but that may be due to overall higher turnout. The Western Boulevard site has the 14th-highest turnout of the county’s 18 early voting sites.
Students at North Carolina Agricultural & Technical State University and University of North Carolina-Greensboro have been marching to the nearest polling site after election boards denied their request to add early voting sites on their campuses.
While both universities have hosted early voting during presidential elections, they have never had midterm early voting sites.
The closest site to both campuses is Union Square, a new site suggested by the county election board. For a site they’ve never used before, Election Director Charlie Collicutt said, it’s experiencing decent turnout.
After a Thursday march to the polls, 369 people voted at the site, he said.
“It doesn’t seem like a lot, but what I think is important is a lot of them were students,” Collicutt said. “And of that, nearly 100 did a same-day registration, and about 47 did an address change.”
Collicutt said election workers  — and even county commissioners, who are not involved in election decisions — have been fielding calls and emails about the early voting decision after videos of the students’ marches have gone viral.
“I’ve seen a lot of different area codes I don’t recognize, and people from all over the place,” he said.
He wants to remind students that while there are no campus early voting sites, there will be campus Election Day sites they can utilize.
How does 2026 feel different? 
Voters this cycle are “extremely friendly,” but feel “a little more determined” than in previous years, said Haywood County election director Robert Inman.
McCall noted that voters seem more informed, particularly about the need to bring a photo ID to vote.
Most election directors said they hadn’t noticed much misinformation circulating so far, but expected it to come soon.
Inman said some voters expressed concerns about voting technology after Dolly Parton’s sister, Tennessean Stella Parton, claimed her voting machine switched her vote.
“I just take people at their word,” Inman said. “What I’ve done is gone through our equipment. We properly tested our equipment, and the functionality was doing exactly what it was supposed to do during testing, and up until now has not been an issue.”
Putting on an election is “like putting on the Olympics or the Super Bowl,” Inman said. It requires year-round preparation to pull off a twice-a-year event.
One of the biggest pieces of the puzzle is staffing enough poll workers to run early voting and Election Day sites. Every cycle, that gets harder and harder, Inman said. Generally, the pool of workers is older, which is becoming an issue. Inman said they need younger people to start signing up.
“It’s time for them to step up,” he said. “Not just students, but younger professionals, younger people. You can take a day off for this kind of work, and then the more of you who do that, the conspiracy theories will kind of diminish and go away because you actually know what’s happening.”
In Mecklenburg County, Dickerson said, they have between 800 and 900 people trained to run early voting sites, and 3,400 lined up for Election Day.
In Jackson County, Allen said they go from about four full-time election workers to 150 employees during election season. The majority of the workforce is retired people, who are beginning to encounter health issues and caregiving needs, she said. However, they recruited 30 new workers this year, which Allen said was “exceptional.”
Election director turnover is common in North Carolina.
Jones County interim election director Sheila Garner started her job this September. The previous director, Jessica Taylor, started the September before the 2024 election.
Once a week, a State Board employee comes in to help Garner, who said Taylor and the county board members are also supportive. But she is in a one-person office right now. She said her biggest obstacle is trying to learn everything she doesn’t know, from what precincts they need on Election Day to how to navigate the software system.
Pasquotank County Election Director Janae Hedgepeth also started shortly before the 2024 election. Now, this will be her sixth election. She said everything is running smoothly.
“Elections, you learn something new every day,” she said. “What you thought you knew, you didn’t know. Now that part doesn’t change, but I feel more comfortable.”
While every election has its “pet issues,” Duncan said she feels like Buncombe County election administration has hit its groove. Right now, they’re dealing with more attention on election changes and more changes to voter registrations in between cycles. But change is normal in the election world, Duncan said. She said voters should feel comfortable coming to them.
“Election officials are your neighbors,” she said. “They’re the people that you see at the grocery store. You can come to the office and see us. If you have any questions, we’re here for you.”
Collicutt also feels the heightened attention on elections in Guilford County, particularly for a midterm year.
“There’s more pressure that I feel from voters, from the people watching, from the people that are more invested in watching the behind the scenes mechanisms of how things work that I don’t normally get in a midterm election, and so that can feel a little bit more like a presidential year,” he said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Citizens’ group wants tolls, tax on rich to finance property tax relief
text:
A citizens’ group called Monday for Connecticut to impose interstate highway tolls and a surcharge on millionaires’ earnings to finance billions of dollars in local property tax relief, including repeal of the municipal motor vehicle levy.
The Connecticut Citizens’ Assembly on Property Taxes also recommended new incentives to promote school regionalization and shifting billions in local special education costs onto the state.
But the group’s most sweeping proposals likely will draw strong opposition from both sides of the political aisle, including from the state’s gubernatorial candidates. And the tolling proposal also could require an overhaul of state budgeting practices and possibly an amendment to the state Constitution.
“It is well known that Connecticut’s property tax system is complex, inequitable and in desperate need of reform,” the assembly wrote in a report released Monday. “To this end, our evidence-based recommendations seek to succeed where all other attempts have fallen short.”
Imposing tolls to send big dollars back to towns
The 98-member assembly, created last July by the Connecticut Conference of Municipalities and by researchers from Yale and the University of Connecticut, wants to revive a tolling plan like what Gov. Ned Lamont pitched — unsuccessfully — shortly after taking office in 2019.
The panel said it believes tolls on interstate highways could generate as much as $950 million yearly.

Dawris Gomez of Bridgeport, a member of the Citizens’ Assembly, seen in a  video press conference on the assembly’s report on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. Credit: Keith Phaneuf / CT Mirror

At the same time, citizens said Connecticut should repeal cities and towns’ ability to tax motor vehicles. And to ensure communities don’t replace the lost revenues, which would also be around $950 million per year, by simply raising property taxes on residences, businesses and equipment, the toll receipts should go to municipalities to keep local budgets whole.
And while Connecticut residents would receive 100% of the benefit from canceled motor vehicle taxes, the group estimated that 40% of the toll revenue would come from out-of-state drivers.
The political hurdles such a plan would face are daunting.
The 2019 General Assembly wouldn’t support Lamont’s tolling plan, and one year later lawmakers also balked at a more limited plan to toll only large commercial trucks. They did pass a more modest mileage fee on trucks in 2021.
But before such a plan could even run the political gantlet, it would have to navigate a maze of legal barriers.
The assembly recognized that federal law requires tolling revenues to be used for transportation purposes. In other words, tolling dollars would have to go into the state budget’s Special Transportation Fund.
But while the citizens’ group noted this would free up other revenues in the $2.4 billion STF, such as fuel and sales tax receipts, to finance repeal of local car taxes, it isn’t that simple.
Connecticut voters in 2018 overwhelmingly ratified the so-called “lock box” constitutional amendment that prohibits redirection of STF receipts outside of the fund.
Legislators could begin the process of repealing the lock box by initiating a new amendment, but that wouldn’t go before voters until 2028.
Taxing millionaires and shifting special education costs onto the state
But the assembly said tolls aren’t the only way to ease burdens on local property taxpayers.
The panel suggested at least a 1 percentage point state income tax surcharge on high incomes, saying Connecticut could raise considerable revenue this way and reverse worsening income and wealth inequality.
“There has been a growing sentiment among the public and policymakers that wealth is an untapped source of public revenue, supported by public infrastructures and the inequities of the current system, which can be more effectively utilized to offset the property tax burden,” the report states.
The assembly was crafted by researchers from Yale and the University of Connecticut to closely mirror the state’s adult population.
The lowest earning 10% of Connecticut workers effectively lost 40% of their income to state and municipal tax burdens in 2022, according to the most recent tax fairness study, done in late 2025 by the Department of Revenue Services. The middle three deciles lost 16% to 20%, and the highest-earning decile lost just 10.6%.
Both Lamont, a Democrat, and GOP gubernatorial nominee Ryan Fazio have said they oppose raising state income tax rates on the highest earners, arguing it would prompt them to flee the state. The Republican minority in the General Assembly and many moderate Democratic lawmakers also oppose such a tax.
Still, a recent poll commissioned by The Connecticut Project, a nonprofit research and policy group, found 76% support “increasing taxes on millionaires and billionaires.”
And tax fairness isn’t the only thing on local taxpayers’ minds, assembly members said.
Cities and towns currently bear about two-thirds of the $3.3 billion cost of special education services statewide each year, an expense crippling many local school budgets.
The citizens’ assembly recommends the state bear the full cost, which would involve far more than an income tax hike on high earners would generate.
State Senate Democratic leaders offered an income tax surcharge in 2025 that would raise about $420 million annually, and it included singles earning more than $250,000 per year and couples topping $500,000. The full legislature and Lamont left the proposal out of the final state budget adopted two years ago.
The citizens’ group noted that to assume billions of dollars in new special education costs, the state also would have to radically change fiscal practices it’s followed since 2017.
Connecticut has used aggressive budget caps to force unprecedented surpluses averaging more than $1.8 billion annually since then, cushions equal to 8% to 9% of the General Fund. Officials have used those surpluses to build reserves and shrink state pension debt, which still exceeds $30 billion and represents one of the largest burdens, per capita, of any state.
But critics say the state has been too aggressive in saving to shrink pension debt, and that these forced surpluses have come at the expense of education, municipal aid and other core responsibilities of state government.
Incentives to regionalize and shifting sales tax receipts to towns
The citizens’ assembly says Connecticut also could reduce education costs if more school districts were to combine services on a regional scale. But members stopped short of endorsing mandated regionalization, instead recommending a new state commission be formed to craft incentives and other plans to encourage change.
Other proposals from the assembly include:

Shifting half of the $110 million the state collects annually from a 1% sales tax surcharge on prepared meals to cities and towns to ease tax burdens. The 2019 legislature, which approved the surcharge, briefly considered giving the funds to municipalities before assigning them to the state’s budget.


Barring future state mandates on cities and towns from taking effect until one year after passage to allow communities to better plan for added costs.


Creating an independent, nonpartisan Council on Local Mandates to provide legislators with cost estimates for new mandates imposed on cities and towns.


And reevaluating the Connecticut grant program that reimburses municipalities for some of the revenues they lose because the state exempts hospitals, private colleges and universities, and state property from local taxation. Legislators also are being asked to consider ending or limiting exemption for certain groups.
