title: Judge rejects AG’s bid to permanently end case against ex-Capitol Police officer
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
A Hinds County judge has blocked the state attorney general’s attempt to permanently drop the manslaughter case against a former Capitol Police officer who admitted killing a 25-year-old Jackson man during a traffic stop.
Hinds County Circuit Judge Faye Peterson ruled the attorney general’s office was showing a “bias” for law enforcement, despite its legal responsibility to prosecute the manslaughter case against the white former officer, Michael Lamar Rhinewalt, for firing the shot that killed Jaylen Lewis, a Black man. After a majority-Black jury deadlocked on whether to convict Rhinewalt at trial last month, the new ruling leaves open the possibility that Rhinewalt could face a second trial and up to 20 years in prison under a future attorney general, once current Republican officeholder Lynn Fitch’s term is up in 2028.
September’s manslaughter trial against Rhinewalt and the other former officer who admitted to shooting at Lewis in self defense, Steven Frederick Jr., marked the first criminal trial from Capitol Police’s record year of shootings in 2022. After the trial ended in an acquittal for Frederick and a hung jury for Rhinewalt, Peterson said she could hold another trial as soon as February.
Attorney General Lynn Fitch discusses her 2027 campaign for governor during an event at the Mississippi Republican Party headquarters in Jackson on Wednesday, Aug. 5, 2026. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
But just hours later, the attorney general’s office announced in a press release that it would not put Rhinewalt on trial again, writing that “in the case of a tie, the benefit of the doubt goes to our law enforcement officers.”
In her ruling Wednesday, Peterson criticized the attorney general’s reasoning, stating that Fitch’s office failed to give a substantive basis to “abandon” its oath and duty to keep prosecuting the case, such as “conflicting evidence.”
“The Court does not operate in (a) vacuum and is aware that on the date the case was announced as a mistrial, the Office of the Attorney General announced it would be abandoning its duty to pursue prosecution of this case due to a bias in preference of law enforcement rather than upholding the oath of the office to pursue prosecutions of cases without bias, sympathy or prejudice,” the judge wrote.
The attorney general’s office did not respond to multiple requests for comment. After Peterson rejected the office’s effort to get a permanent dismissal, the attorney general filed an official request Friday for the judge to temporarily drop the case. 
Jaylen Lewis Credit: Courtesy of Arkela Lewis
“The prosecution is bound to administer justice and protect the public by faithfully, fairly and impartially prosecuting crimes without regard to bias, sympathy, prejudice, preference or favoritism,” wrote Luke Williamson, the special assistant attorney general who handled the prosecution. “The prosecution believes we have exercised appropriate and reasonable measures in the prosecution of this case.”
Peterson has not yet ruled on the new request, according to court records.
Arkela Lewis, whose son Rhinewalt killed, thought the case was over. But when she learned from Mississippi Today there was a chance Rhinewalt could face trial again, she said the judge’s ruling gave her “a little bit more faith.”
“It doesn’t give me peace, but I can breathe a little bit knowing that she’s speaking out for my family, for my son,” she said.
Peterson ruled that she would have considered a request to temporarily drop the case, while allowing another prosecutor to take it up in the future. But in its initial request, the attorney general’s office aimed to shield Rhinewalt from prosecution in the manslaughter case forever — an “unnecessary reach” for Fitch’s office, according to Mississippi Christian University law professor Matthew Steffey.
“What that does is it instructs the next attorney general — whoever that is, and no matter what future evidence comes forward — ‘You may not prosecute this officer,’” Steffey said. “It would be a shame to have to tell a victim, ‘We can’t pursue justice because the previous holder of this office made sure to tie our hands.’”
An ‘unnecessary reach’: Rhinewalt’s critics and allies both find fault with AG
Arkela Lewis, bottom right, mother of Jaylen Lewis, who was shot to death during an encounter with officers of the Capitol Police department, testifies before members of the Jackson delegation of the Mississippi Legislature at the state Capitol in Jackson, Monday, March 6, 2023. Lewis was one of several witnesses who spoke against a bill that would increase state involvement in the Hinds County court system and expand the jurisdiction of Capitol Police inside the city of Jackson. The hearing drew a large number of spectators. (AP Photo/Rogelio V. Solis)
In Mississippi, the attorney general has sole power to prosecute officers for shooting civilians under state law. But both critics and allies of Rhinewalt have found fault with how the attorney general handled the case.
Speaking as Rhinewalt’s friend, Shaun Yurtkuran, a Jackson-based criminal defense attorney and a former prosecutor for the attorney general’s office, has another word to describe the office’s handling of the case: a “mess.”
Since Fitch’s office secured a grand jury indictment in the case last year, Yurtkuran said he has wanted nothing more than for Rhinewalt to finally be free of the case that has “financially ruined” his friend. But he said the attorney general failed to give the judge any valid legal reason for why the case should end forever.
“I don’t fault Judge Peterson because I fault the AG,” Yurtkuran said. “I think they screwed up in the beginning, like indicting him, and even to the end, they couldn’t even do that right.”
In his argument for a permanent dismissal, Williamson justified his request with the jury’s decision to acquit Frederick and the “age” of the case, even though it was the attorney general’s office that waited three years to indict the former officers.



This is not the first time a judge has questioned the fairness of the attorney general’s prosecution of Rhinewalt from his time as a Capitol Police officer with the force’s crime suppression Flex Unit. Another conflict stemmed from an aggravated assault case Rhinewalt faced after prosecutors accused him of shooting Sherita Harris, a Black woman, during an attempted traffic stop a month before he killed Lewis. 
The attorney general’s office was prosecuting the aggravated assault case against Rhinewalt while it was also defending him against a $3 million federal lawsuit that Harris filed, which accused the former officer of shooting her in the head and leaving her with “permanent neurological and facial injuries.”
The attorney general’s office argued that, because separate divisions were handling the cases, there was no evidence of “improper influence” on the grand jury that indicted Rhinewalt in Harris’ shooting. But ultimately, the Hinds County circuit judge presiding over the case, Adrienne Wooten, ruled the discrepancy was an unprecedented “conflict of interest which gravely undermines the integrity and fairness of the proceedings.”
The attorney general appointed the office of Lin Carter, the district attorney of Forrest and Perry counties, to take over the prosecution for Harris’ shooting. After a year and a half of delays, Rhinewalt is scheduled to face trial in that case next month.
Rhinewalt in ‘legal purgatory
Law experts expect that Rhinewalt will be clear from prosecution in the manslaughter case as long as Fitch is attorney general. But Yurtkuran said the judge’s ruling still leaves the former officer in “legal purgatory.”
Steffey said that once Fitch’s term is up at the beginning of 2028, it will be up to the new attorney general to review Rhinewalt’s case and decide whether to put him on trial again. So far, the only name in the race is Republican Sean Tindell, the former public safety commissioner whose department oversees the bureau that investigated Lewis’ killing. 
State Public Safety Commissioner Sean Tindell announces his candidacy for attorney general at the Republican Party headquarters in Jackson on Wednesday, Aug. 19, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
During his tenure over the Department of Public Safety, Tindell also oversaw reforms that gave its law enforcement standards board more power to investigate officer misconduct. He did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Lewis’ father, William Drake, said the attorney general’s decision against retrying Rhinewalt is a “political” move as Fitch runs for governor in next year’s elections. Fitch’s office has so rarely taken officers to court for shooting at civilians that Drake said the attorney general’s decision to indict Rhinewalt and Frederick for his son’s death already “spoke volumes” to him.
According to Fitch’s office, Lewis’ killing was one of only four times during her tenure when officers shot at civilians that the office did not find to be “justified.”
“For her to go against the grain, it was some light for me in some very dark times,” Drake said. “For her to even indict her own.”

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Shapiro signs bell-to-bell cellphone ban for Pa. schools
text:
Governor Josh Shapiro signs a bell-to-bell cellphone ban into law at Lenape Middle School in Central Bucks School District on Oct. 26, 2026. (Photo from PACast)More than 1.7 million K-12 students in public and private schools in Pennsylvania will soon all learn under a new, statewide law: a bell-to-bell cellphone ban restricting device use during the school day. 
On Monday, Gov. Josh Shapiro ceremoniously signed Senate Bill 1014, which passed the House and Senate last week, at Lenape Middle School — part of the Central Bucks School District, which has its own cellphone ban already in place.  
“What we’re doing is taking the example you set, and the model that you set, and now making sure that all schools across Pennsylvania follow that model,” Shapiro told assembled students. “I think students need to spend less time focused on their phones and a whole lot more time focused on learning and developing those social skills with their neighbors; on talking to their friends face-to-face; and on developing the critical life skills they’re going to need to interact with others.”
Sanjana Chamarty, a senior at Central Bucks High School South, shares research supporting a ban on cellphones in schools for herself and other students. (Screenshot from livestream)
Sanjana Chamarty, a senior at Central Bucks High School South, pointed to research findings that having phones on silent or turned off wasn’t enough to mitigate negative effects. 
“Eliminating the distraction altogether really does push forward and propel our idea of removing distractions, and also ensuring our students are receiving that quality education,” said Chamarty. “School is not only about the academics, but it’s also about making the social connections. Putting the phone down and looking up can really do a lot for our students.”
Two dozen states have a bell-to-bell cellphone ban, and most others have some sort of restrictions for K-12 students. PA Unplugged, a coalition of parents and educators in 32 counties, has repeatedly pushed for lawmakers to follow suit. 
Kirstin McGowan, a co-leader with the organization and Bucks County mom of two, pointed to ever-increasing mental health concerns tied to cellphone use, including depression, anxiety and poor self-image. 
“Research shows that teens are spending roughly 70 minutes of each school day on their phones, leading to lost learning, lost education and wasted tax dollars,” McGowan said. “This is a big step, but our work is not finished.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
School officials will need to adopt district policies before the 2027-2028 school year prohibiting cellphones all day, including during breaks and lunch, with a handful of exceptions for students with medical needs or disability accommodations. 
The law allows districts to craft individualized policies, and also requires schools to brief parents on emergency notification procedures. The ability of parents to contact children during a crisis was a point of contention for some, specifically pointing to school mass shootings.
In response to a question on the topic, Shapiro pivoted to another, less bipartisan issue: reducing firearm access for those who might harm another. 
“I don’t think we should accept the premise that a student having a phone in their hand or in their pocket makes a school any safer,” said Shapiro. “What we need to do is get the guns out of the hands of those people who shouldn’t have them. That’s why we need comprehensive gun reform in this commonwealth and in this country.” 
 Unclear reach of a bell-to-bell cellphone ban

The first bell-to-bell law was passed in Florida in 2023, making it difficult to determine whether statewide bans have any impact. An early analysis found that suspension rates spiked in the first year following its introduction, when students didn’t follow the new rule, but fell the subsequent year. 
All the while, learning outcomes improved, according to the study. But more time is needed to assess whether reduced screen time will have the same impact on mental health.
“There are some learning benefits over the long run — but not in the initial period,” Harvard University professor Paul Peterson said in a July article. “And as for the social-emotional side, we know less about that because we can’t observe it easily through the data we have at present.”
Sen. Steven Santarsiero (D-Bucks) holds a cell phone aloft at a press conference on Feb. 4, 2026. The former teacher said the devices are distractions for students in classrooms. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
Other experts told the New York Times last month that small-group tutoring would have the biggest impact on test scores, but costs more than bell-to-bell bans. Interventions like implementing the “science of reading” and universal pre-K were ranked more effective than increasing teacher pay or expanding private school vouchers. 
Anecdotally, Central Bucks High School West teacher Christie Besack said students were more present, engaged in class and talkative with each other following the district’s cellphone restriction. 
“We’ve seen in our district that this works, and I absolutely support making this a consistent expectation across Pennsylvania,” Besack added. 
Sen. Steve Santarsiero (D-Bucks) cosponsored the effort with Sen. Devlin Robinson (R-Allegheny). But he said he noticed many of his colleagues were distracted by their own devices when he spoke about the bill last week from the Senate floor.
“It’s a problem for us too … we’re addicted to it too,” Santarsiero said on Monday. “I didn’t bring mine here today, because we need to be more present with each other. If we’re going to get past this very volatile time in our country’s history, it’s going to be by building those relationships one person at a time.” 
Doing so would “repair our world… country… (and) state,” he continued, calling students “the vanguard for this.”
“You’re going to show us how it’s done, because the success you’re going to have in the schools will carry over to all of us as well,” he added.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: 174 former judges ask for dismissal of DOJ complaint against Minnesota bench
text:
U.S. District Judge Patrick Schiltz speaks at a symposium at the University of St. Thomas School of Law on Friday, Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo by Madison McVan/Minnesota Reformer)Former federal and state judges sent a letter Monday requesting the dismissal of a misconduct complaint filed last month by the U.S. Department of Justice against nearly every federal judge in Minnesota. 
Minnesota’s federal judges, including U.S. District Judge Patrick Schiltz, who was until recently the chief judge for the District of Minnesota, spoke to the New York Times in September about the impact of Operation Metro Surge on the courts. The federal government’s actions during the immigration crackdown — mass arrests of non-criminals, a lack of resources for the courts and local prosecutors, and failure to follow more than 200 court orders — “created a grave threat to the rule of law,” Schiltz said.
The DOJ filed a misconduct complaint with the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, which oversees the District of Minnesota, arguing that the judges who spoke to the New York Times violated the code of conduct for federal judges by launching a “partisan press campaign” and criticizing the government. The DOJ requested that U.S. Circuit Judge Steven Colloton order the judges to recuse themselves from all cases involving the Department of Homeland Security.
The complaint was an escalation of an ongoing battle between the Justice Department and the federal courts, especially in Minnesota, where prosecutors are still litigating cases against people who protested Operation Metro Surge. 
On Monday, 174 former federal and state judges asked Colloton to dismiss the complaint. 
The Minnesota judges’ statements to the New York Times were about the administration of the courts and the rule of law, topics judges are free to speak publicly about, the retired judges wrote. The New York Times article noted that Schiltz declined to comment on any matters pending before him, which would be improper. 
“Instead of dealing with the government’s defiance of judicial orders, the government filed disciplinary charges against the Minnesota judges who lawfully called out their misconduct,” said Nancy Gertner, former U.S. district judge for the District of Massachusetts, who signed the letter. 
In the letter to Colloton, the retired judges also argued that Colloton does not have the authority to force the recusal of judges from pending cases — there’s a well-established procedure for requesting a judge’s recusal from a case, and a misconduct complaint is not a substitute for that process, the letter states. 
Schiltz himself has publicly defended his statements. Two days after the Justice Department filed the complaint against him and others, he spoke at a symposium on state law remedies for federal lawlessness at the St. Thomas School of Law.
“I did not violate any ethics rules,” Schiltz said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: PODCAST: A look at CT’s five congressional races ahead of Election Day
text:
Democrats across the country hope for a blue wave on Election Day. In Connecticut, several delegation members could head to powerful committee leadership positions if Dems take the House.
WSHU’s Ebong Udoma spoke with CT Mirror’s Lisa Hagen about Connecticut’s five congressional races as part of the collaborative podcast Long Story Short. Read Lisa’s coverage here.
WSHU: Hello, Lisa.
LH: Hey, thanks for having me.
WSHU: Okay, well, polls and early voting numbers indicate November 3 might be a good night for Democrats. You’ve investigated five races in Connecticut based on a combination of factors, including district makeup, incumbency, fundraising advantage, and the state’s swing toward Democrats in the Trump era. What did you find? Let’s start with the first district, the only one without an incumbent on the ballot.
LH: Yeah, it’s an interesting one because the state’s delegation has been pretty stable, you know, at least since I’ve covered it, and has been the same membership since pretty much 2018, and so this is the first time in a long time, and especially in the first district based around Hartford, that constituents and voters will have a new member. And so Congressman John Larson (D-CT-1), who’s been there for 28 years, lost the Democratic primary, and so now it is former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin (D) who is favored to get the seat, given the district’s makeup again, how it is one of the bluest in the state, and he faces Republican Amy Chai, who is a doctor. She actually has run before as an independent in the third district. She doesn’t live in the first, but says she would move there if she won. And so it’s between Bronin and Chai. There’s also a Green Party nominee and a write-in candidate. On November 3, a new member will represent the first district, and based on how it’s looking, it will be former Mayor Luke Bronin.
WSHU: Okay, now let’s move over to the second district in eastern Connecticut. What do you see there?
LH: It’s an interesting one. It makes up the entire eastern part of the state. It’s on its face a pretty competitive district. But Joe Courtney (D-CT-2) has held it since 2006, and he won by 83 votes. And now he’s won re-election pretty easily. He’s been able to kind of cobble together a pretty diverse voting coalition. I mean, there’s clearly ticket splitting that happens. People vote Republican in local offices but still vote for a Democratic member in Congress. And so he faces Republican George Austin. He’s a contractor. He’s a first-time candidate, and so he’s trying to kind of cut into, you know, Joe Courtney’s advantages there. Maybe pull some of those Republicans back into the fold, and he’s going for more low-propensity voters. That’s worked for Republicans, especially President Trump, nationally. So we’ll see if he can kind of replicate that on a more local level.
WSHU: And now let’s turn to the third district, where we have the longest-serving member of the Connecticut delegation, Democrat Rosa DeLauro, and she’s running for a historic 19th term. How does it look for Rosa DeLauro?
LH: She still looks favored to win. It’s the district based around New Haven. It is also a pretty blue district, though, you know, as someone who’s been there since she won in 1990, she says, based on how she’s been looking at her district, things are starting to change a little bit. She feels like people are, you know, maybe Democrats aren’t coming out in large numbers like they have been in the past in cities like New Haven, and maybe things are swinging a little bit. But on the whole, it looks like she is poised to get that historic 19th term. And you know, for her and a lot of members who are running for re-election in the delegation, they have their eyes on chairmanships of their committees. If Democrats take back the House, which, at least as things stand right now, looks pretty good for them. And so, as part of her pitch to voters for having another term, she really wants to be chair of the House Appropriations Committee. It is arguably the most influential one, and it makes all the decisions about how the federal government spends money and how money is allocated to agencies. And at a time when there’s been a lot of cutbacks to federal funding, I think she sees herself as someone who would come in if Democrats are in power and try to make up for some of that lost funding. And she faces Republican Chris Lancia, also a first-time candidate, someone who was a Democrat back in the day, but is a Republican Party member now, and you know has kind of made the calls for change for someone who’s been again serving for decades at this point, and has also kind of talked about her age a little bit since she is also the oldest in the delegation.
WSHU: Yeah, now talking about seniority, we have Representative Jim Himes (D-CT-4) in the fourth district in Connecticut, and he’s the ranking Democrat on the Intelligence Committee right now. So he stands a chance of being the chair if the Democrats win. What’s his race looking like?
LH: Yeah, he’s making again a very similar pitch to the rest of his colleagues in the delegation that if he gets reelected again, which again it looks likely in the southwestern part of the state, that he would be seeking the top role on the Intelligence Committee. He’s currently the ranking member for Democrats, but he would stand to become chair if Democrats take back the House. All these committees have very different roles, but there’s a through line in all of them, and it’s an oversight of the Trump administration. So he very much sees himself playing a role in that. He faces Republican Michael Goldstein in a rematch. Goldstein is a doctor and an attorney. And then also an independent nominee, Benjamin Wesley, who has run in the past, and they’re kind of running on opposite sides of the spectrum of Congressman Himes.
WSHU: And now, Lisa, the most contested seat so far has been the fifth congressional district held by Jahana Hayes (D-CT-5). What does it look like for Hayes this time around?
LH: Yeah, the fifth district will always, I think, remain the most competitive. Republicans have had their eye on that for a long time. Hayes was first elected in 2018, and so 2022, that re-election race was her closest. Republican George Logan got very close. That was a year where Republicans did well and took back the House. She managed to survive that, and she faced a rematch from him in 2024, and the margin was just not that close, and that was not a good year for Democrats. So now the party in power faces headwinds in the midterm election. This is a good time for Democrats to be running, and things are definitely pointing in her favor. She faces a Republican, Chris Shea. He’s a retired Navy SEAL. He’s a firefighter. It has gotten less national attention than it has in quite some time, but there is some kind of last-minute outside spending that has been happening on behalf of both candidates. So maybe there’s a little bit of movement. Maybe there’s a little bit of hope left that the needle can move in the last week before the election. But it’s always a tough one, and I don’t think either party ever takes that one for granted.
WSHU: Okay, well, we’ll see what happens November 3. Thank you so much, Lisa.
LH: Thanks for having me.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland rolls out new grant program for solar, battery projects
text:
The Lime Kiln community solar project in Howard County, a 3.2-megawatt project pictured after a ribbon cutting ceremony on July 8, 2025. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)Maryland is beginning to accept applications for a program to bolster solar, wind and battery storage developers with state grant funding.
The program, christened Megawatts for Maryland, was established earlier this year by the General Assembly, using $200 million from an existing state fund.
The grant money is meant for projects that have already completed some initial development steps, including acquiring property, and applying to regulators at the Maryland Public Service Commission or the regional electric grid.
“We want to make sure that these are real projects,” said Kelly Speakes-Backman, director of the Maryland Energy Administration.
Maryland Energy Administration Director Kelly Speakes-Backman speaks with Montgomery County executive Marc Elrich during a December event in Annapolis. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
Officials at the administration will dole out the funds through a competitive auction, selecting the projects that deliver the most megawatt-hours of electricity per dollar.
Maryland policymakers hope that the projects, which must come online within seven years of receiving the grant money, will eventually help reduce electricity prices for customers by bolstering supply.
“This program is an investment in energy affordability for Maryland in the medium to long-term,” Speakes-Backman said. “This is not going to be something that impacts our bill tomorrow.”
Collectively, the projects are expected to deliver “several hundred megawatts,” enough to power about 150,000 homes per year, Speakes-Backman said.
The $100 million per year in funding comes from a trove of “alternative compliance payments” that electricity suppliers make in lieu of complying with the state’s rules governing the percentage of their energy portfolio that must be renewable.
The payments have burgeoned in recent years in part because suppliers are required to devote an increasing amount of their portfolios to solar, and projects haven’t kept pace. Democratic lawmakers have used the extra dollars, which flow into the Strategic Energy Investment Fund, both to balance the state budget — stirring opposition from the right and from climate groups — and to set up additional climate and energy programs, such as the auction.
“We’re using every tool at our disposal to bring Marylanders relief as energy costs skyrocket in our region and across the country,” Moore said in a news release Monday. “This program will tackle rising electricity demand with cleaner, cheaper, in-state energy generation that will drive down costs for the long-term.”
State leaders also hope that the grant funding will help make up for investment tax credits for renewable energy projects that were canceled by President Donald Trump’s administration, which came from the federal Inflation Reduction Act.
“It’s not going to necessarily fully replace the ITC [investment tax credit],” Speakes-Backman said. “But I don’t think it’s just like a drop in the bucket, either. This is a really big deal: $200 million toward in-state generation through a grant process.”
John Magoon, whose Laurel church missed out on a state grant to install solar, speaking in February against lawmakers’ move to shift $400 million from a key clean energy fund, the Strategic Energy Investment Fund. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)
Initial applications for Megawatts for Maryland are due from developers by Nov. 30. After that, state officials will confirm that the developers meet eligibility requirements, and qualified developers will have until Jan. 22 to submit an actual bid.
Throughout the state, renewable energy projects, including solar farms and battery storage facilities, have at times provoked strong pushback from communities.
In the application due in November, developers will need to show that they notified a local elected official about their project. In January, developers will need to provide plans for community engagement and community benefits.
But ultimately, the law requires that the winning projects be chosen purely based on the megawatts they can deliver for each dollar spent, Speakes-Backman said.
Lawmakers, who passed the program in this year’s Utility RELIEF Act, hope their constituents will see the program as a boon for their bills.
“Lowering costs for Maryland families remains our top priority,” Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City) said in a statement. “That’s why we passed Megawatts for Maryland last session — to bring more clean, renewable energy onto our grid, increase supply, and help lower utility bills.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: President Trump to return to SC days ahead of midterms
text:
President Donald Trump arrives for a campaign rally at T. Ed Garrison Arena at Clemson University on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026, in Pendleton, South Carolina. (Photo by Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)COLUMBIA — President Donald Trump will return to South Carolina for the second time in two weeks as the November election approaches.
Trump will participate in a midterm rally in Rock Hill on Thursday, according to a news release from the Republican National Committee. The specific location is yet to be announced.
The event is set to begin at 11 a.m., with doors opening at 9 a.m. Trump is scheduled to begin speaking at 12:30 p.m.
His afternoon appearance will allow the president to get back to the White House in time for the annual Halloween event, when he will join first lady Melania Trump to hand out candy to trick-or-treaters.
The visit comes just over a week after Trump’s last appearance in the Palmetto State. The president, who is traveling the country to drum up Republican support in the lead-up to the Nov. 3 election, rallied for U.S. Sen. Darline Graham in Pendleton last Wednesday.
Graham, who was appointed to the seat following the death of her brother, U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham, is facing Democrat Annie Andrews, a Lowcountry pediatrician, for the term starting in January.
Although South Carolina is generally a Republican stronghold, polls suggest that race might be tighter than expected. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report has the race listed as “lean Republican,” making it nearly a tossup.
Also in play is the 1st Congressional District, where Republican Jenny Costa Honeycutt is facing off against Democrat Nancy Lacore. Republican U.S. Rep. Nancy Mace opted to run for governor instead of reelection to the Lowcountry House seat. The Cook Political Report considers that race to “lean Republican” as well.
This marks the third time Trump will visit South Carolina in three months.
His rally for Graham in Myrtle Beach ahead of the GOP special primary runoff in August is credited with helping boost turnout. Graham defeated U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman by 5 points, winning 34 of 46 counties but losing the state’s northwest corner.
Trump’s appearance will come on Norman’s home turf. Norman lives in Rock Hill, which is part of the 5th District that he represents.
The announcement comes days after Norman’s son, Warren Norman, wrote in a commentary for FITSNews that he will be voting for Andrews. Ahead of last week’s Trump rally, Norman said during a radio interview that he refuses to help her campaign, though he pledged to vote for her since he promised to support the GOP nominee.
State Sen. West Climer, who also lives in Rock Hill, is the Republican nominee to replace Norman in the House. He’s facing Democrat Mallory Dittmer of nearby Fort Mill.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Juvenile arrested after 11 people shot near FAMU homecoming
text:
A mural featuring the sights of the Florida A&M University experience painted at the Efferson Student Union is seen on Dec. 31, 2024. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)Florida A&M University’s homecoming was the setting of shootings that injured 12, including 11 struck by gunfire. Of the 11 struck, six were juveniles, according to Tallahassee Police Department. The suspect is a 15-year-old. 
The shootings occurred just before 8 p.m. Saturday, following FAMU’s homecoming football game, on a street that runs in front of the historically black public university’s football stadium.
Monday morning, TPD announced it had arrested the suspect, charging him with 11 counts of attempted second-degree murder and possession of a firearm by a delinquent. His first court appearance was Monday morning, during which he was ordered to remain locked up, WCTV reported. 
TPD has not announced any deaths related to the shootings.
“What should have been a weekend of celebration in our community instead became a night of fear and violence for the victims and their families,” TPD Chief Lawrence Revell said in a news release. “While this arrest marks a significant step forward, our work is far from over. We remain committed to holding those responsible accountable and getting answers for every family impacted by this tragedy.”
The police department says its preliminary investigation determined “a physical altercation occurred before shots were fired” between “individuals known to one another.” However, as of Monday morning, “none of the victims appear to have been the intended targets.”
During FAMU’s homecoming, TPD and other law enforcement in Tallahassee maintained “significantly elevated police presence” in the area surrounding campus, FAMU President Marva Johnson said.
“I share your outrage and profound sadness at the senseless and despicable shooting that took place near our FAMU campus last night,” Johnson said in a video posted to the university’s social media. 
Although in close proximity to the campus, the shootings were not on campus grounds, giving TPD the lead in the investigation.
Come together: Jolly and Nixon stump on FAMU campus as election draws near

Friday, Democratic nominee for governor David Jolly, his running mate Gwen Graham, Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Angie Nixon, and Democratic nominee for chief financial officer Annette Taddeo were on campus. 
Jolly posted to social media the morning after the shootings that he and his wife were praying for the victims and “the entire FAMU family.”
“To see that beautiful sense of community shattered by senseless violence is devastating, and learning that multiple victims are children is even more horrifying,” Nixon posted to social media, adding, “The gun violence in our country has to stop, and it will take all of us working together to heal our communities and protect our kids.”
Republican nominee for governor U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds, who attended FAMU, also posted.
“I am devastated by this senseless violence at FAMU on homecoming weekend. I walked this campus as a student and cannot imagine why someone would commit such a heinous act.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Advocates urge New Mexico lawmakers to enact stricter regulations on automated commercial vehicles
text:
Advocates highlighted the lack of automated commercial vehicle regulation in New Mexico statute to lawmakers on the interim Transportation Infrastructure Revenue Subcommittee on Oct. 23, 2026. (Photo by Diana Cervantes for Source NM)Advocates on Friday urged New Mexico lawmakers to join a handful of states that have passed public safety regulations for self-driving commercial vehicles.  SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reported 1,199 automated vehicle crashes nationwide in the past year. Driving systems that provide both automated speed and steering input but require a human driver were involved in 1,857 crashes. In total, 16 of the reported crashes occurred in New Mexico.
Daniel Cook, a business agent with Teamsters Local 492 in Albuquerque, began his career driving commercial vehicles in Alaska at age 19. He highlighted to the interim Transportation Infrastructure Revenue Subcommittee last Friday an incident in Arizona in which a semi-truck equipped with automated systems and two safety drivers at the helm veered into a concrete barrier on a highway. 
Cook told lawmakers he drove commercial semi-trucks with similar technology and that the automated system in his vehicle would “read a speed limit sign and it would slam on the brakes,” or, in another instance, dangerously stop the vehicle after falsely detecting a median as a stationary object.
“These systems do affect the way we drive currently and they are not ready to go at this point,” Cook said.
Six states — Hawaii, California, Nevada, Arizona, Texas, and Arkansas — passed self-driving vehicle regulations that require companies to obtain permits and state authorization to test or operate automated vehicles. New Mexico’s current statute allows driverless vehicle corporations to test on public roads if they notify the New Mexico Department of Transportation five days in advance and the vehicle complies with New Mexico traffic laws.
According to the advocates’ presentation, the current law does not require companies operating driverless vehicles to obtain a state permit, submit safety data or demonstrate that the driverless system has passed any preliminary safety testing.
“I didn’t realize our laws are so lacking,” Rep. Joy Garratt (D-Albuquerque) said. She called regulations — like requiring companies testing driverless semi-trucks to obtain a state permit that can be revoked for safety concerns — “common sense.”
Rep. Rod Montoya (R-Farmington) said autonomous vehicles will help fill gaps in commercial trucking shortages and New Mexico should not fully restrict them, but expressed support that something needs to be done.
“There is a need over time for this, but the idea of us being the guinea pigs is not something I’m looking forward to,” Montoya said. “There is a real risk here. We need to put some guardrails.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Jefferson Family Court judge to be suspended for 30 days
text:
A Jefferson Family Court Judge has been suspended for 30 days.
(Stock photo by Greenleaf123/Getty Images)Louisville Family Court Judge Lauren Adams Ogden will be suspended for 30 days after the Kentucky Judicial Conduct Commission found she violated multiple rules of judicial conduct. 
According to the agreed-upon order, released publicly Monday, Ogden will be suspended from the bench for 30 unpaid days beginning at midnight Nov. 8 through 11:59 p.m. on Dec. 8. 
The commission, which can discipline judges in order to “promote public confidence in the integrity, independence, competence and impartiality of the judiciary,” found Ogden had acted in ways that undermined the public’s faith in the court, including “rolling her eyes and smirking while hearing testimony,” speaking in a “sarcastic tone” and speaking over counsel, among other issues. 
Other findings in the order include allegations that Ogden: 

“Conducted a hearing with her judicial robe unzipped revealing a shirt covered with a design of two champagne glasses.” 
“Blatantly violated a parent’s due process rights — without any consideration of or reference to the relevant law” by removing a child from a mother’s custody without notice to the mother. 
Ordered a father’s “unsupervised parenting time with his three children be suspended, without making sufficient findings of endangerment.”
“Ate food and texted during the proceedings” in one case. 

Ogden “has acknowledged the concerns raised in these proceedings and has accepted responsibility for the administration of her courtroom and docket,” the commission’s order stated. 
“She has implemented changes intended to ensure that all parties, including those appearing without counsel, have a full opportunity to be heard, that the record reflects the basis for the Court’s decisions, and that rulings of the Court of Appeals are implemented promptly and completely,” according to the Monday order. 
During her suspension, she cannot appear at the Jefferson County Judicial Center. Within six months she must pay out of pocket for an educational course about “proper conduct of hearings and due process.” 
The last time the commission entered a suspension order for a sitting judge was in April 2025, according to records posted to its website. 
Ogden is the chair of the Child Fatality and Near Fatality External Review Panel, which reviews the worst cases of abuse and neglect — those that result in death or near death — and makes recommendations for policy changes.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Maine Ethics Commission fines Bobby Charles for campaign finance violations
text:
Republican gubernatorial nominee Bobby Charles signs a supporter's t-shirt during a Sept. 23 campaign event. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)The Maine Ethics Commission on Monday fined Republican gubernatorial candidate Bobby Charles more than $22,000 for violating state campaign finance laws.
The Charles campaign accepted more than $45,300 from dozens of individual donors who exceeded the $2,075 limit on individual campaign contributions, the commission unanimously agreed. The Charles campaign did not dispute the findings, but opposed the fine, repeatedly stressing its cooperation with the commission to return the excessive amount to donors. 
“I’m understanding that every contribution over the limit was returned as of this date,” said Commissioner Sarah LeClaire, a Democrat from Woodland. “I don’t think that that’s the salient issue for us. The salient issue was the acceptance and the failure to report.”
The commissioners pointed out that Charles’ campaign cooperation came after the Maine Democratic Party filed a complaint in early October detailing the over-the-limit contributions. Charles’ campaign Treasurer Bill Riley said that he spotted the excess amounts in reports that were uploaded by a national consultant the team hired, but did not explain why the campaign still accepted them. 
A campaign accepting dozens of over-the-limit contributions is a relatively rare occurrence. In a memo last Thursday, Executive Director Jonathan Wayne wrote that during the commission’s compliance reviews, staff “sometimes finds a gubernatorial candidate has accepted a few (over-the-limit) contributions, but current staff cannot recall finding a candidate campaign accepted anywhere near 36 (over-the-limit)  contributions during a report period.”
Given the unique circumstances, the five commissioners discussed Monday what precedent they would set by fining the Republican nominee’s campaign, and how much that fine should be. 
Attorney Brittany Walker Hausle with the national conservative law firm Lex Politica, who represented Charles, asked the commission for more time and to waive the fee, initially proposing a final determination after the Nov. 3 election. A majority of the commissioners denied that extension, saying the campaign had known for weeks about a potential fine.
Eventually, Commissioner Jill Goldthwait, an independent from Bar Harbor, proposed a 50% fine. The memo from Wayne last week had a suggested minimum of $11,329, which represents 25% of the total overage the Republican nominee accepted. The fine amount does not reflect the more than $4,500 in overages the campaign accepted due to processing fees for online contributions.
Wayne said in the meeting Monday that he proposed that amount as a floor because “I thought a message should be sent to all candidates as sort of general deterrence.”
Four out of five commissioners voted in favor of the 50% fine, which amounts to more than $22,000.
Attorney Kate Knox with Portland law firm Bernstein Shur, who represented the Maine Democratic Party, said the fine “is the cleanest message to voters: This happened; they were fined this much money; they did something wrong.”

Nathan Mark LaylandJul 8, 1961 — Oct 8, 2026Laramie, WyomingShared by: Ball Family ChapelNathan Mark Layland passed away peacefully in his home in Laramie, Wyoming on October 8, 2026 at the age of 65, having lived life his own way, with plenty of laughter, coffee, and heavy metal music along the way. He was born July 8, 1961, in Montpelier, Idaho to parents Marquis Layland and Alice Lucille Nate Layland and spent most of his childhood in Ely, Nevada, spending many days as his dad’s sidekick on cowboy and desert adventures.
He moved to Kemmerer, Wyoming in his early teens, and made it his home for over 40 years before moving to Laramie, Wyoming, where he spent the last 10 years of his life.
If there is one thing Nate will always be remembered for, it is how good he was at making people feel special, seen, and accepted for exactly who they were, without judgement. It didn’t matter who you were, where you came from, what you believed, or what kind of life you lived, Nate never judged anyone for being themselves, and he didn’t spend his own life worrying about what other people thought of him either. He was unapologetically himself, even if that meant being different from everyone around him.
He lived life on his own terms and accepted other people in the same way.
The other thing most people will always love about Nate is that he was funny – REALLY funny. He could make anyone laugh, no matter their age, background, or personality. He had a sharp wit and a wonderfully irreverent, unfiltered, and unique sense of humor. He was always looking for an opportunity to stir up a little trouble just to get a reaction. He had a special way of making kids laugh, and Grandma Kay’s daycare gave him plenty of opportunity to do just that.
“Uncle Nate,” as all the daycare kids affectionately knew him, would show up without warning, terrorize the kids, get them riled up and laughing hysterically, and make poor Grandma Kay go crazy and kick him out for bad behavior. If there was one thing you could count on with Nate around, it was plenty of laughter.
Nate had a lot of passions in life, but anyone that knew him knew guns were at the top of the list. He absolutely loved guns. He knew just about everything there was to know about them and loved shooting them (i.e., blowing stuff up!), working on them, buying them, and bonding over them with his closest friends. It was a huge part of who he was, and everybody knew Nate as the gun guy.
Nate was also an incredible and naturally talented artist. During his years in Kemmerer, he created artwork for many people, airbrushing motorcycle helmets and snowmobile hoods; painting signs for local businesses; and even designing headstones for friends and family. His artwork can still be seen throughout Kemmerer and will continue to bring joy to the many people who are fortunate enough to have a piece of it.
Another one of Nate’s passions in life was history. As a self-declared history nerd, Nate would spend much of his time watching documentaries, the history channel, reading books, and just learning as much as he possibly could about the past, especially if it was military history. He loved visiting military museums and would often know more about the artifacts in the museum than the people working there. Dragging him away from a conversation about fighter jets or aircraft carriers was nearly impossible.
Nate’s passion for weapons, the military, history, and art all came together in his favorite pastime – building models. A hobby he picked up as a teenager, he spent the rest of his life honing his skill and creating incredible works of art. His children will remember spending hours with him wandering through hobby shops or watching him at his modeling desk in the deepest concentration as he put together exact replicas of his favorite cars, fighter jets, and tanks.
He put his heart and soul into every model he built and was proud to show off each finished piece.
And then there was the music. Nate was a huge fan of rock and heavy metal music, and his love for the genre was infectious. Tool was his favorite band, and if you knew Nate, you knew that you had better like Tool. One of his favorite questions to ask anyone who came around was “Do you like Tool?” and if the answer was no or they didn’t know who Tool was, he would act like he was personally offended in a way that was unmistakably Nate and then put on a Tool song and make you listen to the entire thing.
If you were going to spend time around him, you had better learn to appreciate Tool.
Sharing his love for music was one of his favorite things to do. Nate and his big brown station wagon were responsible for taking an entire generation of Kemmerer teenagers to rock concerts. He would load up the car with his own kids and as many of their rock-loving friends as they could fit and would drive them to Salt Lake City, make sure they were safe, and rock hard with them all night long. For many, including his own children, his passion for rocking out was a gift that will stay with them forever.
As much as Nate loved his hobbies and interests, however, there was nothing he loved more than his family. He was a caring and devoted father who loved his children unconditionally. No matter what life threw at them, or what they might have put him through along the way, he was there, and he loved and supported them through it all. His children will find comfort in knowing that not a day went by that their father didn’t think of them and love them with everything he had.
His love for his grandchildren was just as strong. He absolutely loved being a grandpa and found true joy in spending time with his grandchildren, corrupting their minds as he would always say. They loved listening to his “old man stories,” laughing endlessly at his jokes, and playing with his big floppy ears. He had a special place in his heart for each of them, and they all knew just how much he loved them.
Nate was also incredibly close to his own father, Mark, and some of his most meaningful memories were made alongside him riding horses, branding cows, working on leather, fixing things, and fighting about who had whose tools. Their bond was strong and lasted a lifetime. Losing his dad was one of the hardest things Nate ever experienced, and there is comfort in knowing that he gets to be with his father again.
Nate was truly one of a kind in the best ways possible and will be missed beyond measure by the many people whose lives he touched.
He is survived by his daughter, Jennifer Scucchi of San Diego, CA; sons, Justin (Kelly) Layland of Lehi, UT and Jordan (Tera) Layland of Evanston, WY; six grandchildren, Jonathon, Matthew, Sydney, Abigail, Degan, and Erin; two great grandchildren, Archer and Birdie; sister Leslie Hayes; stepmother Kay Layland; step-siblings Loyde Cobb, Jacquie Louie, and Mike Cobb; and many nieces, nephews, cousins, and friends. He is preceded in death by parents Marquis Layland and Alice Lucille Nate Layland.
A celebration of Nate’s life will be held at the Kemmerer Stake Center cultural hall November 14, 2026, at 11:00am. This will be an informal gathering to share stories and reminisce about all the laughter, fun, chaos, mischief, and love he gave us all and celebrate Nate in a way that is true to who he was.

Gerald Milton “Gary” RicleyNovember 14, 1946 – October 17, 2026Slater, WyomingShared by: Schrader, Aragon & Jacoby Funeral HomeGerald Milton “Gary” Ricley, 79, of Slater, Wyoming, passed away peacefully in his sleep on October 17, 2026, leaving behind a lifetime of love, laughter, adventure, and stories that will be told for generations.
In Loving Memory of Gerald Milton “Gary” RicleyBorn November 14, 1946, in Denver, Colorado, to Arthur Morgan and Pauline Rose Ricley, Gary was a man of remarkable ingenuity, unwavering determination, deep faith, and an unforgettable sense of humor. He knew how to get things done but never believed life should be taken too seriously.
If asked, Gary would say his greatest accomplishment was the family and life he built with his beloved wife, Karen Sue. They met in 1964, and married after two years of courtship, going on to spend 50 years together. They raised four children and created a life rich in love, laughter, and unforgettable memories.
Summers meant weeks of boating, winters brought family ski trips, and he continually prioritized creating memories through family vacations, hunting adventures, late-night card games, and time spent together filled the years. Gary especially loved deer and elk hunting and believed life’s greatest adventures were even better when shared with family and friends, even including his mom on a trip to Hawaii.
Gary’s professional accomplishments were extraordinary. Beginning his career as a mechanic, he worked his way through the ranks of General Motors to become an executive, retiring at just 52 years old. He possessed the mind of an engineer, a natural gift for problem solving, and a work ethic that he used to be successful across several endeavors, both personally and professionally.
Retirement was hardly the end of Gary’s working years. For more than 30 years, he enjoyed a successful ranching and cattle operation on his rolling Wyoming ranch. Alongside his beloved pet horses, chickens, and cattle, Gary and Karen took great pride in caring for the land and creating a haven for wildlife. Their dedication to wildlife habitat improvements earned them the honor of 2011 Landowners of the Year, a recognition of their commitment to conservation and stewardship.
They also welcomed walk-in pheasant hunting on their property, sharing their appreciation for the land and outdoors with others. The ranch became another chapter in a life defined by hard work, ingenuity, and a deep appreciation for nature.
Wonderfully nostalgic, he loved sharing stories from his colorful life, often telling the same favorites again and again. His family could frequently recite them right along with him, but his enthusiasm and familiar punchlines were part of what made him so endearing. Those stories, and the laughter that accompanied them, became treasured family traditions.
His faith in and love for the Lord were central to his life, providing strength and comfort throughout every season. The passing of Karen eleven years ago profoundly changed Gary’s world. After a lifetime together, navigating life without her was never quite the same.
In his later years, Gary faced the challenges of dementia, particularly difficult for a man who had always proudly described his memory as a “steel trap.” Though the disease gradually changed his world, it never erased the man his family loved. When comfortable and at ease, his familiar humor and quick wit still shone through, offering precious glimpses of the storyteller and jokester everyone knew.
Gary lived a full and vibrant life. He worked hard, loved deeply, laughed often, and filled his years with experiences worth remembering. His greatest legacy isn’t measured by professional titles, cattle raised, or places traveled, but by the family he cherished, and the memories he leaves behind.
Gary was preceded in death by his beloved wife, Karen Sue; cherished granddaughter, Elizabeth Rose Dimzoff; parents, Arthur Morgan and Pauline Rose Ricley; and brother, Ronald Arthur Ricley.
He is survived by his four children, Ronda Dimzoff of Frederick, Colorado; Terry Ricley of Burlingame, Kansas; and David Ricley and Sheila Ricley, both of Cheyenne, Wyoming; nine grandchildren; seven great-grandchildren; and many extended family members and friends.
And though Gary may have told the same stories a hundred times, his family would give anything to hear him tell them just once more.
Rest peacefully, Gary. A life well lived, a job well done, and a lifetime of stories left for us to tell.

name: Mississippi Today
title: From the headache and aspirin department: Please explain college football this season
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
An old adage in college football is that, on any given Saturday, anything can happen. Anybody can beat anybody.
And that certainly holds true in the current season.
Rick Cleveland
How else to explain these occurrences? On Sept. 26, Florida slaughtered Ole Miss 52-28. On Oct 3, Missouri clobbered Florida 45-17. But on Oct. 17, Ole Miss belted Missouri 31-3.
In a matter of three weeks, Florida whipped Ole Miss by 24 points, and Missouri whipped Florida by 28, yet Ole Miss browbeat Missouri by 28.
It’s enough to make you dizzy. I mean, how does this happen? Team A was 24 points better than Team B, and Team B was 28 points better than Team C. Yet Team C beat Team A by 28 points. This does not compute.
But this is not an anomaly, either. Elsewhere in the SEC this season, Alabama slammed South Carolina by 31 points, 49-18. Tennessee trounced Alabama 26-10, yet South Carolina, just this past Saturday, defeated Tennessee 27-24. You’ll get a headache if you think about it too much.
Take some aspirin, because it’s not just happening in the SEC, either, as we shall see.
Earlier this season, Troy slammed Southern Miss 55-34. It was like men vs. boys. The next week, Louisiana pounded Troy 33-6. But then a week later, this past Saturday, Southern Miss stunned Louisiana 35-31.
Southern Mississippi quarterback Landry Lyddy (18) throws during an NCAA college football game in Hattiesburg, Miss., Saturday, Sept. 19, 2026.  Credit: AP Photo/Matthew Hinton
When results are this disparate, you figure there’s got to be a reason, a common thread. Having reported on college football for six decades or so, I figured that reason was turnovers. Experience tells me that when upsets occur, the turnover differential is most often the reason.
So I went back and looked at the nine results listed above. And I was partially correct. Not once among those nine decisions did the losing team win the turnover battle. In five cases, the winners were at least plus-2 in turnovers, but in the other four games, the turnovers were even.
The one common factor in all nine games? The home team won. Like Dorothy from Kansas once said, over and over, “There’s no place like home.”
In college football, the home team does enjoy a definite advantage. You could look it up. I did. So did renowned college football expert Phil Steele, who found that over the past five seasons home teams have won 64.2% of Division I football games. 
Nevertheless, I have heard TV pundits attribute such surprising turn-arounds as those discussed above to the modern version of college football with its unlimited free agency. For most teams, there is now wholesale turnover in rosters between seasons. It stands to reason that especially early in the season coaches are still getting to know the players and vice versa. Players are still learning new formations and new systems. There’s bound to be a period of adjustment when results are uneven and strange things happen.
That might seem like sound reasoning, but it doesn’t explain why this kind of stuff has been happening since long before college players were making more money than college presidents and changing schools faster than girlfriends.
Take 1970, for instance, 56 years ago. Ole Miss beat Alabama 48-23 in Jackson. Alabama beat Mississippi State 35-6 in Tuscaloosa, but State beat Ole Miss 19-14 in Oxford. Furthermore, that same season Ole Miss beat Memphis by 34 points, and Memphis beat Southern Miss by 33 points, yet Southern Miss beat Ole Miss by 16 points. Sounds crazy, but it happened.
And it happened long before that. One hundred years ago, Tulane beat Ole Miss 6-0. And Mississippi State Tulane 14-0. But Ole Miss beat Mississippi State 7-6. Homefield advantage? The home team won only once in those three games.
In college football, there’s only one explanation, which is: Go figure.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: What is the Kansas accent? Depends on whether you ask Kansans or non-Kansans, research finds
text:
Lacey Wade, a linguist at the University of Kansas, speaks with fellow linguist Jeff Holliday on Sept. 17, 2026, in Lawrence, Kansas, during a recording of the Kansas Reflector Podcast. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)LAWRENCE — Linguists at the University of Kansas revealed that the way Kansas speak is much more diverse than some people think, and perceptions of a Kansas accent differ, depending on whether listeners are Kansans or non-Kansans
Yes, Kansans do have an accent.
“There is no such thing as an accentless way of speaking,” said Lacey Wade, a linguist and assistant professor at the University of Kansas, “and we’ve been able to identify a few features that we do see in Kansas speech.”
Kansas is often left out of traditional studies of linguistic variations based on geography. Wade and fellow assistant professor and phonetician Jeff Holliday, along with co-author Tyler Hausthor, published a paper in August in Duke University Press to fill that gap.
In an interview on the Kansas Reflector Podcast, Wade and Holliday said Kansans often associated Kansas speech with a neutral accent, while non-Kansans largely associated it with Southern-accented voices.
“I think what’s going on is there’s a state, a part of the country, that has a name and people know that this place exists, but they don’t know much about it,” Holliday said. “And so when you ask them, well, ‘How do you think they talk?’ they actually don’t have much experience with that.”
Jeff Holliday, assistant professor and phonetician at the University of Kansas appears on Sept. 17, 2026, in Lawrence, Kansas, during a recording of the Kansas Reflector Podcast. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)
Wade pointed to the AppleTV sports comedy sensation “Ted Lasso” as a prime example of the disconnect between the perceptions and reality of Kansas speech. The titular character is a football coach from the Kansas City area, yet he speaks with a distinct “country Southern accent.”
Jason Sudeikis, who has played the character for four seasons, described his hometown as Overland Park, located outside the Kansas City metropolitan area. He graduated from Shawnee Mission West High School and attended Fort Scott Community College, and he doesn’t “actually sound like that in real life,” Wade said. 
His character puts on an accent and plays a character associated with stereotypes of what a rural accent sounds like, Wade said. 
“People will often use accents of characters as sort of shortcuts to whole hosts of personality traits that they want to convey very quickly,” Wade said. “And the quickest way to convey that is through somebody’s accent.”
One of the major takeaways from their research, Wade said, was the finding that Kansas is linguistically diverse, despite perceptions to the contrary. 
In their research, Wade and Holliday played participants clips of accents from throughout the United States. Kansans struggled to identify Kansas speakers from Salina and Dodge City as being from Kansas. They received higher accentedness ratings compared to speakers from the rest of the state or Kansas City. 
One of the Southern accent features Wade and Holliday discovered in Kansas speech was a linguistic phenomenon called the “pin-pen merger,” which occurs when a speaker pronounces “pin” and “pen” the same.
They observed another feature of Kansas speech in pronunciation of the “a” vowel sound that is most commonly associated with California speech, or the typical “valley girl” accent. In their observation, “hat” sounded more like “hot,” especially in younger Kansans. 
Kansans recognize variety in Kansas speech, distinguishing differences in speech between eastern Kansas and western Kansas. Simultaneously, they have a perception that a Kansas accent is neutral persisted, Wade said.
Their research could be classified as “folk linguistics” because of its focus on the way people think and feel about Kansas speech, which Wade and Holliday said was the best way to glean information about how language functions in different dialect regions of the country.
“The words and the sounds that come out of your mouth, that is a reflection of you and all of your experiences,” Holliday said. “I talk this way —the way that I’m talking now — because of where I was raised, where I’ve lived, who has been in my life that influenced me, and how I’m trying to present myself to the world.” 
He added: “That’s a beautiful thing, I think, and that’s true for everyone. What we want to understand is why is language like that?”
Wade and Holliday’s research is ongoing, and people who grew up in Kansas and are 8 years old and up can participate by visiting sociolinguistics.ku.edu/outreach or emailing kusociolab@gmail.com.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Early voting to begin Wednesday in Oklahoma
text:
Voters wait in line outside the Oklahoma County Election Board on Oct. 30, 2024, to cast a vote in the Nov. 5 election. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – Thousands of Oklahoma voters are expected to go to the polls early this week to cast ballots before the Nov. 3 general  election.
Oklahoma’s four-day in-person early voting window begins Wednesday and ends Saturday. Voters will cast ballots for legislative seats, statewide offices, congressional races, county posts, judicial retention and two legislatively proposed state questions.
Oklahoma has one of the shortest early voting periods in the country, and legislative efforts to expand that window have not advanced.
“With four days of early voting plus election day, “there are plenty of opportunities for voters to cast their ballot,” said State Election Board Secretary Paul Ziriax. “Remember, no excuse is needed to vote early. However, you will need to complete an in-person absentee ballot application when you check in at your early voting location.”
Voters may vote for any candidate regardless of party affiliation.
Several county election boards have opened more than one early-voting location.
Oklahoma County has three early voting locations for the first time after some voters reported waiting in lines for more than an hour during the presidential election two years ago.
Oklahoma County Election Board Secretary Doug Sanderson said officials added an additional polling location in the south part of the city.
“So, we’ve kind of got good distribution all over the county,” he said. “It is one per county commissioner.” 
Tulsa County will have four locations.
Tulsa County Election Board officials were trying to serve each of the city’s four quadrants, said Ronni Pierce, communications coordinator.
“So that is why we have located an early voting center in the north, the south, the east and the west, so we could just make sure that everybody was just minutes away from an early voting location,” she said.
Cleveland County has six early voting sites.
Canadian County, which is Oklahoma’s fourth most populated county, has two polling locations. 
Voters must cast ballots in the county in which they are registered.
They must also show proof of identity issued by the state, federal government or a federally recognized tribe before receiving a ballot. Voters may also use their county election board voter card even though it does not contain a photograph.
Those without identification can vote by provisional ballot.
Polls are open from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. Wednesday through Friday and 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. Saturday.
To find their closest early polling site and a copy of their sample ballot, voters can visit the State Election Board’s website.
