name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas Democrats, Republicans lean into voter engagement strategies in top-of-ticket races
text:
Kevin and Becca Peck, center, listen to Democratic Party candidates during a Sunday rally in Shawnee. Becca Peck has knocked on more than 4,000 doors in this election cycle to encourage Kansans to take part in the 2026 elections. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)SHAWNEE — Becca Peck demonstrated personal commitment to getting out the vote by knocking on 4,627 doors for the Johnson County Democratic Party.
So far.
Her total stands as the best this year among party volunteers in Johnson County, but that didn’t include more than 1,400 residences she approached on behalf of individual candidates in this election cycle or the canvassing she planned to finish before Nov. 3.
Instead of hunkering down in her Overland Park home to obsess about polling numbers or the latest campaign news, Peck said, she found purpose in going door-to-door and speaking directly with potential voters about what was at stake on the ballot. While she encountered discontent regarding some candidates, she said informal chats with people registered to voter revealed enthusiasm for taking part in this election.
“Normally in the midterms, I will get a lot of people that say, ‘I’m not voting this year.’ This year, everybody’s voting,” Peck said Sunday in Shawnee during the final stop on the Kansas Democratic Party’s candidate bus tour.
Tracking of advance balloting by the Kansas Secretary of State’s Office offered insight into voter engagement. As of Friday, 154,000 Kansans had submitted advance ballots in-person or by mail. That surpassed advance voting — at this juncture — in the previous two midterm elections. At this time in 2022, 92,000 Kansas had cast votes. By this point in the 2018 election cycle, 119,000 had put pen on paper to vote.
Republicans and Democrats are well aware that registered Democrats made up 73,000 of the state’s preliminary total. The early tally indicated about 60,000 registered Republicans and 20,000 registered independents had taken advantage of the opportunity to vote before Election Day.
 
Attorney General Kris Kobach speaks ahead of President Donald Trump’s rally Oct. 19, 2026, at Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
GOP’s call to vote
During the Oct. 19 rally hosted by President Donald Trump in Park City, Republican Attorney General Kris Kobach and GOP gubernatorial candidate Ty Masterson took turns begging Trump loyalists to get to the polls.
Kobach, who is running against Democrat Chris Mann, pointed to statistics that suggested Democrats were more eager than Republicans to take part in the midterm.
“That means that the opponent got out of the starting blocks faster than us,” Kobach told the crowd before Trump took the stage. “I know everybody here is going to vote, but just call someone. Call a friend. Call a cousin you haven’t spoken to in awhile. Just say, ‘Hey, let’s have lunch and go vote together.’ We need to get our people to the polls.”
Kobach predicted Kansas races for U.S. Senate, attorney general and governor were “going to be extremely close.”
Mann said he was confident his rematch with Kobach would have a different outcome than in 2022.
“It is time to take this office away from one man’s political agenda and bring it back to the people of Kansas,” Mann said, speaking at the Democrat’s rally Sunday in Shawnee.
Masterson, president of the Kansas Senate, relied on Trump’s endorsement to win the GOP primary in August. He said during the Park City event with Trump that strong Republican turnout was essential in his campaign against Democratic nominee Cindy Holscher, who also serves in the Kansas Senate.
“This is all for nothing if you don’t get out and vote,” Masterson said. “Every single person in this arena and 10 of your friends, and 10 of their friends. That’s what makes a difference.”
Holscher, speaking to more than 150 Democrats in Shawnee, said the 2026 election demonstrated how challenging it was to campaign for statewide office. Like Masterson, she made a get-out-the-vote pitch.
“There’s never been a time when we needed good, reasonable people more,” she said. “Thank you for the work you’ve done and what you’re going to do to help us get across the finish line. I’m asking you to make sure that not only do you get out and vote, but you find five friends that you can get out to vote. We can’t just wish for it or think it’s going to happen on its own. I gotta have you making phone calls. I’ve gotta have you knockin’ doors. I’ve got to have you donating.”
 
The ground game
Deann Mitchell, chair of the Johnson County Democratic Party, said the Democrats’ effort to drive turnout began long before the August primary. The goal was to contact potential voters with information about registration, advance ballot acquisition, deadlines for voting and issues that might influence decisions, she said.
She said pressure from Kobach, Masterson and U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall to convince Republican voters to head to the polls could be a reflection of comments Democratic volunteers had been picking up as the general election drew closer.
“We’re hearing from Republicans, you know, that they’re not excited about their candidates, but yet they can’t flip the switch and vote for a Democrat. So, they’re just not going to vote,” Mitchell said.
She said Trump’s sagging favorability rating and Marshall’s strategy of doubling down on his relationship with the president could be significant in the final phase of the U.S. Senate showdown. Vice President JD Vance was traveling Monday to Topeka for his second campaign stop in support of Marshall.
“We don’t want a radical Democrat representing Kansas in the U.S. Senate,” Marshall said during the Trump rally in Park City. “I am asking for your vote. I’m asking you all to get out and vote.”
Adam Hamilton, the church pastor and Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, said Marshall’s campaign was focused on events restricted to GOP supporters. Marshall took part in the Kansas State Fair debate with Hamilton, but generally had avoided open forums with Kansans after walking out of a 2025 town hall in Oakley, where he accused participants of being disrespectful.
During a 20-community bus tour, Hamilton met Sunday with Kansans in Oakley to talk about their concerns, including the cost of living, war with Iran, healthcare access and corruption in Washington, D.C.
“Roger Marshall said that meeting with Kansans is dangerous, but I met the Kansans he ran away from in Oakley,” Hamilton said. “And they’re not dangerous to me. They’re good, decent people who want leaders that listen to their concerns. They expect their senator to fight for them and stand up for them, not run and hide.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico State University students and organizers call for statewide ban on data centers
text:
First-year New Mexico State University student and Stop Project Jupiter organizer Lennie Dupass speaks at a rally on Oct. 25, 2026, on the school's main campus in Las Cruces. (Leah Romero for Source NM)Dozens of New Mexico State University students and statewide organizers rallied against hyperscale AI data centers in Las Cruces Sunday, calling for a statewide ban against the developers. 
NMSU students from Youth United for Climate Crisis Action (YUCCA) gathered on the university’s main campus alongside other environmental and political advocacy organizations, as well as local and state elected officials and southern Doña Ana County residents impacted by the AI data center known as Project Jupiter. 
The rally followed a three-day meeting of organizers from across New Mexico aimed at training organizers and creating a coordinated campaign against data centers and related policy ahead of the 2027 legislative session in January.
Oracle says it will cut Project Jupiter emissions after New Mexico org seeks to toss permit case

“Together we really are stronger than separately, and I think being together in person here in Las Cruces was a great way to see that,” YUCCA member Alex Atcitty told the crowd. He said AI and data centers are “extractors” that take more from the state and its communities than they give back, and are creating a crisis in New Mexico that requires more than a moratorium. “We are trying to be uncompromising with our rejection of AI. We do not want to stop halfway with guardrails or honestly even a moratorium. We want to push for a ban,” Atcitty said. 
Stop Project Jupiter organizer Lennie Dupass, a first-year NMSU student studying criminal justice, said he has followed the development of Project Jupiter since the Doña Ana County Commission voted to approve up to $165 billion in Industrial Revenue Bonds to help fund the data center in September 2026. He said he stayed for seven hours to hear the community provide public comment on the vote, which commissioners should have taken to mean the issue required more review.
“Our local government does not work for us…They made it abundantly clear that the only people I could place my trust in were my fellow community members,” Dupass said during the rally. “We know what New Mexico is worth. Our state has been used for decades solely for its resources, but our value is not determined by how much can be taken from us.”
Dupass told Source NM that he supports Daisy Maldonado, democratic candidate for Doña Ana County Commission’s District 1, and that she is a “turning point” for the commission this election cycle. 
“We’re cautious of our public officials and cautious of our government at this point,” he said, adding that he has never worked closer with government and politics than he is now. “I’m super confident that she can win this and I know it’s definitely going to change some things for us.”
YUCCA officials said the group is organizing and participating in student walkouts and community protests against data centers across the state on Tuesday as well. YUCCA Communications Manager Sophie LaBorwit told Source NM that University of New Mexico students plan to march down Central Avenue in Albuquerque to U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich’s office to protest the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, which protestors argued Sunday will rollback environmental protections. New Mexico School for the Arts students also will lead a protest to the Roundhouse in Santa Fe on Tuesday, while NMSU students and community members will gather at the Plaza de Las Cruces.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Early voting to begin in Kentucky this week ahead of November election
text:
Kentuckians can start voting early on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. Warren County residents, above, cast early votes in November 2024 at the Ephram White Park polling station. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Austin Anthony)For the November general election, early voting in Kentucky begins Thursday. 
All registered voters may cast ballots Thursday, Friday and Saturday through in-person no-excuse voting. Hours may vary by county. To find polling locations by county, visit the Kentucky State Board of Elections website. 
The general election is next week — Tuesday, Nov. 3. The deadline to register ahead of the election in order to vote was in September. 
The ballot will include local and statehouse races, as well as federal elections for the U.S. House and Senate. One constitutional amendment regarding governors’ pardon powers will be on the ballot. The State Board of Elections website also includes sample ballots from around the state. 
Candidates are making their final pitches to voters with days left ahead of the general election. In what has become Kentucky’s most competitive race — the 6th Congressional District in the central part of the state — Democrat Zach Dembo has announced a Lexington rally with Gov. Andy Beshear on Thursday, the first day of early voting. Last week, Republicans held their own rally with volunteers in Fayette County featuring the GOP candidate in the race, Ralph Alvarado, and U.S. Senate candidate, U.S. Rep. Andy Barr. 
In order to vote in Kentucky, voters must show proof of identification with a photo, such as a driver’s license. 
To learn more about candidates in the upcoming election, visit the Kentucky Lantern voter guide.

name: National
title: Brighter streetlights cut nighttime violence, but only for a while, study finds
text:
Streetlights illuminate autumn foliage in a suburban Maryland neighborhood. Brighter streetlights may help reduce nighttime violence, according to a new study. (Photo by Amanda Watford/Stateline)As days grow shorter and darkness arrives earlier across much of the country, a new study suggests that brighter streetlights may help reduce nighttime violence — at least temporarily.
Researchers found that outdoor nighttime violent crime fell by about 46% in targeted areas of Newark, New Jersey, during the first six months after aging streetlights were replaced with LED fixtures. The reductions were driven largely by declines in aggravated assaults and robberies, the researchers found.
But the effect faded over time. The upgrades did not produce a statistically significant reduction in violent crime over two years, and researchers found no significant overall effect on property crime.
The findings suggest that improved street lighting may help cities reduce violence in targeted areas, but that infrastructure upgrades alone may not be enough to sustain those gains.
Researchers point to community violence programs, pandemic recovery in historic homicide decline

Between 2019 and 2021, Public Service Electric and Gas Company replaced 1,419 streetlight fixtures in Newark as part of an initiative that prioritized areas based on past patterns of violent crime. The effort involved the Rutgers University-Newark Public Safety Collaborative, which helped identify locations for upgrades.
Researchers analyzed crime reports from the Newark Police Division between 2018 and 2023, comparing incidents near upgraded streetlights with those near fixtures that were not replaced. They examined crimes reported within 200 feet of each streetlight, including aggravated assault, robbery, homicide, burglary, theft and vehicle-related offenses.
The study used a quasi-experimental research design to estimate the relationship between the upgrades and crime, rather than randomly assigning streetlights for replacement.
The estimated reduction in outdoor nighttime violent crime was about 35% over the first year. By the end of the two-year period, however, the overall estimated reduction before and after the streetlights’ replacement was smaller and not statistically significant.
The researchers also found no statistically significant overall reduction in property crime following the upgrades. While some categories, including burglary and theft from vehicles, declined during certain periods, the results did not show a consistent effect across property crimes as a whole.
Nor did the analysis find significant evidence that crime simply moved into nearby areas after the lights were replaced. Researchers also found no systematic change in indoor nighttime violent crime, which they examined as a comparison.
The findings add to a mixed body of research on whether improved lighting can prevent crime. Some previous studies have found that brighter lighting is associated with reductions in crime, while others have reported less consistent results. A previous review of studies from four countries found an overall reduction in crime of about 14% following street-lighting improvements.
The Newark study suggests that the timing and durability of any effect may be important considerations for cities weighing investments in street lighting.
The researchers offered several possible explanations for why the reductions in violence diminished. People committing crimes may have adapted to the changes, while the underlying conditions that contribute to crime may have remained. The study also noted anecdotal reports of streetlights being damaged, though it did not measure whether damage affected the results.
The researchers cautioned against treating lighting improvements as a standalone solution, suggesting that cities consider them alongside community engagement and other crime-prevention efforts.
Stateline reporter Amanda Watford can be reached at awatford@stateline.org.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Candidates split on priority areas in Southwest Alaska Senate debate
text:
A man untangles his net in his boat on the Kuskokwim River in Bethel, Alaska. October 10, 2023. (Photo by Claire Stremple/Alaska Beacon)Southwest Alaska’s Senate district will see new representation in the Alaska State Legislature next year, after the retirement of the state’s longest-serving legislator, Lyman Hoffman. At a forum this week, four candidates offered different views on the district’s most pressing issues, from fisheries to energy and the rising cost of living in rural Alaska.  
Senate District S, one of the state’s largest districts, spans communities across Western Alaska and stretches to Cook Inlet, Bristol Bay and Aleutian islands that are only accessible by boat and plane. 
The candidates are Dillingham independent Rep. Bryce Edgmon, who currently serves as House Speaker, Republican Darren Deacon of Kalskag, Democrat Wassilie Guy of Napaskiak and independent Richard “Rick” Robb of Bethel.     

Bryce Edgmon, independent candidate for Alaska Senate District S in 2026, is seen in a photo provided by the candidate.
Darren Deacon, Republican candidate for Alaska Senate District S in 2026, is seen in a photo provided to the Alaska Division of Elections.
Rick Robb, nonpartisan candidate for Senate District S in the 2026 Alaska primary election, is seen in a photo published by the Alaska Division of Elections.
 

In the primary election, Edgmon was the frontrunner with 37.9% of the vote, Deacon received 23.9%, Guy received 18.9% and Robb got 11.4%. Voter turnout was 20.3% with 4,184 ballots counted.
Each senator in the 20-member Alaska Senate represents approximately 36,800 residents and serves four-year terms. 
The four candidates participated in an online forum hosted and broadcast by KYUK in Bethel and KUCB in Unalaska on Wednesday, and made their pitch to voters.
Edgmon was born and raised in Dillingham, where he lives when not in Juneau, and has represented the region in the Alaska House since 2007. He is the first Alaska Native to be elected House Speaker, and touted his experience and relationships in the Legislature. 
“I couldn’t imagine replacing the dean of the Legislature, Sen. Lyman Hoffman, with someone who has never served a day as a legislator,” Edgmon said. “My experience is vast. I’m well versed on all the issues. I’ve got credibility among my peers, having been elected speaker multiple times, and I’ve also got relationships I think will greatly enhance the Y-K (Yukon-Kuskokwim) region as well as Senate District S.”
Deacon is Yup’ik Athabascan and grew up in Upper and Lower Kalskag, where he lives and works as a telecommunications installer. He’s run for the Alaska House before, including challenging Edgmon in 2024. 
“I want to fight for a full dividend. I want to fight for our subsistence rights, which always seem to be threatened, especially fishing,” he said. “And I just want to bring a new face, if elected, to the Senate with new ideas and just want to fight and do right for the people.”
Guy is Yup’ik and was born and raised in the village of Napaskiak on the Kuskokwim River where he lives and subsistence fishes year-round. 
“I taught myself local government, state and tribal, and have been advocating ever since,” he said, explaining that his advocacy covers public services through the community assistance program, the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, and the Indian Health Service. 
Robb is a longtime resident of Bethel, where he raised his family and has worked in behavioral health as a licensed professional counselor. 
“I’ve made a career helping people through rough times, mental illness, substance abuse issues, developmental disabilities, suicide prevention,” he said. Robb has also previously served on the local city council, as mayor, and on the board of the Alaska Municipal League. 
The candidates differed in their views on the top three priorities for the region.     

Alaska Senate District S spans from Western Alaska to Bristol Bay and the Aleutian Islands (Screenshot of Division of Elections map)
 

Robb said his top priority would be restoring fisheries. Western Alaska has seen a dramatic collapse in salmon runs on the Yukon and Kuskokwim rivers in recent years. 
“We have to explore hatcheries. We have to explore anything we can do to get our fish, and we need to address trawling,” he said, referring to the industrial trawling industry that has been criticized for its accidental harvest of other species, known as bycatch. He said he would also focus on public safety and funding for schools. 
Deacon said fishing would also be his focus, as would lowering the cost of living, in particular by advocating for a large Alaska Permanent Fund dividend, “which also would help costs and lower the cost of living,” he said. 
Guy said he would also advocate for a large dividend and to protect the Power Cost Equalization program, a state subsidy that offsets rural communities’ high energy costs. He said he would also support reviving a pension for public employees, and state subsidies for bulk fuel purchases.
Edgmon said narrowing priorities to three isn’t realistic. “When you get down to Juneau, you’re going to be dealing with 15 to 20, perhaps 25 different priorities,” he said. “But if I had to condense it down to three priorities, I would start by first saying that my first priority is to put Rural Alaska at the front of the table, not at the back of the table, not in the middle of the table, but at the front of the table.” 
Edgmon said that he would work to increase funding for the state’s Home Heating Assistance Program, a state program that provides emergency and annual assistance to households based on income eligibility requirements. 
“Right now we funded it at $11 million. I think we’re going to have to come back and perhaps double or triple that to make sure that families in need can get the heating vouchers that they’re going to need to get through the winter,” he said. He said he would also focus on education funding, reviving a public pension, election reform, public safety and trawling regulations.
Edgmon said he believes that if he is elected he would be appointed as a co-chair of the Senate Finance Committee, which drafts the state budget and selects priorities, which would benefit the district. That appointment would be up to the members of the Senate majority.  
Alaskans are seeing skyrocketing energy costs, particularly in rural communities, as the U.S. war with Iran is driving up costs for heating fuel, groceries and transportation. 
Later in the debate, in a lightning round where candidates asked questions of each other, Robb responded to a question from Guy about how candidates would address rising costs, and said he would also advocate for emergency heating assistance this year.
“To give every resident or every home, every household a heating fuel credit of at least $1,000, so we can have so people can heat their homes this winter,” Robb said. 
Permanent Fund dividend debate
The four candidates disagreed on the amount and source of funding for the annual dividend from the Alaska Permanent Fund, the state’s sovereign-wealth fund. 
Guy and Deacon said they would seek to address rising costs in rural communities by advocating for a “full PFD,” referring to a payment based on a formula in state law that has not been used since 2015. “People would have between $3,000 and $12,000 per family. That would help out with a lot of costs,” Deacon said. 
But that would come at a multibillion-dollar price that doesn’t fit in the state budget without spending from savings. Since 2016, legislators have opted for a “surplus dividend,” paying a dividend with what’s left over after state government services are covered. This year, the dividend was $1,000 plus $200 in energy relief per eligible Alaskan. 
Edgmon asked the other candidates how they proposed paying for a full PFD. He said a large PFD is impractical and lacks support among legislators who want to fund potentially billions of dollars in other priority areas. 
“The reality is, in Juneau, there are no votes for a full PFD. So any candidate to me that says that they’re going to promise a full PFD is providing basically a false promise. It’s a hollow statement, and it upsets me because we work hard down in Juneau to get full funding for education, for PCE, for public safety, and a very meaningful dividend,” Edgmon said.
Deacon said he was unsure how to fund a full PFD until he could study the budget. Robb said he would support a change in the law in order to pay out a larger dividend, supported by growth in the Permanent Fund. Guy said he would support corporate investment policy to grow the fund and its earnings. Neither of those approaches would generate enough revenue for a full PFD in the short term.
Education, disasters and healthcare
All four candidates said they would support adequate state funding for education. 
Robb said he supports the creation of an education endowment fund to provide designated funding for schools, and forward-funding to create more stability. “It’s one of the biggest responsibilities, constitutionally mandated responsibility, especially out here where it’s all REAAs (Regional Education Attendance Areas) and there’s not a lot of local sales tax or property taxes to support it,” he said. “I would support: forward funding, educational endowment fund, adequate pay for teachers, and growing our own teachers.”
Edgmon emphasized the need to address challenges of teacher recruitment and retention particularly in rural communities, and said he supports the work of the bipartisan task force currently examining how the state funds education. 
“I also want to say that if we do have to reexamine the K-12 funding formula, that we do it very judiciously, and that we have somebody who’s got experience at the helm to be able to defend rural Alaska, so that we don’t get shortchanged should that occur,” he said. “But I think it comes down to getting more adequate funding levels to our schools.”
Guy responded only that he would support adequate funding for schools. Deacon agreed, and said he’d support more investment in school maintenance, citing high-profile cases of deterioration of school buildings in the district in Sleetmute and Aniak. “I believe maybe bringing more legislators out to tour these places so that they can see for themselves what the funding does out in the villages,” he said. Deacon said he also supports changing a law to protect funding for schools that drop below an enrollment requirement of 10 students. 
All four candidates said they’d support working with state and federal agencies to help communities impacted by ex-Typhoon Halong last year continue with recovery, as well as pursue long-term disaster planning and relocation for some communities. 
All four candidates also expressed support for increasing access to healthcare. Deacon noted the need for more dental care. Robb emphasized that unmet needs, particularly for behavioral health and suicide prevention, could be met through expanding telehealth opportunities. Robb and Edgmon noted the impacts of the budget cuts and new requirements for Medicaid enacted in the Trump administration’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
“The expansion population beginning in 2027 is going to have to provide work requirements. The eligibility status is going to be in question for a lot of recipients,” Edgmon said. “There are going to be downstream impacts from the Big Beautiful Bill, and the Legislature needs to be aware of all of them.”
Campaign finance
Edgmon is the front-runner in campaign fundraising, according to campaign finance reports filed one month ahead of the general election with the Alaska Public Offices Commission. He has raised nearly $55,000 this election season, with more than $27,000 raised last year and thousands this year contributed by unions, and seafood, healthcare, realtors and telecommunications executives and industry groups. 
Deacon has raised $150, which he contributed to his own campaign. Robb has raised more than $2,700, with $2,100 in self-funding. Guy reported no funding raised or spent this election.
Early voting has begun for the midterm elections, with 26,450 Alaskans casting votes as of Thursday morning, and will continue until the polls close at 8 p.m. on Nov. 3.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Mack Paul discusses “Miracle Road: The Story of Research Triangle Park”
text:
Mack Paul (Courtesy photo)One of the most successful public economic development projects in modern American history is North Carolina’s Research Triangle Park. Nearly 70 years ago, when a collection of public officials, academics and business leaders unveiled their vision for RTP, the undeveloped region found between the towns of Raleigh, Durham and Chapel Hill was characterized as one dominated by possums and pines.
Today, as is documented in the new book by the late writer Allen Paul and his son, Raleigh-based lawyer and civic leader Mack Paul – “Miracle Road: The Story of Research Triangle Park” — RTP is home to more than 350 companies and 65,000 workers. What’s more, it has been the font of scientific discoveries that have changed medicine, agriculture, computing, and everyday life around the world.
Recently, to learn more about the book, the remarkable story it tells and why he and his late father took on the project, Newsline caught up with Mack Paul for an extended conversation.
Click here to listen to the full interview with Mack Paul, co-author of “Miracle Road: The Story of Research Triangle Park.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Here are the 2 candidates running to be SC’s next chief accountant
text:
Democrat Tiffany Boozer (left) and Republican Mike Burkhold are running for comptroller general in South Carolina. (Photos courtesy of Boozer and Burkhold's campaigns)COLUMBIA — The race to be South Carolina’s next comptroller general pits a certified public accountant in the state agency against the founder of a company that tracks healthcare data.
Democrat Tiffany Boozer and Republican Mike Burkhold are both campaigning on ensuring South Carolina’s financial reports are accurate. Both say they have the experience needed to prevent anything like the blunder that put the normally boring accounting office into headlines. Both also want to expand the office’s online reporting to make state spending easier for the public to understand.
But their resumes differ.
It’s the first time voters are choosing the state’s chief accountant since the discovery of a $3.5 billion accounting error caused longtime Comptroller General Richard Eckstrom to resign in March 2023, just four months after he won a sixth term. His appointed replacement, Brian Gaines, said from the outset he had no interest in running for the job.
The multibillion-dollar overstatements stemmed from years of accidentally double-counting public colleges’ revenue. No actual money was found or lost. And the overstatements did not result in any spending deficit, since the Legislature doesn’t use the comptroller general’s reports for budgeting. But they misrepresented South Carolina’s finances to Wall Street investors, prompting a federal investigation.
The CPA
Boozer said she was hired in January 2025 to help correct the problem.
Her role, as a quality assurance manager, involves strengthening internal checks of the state’s ledgers. If elected to oversee the office, she said, her continued efforts will include using high-tech software for automated checks of the numbers. Artificial intelligence tools can help employees, not replace them, she said.
The errors found in the comptroller general’s reporting stemmed from a chaotic, decade-long transition from the state’s old accounting system to a new one.
“We have to have barriers in place, or even more barriers in place, to make sure that the numbers that are flowing up are as clean as they can possibly be,” Boozer said.
Before joining the comptroller general’s office, she was an internal audit manager at the state Department of Health.
Her main argument is that the comptroller general should be a certified public accountant.
Being the state’s chief accountant is “not red or blue,” said Boozer, who lives in Columbia. Once people “understand what the role is, it’s kind of a no-brainer.”
When no CPA announced a bid, “some office banter turned into a little bit of encouragement, and here we are,” she told the SC Daily Gazette about why she joined the race. She turned in her candidacy paperwork on the last day of filing in March.
In June, she won more than 74% of the vote against Bruce Cole, also of Columbia, to become the Democratic nominee.
The company founder
Burkhold, of Sullivans Island, said the accounting scandal is what prompted him to seek the job. He became the GOP nominee without any primary challenge.
The botched numbers were really an information technology issue, he said. His pitch to voters is that he has the needed expertise in IT and leadership experience from running a company.
The company he founded in 2009, Equiscript, uses technology to track patients’ records and medications to support treatment and help healthcare providers save money on prescriptions. He sold the company in 2019 but remains on its governing board. Tracking millions of healthcare transactions requires an understanding of IT systems, he said.
To increase transparency, he wants to incorporate AI into the office’s online spending records so the public can easily get answers to their questions.
“There should be no mysteries about where our money is,” Burkhold said. “I think it’s really important that the controller’s office be known as the place of monetary truth.
“If people need information, we can just give them the information, and they can rely on it,” he said.
Burkhold says he’ll bring an additional layer of leadership to the job.
He’s put together a “leadership council” of seven business leaders in the state he says are advising his campaign and will function as a board of advisers if he’s elected.
The team includes prominent philanthropist and financier Ben Navarro and Chad Walldorf, a co-founder of Sticky Fingers barbecue restaurants and former adviser to Govs. Mark Sanford and Nikki Haley.
Walldorf told the SC Daily Gazette he signed on to be a “helpful sounding board” for Burkhold in an office that often goes unrecognized.
Beyond making annual reports that close the books on the state’s ledgers, other duties include signing off on the state’s payroll to ensure employees are paid correctly and on time. The comptroller general also sits on the five-member State Fiscal Accountability Authority, a panel that gets the final say on borrowing, purchasing and major improvement projects for all state agencies.
The Nov. 3 election marks the first open contest for comptroller general in 28 years. In 1998, Democrat Jim Lander replaced retiring Comptroller General Earl Morris, a Democrat who previously held office as lieutenant governor and legislator in both chambers. In 2004, he was convicted of securities fraud related to the HomeGold scandal and spent nearly four years in prison.
In 2002, Eckstrom ousted Lander.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: DOJ confirms it’s sending election monitors to Louisiana — and all 50 states
text:
Michael Wolfe waves American flags at the entrance of City Park in New Orleans, one of several busy intersections in the city where the No Kings movement encouraged people to rally Saturday, Oct. 17. 2026, to raise awareness for the Nov. 3 election. (Photo by Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)An unspecified number of election monitors from the U.S. Department of Justice will be sent to Louisiana for the Nov. 3 election, but an agency spokesman said the deployment is nothing out of the ordinary and similar to measures it has taken for decades in previous elections.
A spokesman for the Louisiana Secretary of State said Friday its officials were “indirectly informed” the DOJ will send election monitors to certain jurisdictions, but the state has not received any official notice of its plans or the parishes where they will be stationed.
When asked to confirm its plans, an unnamed Justice Department representative responded via email Friday that the agency will have monitors in all 50 states. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche has previously said roughly 1,000 monitors are being sent across the country, adding that his agency routinely sends out these workers for elections.
“All monitors must meet the same legal and ethical requirements, including that they not interfere with the voting process,” a DOJ spokesperson said in an email to the Illuminator. “Every monitor has the same role: observe for potential violations of federal law and report concerns to the Department, which the Department will review after Election Day and act where appropriate.”
Some states have provided more information on DOJ monitoring plans for the Nov. 3 election. 
In Michigan, Attorney General Dana Nessel issued a news release Thursday that said the DOJ sent notices to communities in the state that federal monitors would be sent to their polling places on Election Day. They include Detroit, East Lansing, Flint, Grand Rapids and Lansing.
Federal monitors are also being sent to three Oklahoma counties, including the two most populous, according to its state election board. 
Salt Lake County in Utah has learned federal monitors will be present on Election Day. Lt. Gov. Diedre Henderson said she expects more but hasn’t learned details of where they will be deployed.
Henderson is among GOP state elections officials who have not met the Trump administration’s demand to provide their voter data.      
Election monitors’ duties include ensuring that polling places are in compliance with federal laws such as the Voting Rights Act and measures that ensure access for the elderly and disabled.
The Trump administration’s every move ahead of Election Day is drawing scrutiny as the president has spent months strongly suggesting the federal government take over elections from states, which goes against what’s laid out in Article 1, Section 4 of the U.S. Constitution.
WIthout any supporting evidence, Trump continues to claim the 2020 presidential election was “rigged” against him that Democrats will cheat in the midterm elections to take control from Republicans in the U.S. House and Senate. 
Courtrooms have become the Trump administration’s most frequent forum to take on state election officials, including some Republicans who have rejected his demands to turn over voter rolls to ensure noncitizens don’t cast ballots. 
Louisiana was the first state to use a new voter list maintenance database from the U.S. Department of Government Efficiency, providing Secretary of State Nancy Landry with information to check voters’ immigration status. Landry, a Republican, confirmed in January detailed information on Louisiana voters would be provided to the Department of Justice. She said state officials determined they had to comply with the DOJ’s request, The Times-Picayune reported.  
The Trump administration has continued to pursue legal action heading up to the Nov. 3 election as polls show Republican candidates losing ground in congressional races. 
Earlier this month, the DOJ sued California to block some 20,000 ballots that the feds claimed were mailed to noncitizens. And on Thursday, the administration filed a lawsuit against Alaska in the event that a Democrat wins its U.S. Senate race.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Commentary: Here’s what to know about potential election related litigation, here and beyond
text:
Voters cast their ballots at Webster Town Hall in Webster, Minnesota during the primary election Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)The U.S. Department of Justice sued the state of Alaska in federal court last week over its U.S. Senate election. In California, the DOJ  appealed a lawsuit judgment against suspected noncitizen voters. These actions are part of a broader push by the administration to block and tackle their way to GOP electoral success in the midterms and beyond.
Last week, I listened to a briefing with the Democratic National Committee’s litigation team. During the first Trump term, the DNC began building out an in-house attorney’s office for the sole purpose of taking the GOP and Trump to court. This is a new role for in-house staff attorneys specialized in high-stakes civil litigation, many with government experience in voting rights protection. This also added capacity on top of the existing voter protection and general counsel teams. This effort could become highly significant this year; more on that in a minute.
Democrats in Minnesota and across the country are fighting legal brushfires in state and federal courts to stop illegal anti-voter actions and preemptively do their own blocking on potential future actions, like the DOJ litigation against Alaska, filed the day after our briefing.
In 2020, the days between the general election and Jan. 20 were highly litigated. We all remember the insurrection on Jan. 6, but there were also court fights trying to block Joe Biden’s earned victory. In all, the Trump campaign and allies filed 62 lawsuits in nine states, including Wisconsin and, infamously, Georgia.
In 2020, then-U.S. Attorney General Bill Barr sowed doubt in the election with false statements about voter fraud and authorized DOJ investigators to look into supposed “vote tabulation irregularities.” When DOJ investigators found nothing, Barr leveled with Trump, and which is how he became persona non grata.
Current U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche — formerly Trump’s personal attorney — has been highly active in the voting sphere. When the DOJ acquired state voter registration rolls, it shared that data with the Department of Homeland Security for cross-referencing citizenship and immigration data in an unconstitutional and sloppy dragnet, sifting through the voting records of millions of Americans who exhibited no evidence of wrongdoing.
In Minnesota, Attorney General Keith Ellison has blocked the DOJ from acquiring the Minnesota voter registration roll, which would include private information not shared with candidates and political parties. A federal judge in the Minnesota district tossed out the DOJ lawsuit in August. The DOJ has not won a single case to acquire voter data when a litigant has opposed them.
The DNC is in a unique position as a national political party. The DNC is in association with thousands of candidates across the country in every state, from DFL candidates for school board to Jon Ossoff running for re-election to the U.S. Senate in Georgia. In 2025, the Supreme Court issued a judgment in Trump v. CASA Inc. that limits the ability of federal courts to block federal statutes and actions. In order to have a nationwide or universal relief (like a temporary injunction), a party must have nationwide or universal “equity.” In other words, they must be a stakeholder in the case everywhere. Because the DNC is the keystone committee of a national party with direct association with every Democratic candidate, the DNC litigation team can win a nationwide injunction.
If only Ossoff filed suit in his Northern District of Georgia in Atlanta, he could not individually have an injunction outside of the equity of his own campaign’s focused relief, whereas the DNC could win a national decision. 
Looking to next Tuesday, Nov. 3, and beyond, we know that the DOJ will deploy 1,000 election monitors to polling places across the country, including in Minnesota. Likely there will be more DOJ monitors in Minnesota next Tuesday than there were for the August primary. By law, these election monitors are unarmed and they must stay at least 100 feet from the building of the polling place. They abided by the law in August. They may not enter the polling place and they may not interfere or harass voters in any way.
Ellison is deploying Minnesota’s own state monitors, who are also required to stay outside 100 feet. Essentially they are attorneys and staff with notepads and cameras, not falling under any special statute for this unprecedented situation.
Inside the polling place, under Minnesota Statute 204C.07, each major political party (the DFL and GOP this year) are allowed one challenger to represent their party at a specific polling place. Both the DFL and GOP have trained poll challengers, and they are assigned to polling sites in their communities or ones of special interest. Poll challengers must be residents of Minnesota, and they may not influence voters, as happened in the Tammany Hall days of bosses pointing where to mark. For the DFL, these poll challengers are the eyes and ears of the DNC litigation team, able to quickly send text-only messages to the switchboards in St. Paul and Washington. 
As the name implies, poll challengers can contest the eligibility of a voter, but only on specific knowledge, not a drafted list of unwelcome voters. The voter has the ability to clear a challenge, and election judges of the precinct make that judgment. That is one of the reasons why Minnesota poll workers are called election judges, because in the most local sense, they are issuing rulings.
When you vote, you are going to court, the most local, democratic court. Your right to vote that day is being protected by your neighbors who are paid a few days a year and may have a potluck for lunch. They raise their right hands and take an oath at the opening of the polls that morning:
“I solemnly swear that I will perform the duties of election judge according to law and the best of my ability and will diligently endeavor to prevent fraud, deceit and abuse in conducting this election. I will perform my duties in a fair and impartial manner and not attempt to create an advantage for my party or for any candidate. I will not share information about voting that I know to be materially false and will not intentionally hinder, interfere with, or prevent a person from voting, registering to vote, or aiding another person in casting a ballot or registering to vote, except as specifically required by law.”
Some may add, “So help me God.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Residents sue CT for using IQ score to deny intellectual disability services
text:
Trumbull resident Edna Borchetta wants for her 20-year-old daughter Carriella what most parents dream of for their children: the chance to go to college, work and explore new opportunities.
But since Carriella lives with intellectual disabilities, she needs extra support to reach her full potential. Her parents offer all that they can so Carriella can lead a fulfilling life. The Trumbull Public Schools system has also supported Carriella’s complex needs throughout her schooling years, her mom said.
“I want her to be seen as the incredible, dynamic young woman that she is,” Edna Borchetta said. “With the potential to be a fully functioning member of society with the right supports in place, and that’s the key right there.”
Carriella is currently in the school district’s transition program for students between the ages of 18 and 22 who graduated high school but aren’t yet ready for college. Through this, she has a job at a bookstore and interacts with her neurotypical peers at Fairfield University.
Borchetta said her daughter loves being around young adults her age, even if she isn’t enrolled as a university student. The experience also shows Carriella what she could potentially do with the right supports in place.
“She has asked about … college and going away,” Borchetta said. “That’s not something that Dad and I can do alone. We need support in order to provide you with that opportunity. And that’s what we’re looking for.”
Connecticut’s Department of Developmental Services offers a range of resources for people with intellectual disabilities through waiver programs. But it utilizes a strict eligibility standard.
In order to qualify, a person must have a so-called “full scale” score of 69 or below on an intelligence quotient, or IQ, test. That score is composed of several subtest scores in areas such as achievement, memory and executive function. To be eligible, participants must also have evidence of deficits in adaptive behavior. Both need to be documented before age 18.
Carriella has had profound adaptive deficiencies since birth, her mother said. She has been diagnosed with an intellectual disability and with Williams syndrome, a genetic neurodevelopmental disorder.
She took several intelligence tests as a child. Her full scale IQ results range from 67 to 76. DDS deemed Carriella ineligible for intellectual disability services – twice.
“There’s no greater wasted resource on this planet than human potential,” her mother said. “That’s what this statute is doing. It’s wasting human potential.”
Carriella is not the only person the state has turned away due to the strict IQ cutoff. She and three other Connecticut residents with disabilities are collectively suing the state for denying services based on their IQ scores.
The complaint, filed Aug. 10, asserts that the state law governing DDS’s eligibility process violates the constitutional right of people with physical or mental disabilities to be equally protected.
Connecticut is one of only a handful of states that still rely solely on IQ scores to determine eligibility for services, according to the plaintiffs. They argue its approach does not align with current medical diagnostic standards established by the American Psychiatric Association.
DDS declined to respond to questions about the ongoing case. In an email, a spokesperson said the agency acknowledges its eligibility process has serious ramifications for applicants.
“DDS recognizes that eligibility questions can be deeply personal and consequential for individuals and families,” the email reads. “We are committed to treating everyone with dignity, listening to individuals and their families, and making decisions with care and respect.”
Edna Borchetta said not only was the extensive application process traumatic, but it was extremely disappointing to see the life-changing decision boil down to a test score.
“It’s so frustrating because my daughter is more than a number,” Borchetta said. “She is a beautiful human being who deserves to be looked at holistically.”
What the state offers to those eligible
The federal government offers several waiver programs to reimburse states for half of the cost of providing disability services and supports.
Available resources include access to case managers, paid family caregivers, jobs, day programs and supportive housing.
Connecticut requires residents to enroll and be found eligible. But being diagnosed with an intellectual disability is not enough; applicants must meet the state’s strict legal definition of the term.
To meet that criteria, a person’s IQ score must be at or below 69, which is two standard deviations below the average. This score must be recorded before the age of 18 to prove that deficits manifested during the developmental period.
If the score is above that cutoff, it doesn’t matter what other behavior deficits the person exhibits. If someone takes multiple tests and most full scores are within range, but one test returns a score above 69, they are still ineligible.
Jennifer Wheeler, an attorney with the Center for Children’s Advocacy who is representing the four residents in the lawsuit, said many people with intellectual disabilities are unable to receive services the state created specifically for them.
“These families go to DDS, they’re expecting to be eligible and DDS says no based on a very arbitrary and outdated definition of intellectual disability,” Wheeler said. “They say no despite a clinical diagnosis.”
How CT compares to other states
Most other states no longer consider IQ at all, or use the score as only one factor for consideration.
Luke Reynolds, another attorney on the case from the firm Koskoff Koskoff & Bieder, said in reviewing how other states determine eligibility, the legal team found it was common to permit higher IQ scores.
“They don’t rely on it as the gatekeeper to whether you’re eligible for services or not,” Reynolds said.
That approach more closely aligns with medical standards set by the American Psychiatric Association, Reynolds said.
The association’s Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders is widely seen by clinicians and researchers as an authoritative source on classifying mental disorders.
In 2013, the association overhauled its classification for intellectual disability in the manual’s fifth edition. Not only did the official diagnosis change from “mental retardation” to intellectual disability (intellectual developmental disorder), it also defined three domains of adaptive functioning that should be analysed for deficits.
More recent revisions lay out that a full-scale IQ test score is no longer required for diagnosis, and may not accurately encompass a person’s intellectual functioning. Instead, it should represent one aspect of diagnosing intellectual disability, along with a person’s conceptual, social and practical skills, the manual notes.
“This was studied for decades to come up with better protocols for assessing and diagnosing intellectual disability,” Wheeler said, adding it’s “embarrassing” Connecticut hasn’t updated its criteria, given how long ago the changes were made.
Dr. Carol Weitzman, co-director of the Autism Spectrum Center at Boston Children’s Hospital, and an attending physician in the hospital’s Division of Developmental Medicine, said diagnosing intellectual disability requires documenting onset during childhood and evaluating three main aspects: intellectual, cognitive and adaptive functioning.
An IQ test can measure intellectual functioning, but testing well in that aspect does not determine whether someone can manage day-to-day tasks, said Weitzman, who is also a partner at the Connecticut Center for Developmental Pediatrics.
Examples include social and practical skills, literacy, self direction, personal care and managing schedules and transportation, she said. Connecticut’s strict cutoff pulls attention away from understanding a person’s functional impairment and support needs, Weitzman said.
“And that’s the whole purpose of this, isn’t it?” she said. “Figuring out who are the people who really need the DDS support to function in life.”
A touch-and-go effort by CT lawmakers
That systematic shift is not lost on DDS officials or state legislators. However, stakeholders point out that any change will come with a high cost, which some believe the state seems unwilling to pay.
Andrew Feinstein, another of the lawyers for the plaintiffs, is a long-time special education lawyer based in Mystic. He is also co-founder and legislative chair of the advocacy group Special Education Equity for Kids in Connecticut, known as SEEK.
“The current system is already underfunded,” Feinstein said. “An increase in eligibility is going to put more pressure on the governor and the legislature to appropriate more money for human services, and that’s not a bad thing.”
State Rep. Jay Case, ranking member of the Human Services Committee, has pushed for years to remove the IQ cutoff from state statute.
“People come in year after year and tell us how antiquated we are by just labeling somebody with an IQ,” Case said. “It shouldn’t come down to money when it’s somebody who needs something.”
But the state keeps hesitating due to the high cost of change, he said.
A law adopted in 2023 called on the Office of Policy and Management and several other state agencies to recommend a new statutory definition for intellectual disability and determine whether IQ should be used as a factor.
As part of the effort, the University of Connecticut examined the eligibility criteria used in every state and the District of Columbia. The study found that eight states, including Connecticut, relied on a singular score. Nineteen states factored in IQ as one aspect of eligibility, while 24 states did not use IQ scores at all.
OPM also hired a nonprofit organization called Altarum to fulfill the statutory requirements. Its November 2024 report offered two options for the state to revise the statute: removing the IQ score requirement; or reclassifying intellectual disability under the broader umbrella of developmental disabilities, which encompasses people with higher IQ scores.
Its report noted the change would have significant impacts on budget, eligibility workflows, enrollment processes and workforce, and recommended additional research and support to address each of them.
Lawmakers continued to debate the issue in 2025 and 2026, but stopped short of revising the state’s definition, instead passing a bill this year that calls on the DDS commissioner to create recommendations for a standard definition of intellectual disability that does not rely on a single test score or measure and aligns with medical standards.
Case said the amendment was made because there wasn’t any funding available.
“So they want to do more studying and find out what DDS can do. That’s the bottom line,” he said. “The definition should be changed.”
The legislative report is due on Jan. 1, 2027.
DDS confirmed in an email that it is talking with stakeholders about redefining the term.
Weitzman, the doctor who specializes in developmental pediatrics, said initial costs may be daunting, but leaving people without the ability to work or live independently will cost the state more in the end.
“Where do you want to pay for it?” she asked.
Feinstein, the lawyer, said Carriella Borchetta and the other plaintiffs shouldn’t be forced to wait for new recommendations to come. The state has been “admiring” the problem long enough, he said.
“Bringing this lawsuit puts more pressure on the legislature to do something,” he said. “We hope that this pressure is enough to get them to move beyond admiration to actual action.”
Carriella has two more years until she ages out of the transition program. Edna Borchetta worries that without access to state services, her daughter will end up sitting idly at home, like so many other children who have been denied.
“This is bigger than Carriella. It’s bigger than the four plaintiffs in this case,” she said. “It is really about all of those kids and all of those young adults who are being denied services that they really need to flourish.”
This story was first published Oct. 26, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

name: California
title: A house divided? California YIMBYs disagree on Prop. 45
text:
Voters line up to cast their ballots in front of the Fresno Registrar of Voters office in Fresno on Nov. 4, 2025. Photo by Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters/CatchLight Local




Does more housing mean more sprawl? Traditional supporters of building more homes are split over a ballot measure that backers say would create more California homes.
As CalMatters’ Ben Christopher explains, Proposition 45 would limit environmental reviews under the California Environmental Quality Act. It would help developers advance projects they deem as “essential” faster and easier by subjecting reviews to time limits, among other things. 
While pro-housing advocates agree that California should build more housing, the rift over Prop. 45, however, comes down to where housing should expand.
Recent legislation to turbocharge housing construction has mostly applied to urban areas where homes and other infrastructure already exist, known as infill development. But Prop. 45 applies to all types of housing projects, including low-density housing located at the edge of metro areas, oftentimes referred to as sprawl.
Critics of sprawl argue that this type of land use houses fewer people over larger tracts of land, renders residents car dependent and has a bigger negative effect on the environment by requiring more freeways and water infrastructure. Bay Area pro-housing advocates Eastbay for Everyone and the Greenbelt Alliance are against Prop. 45.
But not everyone views sprawl as a bad thing, and some Prop. 45 proponents argue that California can’t build its way out of its housing crisis on infill development alone. 

Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, an Oakland Democrat and supporter of Prop. 45: “I’m an ‘all of the above’ person when it comes to housing, I think we need housing of all different types, shapes and sizes.” 

Read more.
More on the election: If you want to learn about the other propositions on the ballot, check out our last-minute guide on all 14 propositions here. Those proposals also include $44 billion across three bond measures, and for a rundown on those, read our explainer here.



We’re bringing our voter guide to life through VotingMatters events across California, in collaboration with on-the-ground partners. We’re holding two events today: In Los Angeles at the LADWP Crenshaw Customer Service Center and South Lake Tahoe at Lake Tahoe Community College.

Other Stories You Should Know


The wheelchair basketball team that’s changing lives inside prison


Members of the wheelchair basketball team practice on the general population yard at the California Medical Facility in Vacaville. Photo by Brian L. Frank for CatchLight/The Marshall Project




Today we’re publishing a story and visual essay that takes you somewhere that few people can go: A wheelchair basketball program inside a California state prison.
Our friends at the Marshall Project and Catchlight gained access to the team at California Medical Facility in Vacaville and met men who said the prison program helped them turn their lives around.

Steven “Scooby Doo” Davis, team co-captain: “For them to hug me and tell me that they see the good in me and I’m a good person, it made me go harder in wheelchair basketball.” 

California is leaning into the rehabilitative potential of sports. On Sept. 30, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed the Second Chance Sports Act, directing the state’s prison system to come up with a plan to expand sports programming.
Read more.



Spending big on CA’s insurance commissioner race


Insurance commissioner candidate Jane Kim speaks during an event co-hosted by CalMatters and UC Student and Policy Center in Sacramento on Oct. 8, 2026. Photo by Fred Greaves for CalMatters




Influential outside groups related to the insurance industry are pouring millions of dollars into California’s insurance commissioner race, report CalMatters’ Levi Sumagaysay and Jeremia Kimelman.
Political action committees have spent a record-high of more than $6 million on the race. More than half of that spending, $3.2 million, has been in support of state Sen. Ben Allen. Some of the PACs’ funders include companies from the insurance industry, and those same groups have spent more than $1.5 million to oppose his opponent, former San Francisco supervisor Jane Kim.
PACs are not directly affiliated nor can coordinate with candidate campaigns. Allen cannot control who gives to PACs on his behalf, and he said his vow not to take money directly from the insurance, utility and fossil fuel industries still stands.

Allen: “I didn’t ask for this and don’t welcome it.”

Nevertheless, Kim is raising alarm over these contributions, arguing that they are “a reflection of what the (insurance) industry believes is the best outcome for them.”
Read more.



And lastly: What do you want public health officials to know?


A person exhales while using an electronic cigarette in Los Angeles on Sept. 23, 2019. Photo by Richard Vogel, AP Photo




Have an opinion on what health issues should be prioritized in California? CalMatters is partnering with Your Local Epidemiologist to make the real concerns and questions from Californians heard by public health officials and journalists.
Every Monday, we’ll ask about health topics affecting Californians, and it’ll only take two minutes to answer.
This week, we’re asking more about Medi-Cal changes and questions you have on California’s ban on single-use vapes, which will go into effect in January. Take the survey.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: You have questions about ballot questions. We answered them.
text:
EPISODE INFO

HOSTS: Jennifer Smith and Chris Lisinski








WE GET IT: achieving a strong-enough understanding to feel confident voting on nine ballot questions is a tall task. Making it easier is the animating principle of much of our coverage since campaigns launched more than a year ago.
But new questions always come up, so this week on The Codcast, we tried to answer them. CommonWealth Beacon senior reporters Jennifer Smith and Chris Lisinski fielded inquiries submitted by listeners, touching on many of the dense topics voters will need to decide this election season.
Could adopting an all-party primary system lead to general elections featuring two Republicans? What would cities and towns do to address housing shortages if a zoning reform measure fails? And why are voters even being asked to weigh in on the complex formula used to calculate the annual limit on state tax collections before rebates kick in?
Listen along to hear answers to those questions and more.
For more insight as you weigh “yes” and “no” on the nine measures, check out our in-depth guide to the ballot questions, packed with information about what each proposal would do, the top donors putting big money into campaigns, and the ways Beacon Hill might respond.
On this episode, Smith and Lisinski discussed the prospect that wealthier candidates will gain a bigger advantage under an all-party primary system (7:00), which communities would be most affected by a proposal intended to kickstart more production of “starter homes” (15:00), and what’s different about the two repeal measures on the ballot (25:00).

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: What Peggy Flanagan’s Senate victory would mean for Indian Country
text:
Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan addresses voters at a Senate campaign event on the White Earth reservation on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Max Nesterak/Minnesota Reformer)NAYTAHWAUSH — Peggy Flanagan took the microphone and began, as she always does, in Ojibwe.
“Boozhoo,” she said, giving her name, her tribe and her clan before switching to English. “Thank you for welcoming me home.”
Flanagan, Minnesota’s lieutenant governor and Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, had traveled hours across prairie, wetland, forest and farmland to reach this town of 504 on the White Earth reservation, where she is an enrolled tribal member.
About 40 people sat in the shade of a large white tent next to the powwow grounds, as smoke wafted over from a grill piled high with hot dogs. Flanagan made her pitch: She knows what it’s like to struggle from a childhood on the margins, she’ll fight to finally raise the federal minimum wage, and she’ll take on President Trump.
The audience hardly needed convincing to vote for Flanagan over Republican Michele Tafoya, a retired sports broadcaster who is giving Republicans their best shot at winning a Senate seat since 2008.
Still, Flanagan showed up, in a commitment to Indian Country and the state’s most remote corners, where people often feel forgotten, to promise them face-to-face that she would take their concerns to Washington.
“I’m not running to make history, but it’s about damn time there was a Native American woman serving in the United States Senate. And she might as well be from White Earth,” Flanagan said to cheers.
Before she left for events at two more reservations, White Earth Chairman Michael Fairbanks gave her wild rice, sage and sweetgrass.
As with former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola, an Alaska Native and Alaska’s Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, Flanagan’s victory would be historic. Just four enrolled tribal members have served in the Senate in its 237-year history, all men.
Yet Flanagan’s candidacy has significance beyond just representation.
As lieutenant governor, Flanagan helped reshape state government’s relationship with the 11 tribal nations in Minnesota. Now, she promises to bring that experience to Congress, to work to uphold the federal government’s trust responsibilities to 575 federally recognized tribes and to advocate for a progressive economic agenda that would have an outsized impact for Native Americans, who face extreme rates of poverty and the lowest life expectancy of all racial and ethnic groups.
Her tenure in Minnesota government was not without friction with tribal leaders, however, and similar tensions are likely to follow her to the Senate. Tribal sovereignty and Native interests are often at odds with the federal government where she’ll be serving in the world’s most powerful legislative body.
Early years
Flanagan grew up in the Minneapolis suburbs, raised by her white, Irish Catholic mother and later a stepfather whose name they took. She was estranged from her Native father, Marvin Manypenny, who struggled with addiction through her childhood.
Nevertheless, her mother, Patricia Flanagan, ensured her daughter was connected to her Native identity.
She enrolled her as a citizen of White Earth Nation, which requires proof of an enrolled parent and one-quarter “Minnesota Chippewa Indian blood.” She also sent her to spend time with relatives on her dad’s side in south Minneapolis, close enough to walk to the American Indian Center.
The area has been an epicenter of urban Indian life since Native Americans began migrating to cities in large numbers in the mid-20th century, spurred on by federal policies aimed at moving Native people off reservations and dissolving tribal governments. Today the vast majority of Native Americans live in urban areas.
It was in south Minneapolis where the American Indian Movement was founded in the 1960s, followed by the only American Indian-preference Section 8 housing development, one of the first Native-controlled schools, a Native-run health clinic and a Native-run legal rights center.
“She really wanted to make sure that I knew who I was and where I came from,” Flanagan said in an interview.
Flanagan was a poor student in high school with a 1.75 grade-point average, but that changed when she got to the University of Minnesota and had her first Native instructor, Brenda Child.
“It literally changed everything,” Flanagan said. “All of a sudden, I was a sponge, and just threw myself into the work and the community.”
She graduated Phi Beta Kappa with a major in child psychology and a minor in American Indian studies and took a job at the Division of Indian Work in south Minneapolis. Then she joined Wellstone Action, the nonprofit dedicated to carrying on the legacy of Sen. Paul Wellstone by training organizers and candidates.
She served on the Minneapolis School Board and led the Children’s Defense Fund of Minnesota, where she advocated for a higher minimum wage, before winning a seat in the state House in 2015 and being tapped to join Walz’s ticket for governor just a couple of years later.
She often points to her Native identity — as well as her Catholic faith and hardscrabble upbringing — as informing her support for progressive policies such as universal childcare, Medicare for All and raising the federal minimum wage from $7.25 an hour to $17 an hour.
At a campaign stop on the Red Lake reservation, Lindsay Johns said she was moved by Flanagan’s story about watching her mom walk across a graduation stage after returning to school to be a phlebotomist. Flanagan has said that progress was only possible because of the stability provided by safety net programs like Section 8 housing and food assistance.
Johns, a member of Red Lake Nation, raised three sons on her own. She said after years of starts and stops, she just graduated with a four-year degree in child psychology.
“She almost made me cry,” said Johns, a member of Red Lake Nation. “I thought about how my kids were watching me graduate last spring.”
Speaks in a Loud and Clear Voice Woman
When Flanagan introduces herself in Ojibwe, she is doing more than sharing her name, Gizhiiwewidamookwe, or “Speaks in a Loud and Clear Voice Woman,” and her clan, the wolf clan. She is practicing a tradition that represents a triumph over the federal government’s concerted efforts to suppress Indigenous languages and cultures through boarding schools, adoption and relocation policies.
Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan speaks after winning the endorsement for a U.S. Senate seat at the 2026 DFL State Convention Saturday, May 30, 2026 in Rochester, Minnesota. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
Speaking on a national political stage, Flanagan is also bringing an Indigenous language to many Americans for the first time. Her introduction — and especially her name — has also drawn ridicule, particularly from conservative commentators, some of whom reduce its meaning to the pejorative “loud woman.” (Flanagan herself sometimes tells a version of this joke, saying her husband was the least surprised to learn her name.)
“It’s not surprising to me at all that it gets weaponized, and it’s really painful,” said Crystal Echo Hawk, who founded IllumiNative, an organization that aimed to improve the public’s understanding of Native Americans.
Echo Hawk says the reaction underscores how little most Americans know about contemporary Native Americans. She led a massive public opinion research project on Native Americans that found nearly 80% of the public knows little about Native people and that most schools fail to teach about Native Americans past 1900.
“When we are given our Native names, it is spiritual … It’s such an important part of who we are,” said Echo Hawk, who is Pawnee.
An Ojibwe name is bestowed at a spiritual ceremony, usually by a community elder or relative. That individual becomes the recipient’s “wen’enyag” or namesake.
Flanagan received her name in 2023, at age 43, from Priscilla Day, a retired professor of social work at the University of Minnesota.
Flanagan’s daughter, Siobhan, received her Ojibwe name at the same time.
“My daughter received her Ojibwe name so much earlier than I did, and feel like that’s a real gift,” Flanagan said.
Siobhan has had many opportunities to be immersed in the language and culture. She starred in a production of “Bowwow Powwow,” based on a book by Flanagan’s first Native college instructor. In the play, she spoke and sang in Ojibwe as the lead character Windy Girl.
Her daughter’s experience shows the progress of language and cultural revitalization that Flanagan has worked to reclaim in her own life — and advocated for in policy.
Working from inside the system
Marvin Manypenny, whom Flanagan became close with in adulthood, spent much of his life fighting the government. He was a prominent White Earth treaty rights activist and organizer in the vein of the American Indian Movement, known for its combative protests.
Peggy Flanagan and her father, Marvin Manypenny, in 2002 outside the Anishinaabe Cultural Center and Gallery in Detroit Lakes, where he was executive director. Courtesy photo.
He helped lead an effort aimed at reclaiming thousands of acres of land that had been swindled away from White Earth tribal members through federal policies and illegal land transactions. Manypenny occupied buildings, was arrested, and invited legal battles, such as when he stopped paying federal taxes.
His daughter has pursued change through markedly different means, as a politician rather than an agitator.
Flanagan often recalls her father telling her, “My girl, I want to burn down the system, and you want to get into the system and change it from inside out.”
For many Native people, that system has long been a source of harm rather than help. Generations of broken treaties, land seizures and federal policies aimed at forcing assimilation into the white mainstream have left a deep ambivalence toward state and federal government.
“We’ve had such a massive distrust of state and federal government, even local government, like that wasn’t for us,” Echo Hawk said.
One of the clearest symbols of that fraught relationship is visible from Flanagan’s office: a statue of former Gov. and U.S. Sen. Knute Nelson.
Nelson is widely regarded by Native people as one of the most destructive politicians, having been a principal architect of the Nelson Act of 1889. It opened up much of Ojibwe land to non-Native settlement and logging and aimed to push Ojibwe people onto the White Earth reservation. Tribal members often referred to him as “agongos” — the chipmunk — because he stuffed his mouth with Native lands, according to Anton Treuer, professor of Ojibwe at Bemidji State University.
Flanagan and Nelson’s statue have shared the Capitol grounds for the entirety of her service in the Legislature and as lieutenant governor, despite calls by Native activists to remove it. Another monument, a statue of Christopher Columbus, was never replaced under the Walz administration, however, after Native activists tore it down in 2020.
Working within the system and tolerating its flaws has allowed Flanagan to help forge a new relationship between the state and the 11 tribal governments in Minnesota that strives to respect tribal sovereignty.
Soon after they took office, Walz signed an executive order requiring every agency — from health to natural resources to transportation — to develop tribal consultation policies, designate a tribal liaison and maintain ongoing consultation with tribal governments. The Legislature codified those requirements in state law in 2021.
Activists led by members of the American Indian Movement tore down a statue of Christopher Columbus at the State Capitol in 2020. (Photo by Max Nesterak/Minnesota Reformer.)
The aim is to ensure tribal sovereignty is respected while avoiding painful and expensive disputes, such as desecrating a burial ground during road construction or illegally arresting Native people for hunting and fishing on treaty lands.
Walz also created an Office of Tribal State Relations so that tribal leaders would have a direct point of contact in the governor’s office.
“Peggy is why the office was created,” said Patina Park, a member of the Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe who led the office for more than five years after its inception.
Park said the Walz and Flanagan administration followed through on its promise to maintain relationships with tribes by visiting all 11 nations — something no previous administration had done.
When Walz visited the Upper Sioux Community, Park said, the chairman told Walz he was the first governor to visit since Henry Hastings Sibley, Minnesota’s first governor who commanded U.S. forces against the Dakota in 1862 and convened the sham trials that resulted in the federal government hanging 38 Dakota men in Mankato in the largest mass execution in American history.
The relationship between the tribes and state was tested during the COVID-19 pandemic. Minnesota officials joined daily calls with tribal leaders to coordinate the response. That stood in stark contrast to the response in South Dakota, where then-Gov. Kristi Noem was embroiled in an ugly standoff with tribal leaders, who set up coronavirus checkpoints on highways entering their reservations in an effort to limit the spread. Later, the leaders of seven tribes banned Noem from entering their reservations after she accused some of benefiting from drug cartels.
