Walz also signed significant legislation favorable to tribes and Native people. For instance, the law legalizing cannabis granted tribes a unique path to opening dispensaries off reservations, which gave them a head start in securing a foothold in the lucrative market.
During Walz’s tenure, Minnesota established the first state office for missing and murdered Indigenous people, created a commission to redesign the state flag and seal, which many Native people found offensive, and increased funding for Indigenous language instruction.
The administration also fostered the return of land to tribal control. In 2021, the Minnesota Historical Society returned 114 acres to the Lower Sioux Indian Community including the site of the start of the Dakota War of 1862. The Department of Natural Resources returned about two square miles that include a burial and prayer site to the Upper Sioux Community in 2024. And earlier this year, Walz signed legislation paving the way for the University of Minnesota to return 3,400 acres of land to the Fond du Lac Band of Ojibwe, which Nelson’s policies enabled to be divided and sold.
Balancing sovereigns
Flanagan’s tenure has not been without conflict with tribes. Even a politician committed to tribal sovereignty can find herself constrained by the government she serves.
“There’s always going to be friction there when two sovereigns are trying to understand the boundaries of their power,” said Bryan Newland, a former assistant secretary of the interior for Indian Affairs under President Biden and a member of Bay Mills Indian Community.
For Flanagan, the hardest test came in her first term during the fight over Enbridge’s Line 3 pipeline. The Canadian energy company sought to replace an aging pipeline with a higher-capacity one carrying Canadian oil across northern Minnesota, including through treaty lands where Native communities hunt, fish and harvest wild rice.
Roughly 2,000 people rallied at the state Capitol Aug. 25, 2021 to protest Enbridge’s Line 3 oil pipeline. (Photo by Rilyn Eischens/Minnesota Reformer)
Tribal leaders and environmental activists mounted an aggressive campaign to halt the project, filing numerous lawsuits, protesting at the Capitol and then blockading construction sites.
They appealed to Walz, but he declined to intervene in the permitting process.
Flanagan largely stayed tight-lipped, though she released a statement saying she was opposed to the project but didn’t have the power to stop it.
This brought on a harsh backlash from Native activists, who expected her to use her proximity to power to pressure Walz to halt construction. Some started calling her “Pipeline Peggy.”
Winona LaDuke, a White Earth member and prominent leader of the Line 3 resistance, said the nickname was unfair, but she shared the disappointment behind it.
“It wasn’t enough,” LaDuke said. “Peggy stuck with Tim Walz.”
The criticism exposed the limits of Flanagan’s influence and a tension at the heart of her politics. Working from within the system creates opportunities for change, but it does not guarantee that a Native leader’s priorities will prevail.
Former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland, the first Native American to lead the agency that includes the Bureau of Indian Affairs, faced a similar tension. She was widely hailed as a champion of sovereignty but nevertheless found herself at odds with tribal leaders at times.
LaDuke nevertheless supports Flanagan and her intention to serve as a check on the Trump administration.
“She’s strong,” LaDuke said. “If you’ve survived this long as an Indian politician, you’re a very strong woman.”
Vision for federal office
If elected, Flanagan would carry on a Minnesota Senate tradition that includes Tina Smith, Al Franken and Paul Wellstone, all progressive Democrats who championed Native issues on the Indian Affairs Committee.
She wants a place on that committee — along with assignments on agriculture and health, education, labor and pensions — which would give her oversight and influence over federal funding and policy for Indian Country, from health to gaming to land management.
Flanagan says her vision for the federal government’s relationship with tribes is straightforward: “The federal government needs to honor the treaty rights and uphold trust responsibilities.”
Straightforward, she concedes, is not the same as simple.
The federal government has obligations to tribes to safeguard their natural resources as well as fund health care, education and social services. The federal government, by its own admission, has persistently failed to meet these obligations.
Flanagan’s job would be to fight for how these obligations are interpreted, funded and enforced, as the Trump administration looks to cut spending and expand mining and oil development.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
While Flanagan would bring a unique perspective on Native issues to the Senate, she won’t have unique powers to solve the myriad problems facing Indian Country. Tribal leaders know this.
It was only in the decade Flanagan was born that the federal government began embracing tribal self-determination. Through the 1970s, Congress passed a series of laws giving tribes greater control over their schools, health care and other federal programs.
White Earth Chairman Michael Fairbanks said his community is focused on blocking copper-nickel mining near the Boundary Waters and maintaining federal protections for the gray wolf, which is spiritually important to the Ojibwe.
“The wolf is really powerful for us, and it kind of drives along the same lines as tribal policies,” Fairbanks said.
The issues have divided Minnesota’s congressional delegation. Republican U.S. Rep. Pete Stauber, whose district encompasses all seven Ojibwe reservations, has sponsored legislation to open up copper-nickel mining near the Boundary Waters and delist the gray wolf to allow for hunting. Smith has opposed both.
(Walz recently issued an executive order aimed at banning mining near the Boundary Waters, but it’s set to expire after he leaves.)
Leech Lake Chairman Faron Jackson Sr. said his central priority is land. Federal policies divided the Leech Lake reservation into a checkerboard of tribal, federal and non-Native ownership, leaving the tribe with relatively small landholdings within its reservation.
Smith helped secure the return of about 11,000 acres the federal government illegally took from Leech Lake members in the late 1940s and 1950s, but there are thousands more acres that haven’t been returned.
“We want to make sure that we get back what’s rightfully ours,” Jackson said.
It’s clear Native tribes are optimistic about her candidacy. Her campaign has drawn support from scores of tribes across the country: the Oneida Nation in Wisconsin, the Cherokee Nation in Oklahoma, the Muckleshoot Indian Tribe in Washington, the Seminole Tribe of Florida.
At a campaign event on the White Earth reservation, Stella Devine said she can’t wait for Flanagan to be in the “upper leagues” of government.
“The little ones are seeing her as an inspiration. I see her as an inspiration,” said Devine, who serves on the White Earth Elders Commission and said she tries to apply what she hears from Flanagan to her own work.
Later, Devine approached Flanagan to give her a hug and a word of encouragement.
“When are you going to come home and run for tribal council?” she asked.
Flanagan demurred. “One election at a time.”
Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan embraces Stella Devine at a Senate campaign event on the White Earth reservation on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Max Nesterak/Minnesota Reformer)

name: Nevada Current
title: Third data center gas plant seeks approval, as gas pipeline expansion advances
text:
Switch’s proposed gas-fired electricity plant is one of a dozen new delivery points tied to a gas pipeline expansion planned by a subsidiary of Southwest Gas Corp. to meet electricity demands of new data centers. (Photo: Switch media gallery)Utility regulators will consider whether to approve a third private methane gas power plant specifically for data center use in Nevada as NV Energy struggles to keep up with a surge of new demand.
Switch, a major data center developer in Nevada, is seeking approval for a 510-megawatt natural gas-fired power plant at the former Sierra Biofuels Refinery in the Tahoe-Reno Industrial Center, according to filings with the Public Utilities Commission of Nevada.
The 20-acre project was proposed in June by Nexus Fulcrum LLC, however, Switch disclosed in September that it was the “ultimate owner” of the project.
The move comes as a proposed gas pipeline expansion in northern Nevada could increase the amount of natural gas flowing into the region by as much as five times.
NV Energy told regulators rapid growth at and near the Tahoe Reno Industrial Center has outpaced available regional generation capacity, according to filings, noting “the existing system has limits.”
Data center operators looking to expand energy capacity in regions with grid constraints are increasingly proposing their own private on-site power plants — or “behind-the-meter” systems—  mostly powered by natural gas.
Unlike the two temporary gas-fired power plants approved by utility regulators last month, the lifespan of Switch’s project would be 30 years or more and would be supplied by a gas pipeline expansion proposed by Southwest Gas Corporation subsidiary Great Basin Gas Transmission Company.
If constructed, the power plant could produce as much as 2 million metric tons of carbon dioxide (CO₂) annually, according to the project application. That’s equal to the CO2 produced by roughly 453,000 gasoline-powered passenger vehicles driven for one year.
In written testimony to the PUCN, Zoë Harrold on behalf of Nevadans for Clean Affordable Reliable Energy, said the facility’s projected emissions would exceed all utility-owned fossil-fueled power plants in Nevada, except the North Valmy coal-powered plant. 
“At the upper end, the Project’s emissions would effectively eliminate the progress made to reduce electric sector emissions in Nevada since 2015,” said Harrold in her written testimony.
Nevada passed the state’s renewable energy standard in 2020, which mandates energy providers utilize 50% renewable energy by 2030. But private on-site power plants are not required to follow the standard because they are not traditional energy providers like NV Energy. 
Emissions from the Switch gas-fired power plant, and the previous two approved by regulators last month, are expected to contribute to the long-term increase of CO2 driving climate change, said Harrold.
Extensive scientific research also shows that long-term exposure to fine particulate matter is associated with heart disease, stroke, respiratory illness, asthma, and premature death.
More high-emissions gas-fired power plants are likely being planned in northern Nevada with the massive expansion of a methane gas pipeline in the region. 
Pipeline expansion map from Fall 2026 Southwest Gas Holdings presentation to shareholders.
Switch’s proposed gas-fired power plant is one of a dozen new delivery points tied to a gas pipeline expansion planned by the Great Basin Gas Transmission Company. 
Great Basin is in the early stages of a federal environmental review to build about 230 miles of new or expanded pipeline that would run across Churchill, Humboldt, Lyon, Pershing, Storey and Washoe counties. 
Great Basin said the project includes an expansion to the Tahoe-Reno Industrial Center and is needed “to meet growing natural gas demand in northern Nevada.” The expansion could supply an estimated 5,000 megawatts of new gas-powered electricity generation.
According to pre-filings with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), the gas pipeline expansion includes plans for 12 new delivery points in Churchill, Storey, and Lyon counties. 
Great Basin did not disclose who has signed agreements to move natural gas through the pipeline to the new delivery points or for what purpose the gas will be used, telling FERC that the information is “privileged and under non-disclosure agreements.”
But filings to the PUCN confirmed that Switch’s planned natural gas-fired power plant is one of the 12 new delivery points that will be supplied gas from the Great Basin Pipeline expansion. 
“Natural gas will be supplied to the site from an interconnection with a new lateral to the Great Basin Pipeline system,” according to an environmental statement submitted to regulators by Nexus Fulcrum. 
In February, Nevada Gov Joe Lombardo also sent a letter of support to FERC saying the gas pipeline expansion would support “future economic development, including data centers.”
NV Energy projects that its overall electricity demand could double by 2030 due to an explosion of artificial intelligence and data center growth in Nevada.
Great Basin expects the expansion to enter service in November 2028. However, the project still requires formal FERC approval before construction can proceed.
If approved by state utility regulators, the Switch gas-fired power plant would still need to acquire additional state permits and approvals, including an air quality permit for construction from the Nevada Division of Environmental Protection (NDEP).
The project is expected to use as much as 15 acre-feet of water during construction, and 145 acre-feet of water per year during operation. An acre foot of water is enough to cover one football field in one foot of water, or enough to supply roughly two average homes for a year.
Other gas pipeline expansions are also being pushed in the west, as power hungry data centers outpace available supply. An Oklahoma-based company that owns one of the largest gas pipeline networks in the Northwest filed with FERC in September to build a new pipeline between two existing gas transmission lines in Idaho and Nevada.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Commentary: In the 2026 midterms, state and local election officials are working hard to protect your vote
text:
Getty ImagesSince 2020, election misinformation and disinformation have become a rallying cry for sore losers and candidates who don’t get the results they wanted. The reality is that these lies have come at a real cost to voters, regardless of their veracity; they have weakened overall trust in our democratic systems and processes. 
As the 2026 midterms approach, lies about elections, including those from the president, will intensify, so it’s time to set the record straight. First, state and local officials run our elections, not the president. State and local election officials not only administer elections, but state and local law also dictates everything from early voting periods to election certification, and the secretary of state’s role is to ensure election administrators, poll workers, and county officials run our elections in accordance with state law. 
If you see sensational headlines or claims about our elections, or content clearly meant to provoke a strong emotional response, take a minute to pause and verify what you’re reading. Think through who the author is and what the motives may be. Then cross-reference the information with a trusted source, such as the Michigan Voter Information Center, your local clerk’s office, or a nonpartisan website like MichiganVoting.org, all of which have accurate, accessible information about Michigan’s elections.  
Despite failed executive orders aimed at overhauling vote by mail, attempts to upend voter registration, and even a Hail Mary attempt to pass federal legislation that would have required Michiganders to provide a birth certificate or passport in order to vote, Michigan’s elections remain protected, and everyone from state officials to local clerks to the pro-voter advocacy organizations is prepared to ensure that Michigan’s elections remain free and democratic. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
As a former Detroit poll worker and current voting rights advocate, I have seen firsthand the dedication of many local clerks to ensuring their communities can vote freely, without intimidation, and know their vote counts. For example, local and municipal clerks provide public logic and accuracy testing of voting machines so anyone can see exactly how our voting machines work. 
Knowledge is power, and it’s so important to get our information from our trusted, nonpartisan election administrators rather than viral videos online meant to scare or intimidate us. 
And it’s not just Michigan’s clerks who protect our elections; our state officials have also fought back. When the Department of Justice tried to access sensitive voter information, our attorney general and secretary of state fought back and won, because it is their duty to protect the information of the voters who trusted them. Michiganders should feel confident in our elections, because we know our officials will continue to protect our freedom to vote. 
That’s not to say the Trump administration’s threats to interfere with how state and local elections are run aren’t real, but it is a call to voters to remember that state and local election officials have our back in Michigan. As voters, our primary role in elections is to show up and make sure our voices are heard. 
This November, I know Michigan voters will do just that.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Financial struggles threaten to close Michigan’s oldest LGBTQ+ community center
text:
Grand Rapids Pride Center (Courtesy photo)For 38 years, the Grand Rapids Pride Center has been a mainstay and vital resource for the LGBTQ+ community in west Michigan. But declining funding, from individual donations to corporate sponsorships, means they may be forced to close for good at the end of the year. 
On Sept. 29, executive director Jazz McKinney posted an emotional message to the Grand Rapids Pride Center Facebook page. With only two months of operating expenses in reserve, Michigan’s oldest LGBTQ+ community center was on track to close by Thanksgiving without immediate financial intervention. Since then, an online fundraiser has raised enough money to keep the center open until Christmas.
“It’s really been something I’ve been paying attention to for the last year,” said McKinney, who uses they/them pronouns. “I started off with six months of reserves and savings this year and I saw that kind of starting to dwindle.” 
McKinney said that’s not unusual. In the first quarter, the center starts preparing for Grand Rapids Pride by putting down deposits for expenses like entertainment and venue rentals. By the second quarter, they usually end up financially ahead after Pride, held this year June 20 and 21. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
This year was different. Between the loss of grants, sponsorships and other funding, “I was just kind of noticing that we were just kind of flipped,” McKinney told Michigan Advance.
In addition, a flood kept the building closed for three months, from March until early June. Although they held office hours and had temporary space, McKinney said their efforts were focused largely on reopening the center when they would otherwise be writing more grant applications and seeking sponsorships for an upcoming fundraiser, their largest of the year.
McKinney explained how the federal funding picture, which has been hostile toward the LGBTQ+ community, affects the center indirectly. “It didn’t have an impact on us necessarily directly because we didn’t have any federal funds,” they said. “I’ve tried to keep us away beforehand from federal funds because I kind of saw this happening the first go round of this presidency.”
Instead, McKinney said, the center has felt the effects indirectly through community partners, corporate sponsors and other nonprofits.
“That’s where we really start to see some of the trickle down effect,” McKinney said. “Maybe we weren’t getting certain sponsors because their DEI dollars got cut. For instance, we just got denied for a grant through a partner that normally worked with us because they receive federal funds. In order to receive the grant, we had to agree to follow Executive Order 14151, which is essentially the order that says that there’s only two sexes.”
Grand Rapids Pride Center Executive Director Jazz McKinney | Photo courtesy of Grand Rapids Pride Center
That former partner, Blue Cross Blue Shield, also provides health insurance to McKinney and the center’s staff. After a partnership that spanned 10 years, the insurance company had to change its rules of engagement in order to keep the money it receive from the federal government. 
The relative success of the online fundraiser (more than $62,000 from 500-plus donors as of Oct. 23) buys time for McKinney and the center. One month of operating expenses costs about $70,000.
“I didn’t go into this thinking that the online fundraiser would be the end all be all,” McKinney said. “It was a bridge to help bridge the gap so that I can continue to work on the bigger things. It helps me to get us to the point that I can continue to do my job, which is to make us sustainable.”
Denise Spivak is executive director of CenterLink, an umbrella organization for LGBTQ+ community centers. She said the Grand Rapids Pride Center is not alone. A small number — perhaps 1% to 2% — of LGBTQ+ community centers, have been forced to close for financial reasons in the past two years; separately, some are taking a pause.
“There’s been a marked decrease [in funding] sector-wide,” Spivak told the Advance, “but especially when we’re talking about community centers, thankfully, LGBTQ community centers have always been incredibly resilient. They’re fighting tooth and nail and they’re gonna do everything they can to stay open. And as we’ve seen with Grand Rapids, communities are stepping up and really helping in that fight.”
Spivak called out corporate sponsors that have abandoned the queer community. “We saw that massive rollback on corporations, that suddenly I guess it wasn’t trendy or cool or I don’t know what happened, but suddenly many of the friends that we had, sort of ghosted us as a community—and that was very unfortunate,” Spivak said.
Grand Rapids Pride Center (Courtesy photo)
McKinney expressed gratitude to the donors and the outpouring of support. “I think that’s what the government or whoever is scared of, right? They’re doing everything they can to break us down and make us tired and all the things and make it so that we can’t work together.”
McKinney said losing the center would mean “the loss of support for everybody, really. It’s the loss of life-giving services. We are supporting people all throughout their life cycle, from the most dire times, if you will, to celebrating some of their biggest accomplishments.”
“We start serving kids as young as eight years old and we have a group that’s dedicated to elders. We’re serving basic needs. On the other side too, we’re pushing policies, we’re pushing to make sure that our community is heard and seen. And so we would lose all of that in our community,” McKinney said.
It would also mean the loss of the Grand Rapids Trans Foundation, a separate organization established in 2015 and housed within the center. In August, a month before McKinney’s announcement, executive director Ximón Kittok posted a Facebook video to share that the foundation was in desperate need of operating funds. McKinney had planned to make their announcement later and both executive directors emphasized they don’t want the two nonprofits to compete for individual donation dollars.
With a staff of six, the Grand Rapids Pride Center serves LGBTQ+ people in 10 counties and offers dozens of groups each week. Special fundraising events this month include The Luminary Crown, held Oct. 24 and the Prism Awards, set for Oct. 30.
McKinney, who has led the organization since 2020, remains hopeful about the center’s future.
“A lot of people would be losing lifesaving services and life-altering services, and people could literally lose their lives,” McKinney said. “You know, sometimes people are coming to us as their last hope. That’s their only hope for whatever services they’re coming to us for.
“I think our community will band together and figure it out. I think that’s the joy of our community.”

name: California
title: Why are pro-housing groups split on Proposition 45?
text:
In summary
Proposition 45 is intended to make it easier to build. But some pro-housing groups worry it will only lead to more sprawl.


For nearly a decade, California’s Yes In My Backyard activists and other pro-development advocates have wanted to overhaul California’s signature environmental law to clear the way for more housing construction.
Now Proposition 45 is on the ballot. Supporters say it would, among other things, overhaul that law, known as the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA, to clear the way for — you guessed it — more housing construction.
So why are YIMBYs divided?
Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, an Oakland Democrat and one of the movement’s most stalwart champions in the Legislature, is for it. So is the bulk of the building industry, including many major for- and non-profit developers.
Bay Area pro-housing advocates Eastbay for Everyone and the Greenbelt Alliance, two typical allies of Wicks, are emphatically against it.
In the uncommitted middle lies the lion’s share of California YIMBYism: Abundant Housing Los Angeles, SPUR, and both California YIMBY and YIMBY Action — the movement’s two flagship advocacy organizations — have all taken neutral positions.
“It’s been a weird campaign so far,” said Ali Sapirman, advocacy manager at the Housing Action Coalition, an urban building industry group that supports the measure. “The housing community has been a little bit fractured.”
Those fissures aren’t over whether more homes should be built across California. Instead, it mostly boils down to a question of where. 
“The central question here is how you feel about sprawl,” Max Dubler of California YIMBY wrote in the group’s non-endorsement statement, referring to low-density housing development at the edge of metro areas. Though some exurban growth “will necessarily be part of solving our housing shortage,” he expressed concern about making it easier to build “car-dependent sprawl housing and the freeways and water infrastructure necessary to serve that sprawl.”
To sprawl or not to sprawl
For nearly a decade, the Legislature has been on a tear, passing “streamlining” bills aimed at speeding up the regulatory approval of new construction. Almost all of those laws have only applied to projects in places where homes and other infrastructure already exist. 
Prioritizing so-called infill development helped wrangle together a coalition of developers and construction labor unions, but also a diverse swath of Democratic-leaning advocates whose interest in seeing more apartments and condos goes beyond the cause of affordability alone. That includes climate activists who want to see less commuter car traffic; transit, bicycle and pedestrian advocates who want more riders and walkers and urbanists who want Los Angeles to more closely resemble Barcelona. 
In breaking from that urban focus, Prop. 45 is driving a wedge inside that coalition. 
If passed, the measure would speed up the review process required under CEQA (pronounced “see-kwah”) for all types of housing projects. That includes transit-adjacent downtown condo towers, but also freshly paved subdivisions at the metropolitan fringe. 
The measure is “a doubling down on essentially 75 years of land-use patterns that we know haven’t worked,” said Jordan Grimes, legislative director with Greenbelt Alliance, which opposes the measure. “It’s a return to the sprawl era.”
Not everyone in the movement necessarily sees that as a bad thing. Among those who want California to build its way out of its current housing shortage, opinions differ over whether more environmentally-friendly infill development alone is up to the task. 
“I’m an ‘all of the above’ person when it comes to housing,” said Wicks, explaining her support of the measure. “I think we need housing of all different types, shapes, and sizes.” 
An earlier version of this rift first emerged earlier this decade when a handful of Bay Area tech investors announced plans to build a brand new city on Solano County farmland in 2023 under the banner of California Forever. Some YIMBY commentators applauded the plan as a welcome injection of much-needed supply. Others decried it as sprawl dressed in urbanist clothing. 
With Prop. 45, that regional debate is now playing out at a statewide scale.
Housing front and center 
Prop. 45 is about much more than housing policy. 
CEQA requires public agencies to review the possible environmental consequences of the decisions they make, including the permitting of private projects. For decades industry groups, developers and, more recently, housing supply boosters have said the law makes it too easy for project opponents to jam up worthwhile projects by repeatedly demanding additional analysis. 
“The clock is endless and the number of people and entities who can challenge you are also endless,” said Linda Mandolini of Eden Housing, an affordable housing developer. 
Prop. 45 would not exempt any projects from environmental review outright. But for projects deemed “essential,” it would narrow the focus of these reviews and require them to wrap up within 365 business days. Any resulting litigation would also face a shot clock; Judges would have 270 business days to resolve them. Such lawsuits would also be made harder to sustain in court. Aside from housing, essential projects include roads, hospitals, schools, clean energy projects, water and broadband infrastructure. 
But housing has loomed large in the electoral debate. The Yes on 45 campaign has touted the support of affordable housing developers and housing advocates, while pointing to housing affordability concerns as the initial impetus for the measure. 
It’s easy to see why. Environmental challenges to often innocuous-seeming housing projects have regularly generated headlines for years, helping to cement the idea among lawmakers and many voters that CEQA is a major cause of the state’s housing woes. 
Environmental justice groups and their allies have spent years fighting against that argument in the Legislature. Though Prop. 45 does not exempt “essential” projects from environmental review outright — it just shortens and hems in the process — these groups have now lined up to oppose it for much the same reason: They reject the premise that CEQA needs fixing.
But for opponents like Grimes, who supported many recent streamlining bills, the argument that the law is holding up desperately needed residential construction is a year out of date. Last year, the governor signed Assembly Bill 130, a Wicks-authored measure that exempted most infill housing from the CEQA. 
Since becoming law in July 2025, developers have used it to entitle 17,913 units of housing, according to the Office of Land Use and Climate Innovation, a state agency.
“When you look at what’s left to do on urban housing, there are absolutely still barriers,” said Grimes, whose organization applauded last year’s exemption. “CEQA just isn’t one of them.” 
The task of the No on 45 campaign, he said, is to convince enough voters that “we’ve actually solved this problem.”
Are we done here?
Many developers and affordable housing advocates, even those working in urban areas, dispute that CEQA is no longer a major obstacle.
Last year’s exemption does not exempt projects larger than 20 acres, which means supersized urban redevelopment projects are still subject to the old process. 
Prop. 45 also applies shot clocks to other permits issued later in the development process and which regularly slow a project more than environmental review.
And while state laws like last year’s infill carveout may grant certain developers the right to ignore CEQA, there is nothing to stop a deep-pocketed opponent from suing anyway. Putting time limits on those lawsuits could be the difference between a project succeeding and being delayed to death, said Mandolini. 
She points to the planned 130-unit affordable housing project that Eden Housing has been trying to and failing to build in the Bay Area suburb of Livermore since 2018 as an example. In 2021, a nonprofit funded by a handful of well-heeled Livermore residents sued the city, arguing that it hadn’t done enough environmental analysis on a housing development that would be built on a former grocery store parking lot behind a row of downtown restaurants. A lower court ruled that the group’s CEQA arguments were “almost utterly without merit.” An appellate court agreed. The state Supreme Court allowed that ruling to stand.
But by then two years had passed. 
“Every year you lose in litigation is real money for real projects and another year that 130 families don’t get to live in that housing,” said Mandolini. “It’s a great way to kill a project.”
Even an infill project. 
But among some pro-housing supporters of the proposition, the infill versus sprawl debate isn’t much of a debate at all.
“We’re not an urbanist organization,” said Mahdi Manji with the Inner City Law Center, a legal aid provider and housing advocacy group in Los Angeles’ Skid Row. The group supports Prop. 45 and doesn’t mind the concept of more housing far from the city’s core. “To the extent it results in housing that is a little more affordable in Lancaster and Palmdale, a lot of our clients live out in Lancaster and Palmdale.”

name: California
title: Gen Z has very different views on taxes than Boomers, but one generation votes more often
text:
In summary
Surveys show an age gap across the top issues on California’s ballot, including taxing billionaires and requiring IDs to vote. But while Gen Z makes up 30% of the state’s eligible voters, they are far less likely to vote than their counterparts age 55 and older.


Gen Z could be poised to paint California a deeper shade of blue this November — if they turn out to vote.  
An age gap exists across the top issues on California’s ballot this November: youth overwhelmingly favor taxing billionaires and not requiring IDs to vote, while seniors would prefer to block new taxes and impose voter ID requirements. Gen Z voters are also opting for the Democratic gubernatorial candidate – albeit reluctantly. That’s all according to a September report from the Public Policy Institute of California, a nonpartisan research organization.
CalMatters spoke with DemocratIc and Republican voters age 18 to 29 about their attitudes toward California’s gubernatorial race and top election measures. Gen Z support for Xavier Becerra, the Democratic pick for governor, is lukewarm, but that same cohort generally seems eager to vote against his opponent and billionaires this fall.
Nonetheless, young people face an uphill battle when it comes to shifting the balance of power. They make up 30% of the state’s adult population but only 21% of its likely voters; adults age 55 and older, meanwhile, represent 36% of Californian adults but nearly 50% of expected voters, according to the research organization.
”We’re not used to seeing representation that takes into account our needs and our struggles,” said Athena Burciaga, 25, a computer science student at Cal State Monterey Bay. She’s also co-chair of the Democratic Socialists of America’s Central Coast chapter and a candidate for city council in the neighboring town of Marina. “So I do empathize with the sentiment that, like, ‘Why give a damn about politics if politics doesn’t care about me?’”
The wide gap over the billionaire tax
Proposition 40, dubbed “the billionaire tax,” represents one of the sharpest political contrasts between generations in California. 
Young voters are arguably a key bloc for the proposition’s passing since slim majorities of likely voters overall back not just the wealth tax, but also its countermeasures, Proposition 41 and 42. Young adults plan to vote overwhelmingly in favor of the measure with around 76% in support, as opposed to 36% of voters age 55 and over that plan to do the same, according to the Public Policy Institute of California. Middle-aged voters, meanwhile, have been generally supportive, with about 59% backing the measure.
To Stanley Shi, a 19-year-old student at UC Irvine, the reasoning behind that generational split is clear.
“I think it’s pretty obvious that older people tend to own property or tend to be wealthier than Gen Z,” said Shi. “Meanwhile, I own nothing… So I’m obviously going to be in favor of a tax that will never threaten to touch me.”
Federal Reserve data indicates that the share of wealth held by the nation’s oldest residents has roughly doubled in the last 37 years, while that of its youngest has been reduced by half. 
According to Burciaga, Gen Z is well aware of their declining economic prospects. She said that may be why youth political organizations on both sides of the aisle have recently seen explosive growth. 
The Young Democratic Socialists of America has grown by over 50% nationwide in the last year, bringing it to the highest membership levels of its 50-year history. 
Meanwhile, Turning Point USA – among the nation’s dominant conservative youth organizations – has also grown tremendously, particularly since the assassination of its founder, Charlie Kirk, last year.
A voter fills out their ballot for the primary election at Sacramento City College on June 2, 2026. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters
While Turning Point did not respond to recent requests for comment, previous CalMatters reporting found that the organization had seen its presence on California campuses nearly triple as of March, with 78 of the state’s 119 active college chapters founded after Kirk’s death.
“Young people these days are a lot more class conscious overall, wherever they fall on the political spectrum,” said Burciaga. “Our generation is a lot more hip and aware of what’s going on right now than previously because of the material conditions under which we live.”
Young voters lack enthusiasm for Becerra
In the governor’s race, the wide lead enjoyed by Democrat Xavier Becerra over his Republican rival Steve Hilton is no surprise due to California’s party demographics. But perceived instability and disillusionment with the Democratic party has left some young voters lacking confidence in Becerra, interviews show.
A September Politico poll surveying 2,418 registered voters in California, including 174 Gen Z voters, showed that only 34% of those Gen Z voters found Becerra favorable while 39% found him unfavorable.  Yet, a much higher percentage of them, 57%, found Hilton unfavorable.
“I don’t like that he seems to have positioned himself more in the center on some issues,” said Shi about Becerra. “I don’t hate centrism… But I’ve heard that rhetoric for so long and it hasn’t resulted in a lot of the political results that I want.”
Carla Fuentes, 28, president of the Los Angeles County Young Democrats and a graduate of Cal State Northridge, said that the abundance of Democratic candidates running for governor in the primary gave the impression to younger voters that the party lacks cohesion and a clear vision.  
“Becerra is the natural choice, and we’re excited to endorse him and support him in his endeavors, but I do wish that there was a little bit more thought put behind it,” Fuentes said. 
Cole Marting, executive director of the San Diego Young Republicans, believes that Hilton has the solutions necessary to alleviate one of the most pressing issues for young people: affordability.“He’s really the one that’s saying fees and CEQA and energy rules need to be reformed… Maybe that’s some of the reason that a 28-year-old today can’t afford a starter home,” said Marting, 29. “At the end of the day, Hilton is the affordability vote.”In an interview with CalMatters, Becerra made an appeal to young voters by saying he will pursue policies to support first-time homeownership, tackle inflation and make healthcare more affordable.“We have to stop the nonsense, the chaos in Washington D.C., so we can make life more affordable here at home,” Becerra said. “I want you to become a homeowner, I want you to develop wealth because that’s what drives the economy of the state of California.”
CalMatters similarly asked Hilton for his plan for youth, which he said is focused on jobs, affordability, $3-per-gallon gas and housing.“[California] should be the home of energy and innovation and entrepreneurialism and business and jobs,” said Hilton. “We’re going to make California the best place in America to start and run a business by getting rid of the regulations that are now driving businesses to other states like Texas.”
Gen Z voters are largely against Voter ID
Proposition 39, which would require citizens to present government-issued identification to vote, has been championed by its proponents as a “common-sense constitutional amendment.” 
The aim of the proposition has been to target alleged election fraud in California, a suspicion largely held among MAGA voters. Efforts to reign in alleged fraud in the state have yet to produce any evidence — and in one case was deemed unlawful. 
Earlier this week, federal prosecutors charged 28 immigrants with illegally voting or registering to vote in California. California Attorney General Rob Bonta told reporters 28 registered voters out of 23 million is a “drop in the bucket” and shows no widespread fraud.
Only 27% of likely voters age 18 to 29 support Prop. 39, as opposed to 46% of voters age 50 to 64, according to the polling conducted by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies.
Fuentes, who is also a board member of the League of Women Voters, takes this sentiment even further by stating that Prop. 39 is a “huge misstep” that will deter voter participation by disproportionately making it more difficult for certain groups who lack the ability to obtain proper identification. The league asserts that such measures negatively impact voter turnout among people of color, low-income voters, Native American communities, students, and particularly women going through name changes and divorces.
Students wait in line to vote on Proposition 50 at the Price Center at UC San Diego on Nov. 4, 2025. Photo by Ariana Drehsler for CalMatters
“I think the idea, the fundamental concept that voting is kind of sacred and voting should be protected, is right. Do I think that this is the way to accomplish that? No,” Fuentes said. 
Jake Krepps, 21, a junior at San Diego State University and president of the campus chapter of College Republicans, said he has no idea if the proposition will pass, but that he and those he knows support it.  
“I think it’s really important to have a good security net to ensure that people who vote … for representatives that are going to represent the American people, that they are themselves American people,” said Krepps.
As many voter ID proponents mention, Krepps said, “you have an ID to drive, you need an ID to fly somewhere. So I think it’s critically important that you have an ID to vote as well.”
Despite his support for the Republican-backed measure, Krepps feels that the majority of the political landscape is deeply flawed and ineffective. When asked how he felt the current state government was serving young voters, he led with one word: “Terrible.”
“Being a legislator and elected official in California is a two-edged sword. You have to address issues and you have to pass policy to accommodate those issues,” Krepps said. “You also need to prove to voters that the policies and the legislation that you’re passing is actually effective … I don’t think the state of California has successfully fulfilled either [of those] issues.”
Dylan Arreola and Tom Nolan are contributors with the College Journalism Network, a collaboration between CalMatters and student journalists from across California. CalMatters higher education coverage is supported by a grant from the College Futures Foundation.

name: California
title: In prison, wheelchair basketball offers a chance at reinvention
authors: Aala Abdullahi of The Marshall Project, with photos and reporting by Brian Frank for Catchlight and The Marshall Project
text:
Before basketball practice begins, Larry Roach calls the men into a circle.
It’s a Wednesday afternoon, and they are gathering inside the gym at the California Medical Facility, a prison about 55 miles from San Francisco for men, including those with physical disabilities and other serious health needs.  
The men come in a mix, some rolling in in the wheelchairs they use every day, others walking in. They ease, one by one, into the low chairs with slanted wheels built for basketball. Roach waits until everyone, at least 15 players and five coaches, settles. He is incarcerated here, too, and able-bodied, but in this gym, he has another role: the “inside” coach.




First: William Rowe was a well-established basketball player when he lost his leg and thought he would never play basketball again. He found wheelchair basketball in prison and credits the program with giving him the mental fortitude to rehabilitate. Last: Rudy “Jump Shot” Martinez is a long-standing member of the team. Photos by Brian L. Frank for CatchLight/The Marshall Project
The team always checks in before they play. The room takes on a focused energy, the faint rustling of bodies shifting in their seats and the soft scrape of wheels gliding across the room. Each man listens attentively as he awaits his turn to speak.If you want to share news from back home, say how your week went, spit out a motivational line or two, or welcome new players, this is the time to do it. 
On this day in late September, Roach talks about effort: “You can’t teach it. You gotta want it.” Then the men, still in their circle, all turn their fists to the men on either side, linking the whole team. Joe Chambers, a two-time Paralympian and one of the “outside” coaches, recites their slogan: “Everything we do, we do together.”
With that, they disperse — and the gym erupts. Basketballs begin to bounce. A low rumble grows, as hands slap wheels to accelerate red, green, black and silver chairs. They collide. Men tip sideways, falling over, and right themselves in a single beat. Someone calls, “Outlet!” to signal he’s open for a pass after his teammate regains possession of the ball.  
Impulsivity works against you in wheelchair basketball. Someone on defense can block the path you wanted to take to the net and you can’t sidestep around him like you do in stand-up basketball. You have to stop, assess what’s in front of you and find another way. 
Roach has come to think about that lesson, finding another way, as bigger than basketball. “In wheelchair basketball … you got to slow your brain down and say, OK, I can’t do that no more,” he says. “So what’s the next best option?” 
It teaches you to find a way out, he says, especially if you grew up feeling like you didn’t have many choices.
Early morning on the court. The team aims to improve the mental health of incarcerated people by providing a place to exercise, see other people, set goals and work together. Photo by Brian L. Frank for CatchLight/The Marshall Project
The program’s core philosophy is painted on the wall of the prison gym. Physical recreation is paired with the idea of re-creation of character. Photo by Brian L. Frank for CatchLight/The Marshall Project
The message is painted in black on the gym wall: “RE CREATION.”
The space is no accident. Jeremiah Holland, creator of the wheelchair basketball program and the facility’s recreation supervisor until about a month ago, believes recreation can be more than movement, that it can be re-creation, an opportunity to practice being a different person.  
It all starts with imagination, he says. Inside prison, where people are cut off from the outside world and expected to follow strict rules and play certain roles, “imagination contracts.”
“People are always larger than the role that was assigned to them,” he says. 
Sports can give people a chance to work on their character and build relationships in a “lonely, isolated” prison, Holland says. You learn something about yourself in how you react to frustration and losing a game — both teaching moments that push players to consider how they would handle similar situations outside of the gym. 
Over time, you learn to respond differently in your relationships with others and confront the painful parts of yourself, Holland says. This is why sports programs can change people for the better and “help people figure out how to look at the most difficult things in their life,” he says. 



First: Coach Jeremiah Holland has spearheaded a character-first approach to sports at California Medical Facility. Team members are selected based on their willingness to be a positive and supportive teammate, instead of solely on athletic ability. Last: Coaches say having able-bodied and disabled men play together creates a community that doesn’t exist anywhere else in the prison. Photo by Brian L. Frank for CatchLight/The Marshall Project
California is leaning into the rehabilitative potential of sports. On Sept. 30, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed the Second Chance Sports Act, directing the state’s prison system to come up with a plan to expand sports programming. Those who participate in organized sports will reportedly be able to earn credits that can lead to early release. 
Holland has spent years weathering storms, like changes in prison leadership and a pandemic, to build recreation programs that embody this philosophy. Among them is this basketball team unlike most found in U.S. prisons, where able-bodied men and men with physical disabilities train for and play wheelchair basketball alongside one another.

A letter from an incarcerated player to Coach Holland explained that he couldn’t attend practice because he had a heart attack. Photo by Brian L. Frank for CatchLight/The Marshall Project

He credits the community he built around the program as the reason it exists and has lasted. Holland brought in coaches and experts from the outside, gave incarcerated men, like Roach, increasing responsibility over the programs they joined, and fought hard to keep the prison administration invested. 
“Community engagement is really what allowed disability sport to happen,” he says.
Leaving behind gang life
When Roach was a boy decades ago in south Sacramento, he played sports with his friend Landon Jackson. Gangs eventually redrew the lines in their neighborhood, and with that, their relationship.
In their late teens, Roach remembers shooting at him.
Their paths did not cross again for many years, until one day, they saw each other coming down opposite sides of a hallway. Men who knew their history watched them, concerned. 
They pulled each other into a hug. “That was the first time I got to hug him in 23 years,” Jackson says. “It’s the dude I played with when we were in middle school and elementary school. Kids. Innocence…”
Larry Roach, the able-bodied “inside coach” who runs the team when the “outside” coaches aren’t there, often spends his extra time mentoring and coaching players. Roach felt called to participate because he felt that the program was a place where incarcerated players who felt uncomfortable with asking for help could feel supported by their peers to do so. Roach was released from California Medical Facility in mid-October 2026. Photo by Brian L. Frank for CatchLight/The Marshall Project
Roach had already begun trying to put that old life behind him. His change of heart had come during visitation one day, when his 5-year-old daughter asked when he was going to leave the gang alone. Bit by bit, he took action; he renewed his faith in God, stopped using his gang name, took a victims’ impact class and trained to counsel other men. 
It was this version of Roach who hugged Jackson and apologized. 
Jackson, by then, had also pulled himself out of the old life. He had become deeply embedded in the wheelchair basketball program, which launched publicly in late 2022. Able-bodied himself, he had joined because friends who used wheelchairs needed help, people to push them through the yard or to get them through a workout. 
“When you start getting in the wheelchair, you see what you can’t do no more,” he says. “It makes you honor people in a different way.” 

Joe Chambers is an American wheelchair basketball star, a two-time Paralympian, and a cancer survivor who coaches the team at the California Medical Facility. Photo by Brian L. Frank for CatchLight/The Marshall Project










First: Chambers plays for the Los Angeles Clippers Chairmen, alongside Lavonte McDowell, who he used to coach on the CMF wheelchair basketball team. He is also a former Team USA Paralympian bronze medalist, but continues to take practice at CMF. Last: Coach Mieko Chambers, the head coach, helped Coach Holland start the program at CMF. She is also the head coach of the Los Angeles Clippers Chairmen, a National Wheelchair Basketball Association team. Both her husband, Joe Chambers, and Lavonte McDowell, play for the Chairmen. Mieko Chambers also won a gold medal as an assistant coach for Team USA’s women’s U25 wheelchair team in 2019. Photos by Brian L. Frank for CatchLight/The Marshall Project

This kind of growth is what the coaches had in mind when they let able-bodied players join the program, says Mieko Chambers, the team’s head coach, and the head coach of the Los Angeles Clippers Chairmen, a National Wheelchair Basketball Association team. “All of a sudden, there’s this newfound respect for somebody that is looked to be weak or hurt.”
At some point, the gym stopped being just a gym to Jackson. The program put him in a space of serving others, he says, which made him visible to people who could see the change he’d gone through. Holland put Jackson’s name up for resentencing, and the warden wrote the judge a letter of support that played a role in Jackson’s release.
In 2024, Jackson walked out of California Medical Facility.
How he and other leaders ran things stuck with the team. “Prison tells you don’t address it if it’s not violence,” Jackson says. “This gym told you address it so it doesn’t get violent.” Which sometimes meant calling a guy out, face-to-face, when he crossed a line.
Once, Roach recalls, a player cursed at a volunteer. The men stopped practice, formed a circle and told him the behavior was unacceptable. They sent the player away for the day to cool off.  
“We don’t just want to single somebody out,” Roach says. “We’re gonna say what behaviors we won’t tolerate, and then go from there.” 
Other times it meant noticing when someone was struggling. At another practice, Steven Davis, an outgoing co-captain known as “Scooby Doo,” recalls walking in and sitting down. Normally, he would laugh, joke with others, get into his chair and get ready to play. The team noticed something was off and asked him what was on his mind. Davis had recently reconnected with his daughter, and he was afraid of losing her again.
The coaches hugged him. “We got you in here … We love you,” Joe Chambers told him. “We don’t want to see you like this.”
Davis still remembers it. “For them to hug me and tell me that they see the good in me and I’m a good person, it made me go harder in wheelchair basketball,” he says. “… It made me want to come in here and be around these guys who actually show that they care.”
‘I like just being physical’
Quentin Murphy moves through the traffic of chairs like a man playing chess, which is how Joe Chambers teaches the game: Think two and three moves ahead. Four years in the sport and over a decade in a wheelchair, Murphy is a co-captain alongside Davis, and considered one of the strongest players, the Michael Jordan of the team. 
Basketball had always been part of his life. But he was run over by a truck during the crime that landed him in prison, he says, and had his leg amputated while in custody. The following years were dark. “There was those times where I had suicidal thoughts,” Murphy says. 

Quentin “Q” Murphy at early morning practice on the yard. He lost his leg right before he arrived at prison. He is co-captain of the team, alongside Steven Davis. Photo by Brian L. Frank for CatchLight/The Marshall Project

Murphy returns to his housing unit after an early morning practice and prepares for his day. Photo by Brian L. Frank for CatchLight/The Marshall Project



First: He practices with his team in the prison gymnasium. Last: Basketball had always been a part of his life, but he had to learn the sport again through a different body. Photos by Brian L. Frank for CatchLight/The Marshall Project 
The recreation options available to a man in a wheelchair were bingo, shuffleboard, resistance bands, chair yoga. “Those kinds of sports to someone like me is some boring stuff,” he says. “I’m really competitive and I like just being physical.” Disabled men who wanted competition didn’t have much to do, he says. 
Murphy had to learn basketball again in a different version of his body. Even though the instincts were similar, the mechanics were not. You have to generate speed using your arms, and make turns while protecting your momentum. You need to coast into your shots to get the ball up to a rim that is still 10 feet high. 
Now Murphy is one of the players others watch. His sisters, daughters and family friends know what he’s up to now and are proud of him, he says. When he comes into the gym, he doesn’t think about anything else. “It’s just a place of peace,” he says. 
Wheelchair basketball also gave him a new way to mull over his future. A decades-long sentence has made a future difficult for him to imagine. But he considers all of the programs he’s done while in prison, and looks to a player who left the gym and played professionally on the outside as a testament to what’s possible for him.
‘Living proof’
That player is Lavonte McDowell, whom the coaches consider the team’s success story. 
In many ways, McDowell’s story unfolded the same way as Murphy’s. He was shot in the commission of his crime, became a paraplegic, went straight from the hospital room to a jail cell, and learned everything about his disability on his own.  
He joined the team as it was finding its footing. It wasn’t too long before coaches were telling him men were starting to look at him as a leader, but McDowell didn’t see it right away. He just knew that he wanted to change and couldn’t do it alone. 
“I felt like I needed people to hold me accountable for my own actions because I couldn’t help myself or hold myself accountable,” he says. 
Quentin “Q” Murphy’s prosthetic leg rests in his everyday wheelchair while he is at practice in his sports wheelchair. He had to navigate prison life for the first time while newly being an amputee.  He found wheelchair basketball to be a solace. Photo by Brian L. Frank for CatchLight/The Marshall Project
His name was the first thing to go. Around the prison, men knew him by a street name from his gang days: “Everybody in the prison knew me by Chaos,” he says. About two months after joining the team, he stopped answering to it. “This is a false belief. This is not even my name,” he says. From then on, he told people his name was Lavonte.
Fast-forward to the fall of 2024: McDowell and Joe Chambers remember the team gathered in a circle. Joe Chambers, who was already playing for the Los Angeles Clippers Chairmen, had some news to share. The Chairmen wanted McDowell to come play for them. McDowell cried tears of joy. 
He was released early November 2024 and has since played for the team during the 2025-26 season, traveling to games in states he had never been to.
Today, he works with Project Rebound, an organization that helps connect formerly incarcerated people with higher education. “I just wanted to be of service,” he says. “I took from so many people. Did so much destruction in people’s lives, and in my own life and my family’s life… I was tired of being evil and stupid.”
As for the coaches, they never cut him loose. They stayed in touch, met his family, and when he needed a chair of his own, they found pieces of old chairs, built one and sent it to him. 
“It’s wonderful to have somebody to actually give you chances. That’s all individuals want in prison,” he says. “… I feel that this program can give people that. I’m living proof.” 
No guarantee coaches can get inside
Partway through last month’s practice, Holland appears near the door holding a stack of identification cards. “Here’s all the IDs,” he tells the players. “I’m putting them up on that door. If you go to chow, grab your ID and meet me at the door.” 
A player looks toward the door. “Hey, coach, what if they don’t want to let us back in?” he asks. 
“They’re gonna let you back in,” Holland responds.
It’s a harmless question about dinner, but it’s also a reminder of the controlled prison environment they’re in. Even for the volunteer coaches, getting through the gate is not always guaranteed. Some drive nearly an hour one way and have at times been turned away, because searches have taken over the gym, lockdowns have wiped out programming for the day or staffing decisions have canceled practice, the coaches say. 







First: Two men reach up high for the basketball during a game at practice. Second: A man speeds by on a wheelchair, the room blurring around him. Third: The men check in before they play, sharing news from back home and welcoming new players. Last: Coach Mieko Chambers counsels players during a practice at the prison gymnasium. Photos by Brian L. Frank for CatchLight/The Marshall Project
Holland coaches Rudy “Jump Shot” Martinez during the early hours of the morning. Photo by Brian L. Frank for CatchLight/The Marshall Project
The state Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation says that it tries to minimize disruptions to programs, but staffing, training and emergencies have sometimes required temporary changes.
Through the uncertainty and the many hours of driving and labor, including fixing the chairs, the coaches still show up, even on days when they or the players can’t get into the gym. 
“I don’t want them to think we’ve given up on it,” Joe Chambers says. 
So far, the team has played only a handful of games against outside teams. Joe Chambers has brought friends in, for example, and a Berkeley-based organization that has taught adaptive sports for decades has also played against them, Holland says. 
The coaches are hopeful for a future where games with outside teams happen more consistently. In their biggest dream for the program, they imagine registering the team with the National Wheelchair Basketball Association, and bringing outside teams into the facility to play enough sanctioned games to ultimately build a record and earn a national ranking. 
If all of those pieces fall into place, there still is one more obstacle: The team can’t travel. So opponents would have to come to them and go through security, just like any other visitor at the facility. 
‘A part of my family now’
In mid-October, after spending more than two decades behind bars, Roach walked out of the prison, uncertain but excited about his future. His family threw a homecoming party for him, and all of the wheelchair basketball program’s coaches showed up. “They’re a part of my family now,” he says.
He’s also reconnected with Jackson and McDowell. Roach knew how much wheelchair basketball meant to him inside prison, but he’s appreciative of the support network it is giving him in the free world. “When you feel isolated and alone, and you get into a program like that where it’s love and it’s support,” he says, “like, yo, my circle expanded.” 
As he adjusts to his new life, he gets a chance to test the emotional regulation and character work he picked up through the program. Getting out and being around so many people so quickly, for example, has called for breathwork. “Breathe, it’s OK,” he tells himself. And having lived for so many years with so few choices in prison, the pressure to spend money on things you don’t need once you’re out is really high, Roach says. Even with small decisions, “not being impulsive” can benefit you, he says, instead of spending money and realizing later that you needed it for something more important. 
He’s approaching his future in the same way: Roach’s already been offered a job at a transitional home, he says, but he doesn’t want to rush into anything. He’s considering the options to make the best choice. 
But one thing he knows for sure is that he wants to stay connected to the wheelchair basketball team. “Whatever role they need me in,” he says. The process for getting approved to go back in, and how long that’ll take, is unclear to him.  
Maybe one day, Roach will be back at the gym, gathering the men into a circle again. But this time, he’ll be an “outside” coach. 
The players reach upward for the basketball during a scrimmage practice. Photo by Brian L. Frank for CatchLight/The Marshall Project
Coach Holland and the players gather in a circle before and after every game to support each other and talk about challenges they are facing. Photo by Brian L. Frank for CatchLight/The Marshall Project
Coaches Jeremiah Holland and Darwin Walters head home for the day after staying late at a practice. “People don’t care how much you know until they know how much you care.” He tries to remind people of their potential. “People are always larger than the role that was assigned to them,” Holland says. Photo by Brian L. Frank for CatchLight/The Marshall Project

name: California
title: Who’s spending money on the California insurance commissioner race
text:
In summary
Jane Kim and Ben Allen have promised not to take insurance money, but an outside PAC supporting Allen has received industry donations.


Both Democratic candidates for insurance commissioner have promised not to take campaign donations from the industry that one of them will soon be regulating. Despite that, insurance money has seeped in. 
Political action committees that operate separately from the official campaigns have poured more than $6 million into the race, including what was spent on the June primary. That’s a record high for the contest for this position, which is responsible for regulating the state’s property and casualty insurance market. 



These PACs have spent about $3.2 million to support state Sen. Ben Allen, and some of their funders include companies from the insurance industry. Those same groups have spent more than $1.5 million to oppose his opponent, Jane Kim.
In the past week, bail bonds insurers made three donations of $10,000 each to a committee supporting Allen, campaign finance records show. Another entity that appears to be connected to the bail bonds industry donated $9,500. And a health insurance PAC donated $48,000 to the same committee, bringing the number of insurance-related donations to five as of Friday.
“I didn’t ask for this and don’t welcome it,” Allen told CalMatters.
Outside groups called super PACs can spend an unlimited amount of money to push their point of view through “independent expenditures,” as long as they do not coordinate with the candidate’s campaign, the result of a Supreme Court decision known as Citizens United.
That also means that the candidates cannot return the money like they can if they receive a contribution directly to their campaign. With Kim and Allen questioning the source of donations to the super PACs that have spent money in the race, CalMatters looked at who has donated to the committees that have supported or opposed each candidate.

Other companies that have donated to groups spending to support Allen include investor-owned utilities such as Southern California Edison and Pacific Gas & Electric.
Allen said his vow not to take money directly from the insurance, utility and fossil fuel industries still stands, but his opponent is raising an alarm. 
“The contributions that come in are a reflection of what the (insurance) industry believes is the best outcome for them,” said Kim, the former San Francisco supervisor. “These contributions are an investment in him and themselves, not for consumers.”
Thomas Holyoke, a political science professor at California State University, Fresno, agrees. He said donors will expect some kind of access. 
“This is what creates cynicism in our politics today,” Holyoke said, referring to the campaign finance system. “This is why people don’t trust elected officials. That’s bad for democracy.”
Early on in his campaign for commissioner, Allen returned some direct insurance industry donations that he said were mistakenly transferred from an old campaign account into his account for this race. During a debate between the two candidates this month, Allen said even though he has taken insurance industry money in the past, he has a track record of consumer advocacy and of holding industries accountable.
“I have taken on the insurance industry directly,” Allen said at the debate. “I’ve run bills against them and won, gotten them just signed into law.” One of those laws boosts the commissioner’s ability to make insurers fix problems the Insurance Department finds after an investigation.
Allen also pushed back against a failed effort to reduce utility industry liability for wildfires they cause; he opposed an effort to take away insurance companies’ right to recoup their costs from utilities, which could affect Californians’ insurance costs.
Kim said at the debate that for this race, she has not taken insurance industry money directly, nor has she accepted corporate PAC donations, which she called an “important distinction” between her and Allen. 
Kim’s campaign website has a section that details insurance-related donations to both candidates throughout their careers; she said at the debate that donations she received from individuals who work in the insurance industry are different from Allen receiving money from insurance companies. She said she has not taken checks from insurance carriers or their PACs.
Jamie Court is president of Consumer Watchdog, the advocacy group whose founder wrote Proposition 103, which voters approved in 1988 and governs insurance law in California. The law made the commissioner position an elected one.
Court, who opposes Kim’s plan for public disaster insurance but says his organization is “publicly agnostic” on the race, said “insurance companies should not be allowed to influence this race, and they haven’t yet, as far as I know.”
He called the bail bond industry money donated to the super PAC supporting Allen a small amount that he described as coming from a “rogue element” because he said Big Insurance has largely stayed out of this race.
“A few bail bonds donations shouldn’t convince anyone,” Court said. “I honestly think they’ll both be impartial and listen to reason.”
Meanwhile, the outside spending to support Kim totals more than $958,000, much of it from the left-wing California Working Families Party. Kim led the organization until earlier this year, when she decided to run for commissioner.
“This isn’t some independent group that happens to like her,” said Joe Arellano, spokesperson for Allen’s campaign. “It’s her own political operation spending on her behalf.”
Kim’s campaign rejected any insinuation of illegal coordination.
“(Working Families Party) has a strict firewall between their independent expenditure and coordinated activities,” said Catie Stewart, spokesperson for Kim’s campaign. “We have no idea who makes their (independent expenditure) spending decisions, because we don’t talk to anyone on that side of that firewall.” 
Donations to the party’s PAC come mostly from individual donors and labor groups. Its biggest donors include Patty Quillin, wife of Netflix co-founder Reed Hastings; philanthropists Wayne Jordan and Quinn Delaney, who own a real estate development firm; and PACs for the National Union of Healthcare Workers and United Domestic Workers of America.
Donations to the outside PACs spending money on Allen’s campaign or against Kim’s campaign also include Google co-founder Sergey Brin; Facebook parent company Meta; a California Business Roundtable PAC; and crypto billionaire Chris Larsen, who gave to three different committees for a total of about $3.5 million, making him the single largest individual outside contributor in this race. These same tech and business donors are spending big on other races in the state, some of which also pit Democrat vs. Democrat. 
Both candidates are endorsed by unions, and some of their top direct donors are labor groups. Allen’s donors include the California State Council of Laborers, a lobbying group for public service workers, and the Southern California District Council of Laborers, an advocacy group of a dozen unions. Kim’s include the California Nurses Association, the California School Employees Association and the California Teachers Association. 
Other top direct donors to Allen’s campaign include the California Democratic Party, which endorsed him. The California Labor Federation endorsed Kim and is one of her top direct donors.

name: California
title: New reforms give California’s next governor a once-in-a-generation chance to reshape education
text:
Guest Commentary written by

Heather Hough
Heather Hough is an independent consultant specializing in education policy, governance and system improvement.


California voters are choosing who will lead the state’s public education system. But the offices they’re voting on — the next governor and the state superintendent of public instruction — aren’t quite what they used to be. A recent change in state law means each will have different responsibilities than their predecessors.
For more than a century, responsibility for California’s education system has been divided between these two elected leaders, each with significant authority, but neither fully in charge.
The governor, working with the State Board of Education and Legislature, sets policy and funding for education. The elected state superintendent has been responsible for running the California Department of Education and implementing state policy. Over time, that division of responsibility has made it difficult to establish shared priorities and determine who ultimately is accountable for results.
It has contributed to an increasingly fragmented system that educators often say is a source of burden rather than support. Teachers and school administrators spend enormous amounts of energy navigating competing initiatives, conflicting mandates, siloed funding streams and duplicative reporting requirements. These bureaucratic demands take time and attention away from the critical work of teaching and learning. 
Students ultimately pay the price. Despite years of substantial investment and ambitious reforms, California’s student achievement rates remain low, with troubling gaps between different demographic groups.
Last year, my colleagues and I published a report last year calling for fundamental change in how California governs public education. Our central recommendation was straightforward: California should align the responsibility for setting and implementing policy in public education, with clearer accountability for results.
In July, California lawmakers took an important step in that direction. Under Assembly Bill 181, the governor will appoint a new education commissioner, who will run the California Department of Education, a responsibility historically held by the elected state superintendent.
Importantly, the first commissioner will be charged with improving the education department and developing a plan to make the broader education system more coordinated, responsive and effective.
For voters, this changes the significance of the governor’s race. The governor will now appoint the person responsible for carrying out state education policy and will have the authority to replace that person if the system falls short. Instead of the responsibility being divided between two independently elected leaders, there will be a clearer line of accountability from the Department of Education to the governor — and ultimately to the voters. 
The state superintendent’s job is changing, too. Beginning in January, the superintendent will no longer run the Department of Education. Instead he or she will focus on representing the public’s interests and will independently assess how well the system serves students and families. This creates an important opportunity for voters — an independent voice that can serve as a counterbalance to the clearer lines of authority and accountability being established under the governor. 
This change represents an important step forward. It addresses a longstanding structural barrier to effective leadership. 
But changing who is in charge is only the beginning. The critics are right: A new organizational chart will not, by itself, improve teaching and learning. That work happens in classrooms. 
But the state can make it easier — or harder — for educators to succeed. 
In my work with educational leaders, I hear a consistent message: California needs clear goals for student success, policies and resources aligned around those goals, fewer unnecessary requirements and a coordinated approach to helping schools improve. 
Achieving that vision will require shifting the state’s role from its current focus on requirements and compliance toward a shared responsibility for improving student outcomes.
That means coordinating efforts across agencies and levels of government, identifying and removing barriers to improvement and ensuring that educators and administrators have the guidance, resources and support they need.
None of this will be easy. The commissioner and state superintendent will enter newly defined roles with important questions about how they will work together and how the broader system should be organized.
Change is especially difficult when it requires eliminating familiar programs, redistributing authority or asking institutions to work differently.
Still, California has a once-in-a-generation opportunity to fundamentally change how the state supports local public schools. Lasting improvement will require leaders, educators, families, and communities to confront difficult tradeoffs and put students’ needs ahead of preserving the status quo.

name: Nevada Current
title: Clark County home price drop among biggest in nation, report says
text:
(Photo: Hugh Jackson/Nevada Current)Home values in Clark County dropped by 5% in the third quarter of 2026, tying with Miami-Dade for the fourth biggest decline among major metropolitan areas, according to a new report from ATTOM, a national real estate data analyst.
Middlesex County, MA, where sales prices declined 11%, led the drop among major metro areas. Orange County, FL (down 10%) was second, followed by Duval County, FL (down 8%). 
The median price of a home in Clark County was $428,000 in the third quarter, down from $440,000 in the second quarter and from $450,000 a year ago.
In Washoe County, the median price of a home in the third quarter was $590,500, up from $588,750 in the previous quarter, and up from $550,000 a year ago. 
Average annual incomes at both ends of the state – $73,970 in Washoe and $67,678 in Clark County – are woefully insufficient to support purchasing a median priced home, according to ATTOM’s affordability analysis.
