“Affordability remained a challenge in the third quarter, even as some of the underlying factors moved in a favorable direction,” Rob Barber, CEO of ATTOM, said in a news release. “Home prices declined nationally and wage growth outpaced price growth in many counties, but those gains were not enough to meaningfully improve affordability across much of the country.”
The report calculated affordability for average wage earners by determining the amount of income needed for home ownership on median priced homes, assuming a 20% down payment. 
Of the 583 counties included in the analysis, major monthly home expenses exceeded the typical resident’s wages in 80% of the counties, ATTOM reported.
The national median home price in a metro area in the third quarter was $368,000 – down 1% from the second quarter and 2% from the same time last year. Interest rates, however, are “approaching highs last seen in 2023 and the consumer price index, a measure of inflation, rose throughout the third quarter,” ATTOM reports.
Owning the median priced home in the U.S. would require an annual wage of $90,191 – based on a  $73,600 down payment, a $294,400 loan, and monthly mortgage, property tax, and insurance payments not exceeding 28% of income, which is the accepted industry standard. 
The average national wage is $79,534, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, far less than the income needed to buy the median priced U.S. home.
Neither Clark County’s average wage of $67,678 nor Washoe County’s average wage of $73,970, would support buying median-priced homes in Nevada’s respective population centers. 
Home prices in Clark County increased more than 40% between 2020 and 2025, says Las Vegas real estate agent Geoff Lavell. “That’s not sustainable because income didn’t go up 40%. We have a disconnect.”
Lavell blames what he calls “the weird mobility of jobs” brought on initially by the pandemic, that allowed people “working in Cupertino or San Francisco or Marin County, and earning a ridiculous income, to live in Las Vegas, where they would pay any price because it was five times less expensive and a home twice the size. They threw our market out of whack, and now we’re paying the price.” 
Real estate agent Diane Varney, who specializes in luxury homes, agrees. Young tech millionaires, she says, are keeping the high-end market rocking. Varney adds she’s “had a great year. But within these last few weeks, pretty much since the last rate increase and rumblings of another one, it seems like the pause button just got hit.” 
“Sales are down, closings are down, and price reductions are up,” Varney said, noting on Friday, according to the Multiple Listing Services (MLS), 161 homes went on the market,  210 homes for sale decreased their prices, and 83 homes sold. 
Las Vegas Realtors reports more than 10,000 homes are for sale, a level unseen since 2014 following the Great Recession. 
Now is not the time to put a home on the market to test its value, says Lavell. “Buyers aren’t going for it. They want to know why the same house is listed at $45,000 more.” 
Owning a home remains a priority for a lot of would-be buyers, he says, adding a fall in interest rates would result in “bedlam. If interest rates went to 5%, for example, which I highly doubt, it would be everybody and their cousin out there trying to buy a house.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: What to know about CT Mirror’s investigation into prison debt
text:
The Connecticut Mirror published an investigation last month into the state’s practice of assessing a daily fee for every day a person spends in prison and then collecting on that debt in certain situations — sometimes over a decade after the person’s release.
Connecticut charges one of the highest per-day rates in the country; that rate was $347 per day for 2022-23. 
State law allows officials to charge formerly or currently incarcerated people for the cost of their room and board when they receive or give an inheritance, in certain lawsuit settlements or if they win the lottery.
This practice, which has its roots in a 1995 law, has led some people to lose their homes or opportunities at further education or starting a business. It also makes it hard for people to build intergenerational wealth. Hundreds of people every year receive these bills, and most didn’t know they owed money.
After CT Mirror’s story published, some lawmakers called for changes or a repeal to this law. Here’s what you need to know about prison debt.
How is the debt collected and what happens to the money?
The Connecticut Comptroller’s Office works with the Department of Correction to calculate the total cost of running the prison system, then divides that cost up between the people who were incarcerated on a given day to determine the per-diem cost.
The Department of Administrative Services then monitors probate court filings to see whether people involved in inheritance cases have been to prison. If they have, the state sends its bill in the form of a lien on the inheritance.
Changes to the law in recent years have put limits on what the state can collect — it has to leave people with at least $50,000 — and prohibit collection on lawsuit cases unless the plaintiff was convicted of certain murder or sexual assault charges.
The money is taken directly out of the inheritance. In some cases, this requires selling an inherited home or property. That money then goes into the state’s General Fund. The state collects an average of $3.3 million per year from prison debt.
What does the state say about this?
The Department of Administrative Services says it is following the direction of the Department of Correction and has no ability to waive or adjust debts. In turn, the Department of Correction said collecting the money was the job of the Department of Administrative Services.
Lawmakers who were initially part of passing the legislation didn’t return CT Mirror’s requests for comment or declined to answer questions.
What do other states do?
Other states charge much less than Connecticut, and most don’t collect the full cost of incarceration. Many take money from inmates’ paychecks while they are incarcerated and don’t collect at all after they are released.
Some states have begun to repeal these laws, saying it’s not practical to collect money and that it makes it harder for people to reintegrate into society after their prison stay if they have this debt.
What are lawmakers planning to do?
It’s not yet clear, although both Democrats and Republicans said they want to take another look at the law in the 2027 legislative session, which begins in January. Some said they want to repeal the law entirely, a proposal that was considered in 2022 but failed to move forward.
Others would rather find ways to ensure people don’t lose their homes or make it easier for people to argue for a waiver due to their financial status. Gov. Ned Lamont has said he’d support changes to the law, but still wants to charge wealthy people convicted of crimes for their prison stays.
“Maybe if it’s Gordon Gekko or some Wall Street titan, yeah, I think they should contribute to the cost of their incarceration. But I think for the other 90% of people, I want to make sure when they’ve served their time, they get back out, they’re not stuck with an incredible burden that is impossible for them to pay off,” Lamont said.
CT Mirror reporter Andrew Brown contributed to this story.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Low-income advocates ask UTA to pause its fare increase proposal
text:
Passengers board and disembark a UTA FrontRunner train in Salt Lake City on Thursday, April 18, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)As the Utah Transit Authority proposes a 20% fare increase, a low-income advocacy group is asking the agency to take a step back and consider putting more resources toward increasing enrollment of available discount passes before hiking fares.
The Crossroads Urban Center sent a letter to UTA last week as part of the public comment period assigned for the authority’s proposed budget, which includes an increase to the base fare for buses and TRAX from $2.50 to $3. If approved, this would be the first fare increase in the services in 13 years. 
However, the increase would come at “a really bad time,” said Bill Tibbitts, deputy executive director at Crossroads Urban Center. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
He pointed to the rising cost of living, which has led close to half of Americans to struggle to pay for basic needs.
“I would feel better about a price increase if I knew that the people who are going to be hurt by it the most were all enrolled in the discount pass program. I am not confident that that’s the case,” Tibbitts said. “And so I think that they should pause, put some effort into making their discounted pass programs work. And then, if that doesn’t increase revenue in ways enough to make a fair increase not necessary, then then they can look at increasing prices.”
UTA proposes an increase to a $3 base fare. But first, it wants to hear from Utahns

UTA has a reduced fare program for people with disabilities, seniors, youth and low-income households, which allows some to pay $1 for local trips and $2 for premium services, like FrontRunner or express and ski buses. 
UTA hasn’t published how many riders use the program. However, nationally, discounted fare programs struggle to attract participants, with fewer than one in three eligible people enrolling, according to the Urban Institute, a think tank.
In Salt Lake City, for example, the Hive Pass, which allowed access to Utah Transit Authority buses, TRAX and other routes for $42 a month, was terminated in the last city budget cycle. The program was available to all Salt Lake City residents regardless of income, but on average it only had 443 users per month.  
UTA’s programs are great, Tibbitts said, especially with the established caps, which could limit riders’ spending to $8 a week. But not many people know about them. 
Crossroads Urban Center gives out one-day UTA passes at its Downtown Salt Lake City food pantry, but there’s a “general lack of awareness” on the programs, Tibbitts said. 
Two Salt Lake City transportation programs didn’t survive budget cuts — here are the updates

“There’s room for real growth,” he said. “I just know that we are seeing over 12,000 people per month in our food pantries. We give away 50 day passes for UTA service in our downtown pantry every Monday through Friday, and they’re always gone within an hour or two.”
With people struggling to afford the cost of living, including high gas prices, the need for public transportation is growing. 
“For low-income people, public transportation can be such a big part of them having healthy and productive lives,” Tibbits said. “If you’re having trouble paying to ride the bus, you’re not going to take an Uber instead. But you could stay home. You could just not go to something.”
UTA officials hadn’t reviewed the letter when they were asked for comment last week. However, Gavin Gustafson, public information officer at the authority, told Utah News Dispatch on Friday that proposals aren’t final and that all received comments will be considered before any final decisions are made. 
“We’re still in the evaluation process at this point,” he said.
The authority will hold a public open house on Monday at 5:30 p.m. at UTA’s headquarters (669 W. 200 South, Salt Lake City). The meeting will also be livestreamed on UTA’s website. Those who wish to participate in the public comment period online must register in advance.

name: Washington State Standard
title: These measures on WA ballots could shake up local government
text:
Voters in a handful of counties and cities are considering significant changes to the charter of their respective local government. Among the measures are ones concerning term limits, taxes, making elected offices nonpartisan and converting the sheriff's position from elected to appointed. (Photo by Donna Gordon Blankinship/Washington State Standard)Voters may evict the sheriff from office in Pierce County, make Snohomish County Council seats nonpartisan and bar residents from serving on the Everett City Council and in the Legislature, even though the Washington state Constitution allows it.
These are among the slew of significant and controversial changes for local governments to be decided Nov. 3 that are receiving far less attention than contests for state Supreme Court seats and statewide initiatives.
The local measures are the handiwork of citizen commissions in the handful of Washington cities and counties governed by a charter. Commissioners, who are elected, have wide latitude to suggest alterations to the manner and structure of the respective local government.
In line with the state constitution, seven counties and 10 cities have adopted charters that undergo review once-a-decade by a citizen commission. Proposed changes require voter approval.
Here are a few charter amendments voters will decide.
Law and order
Keith Swank’s future as sheriff of Pierce County in western Washington is in the hands of an electorate that put him in office two years ago.
Charter Amendment 53 would make the sheriff an appointed position rather than an elected one. That person would be chosen by the county executive and confirmed by the County Council. If the measure passes, Swank, who was narrowly elected in 2024 to a four-year term, would be out of office on Jan. 1, 2027. King County is the only county with an appointed sheriff.
Swank could be appointed and confirmed. But that’s unlikely as he has publicly butted heads with other elected Pierce County leaders including County Executive Ryan Mello. 
He’s incited anger among some in the community for his controversial social media posts, desire to work more closely with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement on deportation efforts than a state law allows, and his views on an array of social issues, including support for a statewide initiative to bar transgender girls from playing girls sports.
A related measure, Charter Amendment 54, would create a new Public Safety Ombuds Office to provide independent oversight of the sheriff and sheriff’s department.
New ground rules for electeds
In Snohomish County, the state’s third most populous, there is a push to ditch political party labels for elected county offices and the people running to serve in them.
Under Proposition 3, “all candidates for a Snohomish County elected office appear on the ballot without a political party designation and that all elected county offices be non-partisan offices.”
If approved, it would be phased in starting next year with the two council seats and the county executive’s position up for election. It would apply for the other three council seats when they are on the ballot in 2029.
Several Snohomish County offices are already nonpartisan. These include treasurer, auditor, assessor, sheriff and clerk.
This measure split the commission along party lines with Republicans using their majority to advance it over the objections of Democratic members. 
With the county’s Democrat-leaning electorate, Republicans have struggled to win countywide offices. They hold two of the seats on the County Council. Some Democrats view the shedding of party identification as a not-so-veiled attempt to boost Republicans’ chances to win the county executive contest next year. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Meanwhile, in Everett, the largest city in Snohomish County, the charter review commission put Proposition 1 on the ballot. If passed, it would prohibit mayors and city council members from simultaneously holding “any other elected public office at any level of government.”
No county, state or federal office, nor school district, fire district, port district, public utility district or an office of another city or town. The only exception is a precinct committee officer.
A mayor or council member could run for another office, like a state legislative seat. If they win, they would be deemed to have vacated their city post once they are sworn in to the new gig.
State Rep. Mary Fosse, D-Everett, served on the City Council, when she won her seat in the House in 2022. She did not seek reelection last year.
Several state lawmakers now hold local offices, including state Reps. Sam Low, R-Lake Stevens, and Strom Peterson, D-Edmonds who are members of the Snohomish County Council.
In southwest Washington, Charter Amendment 19 would limit Clark County council members to three terms in office. However, once they sit out a full term, they can seek to return to office.
“The policy intent is to balance two competing public interests: the value of accumulated experience in elected office and the benefit of periodic turnover that introduces new perspectives and maintains broader access to public service opportunities,” reads the explanation of the measure. “The inclusion of a one-term break preserves the ability of experienced individuals to return to service while preventing uninterrupted long-term incumbency.”
In Clallam County, the behavior of elected officials is the subject of Charter Amendment 2. If approved, it would establish a three-person board to review complaints of alleged violations of the county’s code of ethics by elected county officials.
Money matters
Raising taxes could get a little tougher for leaders of Snohomish and Clark counties.
The Clark County Council would need a supermajority of its five members to raise taxes under Charter Review Amendment 25. It defines supermajority as a minimum of two-thirds support, which would be four of the five members.
In Snohomish County, Proposition 5 would raise the bar as well. It would require a similar supermajority of four of the five-member county council to assess, levy or increase any tax. If approved, it would take effect on Jan. 1, 2027. 
It would not apply for existing taxes that come up for renewal and are not increasing. Fees, rates and charges, and special assessments would not be considered a tax subject to this requirement.
Supporters, writing in the Snohomish County voters’ pamphlet, argue the amendment “simply raises the consensus standard. When every dollar matters, Proposition 5 ensures careful consideration and broad support before asking struggling residents to pay more.”
Opponents counter that it will put too much power in the hands of a council minority.
“When the few can overrule the many, public participation carries less weight, public trust SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLEis diminished, and the democratic process is undermined,” they wrote.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Commentary: Mike Kehoe keeps saying he’s running again. Why does everyone keep asking?
text:
Gov. Mike Kehoe speaks to reporters after signing three bills in his office April 23, 2026 (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).Election Day is less than two weeks away, so naturally we’re talking about 2028.
More specifically, the question that’s been making the rounds in Missouri political circles for months: Will Gov. Mike Kehoe run for a second term?
He’s answered that question so many times it barely qualifies as news anymore.
In June, he was asked whether he planned to seek another term. Kehoe didn’t hesitate. He said yes.
Asked last month during a stop in St. Peters, Kehoe said he intends to run in 2028 “if Missourians will have us again.”
He faced the question again days later and told Nexstar the decision was a family one.
“We thought about it,” he said. “We prayed about it.”
On former House Speaker Elijah Haahr’s radio show, State Auditor Scott Fitzpatrick was asked whether he’d run for governor if Kehoe didn’t. Fitzpatrick said he’d consider it, then emphasized that Kehoe has been “very clear both in public and in private settings” that he’s running.
Kehoe has been consistent and clear. So why does everyone keep asking?
Part of the answer is Andrew Bailey.
The former attorney general returned to Missouri after a reportedly rough year at the FBI and almost immediately began sounding like a candidate. His allied PAC has more than half a million dollars in the bank. He has talked with people in Missouri politics about the governor’s office.
When Haahr asked whether any statewide Republican deserves a primary challenge, Bailey didn’t say no. He said to give him a year at home “and let’s have that conversation.” Then last week, Bailey publicly criticized the decision to give St. Louis’ police chief a substantial raise. The board that approved it is dominated by Kehoe appointees.
Asked by reporters whether he could beat Bailey in a primary, Kehoe said: “I’m not thinking about running against Andrew.”
But Bailey didn’t create all the questions about Kehoe’s future. Those were already circulating.
Andrew Bailey is back in Missouri and talking like a candidate

Kehoe has been remarkably effective at getting a fractious Republican legislature to do what he wants. He persuaded lawmakers to approve a massive incentive package to keep the Chiefs and Royals in Missouri. He secured votes for his tax agenda, helped push through a gerrymandered congressional map and has put his stamp on the state’s education leadership.
The trouble is what happened after lawmakers said yes.
The Chiefs are moving to Kansas.
In August, voters overwhelmingly rejected Amendment 5, which would have put Missouri on a path toward eliminating its income tax. Amendment 4, the effort to rewrite the rules for citizen initiatives, lost badly alongside it.
The congressional map Kehoe signed into law won’t be used Nov. 3, either. A successful referendum effort and a string of court rulings derailed Republican hopes of capturing seven of Missouri’s eight congressional seats this year.
Along the way, Kehoe’s approval rating slipped underwater in the SLU/YouGov poll: 40% approving, 49% disapproving.
None of this proves he’s reconsidering. It does help explain why some Republicans wonder whether he wants to do it all again.
Kehoe has never been a favorite of the party’s right flank. He won the 2024 Republican primary with about 39% in a three-way race. One of his opponents, Bill Eigel, recently called on someone to stop “this derailing train.”
And now comes another Election Day.
Republicans are defending their legislative supermajorities. Losing three House seats would end one; losing two Senate seats would end the other.
Amendment 3, which would restore Missouri’s near-total abortion ban, is personal for Kehoe: His wife, Claudia, is treasurer of the campaign supporting it.
A good night gives Kehoe something to point to. A bad one gives his doubters another reason to keep asking.
For now, the evidence points one direction. He says he’s running. He’s raising money. He has given no sign he’s going anywhere.
He keeps answering the question. The question keeps coming back.
That probably says less about his plans than about how his first two years have gone.

name: Maryland Matters
title: In a quiet Maryland election year, all eyes turn to Lower Shore district
text:
Voters cast their ballots Thursday at Honeygo Community Center in Baltimore County. With few competitive races on the ballot, attention is turning to the more competitive legislative subdistricts. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)Across the U.S., the upcoming election is being described, by American voters and pundits of every political stripe, as an existential exercise.
In Maryland, not so much.
Here in this mid-Atlantic land of Middle Temperament, there are no competitive statewide elections. Only one U.S. House race has garnered attention in recent days, but only because of Rep. Andy Harris’ (R-1st) combative behavior after a contentious public forum, but that’s unlikely to affect the outcome.
The fate of the ballot measure impacting Democrats’ ability to gerrymander Harris into oblivion in a future election is uncertain. But there is no conceivable circumstance under which Democrats lose their 34-13 edge in the state Senate or their 102-39 advantage in the House of Delegates.
Even with most contests a foregone conclusion, however, there are still a handful of races for state House and Senate seats this year that are considered competitive and merit attention.
The hardest-fought House races are largely in subdistricts, with a smaller universe of voters – which potentially makes them more volatile and easier to influence.
One of those is District 38B in Wicomico County, where Wicomico County Councilmember Josh Hastings (D) is challenging appointed Del. Barry Beauchamp (R). Democrat Kamala Harris carried the district by 7 points in the 2024 presidential election.
Most General Assembly contests not likely to be competitive — again, experts say

The Beauchamp-Hastings race is taking place amid multiple political crosscurrents in Wicomico County, including an ongoing civil war between County Executive Julie Giordano (R) and some other area Republicans.
“I think people are interested [in the District 38B legislative election] even though there’s not a lot of up-ballot stuff that’s turning people out,” said Mike Dunn, president and CEO of the Greater Salisbury Committee, a civic organization that co-sponsored a candidate forum earlier this week.
But with so few competitive races on the docket across the state, it means the Beauchamp-Hastings election is getting an inordinate amount of attention from outside forces. It’s something the two candidates have discussed among themselves.
“We are a little uncomfortable with some of the attention that’s come into this race,” Hastings said during Tuesday night’s candidate forum, noting that most of the spending is coming “from the other side of the [Chesapeake] Bay.”
A super PAC looking to boost internet gaming in the state is investing heavily in the race to oppose Beauchamp and support Hastings – part of a spending spree in Maryland from the PAC that has topped $3 million overall and continues to rise.
The political arm of the Maryland State Education Association is also spending in the race, on Hastings’ behalf. House Republican and Democratic campaign committees are similarly involved.
Beauchamp, 65, a local businessman and member of the Wicomico County Republican Central Committee, is a political ally of Giordano’s. He was appointed to the House in September 2024, after then-Del. Carl Anderton (R) joined Democratic Gov. Wes Moore’s administration in an economic development role.
Hastings, 44, is seeking to retake the House seat that former House Appropriations Chair Norman Conway (D) held for 28 years until he was ousted by Anderton in 2014. But in an interview, Hastings eschewed partisan arguments.




Subdistricts, main drama
Other subdistrict races to watch this fall, according to political professionals, are:
District 29B in St. Mary’s County, where Del. Brian M. Crosby (D) is retiring after two terms, has swung between the parties over the past few decades. Democrat Adrianne Mathis will face Republican BJ Hall in the district Kamala Harris carried by 11 points in the 2024 presidential election.
In Anne Arundel County’s District 33B, Democrat Chuck Cook, a longtime union organizer who currently works for the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development, is challenging Del. Stuart Schmidt (R). Harris carried the subdistrict by 8 points in 2024.			



“The broad public despises the two-party system and what it espouses,” he said. “We need to focus on democracy more than political parties.”
Hastings said he would sponsor legislation to create open primaries in Maryland and said he plans to vote against Question 3, the ballot question that would make it easier for legislative Democrats to redraw the state’s congressional map mid-decade.
Beauchamp in an interview and in public appearances has made similar claims to bipartisanship. During the forum this week, he explained that he was wearing a purple tie because he represents all of the constituents in his district.
“You serve everyone when you’re serving in this seat,” Beauchamp said.
He also noted that in his “gerrymandered” district, “I start 7 points behind,” and has to tailor his message accordingly.
Hastings, a two-term councilmember who has worked in agriculture and for conservation organizations, is touting his resume and 400-year family history on the Lower Shore. He argued that he is uniquely equipped to deliver for the district given his ties to and history of working with Democrats, Republicans and political independents. He said his principal focus if voters send him to Annapolis will be affordability and economic development.
But Hastings conceded that he could benefit from the current political environment, with growing voter antipathy toward President Trump and some of the local Republican infighting – which could jeopardize Giordano’s bid for a second term as county executive, even though she’s currently favored to hang on.
In his social media posts, mailers and digital ads, Beauchamp has vowed to protect farmers and watermen and to preserve an Eastern Shore lifestyle that he implies is threatened by Annapolis politicians and bureaucrats.
“Truth is, I could sit in that machine with my dog over in the shade, and that’s the perfect life,” Beauchamp said in one Facebook post, which features a picture of him operating heavy construction equipment. “Instead, I am choosing to serve my community when they need me most. I’m not doing it for a title. I’m doing it because the Shore deserves someone in Annapolis who has actually built things here and will fight to keep our way of life.”
He also argued in an interview that unlike Hastings, he already has a record of accomplishment in Annapolis, as a member of the House Appropriations Committee. “I feel like I have found my footing and have made some pretty good connections and have good relationships with people on both sides of the aisle.”
At the candidate forum Tuesday night, the audience at Salisbury University and watching on community cable TV could have been forgiven for not immediately knowing which candidate was the Democrat and which was the Republican. Only when it came to a conversation on taxes and spending did any significant differences on issues come through, with Beauchamp attacking State House Democrats for high taxes and onerous regulations.
Beauchamp also argued that for all of Hastings’ talk of political independence, the Democrat will have to follow the party line if he is elected to the House.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Each candidate has topped $100,000 in fundraising for the contest. Through Oct. 18, Beauchamp reported raising $111,937 and spending $75,256. Hastings raised $102,539 and spent $99,322. Beauchamp had more money available for the final days of the campaign, reporting $36,781 on hand as of Oct. 18 compared to Hastings’ $7,326 war chest.
The House Democratic Caucus Committee and the Republican House Caucus Committee are also sending literature to voters on their candidates’ behalf. The GOP mailer hits Hastings for his ties to Moore and other Western Shore Democrats.
But the race has been roiled by the heavy spending of American Future PAC, a national political entity connected to the internet gaming industry that supports Democratic legislative candidates across the country. Through Oct. 20, the PAC has reported spending at least $202,630 to defeat Beauchamp and another $38,687 to boost Hastings.
The PAC in its mailers argues that Beauchamp voted for measures in the House that will lead to property tax hikes and against programs that are meaningful for Lower Shore residents. Other spots seek to tie him to Trump. (The industry has a similar national PAC that supports Republican legislative candidates.)
Beauchamp has responded that his vote was against the overall state budget, because of its reliance on higher taxes and fees, not because he opposed particular programs or funding measures. He notes that Del. Sharee Sample-Hughes, an Eastern Shore Democrat, also voted against the state budget this year.
Early in his campaign, Hastings vowed not to accept corporate PAC money for this race – a pledge he says he has kept. The American Future PAC ad spending is being made independently of Hastings’ campaign – the two committees are not allowed to communicate – and enables Hastings to keep his promise even if he is benefiting from the corporate spending.
“I don’t even know who they are,” Hastings asserted in an interview. “But they certainly are working hard to make sure Mr. Beauchamp doesn’t return to Annapolis.”
Both candidates said they have talked with each other about the tenor and tone of the race – at the start of the campaign and in more recent days. Both vowed not to personally attack each other and both have marveled at the intensity of the attention their contest has received from outside groups.
But Hastings said he believes Wicomico County voters would be seeking change this year regardless of the heavy outside spending in his race.
“I think you’re going to see a very strong vote against the status quo in Wicomico County,” he predicted.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ Democrats eye data center, AI regulation if Congress changes hands
text:
People participate in a protest of the CoreWeave AI data center outside the municipal building on October 21, 2026, in Kenilworth. New Jersey Democrats hoping to flip control of Congress say they want to curb data center development. (Photo by Stephanie Keith/Getty Images)[2026 election Voter Guide: Who is running in this November’s midterm elections?]On the second day of early in-person voting for the upcoming midterm elections, Democratic House hopeful Adam Hamawy joined a group of environmental activists to protest a planned data center in South Brunswick.
The campaign stop shows Hamawy, a physician who is hoping to succeed Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman in the 12th Congressional District, recognizes that public anger over data centers is key to energizing Democratic voters hoping to win back control of the House of Representatives.
In an interview last month with the New Jersey Monitor, Hamway said federal regulations on data center construction are needed because the environmental and energy issues they present cross state lines. He said he does not support a ban on data centers, but backs a temporary pause on construction to study their impact.
“We need to slow down. We are moving too fast,” he said. “It’s uncontrolled.”
The election is Nov. 3. All 12 of New Jersey’s House seats are on the ballot, as is Sen. Cory Booker (D), who is seeking a third full term against Republican Justin Murphy.
New Jersey Democrats say if they take back control of the House next year, moving to rein in data center construction and the artificial intelligence industry is a top priority. They say they want to push bills to make data centers supply their own clean power and call AI executives to testify before Congress.
Rep. Rob Menendez (D) is seeking a third term in the 8th Congressional District. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
“I think the entire AI conversation is very high on the priority list,” said Rep. Rob Menendez (D-08), who is running for a third term with no GOP challenger. “We can’t wait another day to have this conversation.”
A new Politico Poll says half of Americans oppose data centers being built within three miles of their home and are more likely to oppose candidates who back data center construction. Democrats are benefiting from the backlash, the poll says.
So far, the fight over data center regulation has played out largely at the local level. In New Jersey, more than 100 of the state’s 564 municipalities have banned or restricted new construction.
There are at least 80 data centers in New Jersey, according to South Jersey Climate News. And while some states are considering moratoriums on data center construction, including neighboring New York, our governor, Mikie Sherrill, a Democrat, has resisted calls for such a ban.
In January, Menendez introduced two bills targeting data centers, one that would require them to generate all the electricity they use, with clean energy targets in 2040, and another that would require them to report how much water is used and greenhouse gases emitted every six months. He also pointed to other legislation introduced that would halt construction of AI data centers until the federal government requires approval for new AI models.
“States are sort of in the laboratory now, and they’re thinking about AI regulations, but we very much need a federal framework,” Menendez said.
Hamawy, a surgeon whose chief opponent is Republican Gregg Mele, said he’s used AI in his medical practice to increase efficiency with paperwork, but sees clear downsides of the technology, like the mistakes it makes when used for research or the impact it’s had on children’s reading and writing skills.
“We need to just kind of make sure that we are doing this correctly, and maximizing the good and minimizing the bad,” he said.
Carmen Bucco is the Republican running in the 10th Congressional District. (Photo courtesy of Bucco)
Carmen Bucco, a Republican challenging Rep. LaMonica McIver (D) in the 10th District, lives in Kenilworth, about a mile from where the cloud computing company CoreWeave is now building a $1.8 billion data center. So he fully understands the community’s concerns about how much water the facilities use, the noise they make, and the energy they consume.
But he finds some hypocrisy in the revolts now raging in communities around the state, noting that no one protests outside golf courses over their water consumption.
People initially complained about the effects of cell phones and microwaves when they were first introduced too, he said.
“And all these things are here now, and maybe they’re affecting our lives, maybe they’re not. We’ll never know the truth. Science is good, but there’s no 100% in science either,” he said.
Data centers are also a hot issue down in the 2nd District, where Rep. Jeff Van Drew is seeking reelection against Democrat Zack Mullock.
Mullock, the Cape May mayor, regards data centers as an environmental justice issue, pointing to the controversial data center in Vineland that state officials recently fined $1 million for installing dozens of unpermitted power generators. The problems that have arisen since that project broke ground earlier this year prove that policymakers must demand more transparency around data center development before greenlighting anything, he said.
“This is a huge, huge, huge project, and that’s not what it was sold to the public,” Mullock said.
Mullock said he would support a moratorium on data center development until policymakers can learn more about their impacts. He opposes tax breaks for developers, noting the multibillion-dollar price tags of bigger projects.
“I think data centers are a part of our future. But we’re at the genesis. We are at the moment where we can choose our future,” he said. “We the people should shape that future. It shouldn’t be made in backroom deals.”
The CEO of the firm behind construction of the Vineland data center has said Van Drew’s support of the facility was critical. Van Drew has expressed support for data centers but has joined some of his colleagues in pushing for guardrails on the industry.
Earlier this year, he joined Rep. Josh Riley (D-New York) on a bill aimed at stopping data center projects from driving up energy bills.
“Artificial intelligence has the potential to do a lot of good for our country, but that growth must be handled responsibly,” Van Drew said in a statement when that bill was introduced. “Families and small businesses are already paying far too much for electricity, and they should not be hit with even higher bills because major data center projects require massive amounts of energy and new infrastructure.”
Bucco said if elected, he would restrict data center development to rural areas, prioritize bolstering the power grid, and require data center developers to generate their own power and water supply. He opposes tax breaks for them, but said their development is inevitable.
“I understand progress. I might get hated for it, but that’s life. If we don’t progress, we sit in the Stone Age, and AI is going to be here,” he said. “It’s just a matter of what towns want them and what towns don’t.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Commentary: Ayoub: Nebraskans can lead to close the fissure
text:
Supporters of Ukraine and the Ukrainian people gather outside the Nebraska State Capitol every Saturday to honor the homeland in its continued resistance to Russian invasion, including this weekend on Saturday, Feb. 28, 2026, marking the four-year mark of the war. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)We interrupt this election season to bring you a seismic, geopolitical event: We have met the enemy … and bought him a gift card. Written in Cyrillic.
What’s up with the president’s latest appeasement of Russia’s Vladimir Putin? The capitulation includes a diesel deal that will help fund its war with Ukraine and its support for Iran but do little to stanch the rising cost of fuel here, and an executive order bypassing a new wave of sanctions against Russia. The result was a windfall for Putin, money to aid a war with our ally and support Iran in its war with the U.S. — where American troops have been killed and injured.
Seriously? We are now carrying water for Russia? For those of us in a certain demographic — one which includes the real missiles of October — the idea addles the mind. This has less to do with “I never thought I would see the day” and more to do with “For the love of Mike, what are we doing?”
There’s more: The Wall Street Journal has reported that presidential pal Elon Musk purposely sabotaged Starshield, Ukraine’s first line of defense against Russian drones and critical to its own prosecution of the war. Musk has threatened members of Congress who are calling for an investigation. To roil the waters further, Reuters has reported that the decision to slow Starshield came from within the White House. Musk and the president deny any involvement, but late last week the WSJ said Trump had asked Musk to remove restrictions to Starshield. Bad business, indeed.
Finally, in an unctuous fit of senseless subservience, Special Envoy Steve Witcoff, during a meeting with Putin, praised him as a humanitarian, a farcical idea that has been widely ridiculed here. Perhaps Witcoff didn’t get the 2023 memo the rest of the world did, the one where the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Putin for kidnapping and transferring Ukrainian children to Russia, a war crime. That’s not to mention the ongoing killing of civilians in Ukraine, most recently a 14-month-old in a stroller in a public park.
Congress — you remember Congress — hasn’t been in session since Oct. 3 and won’t be back until after the midterms, when it will be populated with enough lame ducks that actual lawmaking may have to wait until a new Congress is sworn in in 2027. That may be too late for Ukraine … or for the rest of us. 
Sixty percent of Nebraska’s congressional quintet is campaigning, but to the quintet’s credit, none of them sided with the president on waiving sanctions, diesel or undercutting an ally locked in a battle for its survival. Their political courage in this instance is noted and applauded. 
Putin has suggested that he, the president and Chinese leader Xi Jinping meet in a summit to decide Ukraine’s fate. Wait, what? Thirty-two years ago, in signing the Budapest Memorandum, Ukraine gave up its nuclear arsenal, third largest in the world at the time, in exchange for security assurances from the U.S. Now we would consider its fate without a seat at the table?
Perhaps it’s the latent trauma of being sent home early from junior high during the Cuban missile crisis, so I might be incinerated among family and friends. This was after Russian Prime Minister Nikita Khrushchev had pounded his shoe on a desk at the Polish embassy in Moscow and declared, “We will bury you!” While history and alternative translations have tried to mitigate his threat, no one is disputing that six years later he sent nuclear-tipped missiles to Cuba. The result brought the world to the brink of an atomic war, terrifying seventh graders like me who knew cowering under desks while inside a 50-megaton blast radius was pure folly.
We then lived through glasnost, perestroika and the eventual fall of the Soviet Union in 1991. Eight years later Putin arrived, bringing with him a nostalgic view of the once mighty empire. His 2014 incursion into Crimea and the war in Ukraine underscore his view that Russia should return to its former bellicose self.
Sure, alliances change as do the political fortunes of countries. Consider Japan and Germany, our sworn enemies during World War II but now considered — or at least as many of us would like to believe — strong allies. 
Nothing in its recent behavior indicates we should be playing geopolitical footsie with Russia, however. Its war with Ukraine and ongoing economic hardships have diminished the country in many regards, its nuclear arsenal notwithstanding. Still, its aim seems clear. 
Meanwhile, when Congress does reconvene, perhaps Nebraska’s delegation can lead in putting party, partisanship or patronage aside and go about the business of closing a major fissure in the geopolitical world, lest it widen beyond repair.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri to raise speed limit to 75 mph on stretches of four interstates
text:
(photo courtesy of the Missouri Department of Transportation)Missourians will soon be able to drive a bit faster on some rural roads.
The Missouri Department of Transportation has selected portions of four interstates where drivers can go 75 mph, rather than the typical 70 mph.
MoDOT crews will work to update all speed limit signs in these areas this fall and ask that all drivers abide by the posted speed limit signs in these areas, according to a MoDOT news release.
The speed limit will not be raised until a new sign is posted.
This comes after a new law permitting the department to raise the maximum rural highway speed limit to 75 mph. Senate Bill 1408 was passed on May 15, and Gov. Mike Kehoe signed it into law on July 13.
Each location was reviewed through a detailed process to determine if the location was eligible for a raised speed limit.
Each review looked at current traffic volumes, truck traffic volumes, current speed data, crash history, terrain, road design, the presence of safety countermeasures, existing speed limits of border states in areas near state lines and active construction, according to the news release.
Portions of I-29, I-35, I-49 and I-55 will raise the maximum speed limit. Eight sections of these interstates will have raised limits, according to the release:

A 64-mile stretch of I-29 in Andrew County from Exit 56 to approximately 2.5 miles south of the Iowa border
A 55-mile stretch of I-35 from the northern Cameron city limit to approximately four miles south of the Iowa border
A 24-mile stretch of I-49 from the Arkansas border to Exit 24
A 45-mile stretch of I-49 from Exit 56 to just south of Exit 101 in Nevada
A 17-mile stretch of I-55 from the Arkansas border to mile marker 16.6 just south of the I-55 interchange
A 45-mile stretch of I-55 from mile marker 19.8 just north of the MO 84 interchange to mile marker 64.9 at the Route AA bridge
A 16-mile stretch of I-55 from mile marker 70.5 just north of the Route HH interchange to mile marker 86.6 just south of the Route PP interchange
A 59-mile stretch of I-55 from mile marker 106.4 just north of Exit 105 to mile marker 164.9 at the Jefferson County line

MoDOT said it will monitor and evaluate crash data in these areas and, if needed, will bring the maximum speed limit back down to 70 mph.
“An increased speed limit may allow motorists to reach their destinations faster, but safety must remain a priority,” Missouri State Highway Patrol Col. Michael Turner said.
“The Patrol and our traffic safety partners at MoDOT remain committed to reducing the number and severity of traffic crashes in Missouri. It is each driver’s responsibility to make safe decisions while driving.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Commentary: Building a stronger, more resilient water system for SC
text:
This photo shows South Carolina Water Utilities' wastewater treatment plant in Elgin, S.C. (Photo courtesy of South Carolina Water Utilities)South Carolina’s communities depend on water systems that are reliable, resilient, and financially sustainable.
Whether it’s a family turning on the tap or a business opening its doors, reliable water service is something many of us rarely have to think about, even though it underpins nearly every aspect of daily life.
As our state continues to grow, maintaining that reliability requires more than simply responding to today’s needs. It requires long-term planning, responsible infrastructure investment, and experienced professionals managing increasingly complex water and wastewater systems.
New homes, businesses and economic development all depend on the capacity of those systems, which means the infrastructure needed to serve growing communities often must be planned and invested in well before the demand arrives.
On July 1, South Carolina Water Utilities formally consolidated the systems previously operated by Blue Granite Water Company under the SCWU name.
The consolidation represents an important milestone in work that began when SCWU took over management of these systems in 2024, bringing our South Carolina operations together as one coordinated utility.
SC utility hopes to fix poor reputation of a long-troubled system with merger

Since 2024, our focus has been straightforward: strengthen reliability, modernize infrastructure, and improve operational performance.
The results are meaningful. Boil water advisories have decreased by more than 80%, and customer satisfaction has steadily improved.
Those successful outcomes reflect the work happening every day across our systems: stronger maintenance programs, reorganized operations, updated oversight, and continued investment in the fundamentals that keep water and wastewater service safe and reliable.
Professional utility management is largely a labor that customers never see.
It means monitoring systems and water quality, maintaining infrastructure before problems arise, planning for future capacity needs and ensuring trained operators and technical experts are available when conditions change.
As South Carolina continues to add new residents, homes and businesses, that responsibility becomes even more important.
Reliable water and wastewater infrastructure is not simply a response to growth; it is part of what makes sustainable growth possible.
Drought conditions seen this year across South Carolina and the Southeast offer a timely reminder of why those fundamentals matter.
Rainfall plays an essential role in replenishing the surface and groundwater supplies our communities depend on, and extended dry periods can place added pressure on water systems.
Conditions like this underscore the importance of planning ahead and ensuring utilities have the infrastructure, resources and professional expertise to adapt to changing conditions.
With the consolidation now complete, more than 70,000 equivalent residential connections across the Midlands and Upstate are part of a single, coordinated utility.
Bringing these systems together allows administrative, regulatory, technical and infrastructure-planning resources to be shared more efficiently while giving local teams access to broader statewide capabilities.
That scale matters beyond administrative efficiency.
It gives local systems access to a larger network of operators, engineers, and technical resources, while enabling better coordination of maintenance practices, infrastructure planning, and investments across the organization.
Local teams remain focused on the communities they serve, but they now have greater resources at their disposal when challenges arise.
We are already seeing the benefits of that approach.
Through targeted operational improvements — including closing high-cost facilities and reorganizing field operations — South Carolina Water Utilities has reduced former Blue Granite annual expenses by more than $500,000.
Those efficiencies help strengthen long-term system reliability and support continued infrastructure investment.
The July consolidation is an important milestone, but our work continues.
It provides a stronger foundation to continue improving the systems our customers rely on every day while preparing for the demands of a growing state, aging infrastructure and fluctuating weather conditions.
Ultimately, customers should be able to trust that when they turn on the tap, the water will be there and the system behind it is being responsibly managed for the long term.
That is the standard we are working every day to deliver for the communities we serve.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Commentary: Oklahoma voters can pick between disparate views for governor, but down ballot races matter, too
text:
From right, Cyndi Munson and Mike Mazzei are pictured at public appearances. (Photo of Munson by Janelle Stecklein/Oklahoma Voice. Photo of Mazzei by Jessica Tobias/For Oklahoma Voice)The November elections pose an opportunity for Oklahomans to determine our state’s path forward.
If the two leading candidates running for governor are any indication, our state stands at a crossroads in terms of the vision of what is needed to move our state out of the bottom 10 in all the categories that matter.
That stark divergence was on display earlier this month when Republican Mike Mazzei and Democrat Cyndi Munson met for what was expected to be their lone debate heading into the Nov. 3 election. (There are also three independent candidates running, but they were not invited to participate because they didn’t meet the debate’s fundraising criteria.)
Here’s where Munson and Mazzei stand: 
 Data centers
Munson vows to sign an executive order on her first day putting a moratorium on the construction of the large power-hungry and water-consuming monstrosities that we love to hate. She wants the state to adopt a standardized, uniform approach to how it deals with big tech.
Mazzei is fine with the construction of the centers — if the local community wants them. He said AI is here to stay and for America to “win the battle for supremacy,” it requires processing power. He does think there should be four guardrails —  the centers should be required to provide their own electricity; no taxpayer funds should subsidize them; they must be built on locally-approved industrial sites; and they should use advanced-closed looped cooling systems to ensure they use only as much water each day as a several hundred bedroom hotel would.
 Public school funding
The two also disagree on increasing public school funding.
The debate moderators pointed out that Oklahoma’s per pupil expenditure of about $12,500 ranks the state 49th worst in the nation. They asked if that’s enough to get the job done and fix Oklahoma’s suspiciously similar bottom three ranking in education outcomes.
Munson said the state is not meeting the needs of what it takes to operate a classroom and has nearly 4,000 emergency certified teachers. Those educators don’t have a typical license in the subject area they’re teaching, but are hired anyway because of severe teacher shortages. She said the state recently ranked last in education because it’s not making proper investments to take care of teachers. She’d also work with the Legislature to create targeted funding around mental health care access and special education services. 
“If we want more business and industry to come to the state of Oklahoma, we’ve got to get out of last in the nation for public education, and that starts by making critical investments for our public schools,” she said.
Mazzei said his five children’s education included public schools, homeschooling, and private schools, which is why he supports school choice. Parents, he said, know what is best for their kids. He said the state needs to improve literacy rates. 
“Herein do lie some big difference between Rep. Munson and myself,” Mazzei said. “She wants to pour more and more money into an already dysfunctional system. She doesn’t support school choice.”
 Corporate and foreign tax breaks
And when the moderators questioned Mazzei about whether he is a hypocrite for campaigning against foreign-controlled companies owning Oklahoma land, yet supports an aluminum smelter in Inola whose majority owner is affiliated with the United Arab Emirates, he basically said that didn’t count. This foreign ownership is OK because it would create thousands of jobs and develop aluminum for our military jets and warships, he said. 
He believes Oklahoma’s smelter, which is a Trump priority, would not pollute as much as others. And despite local opposition and concerns, Mazzei indicated he doesn’t believe it would endanger the health, people, cattle and hay in eastern Oklahoma.
Munson said she opposed the $255 million “tax giveaway to a foreign corporation.”
 Personal income taxes and the state budget
Mazzei’s solution to make the state more attractive and affordable is to eliminate the income tax. He said the state can begin doing that by “cleaning out a ton of the $2 billion worth of tax giveaways” in Oklahoma’s tax code. 
Munson said it’s easy to campaign on cutting taxes, but governing is more difficult. She said previous Republican income tax cuts created a massive budget hole and wound up benefiting the wealthiest residents. They also resulted in massive cuts to public education, healthcare, infrastructure and other programs that working families relied on.
She said Mazzei’s plan to cut taxes is not going to help the average Oklahoman who wants their child to have access to quality public education.
 Down ballot races and turnout
Regardless of which vision voters select, I am just really glad that Oklahomans have options up and down the ballot this year because our state is at a critical junction.
Too often Oklahoma elections are determined in our closed primaries, with a small number of Republicans and Democrats deciding who represents them in our Legislature. That’s a disappointing outcome given lawmakers play the most key role in determining policies on critical issues such as healthcare and education.
The governor can recommend an agenda, but ultimately it’s our legislators who give it the thumbs up or down.
This year a staggering number of 55 out of the 101 House seats have at least two candidates running on Nov. 3. On the Senate side, 14 of the 25 seats that are eligible to appear feature a competitive general election.
That’s great news for Oklahomans because now they can vote for the candidate that best aligns with their vision for the future, instead of being stuck with the one selected by only Democrats or Republicans.
But it does require Oklahomans to vote. Ours is a state that traditionally boasts some of the lowest voter turnout rates in the country and high amounts of apathy.
Oklahoma does not make it easy to vote. In recent years, some Oklahomans have waited in line for hours to vote early. And ours is a state that offers fewer early voting options and a much shorter window to those cast ballots.
With so many options on the ballot and with Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt leaving us with a plethora of bottom 10 rankings in all things that matter and with a growing number of hospitals at risk of closing, we have plenty of reasons to cast a ballot this year.
The question, though, is will Oklahomans take the time to do so?

name: WyoFile
title: What are Wyoming’s key legislative races? Here are five to watch.
text:
While voters determined most of the incoming Wyoming Legislature’s composition in the primary election, 32 legislative races will be decided in November. 
The contests vary widely in competitiveness with progressive candidates running in deep-red districts, Republican hopefuls challenging incumbents in Democratic strongholds and a couple of three-way races involving minor party candidates. 
Regardless of the outcome of November’s races, the 69th Legislature will look different than the last one after the Wyoming Freedom Caucus lost its House majority and backslid in the Senate in the primary election. As such, voters’ choices next month will largely decide to what extent Republican lawmakers retain their statehouse power. 
Here are five races to watch. 
House District 33 is one of the Legislature’s few swing districts. 
Stretching across Fremont County, House District 33 encompasses the Wind River Indian Reservation towns of Fort Washakie, Ethete and Arapahoe, as well as the small non-tribal communities of Atlantic City, Crowheart and Hudson. Over the years, its representation has flipped back and forth between Democrats and Republicans, as well as enrolled tribal members and white ranchers. 
Earlier this year, Secretary of State Chuck Gray called for a reexamination of the district’s boundaries in light of a U.S. Supreme Court decision on racial gerrymandering. Lawmakers declined his request after several of the district’s constituents, including non-tribal members, argued the boundaries weren’t simply drawn with consideration to race but also to keep communities of interest, such as sovereign governments, intact.  
Members of the House of Representatives work through the 2026 Wyoming Legislature budget session in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata/WyoFile)
Rep. Ivan Posey, a Democrat and Eastern Shoshone educator, has represented the district since 2024, when he ousted a Freedom Caucus-backed incumbent Republican. Posey is now running for a second term against Republican Justin Morgan, a Marine Corps veteran who owns and operates a horse training business. 
In their responses for WyoFile’s 2026 election guide, the two candidates diverged on campaign finance reform, public land transfers and what the Legislature can do to make healthcare more affordable and accessible. 
House District 37 will have a new representative for the first in over two decades.
Since 2003, Republican Rep. Steve Harshman has represented Natrona County’s House District 37, including two terms as speaker of the House. The district spans Casper Mountain and several west-side neighborhoods, including Wolf Creek and Valley Hills. 

Rep. Steve Harshman, R-Casper, durimg the 2026 Wyoming Legislature budget session in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata/WyoFile)

Harshman’s decision to run for superintendent of public instruction this year left his longtime House seat open. Three Republicans vied for the nomination with Brian Costello, an educator, ultimately winning the primary election against the two candidates more closely aligned with the right flank of the GOP. Costello will face Democratic candidate Betsy Erickson, who is also an educator in Casper. 
In their responses for WyoFile’s 2026 election guide, both candidates pointed to young people leaving the state — sometimes called brain drain — as one of the biggest challenges and opportunities facing Wyoming today, but diverged on how to address the problem. 
For over the last decade, a Democrat has represented House District 23. 
Since 2015, voters in Teton County, one of Wyoming’s two blue bubbles, have sent a Democrat to Cheyenne to represent its northern half, including Teton Village, an eastern section of Wilson as well as the communities of Kelly, Moran and Moose. 
Democrat Rep. Liz Storer has represented House District 23 since 2022, when the race between her and Republican candidate Paul Vogelheim set a new campaign-finance record for a Wyoming legislative race. As a lawmaker, Storer has largely focused on abortion rights, tourism and tax reform. 
(Storer is the president and CEO of the George B. Storer Foundation, a financial supporter of WyoFile. The foundation has no role in WyoFile’s editorial content.)
Republican candidate Shannon Brennan is challenging Storer in the general election. Brennan did not respond to WyoFile’s candidate questionnaire. She works as an energy and environmental management consultant and identifies as a constitutional conservative, according to her campaign website. 
The Wyoming Capitol interior is pictured during the opening days of the 2026 budget session. (Mike Vanata/WyoFile)
House District 14 will also host a showdown between a Democratic incumbent and a Republican challenger. 
Voters first elected Democratic Rep. Trey Sherwood in 2020 to House District 14, which spans north Laramie and the Albany County communities of Rock River and Bosler. Until then, the district had been represented by a series of Republicans for the last three decades. In 2022 and 2024, Republican candidates failed to recoup the seat. 
As a lawmaker, Sherwood risen through the ranks of the minority party while focusing on housing, supporting rural schools and suicide prevention. Most recently, she served as the sole Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee — the Legislature’s most powerful panel and one responsible for crafting the budget bill. 
Sherwood will face Republican candidate Emily Study in the general election. Study did not respond to WyoFile’s candidate questionnaire. According to her campaign website, Study has worked with the military and the Department of Veterans Affairs for over two decades. 
Voters in House District 11 will decide a three-way race. 
Republican Dan McIntosh, Democrat Britney Tennant and Libertarian Ryan Shollenberger are all competing to represent Laramie County’s House District 11, which spans a central section of Cheyenne. 
Republican Rep. Jacob Wasserburger, who currently represents the district, did not run for reelection after serving one term. 
The district’s boundaries shifted significantly during the Legislature’s 2022 redistricting process. Years before then, several Democrats represented the district, but for the last decade, it has favored Republicans. 
McIntosh works as an educator at Laramie County Community College, Tennant runs the Cheyenne Animal Shelter and Shollenberger is a wildland firefighter and substitute teacher. 
In their responses for WyoFile’s 2026 election guide, all three candidates highlighted the economy, the state’s workforce and community development when asked about Wyoming’s biggest challenges.

name: WyoFile
title: Lead doesn’t suit us anymore
authors: By Ted Kerasote, Writers on the Range
text:
Opinion

There are about 15 million hunters in the United States (I’m one of them), and an estimated 13 million of us still use bullets made of lead despite its toxic effects on wildlife and human health, which is why I switched to nontoxic ammo years ago.
Hunters are not alone in loving lead. The Romans employed lead in their plumbing, Gutenberg made printing type from a lead-tin alloy, and lead-acid batteries worldwide start our cars. Lead is especially suitable for making bullets. Because of its low melting point, lead is easy to pour and cast; it retains its kinetic energy over long distances; and it deforms on impact.
But even in tiny dosages, lead is toxic to all living organisms, damaging nervous systems, impairing the creation of blood, harming kidneys and liver, impeding reproduction and diminishing the cognitive development of children. The amount of lead discharged by hunters isn’t trivial. We spew an estimated 12-20 million pounds of lead across America’s fields and forests each year. Imagine 444 fully loaded semitrucks stretching for six miles. That’s 20 million pounds of lead.
Most of this massive tonnage falls in the shape of shotgun pellets discharged by bird hunters in pursuit of doves, pheasant, grouse and quail. (Waterfowlers were required to switch to nontoxic shot in 1991.) Since birds have no teeth, they pick up grit to grind seeds and plants in their gizzards. Thus, while foraging, they ingest shotgun pellets and can die from consuming as little as one of them.
The balance of lead falling upon the American countryside is composed of bullets that have brought down big game animals and prairie dogs. On impact, these bullets shed dozens and sometimes hundreds of microscopic lead shards. A substantial number of these fragments may end up in our steaks and burgers; the rest are left behind in big game gut piles or in the carcasses of prairie dogs. This feast of lead-scattered remains is subsequently eaten by a wide variety of scavengers. All told, this annual jetsam of lead causes 10-20 million wildlife deaths, perhaps 15 million doves and other upland birds, tens of thousands of raptors, and countless mammals, such as ferrets, coyotes, badgers, weasels and bobcats.
When it comes to human beings, no one knows how many Americans are harmed by eating meat contaminated by lead bullets. Recently, synchrotron X-ray imaging, which can detect far smaller particles than standard X-rays, has revealed that deer and birds downed with lead bullets or lead shot are seeded with nanoparticles of lead that far exceed levels set by the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention for lead poisoning, especially lead poisoning in children.
There is also no safe level of lead exposure, a reality that has led to national bans on lead paint in 1977, lead plumbing in 1986, lead shot for waterfowl hunting in 1991, leaded gasoline in 1996, and the U.S. Army’s transition to lead-free ammunition in 2003.
Taking all this into account, I made the switch to nontoxic ammunition and have now shot 13 elk and a bison with a variety of Barnes X copper bullets, all of the animals dropping in their tracks, as well as many dozens of upland birds with bismuth shot. I am not alone in thinking that these bullets provide superior accuracy and one-shot kills. “American Hunter,” one of the National Rifle Association’s flagship publications, has unabashedly praised the Barnes line, saying, “Every now and then a new bullet comes along that redefines what we think we know about hunting projectiles.”
It’s true that copper ammunition is more expensive than lead (about a dollar more per round than premium lead ammo), but how many shots do hunters need to fill their tag — one or two? And nontoxic shotgun shells are now priced cheaper than some equivalent lead-shot loads.
In this light, I can’t think of a single reason not to switch to nontoxic bullets and birdshot for hunting while we continue to use lead ammunition at rifle ranges, and at trap and skeet fields, where lead won’t enter the food chain. It’s the right thing to do for wildlife and for our own health and that of our families.
Yet on Sept. 17, President Donald Trump grandfathered hunting with lead ammunition on 640 million acres of federal lands. The NRA cheered his executive order as a “historic moment.”
