name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho politicians are using AI to write for them
text:
AI detectors flagged dozens of op-eds and other statements published under the names of state constitutional officers and lawmakers, some of whom employ professional writers earning six-figure salaries. (Photo by Getty Images)This story was 0riginally posted on IdahoEdNews.org on Oct. 21, 2026.
The next time you come across an op-ed by an Idaho politician, think twice about the source. It may not be human. 
Op-eds and other online posts from some of Idaho’s most powerful elected officials contain heavy doses of artificial intelligence, according to AI detectors, tools that distinguish between writing by humans and writing that comes from machines like ChatGPT. 
Idaho Education News started using these detectors last week after a series of stories from RANGE Media exposed a “startling” amount of “AI slop” in the opinion pages of Spokane newspapers and in written statements from candidates for political office. 
EdNews turned up similar results. AI detectors flagged dozens of op-eds and other statements published under the names of state constitutional officers and lawmakers, some of whom employ professional writers earning six-figure salaries.
It’s common for high-ranking politicians to task staffers with communicating on their behalf. They write speeches, social media posts, op-eds and press statements. But if those staffers are outsourcing that work to artificial intelligence, it would raise questions around authenticity, transparency and accountability, particularly when machine-generated content isn’t disclosed. 
Gov. Brad Little’s office this year published three op-eds that included AI-generated content, according to Pangram and GPTZero, two different commercial AI detectors. Attorney General Raúl Labrador’s office also published three, and State Superintendent of Public Instruction Debbie Critchfield’s office had two. 
None disclosed that they used artificial intelligence. 
The detectors flagged several other elected leaders, too. But many didn’t answer requests from EdNews to discuss their use of AI. Writing from Rep. Mike Simpson, Lt. Gov. Scott Bedke, Secretary of State Phil McGrane, state Rep. Josh Tanner and state Sen. Brian Lenney triggered the detectors.
Those who did talk to EdNews cast doubt on the reliability of AI detectors. Critchfield’s spokeswoman denied using AI at all. Spokespeople for Little and Labrador conceded that they use AI tools but not to the extent that the detectors suggested. 
 Spokespeople acknowledge some AI use

Daniel Estes, communications director for Labrador, acknowledged that he and Damon Sidur, director of external affairs, use AI when they write op-eds for Labrador. 
ChatGPT and Claude help make their writing clearer and distill complex legalese stemming from the cases they often write about, Estes said in an interview at his Statehouse office. But he denied that AI does most of the work. Labrador edits the op-eds himself before they’re published, he said. 
“There’s nothing that we’ve cranked out that hasn’t been reviewed and edited and changed, often substantially,” Estes said. “I disagree, vehemently, that these are AI-written.” 
Pangram determined that Labrador’s op-ed celebrating Idaho’s settlement with Meta was entirely AI-generated. Two others included a majority of AI writing mixed with some human contributions, according to Pangram. The detector estimated that an op-ed about banking scams was 92% AI, while a letter reflecting on the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks was 81% AI.   
Read Pangram’s reports here, here and here.
Most of the writing from Labrador’s office that EdNews tested was not primarily AI-generated, according to the detectors.
The same goes for Little’s office, although the detectors did flag three op-eds from the governor. Pangram determined that one on nuclear energy was 100% written by AI. Another op-ed applauding the state’s “fiscal discipline” was 88% AI, and a third on investments in teacher pay was 67% AI, according to Pangram.
Read Pangram’s reports here, here and here.
In response to EdNews’ request for an interview, Emily Callihan, the governor’s communications director, recited a prepared statement. EdNews did not accept written comments from the elected leaders and spokespeople mentioned in this story. 
“AI detectors are frequently wrong,” Callihan said by phone. “That said, AI did not write the three op-eds you noted, but AI has replaced the use of other writing resources, such as an online thesaurus and editing tools. So it is accurate to say the governor’s office uses AI to assist with some writing.”
Gov. Brad Little delivers the 2026 State of the State address. This speech was written by humans, not written by artificial intelligence, according to Pangram, an AI detector. (Sean Dolan/EdNews)
 The ‘stylistic quirks’ of AI

AI detectors aren’t foolproof. Estes pointed out that earlier versions of the detectors flagged the U.S. Constitution as being AI-generated. 
But that was three years ago, and the technology has improved. 
The detectors, which are AI-powered themselves, have been fed millions of texts written by humans and millions of texts written by AI models like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok. Then they were trained to identify common writing patterns from each source. 
“AI models have many visible and invisible stylistic quirks unique to them that determine how they write, and that is what Pangram picks up on,” Annamieka Aerts, a technical writer at the company, said by email. 
When Pangram released the fourth iteration of its AI detector this summer, the company touted a false positive rate — when human writing is incorrectly labeled as AI — of just 0.0041%, or roughly one for every 24,000 documents. 
An independent study of commercial AI detectors by researchers at the University of Chicago last year found that Pangram’s software achieved “near-zero” error rates when analyzing texts that were medium-length (news stories and blogs) to long (novel excerpts).
Lauren Necochea, chairwoman of the Idaho Democratic Party
Still, the detectors can be wrong, so EdNews didn’t rely on just one. EdNews tested writing that Pangram flagged as AI-generated with a second detector, GPTZero, which confirmed Pangram’s results. 
Both determined that humans wrote the U.S. Constitution.
The detectors can distinguish between texts that were entirely AI-generated, a mix between AI and human writing or only edited by AI.
They noticed, for instance, that a recent op-ed by Lauren Necochea, chairwoman of the Idaho Democratic Party, was “AI-assisted.” Ironically, the article argued that data centers shouldn’t get tax breaks, in part, because of their environmental impact. Necochea told EdNews that the Democrats’ communications director, Avery Roberts, uses an AI tool to “polish” op-eds. 
“I don’t seek out AI tools, in general, as a personal policy,” Necochea said by phone. “I worry about my own (writing) skills degrading. I think we all need to be conscious of not becoming dependent on AI. That’s what these companies want.”

Testing Pangram’s AI detector
When Pangram’s AI detector analyzes a text, it parses the writing into three possible categories: AI-written, AI-assisted or human-written.
EdNews took one of its own articles — last week’s coverage of a televised debate between candidates for state superintendent — and inserted changes made by ChatGPT to test how this works. We asked Pangram to analyze the article each time AI made changes.
First, we asked Pangram to test the original article for AI.

Pangram result: 100% human-written.

Second, we asked ChatGPT to edit the original article.

Pangram result: 23% AI-assisted and 77% human-written.

Third, we asked ChatGPT to rewrite the AI-assisted article. 

Pangram result: 12% AI-written, 55% AI-assisted and 33% human-written. 

Lastly, we asked ChatGPT to write its own article based on the superintendent debate.

Pangram result: 100% AI-written.


 ‘We write our stuff,’ says Critchfield spokeswoman

Pangram also flagged two op-eds from Critchfield — one highlighting student success was entirely AI, according to the detector, while another op-ed about Critchfield’s recent funding formula listening sessions was primarily AI.
Read Pangram’s reports here and here.
Andrea Dearden, communications director for Critchfield, denied that her office uses any AI tools to write op-eds. She writes them with Maggie Reynolds, public information officer for the Idaho Department of Education, and Critchfield. 
“These articles, specifically, are very personal to her,” Dearden said of Critchfield. “She wants the community to understand her perspective.” 
Dearden shared drafts of the op-ed, passed back and forth between herself, Reynolds and Critchfield, to demonstrate that humans wrote it. And Pangram showed that an early draft was 100% human-written. But the detector also showed that a later draft, which included significant edits to the original, was 74% AI-written. 
Dearden appeared perplexed by the results, but she stood her ground in a follow-up interview. 
“We don’t use AI. We write our stuff,” she said by phone. “We go through multiple iterations, through multiple people, and if we used it, we would tell you.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: In Tennessee’s 2nd Congressional District, Democrat Barnett tries to flip a long-held GOP seat
text:
Knoxville engineer and business owner Michaela Barnett, right, is the Democratic nominee in the 2nd Congressional District. She's challenging four-term incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Tim Burchett for the seat. (Photo: Burchett by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout; Barnett submitted by campaign.)Michaela Barnett, a Knoxville small business owner and scientist, is attempting to overturn more than a century of Republican domination in Tennessee’s 2nd Congressional District  by beating U.S. Rep. Tim Burchett in November.
Barnett, the Democratic nominee, began thinking about taking Burchett on in 2025 when she worked in Congress as a Science Policy Fellow in the office of U.S. Rep. Paul Tonko, a New York Democrat. There, she worked on issues advancing science-based policy. The experience also endeared her to the concept of running for office.
On a personal level, she found Burchett “embarrassing” after watching him theorize about the existence of aliens and other such things, she said. Working in Congress gave her the idea she could do the job herself.
“I saw really how ineffective at his job, and how ineffective he was at delivering for the people of East Tennessee,” she said. “I am not someone who complains about problems. I think it’s much more effective to propose a solution, rather than point out a problem.”
Barnett has no legislative experience. She has a Ph.D. in Civil Engineering from the University of Virginia and her day job is running KnoxFill, a refillery selling alternatives to various household products, reusing products that would’ve been thrown away to make soaps, cleaning solutions and pet products.
Michaela Barnett, right, the Democratic nominee for Tennessee’s Second Congressional District, is joined by a volunteer for door to door canvassing. (Photo: MichaelaForTennessee.com)
Speaking with Tennessee Lookout, she criticized President Donald Trump’s war in Iran for raising prices on gas and other necessities, and said she’d work hard to fix local problems with health care (“there are people in my district who have to drive 90 minutes to get care”) and infrastructure, which she said hasn’t been kept up as more people move to the district.
Elsewhere, her priorities range from supporting abortion rights and LGBTQ+ rights, which includes banning conversion therapy and discrimination, and supporting veterans through more VA funding and job training.
She pledges on her website to “return ICE to 2024 funding levels” and hold them accountable for crimes, and on education, states she wants to raise teacher pay and make college more affordable.
Money talks
Barnett has raised $638,378 as of September 30, nearly all from individual contributions.
That is still far in the shadow of the over $3 million Burchett has raised, which includes tens of thousands of dollars from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, AIPAC, just this year. AIPAC is by far his biggest donor.
Burchett has handily won all of his elections in the district since his election in 2018, taking over 60% of the vote every time against Democratic challengers.
No debate
Barnett said Burchett has refused to debate. Burchett did not respond to multiple requests for an interview by Lookout for this article.
Barnett told Lookout that she challenged Burchett to do a town hall where she wasn’t present, so as to avoid platforming her as he claimed he feared. Yet Burchett hasn’t done that either.
“Voters deserve to hear from those who represent them,” she said. “The way I like to put it, this is a job interview, and I’m the only one showing up for the interview.”
She called it “really quite baffling” that Burchett was refusing to hold town halls or participate in debates, given how much money he’d been raising.
“He’s both raising and spending more money than ever before,” she said. “But we’re not seeing where that money is going. He’s very absent from the district. I’ve seen a couple yard signs, but I’m not seeing ads or mailers.”
She said it seemed like he “doesn’t think he has to, thinks he can win no matter what he does.”
Burchett’s record
Burchett was elected in 2018, after U.S. Rep. Jimmy Duncan retired from Congress. Jimmy Duncan represented the district from 1988 until his retirement; his father John Duncan, held the seat from 1965 until his death in 1988.
Burchett initially said he was “probably a no” on Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act in 2025, though he changed his tune after meeting with Trump in the White House later that year.
Burchett said Trump “answered all our questions, was very informative. It was a very good day,” and said they’d “hopefully get this worked out and do some great things for this country.”
U.S. Rep. Tim Burchett of Tennessee’s 2nd Congressional District, is running for his fifth term in Congress in 2026. Lookout)
Amid the burgeoning war in Iran, Burchett has wavered in his support. He called his colleagues in favor of bombing Iran “war pimps” last year, but then later said he was “comfortable” with Trump’s strikes on Iranian nuclear sites later that year.
“Any time there’s a loss of life, I’m a little hesitant,” he said, but added that he knew “first hand” from his parents’ experience in wars “what impact a war can have on a country.”
This year, he said he opposed the idea of sending ground troops to Iran, but voted against a measure that would’ve forced the White House to stop the war.
He’s also introduced a pair of bills which would attempt to address the rising gas prices from the war — one which would ban exported diesel fuel and another which would ban it in the event of gas prices rising to $5 a gallon nationally, and would end the ban after those prices lowered to below $4.50 a gallon.
Recently, he introduced a bill, HR-10225, which would prevent federal money from being used to provide housing assistance to undocumented people living in the U.S.
He’s one of 12 co-sponsors on HR 9160, the No Safe Haven for Terrorist Families Act, which would ban family members of known terrorists from entering the country.
And he has co-sponsored U.S. Rep. Nancy Mace’s Preserving Social Security and Medicare for Citizens Act of 2026, which would limit Social Security and Medicare benefits to U.S. citizens and immigrants who have been lawfully admitted for permanent residency.
The road ahead
Barnett knows it’s a tough road ahead if she does manage to win — facing “a lot of establishment interests in both parties who want to maintain the status quo.”
But she thinks there’s “a degree of social and political capital” to be had if she wins the district, which has been held by Republicans since 1855.
“Democratic leadership might want to keep the seat, so they might throw me a bone they might not throw other freshmen,” she said.
She has some aces up her sleeve in case, though, describing coalition building with other aspiring political outsiders in this year’s midterms, planning to have a bloc that can vote for various issues if they win.
Democratic congressional candidate Michaela Barnett drew hundreds of attendees to an Oct. 12 town hall meeting in Farragut, Tennessee. (Photo: MichaelaForTennessee.com)
“It’s a voting bloc,” she said. “We’re not just striking out on our own. It’s absolutely critical if we want to deliver on common issues constituents are asking us to work on. We have to be doing coalition work right now.”
On the campaign trail, she’s talked to people of all political alignments who are dissatisfied with the status quo — and she thinks she can get them on her side.
“I was raised in a very conservative Republican family,” she said. “That’s helped me reach across the aisle. Republicans feel politically homeless. They feel they were sold a false bill of goods by this president who told us he’d bring prices down and ran on not getting us into more forever foreign wars, and what do we have? Still high prices and more foreign wars.”
Barnett, who was born and raised in Ohio, called East Tennessee her “chosen home,” joking that she “couldn’t coordinate it with her parents” to be born there originally.
“I tell folks who were born here, ‘I didn’t have the good fortune to be born here but I got here as fast as I could,’” she said. “This is my chosen home. I started and grew my business here, I met my husband, we got married, he got his Ph.D. I have so much love and appreciation for my chosen home, I want better for my neighbors than what we have right now.”

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Tolls on Mobile Bridge and Bayway project become election issue in coastal Alabama
text:
The Mobile Bay causeway and city skyline at sunset. A new Mobile bridge and Bayway is expected to be completed by 2031, but a plan to pay off federal loans with tolls has become a major issue in coastal Alabama as Election Day approaches.  (Getty Photos) 


Key Points

Both Democrats and Republicans oppose tolls planned for the Mobile Bridge and Bayway project.
The tolls are not expected to take effect until 2031, when the first phase of the project is completed.
Candidates have politicized the issue. Democrats placed the blame on President Donald Trump and Sen. Tommy Tuberville, R-Alabama, the Republican nominee for Governor. Republicans praised Trump and U.S. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy for making a federal loan available for the project.
Many of the local elected officials accepted the tolls after an agreement to reduce the original rate and to preserve other routes that did not include a fee.




If there’s one issue that can bring Democrats and Republicans together in coastal Alabama, it’s the plan to impose tolls on the new bridge and Bayway project to cross Mobile Bay.
Republicans equate it to imposing a tax that disproportionately affects locals. Democrats express concerns about placing an additional cost on the working class during a period of high inflation.
“I believe we have already paid for these roads with our federal tax dollars, our state tax dollars,” said Danielle Duggar, the Republican nominee for Alabama House District 96, in an interview on Wednesday.
Her opponent, Democratic nominee Terri Osborne, also opposed the tolls.
“If a toll has to be imposed, it should be as low as possible for the shortest amount of time, especially on the residents of Baldwin and Mobile counties who have to commute back and forth across the bay,” she said in an interview on Wednesday.
Local and state officials have recognized the need for another route for commuters to cross Mobile Bay since the early 2000s as traffic through the Wallace Tunnel, a key artery for Mobile, increased. The bridge would offer commuters another option and, ideally, relieve traffic in the tunnel.
The project is being funded with a federal loan; money from tolls would be used to repay it. While no tolls would be charged until the first phase is completed, expected in 2031, commuters and House Democrats from the area have concerns that the tolls automatically increase annually without a cap.
Former Mobile Mayor Sam Jones, now a Democratic state representative for the city, said he would not have preferred the toll either.
“I would think that with Mobile and Alabama being considered one of the reddest of red states, we shouldn’t have to pay a toll,” he said in an interview on Wednesday. “With our Congressional delegation in Washington, our Senate delegation, if we had Sen. (Richard) Shelby, we probably would not have had a toll, but now, someone is suggesting we borrow tax dollars and pay interest on our own tax dollars to get the bridge built. I have a problem with that.”
Other Alabama House Democratic candidates banded together to express their opposition to the tolls in a Facebook post.
“This bridge should be uniting the region, not putting a tear in our pocketbooks,” said Rep. Adline Clarke, D-Mobile.
The project
All agree that the new project is needed to address the traffic congestion along Interstate 10 at peak travel times. The project also aims to reduce roadway crashes, provide a direct interstate route, address the impact of the ships on traffic and minimize the effects of storms and sea level rise.
According to a grant application for the project, the Wallace Tunnel, built to accommodate about 35,000 vehicles per day, now sees 65,000 vehicles per day on weekdays. It increases to 75,000 vehicles per day on the weekends. By 2040, traffic is projected to be 95,000 vehicles per day.
Gov. Kay Ivey gets power to approve new I-10 bridge design

The project aims to give commuters another option to cross the river. According to a fact sheet from ALDOT, the first phase of the plan is to build a bridge with six lanes, three in each direction, and to restripe the existing Bayway from four lanes to six. The second phase of the project would create a new six-lane Bayway.
“The one thing it does for the city of Mobile, it keeps from blocking the tunnels,” said Jones. “When you block the tunnels, you block up traffic in downtown Mobile, you back up traffic on the Bayway. It has a purpose, it is needed.”
ALDOT said in a statement that the tolls are necessary “for the project’s financial viability.”
“Its Phase I cost is roughly double the entire state of Alabama’s transportation budget, and rapidly rising inflation on construction materials further limits the state’s ability to fund the project without revenue sources,” the statement said.
The construction cost for the first phase is about $3.2 billion. Details and financing of the second phase of the project still need to be finalized. The project will be paid for in part by two federal grants totaling $675 million. ALDOT will contribute at least another $250 million.
The remaining amount will be obtained from a $2.52 billion federal loan called the Transportation Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Act. The tolls would service that loan and other debts associated with the project.
A long process
Residents and officials hesitated to impose user fees in the past. The project requires the metropolitan planning organizations to include the project in their transportation plans for it to move forward. In 2019, the Mobile Metropolitan Planning Organization had tabled a vote on the project. The Eastern Shore Metropolitan Planning Organization voted 8-1 to remove the project that prevented it from moving forward.
“It was that they were advertising that the toll would be $6 in each direction,” said Jack Burrell, Fairhope city councilman and chair of the Eastern Shore MPO, in an interview earlier this month. “There was no mention of a monthly pass.”
However, the MPO wrote a letter to Gov. Kay Ivey to resurrect it in 2021.
“The traffic congestion just to make a simple trip across the bay on a Friday or any given weekend, you have to plan for a couple more hours for your trip,” Burrell said. “I think the need to solve our traffic congestion was the reason that we needed to pursue a solution.”
Under the current proposal, commuters can pay for a $60 monthly unlimited ALGO Pass that will not increase in price for the first decade once tolls are in effect. Those who decide not to purchase the monthly plan but have an ALGO Pass who drive passenger vehicles will pay $3 per trip.
Commuters who do not have an ALGO account but use another system for paying tolls will pay $7.70. Those not on any plan will pay $15.40 per trip. No tolls will be implemented until the project opens in 2031.
Burrell said he was open to considering a toll but wanted it capped at $2.50 and pressed to preserve non-toll routes. He also wanted to remove the option for a public-private partnership.
ALDOT considered partnering with a private firm to help pay for the cost of the project and allow a firm to charge a fee for crossing the bridge, but that plan was abandoned.
“In that agreement, it was stated that they could toll any access across the bay, now and into the future,” Burrell said. “We found that totally unacceptable. With the new framework, that went away and we preserved toll-free options.”
Burrell also said he wants to ensure all toll money is used for the project and not disbursed to other spending by the state.
ALDOT said that toll prices will eventually increase to help pay for the federal loan. The monthly pass will remain $60 for the first 10 years but will increase after that. Other toll options will increase each year as soon as the toll takes effect. It will be either 5% or the change in the CPI for the south region, whichever is higher for the first 10 years. It will then be 2.5% or the CPI for the south region, whichever is greater, after that.
Will Congress ban ‘mud dumping’ in Mobile Bay?

Republicans praised President Donald Trump for opening the financing option for the project.
“Thanks to President Trump and Secretary (Sean) Duffy’s leadership, we are seeing real progress,” U.S. Sen. Katie Britt, R-Alabama, said in a video on the ALDOT website regarding the project. “I have been proud to work alongside them to ensure that Alabama’s priorities are heard in Washington.”
Jones laid the blame for the cost and tolls on the president’s administration.
“I have been listening to the president say we have trillions of dollars in tariffs, let’s spend some of it on the bridge,” he said. “Let’s delegate some of that to infrastructure and put some of it toward the bridge.”
Local House Democrats in their video linked the toll to U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville, R-Alabama, because he helped secure the federal loan.
“We were promised a flat toll of $2.50, but Sen. Tuberville raised that to $3,” Jones said in the ad. “And now Trump’s new federal loan locks us into automatic increases based on inflation.”
The campaign for Tuberville referred the Alabama Reflector to an article from al.com that said Tuberville opposed the tolls and he would work to reduce them.
Duggar and Sen. Chris Elliott, R-Josephine, have proposed legislation that would give drivers a chance to claim a tax credit for tolls, capped at $15 million a year for five years.
Local officials are resigned to accepting the tolls to help alleviate traffic that continues to be a problem.
“We don’t want any tolls, but we understand the situation that we are kind of in,” said Daphne Mayor Robin LeJeune. “We hope that the federal government will come in with additional funding. We hope whoever the next governor is will work with the next ALDOT director and work to limit tolling.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee officials urge caution amid reports of ballot problems
text:
Voters in several counties have reported their selections default to a candidate they didn't select, and a spokesman for the  Tennessee Secretary of State's office urges voters to avail themselves of all safeguard measures. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)A Tennessee Democratic lawmaker is calling for election officials to resolve complaints that voting machines are defaulting to candidates they didn’t want to select but stopped short of saying ballots are rigged.
“Obviously, this keeps coming up and it needs to be addressed after this election, because it’s not acceptable that people are having these problems,” state Sen. Heidi Campbell said Friday. “However, I don’t think it’s indicative of any foul play.”
Campbell said she spoke with Davidson County Election Office officials after receiving multiple complaints about ballots during the midst of early voting leading up to the Nov. 3 election. Officials confirmed the machines are not connected to the Internet and that the machines are calibrated properly, she said.
“I feel confident having talked to them that it’s user error,” Campbell said. 
Nashville TV stations, including NewsChannel5, and WSMV, reported some voters said when they touched the voting screen an incorrect name appeared. The changes required them to push the correct button two or three times before confirming their ballot, they said.
In light of the complaints, Davidson County Election Office is urging people to check their ballots before completing the vote and requesting a printout to make sure their selections were correct, she said. Davidson County voters also will be given plastic sticks to cast ballots.
“I Idon’t think it’s indicative of any foul play,” said state Sen. Heidi Campbell, a Nashville Democrat, of reported ballot errors. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Chad Gray, Williamson County Administrator of Elections, said his office is providing voters with styluses at all polling locations.
“All voting equipment undergoes thorough logic and accuracy testing by both Republican and Democratic representatives before being used in an election,” Gray said in a statement.
The Secretary of State’s Office also is encouraging voters to make sure their votes are recorded correctly before confirming their choices.
Responding to questions from the Lookout, Secretary of State Tre Hargett’s spokesperson Ben Hill said the office “takes any and all complaints seriously.”
“Tennessee’s voting systems are designed with multiple safeguards to help ensure that ballots are recorded consistent with voter intent. The process includes several opportunities for voters to verify their selections before casting their ballot,” Hill said in a statement.
First, when a voter makes a choice, the selection is clearly displayed on the machine’s screen. Then, before casting a ballot, voters are given a summary screen displaying all their selections. Third, voters should review a paper ballot generated by the systems to confirm their choices are accurate before casting a ballot.
Voters who believe they have a problem with their ballot should notify a poll official immediately, before casting their ballot, he said.
In addition, the state is encouraging voters to know what is on the ballot before going to vote, including familiarizing themselves with three constitutional amendment questions.
Richard “Rique” Patire, a Nashville entertainer and stylist, said he experienced a similar situation in August when he tried to vote in the Democratic primary. He filed a complaint with the Davidson County Election Office.
Patire said he told election workers he wanted a Democratic ballot but when he pressed a button three times to vote for Democrats, the machine failed to work correctly. An election worker then pressed the machine button and said it went through.
Yet when got his ballot and went to the booth, another election worker said it appeared he didn’t want to vote for the gubernatorial candidate. He was then informed he received the wrong ballot.
When he said, “I don’t understand this,” an election worker responded, “Neither do we.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Midterm early voter turnout tops 2022 stats by 57% in first 8 days, but lags behind 2018
text:
Casa Azafran, a cultural community center in South Nashville, serves as a precinct during elections and drew 'No Kings' attendees Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Eight days into early voting, turnout was more than 57% higher for Tennessee’s Nov. 3 midterm election than it was in 2022, according to state data. 
More than 665,600 people cast their ballots as of Thursday, representing 13.85% of registered voters in Tennessee. The early voter turnout still lags behind 2018’s 8-day total of 810,056.
The higher turnout comes after state lawmakers redrew Congressional districts this spring in an effort to give Republican candidates a boost at the polls. This year’s ballot includes multiple high-profile races with no incumbents.
Republican U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn faces Democratic contender Jerri Green, a Memphis City Council member, and a field of independents including David Hatley and Lauren Pinkston for the state’s open governor seat.
Voter Guide: 2026 Midterm General Election

Voter turnout in Shelby County, which was divided into three congressional districts, is nearly 70% ahead of 2022 with almost 89,000 ballots cast as of Thursday. The county’s turnout is still about 9.6% behind turnout in 2018.
In West Tennessee, Haywood County’s turnout is nearly 92% higher than in 2022, with 1,582 votes cast. Hardeman County’s 2,034 votes puts it 61% of 2022 turnout statistics. Both counties remain about 12% behind 2018 early voting numbers. In this year’s primary election, Haywood County saw more total Democratic ballots pulled than Republican by a narrow margin.
Williamson County is also outpacing its 2022 turnout by nearly 69% with 35,982 ballots cast. It, too, is behind 2018 turnout by about 12%.
Eyes are on the vacant seats in Congressional Districts 5 and 9, both of which now stretch from left-leaning Memphis through rural West Tennessee and conclude in Williamson County, the wealthiest county in the state and a stronghold for conservatives. Democrats and Republicans alike have poured money into the races in the last 90 days to fund final pushes before Nov. 3.
In District 9, State Rep. Justin Pearson, a Memphis Democrat, is competing with Republican Shelby County Sen. Brent Taylor. 
Former Tennessee Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher unseated District 5 incumbent U.S. Rep. Andy Ogles in the Republican primary in August in a notable upset. Hatcher has since been endorsed by President Donald Trump and faces Democratic candidate Chaz Molder, mayor of Columbia.
The 8th Congressional district also encompasses part of Shelby County and parts of West Tennessee. Republican U.S. Rep. David Kustoff, the incumbent, faces Democratic nominee former Shelby County Criminal Court Clerk Heidi Kuhn and a slate of independent candidates. 
Early voting runs through Oct. 29.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: In Arkansas’ US Senate race, rivals paint Cotton as not focused on the state
text:
Republican U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton faces challenges from Democrat Hallie Shoffner and Libertarian Jeff Wadlin in his bid for reelection. (Courtesy of the Arkansas Secretary of State's office)Twelve years after he was elected in one of the most expensive Senate races in the country, Sen. Tom Cotton has become one of the most prominent Republicans in Washington and a leading defender of President Donald Trump.
His rivals, Democrat Hallie Shoffner and Libertarian Jeff Wadlin, say Arkansas has fallen by the wayside as Cotton’s raised his profile.
Shoffner and Wadlin are criticizing Cotton as absent from the state, and point to his refusal to participate in debates with them as emblematic of that absence.
“My personal opinion is that he’s a coward… and he should make himself available to his constituents,” Wadlin said.
Republicans have held every statewide and federal office in Arkansas for over a decade. But Trump’s low approval rating and rising concerns about affordability have put Republican states in play and have Arkansas Democrats believing the race is competitive. Shoffner’s campaign has caught national attention, though not the national spending seen in other states.
Cotton and Shoffner had agreed to a debate hosted by Salem Media Group, a conservative Christian outlet. Salem Media did not invite Wadlin to the debate, he said, and the outlet retracted the offer to Cotton and Shoffner this month.
A Cotton spokesperson said the senator had been hoping to make Shoffner answer for her comments on illegal immigration. In September, Cotton’s team began running TV ads quoting Shoffner saying in a podcast interview that Arkansas farmers would “trade five Americans for just one” undocumented immigrant worker.

Cotton’s absence takes center stage at debate between Arkansas’ US Senate candidates

 

Shoffner’s family farmed soybeans in Jackson County for 150 years until she closed the farm due to financial strain last year. She told the Advocate she was relaying another farmer’s words rather than speaking for herself or her family.
“Tom Cotton is going to clip up everything that I say, and he’s going to mischaracterize it,” Shoffner said. “And he’s doing it because he’s scared, because he hasn’t had a town hall in nine and a half years, because he hasn’t shown up for the people of Arkansas.”
The idea that Cotton doesn’t truly represent the state has been a consistent refrain of his opponents throughout the election cycle, including the primaries. Shoffner and Wadlin said they have met people frustrated with the high costs of necessities.
The Arkansans Shoffner has met while campaigning don’t talk to her about how Cotton’s ads portray her, she said.
“With gas being over $4 a gallon in a state in which we drive 30 minutes to an hour to get anywhere, with grocery prices the way they are… These are the things I hear about on the campaign trail,” Shoffner said.
Wadlin said he has traveled to all 75 counties and found “an interesting mix” of Arkansans enthused by his campaign, including “center-right conservatives who are frustrated with Tom Cotton.”
“I get this heterogenous mix of people who are independents, Libertarians and disengaged voters who otherwise wouldn’t vote at all,” Wadlin said.
Cotton’s team did not respond to a list of emailed questions from the Arkansas Advocate.
On his campaign website, Cotton touts himself as someone who “uses his influence in the U.S. Senate to deliver for Arkansas,” citing his support for tax cuts and the growth of the state’s defense industry since he took office.
“[These] are the popular things that Arkansans want their senator to be doing: putting money back in their pocket through tax cuts, supporting our military, supporting our law enforcement, securing our border, keeping them safe and helping their families prosper,” Cotton told 40/29 News in a September interview.



Quotation







Tom Cotton is going to clip up everything that I say, and he’s going to mischaracterize it, and he's doing it because he's scared.


– Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Hallie Shoffner


 Cotton, Republicans outspending rivals in race

Democrats have not won a statewide or U.S. House race in Arkansas since 2010. 
Cotton unseated Democratic U.S. Sen. Mark Pryor in 2014 and easily won reelection in 2020 against only a Libertarian opponent after the Democrat challenging Cotton dropped out after the filing period. He is the Senate’s third-ranking Republican and chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee.
Democrats see rare signs of hope in solidly red Arkansas’ midterms

Most national political forecasters have rated Arkansas’ Senate race as solidly Republican, though the Almanac of American Politics moved it from safe to “likely” Republican.
A Hendrix College and Talk Business & Politics poll indicated a tight race between Shoffner and Cotton in August, raising Democrats’ hopes for an upset, but the gap widened to show Cotton leading by 9 percentage points this month. The poll had a margin of error of plus or minus 5 percentage points.
Cotton and groups backing him have routinely outraised and outspent his opponents. America One, a conservative super PAC, has spent more than $4.4 million this year on the race, according to Federal Election Commission filings.
Cotton and the Republican Party of Arkansas announced a $1 million effort to get out the vote Oct. 15, days before early voting began.



Quotation







I get this heterogenous mix of people who are independents, Libertarians and disengaged voters who otherwise wouldn’t vote at all.


– Libertarian U.S. Senate candidate Jeff Wadlin


 Healthcare access and costs

Cotton supported the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the sweeping 2025 federal tax and spending legislation Trump signed that will cut Medicaid spending starting Jan. 1. Medicaid serves more than 800,000 low-income and disabled Arkansans.
Shoffner said “the most heartbreaking” conversations she has with Arkansans have been about the future of Medicare and Medicaid. Arkansas was the first Southern state to expand Medicaid, but the Trump administration denied a five-year extension of the program in July. The state is now seeking a temporary two-year extension.
Uninsured and underinsured people delay seeking healthcare because they cannot afford it, only to pay more when they have a medical emergency, and sitting members of Congress have not done enough to fix this, Shoffner said.
“It is time for them to go and be replaced by someone who understands what life is like on the ground, and I do,” she said.
Wadlin said the healthcare system “needs to be totally overhauled” and suggested a “hub-and-spoke system” requiring certain types of care to be available within specific distances of where people live. He acknowledged that the idea is “not the most Libertarian solution” and would take a great deal of effort, but he considers himself a “pragmatic centrist.”
“I want to actually solve problems, and sometimes that does take a public-private partnership,” he said.



Quotation







(These) are the popular things that Arkansans want their senator to be doing: putting money back in their pocket through tax cuts, supporting our military, supporting our law enforcement, securing our border, keeping them safe and helping their families prosper.


– Republican U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton


 Agriculture, tariffs and the Iran war

Shoffner has regularly criticized Cotton’s past votes against the Farm Bill, the federal agriculture spending and policy package that Congress regularly renews. 
Cotton has said past versions of the bill allocated too much money to food aid programs such as the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, which will face spending cuts and higher administrative costs as of Jan. 1.
Senate Democrats have opposed the current Farm Bill recently endorsed by the Senate Agriculture Committee because of SNAP cuts. Shoffner has said she would have voted to advance the bill to get farmers the financial support they need.
The current Farm Bill expired Sept. 30, and Congress recessed without renewing it. Last year, Cotton asked U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins to speed up aid to farmers.
Cotton has distanced himself from one of Trump’s stances on agriculture, opposing the president’s plan to allow more foreign beef in the U.S.
Cotton has broadly supported the Trump administration’s tariffs. He told KATV last week that the U.S. should tariff imported rice “being unlawfully subsidized by other countries,” blaming these subsidies for east Arkansas rice farmers’ financial struggles.
Shoffner’s opposition to Trump’s tariffs, which forced her to close her family’s farm, is a key pillar of her campaign. Wadlin said he would support targeted tariffs on products subsidized by other countries, but he opposes Trump’s “blanket tariffs.”

Issue Spotlight: Where Arkansas’ U.S. Senate candidates stand on the Iran war

 

Additionally, Cotton has been a vocal supporter of the war in Iran that Trump started in February, while Shoffner and Wadlin oppose it. Wadlin said the money that went into the United States’ wars in the Middle East during the past two decades could have funded Social Security, which is expected to have insufficient funds to provide full benefits to beneficiaries in 2032.
“We should be spending money on things that are actually killing people [here] — diabetes, cancer, dementia, heart disease — not nuclear weapons from Iran,” Wadlin said.
Disrupted commerce in the Middle East during the war has caused gasoline and fertilizer prices to spike, and Shoffner said this fuels much of the frustration drawing Arkansans to her campaign.
“A lot of folks who come to my events walk up to me and they’re feeling a lot of anxiety, a lot of sadness, and they’re ready for something different,” she said. “I hope that my campaign provides them with a vision for the future in which they feel that they can not just survive but thrive.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Valley North’s proposed transmission line has sparked a familiar debate over land, resources, power
text:
Along the Shenandoah River in Jefferson County, West Virginia, a roadside sign delivers a pointed message about the proposed Valley North transmission line, which has become the focus of a growing grassroots opposition movement. (Photo by Mike Chalmers for West Virginia Watch)The view from Marc and Elizabeth Shockley’s front porch could easily land in an outdoor magazine. The historic landscape slopes gently downhill away from their home (circa 1790), and tumbles like a painting across Bloomery Road in Charles Town, West Virginia, eventually spilling into the Shenandoah River at the base of the Blue Ridge Mountains on Jefferson County’s eastern edge.   

For 13 years, the Shockleys have lived and farmed hay, beef cattle and corn on their 96-acre postcard of a plot, which they named Mulberry Hill Farm — just 15 minutes from downtown Charles Town.  

Like their neighbors, the land in this part of the county represents many things — above all else, a living, a dream setting. A forever home. 
As fate would have it, the swath also means something else to someone else — a potential opportunity for Valley Link Transmission Company LLC, a joint venture among Dominion Energy, FirstEnergy Transmission and Transource Energy. Its proposed Valley North Project would span approximately 260 miles, carrying new 765-kilovolt transmission lines from the coal-fired John E. Amos Power Plant in Putnam County, West Virginia, to Frederick County, Maryland — a colossal infrastructure undertaking that could cut through 20 West Virginia counties and gobble up nearly 7,000 acres of farmland, forests, and residential property along the way.
Elizabeth Shockley stands beneath existing high-voltage transmission lines on her family’s 96-acre farm Charles Town, West Virginia. Shockley and her family fear the proposed Valley North Project will bring additional transmission infrastructure to their property, threatening their agricultural operations, water resources, and way of life. (Photo by Michael Chalmers for West Virginia Watch)
When the Shockleys sit on their front porch in the evenings, like many nearby, they’re reminded of why they chose this part of West Virginia to call home. When they spend their days working out back — already bordered by power line towers over 100 feet tall — they can’t help but wonder what the future holds, and if there’s even a place in it for them and their family. 
“Between here and the highway, which you can see through the trees in the winter, there could be four sets of transmission lines within walking distance of us if Valley Link gets approved,” Elizabeth said. “What’s the ramifications of that?”
For Shockley, the prospect of another transmission corridor raises questions that extend well beyond the view from her back door. Mulberry Hill Farm is a working agricultural operation, with hay and corn fields and a cow-calf business that helps support the family, including a son-in-law employed in the operation. The possibility of massive transmission towers rising through those fields presents a host of practical concerns.
“There have been things written about fertility in cattle, and that’s what we do,” she said. “That’s a serious worry for us.”
Water is another pressing concern. The Shockleys recently drilled a replacement well that had to reach six times deeper than the original. The experience has heightened their anxiety about what extensive drilling required to stabilize towers that could reach nearly 200 feet high might mean for the underground water sources sustaining their farm.
“What will all that drilling do to the water table here and the aquifer system?” she asked. “We can’t survive here without water for our cattle.”
Beyond water and livestock, the family has reservations about navigating farm equipment around transmission structures in cultivated fields, the potential for wildfires, and the possibility of herbicide applications along maintained rights-of-way. The latter is particularly troubling for a family that tries to minimize chemical interventions in its agricultural practices.
“We try really hard to avoid that stuff,” Shockley said, referring to the potential spraying within Valley Link’s projected 200-foot easement surrounding either side of the proposed towers. “We try to keep our cattle as free of antibiotics or anything else as we can.”
And then there are questions about exposure. While the health implications of transmission-line exposure remain a subject of scientific research and debate, the uncertainty itself weighs heavily on Shockley and her husband. “My grandkids run around here. What are the health risks for them? That’s a real concern for us.”
Dan McGinn stands on his 270-acre Jefferson County, West Virginia, property, where proposed Valley North transmission routes threaten historic farmland dating to the 18th century. McGinn has become a leading voice in the growing opposition to the project. (Photo by Michael Chalmers for West Virginia Watch)
Land, legacy and leverage  
For Dan McGinn, the fight against Valley North is about more than transmission lines. It’s about history, property rights and an all-too-familiar West Virginia predicament — sacrificing land and resources for the benefit of someone somewhere else.
McGinn and his wife moved to Jefferson County in 2012, undertaking an extensive restoration of a 270-acre property overlooking the Shenandoah River. The land, anchored by a home dating back to approximately 1740, has documented ties to George Washington and the region’s early westward expansion. Under two proposed route alternatives, transmission towers and the 200-foot easement could cut through the property’s fields or pass directly in front of the historic home.
“We came here because we love history,” McGinn said. “We feel like the history in this county is underappreciated and under-promoted. This is one of the five most historic counties in America, and I say that without any hesitation.”
McGinn has since become one of the project’s most vocal opponents, publishing commentary through his Substack and the website Say No to Valley Link, organizing residents, and personally funding research and mailers throughout Jefferson County. Alongside groups such as Jefferson County VOLT (Voices Opposing Line Transmission), opponents have been pressing elected officials and raising public awareness about a project they believe offers little to no local benefit.
At the center of their argument is a fundamental question: Why should West Virginians surrender thousands of acres of land to accommodate growing electricity demand elsewhere — particularly northern Virginia’s sprawling data center industry?
“This is just an extension cord,” McGinn said. “No one can give you any legitimate reason why this benefits the state of West Virginia.”
Opponents argue that without a local substation to deliver electricity to Jefferson County, residents would bear the environmental and property impacts without receiving a corresponding direct power supply. McGinn also disputes the project’s underlying demand projections and warns that West Virginia ratepayers could face substantial costs for infrastructure he believes primarily serves northern Virginia.
“This is not just a power line fight,” he said. “It’s an electric utility bill tax fight because every single resident and every single business is going to pay a higher electric bill to support this.”
Through McGinn’s reach, the movement has attracted support from prominent figures, including filmmaker Ken Burns, author Malcolm Gladwell, musician Marty Stuart, and Bass Pro Shops founder Johnny Morris. Yet McGinn maintains that the opposition’s greatest strength lies with ordinary residents — farmers, tradespeople, teachers, veterans and families facing the possibility of losing control over land they’ve spent generations maintaining.
“Who’s going to fight for them?” he asked.
For McGinn, the disparity is especially troubling given the possibility of eminent domain, which could ultimately allow the acquisition of property rights without landowners’ consent.
“It’s a ridiculously imbalanced fight that we’re trying to wage here,” he said. “But what I told the community is we have the moral high ground, and I don’t say that lightly. We do.”
And increasingly, he believes, the public agrees. “The more people know about it, the more opposed they are,” he said.
Jefferson County Commissioner Cara Keys shares McGinn’s concerns. Although the commission has formally opposed Valley North, submitted public comments and held town halls, it has no direct authority to approve or reject the project — a reality Keys finds particularly troubling given the potential consequences for local landowners and the county’s long-term planning.
“I think it’s frustrating as a local leader when decisions, in this case at the West Virginia (Public Service Commission), and of course the PSC in other states, and federal, have the authority to negate our planning for economic development — our planned areas to remain agricultural in nature,” she said.
Like McGinn, Keys questions the absence of any direct energy benefit to Jefferson County, comparing the proposed transmission corridor to “… highways in the sky that have no on- or off-ramp. Without a local substation, the county would bear the impacts of infrastructure intended to serve electricity demand elsewhere.”
Still, Keys believes coordinated opposition from affected counties across West Virginia, Virginia and Maryland could influence the regulatory process. “Though county commissioners don’t have a codified voice, potentially working with all of the impacted counties as a whole package will show strength to the PSC.”
Promises and property lines 
Valley Link, however, disputes the characterization that Valley North is primarily intended to serve northern Virginia’s data centers.
“The Valley North Project is not being developed for a specific data center, county, customer or industry,” said Lauren Siburkis, spokesperson for the project. She explained that PJM Interconnection, the regional electric grid operator, selected Valley North to address long-term reliability needs driven by growing electricity demand from manufacturing, economic development, population growth and emerging technologies.
Siburkis also pointed to projected economic benefits, including nearly $14 million annually in property tax revenue across West Virginia, with approximately $9 million supporting schools. Jefferson County alone could receive nearly $1 million annually, according to the company’s estimates.
She emphasized that no final route has been selected and that public feedback is helping shape the process.
“The goal is to avoid or minimize impacts to homes, farms, businesses and important community resources wherever feasible,” she said. “If a property is ultimately located along an approved route, Valley Link would work directly with the landowner to discuss easement needs, property-specific considerations and fair compensation. In most cases, landowners retain ownership of their property and can continue many of its existing uses.”
For Jefferson County resident Lisa Boyer, those assurances offer little comfort.
She and her husband, James, own a 113-acre Jefferson County farm that has been in his family for more than a century. Alongside their dog-boarding business, the couple raises hay for their animals and for sale, while maintaining roughly 5 acres of wildlife habitat threaded with trails where Boyer rides her horse.

Lisa Boyer stands beside a sign opposing Valley Link on her family’s 113-acre Jefferson County farm. Under one proposed route, transmission towers would follow the road in the right side of the photo, cutting through the property behind her and threatening farmland and wildlife habitat maintained by the family for generations. (Photo by Michael Chalmers for West Virginia Watch)
Boyer said neither she nor her husband have been contacted directly by Valley Link. From conversations with neighbors, she believes others in the area have been similarly overlooked. 
“It just feels like this giant corporation is coming in and doing whatever it wants, without any consideration for the people who actually live here,” she said.
Under one proposed route, Boyer fears losing a substantial portion of their hayfield and much of the habitat, along with facing potential impacts to their well, property value, and retirement plans.
“It’s devastating,” she said. “It’s the last thing I think about when I go to bed, and the first thing I think about when I wake up in the morning.”
Already crossed by existing transmission lines, the property could ultimately be surrounded on three sides by high-voltage infrastructure. Boyer questions why alternatives along existing utility corridors, highways, or railroads weren’t pursued instead.
“It’s exhausting to think that we’ve taken care of this land for a hundred years in the family, we’ve paid taxes on it and they’re allowed to come and bulldoze through it,” she said.
For Boyer, the uncertainty has shaken something more fundamental than the future of the farm itself. “You think you’re protected on your own land. And then one day, you realize: do I even really own it?”
Looking ahead
Ultimately, the Valley North Project’s future rests with state utility regulators. Although regional grid operator PJM Interconnection selected the project to address electric grid reliability needs, Valley Link must still obtain separate approvals from the West Virginia Public Service Commission, Virginia State Corporation Commission and Maryland Public Service Commission before constructing the proposed transmission line.
In West Virginia, regulators must determine whether the project addresses electricity needs or regional reliability, serves the best interests of West Virginia customers and citizens and strikes an acceptable balance between power demands and environmental impacts. Proposed routes, landowner concerns and evidence submitted by opponents could all factor into that review.
Valley Link currently anticipates filing regulatory applications in early to mid-2027. Until then, residents can continue submitting comments, attending public meetings, gathering evidence and pressing elected officials. Once applications are filed, the process will shift toward formal regulatory proceedings, where testimony, technical evidence, and legal arguments could play decisive roles. Under West Virginia law, property owners within the preferred transmission corridor must also receive notice by certified mail at least 30 business days before the PSC’s deadline for filing petitions to intervene, giving affected landowners an opportunity to participate formally in the proceedings.
For opponents, those proceedings will represent a critical opportunity to challenge the project’s necessity, proposed routes and impacts. And should West Virginia regulators deny the required certificate, that decision could present a major obstacle to Valley North’s construction along its proposed corridor.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Dickinson State finance investigation calls for more oversight, support from University System
text:
Meredith Larson, chief operating officer for the North Dakota University System, speaks during a committee hearing on Oct. 6, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)An accounting firm’s investigation into the financial management and reporting at Dickinson State University has yielded a group of recommendations, including more support and oversight from the North Dakota University System.
The University System, led by Commissioner Brent Sanford, has been discussing creation of a shared services system to support North Dakota’s smaller colleges that have struggled to attract and retain employees with expertise in areas such as accounting, payroll and financial aid. 
The investigation was triggered by the dismissal of the vice president of finance at Dickinson State University in December 2025, Deputy Commissioner Meredith Larson told the Legislature’s Higher Education Funding Review Committee earlier this month. Larson, Sanford and Dickinson State President Scott Molander discussed the results of the investigation by investigative firm CliftonLarsonAllen with the committee.
North Dakota University System envisions more collaboration, efficiency

University System officials told investigators that poor cash flow management put the university at risk of not being able to meet payroll obligations in December 2025.
Larson said the report shows that there needs to be “a layer of validation” at the University System office.
“I think we have learned that it is really critical to engage in more aggressive performance management with people when there are signs that somebody is not — particularly your VP of finance — is not responding to requests, doesn’t seem to have the requisite knowledge,” Larson said. 
The man at the center of the investigation, Leslie Wietstock, the former DSU vice president, said in an interview that he warned DSU officials that cash flow was an issue because of construction and other spending. He said he secured a line of credit to ensure the university had cash until it could hold a bond sale to raise money for the construction projects. 
The investigative report says Dickinson State’s finance office had a high degree of turnover before Wietstock was hired as vice president in September 2022.
The report said the decision to remove Wietstock “was initially driven by concerns regarding workplace conduct, communication, and professional relationships.” After Wietstock left, “additional concerns regarding DSU’s financial condition, cash position, capital project funding, and financial reporting practices came to light, prompting further review,” the report said.
Scott Molander, president of Dickinson State University, speaks during a committee hearing on Oct. 6, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Molander told the legislative committee that he was not happy with the budgeting process he inherited at DSU when he became president in 2025. 
Wietstock was notified in December 2025 that he would be fired, according to documents obtained by the North Dakota Monitor. The documents regarding Wietstock’s termination and a subsequent appeal were not included in the report. 
Molander cited in a letter to Wietstock “substantive deficits in subject matter area expertise, such as the admitted lack of knowledge on bank reconciliations and errors — either intentional or negligent — in critical procurement areas.” 
Wietstock disputed the firing and the findings of the investigation.
“They seem to continue to imply that I don’t know how to do a bank reconciliation,” Wietstock said in an interview. “I’ve been an accountant for 40 years. I think I know how to do a bank reconciliation.”
Since Wietstock’s departure, Dickinson State has since been using financial office staff at North Dakota State University. 
Sanford said that while there have been arrangements where larger colleges have helped smaller colleges with administrative tasks, the system office has not always been looped in on communication as those arrangements evolve. 
The report recommended formal service agreements and periodic performance reviews to promote accountability.
North Dakota University System Commissioner Brent Sanford speaks during a committee hearing on Oct. 6, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Sanford told the committee that while the University of North Dakota and NDSU are large enough to adequately staff key financial expertise positions, the problems at Dickinson State could have happened at any of the nine smaller colleges in the system. 
He said the State Board of Higher Education will evaluate whether shared services positions to help the smaller colleges should be part of the University System office or with UND or NDSU. 
Sanford said the University System doesn’t plan to ask the Legislature to fund new positions, though some positions could shift from campuses to the system office.
The report also highlighted the need for better performance monitoring for key financial leadership positions and fraud and ethics training for leadership and the state board. 
Larson stated the University System is working to become more collaborative among the 11 campuses with a plan called “One NDUS.”
“Within that plan, we will engage in more centralized oversight and accountability for back-of-house services,” Larson said. 
The University System said that through September, it has paid CliftonLarsonAllen more than $80,000 for the investigation.
NDSU, Minot State shoring up shaky bookkeeping at Dickinson, Bottineau

Legislators had different responses to the report. 
Rep. Jamie Selzler, D-Fargo, thanked Molander and Sanford for addressing problems that existed before entering their current roles. But said he had concerns about the system’s responsiveness under previous leadership and wants to ensure that doesn’t happen again. 
“I’m very concerned about performance management going forward,” Selzler said. 
Rep. Steve Swiontek, R-Fargo, said his reading of the report indicated that Molander did not react quickly or aggressively enough after seeing red flags about DSU’s finances. 
Larson agreed that action should have been taken more quickly. 
“We are impressing upon the leaders of our institutions that we must act sooner, and we are going to put in place more consistent oversight,” Larson said. 
The report says that in hindsight, Molander “stated that he wished he had ‘pushed harder’ and more thoroughly evaluated Mr. Wietstock’s financial capabilities earlier in his tenure.”
After being informed in December by Molander that the termination would stand, Wietstock sent a letter in January to the University System office appealing the decision, arguing that the reasons provided by Molander were “inaccurate, undefined, and in some cases untrue.” 
In his appeal letter to Sanford, Wietstock said he felt targeted by co-workers and Molander for ongoing staffing and administrative problems at the college. 
He also said there were no training or procedure manuals to show how to find information he needed in the NDUS PeopleSoft Finance System. 
The report shows that as early as 2023, Wietstock, in an email to University System office finance personnel, said he found the Dickinson State system overly convoluted.
Wietstock was interviewed by CliftonLarsonAllen, but he said most of the accounting firm’s questions were about the bank reconciliation process and not other issues identified in his termination. 
By the time of his firing, Wietstock said had hired a controller and he felt the finance team had been making “significant progress” on DSU accounting. 
Wietstock was informed by Sanford on Oct. 6, after the report was finalized, that his appeal for being terminated was denied. 
Wietstock, who now lives in Fargo, said he doesn’t plan to challenge the termination in court.

title: North Dakota tax commissioner candidates differ on eliminating income tax, direction of the state
text:
From the left, Republican Tax Commissioner Brian Kroshus and Democratic-NPL tax commissioner candidate Mark Nelson (Photos provided by the campaigns)North Dakota voters have a choice for the state’s tax commissioner between the incumbent who says he wants to explore more tax reductions and a challenger who says the Republican-dominated state government is moving in the wrong direction. 
Republican Brian Kroshus is seeking a second four-year term, challenged by Democrat Mark Nelson. North Dakota is the only state with an elected tax commissioner.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The info you need to cast your ballot.]
Kroshus was appointed tax commissioner in late 2021 by then-Gov. Doug Burgum. He had previously served nearly five years on the Public Service Commission. Before then, he worked in the private sector, including as publisher of The Bismarck Tribune. He also owns a cattle and grain operation in western North Dakota.
Kroshus said he wants to keep working with state lawmakers to advance a “low and reasonable tax environment” and make improvements in various tax credit programs. He said he also wants to keep improving everyday interactions with his office, such as keeping call wait times short or nonexistent.
Nelson, a retired Rugby-area farmer, said he is running because “everything in the state is going in the wrong direction and the state is also in crisis.” He cited Trump administration tariffs hurting North Dakota’s farm communities and the president’s trade war with Canada turning away tourists.
He said North Dakotans have told him they want state officials “to stop being stupid with our money.” 
Nelson opposes eliminating the state individual income tax, saying it would put too much pressure on property taxes and give “more welfare to people who can actually afford to pay the bill.”
Kroshus said officials should explore eliminating the state income tax, and he is not opposed to doing so. But many citizens would argue that additional property tax cuts are more important, he said.
Property taxes eliminated for 50,000 North Dakota households under new legislation

“I think we have to be careful when it comes to making sure that we still have the appropriate revenue collection tools in place to fund the services that the state provides,” Kroshus said.
Renters probably didn’t see any reduction after the 2025 Legislature boosted the primary residence property tax credit for homeowners, Nelson said. Since the Bakken oil boom, there’s barely any place a person can rent affordably, he said.
Kroshus said he would look for ways to increase the credit amounts for the primary residence, disabled veteran and homestead tax credits. The renter’s refund program also deserves more attention, he said.
Nelson criticized North Dakota’s Republican supermajority control. No Democrat has won a statewide election since Heidi Heitkamp’s 2012 U.S. Senate run. Nelson said, “There are so many people who are just tired of living in a failed red state.” 
Kroshus said he is focused on his own work, and it’s up to voters to decide who will hold state offices and legislative seats. 
“My job as an incumbent is to continue to work hard on behalf of the citizens, stay focused on what I’m tasked to do, and I’ll just leave it at that,” he said.
The tax commissioner oversees a two-year budget of more than $127 million and an office of 117 full-time employees. The annual salary is $145,314.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Commentary: What the town kept and what it couldn’t lend
text:
Book bans, like a recent one in Jefferson County, Tennessee, in which school administrators removed 32 titles from book shelves, deprive children of finding versions of themselves they can't see elsewhere. (Photo: Holly McCall/Tennessee Lookout)I was raised in Erin, Tennessee, by people who would drive forty minutes with a casserole to a family they had never liked, and I want that said before anything else, because everything I’m about to describe happened inside a place that loved me in the only currency it had on hand.
A small town gives a kid a kind of attention a city can’t afford. Everyone knew whose boy I was, so when I walked to church on a Wednesday there were six porches that would have noticed if I hadn’t arrived. I learned to sing in that building. I learned what it sounds like when a whole room agrees on something, and I learned that a casserole dish returned unwashed is a small insult while one returned clean with something in it is a conversation. Most of what I know about plot I took from the women at the folding table in the fellowship hall, passing the news down the line the way you pass a plate, with the worst part saved for whoever sat last.



				I remember the first book I took home that nobody at church would have approved of, and how I carried it against my stomach under my shirt, the way you carry something warm that might still be alive.			


I was also a Black gay boy in a place where the pulpit had already decided what I was, and nobody was cruel about it, which made it harder to argue with. Nobody had to be. The whole town was kind to a version of me that did not exist, and I spent my childhood learning to answer  to him, to fold my hands the way he would, to laugh at the right pause, to keep the other boy in the back room like a coat I wasn’t ready to be seen owning.
What I needed was proof that the coat could be worn, and proof lived in books. The books lived forty minutes away, or in a library that kept hours built for adults with cars. I remember the first book I took home that nobody at church would have approved of, and how I carried it against my stomach under my shirt, the way you carry something warm that might still be alive. I read it in the bathroom with the fan on. The fan was louder than I needed, and I think part of me wanted the house to hear that something was being kept in there.
It was a love story, and I didn’t know until I was grown that it had been a very ordinary one. What it gave me was the plain fact that a person like me had been written down, on purpose, by someone who stayed alive long enough to do it. Nobody in Erin could have given me that. They didn’t have it to give, and I have never held that against them.
Last week, Jefferson County Schools pulled 32 books from its libraries under Tennessee’s Age Appropriate Materials Act. The director of schools said that with 25,000 books and two librarians, nobody can know every word of every one, and I believe him, and I thought about the fan. I don’t know which 32 they were. I know there is a boy in that county tonight who is going to need something small and warm to carry home against his stomach, and that the shelf he would have reached for is a little emptier than the one I had, and mine was not full.
I don’t think the people deciding are villains, because I grew up among them and they brought me food when my grandmother died. That is what makes this hard to write. The same hands that held the dish are the hands that close the cabinet, and both are acts of love as they understand it, and neither one reaches the boy.
My family is still in Erin. When I call, they tell me who died, who got saved, and whose boy is home, and when they ask what I’m working on I say a book, and they say that’s nice, and we both let the pause do what it has always done. I love that town the way you love a house with one room painted shut. I don’t need it to stop being itself. I only wish someone had left one shelf low enough, and quiet enough, and nobody’s business, so that a boy could take what he needed home under his shirt and not have to wonder whether it would still be there the next time he was brave enough to go back.
