name: Alabama Reflector
title: Commentary: The lasting damage of anti-transgender hysteria
text:
Advocates for transgender rights rallied outside the Statehouse in Trenton, New Jersey, on Jan. 5, 2026. (Dana DiFilippo / New Jersey Monitor)This era of cruelty and corruption will end. 
But we all see the damage it’s wrought. The aggressive nihilism. The smug elevation of power, trampling rights and restraints to suit those who rule. 
Many Americans have seen this brutality engulf their loved ones or felt it in their bones. The destruction wrought by anti-transgender hysteria might be among the hardest to repair.
It’s denied Alabamians critical healthcare. Federal judges gave our Legislature sweeping power to ignore medical consensus when moral panic rules the day. Transgender youth are now second-class citizens, denied access to activities because they exist, not due to any scientific determination.
And the attacks keep coming. One study estimated that between August and October, over $100 million was spent on political spots containing the phrase “sex change.” Alabama’s U.S. senators use valuable time in the upper chamber to threaten the civil rights of transgender people. The chair of the Alabama Republican Party said two candidates for the Alabama House who are transgender had “mental disorders.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
For all that, few voters appear to share the priorities of the gonad obsessives. A CNN poll last month found the issue ranked last in importance for those surveyed. A poll released last week found Democrats more trusted on transgender issues than Republicans. A prominent Republican in Texas — where anti-transgender advertising has taken the place of nitrogen in the atmosphere — says the attacks seem to be having little effect.
Does this mean we’ll get some relief from this ceaseless dehumanization of a small group of people? 
I doubt it. If this were simple political opportunism, Alabama Republicans would drop the hysteria as quickly as they erased Jeff Sessions from their memories.
But it’s more than that. The anti-transgender hysteria is the most recent eruption of an Alabama mindset, one that’s taken a feverish intensity in the post-COVID era: There is one way to live, and it is the way our leaders live.
Alabama is a diverse state with a government that generally rejects plurality. We stopped issuing marriage licenses because a handful of probate judges hate same-sex marriage. The state Legislature immediately overrode Birmingham when it tried to create a local minimum wage.
But pre-COVID, non-conservative spaces were tolerated. Former state Supreme Court Justice Roy Moore and the probate judges aside, no one seriously challenged the fact of same-sex marriage. Cities had broad scope to rule themselves, provided they didn’t cross the Business Council of Alabama.
Now look at what we’ve seen since 2021.
First came the laws limiting transgender Alabamians’ ability to use the bathroom. Then the Legislature made it a felony for a doctor to provide gender-affirming care to a transgender youth. And finally, they banned transgender youth from playing sports in a way that’s consistent with their gender identity. Nothing less than a public effort to drive a group of citizens into shadows and silence.
This was revolting. But it worked. The federal courts blessed the offensive. And it emboldened those demanding uniformity in Alabama civic life. The cruelty and humiliation of the anti-transgender campaign quickly spread.
University instructors can now lose their jobs if they teach from a hazy list of “divisive concepts.” Our flagship universities drove Black and LGBTQ+ students out of public spaces. Professors now face post-tenure reviews. Their ability to decide how they teach students has been limited, if not curtailed.
State lawmakers revived the state’s Jim Crow traditions of treating Black Alabamians’ political views as inherently illegitimate. Our Legislature worked to reduce their representation in the congressional delegation. They’ve moved heaven and Earth to make voting harder, banning ballot drop boxes and criminalizing certain forms of assistance. And now we hear a gubernatorial candidate threaten to send the National Guard into the state’s major cities. 
Crime is down. A militia is not law enforcement. The leadership yawns. Voter fraud is almost nonexistent in Alabama. They shrug.
Because none of this is rational. But transgender hysteria isn’t rational, either. It is a rejection of reality for ideology; an angry swipe at a minority and, by extension, the plurality that rebukes a vision of conformity. Contradictory evidence does not disturb a zealot’s convictions. 
That’s why the attacks keep coming, even when Alabamians reject them. That’s why the attacks get more vicious, and the ethical floor for discourse keeps falling. A small group of leaders have been given the power to make the state into a Thomas Kinkade painting: Saturated, quaint and void of humanity. The vision must come to life.
It’s an impractical project. Alabama is home to many different people whose rights must be upheld. Whose right to exist is not open to debate. And who keep demonstrating resilience.
But that never stopped irrational creeds from shoving individuals into a cramped forgery of life. The wounds from this effort will take a long time to heal. 
And as long as that obedience-first mindset reigns in Montgomery, the damage will grow. And make repairs even more difficult when this cruel era ends.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Palmer, Mercer face off in Alabama’s 6th Congressional District
text:
U.S. Rep. Gary Palmer, R-Hoover (left) is seeking his seventh term representing Alabama's 6th Congressional District. He faces Democratic nominee Maurice Mercer (right), a former member of the Pelham City Council. (Photos courtesy of the candidates; photo illustration by Brian Lyman)The race for Alabama’s 6th Congressional District features a longtime incumbent against a former president of the Pelham City Council. 
U.S. Rep. Gary Palmer, R-Hoover, seeking his seventh term in office, will face Democratic nominee Maurice Mercer, who won the Democratic nomination for the district against Ashtyn Kennedy in the August 11 Democratic special primary. The district is among the most conservative in the country. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report lists the district as “Solid Republican.”
The 6th Congressional District spans portions of Jefferson County outside Birmingham, alongside Autauga, Elmore, Coosa, Chilton, Shelby, and part of Talladega counties. The district saw some alteration after Republican lawmakers implemented its controversial and previously contested 2023 congressional maps earlier this year.

The candidates

Palmer is a stalwart conservative who supports abortion restrictions, gun access and opposes measures that would give legal status to immigrants. He has called for repealing the Affordable Care Act and reducing regulations on businesses.
Questions for comment were sent to Palmer’s campaign on Monday. As of Friday, he had not responded. 
In a March 5 press release, Palmer praised the attacks on Iran.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“I’m thankful that President Trump, as the Commander in Chief, approved Operation Epic Fury and took action to protect our nation, neutralize this threat, and hold Iran accountable for their decades of attacks against America,” Palmer said. 
On June 3, Palmer voted alongside Republicans to block the War Powers Resolution to end hostilities with Iran. 
“The people of the 6th District are hardworking, faithful, and conservative to the core,” Palmer said on social media of his primary victory on August 11. “They are small business owners, farmers, parents, veterans, and neighbors who get up every day and do the right thing for their families and their communities
Palmer, who has served since 2015, drew criticism from candidates in both parties for running for a sixth term in Congress in 2024 after saying in 2014 he would only serve 10 years. Palmer claimed that it was God’s plan for him to stay in office. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The cost of living—of gas, groceries, utilities—is drawing opposition from every corner of the political spectrum. Since January of last year, gas prices have risen by roughly 33% amid the ongoing war with Iran. Trump’s tariff war is also projected to cost households an average $820 in 2026. 
Mercer, like Democrats across the country, is heavily centering his campaigns on economic affordability to challenge sitting Republicans.
“[Affordability] is a central theme that everybody’s heard, it doesn’t matter what political party you normally subscribe to—pain at the pump and at the grocery store,” said Mercer, a former president of the Pelham City Council, in an interview on Monday.
Palmer has also said in the past that affordability concerns and rural health care are among his top priorities. He voted in favor of budget reconciliation measures aimed at dismantling parts of the ACA and reducing federal health spending, maintaining that his positions were focused on reducing the national deficit and curbing government overspending.
Palmer has said that addressing economic affordability and rural healthcare access remain among his top priorities. He has also pursued efforts during his tenure to dismantle key parts of the ACA and Medicare.
Mercer argued that domestic financial strain has less to do with federal programs and more to do with international obligations. 
“Things are unaffordable for Americans, but we’re spending money overseas,” he said.
If Democrats restore a majority in the House, Mercer pledged to reclaim Article 1 constitutional powers by leveraging the War Powers Act to restrain executive overreach, subpoenaing officials, and prioritize a complete withdrawal of troops to redirect resources back home.
However, Mercer said the war is not the only reason for all the economic hardship; he points to the rollback of social programs. 
The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) caught Pelham residents before they fell on hard times, Mercer said. Last year, congressional Republicans, including Palmer, voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which pushed more of the costs of maintaining the program to the states and required them to fix “error rates” or face penalties.  
“We’ve really got to think. Hey, these tax cuts that we gave to the ultra-wealthy Besos, Zuckerbergs, Elons of the world—the trickle-down is not trickling,” Mercer said.
He said more should be done to protect these programs as well as everyone who pays into them, including immigrants.
“I think everybody that I talk to agrees that the current way that ICE is handling the situation is inhumane,” Mercer observed. “There’s no due process. Families are being separated. Some people have been unalived in this process, and that needs to stop. We can secure our borders without unaliving people, separating families, and creating stress And having members of our community distraught.”
In an August Facebook post, Palmer characterized the Democrats as part of a “radical socialist agenda of the Democratic Party that wants to take money out of your pockets, open your borders, and grow the government into every corner of your life.”
Mercer said there is nothing radical about representing all people, making sure more people have access to healthcare, an affordable life and an end to ICE brutality. 
“We’re on the agenda of the people and making sure we represent all people. I’ve got a history of working across the aisle and representing all people—and that’s what we’ll do,” he said.

Fundraising

According to the most recent campaign filings, Palmer raised $1,138,127.83, of which 51% ($581,693.46) came from individual contributions. He has spent $1,187,383.43, with no funds remaining as of September 30. 
Maurice Mercer has raised $30,338.54 of which 79% ($18,789.58) came from individual contributions. He has spent $17,231.53, with $13,107.01 as of September 30.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Commentary: What happens when Kentuckians have the chance to work through their differences?
text:
Last March, CivicLex organized the first Civic Assembly in Lexington to review Lexington's merged government charter. (Photo courtesy Brandon Turner, Unsung Hero Media)Earlier this year, 30 Lexington residents, selected at random, spent more than 30 hours together talking about something that most of us don’t think about at all: the rules that underpin our local government.
These residents were Republicans, Democrats, and independents. They were younger and older, from different socioeconomic backgrounds. Some followed local issues closely. Others came knowing absolutely nothing about local government. And yet, after seven sessions of learning, discussion, and plenty of debate, they reached 85% agreement on three recommendations to change Lexington’s city charter.
At a time when much of our national conversation focuses on how divided we are, Lexington’s First Civic Assembly shows that real people can still come together and solve real problems.
This process was organized by CivicLex, the nonpartisan nonprofit that I run. A few years ago, members of Lexington’s Urban County Council approached us about reviewing Lexington’s charter, the document that lays out the basic rules for our merged city-county government. The last comprehensive review of the charter took place in 1998, and the only recommendation to reach the ballot then – a measure to expand council terms to four years – was soundly defeated.
We knew charter reform would be difficult. Most residents don’t have the time or inclination to study such a complicated document. But, we believed decisions about the basic rules of government shouldn’t be left entirely to elected officials or appointed “experts.”
In looking around at potential examples for tackling an issue like this, we learned about citizens’ assemblies, which bring together residents selected by a representative lottery to learn about an issue, deliberate, and develop recommendations. 
We thought this could be the perfect solution. So, we spent three years organizing one in Lexington.
We mailed 10,000 invitations to randomly selected Fayette County addresses. From those who applied, we used a software to select a randomized group of residents that closely reflected our community across political registration, age, race, income, education, and more to be our Assembly. Throughout March, participants learned about local government, heard from experts, debated different solutions, and developed their own recommendations. You can watch recordings of these sessions online.
This is quite different from the way we typically ask people to participate in government. Most public meetings give residents a few minutes at a microphone to share opinions, often about decisions already largely developed.
The Assembly was a big ask. Residents spent evenings and weekends learning about the complicated ins and outs of local government. They built new friendships with people they’d just met and who came from vastly different life experiences. They found points of disagreement and compromised, merging together the proposals they generated into ones that could pass the voting threshold they themselves set: no recommendation would be adopted without 80% support.
One question they had to answer was whether Lexington should change Urban County councilmember salaries. On one hand, low compensation can make public service difficult for people who can’t afford it. On the other, asking residents to support higher pay for politicians is…a difficult proposition.
After weeks of deliberation, the Assembly arrived at a recommendation that 85% supported: raising Council salaries from roughly $42,000 to $59,987, the average annual wage in Lexington, beginning in 2031. The Assembly also recommended public attendance and accountability standards for councilmembers, which received 89% support.  
The third recommendation? That Lexington adopt the very process they were going through as a way to review the charter on a fixed schedule, every eight years. This recommendation also received  89% support.
These weren’t unanimous decisions. Some of the participants disagreed — but everyone agreed that the process itself was a success. An independent evaluation by an organization called FIDE found that participants’ knowledge of the issues nearly doubled. Seventy-four percent of participants said their views on council compensation changed during the Assembly, while 65% said the same about charter review. Perhaps more interestingly, the percentage of participants who believed ordinary residents could develop strong policy recommendations rose from 60% to 83%. And 96% said they gained a sense of community through the process.
In so much of our political discourse, it feels like people just show up with their preexisting opinions and defend them. In our Assembly, participants were listening and reconsidering what they thought. People actually changed their mind — in opposite directions — when receiving new evidence. They debated respectfully and found common ground, all while building bonds with those they disagreed with.
The process wasn’t perfect. Some participants wanted more time, and 30 Lexington residents certainly haven’t solved political division in Kentucky, much less America.
But I wonder how much of our difficulty working across differences has to do with the way we ask people to participate in public life. What happens when we give people time to really wrestle with local civic issues, equip them with good information, let them build relationships, and give them the real responsibility to develop something together?
In this case, their three recommendations are now on the November 3 ballot, where Fayette County voters will have the final say.
We won’t always agree about what our communities should do. Nor should we expect to! But maybe we can do a better job of creating opportunities for Kentuckians to take on difficult questions together.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Not a ‘David and Goliath race’: Dems challenge long-standing Republicans in KY House races
text:
Democratic Congressional Candidate John Drew Williams speaks on Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026, at the annual St. Jerome Picnic in Fancy Farm, Ky. (Austin Anthony / Kentucky Lantern)John “Drew” Williams has put around 140,000 miles on his car since he began running as a Democratic challenger to incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. James Comer last year. 
That’s amounted to about 15 oil changes, but Williams has traveled across the 1st Congressional District, which spans from West Kentucky to Frankfort. 
“I knew that even if it was just me and my car and $30,000 by the end of the campaign, I would at least be able to put a different kind of bend into it than typically was done,” Williams said of his campaign. He previously worked on Democratic campaigns in the district and with a county Democratic party. 
Williams is not alone in challenging a Republican in what are considered solid red congressional districts in Kentucky. Race raters like The Cook Political Report call Kentucky’s 1st, 2nd, 4th and 5th Congressional Districts very safe Republican territories. The Kentucky Lantern spoke to some of the candidates running what appear to be long-shot campaigns. Democratic U.S. Rep. Morgan McGarvey appears to be safe in the 3rd Congressional District and faces GOP challenger Maria Teresa Rodriguez. The 6th Congressional District, an open seat, is close between Democrat Zach Dembo and Republican Ralph Alvarado. 
Megan Wingfield, who is the Democrat running against U.S. Rep. Brett Guthrie in the 2nd Congressional District, said she disagreed with the notion that the district is solid red. Guthrie has represented the area since first being elected in 2008. 
“I tell folks all the time, Congressman Guthrie has no one to blame but himself for me stepping into this race because had he just listened to us, perhaps I wouldn’t have felt it necessary to try to go and be the voice for my community, and try to fight for everyday working-class Kentuckians, regardless of what the little letter is beside their name,” Wingfield said. 
She added that she’s heard a lot from voters in the district on local issues, like data centers. In recent months, a proposal by Kentucky Industrial Alliance to build a hyperscale data center near Mammoth Cave National Park in Barren County has raised a lot of controversy. Other topics include affordability issues like buying groceries and gas, paying bills and having access to health care. 
“So, if he feels safe and secure in his seat, then to me, that’s just another testament of how he’s not actually paying attention to what’s happening here,” Wingfield said. 
Out in Eastern Kentucky, Prestonsburg attorney Ned Pillersdorf is running against incumbent U.S. Rep. Hal Rogers, who has become known as the “Dean of the House” as the body’s longest serving member. He was first elected in 1981. 
Democratic congressional candidate Ned Pillersdorf speaks to voters in Knott County. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)
While Rogers is widely expected to get another term in Congress, Pillersdorf has gained support from notable Eastern Kentucky Democrats, like former Gov. Paul Patton. In an ad supporting Pillersdorf, Patton made an issue of Rogers’ age, saying: “I’m 89 years old — about the same as Rogers — and I’m too old for Congress.” 
Before releasing the ad online, Pillersdorf held a small town hall in Knott County. Afterwards, he told the Lantern “I don’t think it’s a David and Goliath race” and he was seeing an increase in donations to his campaign amid Trump’s war in Iran and rising gas prices. As of Oct. 22, Pillersdorf’s campaign had about $368,000 while Rogers’ had about $973,000. 
“Admittedly, when I first started out, I had people tell me it’s uphill. I’m not hearing that anymore,” Pillersdorf said. 
‘It’s not about winning all the time’
Wingfield, who is a mechanic and an activist in her community, said that she has heard some Democrats view running in what’s seen as Republican territory as a “lost cause.” Some candidates have even tried to switch parties in hopes of getting elected. 
She said she tries to tell others that “it’s not about winning all the time.” 
Megan Wingfield of Bowling Green chants and marches while holding a banner reading “Free Ernesto” during the “No Kings” protest in Bowling Green, Ky., on Saturday, June 14, 2025. The banner refers to the recent detainment of local teenager Ernesto Manuel-Andres by ICE, despite his legal status. He was later released. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Austin Anthony)
“It’s more important that we challenge these folks, challenge these incumbents who’ve been comfortable and sitting there for a long time, and make them less comfortable and actually perhaps maybe make them work a little bit for the first time in a long time, and if we can even just move the needle just a little bit, then that is a win to me,” Wingfield added. 
Back out in West Kentucky, Williams said he felt like his own campaign was partly about building infrastructure to “move the needle more to the center, even if we don’t win.” That connection with voters can play a role in future elections, he said. 
“Where a lot of these counties started off in May of last year compared to where we are now is a completely different beast, and so I’m excited about that and whatnot,” Williams continued. “And so we’ve gained ground regardless of whether or not we change seats … I mean politics is really 10- and 15-year projects and a lot of people think it’s always election after election, but  you got to take those lumps.”
Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3. Early voting in Kentucky begins Thursday, Oct. 29.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginia Mercury readers head toward midterms with rising bills and doubts about Washington
text:
Virginia Mercury readers who responded to an election survey cited concerns about rising costs, healthcare access and whether congressional candidates would address their priorities. (Photo illustration by States Newsroom)Rising bills, concerns about the state of democracy and frustration with both political parties are weighing on Virginia Mercury readers ahead of next week’s midterm elections, with many questioning whether the candidates can deliver the changes they want. 
More than 350 readers responded to The Mercury’s online survey between Sept. 22 and Oct. 17, describing the issues that matter most to them and whether congressional candidates are paying attention. 
The voluntary survey was not a scientific poll, and its findings do not represent Virginia voters as a whole. Many respondents voiced opposition to President Donald Trump alongside concerns about healthcare, food prices and energy costs. 
Longtime Virginia political analyst Bob Holsworth said voters are feeling squeezed on several fronts. 
“I think what happens is that people feel they can’t get a break. And everything keeps moving up,” he said, referring to the rising cost of living. 
Some readers expressed confidence in Democratic candidates, while others criticized the left or questioned whether either party could address their concerns. 
 Trump and democracy

Some respondents view the election as a chance to rein in presidential power. 
Ann McMillan of Henrico County in the 1st Congressional District listed her top concern as “Restore checks and balances in national government.”
McMillan also supported all three constitutional amendments on Virginia’s November ballot, which would protect reproductive rights, including abortion access; remove the state’s unenforceable ban on same-sex marriage and guarantee marriage equality; and automatically restore voting rights to people convicted of felonies upon their release from incarceration. 
Richard Sellers, an 11th District respondent who identified rising energy costs as his leading concern, said his own party needed to change course. 
“As a Republican, we need to stop MAGA,” he said, referring to Trump’s Make America Great Again movement. 
Stephanie Fuller of Franklin County worried about allegations that could erode public confidence in elections.
Elections chief says Virginia is ready for midterms, potential federal interference

“I am concerned about the misinformation about election fraud that the GOP and other entities are spreading,” Fuller wrote.
Attorney General Jay Jones recently created a new Voter Protection Section to investigate potential complaints of voter intimidation, improper registration cancellations and other obstacles in voting. 
 Healthcare access and costs 

Healthcare was another concern, with some readers backing candidates they believe would improve access and others saying neither party was offering enough. 
State officials estimate that 300,000 Virginians could lose Medicaid coverage next year under new eligibility and verification requirements. 
Meanwhile, U.S. Rep. Rob Wittman, R-Westmoreland County, joined Democrats in supporting an extension of enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies, although the measure failed in the U.S. Senate. 
Sheila Blackford, a 5th District respondent, said she trusted Democratic candidate Tom Perriello, who faces Republican U.S. Rep. John McGuire of Goochland, to address the issue. 
“Yes, I believe that Tom Perriello will work to expand health care access and lower prices,” she wrote. 
John Meszaros of Midlothian wants universal coverage and said neither candidate in his district, the 1st, supported it. 
“My main issue is getting universal healthcare coverage for all and neither candidate (Wittman or Democrat Shannon Taylor) speaks to that,” Meszaros wrote.
Meg Heubeck of Waynesboro urged candidates to consider proposals from both parties when addressing healthcare costs. 
“Not just say, ‘no’ to any Republican ideas,” she wrote.
Casandra Oldham, a 10th District respondent, identified her priorities as “disabled adults, specifically level 3 autism.” Asked whether any congressional candidate would effectively address that concern, she answered: “No.”
 Government waste and fraud

Readers concerned about government waste and corruption had differing views on whether  a change in congressional leadership would make a difference. 
Mike Harton, a 1st District respondent, expressed confidence in Taylor, who currently serves as Henrico County’s commonwealth’s attorney, but said he considered himself politically open-minded.
“I am an independent, but I’ve never seen the GOP cave so completely to a crazy president,” Harton wrote.
Luria and Kiggans rematch in Va.’s 2nd Congressional District among most-watched races in nation

Thomas Rein, a 2nd District respondent, was critical of both parties. He argued that corruption would persist without changes to the two-party system and doubted candidates would address his concerns. 
“The current system is not sustainable and it’s heartbreaking to see the amount of lies being spread from both sides,” he wrote. 
Similar criticism has come from independent 5th District candidate Cooke Costa Harvey, who has blamed partisan divisions for congressional failures and argued that voters need an alternative to the two major parties. 
 Food prices and affordability 

Grocery bills were another source of frustration, although readers disagreed about what was driving prices and whether Congress could bring them down. 
A recent statewide survey found that 51% of families with children experienced food insecurity. Food bank leaders have also reported growing demand for assistance. 
Skye Whitcomb of Richmond believed Democratic U.S. Rep. Jennifer McClellan, the 4th District incumbent running for another term, would try to address affordability but doubted she could make much difference soon. 
“I feel McClellan will attempt to do so, but the damage has been done, and there’s not much she can do in the short term,” Whitcomb wrote. 
Skip Ressel of Franklin County in the 9th District criticized the far left and predicted prices would fall once the Iran war ended. He argued that the costs were justified by the need to confront Iran’s nuclear ambitions. 
Wally Bunker, a 7th District respondent, named higher food prices as his top concern but doubted any congressional candidate could effectively address them.
He still plans to cast a ballot Nov. 3. 
“A vote is the only way to hope things change. If you don’t vote, you have no right to complain,” Bunker wrote. 
 Energy costs and data centers

Higher electricity bills and the growth of data centers also drew concern from readers. 
In a rare bipartisan move, lawmakers from both parties have recently proposed moratoriums on data center development, citing noise, electricity demand, water consumption and other environmental impacts. Industry supporters and electrical workers warn that restrictions could cost jobs and tax revenue.
Data center moratorium bills stack up ahead of Virginia legislative session in January

Sarah Ovink of Montgomery County in the 9th District identified rising energy costs as her biggest worry. She supports Democratic candidate Joy Powers. 
“Yes, Joy Powers addresses this concern. The incumbent does not,” Ovink said, referring to Republican U.S. Rep. Morgan Griffith of Salem.
Fuller, who also prioritized energy costs, said the Democratic candidate in her district would consider how decisions in Virginia would affect Virginians rather than follow the MAGA agenda. 
Diana Diehl of Loudoun County in the state’s 10th District selected data centers as her top issue and expressed confidence that her congressional candidate would address it. She also worried about “the effect the president and his administration’s poor governing is having on Northern Virginia, the state, country and world.”
Tony Dunsworth of Essex County, located in the 1st District, doubted candidates could do much about rising energy costs. 
“Too many other forces at hand,” he wrote. 
Still, he considered participating in the election worthwhile. 
“Voting is our way to speak directly to those who govern us,” Dunsworth wrote. 
Holsworth, the political analyst, said many voters were struggling to find political leaders who represented their interests. 
“I think there’s a disenchantment with what’s going on, because people don’t know who’s speaking for them,” he said. 
But he suggested that frustration could bring people to the polls rather than keep them home. 
“They’re giving it something like a final shot in this election. People think the system is broken because it’s not serving them very well,” Holsworth said. 
Election Day is just over a week away. Early voting ends Oct. 31. If you haven’t voted yet, read The Mercury’s voter guide to learn more about the races, candidates and constitutional amendments that are on the ballot

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Law enforcement agencies’ use of license plate reader data faces fresh scrutiny
text:
A view of an automated license plate reader in Northern Virginia. (Photo by Nathaniel  Cline/Virginia Mercury)A Virginia prosecutor’s recent decision not to charge a police officer for sharing license plate reader data with federal authorities without authorization could spur reform efforts in the commonwealth.
Automated license plate readers, commonly used to identify vehicles and investigate crimes, have drawn criticism over privacy concerns and alleged misuse, sparked disagreement over how they’re used by authorities, and forced local governments to reconsider contracts.
Under state law, law-enforcement agencies may share data obtained through ALPR systems under certain circumstances. The statute prohibits sharing or disseminating the data to “any database of any other state, federal, private, or commercial entity.” 
The statute does not, however, expressly prohibit sharing or disseminating the data directly to out-of-state or federal law-enforcement officers.
Although the recent data-sharing case in Isle of Wight was intended to support an investigation, Senate Majority Leader Scott Surovell, D-Fairfax, said localities should face penalties if they don’t share data the right way. 
“I think there needs to be consequences for localities that improperly share data,” Surovell said after Thursday’s crime commission meeting, adding that some law enforcement agencies have not followed the laws governing ALPR use that took effect July 1, 2025.
Nearly 13% of law enforcement agencies using ALPR systems in the state reported providing continuous access to out-of-state law enforcement, and nearly 6% reported providing continuous access to federal law enforcement, according to the crime commission’s 2025 survey 
About 30% of the 361 total agencies did not respond to the survey. None of the agencies were identified in the survey results.
Of the 361 law-enforcement agencies surveyed, around 70% responded (251), and 44% (159) reported using ALPR technology. 
Among those agencies, 20% reported retaining ALPR data for longer than the law’s general 21-day limit. State law allows data to remain if it’s needed for an ongoing investigation, prosecution, or civil action until the investigation concludes.
ALPRs are different from automated speed enforcement and red-light enforcement cameras that capture speeding vehicles or vehicles entering intersections after the traffic signal turns red and issue citations.
A view of two automated license plate readers in a retail space. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)A view of an automated license plate reader. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)A view of two automated license plate readers in a retail space. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)A view of an automated license plate reader. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)A view of an automated license plate reader. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)A view of an automated license plate reader in Northern Virginia. (Photo by Nathaniel  Cline/Virginia Mercury)
 ALPRs in practice

One of the most high-profile instances of ALPR use in the state came in 2015, when Virginia law enforcement used the technology to help find the gunman who shot two journalists in Roanoke during a live broadcast and then fled three hours away to Northern Virginia.
Nationally, similar cases show how ALPRs have been used to improve and solve investigations. 
But Chris Kaiser, policy director for the ACLU of Virginia, said claims that ALPRs help solve cases are hard to assess because it is often unclear whether the technology actually made a difference.
More importantly, Kaiser warned, Virginia’s ALPR safeguards may not prevent unauthorized out-of-state access, and the cloud-connected system could expose statewide data if one agency fails to comply, raising broader privacy and oversight concerns.
“If one agency or even one officer allows unauthorized access to the system, that means the whole state’s set of data is compromised,” Kaiser said.
He also argued that ALPRs enable broad, warrantless surveillance that threatens privacy and can negatively impact people’s activities, while evidence that they significantly improve crime-solving is weak.
Last year, House Majority Leader Del. Charniele Herring, D-Alexandria, carried legislation that allowed the use of license plate reader systems, like those operated by Flock, by establishing statewide approval, restricting police use of ALPR technology, requiring documentation and reporting and creating oversight to monitor use and accountability.
The measure was signed into law by Gov. Abigail Spanberger earlier this year.
Under the new law, the system’s uses are limited to investigating suspected criminal violations when there is reasonable suspicion that a crime occurred, investigating missing or endangered persons or people associated with human trafficking, and receiving notifications involving missing or endangered persons, outstanding warrants, human trafficking, stolen vehicles, or stolen license plates.
Data may be shared with other Virginia law enforcement agencies, commonwealth’s attorneys, a criminal defendant or their counsel, or their ALPR vendor.
ALPR data may also be shared if officers receive a court order or court-issued subpoena, or to alert the public to an emergency situation, a missing or endangered person, a person associated with human trafficking, or a person with an outstanding warrant.
Herring, chair of the crime commission, nor her office responded to multiple requests for comment about the use of ALPRs in Virginia since the law was passed. 
 Notable cases

Police departments in Richmond and Smithfield are among the most prominent agencies to share data from their Flock system, which has received the most public attention.
Recently, Isle of Wight Commonwealth’s Attorney Georgette Phillips said her office would not bring any charges against the Smithfield police officer, who shared data from its ALPR system with the FBI, which was investigating the March 12 shooting at Old Dominion University that killed one person and injured several others.
Phillips wrote to the Mercury that the officer was not found in violation because the officer had no criminal intent to violate the statute after the department was contacted to assist with the investigation.
She said the department was contacted after the investigation determined a resident purchased the firearm used in town.
“A law-enforcement agency may share system data with another law-enforcement agency as part of a criminal investigation of Virginia Code,” Phillips said.
The attorney said the department now knows about the prohibition on sharing system data with federal law-enforcement partners and has implemented additional safeguards to prevent future incidents.
In an Oct. 12 statement, town leaders emphasized that the officer shared the information for a legitimate investigative purpose.
“However, a legitimate purpose does not remove our responsibility to understand and follow the requirements governing that information,” the statement added.
The town’s authorities said that when the information was shared with the FBI, the department believed the FBI was included in the definition of law enforcement agencies. However, the town later learned that was not the case and that it requires a court order or subpoena before it can share this information with the FBI.
“Since this issue was identified, we have taken steps to ensure our officers understand the statute’s restrictions on sharing license plate reader data, including the requirements that apply to requests from federal and out-of-state agencies,” the  statement read. “We have reinforced the expectation that officers seek guidance before releasing information whenever there is uncertainty about what the law permits.”
A similar data-sharing case occurred in the city of Richmond earlier this year when a police sergeant shared data with the FBI on a homicide investigation. 
On Oct. 10, Richmond Mayor Danny Avula said the city would not renew its contract with Flock Safety for ALPRs, citing public concern over surveillance, data privacy, and police access to vehicle-tracking information. The city has not decided, however, to abandon license plate reader technology altogether.
 What’s next

The Virginia State Crime Commission is expected to submit results of a statewide survey detailing the use of ALPR systems to lawmakers by Nov. 1. 
Lawmakers will return to Richmond in January to discuss related legislation. Some lawmakers, including Sens. Lashrecse Aird, D-Henrico, and Glen Sturtevant, R-Chesterfield, have publicly expressed interest in banning the readers, signaling bipartisan interest in further action. Others have called for more transparency.
No legislation has yet been filed as of Thursday afternoon.
Following the Smithfield Police case, Aird said Virginia’s rules already restrict sharing license plate reader data, but the decision not to prosecute raised doubts about whether the rules would be enforced and strengthened the case for banning the technology. 
“There really is nowhere to go from there, but to revoke the use of the technology,” she said.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Sentara hospitals are using AI to help monitor patients, determine discharge timelines
text:
Sentara Heart Hospital in Norfolk. (Photo by Ned Oliver/Virginia Mercury)Virginia-based nonprofit health system Sentara announced last week that it has started using artificial intelligence technology to assist with patient monitoring and  discharges. 
Regard is an AI system that integrates with electronic health records. Co-founder and president Nate Wilson said it’s used by more than 150 hospitals across the country. Dr. Rollin Reeder, chief health information officer at Sentara, said that all 12 of the health system’s hospitals now use Regard. 
The tool helps physicians and case managers more easily parse through patients’ hospital admission charts, monitoring notes during their stay and their medical histories, both men said. The goal is to help diagnose new or worsening symptoms sooner and think proactively about patients’ discharge times and follow-up care. 
“If a patient is going to need rehab or help at home, you want that on the table at admission, not the afternoon they’re medically cleared to leave,” Reeder said. “Catching it early gives the case manager time to find a bed, arrange services and walk the family through it.”
Discharge planning begins as soon as a person is admitted for inpatient care. Case managers analyze health data about the patient to help determine when it may be safe for them to go home or whether they may need to transfer to a rehabilitation facility first. 
Case managers also begin the work of determining what services are covered by patients’ insurance. But the information is scattered, Reeder explained. 
“Most of those answers are buried” in patients’ charts, medical history, screenings and doctor’s notes, he said. 
“The hard part has always been that it’s spread out everywhere, so case managers spend a lot of their day clicking around just to get the basics before they could start planning,” Reeder explained. 
Regard helps scan and filter information, Reeder said, and case managers appreciate a feature that allows them to pull up rundowns of what may have changed with the patient since the previous day. 
 Sentara emphasizes AI is a tool, not human replacement

A press release announcing the adoption of Regard implied that it’s estimated to save “nearly 90,000 hours of staff time – the equivalent of hiring 40+ full-time employees.”  
When asked if use of the technology may lead to reduced case manager staff, Reeder said “no one is losing their job over this.” 
Staffing levels and certain services have been in flux for some hospitals and clinics over the past year following H.R. 1, a reconciliation bill Congress passed last summer that entails changes to hospital funding mechanisms and puts roughly 300,000 Virginians at risk of losing Medicaid insurance. 
Citing the bill as a contributing factor, Valley Health changed staffing contracts and trimmed services this past spring. Last winter, Centra closed its labor and delivery unit at a hospital in Farmville. Last fall, Shenandoah Valley’s Augusta Health closed three clinics. 
Virginia hospitals amplify risks federal shifts pose to patient care

Thirteen rural hospitals — including a Sentara hospital in Halifax —  have also been identified as vulnerable to service cuts or closure over time, a state report indicated. 
Reeder said the estimate of 90,000 hours Regard saves being equivalent to hiring more than 40 full-time staff was meant to reflect how case managers can spend less time glued to a computer screen and more interfacing with patients. 
“The 90,000 hours is a forecast of time our case managers can redirect to patient care, based on pilot data we haven’t confirmed yet,” he said. “Our goal is for every case manager to reach more patients, catch problems earlier and spend more time with the people they’re caring for.”
 ‘There’s just so much going on’

Wilson, Regard’s president and co-founder, shared how the technology can also help identify sudden, deadly health conditions like sepsis, an infection that can be triggered by underlying health conditions or that manifests post-surgery in some patients. 
“There’s just so much going on with the scale of data on every single patient that humans can’t keep up anymore,” he said. “There’s 50,000 data points in every patient. Imagine a 100-page book, and we have time to flip through the first three pages. When we were able to catch things earlier, we’ve seen it move (the) length of stay.”
A case study compiled by Regard amid Sentara’s pilot use of the program revealed how a doctor in their Norfolk location used the technology to solve a patient’s condition. 
Dr. Colin Findlay had suspected lack of adherence to prescribed medications was the root cause of an admitted patient’s  uncontrolled heart failure, but Regard’s comb-through of the person’s records revealed a separate condition. 
It turned out that doctors had previously paused the patient’s use of hypothyroidism medication for other reasons.  When left untreated for too long, hypothyroidism can cause rapid heart rates. Regard helped Findlay confirm that it was time for the patients’ prescription to be resumed. 
While AI use has been growing across multiple industries in recent years, it has presented a series of pros and cons. 
Theresa McDonnell, chief nurse executive at Duke University Health System, has emphasized that AI tools can reduce staff burnout, but cautioned about the technology’s potential to depersonalize care or weaken patient trust.
Likewise, a National Institutes of Health study labeled AI “the opportunity for health care revolution,” but said that it also presents ethical, regulatory and safety challenges to address when integrating it. 
 Regulating the tech

In Virginia’s legislative session earlier this year, Del. Irene Shin, D-Fairfax, and Sen. Jeremy McPike, D-Prince William successfully carried legislation to prohibit downcoding insurance claims without a healthcare provider providing reasons for the decision. 
The new law is meant to ensure human decisions factored into insurance claims rather than allowing AI technology to carry out the action on its own. 
“Applications where it’s an assistive tool and not deciding is what’s appropriate,” McPike said. “We have licensed practitioners, and that’s why we hire them. That’s why we folks go to school in very sophisticated and specialized areas.”
Further action is expected in the state’s 2027 legislative session, Virginia’s Joint Committee on Technology and Science director Jodi Kuhn said. The committee outlined a series of recommendations for lawmakers to explore.
One suggestion is to establish an enforcement agency that can receive complaints from the public, investigate potential noncompliance with regulations and impose penalties. 
Other ideas include requiring disclosure of AI use in healthcare or human-involvement bills, like the ones McPike and Shin have already explored. 
Del. Rodney Willett, D-Henrico, who chairs the House of Delegates’ Health and Human Services Committee, said he will be introducing the public disclosure bill soon. 
“It’s one of those guardrail things, but it’s not prohibiting AI use,” he said.

title: Commentary: Virginia’s chief pundit predicts gloom for one party, and he fears for our collective discourse
text:
University of Virginia political analyst Larry Sabato, seated, explained his projections for the upcoming midterm congressional elections to a crowd of nearly 250 last week in Norfolk. At left is former Norfolk Mayor Paul Fraim. (Photo courtesy of Alexander Chen)Larry Sabato, the decades-long University of Virginia political analyst, had a dire warning for Republican congressional candidates last week: 
You’re going down in the U.S. House of Representatives. And you might lose your slim majority in the U.S. Senate, too, after the Nov. 3 elections.
“It’s either going to be a sizable blue wave, or it’s going to be a tsunami,” Sabato, founder and director of U.Va.’s Center for Politics and head of the eponymous Sabato’s Crystal Ball, told nearly 250 people at The Slover building in downtown Norfolk last week. The perennial prognosticator relayed similar comments to me in a brief interview just before his address.
The Crystal Ball, a nonpartisan political analysis newsletter, forms its projections by polling, reporting, studying electoral history and other factors. Sabato said Democrats could win at least 224 seats in the House of Representatives (they now trail Republicans 218-214, with one independent and two vacancies). In the Senate, he said, Democrats should do no worse than 50-50. (The GOP currently holds a 53-47 advantage.)
Sabato’s Crystal Ball recently rated the seat held by U.S. Rep. Jen Kiggans, R-Virginia Beach, as “leans Democratic.” She’s in a rematch with former Democrat U.S. Rep. Elaine Luria, and it’s one of the more-competitive contests nationwide. The group rated the race of longtime incumbent U.S. Rep. Rob Wittman, R-Westmoreland, as a toss-up. He’s battling Democrat Shannon Taylor.
Such predictions and the latest polls explain why President Donald Trump has undermined the electoral process – including demanding uncustomary mid-decade redistricting in red states to try to gain more Republican seats in the House. He’s also lied incessantly about voting security and accuracy. More on that later.
Sabato told those gathered that a “national funk” often haunts the president’s party during the midterms – especially, he said, in the sixth year of an incumbent’s time in office. (This is Trump’s sixth year over two non-consecutive terms.)
I’d add that there’s despair coupled with outright fear among many Americans because of Trump’s policies that have caused so much havoc:

A war of choice in which the United States joined Israel against Iran. It was poorly conceived, the president hasn’t sufficiently explained why our country is even waging it, and the conflict has no end in sight. The war has boosted gasoline and diesel prices astronomically nationwide. For example, AAA reported regular gas cost an average of $4.09 a gallon in Virginia on Friday; diesel totaled $6.27 a gallon.


Trump’s misguided fascination with and implementation of tariffs. A recent Cato Institute/​Morning Consult survey of 4,150 registered voters found 74% say that Trump’s tariffs increased the prices of things they buy – including 66% of Republicans and 84% of Democrats. A majority believes the tariffs have weakened the U.S. economy. Americans see the effects in their wallets.


A brutal, racist roundup of suspected undocumented immigrants that has targeted people who haven’t committed major felonies. Federal agents have killed U.S. citizens who have protested their actions, and they’ve detained hundreds of other citizens, too. We’ve witnessed the Kafkaesque spectacle of migrant children as young as 2 years old trying to represent themselves in deportation proceedings.

 Sabato, a Norfolk native, also worried about the fate of our democracy – regardless of elections.
“We’ve lost the ability” to have meaningful conversations about the public good, he told me. “We’re at the point where it is very possible to construct the decline and death of the Republic. … You can see how it might” happen.
Later, fielding a question from the audience about the lack of civility in public speech, Sabato added, “We’ve gone down some notches. And we’re so nasty to one another.” 
That brings me back to Trump and his administration’s machinations going into the midterms. The president has brayed about electoral problems – knowing he’s exaggerating or outright lying. He’s doing this because his haphazard and narcissistic leadership has alienated many Americans and threatened their day-to-day living conditions.
The worst actions, which a GOP majority in Congress approved, targeted low-income people with cuts to Medicaid and food stamps. The cruelty was unnecessary.
That’s why Trump demanded, starting in 2025, that GOP-controlled states overhaul congressional boundaries to create more Republican-leaning districts. The decision defied customs. It led to a backlash from Democratic-controlled states that fought the craven map-drawing with their own craven map-drawing.
Democrats in Virginia embarked on a similar crusade, and a referendum passed by 3 percentage points to allow drawing of new districts in the commonwealth. But the Virginia Supreme Court overturned the electorate’s decision.
The president also has tried to pre-empt his party’s inevitable losses next month by relying on a well-worn practice: denigrating the very voting systems that placed him in office not once, but twice. He’d rather throw doubt on the upcoming results than concede defeat – leading us down the path of becoming a Banana Republic.
What else should we expect, however, from the person who incited the Jan. 6 attempted overthrow of the 2020 elections?
His wild-eye conspiracy theories usually don’t stand up to judicial muster: The Supreme Court this year blocked his attempt to have the U.S. Postal Service screen mail ballots.
That hasn’t stopped him mucking up things, even as his favorability ratings crater. He’s threatened local officials with criminal prosecution over their voter rolls. In Virginia last week, Arlington County officials sued the administration to prevent it from sending armed federal agents to polling places.
 That’s why Sabato’s predictions aren’t a surprise.
People are suffering across Virginia and the country. They’ll express that discontent during the midterm elections.

title: In Cumberland, questions swirl over water sources for newly-approved Dominion gas plant
text:
Cobbs Creek Reservoir in Cumberland County August 2026. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)Cumberland County has promised Dominion Energy two million gallons of water a day from Cobbs Creek Reservoir for its proposed three gigawatt natural gas plant. But technically, the water is not yet theirs to give away.
The county board of supervisors voted 3-1 on Tuesday night to approve the conditional use permit for the natural gas plant that would become the second largest in the nation if it is fully approved by regulators and state agencies. 
Board Chair John Newman, a former Dominion employee, recused himself from the vote. 
The CUP permit approval came after months of public meetings and hearings about the project. The room was split between residents from Cumberland and the surrounding counties who support and oppose the project. 
The supervisors’ vote will allow portions of the land where the plant will be located off of Duncan Store Road bordering the James River and Buckingham County to be rezoned, as well as a laydown site nearby.
The massive gas plant will run full time and provide enough electricity for up to 750,000 homes, with the utility predicting power demands to more than double by 2045.
“The proposed Cumberland Energy Center is a vital piece of our all-of-the-above strategy to meet our growing customer demand reliably and affordably by decreasing reliance on more costly purchases from the PJM market,” said Dominion spokesman Jeremy Slayton.
Board member Bryan Hamlet was the only supervisor to vote against moving forward with the permit. While he was not against the plant as a whole, he said he wanted to nail down details on where the water will come from. The county should have continued its due diligence before advancing the project, he stated. 
“I see the benefits. Absolutely. I can’t deny that. When you look at the revenue in a county such as Cumberland, when you look at what this board is tasked with when it comes to pinching pennies and making sure that we’re fully funding the offices of this county, our schools, our sheriff’s department, EMS, and our wonderful volunteer firefighters,” Hamlet said during the Tuesday hearing. 
But, he asked “What happens to this project if we go ahead and prematurely authorize the conditional use permit and that water deal is not in place?”
The reservoir at Cobbs Creek, otherwise known as the Virgil R. Hazelett Reservoir, was completed just last year and is owned by Henrico County, despite being within Cumberland’s borders. 
The 14.8 billion gallon reservoir will release water into the James River in drier months. The construction of the reservoir led the Department of Environmental Quality to increase the amount of water that could be taken from the James River for drinking water by 47 million gallons a day on average. 
According to the Henrico County website, with the new agreement Henrico could withdraw 75 million gallons per day on average, an increase of 30 million gallons per day. The remaining 17 million gallons per day increase can be sold to its partners, Powhatan County and Cumberland. 
But the official deal to allow Cumberland to use that water has yet to be completed.
When asked where the water for the gas plant will come from, Slayton said “We are still working through those details.”
Henrico and Cumberland County officials did not respond to requests for an update on the water purchasing negotiations as of Friday afternoon.
Some residents who have staunchly opposed the gas plant, like Katie Hoffman and Steve Haring, said that approving the CUP before having all the facts was irresponsible.
“I would never be allowed to build a house without having a well site located. And so for Dominion to be able to use the equivalent of thousands of houses… the county said ‘you guys are good to go.’ But they don’t have one of the most important pieces locked down,” Haring said.
Haring said that members of the community have many outstanding questions related to the project.
“I think that the route, size and design of transmission lines, which could involve eminent domain, that’s a big one,” Haring said. “Also gas pipelines and potentially water pipelines from whatever water system they choose.”
Dominion still needs to file an official request for the project with the State Corporation Commission;  the panel of commissioners will then determine if the gas plant is in the public’s best interest. The project will also need approvals from DEQ for an air permit for the turbines. 
The project is anticipated to be completed in 2033-34 if all permits are approved.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Recruitment efforts bring mixed results for state law enforcement agencies
text:
A Division of Sheriffs recruitment billboard in Providence’s Jewelry District in July 2025, part of a $56,278 advertising campaign for the academy that graduated 11 recruits in April 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)The Rhode Island Division of Sheriffs spent less on a recruitment advertising campaign to address staffing shortages than the Rhode Island State Police did and ended up with more applicants.
That gave Rhode Island’s top sheriff some bragging rights since the sheriffs division had fewer training spots, resulting in a much more competitive selection process.
“I’ve busted a little bit of their chops,” Chief Sheriff Paul Martellini said.
State police received nearly 300 applications by the Sept. 30 deadline for 23 spots in its 22-week academy scheduled to begin next March, its lowest total in years. 
But 342 applications were received for the Sheriffs Division’s February academy for deputies who provide security inside Rhode Island’s courts following a two-month ad campaign. Eleven deputies graduated in April. Another 300 applications were received for the 13 spots in an eight-week training academy which began Oct. 19.
The sheriffs’ applicant pool has fluctuated in recent years, but the division has made headway in filling vacancies through a broader recruitment push, Martellini said
“I knew it was going to be an uphill battle,” he said. “But we’ve made strides.”
The sheriffs division, along with state police and Rhode Island Capitol Police, are housed under the Department of Public Safety. The department’s proposed fiscal year 2028 budget lists a total of 57 vacancies in sworn positions between the three agencies as of Sept. 21. There were 24 in the state police, 22 in the sheriffs division and 11 Capitol Police officers.
 

 Active sworn personnel in the Department of Public Safety


Rhode Island State Police: 258
Division of Sheriffs: 156
Capitol Police: 40




In a cover letter accompanying the budget, Col. Darnell Weaver, who serves as the department’s director and state police superintendent, called staffing shortages his “greatest concern moving forward.” But Weaver noted “tremendous progress” within the sheriffs division.
Martellini inherited 47 deputy vacancies when he took over the sheriffs division in October 2024. There are now 22 vacancies. A $689,245 request under salary and benefits seeks to bring the division to 174 deputies, leaving just five vacancies by the end of fiscal 2028.
For years, deputy shortages left some courtrooms without enough security for judges to take the bench. In 2025, the Rhode Island Bar Association urged Gov. Dan McKee in a letter to prioritize courthouse security funding, warning that understaffing would only cause further delays and disruptions at the judiciary.
Bar Association President Dana Horton said in a statement to Rhode Island Current that court administrators now report the lowest number of deputy vacancies in the sheriffs division in some time. But gaps in hallway security and courtroom coverage remain, she added.
“We hope continued recruitment and retention efforts will translate into sustained improvements for attorneys, litigants, and others who rely on the courts,” Horton said.
Rhode Island State Police received nearly 300 applications by the Sept. 30 deadline for 23 spots in the academy scheduled to begin next March, its lowest total in years. (Photo by Janine L. Weisman/Rhode Island Current)
Combined recruitment campaigns cost over $175K
Martellini credited the sheriffs division’s progress to a combination of advertising, expanded recruitment and a push to bring in experienced hires. Figures provided by the Department of Public safety shows the sheriffs division spent a total of $75,243 advertising its two 2026 academies, using buses, billboards, radio, newspapers and social media. 
The first campaign ran in June and July 2025 and cost $56,278. A second campaign, which ran in May 2026, cost $18,965.
“We’ve done a full-court press,” he said.
So has the Rhode Island State Police, which launched a $100,000 ad campaign between July and September 2026 consisting of billboards along the state’s highways and digital commercials featuring troopers patrolling highways, piloting drones, conducting scuba operations, working with K-9s and processing crime scenes.
The campaign managed by Cromwell Public Affairs drew 296 applications by the Sept. 30 deadline, state police spokesperson Lt. Col. Erik Yanyar confirmed in an email to Rhode Island Current.
That continues a multiyear decline in applications, which fell from 629 in 2023 to 456 in 2024 and 323 in 2025. 
R.I. State Police trooper applications fall despite new recruitment campaign

Yanyar acknowledged the declining numbers were concerning, but said the state police remains focused on attracting qualified candidates rather than maximizing applications.
“Our standards have always been high, and the selection process remains competitive,” he wrote. “We believe that is what the public should expect from their law enforcement officers.”
The Rhode Island State Police budgeted $551,448 to train the 23 recruits who will be accepted for its 2027 academy. For fiscal 2028, the agency is requesting $492,880 to train 12 recruits.
Capitol Police, the smallest agency within the Department of Public Safety, received 90 applications for its 2026 academy, with six recruits currently in training, Yanyar wrote. 
Because of its size, Yanyar noted the agency does not pay for advertising. Instead, Capitol Police promote openings on social media and by posting flyers in state buildings where its officers screen visitors and employees and provide security at entrances.
Senate Majority Whip David Tikoian, a Smithfield Democrat who served for 23 years in the state police, said he wasn’t surprised by the ongoing recruitment challenges, pointing to the lengthy hiring process and changing career landscape.
Becoming a state trooper means committing to 22 weeks of classroom lessons, physical conditioning and hands-on training at the state police academy in Foster. Recruits are allowed to leave campus only on weekends, according to the agency’s website.
“A lot of jobs today, you have an interview and follow-up interview — you’re in, you’re out,” Tikoian told Rhode Island Current.
Even so, Tikoian expects the state police will eventually get over its staffing recruitment woes. He said law enforcement offers a wider range of career paths than when he joined the agency in 1990, including cybercrime investigations and assignments with federal task forces.
“The advance of law enforcement has really broadened the opportunities,” he said. “I think you’re going to see an uptick in recruitment.”
Newly hired Rhode Island State Police troopers earn a starting annual salary of $81,579. Starting pay for Capitol Police officers is $59,683 a year, while deputy sheriffs earn $65,475 upon appointment.

name: National
title: Rising prices squeeze more Americans ahead of pivotal midterm elections
text:
General Manager Brian Horak walks down an aisle at Post 60 Market in Emerson, Nebraska. A new national report shows how everyday costs have increased for Americans. (Photo by Kevin Hardy/Stateline)Americans’ growing frustration over high prices has defined many political campaigns ahead of November’s midterm elections.
Rising costs of healthcare, gas and groceries during President Donald Trump’s second term have put Republicans on defense, not only in Washington, but in statehouse and gubernatorial races across the country.
As the political environment continues to sour for Republicans, a new analysis released by the Urban Institute on Monday underscores just how expensive everyday life has become in America: Gas and electricity prices are rising much faster than paychecks. Housing, childcare and healthcare are becoming a bigger strain for millions of people. 
And affordability pressure is worsening in once-affordable havens such as Atlanta; Louisville, Kentucky; and Rochester, New York, where costs of housing, groceries and healthcare are increasing faster than the national average.
The latest installment of The American Affordability Tracker from the left-leaning think tank details how costs of food, housing, energy and healthcare have changed across all 50 states over recent years. High prices are pinching people across income brackets, with an estimated 49% of families unable to afford the basic costs of living. That’s according to Urban Institute’s true cost of economic security calculation, which measures how much is needed to live securely.
Americans’ water bills are growing faster than groceries, overall inflation

“We’re not saying that 49% of people are poor. We’re saying that they’re not secure,” said Gregory Acs, an Urban Institute fellow who worked on the research project. “Even if they’re paying all their bills, they’re paying all their bills at best.”
He said the analysis confirms that the economic angst so many people feel is justified — despite strong national economic indicators such as low unemployment and growing gross domestic product.
“They are not crazy. They’re not making it up,” Acs said. “They’re not being marketed into feeling bad. They really do have struggles.”
Among other findings, the report shows that average annual childcare costs for two young children have risen $6,600 over the past decade. Since January 2025, gas prices have risen by 33% — an average increase of $1.02 per gallon nationally. And premiums for benchmark plans on the Affordable Care Act Marketplace are up 22% since last year, now averaging $611 per month.
Affordability politics
Those struggles have become a political liability for Republicans, who control the White House, both chambers of Congress, most state legislatures and a majority of governor’s offices. 
All midterm elections, as a referendum on the sitting president, are difficult for incumbents in the majority. But this cycle is particularly charged because of Trump’s promises to improve the economy during his 2024 campaign, said Todd Belt, a professor of political management at The George Washington University.
“He hasn’t done that. In fact, in a lot of ways, he’s made things worse,” Belt said, citing Trump’s unilateral war in Iran and tariff policies — both of which have driven up costs. “And so Donald Trump is bringing down the Republican ticket.”
Democrats could win majority of governor’s offices for first time in 16 years

Some Democrats have proposed new policies to help lower costs, following the lead of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani whose winning campaign last year promised free buses and childcare. But many others are simply benefiting from the sinking approval ratings of the president — driven largely by high prices. 
“For the Democrats, it’s enough to not be Donald Trump,” Belt said. “People are feeling it, and you can’t out-message it. You can’t out-message what people are feeling in their finances and what they know prices to be as they go to the gas station every week, as they see it in the grocery store.”
Republican officials have recognized the political drag of rising prices. 
Vice President JD Vance has publicly acknowledged Americans’ growing frustration with high prices, particularly for gas, telling voters “we’re working on it,” during a CBS News town hall in Michigan earlier this month. 
But Trump has often downplayed such concerns, calling affordability “a hoax” promulgated by Democrats. Campaigning for Kansas Republican Sen. Roger Marshall last week in an unexpectedly competitive race, Trump blamed previous President Joe Biden for rising prices. Trump pledged that the war in Iran would end soon.
“And when it does, you’re going to see the biggest drop in oil that anyone’s ever seen,” he said. 
Wide-ranging impacts
Rising prices are hitting consumers and businesses alike.
Earlier this month, Small Business for America’s Future, a coalition of business owners across the country, released results of a new survey that found many small employers are struggling with high costs of utilities, fuel, business supplies and employee healthcare.
Nearly two-thirds of the 1,171 businesses owners surveyed said they had recently cut or skipped their own pay to keep their operations afloat. Nearly half said customers are spending significantly less, and more than two-thirds said they had delayed, canceled or scaled back investments because of uncertainty about federal economic policy. 
Walt Rowen, co-chair of that coalition, said in a news release his own business exemplified the challenges facing Main Street operations across the country. He’s the president of the 116-year-old Susquehanna Glass Company in Columbia, Pennsylvania. Tariffs have disrupted supply chains, he said, and driven up heating oil costs.
“We’ve lived through the Depression, wars, and recessions,” his statement said. “Heating my factory in this current economy is some of the hardest math I’ve ever had to do, and I’m expecting the bill to jump 30% to 40% this winter.”
Relief from energy bills unlikely as utilities request billions in rate hikes

High prices are hitting consumers across demographic and geographic borders.
Acs, the Urban Institute researcher, said rising prices squeeze more than just the poorest Americans. Many middle income earners are struggling to cover the costs of healthcare, higher education and housing, “feeling like they’re on a treadmill at best,” he said. 
The Urban Institute’s recent analysis also highlighted rising price challenges in regions long considered affordable. 
In Arizona, gas and electricity price increases are outstripping other parts of the country: Arizonans pay an average of $219 per month for electricity, the highest in the U.S. and nearly $50 more than the national average. 
In the battleground state of Wisconsin, where gas and electricity costs are well below the national average, parents face disproportionately high costs for childcare: Parents there spend an average of $30,800 per year for care for two young children — $6,900 more than the national average.
“I think there is an old story that affordability really is a coastal problem,” Acs said. “What we’re trying to illustrate is that it’s not just high-cost areas where costs are an issue. Costs are an issue throughout the country.”
Stateline reporter Kevin Hardy can be reached at khardy@stateline.org.
