name: Michigan Advance
title: Democrats are rallying the troops in Michigan’s solidly Republican 1st Congressional District
text:
Rep. Jack Bergman (L) and Callie Barr (R) | Office/courtesy photosWhile much of the national attention headed into Election Day is centered around battleground districts in Michigan’s Lower Peninsula, Democrats are making a push to flip the state’s largest congressional district, which has been solidly controlled by Republicans for over a decade.
Michigan’s 1st Congressional District is made up of the entirety of the UP and several counties in the northern Lower Peninsula, encompassing communities like Traverse City, Petoskey, Cheboygan and Alpena. 
While the nonpartisan Cook Political Report has rated the district “Solid Republican,” the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, U.S. House Democrats’ campaign arm, has added the 1st Congressional District to its list of districts in play.
U.S. Rep. Jack Bergman (R-Watersmeet), a retired U.S. Marine Corps lieutenant general, has represented the district since 2017, succeeding the late U.S. Rep. Dan Benishek (R-Crystal Falls), who served for three terms before that.
In 2024, Bergman faced off against Callie Barr, an attorney raised in Traverse City and Cheboygan who helped veterans access free legal support. Bergman was reelected in a landslide victory, defeating Barr by more than 20 percentage points.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
However, Republicans are facing headwinds. Historically members of the party in opposition to the president have gained House seats during the midterm, and rising costs on gas, groceries and other everyday needs amid the war in Iran have soured voters on President Donald Trump and his promise to lower costs while in office.
Barr’s campaign has also received a boost from former Democratic U.S. Sen. Debbie Stabenow, who now lives in Elk Rapids.
Gongwer News Service reports that Stabenow has appointed her former campaign manager, Dan Farough, to run Barr’s campaign. Barr has also received ad support from VoteVets, a political action committee focused on electing Democrats to support veterans and military families.
“People kind of write off Northern Michigan, but the reality is it was a seat held by a Democrat for 18 years, Bart Stupak, and then he retired, and it became the era of Trump, and it became Republican and Jack Bergman’s been there for 10 years, and not really had anybody focus on him,” Stabenow told reporters on an Oct. 15 press call.
Speaking to reporters after an Oct. 17 roundtable in Michigan’s 10th Congressional District with battleground candidate Christina Hines, U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York) said Stabenow had been in touch.
“Listen, we’re very excited about the opportunities here in Michigan … I’ve been in touch with Senator Stabenow. She encouraged me to send financial support and I recently did just that,” Jeffries said referring to Barr’s campaign.
Bergman’s record becomes a campaign target
Barr, Stabenow and the Michigan Democratic Party have also sought to highlight multiple controversies over the course of Bergman’s time in office, referencing news articles raising questions on Bergman’s participation in a taxpayer funded program reimbursing the representative’s meal and housing expenses and scrutinizing his chief of staff for running a political consulting firm in Michigan while avoiding financial disclosures around the business.
More recently, The Detroit News reported that Bergman was living in a Washington, D.C., home sold to Bergman’s daughter by campaign supporters, although his campaign has said Bergman paid fair market value for his rent on the home “and is in full compliance with House Ethics.”
“The people of Northern Michigan and the Upper Peninsula face terrible challenges because of tariffs and fuel prices, and Jack Bergman voted for all of it,” Barr said in a campaign statement touting the campaign’s recent fundraising haul. “People are frustrated by his corruption in office and complete failure to fight for us. Voters are ready to fire him on Tuesday Nov. 3.”
U.S. Rep. Jack Bergman (R-Watersmeet) speaks to Michigan Republican Party donors, elected officials and activists at the Straits Area Lincoln Day Dinner event in Mackinaw City on June 7, 2025 | Photo by Ben Solis
When asked about Democrats’ efforts to flip the seat and the accusations of corruption leveled against the incumbent, Bergman spokesperson James Hogge said the race “isn’t even close.”
“Crooked Callie Barr’s campaign has spent four years attacking General Bergman’s record, and her latest ad is another example of just how far she’s willing to stretch the truth,” Hogge said, referencing an ad in which Barr blames Bergman for delays in PFAS cleanup at Michigan military bases.
“Her newest ad literally claims General Bergman ‘chairs the Air Force Subcommittee,’” Hogge said. “There’s just one problem – that subcommittee doesn’t even exist. This isn’t a matter of opinion – it’s a basic fact anyone can verify.”
Bergman serves on the U.S. House Committee on Armed Services on the Readiness Subcommittee and the Seapower and Projection Forces Subcommittee. While there is no Air Force Subcommittee, there is a Tactical Air and Land Forces Subcommittee.
While Democrats are talking tough on the campaign trail, some Michigan political consultants say Barr’s victory remains a longshot.
Democrats may need a ‘blue tsunami’
Dennis Lennox, a Republican public affairs consultant based in Cheboygan County, said he expected to see another Bergman victory in November. 
“Now that’s not to say that Jack Bergman is going to win by 21 points again,” Lennox told Michigan Advance. “It very well could be, you know, a seven-point victory or an eight-point victory based on the national trends and the generic ballot lead that Democrats unquestionably have.”
Lennox theorized that talk of flipping the 1st Congressional District is more of an attempt to draw Republican spending away from supporting incumbent candidates in hotly contested seats.
“I’ve seen this play before,” he said. “This is a pretty well played trick that both parties will spend a little bit of money in the final stretch in one of these out-of-reach seats to try to deke the other side and get them to redeploy resources.”
Rather than watching what the political parties or candidates are saying publicly, Lennox said people should be watching what they’re doing.
“I think if Jack Bergman thought he was going to lose, you would be seeing Donald Trump or JD Vance flying into Traverse City or Marquette, and you don’t see that yet, which tells me that the internal polls don’t show this to be a close race,” Lennox said.
The biggest difficulty Barr faces in attempting to flip the district, Lennox said, is that she hasn’t demonstrated herself to be a “different kind of Democrat.”
He later noted that Bart Stupak, the previous Democratic representative who held the seat from 1993 to 2011, was an outlier within his party, supporting the Second Amendment and opposing abortion, earning endorsements from groups like the National Rifle Association and Right to Life of Michigan.
“If you’re a Democrat and you align with those two issues, you tend to do well in northern and upper Michigan,” Lennox said.
As for Bergman, he’s facing the same issue as other Republicans, Lennox said.
“He is swimming against the tide,” Lennox said. “It’s just a question of how big are those waves? To defeat Jack Bergman, you don’t need a blue wave, you need a blue tsunami.”
In an interview with the Advance, Adrian Hemond, a Democratic consultant and CEO of the bipartisan advocacy firm Grassroots Midwest, called the 1st Congressional District a “stretch-goal seat,” which was potentially attainable at the outside edge of a very good election night for Democrats.
Stipulating that he wrote a “fairly-sizable” check to Barr’s campaign at Stabenow’s request, Hemond said the odds of a Democratic victory in the district were “maybe one chance in 10.”
Jodi Decker, left, and others hold a protest outside Audie’s Restaurant in Mackinaw City, which hosted the Michigan Republican Party’s Straits Area Lincoln Day Dinner event. U.S. Rep. Jack Bergman (R-Watersmeet) spoke at the event on June 7, 2025 | Photo by Ben Solis
However, there are multiple factors that put this district in play for Democrats, Hemond explained, pointing to the war in Iran and its impact on fuel costs as one example.
“Public transport is functionally a fiction up there,” Hemond said. “If you’re going anywhere in the 1st Congressional District, you are driving there.”
Additionally, the biggest industries in those parts of the state are tourism and agriculture, both of which have suffered under Trump’s policies, Hemond said.
“We’re just coming off a harvest season. Every one of those crops comes out of the ground with a diesel-powered machine, then it gets trucked to market in a diesel-powered semi, and then you have to try and sell it into the state’s largest trading partner, Canada, while we’re embroiled in a tariff war with them. Also, the Canadians aren’t coming to visit right now for some fairly obvious reasons,” Hemond said. “So the president has, in a very meaningful sense, put this district in play.”
Alongside those factors, more Democrats are moving into the northern part of the state, Hemond said, pointing to Stabenow as one example. 
“You’ve got people from Chicago and Madison and Milwaukee and Green Bay that are buying property in the southern UP, right? On the north coast of Lake Michigan,” Hemond said. “So the people who are moving into this district are by and large Democrats.”
He also pointed to the heavy concentration of Dem-adjacent voters in Marquette County and the northwestern Lower Peninsula’s shift toward Democrats, while emphasizing that a Democratic victory in the district would still require an amazing night for Democrats.
In addition to mobilizing new supporters and winning over a significant margin of independents, Hemond also noted Trump supporters’ turnout will also be a factor.
“There are Republicans and there are Trump supporters, and there’s a great deal of overlap between those two things, but they are not qualitatively the same thing,” Hemond said. “Part of Donald Trump’s electoral success is getting people to show up who are not typically voters. And the other thing that Callie Barr needs in order to win this race is for enough of the president’s supporters to decide it’s not that important to vote this year.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Commentary: AI isn’t going to erase low-wage jobs. It’s going to split them
text:
Indiana job postings in occupations most exposed to artificial intelligence have fallen 41% since 2022. (Photo by Brandon Bell/Getty Images)Most of the talk about artificial intelligence and work asks how many jobs will disappear. For the families United Way works with, a better question is which jobs, and what the ones left behind pay.
Start with who is exposed. Nationally, about 54.5 million households, 41%, don’t earn enough to cover a basic household budget. Sixteen million of them are in poverty. Another 38 million are ALICE households: Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed. They work, and they earn too much to count as poor, but not enough to cover rent, childcare, food, transportation and healthcare. These are the households with the least room to absorb a bad month, let alone a changing labor market.
The jobs many of them hold are heading in two directions at once. Federal projections for 2025 to 2035 show cashier jobs falling 6%, bank teller jobs 13% and customer service jobs 5%. The Bureau of Labor Statistics ties those declines to technology: self-checkout, mobile banking, automated customer service. Over the same decade it expects home health and personal care aide jobs to grow 18%. Those jobs are in demand and hard to automate, and they pay a median of about $35,800 a year.
So, the pattern isn’t a wave of unemployment. It’s a narrowing of the opportunities available to everyone in the job market. The easiest jobs to automate shrink, and the work that grows is steady but often pays too little to get a family ahead.
Indiana shows how easy this is to miss. On paper the state looks healthy: labor force participation of 63.2%, above the national 61.8%, and unemployment of 3.3%. Underneath, there are signs of change. Indiana job postings in occupations most exposed to AI have fallen 41% since 2022, compared with 35% for less exposed occupations. Postings aren’t layoffs, and the gap between the two groups is modest, so it is too early to read it as a verdict. But it is the kind of early signal worth watching.
The larger issue is pay. In the first quarter of 2026, Indiana’s average weekly wage was $1,356, about 82% of the national figure, and it grew 2.7% over the year compared with 3.9% nationally. A state can have plenty of jobs and still leave families short if wages keep falling behind. That gap, more than any single technology, is what pushes working households into ALICE territory.
There is a practical way to respond without waiting for the technology to settle. It starts with a plain test for every training program, apprenticeship and hiring push in the state: does it raise what people earn?
That means tracking results beyond placement. Finishing a program and landing a job is good, but the number that matters is what a worker earns a few years later. Indiana employers already report wages to the state every quarter, which makes that kind of follow up possible. When employers, colleges, workforce boards and funders can see which paths lead to real raises, money and attention can move toward them and away from the ones that don’t.
It also means building ladders inside the jobs that are growing. Home health and personal care work will add jobs, but a job that stays at the same pay for years only deepens the problem. Employers and training providers can make it easier for an aide to move into a better-paid role, with tuition help, flexible schedules and credentials that count toward the next step. Next Level Jobs and Indiana’s apprenticeship system have already shown that training aligned with in-demand careers can work. The task now is to point that same approach at the places where wages are lowest.
AI will change work in ways nobody can fully predict. The families most at risk aren’t waiting on a forecast. They’re making decisions now about rent, child care and whether a second job is worth the hours. If we want AI to leave them better off, the measure that matters isn’t how many jobs exist. It’s whether the jobs that remain pay enough to build a life on.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: The ties the bind, the feuds that separate in Cranston’s House District 15
text:
From left: Democrat Colleen Crudele, Republican Rep. Chris Paplauskas, and independent Allan Fung are running to represent Cranston's House District 15. (Courtesy photos)Editor’s note: This is the first in a three-part series on state legislative races, chosen based on competitiveness between candidates and relevant district issues. Of the 113 seats in the Rhode Island General Assembly, all of which are elected every two years, 24 seats feature at least two candidates on the Nov. 3 ballot. 
Family ties underpin the three-way race for Cranston’s House District 15.
Republican Rep. Chris Paplauskas is seeking a second term after winning an open seat race in 2024 by just 26 votes. 
His challengers include Republican-turned-independent Allan Fung, whose wife, Barbara Ann Fenton-Fung, held the seat from 2020 to 2024 until her unsuccessful challenge to Cranston Mayor Ken Hopkins in the 2024 Republican primary. 
Paplauskas now works as deputy chief of staff for Hopkins, who first became mayor in 2022 with Allan Fung’s endorsement. Fung, an attorney, was term-limited, after serving four terms as the city’s Republican mayor.


About House District 15
Represented by Rep. Chris Paplauskas since 2024
Geography: western Cranston
Population: 15,203 residents; 11,180 registered voters
Partisan breakdown: 60% unaffiliated; 22% Democrat; 18% Republican 
Demographics: median age: 44; 78% white; $113,727 median household income (2024)


Then there’s Democrat Colleen Crudele, an attorney whose cousin, Frank Montanaro Jr., held the same House seat for 18 years, and later served as head of the powerful Joint Committee on Legislative Services under former House Speaker Nicholas Mattiello. Mattiello was ousted in 2020 after he lost his reelection bid to Fenton-Fung.
Each got their start on the Cranston City Council: Crudele with a single term in 1996, Fung from 2003 to 2007, and Paplauskas from 2014 to 2024. 
All three emphasize affordability concerns and say they want to reduce unnecessary government spending. None of them supported the millionaire’s tax included in the state’s fiscal 2027 budget, though Crudele gave the caveat that she would need more information about how the revenue from the tax would be used.
Their differences are, for the most part, personal, rather than ideological.
Paplauskas, who has a side gig delivering pizzas to help support his family and keep in contact with constituents, distinguished himself as the only candidate with children; his son just started at the University of Rhode Island while his daughter is a junior at Cranston West High School.
“I understand what it’s like to need a little extra to make ends meet, especially with the cost of college and supporting a family,” Paplauskas, 43, said. 
Not an important distinction to Crudele and Fung. Both said they understand the child-rearing experiences and costs from nieces, nephews and godchildren.



Quotation







“I understand what it’s like to need a little extra to make ends meet, especially with the cost of college and supporting a family


– Republican Rep. Chris Paplauskas


Crudele, 63, said she understands the financial strains for parents through her work as a divorce lawyer in her own family law practice in Cranston. She pointed to her legal background, which includes serving as legislative legal counsel at the State House from 2016 to 2023, as reason why she is the best candidate for the job.
“I’m not a career politician, but I have a lot of experience in the law, in Supreme Court law, case law, seeing how legislation is drafted,” she said.
Crudele ran for the same seat once before, in 2006, losing to Mattiello by 68 votes. 
Fung, 56, an attorney with Warwick-based Lepizzera and Laprocina, is a perennial candidate. In addition to his 16 years in Cranston as a city councilor and mayor, he has also run twice for governor in 2014 and 2018. In 2022, he ran for the open seat representing Rhode Island’s 2nd Congressional District.
But, this will be Fung’s first time on the ballot as an independent, having disaffiliated a few months before the June 30 declaration deadline.
Fung said he’s “transcended” party politics.
“Voters don’t really care whether you’re a Republican, a Democrat, or an independent,” Fung said. “They’re looking for common sense.”



Quotation







I’m not a career politician, but I have a lot of experience in the law, in Supreme Court law, case law, seeing how legislation is drafted


– Democratic challenger Colleen Crudele


Fung said he was concerned with the direction the state was headed, criticizing Paplauskas for voting against the state budget and “dropping the ball” on Cranston’s Meshanticut State Park, overrun by invasive aquatic plants and in need of infrastructure repairs. 
Paplauskas sponsored a resolution in the 2026 session for $3.5 million to restore the park’s 0.8-mile paved walking path. The proposal failed to advance out of committee and was not in the final budget.
Fung said Paplauskas’ proposal did not succeed because he did not work across the aisle and win support from legislative leaders. The resolution had seven co-sponsors, five of them Democrats.
Accusations over city contracts, unpaid state taxes
On Monday night, Fung, who loaned his campaign $50,000, sent a text blast to district voters. The accompanying, 38-second video, shared with Rhode Island Current, suggests Paplauskas helped direct the “tens of thousands of dollars” in no-bid city contracts awarded to his family’s sign and graphics company when Paplauskas was council president. The video also notes the company, Bori Graphix, owes $1.2 million in unpaid state taxes.
Paplauskas did not dispute the taxes owed by his parents’ company. But he said their financial hardship was irrelevant to his candidacy. He has not worked for the business since 2025, and said he had no knowledge of the company finances.
“I’m the candidate, not them,” Paplauskas said, calling Fung’s attack “despicable.”
Paplauskas also noted that the city awarded contracts to his family’s business during the time Fung was mayor.



Quotation







Voters don’t really care whether you’re a Republican, a Democrat, or an independent. They’re looking for common sense.


– Independent challenger Allan Fung


On his vote against the state budget, Paplauskas said there were things he wanted the state to “do a better job at,” naming taxes and overall spending as areas of concern.
Paplauskas is also unhappy with state education policy mandates that leave local school districts to pick up the tab. If reelected, he plans to reintroduce legislation requiring the state revenue department to publish a report calculating any unfunded or partially funded mandates for local education. The Republican-backed bill failed to advance out of committee in the 2026 legislative session. 
Paplauskas had his own critique of Fung.
“He was a Republican for so long, to turn his back on the party that supported him, I think is unfortunate,” Paplausakas said.
Crudele distinguished herself as the only candidate who is pro-choice.
Fung calls himself a “centrist” on abortion, though he said he opposes late-term abortions. Paplauskas identifies as pro-life.
But more than hot-button issues, Crudele was focused on the challenges of small business owners, seniors and working families.
“Not being an elected official, I think I have a lot of independent experiences to know what everyday people are facing,” she said.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Commentary: Time is running out to have a say in new Census 2030 rules. What’s at stake for Rhode Island kids.
text:
Proposed changes to Census 2030 rules could lead to significant undercounts of children in Rhode Island, which translates to less federal money available for schools, hospitals and public services that support their wellbeing. (Getty illustration)I lead an organization that relies on the power of data, to inform policies that improve the lives of all Rhode Island children. Every kid counts in our state.


How to submit a comment
Over 95,000 comments have been submitted since the public comment period opened Sept. 10 for proposed changes to the Code of Federal Regulations governing data collection  by the U.S. Census. The comment period ends on Nov. 2. 
To submit comments online:
Go to https://www.regulations.gov.
Enter USBC-2026-0628 in the search box. 
Click on the “Comment” icon.
Complete the required fields and enter or attach your comments.
Written comments should indicate Docket No. USBC-2026-0628 and can be mailed to 4600 Silver Hill Road, Designation: ADDEMO/FRN, Washington, D.C. 20746.


But the Trump administration is working hard to make sure our kids don’t count in the next Census. It is our collective duty as adults to speak up and make sure they are. 
For every child counted in the Census, Rhode Island receives federal funds for essential programs that support children, families, and the communities where they live, learn, play, and grow. Undercounted children mean a loss of federal money to support schools, hospitals, transportation, emergency services, and more.  
The Census Bureau is proposing major changes for how the 2030 Census is conducted. These new rules would:

End the collection of race and ethnicity data.


Ban questions on sexual orientation.


Exclude U.S. residents like visa holders, refugees, and asylum seekers from the count that determines the number of seats in Congress and Electoral College votes.


Add a legal status or citizenship question.


End guidelines for a variety of living arrangements.


Use tax records to determine place of residence.


Count incarcerated people at their facility instead of at their home.

Every Census since 1790 has collected race and ethnicity data. The 2020 Census reported that nearly half (47%) of Rhode Island children under age 18 were Children of Color, allowing all to know and understand demographic shifts and community needs.
A lack of routine data collection makes it difficult to understand the changing needs of the LGBT+ population, leaving federal and state leaders less able to create effective polices for LGBT+ people and their families.  High suicide rates among LGBTQ+ youth will not go away just because the data is not there, but not having the facts will make it harder to understand and solve these problems together.



Quotation







Undercounted children mean a loss of federal money to support schools, hospitals, transportation, emergency services, and more.


The Constitution requires that every person living in the U.S. be counted. Excluding visa holders, refugees, asylum seekers, and others will lead to a serious undercount. In Rhode Island, the number of public-school students identified as immigrants more than tripled from 2012 to 2025 (1,893 to 6,105). This proposed change would harm immigrant children as well as every U.S. citizen child living in a community with a high number of immigrants because that community will not get the resources it deserves.
The proposal to end 2020 guidance for shared custody of children and other complex living arrangements will also lead to substantial undercount. According to the 2020 Census, over 17,000 Rhode Island children live in multigenerational households and more than 1,400 live in out-of-home placements such as foster care. 
The administration has proposed using tax records to determine residency. However, some tax records reflect a mailing address instead of a residential address. Reliance on tax records risks missing military children, which can unfairly hurt communities like Newport and Middletown.
The proposed changes would increase the population count where prisons are built and decrease it where those incarcerated normally reside. Our state prisons are in Cranston, but among incarcerated individuals who are parents, 68% live in the five core cities of Central Falls, Newport, Pawtucket, Providence, and Woonsocket, compared to just 9% who live in Cranston. If incarcerated people in Rhode Island are counted in Cranston and not in their home communities, the result will be a substantial decrease in resources where their children live. 
Lastly, if the 2030 Census includes a question on citizenship, we expect a significant young child undercount. Even before a potential citizenship question was proposed, Census staff warned that the current political environment would make it harder to persuade people to fill out the Census. If the Census form asks about citizenship status, that effect will be much stronger and may result in 11% of Rhode Island children not being counted.
Proposed changes to the 2030 Census will affect the lives of an entire decade of children. A missed preschool child will not be counted again until high school, leaving communities without resources intended to support them during their most important developmental years and leaving our policymakers without valuable facts needed to make informed policy decisions.
Rhode Islanders can submit a public comment on these proposed changes by Monday, Nov. 2. Comments from parents, educators, providers, and community members show federal officials how these changes would affect real families. You don’t need to be an expert.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: More Hoosier women are delivering at home. Is it safe?
text:
A growing number of Hoosier women are seeking midwives to deliver their babies at home. (Getty Images)A series of infant and maternal deaths overseen by unlicensed midwives led Hoosier lawmakers to a conclusion in 2013: legalize and regulate the practice to make it safer.
The deaths included a Columbia City mother who died with her baby in 2003 after the woman’s uterus ruptured during a delivery at her home, and the 2007 stillbirth delivered by a Goshen mother who suffered repeat seizures during a three-day home birth.
Both were attended by an unlicensed midwife in Indiana with no formal training who was recently ordered to cease and desist. Neither were taken to the hospital.
Would a path to licensure with formal training protect women who want to deliver their children at home?
Thirteen years later, Hoosier women are increasingly turning to midwives for care, as fewer obstetricians practice in the state and women report declining trust in the medical system.
Supporters say the outcomes show home birth is a safe option for low-risk pregnancies when attended to by a certified direct-entry midwife, but unlicensed midwives continue to work underground.
Out from underground
Lay midwives deliver babies outside the hospital, typically at the mother’s home with little to no medical intervention, under the belief birth is a natural process.
They did so at risk of prosecution for decades. Only registered nurses with advanced degrees could practice midwifery in Indiana until 2013, when lawmakers legalized direct-entry midwifery.
The term itself is a source of confusion: midwives care for women through pregnancy, childbirth and postpartum periods, but their training, educational background and scope of practice varies widely.
Indiana Midwifery Committee member April Brake (Courtesy photo)
Unlike a certified nurse midwife, there was no formal standard of training for lay midwives, who often learned through self study or apprenticeships with other midwives.
The direct-entry certification offered lay midwives the chance to get on the right side of the law, so long as they underwent formal training and reported outcomes to the state’s newly formed midwifery committee.
Licensed midwives have delivered or assisted with more than 3,200 live births since Indiana issued its first direct-entry midwife certificate in 2017, with seven stillbirths and zero maternal deaths reported to the Indiana Department of Health in that time.
Women are choosing this option because “they want individualized care and the continuity of care,” said April Brake, president of the Indiana Midwives Association and the newest member of the state’s midwifery committee.
“You hire a provider to be at your birth and to walk with you through pregnancy, labor and postpartum with your newborn, and that provider is consistent. We aren’t doing prenatal with a provider that you’re never going to deliver you.”
What it takes to become a direct-entry midwife
Indiana requires midwives to be at least 21 years old.
Applicants must obtain an associate’s degree or higher in nursing or a midwifery program accredited by the Midwifery Education Accreditation Council.
An apprenticeship consisting of at least 80 births and certifications in emergency skills like CPR and neonatal resuscitation are also required, as is liability insurance and continuing education.
The final qualification: a supervising physician willing to examine a midwife’s clients and consult throughout the pregnancy.
“Indiana expects us to have more births and more experience to be a licensed midwife here, and I believe that’s only made our outcomes even better,” Brake said.
Only 24 direct-entry midwives in Indiana have an active license, according to the Professional Licensing Agency.
These midwives are supervised by the midwifery committee, a three-member board comprised of professional midwives who review annual reports and consumer complaints.
Unlicensed midwives are not held to the same standards, often operating outside the notice of authorities until there is a death or complaint.
‘Called by God’
Becky Cantieri says she was called by God 36 years ago to deliver babies for Christian women without medical intervention, relying instead on the “power of prayer.”
A homemaker and doctor’s wife in Mishawaka, Cantieri underwent one year of training toward a licensed practical nurse certification before she started delivering babies — 3,000 to date by her estimate.
At a cease-and-desist hearing last week, Cantieri said she does not advertise her ministry or accept payment, other than occasional gifts.
She did not seek certification when Indiana legalized direct-entry midwifery, becoming one of an unknown number of unlicensed midwives who continued to practice outside state oversight.
“I would not jeopardize the women and babies without the power of God to protect them,” she said, “because I know. I’ve seen it. I see how a woman can die.”
Carah Rochester, an attorney in the consumer protection division of the Indiana Attorney General’s Office, proceeded to ask Cantieri about six stillbirths and a maternal death.
Only one of the women went to the hospital.
In one case, Cantieri admitted she did not call 911 or check for fetal heart tones when a Goshen woman suffered 14 seizures during a three-day home birth she attended in 2007.
Cantieri said the woman refused to go to the hospital when she learned of her high blood pressure, a sign of preeclampsia.
Becky Cantieri, left, sits with her attorney Tom Dixon at a cease and desist hearing Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. (Screenshot courtesy of the State of Indiana Zoom)
Cantieri and the couple failed to notify police of the stillbirth for two days, according to Rochester.
Cantieri failed to call the police for four days following the 2003 deaths of a Columbia City woman and her baby, a delay she attributed to her prayer vigil over the woman.
“I just didn’t think I’d ever lose a mom,” she said. “I thought God would protect every one of them, but he didn’t. That was a real crisis for me. I stayed and prayed for that mother while she decomposed — prayed and prayed and prayed until God finally spoke to my heart and said, ‘Call.'”
The mother underwent cesarean sections for at least three previous pregnancies, which put her at high risk of uterine rupture.
Dr. Erin Cleary, a maternal-fetal medicine specialist for Riley Children’s Hospital and assistant professor at Indiana University Medical School, said women who undergo one or two c-sections can safely attempt to labor vaginally in the hospital if the incision was made through a thin part of the uterine muscle, but the risk of uterine rupture increases with each additional cesarean.
“That is absolutely a life threatening emergency for both the fetus and the pregnant patient,” she said. “Access to an operating room can be live saving.”
Cantieri said she informed the mother of the risks, as she does for the other women she ministers to, repeatedly telling the committee she “gladly” takes women to the hospital when asked.
But it has to be the mother’s decision, she said.
Cantieri said the woman wanted to stay home because she had contracted an infection and nearly died at the hospital during a previous delivery.
“I can’t make them go in. If they choose to stay home, then God has told me you stay with them and you support them and you help them.”
‘Cease and desist’
The case is familiar to Alicia Diane Holmes, a certified professional midwife who was appointed to the state’s midwifery committee in 2013, who said the woman had sought her assistance too.
“She said, ‘Diane, will you attend to me,’ and I said, ‘No, you’ve had four c-sections. That is not safe. I will not,'” Holmes recalled during the hearing.
Holmes said the coroner notified her the mother’s body had been left in the home for days, asking her advice for how to prevent such a delay in the future.
The Indiana Midwives Association started to work with lawmakers on legislation to require timely death notification, eventually culminating in the 2013 law on certification, she said.
Tom Dixon, a St. Joseph County attorney associated with the Alliance Defending Freedom, argued Cantieri’s practice is a ministry protected by the U.S. Constitution. Her refusal to accept compensation separates the activity from practicing midwifery without a license, he argued.
“My client has had thousands of successes — not just a couple, but thousands,” Dixon said. “So, in the entirety of her career, we have six or seven stillborns and one mother who died.” Investigators cleared Cantieri in each case, he said, and in some instances the stillbirths “occurred before she even got on the scene.”
The midwifery committee issued a cease-and-desist order to Cantieri.
Dixon said he is considering an appeal.
Other disciplinary cases
Cantieri is not the first midwife subject to discipline.
The committee reprimanded a midwife for performing a tongue tie procedure on an infant who was later rushed to neonatal intensive care for a severe hemorrhage. The infant survived, and the midwife later paid a $5 settlement to resolve the complaint.
Another midwife spent 17 months in probationary status following the stillbirth of a breech fetus, as the committee concluded she waited too long to initiate transfer to the hospital and did not develop a written emergency plan prior to the delivery.



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



The attorney general’s office is investigating three consumer complaints against other midwives, though details of those cases are not public.
A DeKalb County judge sentenced a St. Joe woman to a year of probation for practicing midwifery without a license in the 2012 delivery of four infants, two of whom died, though her attorney argued she did not contribute to the deaths.
A similar fate awaited two elderly Adams County Amish women convicted of practicing midwifery without a license in 2018.
Informed consent
Women must sign consent and disclosure forms before a certified midwife can work with them.
The forms outline an emergency plan, including with hospital the mother will go to in an emergency, and collaborative agreement with a nearby physician.
While midwives cannot prescribe medications, their supervising physician can order them local anesthetics, oxygen, vitamin K, anti-hemorrhagic and other medications.
By law, certified midwives must refer women with high-risk pregnancies like preeclampsia or hypertension to an obstetrician.
“It’s pretty apparent if they’re going to be high risk,” Brake said, “and at that point we turn them away.”
The same is true for labor and delivery: If a complication exceeds the midwife’s scope of practice, they transfer the mother to the nearest hospital, she said.
How safe is home birth now?
Certified midwives have reported zero maternal deaths since 2018, and while stillbirths have increased slightly since then, so too have the total number of live births they attended, according to annual midwifery reports.
Reports show midwives are referring women to obstetricians for high blood pressure, breech fetuses, twins, gestational diabetes, fetal distress and other complications before a woman goes into labor.
Midwives initiated 32 emergency transports during labor or postpartum last year, including eight newborns who were rushed to the hospital with respiratory distress, a slow heart rate and other complications, according to the 2025 report.
Jill Inderstrodt, a research scientist and assistant professor at Indiana University-Indianapolis, said the home birth population is too small to compare to hospital births, but the data that does exist looks good.
“If there were low transfers and high infant, fetal or maternal mortality, then we might be concerned,” she said.
Data on stillbirths isn’t a great metric of safety, as stillbirth can occur at any time after 20 weeks gestation. “So we don’t know when it’s happening and we don’t know who it’s happening to,” she said.
Maternity care deserts
Even uncomplicated pregnancies can become dangerous.
A woman may develop postpartum hemorrhage, or heavy bleeding after delivery that can become life-threatening in a short period of time, said Cleary, the maternal-fetal medicine physician.
Other complications like fetal distress can also arise during labor, which she said can be difficult to properly assess without the monitoring and quick intervention available in a hospital.
“Patients can be at risk for hypertension complications like preeclampsia that may not really appear until the end of pregnancy, or even for the first time during labor,” Cleary said.
The farther away the woman is from a hospital, particularly one with a dedicated labor and delivery unit, the less time doctors have to intervene.
One in four Indiana counties are considered maternity care deserts, either due to the lack of clinicians, insurance or birth facilities, according to the March of Dimes.
The group found that while Hoosier women travel an average of 14 minutes to reach the closest hospital with labor and delivery services, women in maternity care deserts travel twice as long than those in counties with full access.
Freestanding birth centers are closing as maternity care gaps grow

Some 71,000 women live more than 30 minutes from the nearest hospital with labor and delivery services, the report found.
In response, the March of Dimes is pushing for policies to make it easier for trained midwives to work with low-risk obstetric patients.
Dr. Nathan M. Riley, a Louisville obstetrician who acts as the supervising physician for nine certified midwives in Indiana, said women are leaning into the idea that their bodies are capable of giving birth on their own.
“If we’re only looking at deaths, a lot of people can make a pretty good argument for the hospital system as the default,” he said. “But if we’re looking at the whole person, its really, really hard to make that argument, because a lot of women feel like they don’t have much autonomy” in the hospital.
Riley supports midwifery in 18 states. He estimates he supervises or consults with 100 or so midwives at any given time—ordering labs, medications and referrals to high-risk obstetricians as needed.
Supervision is minimal: Midwives call Riley when they have a question or need medication, but he doesn’t order them around.
“There isn’t a ‘Do it this way’ attitude from me,” he said. “It’s, here’s what the (American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology) says. Here’s what the medical board says. Here’s what my experience says. The midwife then takes that information, presents it to the family, so that the family can feel fully informed before they make a decision.”
In March, the medical board granted a waiver to Riley, allowing him to supervise more than four midwives in Indiana at once.
The alternative, Riley said, would be for women and midwives to go underground and practice without a license.
“Midwives, fortunately, are available. Otherwise, women would say, ‘I’d rather have a baby in my own backyard or in a cabin in the woods than go to the hospital, because they’re not oriented toward my interests.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Facing an ongoing snowplow driver shortage, New Hampshire to increase private contractor pay
text:
A plow clears a road in Bartlett during a storm on Jan. 17, 2024. (Photo by Spencer Platt/Getty Images)The leaves have only just begun to fall, but New Hampshire’s Department of Transportation is already raising concerns about snowplowing season.
For years, the agency has struggled to recruit plow drivers and has turned to private contractors to make up the gap. 
On Wednesday, the department presented its latest maneuver to the Executive Council: a plan to increase the amount it pays those contractors by 15%. That move would raise the hourly rate for private plow operators with a commercial driving license from $26.45 per hour to $30.42 per hour. 
The increase will cost the state an additional $2 million to $3 million for the 2026 to 2027 winter season, the department estimates. That money could come from the New Hampshire Highway Fund, funded by motor vehicle registration fees and gas taxes, or the Turnpike Fund, funded by tolls. 
Department of Transportation Commissioner David Rodrigue told councilors the increases are necessary to help combat an intractable workforce shortage. The department is facing an overall 26% vacancy rate, one of the highest in the state, but the vacancy for plow drivers specifically is “significantly higher than that,” Rodrigue said. 
“The department has always and — from what I see, for the foreseeable future — will continue to rely on engineering consultants and hired equipment to help us achieve our mission,” Rodrigue said. 
The Executive Council approved the plan last week. But councilors in both parties raised objections with the department’s use of private contractors and urged Rodrigue to do more to increase the ranks of Department of Transportation employees. 
“I am concerned that we are getting ourselves into a sort of downward spiral,” said Councilor Karen Liot Hill, a Lebanon Democrat. 
“We’re not investing adequately into our own personnel, and then we end up having to hire contractors, and we pay them more to do the same job that if we had personnel on staff that they would be able to do.”
Councilor John Stephen, a Manchester Republican, echoed that concern, noting that the private contractor rate is higher than the hourly rate for state plow drivers. 
“What does this say to the DOT employees that are out there, that are going to be driving alongside these contracted-out plow drivers and equipment, and they receive a 15% increase, and the DOT employees are not receiving that increase?” Stephen said. 
Rodrigue said he heard those concerns. “We represent the citizens of New Hampshire at the end of the day who own our infrastructure, and we need a solid, competent workforce in order to do that,” he said. 
New Hampshire’s plow driver recruitment problem is not new. The number of potential employees with commercial driver’s licenses has dwindled, and the state has faced increased competition from towns and cities for the same drivers. Meanwhile, the neighboring state of Massachusetts pays, in some cases, more than twice as much for its private contract snowplowing work, further complicating New Hampshire’s recruitment pitch.
In 2023, those same problems forced the department to make a similar move: It increased private contractor pay by 15%.
The workforce problems have affected the private sector as well as the public sector. 
“The Department has had similar difficulty contracting drivers with rental equipment to supplement the Department’s internal staff shortage,” Rodrigue wrote in a document explaining the 15% increase to the council. “Our limited pool of available CDL drivers with plowing experience only serves to heighten the need for recruiting and retaining sufficient contractors and equipment.”
The New Hampshire department is responsible for maintaining more than 4,000 miles of state highways. During a snowstorm, the agency divides those roads into priority tiers: “Type 1-A” roads, such as Interstates 89, 93, 293, and 393, must be plowed every 90 minutes during the day and every four hours at night, while low-volume roads that see fewer than 1,000 cars a day require plowing every 3.5 hours during the day and 7 hours at night.
To accomplish those goals, more than half of New Hampshire’s plow trucks every year are rented and staffed with private contractors, according to the department. 
Last winter, the department was hoping to deploy 667 trucks — 300 of which the state owns, and 367 of which would be rented — Rodrigue explained to the council. But the department was able to find drivers for only 323 of those 367 rental trucks. 
That shortfall had consequences. “The existing shortage increases the time it takes for us to respond during ice storms and increases the snow on the road during snowstorms due to other state and rental trucks having to cover multiple routes,” Rodrigue wrote.
The differences between New Hampshire and Massachusetts rates are stark. For a one-ton truck, the smallest in the fleet, New Hampshire paid $77.79 per truck per hour last winter. Massachusetts paid $126.34. New Hampshire paid $105.29 per hour for each 3- to 5-ton truck — the medium-sized option — compared to Massachusetts’ $222.83 rate.
Under its plan for the coming winter, New Hampshire would increase the 1-ton hourly rate to $89.46 and the 3- to 5-ton rate to $127.28.  Those two states’ numbers include both the rental cost of the truck and the contracted driver’s salary. 
Massachusetts has had higher contract rates for plow drivers for years, according to graphs provided by the department, but in recent years, the Bay State has also increased its pay at a faster rate than New Hampshire has, the graphs reveal.
While the department estimated a $2 million to $3 million annual increase, that number is not a guarantee. Having now announced its plan to increase the private contractor rates, the department will return to the council this winter to request transfers from the Highway Fund or Turnpike Fund, depending on how much it needs.
On Wednesday, Liot Hill and Stephen both suggested that Rodrigue make a greater effort to increase pay for state plow drivers and to make it a priority in the next proposed Ten-Year Transportation Improvement Plan. 
Rodrigue said he would focus on recruitment “as vigorously as I can,” without issuing specifics. 
“You have my 100% commitment, and our DOT teams’ 100% commitment to continue to do our best to tell our story about what we need to do to reduce the vacancy rate at the DOT,” he said.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Golden built a reputation as an outlier, but his potential successors are taking a different tack
text:
Maine's 2026 November ballot lists the candidates for the 2nd Congressional District, Democrat Matt Dunlap and Republican Paul LePage, along with space for a write-in candidate. (Photo by Kaitlyn Budion/Maine Morning Star)[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: How to register, key dates, who’s on the ballot and where the candidates stand on the top issues facing Maine.]Maine’s 2nd Congressional District was always expected to be a competitive and closely watched race this November. But when Democratic incumbent U.S. Rep. Jared Golden announced he wasn’t seeking reelection, it left the district in even more of a state of flux. 
Compromising the geographic majority of the state north of Augusta, the district has routinely split tickets, reelecting Golden while backing President Donald Trump each time he has run for president. 
Much of that has been credited to Golden’s position as a moderate Democrat who works across the aisle, casting votes with Republicans more than the vast majority of his party. While occasionally angering Democratic House leadership, such as over his recent endorsement of a Republican colleague, Golden maintained strong party support throughout his four congressional elections.
In the Bangor Daily News op-ed announcing his decision not to run, Golden himself noted that the district has resisted national trends, writing, “as competitive as it is, it remains true that most people are neither diehard right-wingers or resistance progressives.”
But neither candidate seeking to replace Golden has tried to emulate his unique relationship with his party. Instead, Republican Paul LePage has campaigned hard on the backing of national party leaders. And while Matt Dunlap is more progressive than Golden on many issues, the Democratic party was slow to back him, and Dunlap hasn’t embraced their support on the campaign trail.
Golden did not respond to questions about his bipartisan approach or his potential successors, but in the op-ed announcing his retirement, he wrote, “I have spent almost eight years in Congress opposing the forces of polarization. This is critical to fair leadership in a district like Maine’s 2nd, where robust ideological diversity requires elected officials who are willing to represent the district as it truly exists — not as their party’s most vocal extremes might wish it did.”
In the conservative-leaning district, it will soon be apparent which approach voters prefer. 
Golden himself was not impressed by Dunlap or LePage, writing last fall, when they were the only two who had announced their run, that they “are a far cry from being standard bearers of the generations that will inherit the legacy of today’s Congress.”
The race has implications beyond Maine, as it is  one of a few dozen races considered a toss up or leaning slightly towards either Republicans or Democrats.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.The Cook Political Report earlier this month moved the race in Democrats’ favor, now considering it leaning Republican, making it one of just 11% of House races considered somewhat competitive. 
That uncertainty is drawing outside attention. Data from AdImpact, analyzed by the Wesleyan Media Project, found that from Sept. 28 through Oct. 11, $5.67 million was spent in the 2nd District. And of that, $4.53 million came from outside groups. 
LePage and national Republicans
Numerous national Republican figures have made stops in Maine to campaign with LePage, lauding his experience serving two terms as governor. Throughout his campaign, LePage has also emphasized his relationship with President Donald Trump. 
I know him personally, and I will say right now, I will be able to get into the Oval Office,” LePage said during the Oct. 1 debate. “My opponent will not.”
Across appearances, party leaders have offered effusive support of LePage and painted him as a common-sense Republican — even as they said LePage would be an independent voice for Maine.
During an August rally at the Bangor airport, Vice President JD Vance highlighted what he described as LePage’s record of combating fraud in state programs. 
State and national Republicans have alleged widespread fraud in Maine’s healthcare programs and have tried to make it a key issue throughout the midterm campaign, despite the most recent federal review finding that Maine’s payment error rate was lower than the national average. 
“I need the help, ladies and gentlemen,” Vance said. “You got to send Paul to help me.”
Minnesota Republican Tom Emmer, who serves as majority whip in the U.S. House of Representatives, similarly touted LePage’s experience during a roundtable discussion in September.
“The fact that you have already served, you have already stood in the crosshairs and dealt with these public issues, the fact that you would be willing to offer yourself again in this capacity … you guys know what’s right for Maine,” Emmer said. 
And Republicans are doing more than just campaign appearances to support LePage. According to Federal Election Commission data on independent expenditures, several Republican political action committees are spending to boost his candidacy. 
From September to mid-October, Elon Musk’s America PAC spent more than $160,000 to support LePage, and the No Going Back PAC, an affiliate of Trump’s MAGA Inc. super PAC, spent nearly $200,000 in support of LePage. 
And in just one week this month, the Safety and Affordability PAC, another Trump affiliate, spent $3.5 million opposing Dunlap. 
But even as those national leaders emphasize LePage’s support for the GOP’s agenda, they  have also attempted to portray him as someone who would prioritize the state above the party. 
“A guy like Paul LePage, he is not a go along to get along politician,” Vance said. “He is an independent-minded guy, but he is independent for you.”
And that’s a point that LePage himself has emphasized on the campaign trail. When asked in August how he would navigate a situation where Maine interests conflict with Republican priorities, he said constituents will come first. 
“I navigate it for Maine businesses. Period,” LePage said. “And I spoke to Speaker (Mike) Johnson this week, and that conversation came up. I said I’m going down there, number one to help Maine business. Number two is to help the party.”
Former Gov. Paul LePage, Republican candidate for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, speaks to reporters at Augusta City Hall on Oct. 22, 2026, after voting early in the November election. (Photo by Kaitlyn Budion/Maine Morning Star)
Maine Morning Star asked the LePage campaign how he would respond to voters who feel his closeness to party leaders conflicts with his independent rhetoric, and how LePage would follow Golden’s record of bipartisan work. 
In a statement, campaign spokesperson Brent Littlefield pointed to the former governor’s record in office. 
“Gov. LePage just this year worked with Congressman Golden to help pass legislation protecting Maine’s lobstermen and women,” Littlefield said, referring to a bill Golden introduced that would continue shielding lobstermen from new regulations to protect North Atlantic right whales until 2035. 
Littlefield also said that as Waterville mayor, LePage worked with a Democratic city council as well as Democratic leaders when he served as governor, though that relationship was often fraught.
House Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana has also made two appearances in CD2, an August press conference alongside LePage and several fellow members of Congress and a Get Out the Vote stop in Bangor. 
“There are a lot of people running for Congress this cycle,” Johnson said in August. “There is no one who is as qualified as this gentleman is … He’s one of the most qualified, competent people who have ever run for the House of Representatives in the history, since 1789.”
It’s a rebrand for a man who in 2016 called himself ‘Trump before Trump’ and has a history of controversial remarks, including some that made national headlines while he was governor. 
In 2011, the state NAACP criticized the then-governor for turning down invitations to Martin Luther King Jr. Day events. In an interview, LePage responded, “Tell them to kiss my butt.”
In 2016, LePage left an obscenity-filled voicemail for a Democratic state legislator and later told reporters he would have liked to challenge the Democrat to an armed duel.
“And we would have a duel, that’s how angry I am, and I would not put my gun in the air, I guarantee you, I would not be (Alexander) Hamilton,” LePage told the Portland Press Herald at the time. “I would point it right between his eyes, because he is a snot-nosed little runt and he has not done a damn thing since he’s been in this Legislature to help move the state forward.”
And in 2022, LePage threatened to “deck” a Democratic Party staffer recording him on video. 
But that was not the way Vance portrayed the former governor in Bangor. 
“So I’m going to say very simply, my friends, everything that we’ve accomplished over the past couple of years, it could be undone if you send a lot of crazy people to Congress to fight against us,” Vance said. “Send Paul LePage to Congress, and let’s get to work to save our country.”
Johnson struck a similar tone during the campaign stops, describing the 2nd District race as “a contrast between common sense and crazy.” 
“Paul LePage represents common sense,” Johnson said. 
In his attempt to return to the Blaine House in 2022 , LePage sought to erase his fiery image, with the campaign presenting him as a more mellowed, policy-focused candidate. That has continued into the 2nd District race, with the former governor holding relatively few events with the press, often sticking to written remarks at those appearances and during the two debates with Dunlap. 
When asked at an August press conference about a comment from Dunlap, LePage seemed to refer to his history of off-the-cuff, controversial statements as he paused in the middle of his response, and said, “I’m changing my habits here.”
Dunlap and Democrats 
Across the aisle, Dunlap has had a much more tepid relationship with the Democratic Party — they opposed him in the primary and were slow to back him in the general election. And even though the party is now on board, Dunlap doesn’t tout that support as much as LePage, at times keeping the party at arms length, and is much more likely to focus on what he’s hearing from voters. 
“I don’t really think Mainers are gonna get swayed by the same DC politicians who got us into this affordability crisis,” Dunlap told Maine Morning Star last week. “I have a good working relationship with the (Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee) and I’m grateful for their support, but I’m focused on the people of this district above anything else.”
Dunlap, the state auditor and former secretary of state, was at odds with national leaders even before he officially began his campaign. 
When he was first considering his run last fall, national Democrats were reportedly irked that he would challenge Golden in the primary. And the DCCC, the official campaign arm of House Democrats, made it clear the group would support Golden.
And after Golden announced he would not seek reelection last November, national Democrats were still not on board with Dunlap. In December, a source familiar with Democratic recruiting efforts said the DCCC was still looking for the “strongest possible” candidate to represent Maine, eventually endorsing his primary opponent, Maine Sen. Joe Baldacci.
Dunlap criticized the DCCC for endorsing in the primary, and said the party was trying to influence the race. 
“It’s undemocratic for national establishment Democrats to put their thumb on the scale in any primary,” Dunlap said in a May statement. “Just like in certain other races across Maine this year, they won’t decide this one — the people of Maine will.”
In the primary and the general election, Dunlap’s stances are not always in lock-step with the national party. He’s a strong advocate for Medicare for All, but doesn’t support gun control measures. 
“People are obsessed with labels like progressive or conservative and I don’t think they’re really helpful,” Dunlap said. “I led a pro-Second Amendment group for sportsmen, and I probably own more guns than every member of my party combined in the House. But I also support Medicare for All because in a rural district like this, our healthcare system is failing us and leaving people behind.”
Matt Dunlap, Democratic primary candidate in Maine’s 2nd congressional district, takes a photo with Erin Oberson (left), co-president of the Maine State Nurses Association, and Cokie Giles (right), vice president of National Nurses United. (Photo by Kaitlyn Budion/Maine Morning Star)
It’s another way that Dunlap has made it clear that he isn’t relying solely on the Democratic Party — its reputation or its support — to win the district. And Dunlap said he thinks that approach is an advantage in rural Maine.
“I’ve heard from thousands of voters, and I think people respect that I show up, I listen, and I’m gonna do my best to fight for them,” Dunlap said. 
The primary ultimately went to a ranked-choice count, and although Baldacci led in the first two rounds, Dunlap came out ahead in the final round of tabulations, winning by less than three thousand votes.
However, the DCCC was notably slow to shift its support. 
Jordan Wood, another primary candidate, posted a social media video in late July where he called out the party for not endorsing Dunlap, and said national Democrats were “f-ing up another race in Maine and they need to stop.”
“They are just sore losers, they’re upset that the candidate that they incorrectly backed in the primary lost,” Wood said. “And so they’re just ignoring our district. It’s sabotage.”
But at a press conference a few days later, Dunlap said he wasn’t concerned about it, making clear the campaign wasn’t waiting for a green light from the national party. 
“I think people have been frustrated by the delays, but we are doing very well,” Dunlap said. “We’re very competitive. We’ve been doing well on the campaign trail with our fundraising and generating a little bit of support here and there.”
The DCCC eventually added Dunlap to the organization’s ‘Red to Blue’ program in late August, and endorsed him in the race.  
“He’s the independent, Maine-first leader the Second District needs to lower costs, protect affordable health care, and stand up to the billionaires rigging the economy against working families,” DCCC Chair Suzan DelBene said in a press release. 
And since, the party has shown up for Dunlap. According to Federal Election Commission data on independent expenditures, the House Majority PAC, the Democrats’ major super PAC, spent a whopping $7.1 million in the last month to oppose LePage.
But it’s not the only group spending on Dunlap’s behalf. The Campaign for a Family Friendly Economy and National Nurses United for Patient Protection have also been active in the District, underscoring that he isn’t relying solely on the party. 
The Campaign for a Family Friendly Economy spent more than $450,000 in September and early October, and National Nurses United for Patient Protection spent $385,000 on digital ads and production last month. 
Even with Democratic Party support, Dunlap doesn’t spend much time explicitly campaigning on it and at press conferences, debates and town halls, he is much more likely to turn the conversation to voters and their personal experiences. 
“I’m gonna do what’s best for Maine, regardless of where my party stands on the issue,” Dunlap said. “Just last month a former GOP state senator was on local TV praising my work as auditor because I stood up to my own party when they got it wrong. That’s the kind of leadership I’ll bring to Washington.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Republican Tom Tiffany proposes parents’ bill of rights
text:
U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany released his proposal as in-person early voting kicked off last week and with a little over a week to go before Election Day. Tiffany at a press conference with Sen. John Jagler and Rep. Amanda Nedweski in October 2025. (Photo by Ruth Conniff/Wisconsin Examiner)Republican gubernatorial candidate Tom Tiffany is proposing a bill of rights for parents and teachers, which includes requiring parental permission for students who want to change their names and pronouns at school and banning transgender students from bathrooms and locker rooms that match their gender identity.
Tiffany released his proposal as in-person early voting kicked off last week and with a little over a week to go before Election Day. Tiffany has sought to leverage divisions over cultural policies in schools since he launched his campaign last year. 
Under his proposal, transgender girls would be prohibited from participating on girls’ sports teams and using girls’ locker rooms and bathrooms in schools, schools would be prohibited from placing tampons in boys’ bathrooms and “gender transition procedures” would be prohibited for those under 18.
“Every child deserves a safe classroom, every teacher deserves the authority to maintain order, and every parent deserves to know what is happening in their child’s school,” Tiffany said in a statement.
Last month, Tiffany appeared at a town hall hosted by Moms For Liberty, a right-wing organizing group for parents well known for supporting book bans and targeting schools over policies related to transgender children. Keeping transgender girls out of girls’ sports was one of the first priorities Tiffany mentioned at the Moms For Liberty town hall.
Tina Descovich, one of the founders of Moms for Liberty, who traveled to Wisconsin from Florida for the event, said that the organization is targeting women who don’t ordinarily vote in get out the vote efforts in Wisconsin. She said the election presents voters with a choice that could take the state in two very different directions.
“You can continue with someone who believes that boys should be playing with girls in sports. You can continue with someone that thinks mothers should be called inseminated persons,” Desovich said, using terminology that Tiffany’s opponent, David Crowley, has in fact not endorsed. (Gov. Tony Evers was criticized for the use of the term in budget language referring to artificial insemination.)
Noting Tiffany’s plane crash, Descovich said she thought God saved Tiffany for the state of Wisconsin. 
Tiffany’s proposal would also require that parents be able to review instructional materials, that schools notify parents and obtain consent before letting a student go by a different name or use different pronouns in school, require schools notify parents about violence, threats and crimes that occur on school grounds, implement school report cards, require schools to give parents information about their child’s academic proficiency and classroom behavior twice a year. 
His proposal would allow teachers to remove violent or disruptive students; require behavior intervention plans before a student could be returned to a classroom; prohibit retaliation against teachers for enforcing classroom rules, reporting unsafe conditions, requesting assistance or taking appropriate action to protect students; and establish school safety and parental notification requirements. 
In contrast, Democratic candidate and Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley has focused his education platform on increasing funding for public schools, including for special education, and providing universal early childhood education for Wisconsinites.
Tiffany’s campaign pointed to the New Richmond school district, which has been the target of an investigation by the Trump administration over its bathroom policies, and a report in the conservative Heartland Post, an online outlet run by talk radio host O’Donnell, about Winneconne High School, where a superintendent retired after controversy over the school district allowing an 18-year-old student to use a preferred name, instead of a legal name, used in the school’s graduation ceremony without the parents’ permission.
Wisconsin Republicans have repeatedly introduced bills that would implement a parents’ bill of rights and require permission before students could go by different names. In the past, lawmakers received help with drafting these measures from the conservative Wisconsin Institute for Law and Liberty. 
Gov. Tony Evers has vetoed those bills. In one veto message, he said the bill was “neither aimed at supporting our parents, our kids, and our schools, nor improving student outcomes, nor fostering collaboration and communication to do what is best for our kids,” but was rather “another attempt to divide our schools and communities and inject political ideology in the very last place it belongs — in our classrooms and our schools.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: As US Senate race boils over, here’s some advice for Kansans from a swing state veteran
text:
Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, right, and Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Adam Hamilton participate in an Oct. 21, 2026, debate at WDAF-TV in Kansas City, Mo. (Pool photo by Charlie Riedel/Associated Press)Greetings, fellow Kansan! You may feel disturbed and uncertain upon learning that our state has now entered that curious category known as swing.
No worries, though. I can help! As a journalist, I spent 14 years in two states that were classified as swing. I first worked in St. Petersburg and Tampa, Florida, as the state wrestled with the fallout of the essentially tied 2000 presidential election. I then spent a decade in evenly divided New Hampshire, covering the 2006, 2008, 2010, 2012, 2014 and 2016 elections.
I found the experience riveting, educational, disconcerting — and occasionally annoying. Here are a handful of applicable lessons. Bear them in mind as you watch your 5 millionth anti-Roger Marshall or anti-Adam Hamilton ad.
 
Ads don’t intersect with reality — or Kansas
As you’ve probably figured out by now, many ads in tight races like the Marshall-Hamilton contest don’t come from the state where they run. They receive precious little input from the candidates they supposedly boost.
The overhyped messaging has been cooked up in Washington, D.C., laboratories where political consultants pore over focus group reports and ask AI models what Kansans respond to. Then they looked at the calendar and just decided to run as many ads featuring the word “pedophile” as possible.
At least that’s what I imagine. Seriously, forget the ads. They target folks who don’t read the news or know about the candidates.
 
National news outlets treat us like yokels
Believe me, I saw plenty of stereotyping while living among flannel-loving New Hampshire residents and beach-going Florida seniors. Reporters from Washington, D.C., and New York City love to treat residents of other states like butterflies pinned to a sheet of poster board.
“Ruby red.” “Rural” “Fly-over country.” These oversimplifications occasionally verge on outright falsehood.
But don’t look for national outlets to explain what’s really going on or add depth to their reporting. That might require spending more than a weekend in (ugh) Kansas. Reporters have another swing state to get to and another verging-on-viral story to tell.
 
Folks obsess over meaningless numbers
Fluctuating polls, early voting metrics, shifting demographics — all of these numbers will be sifted through and scrutinized in the days before the the Nov. 3 midterm election.
But as those outside the swing state bubble understand these numbers only go so far. Polls depend on whoever answers the phone or responds to a text. Early voting depends on whoever shows up — with most voters still casting their ballots on Election Day. Demographic trends flatten diverse individuals into a faceless mass of humanity.
Don’t get me wrong. As sports fans prove, everyone enjoys sorting through the numbers. Everyone enjoys making their little predictions. But does any of it mean anything? I mean, really?
 
The last couple of weeks become unbearable
In New Hampshire and Florida, the days before a big election transformed into a nonstop barrage of TV ads, breathless news coverage, glossy mailers and conversations best summarized as: I don’t know what’s going to happen, but I am hopeful/fearful.
The best advice I gained after 14 years of this cacophonous din? Tune it out. Ignore the final stretch as much as possible. It will play on your emotions with nonsensical drama. Your engagement or lack thereof will make absolutely no difference to the outcome (unless you’re a candidate or staffer, I suppose).
We will know the outcome soon enough. Then we can chew over actual facts.
 
It will be lovely when the madness ends
Either Marshall or Hamilton will be our U.S. senator. Either Cindy Holscher or Ty Masterson will be our governor. Up and down the ballot, some will win while others will lose.
Most importantly, Kansans will have made their choices. We will know the shape of the next two years of Kansas politics. We can all go back to doing whatever we were doing before.
Perhaps sipping on a ruby red beverage out in the rural areas of this lovely fly-over country.
Clay Wirestone is Kansas Reflector opinion editor. His first book, “Opinionated: Kansas Journalists Who Proved Why Commentary Matters — Then and Now,” was published in September 2026 by the University Press of Kansas. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate.
